Céline Dion moved to tears on stage as sellout Paris residency begins
Thousands of fans crowd into Europe's largest indoor venue for Canadian singer's comeback
Eleven minutes before 9 p.m. local time, the lights went down and screams erupted as Céline Dion took the stage in a Parisian suburb for her first concert in six years.
Dion, 58, opened the show at at Europe's largest indoor concert venue with a rendition of 1998's On Ne Change Pas, stopping partway through as she was moved to tears.
"I promised not to cry," she told the crowd in Nanterre, wearing a black gown and diamond necklace.
"Tonight I want to sing for you, for me, for life."
Thousands of devoted fans packed Plenitude Arena on Saturday to watch Dion's return to the stage, opening a sellout Paris residency after a battle with a rare neurological disorder sidelined the singer's career.
"Finally. It’s amazing we’re all together. I made a promise. I made a promise to come back and be back on stage," Dion said, speaking in French and then English.
“Thank you so much for your support, your patience and, if I may say so, I am everything I am because you loved me," she continued, quoting her own 1996 song.
Concertgoers, who made their way through thousands of feet of barricades to get inside the venue, were wearing anything from jeans and graphic T-shirts to sparkly mini skirts and floor-length gowns.
One woman wore her wedding dress.
"I cancelled the party with all my family and friends to come see Céline," said Fanny Sucheyre, who celebrated her one-year wedding anniversary at the concert.
"I said to myself, if one day I had the chance to see her, I would wear my best dress. So it's my most beautiful dress."
Inside, special edition Céline champagne glasses sold out within minutes and the lines for champagne itself stretched more than 30 metres. Even the men's washroom had snaking line ups.
"It's a dream. I haven't slept for three days. I'm 50 years old and right now I feel like I'm 15," said Guylene Richardson, heading into the arena with her daughter, both in Dion concert tees. "With [Dion's] disease, I didn't think she would come back, so it's great. I'm really happy for her. I'm happy for us."
One of the best-selling artists of all time, she announced a diagnosis of stiff person’s syndrome — which causes stiffness and muscle spasms — and disappeared from the spotlight in 2022. She broke her hiatus to perform Edith Piaf's Hymne à l'amour from the Eiffel Tower during the opening ceremony of the 2024 Paris Olympic Games.
Dion is scheduled to perform a series of 26 concerts over the next eight months. The City of Light has buzzed with anticipation for the singer's comeback, with signs dotting the length of the Champs-Élysées or along the famed river Seine.
With files from Sarah Leavitt and Carly Thomas

Reo Morimoto, a Japanese actor and narrator known for his gentle voice, died on Sept. 4. He was 83.
Morimoto, whose real first name was Haruyuki, was from Nagoya.
His agency said Friday that he died suddenly of an unknown cause.
Morimoto made his acting debut in the 1967 drama series “Koukousei Jidai” on public broadcaster NHK.
He gained popularity as a narrator thanks to his distinctive and calm delivery.
His notable roles include those in the television drama series “Kiiroi Namida” (Yellow Tears) and “Ai to Iu Na no Moto ni” (In the Name of Love) as well as the film “Kids Return.”
He narrated a number of variety shows and commercials and was well known for his narration in the children’s series “Thomas & Friends.”

A Bengaluru commercial court has temporarily restrained hyperlocal news startup Way2News from using confidential information and intellectual property belonging to AppsForBharat, the operator of spiritual tech platform Sri Mandir. The court passed the ad-interim ex parte injunction on Thursday (September 10) in a commercial suit filed by AppsForBharat against Way2News and its former employee Shivam Kumar Singh. The order restrains Way2News, its directors, employees, agents, and others acting on its behalf from using AppsForBharat’s confidential information, intellectual property, and other data allegedly received from Singh until the next hearing. Since the order was passed ex parte, Way2News and Singh were not heard before the interim relief was granted. Inc42 has reached out to AppsForBharat and Way2News for comments on the development. The story will be updated on receiving a response. What AppsForBharat Has Alleged According to court filings accessed by Inc42, Singh worked as a senior operations associate at AppsForBharat and was involved in coordinating with priests and temples and managing on-ground pooja operations. He resigned on August 3, 2026, citing “personal exigencies”, and his last working day was August 7. AppsForBharat alleged that one of its employees received a request from Singh on August 25 seeking access to the startup’s Google Drive. The request was allegedly sent using a Way2News email address, prompting AppsForBharat to launch an internal investigation. The startup claimed the drive contained videos, marketing material, operational information, financial data, and details of suppliers and customers. AppsForBharat further alleged that Singh joined Way2News in violation of the non-compete provision in his employment agreement and shared its confidential information with the platform. It also accused Way2News’ spiritual tech platform Veda Mandir of publishing promotional videos identical to marketing material created by Sri Mandir. AppsForBharat also accused Way2News of approaching its employees and customers and sought separate ex parte injunctions against such solicitation. However, the court declined to grant these two injunctions without hearing the defendants and issued notices to them instead. The current injunction is limited to Way2News’ alleged use of AppsForBharat’s confidential information. The interim order does not constitute a final finding of data theft or copyright infringement. AppsForBharat Seeks ₹1 Cr AppsForBharat has sought ₹1 Cr in compensation for alleged losses and contractual breaches. It has also sought the return of its confidential material, permanent injunctions against its misuse and the solicitation of employees and customers, and an account of revenue generated through its alleged unauthorised use. Founded in 2020 by Prashant Sachan, AppsForBharat’s Sri Mandir app enables users to book online pujas and offerings, receive prasad, and access devotional content. In July 2025, AppsForBharat raised ₹175 Cr in a Series C round led by Susquehanna Asia VC. It has raised about $65 Mn to date. Meanwhile, Way2News was founded in 2015 by Raju Vanapala. It primarily offers short-format hyperlocal news in vernacular languages. It later entered spiritual tech with Veda Mandir, which facilitates pooja, chadhava, and daan offerings at temples. The startup raised $14 Mn in a WestBridge Capital-led Series B round in 2024 and has raised nearly $30 Mn to date.

CJP founder heckled by content creators during visit to tribal families in Madhya Pradesh
A viral video of the incident showed a woman influencer thrusting a microphone at Dipke as he was leaving in a car and asking if he had come there to "do politics on corpses"
Cockroach Janta Party founder Abhijeet Dipke was heckled by a group of people who appeared to be social media influencers or content creators during his visit to Madhya Pradesh's Balaghat district on Saturday. Dipke had gone there to meet families of tribal children who allegedly died due to infectious diseases and to gather information about local healthcare facilities.
A viral video of the incident showed a woman influencer thrusting a microphone at Dipke as he was leaving in a car and asking if he had come there to "do politics on corpses" and why he was visiting the area so late. Dipke was heard saying he apologised for arriving late.
Dipke visited Adori, Korka and Bondari villages during the trip. In the video, the woman was also heard saying, "A good road has been constructed here. Can't you see it?" As the situation escalated, CJP workers accompanying Dipke moved him into another car and took him away. As he left, the woman was heard saying, "He ran away, he ran away."
Local journalists said they were surprised to see this group of social media influencers from outside turning up in the remote village, and wondered if they had been sent by someone to disrupt the CJP founder's visit.
Earlier this week, the Jabalpur bench of the Madhya Pradesh High Court sought a response from the state government over the deaths of more than 30 children in the region. A division bench of Acting Chief Justice Vivek Rusia and Justice Pradeep Mittal issued notices to the state Health Department, Women and Child Development Department, Balaghat collector and others while hearing a public interest litigation. The PIL alleged that children were not receiving adequate treatment and that around 400 children were being treated at a hospital with a capacity of 50 beds.
The visit, the confrontation caught on video and the court proceedings have kept attention on the reported child deaths and the condition of healthcare facilities in the area.

It turns out Jean-Luc Picard was an even better starship helmsman than the writers knew. A physicist has gone through the details of a warp-speed trick from the first season of Star Trek: The Next Generation and found a subtlety the show missed. But instead of a plot hole, the detail he found actually makes the maneuver more impressive… as well as a great opportunity to teach about a lesser-known feature of the theory of relativity.
Níckolas de Aguiar Alves, a physicist at the Federal University of ABC in Brazil, first watched Next Generation as a master’s student. When he got to the episode “The Battle” in the show’s first season, the plot reminded him of his relativity coursework.
In “The Battle,” a Ferengi leader reminds Picard of a battle he fought years ago as captain of a ship called the Stargazer. Under fire from a mysterious attacker, Picard’s ship’s shields were down. He had to get closer without taking a hit, so he made a gamble. Picard ordered the Stargazer to charge the enemy ship at warp speed (meaning faster than light), then stop abruptly and fire. By going faster than light, Picard anticipated that the other ship would see two images of the Stargazer: where it reached warp speed and where it stopped. If they fired on the wrong image, they would miss the Stargazer, and Picard could win the battle.
Later in the episode, Riker mentions that the trick had been immortalized in Starfleet textbooks as the “Picard maneuver.”
As it turns out, it’s also not that far from what you can find in some physics textbooks. While warp speed is pure science fiction, physicists sometimes need to consider what happens when an object goes faster than light, and such an object really does leave two images.
Something about the story bothered de Aguiar Alves at the time. But he forgot about it until years later, when he was working through a more practical problem involving particles in a medium with a slower speed of light. Not trusting that he had done the math right, he started trying to work out the situation visually.

Indore (Madhya Pradesh): A 73-year-old labourer fell victim to online fraud after an unidentified person activated a UPI app on his lost mobile phone and siphoned Rs 3.34 lakh from his bank account over five days under the Sanwer police station's jurisdiction.
The victim, Madanlal Chauhan, a resident of Ganesh Colony in Dharampuri, reported that the incident occurred after he lost his phone at the Dharampuri weekly market on March 16. Despite extensive searching, he could not trace the device. He subsequently obtained a replacement SIM card for his registered number.
The fraud came to light when Chauhan visited his bank branch to withdraw money and discovered that unauthorised transactions had cleared his savings between March 16 and March 21, 2025.
According to the complaint, the unidentified suspect utilised Chauhan's lost phone and linked SIM card to set up a PhonePe account without his authorisation, illegally transferring a total of Rs 3,34,270 from his linked bank account.
Chauhan initially lodged a cybercrime complaint on the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal (NCRP). Following a preliminary inquiry, Sanwer police registered a case under section 318(4) of the BNS and section 66D of the IT Act.
Police have launched an investigation to trace the fraudulent UPI transactions and identify the suspect.

Going into the summer transfer window as Premier League champions, hope sprang eternal for Arsenal.
An opportunity to capitalise, encouraged by a sense at Emirates Stadium that their competitors were in transition because of managerial instability.
If ever there was a moment to strike in recruitment, this was it.
The plans were ambitious: a shortlist with more than 20 players on it. They were targets at Real Madrid and Atletico Madrid, even at Chelsea and Tottenham.
But as the window shut on Tuesday night, you could not escape the sense of unfulfillment - certainly from a section of supporters.
Arsenal's close season was one characterised by some unquestionable successes, but also riddled by difficulties and frustration.
Ahead of their home match against Chelsea on Sunday, BBC Sport details Arsenal's transfer window and whether manager Mikel Arteta, sporting director Andrea Berta and, perhaps most pertinently, owners Kroenke Sports Entertainment can deem their summer operation a success.
Why it became Guimaraes and not Anderson, Tonali or Scott
Bruno Guimaraes's £75m capture from Newcastle United was Arsenal's most eye-catching signing.
Heading into the summer, Arsenal were keeping abreast of Guimaraes' situation at Newcastle, although others were considered a higher priority.
For instance, their interest in Elliot Anderson was widely reported, but it was clear the England international was joining Manchester City.
Guimaraes' former Newcastle team-mate Sandro Tonali and Bournemouth's Alex Scott were also among the midfielders explored before a move for the South American accelerated.
At the ages of 26 and 23 respectively, Tonali and Scott are younger than Guimaraes, who turns 29 in November.
But numerous factors, including availability and price - Tonali joined Spurs for a minimum £92m - made their signings difficult.
Aston Villa's Amadou Onana was also among the options considered, but the Belgium international suffered a serious knee injury at the World Cup.
By mid-June Guimaraes, who had universal backing inside the Emirates, emerged as the club's primary focus.
Berta knew the player's camp well and Guimaraes was admired by Arteta, who had made it clear he wanted proven talent to take his starting XI - rather than the wider squad - to greater heights.
Berta used his strong relationship with Guimaraes' representatives to facilitate Arsenal's move, hence why Newcastle maintained they had had no direct contact from the London club until days before his move was completed.
It is not uncommon for Berta to lean on intermediaries to conduct negotiations, although the approach has had varying degrees of success.
For instance, Arsenal actively sought moves for Leicester City teenagers Jeremy Monga and Louis Page over the summer.
But sources insist that the lack of club-to-club discussions meant both players ultimately did not join Arsenal, with Monga eventually signing for Manchester City when he appeared to be on the verge of moving to the Emirates.
That said, Berta's success in pivoting the club towards a deal for Guimaraes when it became clear other targets were not viable was well received behind the scenes at Arsenal.
Konsa was first-choice defensive option
The signing of Ezri Konsa was equally complex. Konsa was viewed internally as Arteta's first-choice defensive option.
Arteta wanted players used to the rigours of Premier League football - hence the moves for Guimaraes, Konsa and the failed efforts to land Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa.
Konsa's ability to play at right-back was also viewed as a major benefit. Arsenal considered signing an orthodox right-back, with Ivan Fresneda among the options, but Konsa's versatility was a key factor.
But Berta appeared reluctant to meet Villa's valuation. A week before the Konsa deal was confirmed, Arsenal made a £40m offer, which was duly rejected.
Sources claim the deal was eventually sealed by the ownership at both clubs, and the transfer was agreed at £51m, with £4m in add-ons.
In the event of not reaching an agreement for Konsa, it is understood Tottenham duo Cristian Romero and Micky van der Ven were identified as targets – but Arsenal's north London rivals would not consider selling to them.
Como centre-back Jacobo Ramon is a player the club will continue to monitor, but clauses attached to his current contract make the deal difficult.
Tarik Muharemovic, who joined Leeds United, was another considered.
In attack, Christos Tzolis' impact since arriving from Club Brugge in a deal worth about £35m means the Greece international has been heralded as one of the discoveries of the summer.
It is understood the potential deal for the former Norwich winger was initially raised by an intermediary close to a senior member of the coaching staff during the close season.
Berta's number two, Maurizio Micheli, watched Tzolis play for his country against Sweden in June and was suitably impressed.
So far, the 24-year-old looks a positive addition to Arteta's squad.
Arsenal, who also made Piero Hincapie's loan deal permanent and signed Illan Meslier on a free transfer, are happy with the signings they have made.
The captures of Guimaraes and Konsa, who will both be 30 by the end of next season, have raised eyebrows given the combined £126m fee, amid concerns over how the pair's longevity may impact the natural evolution of the squad.
Yet it is undeniable that Guimares and Konsa add elite quality and experience to Arsenal ranks, and ultimately the club feel they paid the going rate to get those deals over the line.
Arsenal miss out on marque attacker
While the club delivered proven talent for Arteta in defence and midfield, Berta's remit of adding an elite attacker ended in disappointment.
Rogers was the club's primary target heading into the window, and the early indications were positive amid a strongly held view internally that the forward wanted to join.
At the start of the summer, it was Arsenal's understanding that Villa valued Rogers at £100m. Arsenal valued Rogers at £80m.
Berta, however, was confident of negotiating the price down to a level he and the club believed could get the deal done.
In the meantime, however, Berta explored alternatives - Bradley Barcola, Kenan Yildiz, Yan Diomande and Nico Paz were admired.
Anthony Gordon was a long-term target, but he had agreed before the World Cup to join Barcelona.
Yildiz and Paz will continue to be realistic targets moving forward. Eli Junior Kroupi is another the club will watch once he returns from injury for Bournemouth.
Anderson's move from Forest to City for £116m, however, altered the complexion of Villa's outlook on Rogers' future.
Villa increased their valuation to £120m and ultimately Chelsea ended up signing the attacker for £117m.
Arsenal, it is understood, were given the opportunity to match Chelsea's offer but refused, believing their £80m valuation was fair - but it does beg the question of whether Rogers would be a Gunners player now if Berta had acted sooner.
Ultimately, the failure to land Rogers arrived as the first of a series of blows to Berta in his efforts to deliver a top-class left-sided attacker for the team.
Arsenal genuinely believed they had a realistic chance of signing Vinicius Jr before he decided to sign a new contract at Real Madrid.
Berta and Arteta were all in on the Brazil icon. The club were prepared finance the deal too.
While the transfer would likely have cost a British record fee and been one of the most lucrative remuneration packages in Premier League history, the benefit to Arteta's team and the Brazil superstar's commercial value meant Arsenal were absolutely prepared to complete the deal.
Yet well-placed sources expressed to BBC Sport over the summer that Vinicius did not want to leave Real, while others feared Arsenal were being used to strengthen the attacker's efforts to secure a more lucrative contract at the Bernabeu.
Those concerns came to fruition as Vinicius signed a new long-term contract in Spain in another Arsenal disappointment.
There were similar reservations about Arsenal's well-documented pursuit of Julian Alvarez.
The Atletico Madrid forward showed very little indication that he was willing to join Arsenal; his preference to join Barcelona was one of the worst-kept secrets of the window.
But Atletico's point-blank refusal to sell to Barcelona was deemed reason enough by Berta and Arteta to persist with their interest in the hope of Alvarez changing his mind until the closing days of the window.
Alvarez, however, preferred to stay at Atletico, even though his relationship with the club is at an all-time low.
Did Arsenal waste their time with Vinicius and Alvarez? The answer varies depending on who you speak to.
When it became clear Alvarez was unlikely, Berta explored his options.
Intriguingly, Arsenal have admired Chelsea striker Joao Pedro, who was deemed not for sale over the summer, although there were concerns over how he would fit into Arteta's system.
It is claimed Berta relies significantly on his vast network of agent connections rather than acting on the club's existing scouting information when analysing the market.
For example, last summer, when all the scouting information pointed towards a move for Benjamin Sesko, Berta's arrival meant the club pivoted to Viktor Gyokeres, who is currently second-choice striker.
This summer the club's late dalliance with Lyon winger Malick Fofana provided a further example of Berta leaning on his agency connections after management agency Roc Nation offered Arsenal an opportunity to sign the Belgium international.
Berta's relationship with Roc Nation was particularly prevalent this summer given Arsenal's pursuit of Vinicius and the sale of Gabriel Martinelli, who are both clients of the agency.
It remains to be seen how much of an impact Arsenal's failure to sign a recognised top-level attacker impacts their season, particularly in light of Martinelli and Leandro Trossard's departures.
Arsenal will move towards player trading model
Arsenal headed into the window with a clear remit of ensuring the club become more sustainable and adept at trading.
Part of that directive is to ensure the club remain compliant with domestic and European financial regulations.
Depending on who you talk to, the size of the potential deals for Vinicius or Alvarez would have raised doubts over Arsenal's ability to stay within the regulations.
Nevertheless, ensuring they maximised the benefits of player trading will become an increasing part of Arsenal's financial operation in the future.
There was already evidence of that through the sale of Martinelli, whose £60m exit to Al-Hilal was the club's record departure. Arsenal have also secured a sell-on clause in the deal.
The exits of Martinelli, Trossard, Gabriel Jesus, Christian Norgaard, Jakub Kiwior, Fabio Vieira and Karl Hein secured the club in the region of £114m.
Through intermediaries, a possible exit for Myles Lewis-Skelly was explored, with a fee of about £80m believed to have been mooted for the midfielder.
Manchester United, who were attracted to Lewis-Skelly's ability to play at left-back, were interested but ultimately deemed his valuation too high.
Of course, it is Berta's job to have a firm grasp on the level of interest in the club's players and their market value but, nevertheless, the thought of Lewis-Skelly's departure resulted in huge uproar from supporters.
As BBC Sport revealed last month, the Gunners resisted any temptation to sell Ethan Nwaneri on a permanent deal, the academy graduate landing a season-long loan deal to Borussia Dortmund that includes a January recall option if required.
The minimum £15m fee secured in Trossard's deal to Besiktas is also viewed as a good deal inside the Emirates given the Belgian turns 32 in December.
Having spent nearly £450m in 12 months, Berta's work in the market has helped the club deliver their first league title in 22 years.
Yet, despite the money splashed, there remain clear issues in the squad - certainly in attack.
The summer window has left many supporters feeling questioning Berta's body of work at Arsenal.
And with the average age of the squad increasing following the captures of Konsa and Guimaraes, can the current options build a dynasty of success before the club need to spend heavily again on regenerating the team?

Mental health conditions that may develop following a traumatic incident could contribute to a higher risk of future cardiovascular issues such as non-fatal heart attack and stroke or a fatal cardiac event, according to new research.
"Traumatic events are common experiences and can include serious fires or explosions, physical assault, transportation accidents, the suicide or death of a loved one, and severe medical illnesses or injuries," lead author Jennifer A Sumner, an associate professor in the department of psychology at the University of California Los Angeles, said.
"Experiencing traumatic events can significantly affect mental health as well as cardiovascular health. Although most work to date has focused on PTSD and cardiovascular health, our research suggests that we should think about a wide range of mental health consequences when looking at cardiovascular disease risk after trauma," Sumner said.
The study, published in the Journal of the American Heart Association, examined national health registries in Denmark, looking at 2,19,866 adults who did and did not develop major heart or brain conditions following a traumatic event.
About 44,000 of the 2,19,866 participants experienced a non-fatal heart attack, non-fatal stroke, procedures to restore blood flow to the heart or cardiovascular death between 1995 and 2019.
Researchers compared 1,75,872 people who experienced a trauma but not a cardiovascular event to peers who experienced a heart attack, stroke, procedures to restore blood flow to the heart or cardiovascular death during the 24-year period.
A wide range of mental health conditions were considered as possible cardiovascular predictors, and machine learning was used to identify the 15 most important mental health disorder predictors of heart and brain outcomes.
Alcohol abuse was found to be the most important mental health risk linked to serious heart or brain conditions for men and women.
"For men and women, the most important psychiatric predictor of MACCE (major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events) was alcohol use disorders," the authors wrote.
"After a traumatic life experience, individuals may turn to alcohol to cope and help manage their emotions. Over time, this new behaviour might develop into alcohol abuse, thus increasing their risk of a serious heart or brain condition," Sumner said.
Mood disorders, including depression, were found to be strong indicators of post-traumatic psychiatric issues associated with cardiovascular outcomes for both men and women. However, mood disorders were a more prominent predictor for women, compared to men.
Psychological conditions that can arise after a traumatic event connected to a higher risk of heart and brain conditions in the future included PTSD, mental disorders caused by brain or physical issues, non-substance-induced confusion, different substance use disorders, personality disorders, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and anxiety disorders.

Trump shadow looms large over Brics as Modi hosts Putin and Xi in Delhi
- Published
The US is not a member of Brics, yet President Donald Trump's shadow will loom large over the group's summit in Delhi this weekend.
Leaders from 11 Brics nations - including host India, China, Russia, Brazil, South Africa, the UAE and Iran, with Saudi Arabia attending as an invited member - will hold talks on a wide range of issues. But few will be as consequential as the impact of President Trump's policies.
The war in Iran and the ever-present threat of White House tariffs, directed at both US adversaries and allies, have destabilised global energy markets and has often left the global economy guessing the future.
It is against this backdrop that Brics leaders are meeting. Yet the group is unlikely to produce a consensus statement that openly calls out the US or lays out a coordinated strategy to counter President Trump's policies and geopolitics.
That is partly because Brics itself is deeply divided over how far it should go in challenging Washington.
"India cannot afford to have a joint statement that rails against Washington," Michael Kugelman, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, told the BBC. He expects any criticism of US policies to be "vague and indirect", reflecting the sharply divergent interests within the expanded group.
While Russia and Iran may push for the group to take a clearer stand against President Trump, the geopolitical realities within Brics are likely to make that difficult.
India, which is reportedly in the final stages of a trade deal with the US, will not want a statement that could upset the White House. China, too, may be wary of being seen as using Brics to target Washington.
Then there is the UAE, which has come under Iranian attack during Tehran's retaliation against US and Israeli strikes. The Gulf state, which hosts US military bases, is unlikely to support a statement that helps Tehran's cause.
Kugelman says Brics has become more significant through its expansion, but that has also made consensus harder.
"You've added a number of members that don't get along," he said, describing the challenge for India as bringing together countries with "a wide array of views and positions on the global order".
Trump has also been quite vocal against Brics, particularly its efforts to reduce global trade's dependence on the US dollar, commonly known as de-dollarisation.
He has often warned the group against trying to come up with an alternative currency or take measures to weaken the dollar's dominance in global trade.
In one such threat, Trump said in November 2024 that Brics countries would face "100% tariffs" if they backed another currency to replace the "mighty US dollar".
Under these circumstances, what can the group realistically deliver?
Brics' geopolitical and economic heft has grown substantially over the past decade. While it will be reluctant to take an openly anti-US or anti-Western position, the group will be looking to build on its existing achievements and demonstrate that it can emerge as an alternative blocs like the G20 and G7.
Brics now accounts for 49% of the world's population, 40% of global GDP and 26% of international trade, according to BBC Monitoring's analysis.
Its most tangible achievement remains the New Development Bank - which has approved billions of dollars in infrastructure and development projects - many of them in countries of the global south.
The group has also created a $100bn contingency reserve arrangement to help members facing financial crises, although it has yet to be tested.
The leaders are also likely to explore ways to make cross-border payments in local currencies easier. That will be of particular interest to Moscow and Tehran, both of which face severe US sanctions.
Brics is also expected to continue positioning itself as a voice for the developing nations, collectively pushing for reforms to institutions such as the United Nations, International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, which many developing nations feel do not accurately reflect the new global order.
For India, in particular, the summit offers an opportunity to strengthen its claim to leadership of the global south.
Many of Delhi's own foreign policy priorities, including multilateralism, a more multipolar world, greater representation for developing countries and freer global trade, align closely with Brics' wider agenda.
But India will also have to find ways to work around China's considerable influence within Brics and its stronger presence across much of the developing world.
The Modi government has placed a strong emphasis on becoming a "leader or a voice of the Global South", Kugelman says. But India's efforts have had "limited success" in making deeper inroads in Africa and Latin America, where China has been more successful.
With most Brics members coming from developing economies, Kugelman says the expanded grouping gives India an opportunity to deepen ties with countries such as Ethiopia, Brazil and Indonesia and build a stronger profile across Africa and Latin America.
For Delhi, the test will be whether it can secure a consensus statement - often seen as a measure of a host nation's diplomatic success. That will be difficult given sharp differences over the Iran war, relations with the US and the future of global trade.
The scale of the challenge was evident in May, when Brics foreign ministers failed to agree on a joint statement after their summit because of differences over the Iran war, leaving host India to issue a chair's summary instead.
India will take confidence from its experience as G20 host in 2023, when it managed to secure a joint declaration despite deep divisions over Russia's war in Ukraine.
But Delhi will also want substantive announcements and to highlight what Brics has already achieved. On this, members are likely to agree: none will want the grouping dismissed as merely a "talk shop".
Leaders are expected to explore ways to strengthen financial cooperation and may make substantive announcements. They are also likely to address major geopolitical developments, with any language on the US is expected to be carefully crafted to avoid confrontation.
Washington, for its part, will be watching closely.
The summit will also provide the setting for several important bilateral meetings. Chinese President Xi Jinping's meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday will be keenly watched. The two countries have been slowly rebuilding ties, although progress has been more cautious than either side might have hoped.
Modi is also due to meet President Vladimir Putin, with the war in Ukraine likely to feature prominently in their discussions.
Modi made a highly public appeal for peace when he met Putin last month on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Bishkek. While some interpreted his remarks as a rebuke to Moscow, Russia did not see them that way and publicly welcomed Modi's efforts.
Beyond geopolitics, India's growing trade deficit with both Russia and China is also likely to feature in the bilateral discussions.
But in the end, the group's focus will be on concluding a successful summit as it would add further weight to Brics' influence.
And for host India, it would also be a diplomatic and geopolitical achievement at a time when Delhi is seeking to reassert its international influence.
Kugelman says the stakes are particularly high for India at this summit.
Delhi, he argues, has been somewhat overshadowed by Pakistan's recent diplomatic role in the Middle East, including its involvement in mediation efforts around the Iran war.
"This is an important opportunity for India to reassert its global significance and its global leadership," he says. "That is one reason why the stakes are high."
The summit, he adds, is in some ways "more important for India as host than it is for the Brics grouping as a whole".

Doug Kreuzkamp was shocked when news outlets reported that Google won an auction to buy a huge amount of operational data as part of Spirit Airlines’ bankruptcy proceedings.
Kreuzkamp founded a startup called Springshot in 2011, which created a widely used proprietary platform that helps humans and AI systems improve airline efficiency and quickly solve logistics problems so flights can stay on time and airlines can operate as smoothly as possible. Hundreds of airports use it globally.
Springshot powered Spirit’s technology stack for the last three years, right up to the “very last flight,” Kreuzkamp told Ars. Yet his company got no notice when Spirit prepared to auction off a massive dataset that he thinks likely improperly includes a substantial amount of data and intellectual property (IP) that Springshot owns—not Spirit.
In a limited objection filed last month, Springshot argued that Spirit’s sale agreement does not make it clear what data is being sold. It only vaguely references categories of data that would possibly rope in Springshot data, including “productivity and collaboration data,” “core business systems and business application data,” and “workflow and process data.”
“This expansive definition does nothing to differentiate between Springshot’s intellectual property that exists within Spirit’s data repositories and systems, but Spirit does not own, and Spirit data that it actually owns and has the capacity to sell,” Springshot argued.
Springshot urged the court to pause Spirit’s data sale until a transparent forensic process establishes that none of the data Google is grabbing is actually owned by third parties.
If the bankruptcy court does not “pump the brakes,” it risks sanctioning an “unauthorized acquisition and use of trade secrets” that could doom startups, Springshot alleged. In an email to Ars, Springshot summarized its fears as the court possibly creating “a precedent where startups see massive amounts of IP transferred to the world’s richest and most monopolistic companies via bankruptcy courts.”
“Bankruptcy cannot become the new land grab for AI,” Kreuzkamp told Ars. “The possession of IP is not ownership.”
Asked for comment, Google’s spokesperson declined to discuss mounting objections and repeated a prior statement provided to Ars that did not address any of the concerns raised.
“We acquired part of an enterprise dataset from Spirit Airlines, which can be helpful in improving our products and AI models,” Google’s spokesperson said. “We will not receive any personal information from this dataset.”
Google may use Springshot data to make AI rival
It seems likely that a wide range of Spirit vendors could be in the same spot as Springshot, Kreuzkamp suspects, and his firm is not the only one complaining.
Citing Springshot’s concerns in a separate objection, the International Aero Engines LLC and the IAE International Aero Engines AG alleged that the dataset might also include its proprietary commercial information, technical data, and financial data. Both vendors cited confidentiality provisions in Spirit agreements that appear to have been completely ignored in the push to get the data sale approved.
Top concerns are that proprietary data could be transferred to Google without consent, giving firms no chance to guard against Google—or a third party later gaining access to the data—infringing ownership rights and exposing trade secrets. Both vendors said they risked irreparable harm through the sale to Google and then again through possible resales to future third parties.
For Springshot, it also seems possible that Google could use its valuable IP to create a rival product. In August, just a week before the controversial Spirit auction, Europe’s largest airline, Ryanair, announced a five-year partnership with Google. Under the deal, Ryanair will share operational data to improve Gemini Enterprise tools. That “is precisely the function Springshot served for Spirit,” the startup said in a footnote in its objection, while alleging that “Springshot’s data may be among the most AI-relevant assets to be purchased.” As Springshot argued:
“Should the sale proceed without such safeguards, and should Google obtain Springshot’s intellectual property and ingest that data, Springshot would forfeit the value of its technology it has spent 15 years developing. That existential threat is only amplified by the fact that Google has recently announced its desire to operationalize its own AI platform for airline operations, placing it in direct competition with Springshot.”
Adam Schwartz, a privacy litigation director for a digital rights nonprofit called the Electronic Frontier Foundation, told Ars that allowing Google to buy this dataset via bankruptcy proceedings is unusual.
“This is the first time I am aware of so public a bankruptcy proceeding regarding whether a bankrupt company may sell off the personal data it has amassed as an asset in bankruptcy,” Schwartz said. “It is also the first time I am aware of a company seeking to sell its employees’ data (as opposed to its customers’ data) as an asset in bankruptcy.”
Kreuzkamp is worried that because bankruptcy courts have not deeply considered this issue before, the system is just not set up to protect vendors like his company. In the past, it was straightforward to determine who owned an asset. Consider how Spirit is selling airplanes, which bills of sale clearly demonstrate that it owns, he said. His experience suggests that when it comes to digital assets, courts don’t have the proper notice provisions that are necessary to ensure vendors can advocate for IP to be segregated from sales, should purchases like Google’s become the norm.
“Our main concern with everything is if you want startups to continue building, you need to protect what they built,” Kreuzkamp told Ars. “If they spent 15 years building IP, that IP should not be misappropriated because their customer went bankrupt.”
Springshot and the IAE objectors both want the court to require Spirit to segregate any proprietary vendor data before approving the sale to Google. Springshot argued that it should include any data or information generated by its service or software, including data “likely commingled with much of Spirit’s own operational data (like its employees’ emails, chat histories, etc.).”
“To ensure Springshot’s intellectual property is not among the data acquired by Google (or any other potential buyer) a forensic process is necessary to first identify, and then segregate, Springshot’s intellectual property from that actually owned by Spirit,” Springshot argued.
Kreuzkamp told Ars that Springshot engaged with Spirit every day before it shut down.
“We were very tightly coupled with them, did a lot of great work helping that airline,” he said. “And so, I know there are tens of thousands of emails and documents that I’m sure are in their servers.”
Pilots warn of public harms from sale
If Spirit is forced to segregate a large chunk of data, the value of the dataset may substantially depreciate for Google. In its sale agreement, Google stipulated that Spirit ensure that “no portion of the Assets has been deleted, modified, or removed,” other than through planned processes like the deidentification of customers’ personal data and “de minimis” removals preserving privileged materials.
Kreuzkamp told Ars that prior to reading the Spirit-Google sale agreement, he assumed that if one of the companies he partnered with became insolvent, that either vendor data would be destroyed or that agreements would be honored to prevent transfers to third parties.
On September 16, there will be a hearing where the court will mull objections to the sale. Along with vendors, unions and groups representing many former Spirit employees have joined flight attendants who quickly opposed the sale out of fears that Google or a third party could possibly link them to scrubbed data.
Troublingly, the sale agreement only required de-identification of customer personal data, and former Spirit workers worried that Google’s AI system may combine confidential worker data in ways that may expose information that they might not want public. As groups representing machinists, aerospace workers, and transport workers noted, workers aren’t even aware of all the risks, since “the proposed sale raises novel technological and legal concerns on very short notice.” Seemingly, not even Spirit knows the “ultimate uses” to which the data “may be put after it is sold and processed through artificial intelligence,” they warned.
Schwartz told Ars that Spirit should have gotten consent from workers before selling 80,000 email accounts, 100 million emails, 20 million SharePoint documents, and 500 million Teams messages.
“My top concern is that data privacy is a fundamental human right, enjoyed for example by employees in relation to their employers,” Schwartz said. “This includes the norm that data collected from a person for one reason should not be used or disclosed for another reason without first getting their opt-in consent. Therefore, it is the Spirit Airline employees themselves who should be making the decision whether they want to bear the risk to their privacy of their emails being turned into AI training data.”
Some former workers are alarmed that the data sale could possibly harm the public.
Most ominously, the Air Line Pilots Association, International warned that if Google’s AI system re-identifies pilots in the data set, airways could become more dangerous.
Flight safety programs depend on pilots feeling comfortable sharing in-depth incident reports without fear that confidential information may become public, the Federal Aviation Administration has found. Therefore, any “disclosure of confidential flight operations data through the Sale Agreement can be expected to chill voluntary compliance by pilots across the industry as it becomes known that such data can be sold to third parties with no expertise or interest in aviation safety and presumably included in databases accessible by the public using artificial intelligence software,” the association warned.
Late Google rival vows to resolve objections
Last week, an AI training data lab, Micro1, put in a last-minute competing bid that it claims resolves all objections to the data sale. Outbidding Google by 25 percent, Micro1 offered $12.5 million in cash, while promising that if debtors pick Micro1 over Google, the bankruptcy proceedings can avoid any further delays.
However, Micro1’s plan notably includes de-identifying the data in-house, which Spirit debtors were opposed to in the auction process. Spirit even chose a lower second bid should the Google sale fall through because the de-identification was completed by independent third parties. It seems, then, that even if the late bid is considered, it’s less likely to tempt debtors. Additionally, Micro1’s claims to resolve all objections may be somewhat exaggerated. In Springshot’s case, Micro1 does not promise to segregate IP, trade secrets, or proprietary data. Instead, Micro1 only says that it will not use Springshot data to create a rival product or ever sell the data to a would-be rival.
Ars could not reach Micro1’s lawyers for comment, but the data lab said it plans to attend the upcoming hearing to entice debtors to take their offer.
Kreuzkamp told Ars that he appreciates that Micro1 acknowledges Springshot’s concerns, but his objective remains scrubbing Spirit’s dataset of any data that Springshot owns.
His company’s lawyers have been in contact with Spirit debtors’ legal team and plan to defend Springshot’s proprietary data at the upcoming hearing. They feel confident the court will take their concerns seriously. But there are no guarantees, as the bankruptcy court prepares to approve this unusual sale. Kreuzkamp said it remains unclear what process a bankrupt company like Spirit should be taking to “ensure that it extricates everything that is proprietary from a dataset.”
“I just think it’s a very complex issue when it comes to extricating the data that’s owned by somebody else,” Kreuzkamp said. However, now’s the time to do it, he suggested, since “once you throw data into an AI model, it’s impossible to trace what the model did with that.”

When I was a child, the Jersey Shore was my magical place. My great-grandmother, her siblings, and a few other relatives lived there in a high-rise apartment building, so every summer we'd visit for a week. Looking out from the balcony, I believed the ocean went on forever. On the bottom floor, the community pool brought children together in carefree, summer bliss.
At the beach, my brother and I used our boogie boards like 16-year-olds with fresh permits, owning the waves until sunset. I built sandcastles while he dug a never-ending hole to China, and we devoured peanut butter and jelly sandwiches that somehow tasted superior in the salty air. At night, the boardwalk signs lit up the sky, and Kohr Bros soft serve always hit the spot. As a kid, there was nowhere else I'd rather be.
When we became parents, we started taking our own summer trips
After our kids were born, my husband and I started a Jersey Shore tradition of our own. We filled our SUV with duffel bags, sand buckets, and shovels, and every gadget needed to take toddlers away. Our boys enjoyed the beach — and it triggered a sweet nostalgia for me — but hauling the kids and all the gear across the sand was tiring, only for the sun to wear them out quickly, and the heat weakened my body with multiple sclerosis (MS). After eight years of annual beach getaways — when my boys were 9 and 6 — we switched gears completely.
My husband is an avid hiker, and living with chronic illness, I yearned to get away from the hustle and bustle. A higher elevation provides a drier, cooler atmosphere, which helps keep my symptoms at bay. So, our summer family vacation shifted to the Catskill Mountains. Only a three-hour drive from our home, it was equally as accessible as the beach.
We found a place to go that works for our family
From the moment we arrived for our first trip in the summer of 2020, I felt like we were at our second home. It was a great place to spend some of those early pandemic months, offering a beautiful change of scenery while also allowing us to keep our distance from others. We thought it was the perfect COVID-era getaway, but the instant we returned home, we couldn't wait to go back.
We've returned to the Catskills multiple times a year since then — and during every season. Our visits always include biking along the Ashokan Reservoir, swimming in Peekamoose Blue Hole, a natural swimming hole in the Sundown Wild Forest, and eating at our favorite spot, Yum Yum Noodle Bar.
We peruse the shops in Woodstock, New York, and my kids enjoy ice cream from their favorite creamery, Sweet Dreams. In October, we head to the Bethel Woods Center for the Arts — the location of Woodstock in 1969 — for their annual Peace, Love, and Pumpkins festival featuring thousands of hand-carved jack-o'-lanterns. While my husband takes the boys hiking, I rest in a peaceful atmosphere that provides a calmness I never found at the beach.
I hope my kids look back on these trips fondly
The Jersey Shore will always remind me of my carefree summer days in the 90s, and I have no doubt my family will enjoy a beach getaway again. But now, my kids have their magical place, too. As adults, when they think of their childhood, they'll recall the pools at our Airbnbs where we swam beneath the orange sunset.
They'll remember our favorite bike path with views of the reservoir, and they'll reminisce about winter days hiking through the snow. I bet they'll almost taste the sweetness of a roasted marshmallow when they recall our time around the fire pit in the crisp October air.
I hope their magical place feels as wondrous and perfect as the beach always will to me.

He arrived with nothing other than the clothes he wore that morning. Hours later he was banged up in a detention centre close to a Stockholm airport to await deportation.
Charles, a former business director from Cambridge, who did not want his full name published, moved to Sweden in 2017 to be with his Swedish wife, Lily, and applied to remain after Brexit, before the deadline of December 2021.
But the migration agency rejected his application, and he and his wife have been fighting with the Swedish authorities ever since.
In a message passed on by Lily, he said he was the only Briton in the detention centre, where he described being hemmed in by three lines of fences separated by a “no man’s land”.
“I arrived here with nothing apart from the clothes I had on,” Charles said. “We were told the meeting … with the border police was to discuss my case. They then said they thought I would abscond, which is why they were going to detain me.”
Lily, a lawyer, questioned whether Sweden, considered a global leader in human rights and progressive politics, was now like Afghanistan. “They have hunted us for five years,” she said.
Charles could be deported in the next week unless his latest legal challenge delivers a reprieve.
He joins a list of 2,490 Britons – of an estimated 14,000 in Sweden – deported from the country between 2020 and 2025, as questions are mounting as to why Sweden appears to have taken such a hardline approach to the Brexit withdrawal agreement (WA) over migration.
In total, Sweden is responsible for 33% of all British nationals deported from the EU between 2021 and 2025, compared with France, which accounted for 6% of all British deportees, Spain at 3% and Germany at 2%. France deported 450, Spain 250 and Germany 160, while Italy deported just 15 Britons in that period.
Different countries collate data in different ways, but Eurostat data suggests the Netherlands is another outlier, with 2,270 Britons deported in the same period.
Data shows 2,100 removal orders were also issued in Sweden, though it is not clear how many of these resulted in voluntary departures or progressed to deportations.
People served with removal orders include Joyce Thomas, a 78-year-old widow who has been in Sweden for 22 years, and George Mason, a 74-year-old with dementia who has been in Sweden for 25 years, both of whose applications missed the deadline to apply to remain in Sweden post-Brexit.
John Sellers, a 34-year-old Briton who has lived in Sweden since he was 10, was deported in January.
The cases also raise the question of whether the WA delivers the political promise made by the Brexit negotiator Michel Barnier and others promising citizens should not be collateral damage of Brexit.
“The level of protection afforded under EU law must not be watered down. Brexit should not alter the nature of people’s daily lives,” Barnier said in 2017.
Nine years on, some have asked if Sweden’s approach has been infected by its apparent lurch to the right more broadly, serving deportations on children and even a 95-year-old Iraqi woman who had lived in Sweden for 20 years.
“The number of absurd, hardline calls from the migration department just keeps piling up,” the Swedish author and journalist Martin Gelin wrote this week ahead of the general election on Sunday.
British citizens who lived in the country before Brexit have unique protection under the WA, but activists have noted that they appear to be subject to the same treatment as other foreign nationals.
“The question is, has national migration policy affected the way in which they apply the withdrawal agreement in edge cases? And has it affected the culture in Migrationsverket [the migration agency] and perhaps in the courts as they apply the withdrawal agreement?” asked James Savage, the editor of the Local, which recently revealed the pressure applied to Sweden by the European Commission.
Family members acting on behalf of Mason turned to the general migration route for residency after the migration agency rejected the withdrawal agreement request for him to remain in the country. The judge’s ruling was clear: “The state’s interest in regulated immigration outweighs Horace [George] Mason’s interest in continuing to reside [in Sweden].”
Since the surge in publicity surrounding deportations of British citizens in Sweden, all three opposition parties have pledged new laws to reopen the application process for Britons, and the incumbent government has said it would look at doing the same.
Niels Paarup-Petersen, the migration spokesperson for the Centre party, has promised new laws if his party retains power. “Some of these cases are just stupid,” he told the Guardian. “They [the migration agency] should not be lenient, but the present decision-making leans towards deportation.”
The Swedish migration agency insists it has only deported 458 British people in strict Brexit-related cases but activists – who have been trying to get granular detail on the remaining cases – say that data may not include Britons who upon rejection from the agency then applied to stay under different routes and ended up with deportation orders.
The agency also says there is “no indication that Sweden has in any way interpreted the withdrawal agreement in an extreme manner or differently from other [EU] member states” and that it has “applied applicable law” with appeal processes.
Savage notes that promises to change the law were made three years ago after other cases emerged.
David Milstead, who runs the activist group Brits in Sweden, has welcomed promises of action but is concerned that politicians might provide a fix for future British applicants without giving a second chance to those already deported or who have left voluntarily.
A spokesperson for the European Commission said: “Correct implementation of the withdrawal agreement is very important to us,” but added: “Reasonable grounds that may justify a late application for beneficiary status are not defined in the withdrawal agreement.”
This means “host states have a certain margin of discretion in deciding what they accept as reasonable grounds”.
In other words, Sweden has not breached the withdrawal agreement but rather is exercising allowable discretion.
Catherine Barnard, a professor of EU law at Cambridge University, says the withdrawal agreement is “unique”, as no other member state has ever left the EU, and will take time to test. But decisions by migration authorities have to be proven to be “proportionate”.
While Swedish courts have not referred their decision-making upwards to the European court of justice, Barnard says a case in the UK may provide precedent for EU citizens affected by the WA.
In the case of “CG”, the European court of justice ruled that the UK breached the EU charter of fundamental rights in denying benefits to an EU citizen in Northern Ireland.
“In a 2021 case … the court ruled that the charter would apply to those who had moved to another member state before Brexit and lived there,” Barnard said.
“While the facts of the case were somewhat different, the principle should remain: the state’s interest in protecting its immigration must be balanced against the rights to family life of vulnerable individuals.”
The Swedish migration authorities and police have been approached for comment on the detention of Charles.

Uganda is withdrawing from the Duke of Sussex’s Invictus Games, the country’s military chief said, out of respect for King Charles amid division over the “Harry-Meghan nonsense”.
Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, son of the Ugandan president, made the surprise announcement in a post on X on Wednesday.
Kainerugaba wrote: “In order not to be construed as being opposed to His Majesty King Charles III of the United Kingdom, whom we deeply revere, Uganda hereby withdraws from the Invictus Games. We shall not participate in anything that does not have His Majesty’s approval.”
The timing of the post suggests it may be in response to an official letter to UK senior government and military officials on behalf of Charles which reiterated the Duke and Duchess of Sussex were not working royals and would not use their HRH styles.
When asked by the Times about what had motivated the move, Kainerugaba is reported to have said: “I have factions in the Ministry of Defence that support that Harry-Meghan nonsense. I had to quash it straight away. I support the monarch. Period.”
The news, first reported by Uganda Pulse news website, will undoubtedly be a blow to Harry, who two months ago stood alongside Uganda’s defence minister, Kiryowa Kiwanuka, at an Invictus Games event in London to announce that the East African nation would be the 26th country to enter the multi-sport event for wounded service personnel.
At the time, Kiwanuka credited President Museveni for his “visionary leadership” and Kainerugaba, a Sandhurst graduate, for “championing our teams entry” adding their support “marks a new chapter for our service men and women.”
The decision to withdraw may be an unintended consequence of the official letter, issued on Monday by head of the royal household , the lord chamberlain, Richard Benyon, at Charles’s behest, and clarifying the position of the Sussexes after their return to the UK two weeks ago.
The letter directed that the couple were “no longer working members of the royal family”, that their charitable work “is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity,” and “their position is akin to private citizens with commercial and charitable interests.”
Kainerugaba was appointed army chief in 2024, and is widely seen as his 81-year-old father’s successor to the presidency. He has made several provocative posts on X, including threats to invade neighbouring Kenya, demands that Jay-Z hand over his wife Beyoncé so he could marry her, and threats against Bobi Wine, Museveni’s principal political rival.
The Invictus Games and representatives for the Duke of Sussex have been approached for comment.

Addressing the heads of state and other senior leaders, including Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, at the inaugural session of the two-day Brics Leadership Summit in New Delhi, Modi proposed that the group work together to formulate ten proposals for global governance reforms, focusing on three key aspects: representation, responsiveness and rule-making. These proposals could be developed into a reform roadmap by the next Brics Summit in 2027, he said. Voting rights, leadership positions and policy priorities at global financial institutions must reflect today's realities, he said. Countries that act as the current engines of global growth must also be given a proportionate role to shape the world's economic policy direction, the Prime Minister added. The existing global governance structure resembles a pyramid where a few dictate the rules at the top for others to follow, he said. The Global South, he underscored, is now at the "front row of the global crisis" but at the "back row of decision-making". While the 11 members of Brics collectively account for about 40% of the global gross domestic product, their voting rights at the International Monetary Fund (IMF) are less than a fifth of the total. Flash floods at the Nepal-Tibet border have killed at least 543 people and more than 1,500 are missing. Hundreds were foreigners in the area to work, take guided treks or make pilgrimages.
Thousands have been rescued, with some of the injured taken to hospitals in Nepal’s capital, Kathmandu. The number of missing may vary because of progress in the ongoing rescue efforts and differences in how data has been collected and verified among agencies.
Here is how different countries have been affected.
Nepal
Nepal’s disaster management authority said on Friday the death toll in that country had risen to 538, with 977 people missing. The authority said 3,253 people had been rescued by helicopter, and more than 150 of the injured were taken to hospitals in Kathmandu and the districts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading.
Local reports cited the National Emergency Operation Centre as saying on Thursday that the missing included 113 Nepali tourists, 85 personnel from the army and police, 161 residents from the Rasuwa district and one from the Nuwakot district.
China
State media reported on Friday that at least five people had died and 558 were missing in Gyirong County, Tibet. The state broadcaster CCTV reported that 260 of the 558 missing people were foreigners. In addition, nearly 100 Chinese citizens were missing on the Nepal side, China’s foreign ministry said.
India
India’s foreign ministry said 288 Indian nationals remained uncontactable, including 73 people who were working on a power project. Nepali officials said many Indian tourists were on pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus.
US
The US state department said 90 of its citizens were unaccounted for in China and Nepal, but that it was not aware of any US deaths. Three Americans have been rescued.
Malaysia
Officials said 51 Malaysians were missing.
Ukraine
Ukraine’s foreign ministry said 55 Ukrainians were missing. The number includes two tourist groups, of 47 and seven people respectively, in addition to one Ukrainian woman travelling with a foreign tour group.
Australia
The Australian government said 39 Australians were missing.
Britain
Officials said 33 of the missing were from Britain.
Canada
The Nepal tourism board (NTB) said 25 of the missing were from Canada.
South Korea
South Korean government officials said nine citizens working on the construction of a hydropower plant in Nepal were missing.
Singapore
Eight Singaporeans were missing, according to the NTB.
Germany
The NTB said eight tourists from Germany were missing.
Russia
The Russian embassy in Nepal said eight of its citizens were missing.
South Africa
The NTB said six South Africans were missing.
Latvia
The NTB said six tourists from Latvia were missing.
Japan
Japanese media said five Japanese tourists were missing, made up of a couple and their children.
New Zealand
Five people from New Zealand were missing, the NTB said.
France
The NTB said four French citizens were missing.
Belgium
The NTB said three people from Belgium were missing.
Spain
The NTB said three visitors from Spain were missing.
Others
The NTB said two people each from Italy, Kazakhstan, Portugal, Ireland and the Netherlands were missing. It said 10 others – one each from Belarus, Finland, Hungary, Israel, Lithuania, the Philippines, Bulgaria, Switzerland, Serbia and Sweden – were also missing.

An Israeli soldier shot a Palestinian man, wounding him in the leg, as settlers confronted villagers by grazing livestock on Palestinian-owned land in the town of Faqqua in the occupied West Bank.
Eyewitnesses said that a group of settlers had entered the area with their livestock, prompting residents to try to stop them. Israeli forces then intervened and, according to men at the scene, opened fire at residents. One of them shot Qassem Hussam, a Palestinian man in his mid-30s, wounding him in the leg.
Reached by the Guardian, the IDF confirmed it had received a report of the incident and that the person who fired was one of its soldiers.
“Earlier today [Saturday], a report was received regarding friction between Israeli civilians and Palestinians near the area of Faqqua,” the IDF said. “An IDF force that was at the scene fired into the air and toward a Palestinian.”
Mohammed al-Sheikh, 34, who was standing next to Hussam, told the Guardian the confrontation began when villagers encountered Israeli settlers grazing livestock on Palestinian-owned land.
“Then the Israeli soldiers came,” al-Sheikh said. “They started shooting. One soldier shot Hussam and he fell to the ground. We immediately went to help him and move him away. We couldn’t get an ambulance to the area, so we took him to hospital in a private car.”
Hussam was taken to hospital in a light-to-moderate condition, according to the Palestine Red Crescent.
The Israeli military said the incident was being reviewed by commanders and that its findings would be forwarded to the relevant authorities for examination. The IDF added that the military was investigating the soldier who shot the Palestinian man, apparently in breach of army protocol, according to the Times of Israel.
Video of the incident shows a group of Israeli soldiers and settlers confronting unarmed Palestinian men before shots are fired.
The incident is the latest to raise questions over the Israeli government’s ability or willingness to curb violent settlers in the occupied West Bank, where attacks have continued to increase.
On 8 September, the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, said he would “not stand by” as horrific suffering continued, writing in the Guardian that for too long the UK had been hesitant to act, “fearful of being accused of being anti-Israel”.
Ed Miliband, the UK’s foreign secretary, said the government would now take the official position that Israel’s occupation of the West Bank was unlawful in its entirety, and announced sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements.
The dramatic shift in the UK’s position came after a summer of intense diplomacy against a backdrop of rising settler violence in the West Bank, which led 12 countries, including France and Canada, to announce sanctions.
After Miliband described violent Jewish settler activity in the occupied West Bank as “ethnic cleansing” carried out with the tacit backing of the government of the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, announced retaliatory measures including the closure of the consulate and entry bans on several MPs.
It marked the latest stage in a rapidly worsening dispute between the two countries, with diplomatic relations at their lowest point in years, even as violence in the West Bank has continued.
Israeli forces also carried out raids across Jenin governorate on Saturday, arresting six people and injuring a 14-year-old boy, who suffered a broken hand, according to the Palestinian news agency Wafa. Soldiers also raided several villages around Jenin, while forces entered at least five towns in Bethlehem governorate and set up a checkpoint at Za’atara.
East of Ramallah, Israeli settlers attacked the outskirts of Burqa, throwing stones at homes and vehicles.
On 4 September, two Palestinian teenagers were shot dead in al-Mughayyir after settlers entered the village under police and military escort and took dozens of sheep from a Palestinian home, residents and Israeli activists said.
The victims were Khalil Abu Alia, 16, and Omar al-Nassan, 19. Three other pupils from their 470-strong school had already been killed by Israeli soldiers and settlers this year.
According to the UN’s Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), more than 1,111 Palestinians, including at least 243 children, have been killed in the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, since 7 October 2023.

For some people, particularly youngsters, an AI chatbot is becoming the first place they turn to when they are distressed. It has its advantages: it is available at any hour, does not appear to judge them and can respond instantly. But when conversations involve thoughts of suicide, the limits of this interaction become consequential. Every conversation with an AI chatbot may not be harmful, but an apparently empathetic response could reinforce hopelessness, prolong rumination, or delay professional help in some people already at risk, say experts.
What the evidence shows
AI use for mental health support is now common. A U.S. survey of 1,009 people aged 12 to 21, published in JAMA Pediatrics found that 19.2% had used AI chatbots for mental health advice in 2025. Nearly 43% of these users did so at least monthly, while 5.8% used them daily or almost daily. Nearly two-thirds had not told anyone about this.
Another analysis of more than 620,000 publicly available ChatGPT conversations found that 4.9% could be classified broadly as involving mental health, although only 0.21% met a stricter definition involving an identifiable person explicitly seeking mental health help.
Studies have also found that chatbots are generally better at recognising very low- and very high-risk scenarios, but struggle to distinguish between intermediate levels of suicide risk. This is particularly concerning for psychiatrists, as suicidal distress is rarely expressed in a single, explicit statement and often emerges through a combination of subtle or changing cues.
When reassurance becomes a loop
“Suicidal distress is not always direct; people may hint, use humour or gradually disclose their thoughts,” said Mithun Prasad, consultant, psychiatry, SIMS Hospital, Chennai. Keyword recognition alone, he said, is therefore inadequate; the context and consistency of a conversation matter.
Sabaresh Pandiyan, consultant, psychiatry, Rela Hospital, Chennai, pointed to another issue: the ‘internal loop’, particularly among younger users, who may derive comfort from the empathetic part of an AI response, while ignoring advice to seek professional help. Repeated reassurance can also make suicidal thinking seem less urgent. “Talking about suicide or venting about suicide is not the problem, reinforcing hopelessness is,” he said.
Nithya M., consultant psychiatrist, Apollo Speciality Hospitals, Vanagaram, Chennai, emphasised that AI could amplify existing distress, prolong rumination or substitute validation for intervention.
In clinical practice, psychiatrists see patients use AI to discuss relationships, workplace problems and other personal concerns before speaking to family or friends. Dr. Pandiyan said around 60-70% of patients in his setting discuss such matters with AI first. For some, this may help them recognise a problem and seek care earlier. Others may spend months trying to manage difficulties themselves before consulting a professional.
Dr. Nithya said warning signs can include patients quoting AI responses verbatim, withdrawing from human confidants, resisting professional help or developing a rigid view of themselves or their relationships based on chatbot responses.
Not a substitute for care
There may be limited situations in which patients use AI alongside clinical care. Dr. Prasad said some patients use chatbots between appointments to record medication effects or organise their thoughts, and later bring a summary to their psychiatrist. This can provide the clinician with information about what happened between consultations.
But such use does not make AI a substitute for psychiatric assessment. A chatbot does not have access to a person’s psychiatric history, personality, psychological defences, adverse life experiences, protective factors or current mental state. It may validate an emotion without recognising when urgent assessment is needed. This is particularly concerning when a person has psychosis, mania or distorted beliefs.
Need for safety checks
Psychiatrists call for mandatory safety audits, independent clinical assessments and clearer liability frameworks. Companies should be required to investigate and report serious safety incidents. . Public education should also explain where AI is and is not appropriate.
Experts add that any response must also address the stigma that prevents people from seeking mental healthcare. Families and communities need to create safer spaces for people to talk about distress and seek help.
When a person is in a mental health crisis, experts said, the priority should remain timely human assessment and support. AI cannot take the place of that care.
