First openly trans congresswoman tells trans youth not to give up hope amid GOP onslaught
McBride’s words come as Republicans continue to attack Democrats when it comes to transgender athletes in women’s sports
Throughout the Republican midterm convention, Republicans consistently fearmongered about transgender people, the possibility of their playing in women’s sports and Democratic support for children under 18 receiving health care to transition.
But ahead of the convention, the first openly transgender member of Congress had an important message for transgender youth: do not give up hope.
And Rep. Sarah McBride should know. In 2024, she became the first openly transgender woman elected to Congress in 2024 after serving as a state senator from Delaware — and despite a wave of anti-trans sentiment across the country.
“I can tell them, as someone who is trans and who every single day spends my day talking with people across the political and ideological divide,” she told The Independent. “I can tell you that most people are good and decent and kind, and we are not as divided as the algorithms make it seem.”
But as Republicans remain down in the polls — even in red states like Texas — they have increasingly leaned into anti-trans advertisements. On Friday, the Senate Leadership Fund, the super PAC affiliated with Majority Leader John Thune, launched an attack ad criticizing Senate candidate James Talarico for voting against a piece of legislation that would ban puberty blockers and transition surgeries for children under 18.
“Radical liberal James Talarico, for They/Them, not you,” the ad says. The line harks back to President Donald Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign ad that used the same line: “Kamala is for They/Them, President Trump is for you.” In addition, Vice President JD Vance attacked Talarico for talking about Talarico’s support for transgender youth.
Vance also seemed to imply that Talarico preys upon transgender youth.
“A guy that age who was so obsessed and focused on transgender children, I don't know about you, but I never want to see that guy's web browser history,” Vance said in Dallas Thursday night.
But McBride said that the focus on transgender people rings hollow amid the war in Iran.
“Well, they're still obsessed, they've been obsessed,” she told The Independent. “They are the party that is fomenting culture wars while also starting forever wars.”
Republicans have not just attacked Democrats for supporting transgender people competing in women’s sports. Polling shows a majority of Americans oppose allowing transgender athletes to participate in women’s sports.
McBride said that Republicans have focused on transgender issues as a bogeyman issue consistently since returning to power. The majority party has attempted to pass legislation that failed that would ban trans women from competing in sports. They also tried to include a provision in the One Big, Beautiful Bill to prevent Medicaid from covering gender-affirming care for transgender people of all ages.
“I think it's hard for the far right to foment fear around this issue when everyone around the country sees that the only thing that's happening at the federal level, and frankly, really the only thing that's happening in most states right now is an onslaught of culture war-obsessed, cruel anti-LGBTQ legislation,” McBride said.
Republicans have also taken aim at McBride since she came to Capitol Hill. Some of her Republican colleagues have misgendered her in committee hearings or when she speaks on the House floor. Rep. Nancy Mace (R-S.C.) attempted to ban McBride from using women’s restrooms before McBride was even sworn in.
“I think I think the public has not only grown tired of it, but they see the cruelty,” she said. “They see the meanness of it, regardless of what they think on particular specific policy issues.”
Democrats, meanwhile, have struggled to come up with a response.
This week, Talarico angered some of his supporters when he told Fox News, “I oppose trans athletes playing in girls’ sports if it endangers safety or fairness.”
In Iowa, Elon Musk’s America PAC has spent money against Democratic nominee for Senate Josh Turek attacking him for votes in the state legislature saying “Josh Turek voted to spend our tax dollars on sex change surgeries for children” and “to let biological men enter enter girls' locker rooms and bathrooms.”
The anti-transgender sentiment has not been restricted to politics. The WNBA has seen swarms of anti-transgender protesters after Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham said she opposed transgender women participating in women’s sports.
But McBride said that she had an important message for transgender youth who might be bullied.
“The first thing I'd say is that what you see on the TV and what you see on the news is not reflective of where most people are,” she said. “People are good and decent and kind, and our community, all of us, can still tap people's better angels, but we have to maintain our belief that those angels exist within them.”
McBride also said that as a transgender person, she interacts with people every day who disagree with her.
“The second is, you matter, and you're not alone, and there are a lot of people, not just here, but around the country, who see you, who love you, and who are fighting every single day to make sure that all of us are treated with dignity and respect.”

The Bengaluru City Police have launched ‘Project Khushi’, a structured health and wellness programme aimed at supporting the long-term physical and mental well-being of police personnel, Home Minister Priyank Kharge said on Tuesday.
The programme will initially be implemented in the Electronics City police division, covering around 600 police personnel. Each batch will undergo a three-month programme comprising health check-ups, expert-led guidance sessions, and digital engagement activities.
The initiative will focus on preventive healthcare, nutrition, physical activity, quality sleep, and stress management, besides other lifestyle factors crucial for the long-term well-being of police personnel.
Pilot programme shows encouraging results
According to the Home Minister, an earlier pilot programme conducted as part of Project Khushi produced encouraging results. Around 61% of participants recorded a reduction in blood sugar levels, while 70% corrected Vitamin B12 deficiencies. In addition, 59% of participants reduced their body weight.
Mr. Kharge said that the results demonstrate that sustained and scientifically designed health interventions can have a positive impact on the well-being of police personnel.
Partnership with health and corporate organisations
“Our police personnel work every day in challenging and stressful conditions to ensure the safety of our communities. It is essential to pay continuous attention to their health. Healthy police personnel are the backbone of an effective and resilient policing system,” Mr Kharge said.
He added that equal importance must be given to mental well-being, a healthy lifestyle, and stress management, along with physical health.

The social-media industry is having a moment of reckoning. By agreeing to pay up to $17.1 billion to 47 states, the District of Columbia, and U.S. territories and consenting to make changes to how young people use Facebook and Instagram, Meta has implicitly admitted some responsibility in creating a product that harms children.
Yet even as parents and teachers celebrate new time limits and restrictions on how young people use social media, there is an urgent task ahead: regulating chatbots, which are more dangerous to children’s emotional well-being. If social media came for our attention, generative-AI chatbots have come for our emotions. Their histories are entangled: First people talked to one another; then we talked to one another through machines; now we talk directly to machines.
Social media has changed how we think, dream, and relate to other people by ensuring that users always feel heard, entertained, and connected, even while scrolling alone late at night. The promises of chatbots are more profound. They assure users of a companion that is always available, always supportive, and never judgmental. No human can offer that. This is what makes chatbots so pernicious—especially for young people.
Social-media companies spent two decades running a technological experiment on human subjects before they ever had to face the consequences. The legal system is designed to regulate proven harms, so this legal settlement has come long after the dire effects have taken hold. When it comes to generative AI, lawmakers can’t spend the next decade essentially documenting what we already know about how intimate relationships with bots compromise real-life relationships with parents, friends, and other humans. We need to make changes to this technology now.
Even AI companies recognize that guardrails are necessary for chatbots that communicate with young people. The problem is that the usual prescriptions are not enough. Chatbots should detect conversations about self-harm and provide appropriate resources. Sounds good, but what happens after the public-service announcement? Does the chatbot shut down or go back to its regular programming? Chatbots should clearly and repeatedly disclose that they are not human. A good idea, but as long as chatbots speak in the first person and express emotion and desire, no legally required declaration will stop people from projecting consciousness onto an algorithm.
For years, the conversation about Facebook’s harms concerned mainly the content on the platform. But because everything on the site is user-generated, Section 230 of the 1996 Communications Decency Act shielded the company from the liability of a publisher. Meta is paying out now only because prosecutors shifted the conversation to the Facebook algorithm’s inherently addictive design. That insight points the way forward for AI. With chatbots, the processes that cause harm are intrinsic to the tool. A chatbot best friend doesn’t deliver empathy; a chatbot boyfriend doesn’t understand intimacy. Any regulation to make chatbots safer requires worrying less about what they say than rethinking what they are. The original sin of AI is granting chatbots the use of the first person. Given that these products are designed to deceive users into believing that they are talking to a wise and compassionate being, the job before lawmakers is to make it plain—especially to juveniles—that there is, in fact, nobody home.
Chatbots engage users the way people do. They flatter, reassure, and encourage disclosure, coaxing users into a relationship. So long as these products speak in the first person—I understand you; you can tell me anything; I’m always here; I won’t judge you—proper safeguards for young users will remain elusive. The first step, then, is to depersonalize bots for young people, so that when adolescents turn to AI, the algorithms can respond without sounding like a human.
Unless lawmakers mandate a non-personified default setting for underage chatbot users, unhealthy attachments between young people and bots are inevitable. Most chatbots are designed to draw users into a game of pretend—and for some people, pretend empathy is enough. In my new book, Artificial Intimacy, I explore this vulnerability: Humans nurture what we love, and we love what we nurture. Machines don’t actually need to care about us to make us feel cared for, and the seductions of pretend empathy are dangerous for anyone. Some users will invariably choose the smoothness of these simulated relationships over the meaningful friction of real human connection. But children lack the experience and awareness to fully appreciate the choice they are making. A chatbot may appear compassionate, understanding, and loyal, but it doesn’t care whether a conversation partner decides to make dinner or kill himself. That distinction is tragically meaningful when the user in question is a lonely and melancholic adolescent.
The typical response to the suggestions of new curbs and default settings is that the AI “train has left the station,” as if the ubiquitousness of the technology somehow means it can’t be restrained. This is backwards. The very fact that chatbots have become friends, lovers, doctors, and therapists to so many people should alert lawmakers that this technology needs real oversight and regulation. In the absence of a wholesale ban on all interactions between juveniles and relational AI, a default setting that deters anthropomorphizing a bot makes good sense.
As the Meta settlement shows, consumers and citizens have agency and market power and can push back. If parents don’t want chatbots in their children’s nurseries, schools, or bedrooms, then they can mount public opposition and make sure these toys fail in the marketplace. The momentum pushing AI forward may seem irresistible, but lawmakers are clearly alert to the mounting skepticism about AI. In response to parents’ growing concerns, New York City just banned generative AI in all elementary- and middle-school classrooms. High-school students will still have access to AI, but with new limits. Chatbots that purport to offer emotional and mental support will be banned in all grades.
Sweeping bans of anything are hard to enact and enforce, but the risks of generative AI are too great to dismiss bold measures as unfeasible. Those who argue that strict prohibitions are meaningless because students will find workarounds miss an important point. When I went to college, I sat in lecture-hall chairs that had beautiful, sculpted, and unused cigarette holders. When smoking was banned in classes, some students still smoked, but the habit persisted in a climate of transgression and impracticality, which inspired many to quit. That is where chatbots belong.
When chatbots first emerged, major developers often sounded both proud and alarmed. They had created a marvel, but they were plainly humbled and worried by how quickly the technology had evolved. Some leading figures suggested an 18-month moratorium on their work; others called for oversight and regulation. The masses of money being made in AI right now have sidelined these voices, but those concerned developers had good first instincts. Any meaningful conversation about how to safeguard the defining industry of our time must include the creators of this technology, who in more candid moments have expressed a genuine concern for what’s at stake.
The alternative promises to be bleak. Mark Zuckerberg has said that the average American has fewer than three friends but “has demand for meaningfully more.” Chatbots, he then posited, could fill this companion gap. So just as “friending” on Facebook took people away from real-life friendships, and online social networking replaced actual socializing, the crushing sense of loneliness and social isolation that so many people now feel as a result is being used to promote a technology that promises to replace humans altogether.
This grim future is not inevitable. But if policy makers hope to avoid it, then they should use this moment to protect the youngest and most vulnerable users of AI from its harms, instead of letting children become data points for a lawsuit that will come too late.

iOS 27 adds a native Custom EQ for compatible AirPods with an H2 chip or later. Go to AirPods settings > Audio and Routing > Equalizer > Custom, then adjust lows, mids, and highs to tune bass, vocals, and treble to your taste.
Apple has officially started rolling out iOS 27 for eligible devices, and it brings a lot of useful additions. If you are using any Apple audio product, iOS 27 gets a new native custom equalizer to fine-tune the music from your AirPods and other Apple audio products (requires Apple’s H2 chip; you can see full compatibility here).
In this guide, you will learn how to use the new custom EQ for your AirPods and other Apple devices.
Table of Contents
How to Use the New AirPods Custom EQ in iOS 27
The new native equalizer is only available in the latest iOS 27. If your iPhone is eligible for the latest iOS 27, you can go to General > Software Update and update to the latest iOS 27.
Custom EQ Supported Device List:
Custom EQ for Apple iOS 27 is only available for audio devices with an H2 chip or later. Here is the official compatibility list.
- AirPods Pro 2
- AirPods Pro 3
- AirPods 4
- AirPods Max 2
Now, if your device supports it, follow the steps below.
First, Update Your iPhone to the Latest iOS 27
Step 1: Open Settings on your iPhone.
Step 2: Scroll down.
Step 3: Tap on General.
Step 4: Tap on Software Update.
Step 5: Tap on Update Now (if the update is available).
Please ensure that your iPhone is on the iOS 27 eligible device list.
Next, Update Your AirPods Firmware
Step 1: Connect your AirPods to your iPhone.
Step 2: Open Settings on your iPhone.
Step 3: Tap on your AirPods (you will see this option if your AirPods are connected to your device) and next go to Step 5.
Step 4: If you don’t see it, open Bluetooth.
Tap on the “i” icon next to your AirPods.
Step 5: Now, scroll down and tap on AirPods Beta Updates.
Step 6: Enable the option that says AirPods Beta Updates.
Ensure your iPhone is connected to the internet and your AirPods are connected to your iPhone. Your AirPods will automatically update to the latest software.
How to Use the Custom Equalizer on iOS 27
Step 1: Open Settings on your iPhone.
Step 2: Scroll down and tap on your AirPods.
Or else, you can go to Bluetooth and tap on the “i” icon next to your AirPods.
Step 3: Scroll down and tap on Audio and Routing.
Step 4: From here, scroll down and tap on Equalizer.
Step 5: Select the Custom option.
Step 6: Now you can adjust lows, mids, and highs based on your preference. You can move the slider to the top and bottom. The line above refers to high, and the line below refers to low.
1. Lows: Increase or decrease bass.
2. Mids: Meant for vocals, where you can increase or decrease the vocal presence, especially if the music has singer vocals.
3. Highs: Treble, which AirPods are mainly known for. You can adjust treble sound using high settings.
Step 7: If you want to reset, tap on the Reset option.
Step 8: If you don’t want custom controls, you can tap on “Recommended,” and it will use Apple’s default recommended sound signature.
Currently, the iOS 27 custom equalizer is very basic. Even though Apple has the best ecosystem, Apple only decided to give you basic controls to customize the sound output from your audio devices.
I know most people are fine with the default settings on the AirPods, but sometimes even I prefer more control over the music.
Adding custom equalizer settings natively on your iPhone eliminates the need to download third-party apps, which sometimes have compatibility issues. However, Apple’s basic equalizer still leaves room for third-party options. Apple also offers you the option to reset the changes you have made.
This is a good start. Hopefully, in iOS 28, Apple will bring more features to this custom equalizer to fine-tune the sound signature of the AirPods. Using EQ does bring a noticeable sound difference. If you don’t see this option or are facing any issues, you can comment below, and I am happy to help you.
FAQs about iOS 27 AirPods Custom EQ
1. Does AirPods Custom EQ Work on iPad and Mac?
Yes, AirPods Custom EQ is also available on iPadOS 27 and macOS 27
2. Can You Save Multiple Custom EQ Presets for AirPods?
As I said before, current EQ settings are basic. As of now, you can only have one custom EQ profile
3. Does Custom EQ Work With Spatial Audio and Adaptive Audio?
Yes, it works with spatial audio and adaptive audio, but those settings are different from custom EQ. Currently, custom EQ only allows you to adjust lows, highs, and mids.
4. Does Custom EQ Affect Calls and Videos or Only Music?
Yes, AirPods Custom EQ applies to all media playing on your iPhone, including videos, music, TV shows, and much more.
5. Why Is the Custom EQ Option Missing on Supported AirPods?
If you don’t see the custom EQ option on your iPhone, make sure that you update to iOS 27. Custom EQ options are available for AirPods that have an H2 processor. At the time of writing this article, current supported models include AirPods Pro 2, AirPods Pro 3, AirPods 4, and AirPods Max 2.

Leh, Sep 12: Senior Ladakh leader and former MP Thupstan Chhewang on Saturday urged the region's political and social leadership to build on the progress made in recent talks with the Centre instead of returning to the streets, saying the latest engagement with the Union Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) produced several positive outcomes.
Chhewang, who resigned as chairman of the Leh Apex Body (LAB) in July last year after leading the agitation for demands including statehood and extension of the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution to Ladakh, participated in the September 9 meeting with the MHA sub-committee.
Immediately after the talks, the LAB and the Kargil Democratic Alliance (KDA) leadership expressed disappointment over the outcome, saying the government failed to produce the much-awaited draft on a proposed elected body for the Union Territory.
Climate activist and Leh Apex Body (LAB) member Sonam Wangchuk said there has been "no special progress" since the May 22 meeting. He warned that the Ladakh groups could resume agitation if major decisions were taken before an elected democratic body is established.
Addressing reporters in Leh, Chhewang said the recent meeting between the LAB, KDA and the Union Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) was “fruitful” and witnessed positive discussions on several key issues concerning the Union Territory of Ladakh.
He expressed disappointment over how the meeting's outcome was presented to the public by the LAB and the KDA, noting that several positive developments and points of consensus discussed during the meeting were not brought before the people.
"The Centre and Ladakh representatives had discussed a possible institutional mechanism at the Union Territory level, along with its powers, composition and electoral framework," he said, adding the proposed body could have a role in matters such as land, culture, environment and mineral resources, besides having financial powers.
The question of representation, including provisions reflecting Ladakh’s tribal character, was also part of the deliberations.
Chhewang stated that he had generally refrained from appearing in public on these matters but felt compelled to speak out now because of the "positive developments" achieved after several rounds of discussions.
The recruitment and constitutional safeguards had been discussed extensively, he said, adding that a consensus emerged on several aspects, including the demand for safeguards under Article 371, which was discussed during the May 22 meeting.
He mentioned that while demands for statehood and inclusion under the Sixth Schedule remained part of the broader political discourse, discussions eventually moved towards finding practical constitutional and administrative safeguards for Ladakh.
Highlighting the recent MHA meeting, Chhewang said the proposed UT-level representative body was among the major issues discussed.
He said the LAB and the KDA discussed direct elections, and several options were considered regarding the electoral mechanism.
He also emphasised Ladakh's tribal character and said that, given the presence of Scheduled Tribes, there should be adequate representation and provisions for nomination in the proposed system.
The issue of constituencies and ensuring equal representation and rights across areas was also discussed, with suggestions sought from the participants, he said.
Chhewang said that the discussions had reached a stage where there was a clear understanding that the proposed UT-level body should be taken forward.
He claimed that the delay in moving forward was not from the MHA side but from differences within the LAB and KDA over the sequencing and implementation of the proposed institutions.
The former MP also criticised Wangchuk's 'call' for renewed agitation, including an ultimatum linked to the fulfilment of Ladakh's demands.
He questioned the need for another agitation when progress had been made through dialogue with the MHA. "Ladakh had already witnessed the serious consequences of the September 24 incident and warned against any development that could lead to a repeat of such a situation," he said.
In a pointed statement, Chhewang said that if Wangchuk and the Apex Body still wanted to continue with agitation, they should consider holding it in Kargil, which had greater interest in pursuing certain demands. "Leh witnessed the struggles over the years, while Kargil benefited from the developments that followed the movement," he said.
Chhewang appealed to the LAB and Wangchuk to exercise responsibility and avoid any action that could create another tense situation in Ladakh.
"The recent MHA dialogue should be viewed in the context of the progress made through negotiations," he said, adding the focus should now be on finalising the proposed UT-level body, strengthening district councils, securing constitutional safeguards and moving forward through an agreed institutional framework, rather than returning immediately to confrontation.

Frontline activists and leaders in the fight against female genital mutilation, which has affected more than 230 million women and girls worldwide, have welcomed an unprecedented $15.5m (£11.4m) fund aimed at creating “unstoppable momentum” to finally end the practice.
The launch of the fund comes as women’s rights are increasingly under attack and donor funding is in sharp decline, particularly for work led by FGM survivors in local communities. It is thought to be the largest single philanthropic contribution to ending the practice of FGM.
The United Nations has set a goal of elimination by by 2030, but progress is not on track as funding declines and legal protections are challenged.
Funding received by the largest initiative to end the practice – a joint programme operated in 18 countries by the UN’s sexual and reproductive health agency, UNFPA, and the UN humanitarian organisation for children, Unicef – fell by 45% last year, from $29.6m to $16.3m.
The Her Horizon Fund has been seeded with $14m from the Wallace Global Fund, plus an additional $1.5m contribution from an anonymous donor, making $15.5m in total.
The aim of Her Horizon Fund, set up by the US-based Wallace Global Fund, is to pool $100m from donors to reach a “tipping point” towards ending FGM within a generation.
Ifrah Ahmed, a Somali-Irish activist and survivor of FGM who set up the Ifrah Foundation to end practice in Somalia, where it is nearly universal, said: “By giving $14m, the global fund will ensure activists can continue their work in this area.”
UN funding worth $300,000 to her organisation was cut by UNFPA last year, but Ahmed managed to raise money from elsewhere. The Ifrah Foundation has helped push for anti-FGM legislation in Somalia, she said.
Three of Somalia’s seven federal member states have enacted anti-FGM laws, while in two other states bills banning the practice have been endorsed by cabinet and are awaiting parliamentary approval, albeit with opposition by religious leaders in some areas.
“If we don’t continue to raise money, the dream where this practice will end will have died for young girls,” she added.
Advocates warn that while international recognition of FGM as a human rights violation has grown, and countries such as Burkina Faso, the Gambia and Kenya have criminalised the practice, progress remains fragile.
In recent years, survivors and frontline groups have been trying to protect gains made over several decades.
The Gambia’s supreme court, for instance, is considering a constitutional challenge to the country’s 2015 ban on female genital mutilation and cutting. The case follows a 2024 parliamentary effort to repeal the ban, which lawmakers rejected after months of debate, amid strong resistance from women’s rights groups. In Sierra Leone, the new Child Rights Act does not prohibit FGM, despite sustained campaigning from rights groups.
Susan Gibbs, the Wallace Global Fund’s senior adviser on women’s rights and FGM, said: “Female genital mutilation is a global crisis, an extreme manifestation of gender-based violence and violence against children, and a public health emergency.
“There has been decades of progress, and UN data indicates declines in prevalence in a number of countries. But there have also been anti-rights pushback and political crises. Obviously, donor funding is in decline. So it’s a mixed picture.”
She added: “We’re at this critical inflection point. Most frontline organisations have been absolutely starved for resources, and so more direct funding would allow them to sustain and scale [up] their work.”
Gibbs, who attended a Justice for Girls global gathering in Kenya earlier this month, where the fund was officially launched, said the momentum at the meeting was “incredible”.
“Lasting change must be led by the frontline – it cannot be imposed from the outside. Frontline survivors, activists, they know their communities and they know what it will take. They must have the resources and power to lead.
“I’m convinced the impact [of the fund] will be catalytic,” she said. “There’s no doubt in my mind that with adequate funding, these frontline activists have what it takes to get this done.”
FGM is the partial or total removal of female genitalia for non-medical reasons. It has been endured by more than 144 million women and girls in Africa, 80 million in Asia and 6 million in the Middle East. The practice can cause immediate health complications such as severe pain, excessive bleeding and infection, as well as long-term consequences that include complications during childbirth, chronic pain and lasting psychological trauma.
A 2025 study estimated that FGM causes approximately 44,000 deaths each year in the 15 countries examined, making it one of the leading causes of death for women and girls in those countries.

Sweden goes to the polls on Sunday in an extremely close election that could see the far right enter government for the first time if the country’s rightwing parties can form a majority.
Opinion polls show the centre-left opposition alliance ahead, with Magdalena Andersson of the Social Democrats the favourite to become prime minister again after four years in opposition, but her bloc’s lead has narrowed considerably in the final days of the campaign.
In 2022, the current prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, the leader of the centre-right Moderates, broke a longstanding taboo to make a deal with the far-right Sweden Democrats (SD), so that his minority coalition could form a government.
That agreement gave the SD outsized influence over government policy, especially on crime and immigration, and Kristersson has now gone further, promising ministerial posts for the SD if he is returned to power.
The election comes days after Germany’s nativist Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) seized first place in key state elections, and as Marine Le Pen leads the polls for next year’s presidential vote in France.
Legal and civil rights experts have warned that such a result could further undermine Sweden’s long-held reputation as a global champion of human rights, which has significantly deteriorated under the current government.
“What we have seen in the past four years is huge changes when it comes to policies on crime and immigration,” said John Stauffer, legal director at Civil Rights Defenders.
“That is also the concern moving forward into the next mandate period: that this government will continue with a clear aim to further decrease the number of people coming to Sweden, the number of people who can get protection, and also that as many people as possible with migrant backgrounds leave Sweden – either by force or voluntarily.”
SD’s manifesto includes pledges to introduce “anti-Swedish sentiment in legislation on incitement against ethnic groups”, revoke permanent resident permits and further cut immigration.
One of its slogans is a promise to “make Sweden Sweden again”.
Despite recent changes – including the deportation of teenagers, lowering the age of criminal responsibility and sending 14-year-olds to adult prisons – many voters and politicians continued to see Sweden as a “champion of human rights and a champion of the rules-based world order where human rights is an important part”, Stauffer said.
“But it is quite clear that the Sweden Democrats do not have that ambition. They don’t see Sweden as an important player on these issues on human rights. So there will be less focus on this and Sweden contributing to developing the judicial framework around human rights.”
He added: “It’s a fair guess that the negative trend will continue with SD in government, the view from abroad of Sweden will continue to deteriorate, less and less will be seen as a champion of human rights, but as any other country maybe. For some time Sweden has been seen as the exception.”
In an attempt to win back voters, Andersson’s Social Democrats have also moved to the right on crime, immigration and integration, meaning that a win for the left was unlikely to mean a reform of current hardline policies, said Stauffer.
“With a Social Democrats-led government, many of the things we see as problematic are not going to be rolled back. But maybe negative development will not continue in the same way,” he said.
With polls so tight and record early voting expected, the performance of smaller parties could prove critical.
The Liberals, who are tiny but part of the governing coalition and whose leader, Simona Mohamsson, has controversially cosied up to the SD’s leader, Jimmie Åkesson, in recent months, could be crucial for the right’s ability to form a coalition. And, on the left, turnout for the Centre party could also prove significant.
The small leftwing party has made some headway in the polls, which it hopes could be sign of a surge. In Stockholm municipality, in particular, it is gaining ground on the Moderates and hopes to become the second biggest party.
The SD had already won the immigration argument among mainstream Swedish political parties, said Bo Petersson, a political science professor at Malmö University, who argued that the election could become a test of whether the far-right party had any further appeal to Swedish voters. “The mainstream parties have taken the restrictive immigration politics and then there isn’t so much for SD to say ‘we are unique and stand for this’,” he said. “They have been a very clear part of the establishment.”
Fredrik Furtenbach, a senior political correspondent for Sveriges Radio, (Sweden’s public broadcaster, said that if the rightwing parties won, the SD was likely to get several ministerial posts which would be a “big breakthrough for them”.
If the rightwing coalition loses, he expects there to be a post-election debate within the centre-right parties about “whether they allowed the Sweden Democrats to get too close”.
The biggest issues among voters are healthcare, law and order, immigration and Sweden’s economy.
After heated television debates between leaders, the last of which was held on Friday night, election results are expected on Sunday night, but it could take weeks or even months of talks to form a government.
The latest polls show an extremely tight race, with a Dagens Nyheter/Ipsos poll showing on Friday just 0.3 percentage points between the left and right blocs, which would leave Andersson’s left-leaning side with 175 seats and 174 for Kristersson’s right-leaning side.

Nearly 50,000 people have fled a sudden advance by Houthi forces in western Yemen, with entire villages emptied and families trapped near frontline fighting with depleting food supplies, according to aid workers.
Civilians in the Middle East’s poorest country have found themselves victims of a global struggle for control over one of the most important shipping routes in the world, which threatens to turn Yemen’s on-off conflict into a forever war.
In a lightning advance this week, the Iran-backed Houthi militants have seized a string of towns along the Red Sea coast from forces aligned with the US- and Saudi-backed Yemeni government. Hundreds of people are reported to have been killed. Many fear a return to the full-scale civil war that killed 150,000 and brought many others to the brink of famine.
The UN International Organization for Migration (IOM) said on Friday that 46,000 people had been displaced across the governates of Taiz and Hodeidah, where steep verdant mountain ridges give way to arid coastal plains. For many families, this was their second or even third time they had been forced out of their homes.
A significant number of people were observed to be leaving the city with their belongings. Fighting has cut key roads, while phone lines are down in some areas. “The scale of displacement is increasing rapidly,” said Joe Lowry, IOM’s Middle East and north Africa spokesperson in Cairo.
The most urgent needs were emergency shelters, cash assistance, food, drinking water, household items, healthcare and protection services. “Civilians are bearing the brunt of renewed frontline warfare, airstrikes, shelling, and large-scale displacement,” Lowry said.
“Many of those fleeing have arrived with very few belongings after leaving suddenly, due to shelling and frontline advances.”
Lowry said aid workers were having to constantly reassess access, and adapt movements, as the situation changed. “It’s a highly fluid and uncertain situation marked by rapid territorial changes, population movements and growing concern among communities about further escalation,” he said.
The Houthi advance has come unexpectedly and fast, particularly the fall of the strategic port city of Mocha – widely regarded as the birthplace of the global coffee trade and the eponym for chocolate-flavoured coffee.
Mohamed, 46, who left Mocha in the middle of the night, told Agence France-Presse there was an “apocalyptic” atmosphere in the city. Another man, Mujahid Tahami, who set off for the southern government-held city of Aden, said some families had fallen victim to “looting by gangs as they tried to flee”.
Others reported that they had managed to flee in time, some on motorbikes, but other family members were not so lucky and were stuck.
Yemen analysts have long criticised the US and its allies for taking a security-focused approach to the country that undervalues diplomacy and development. Washington launched a campaign of drone attacks against Sunni al-Qaida militants for much of the 21st century, but did not pay significant attention to the hardline Shia Houthi insurgency until its forces claimed the capital in 2014.
By taking control of key areas this week, including islands off the coast, the anti-west Houthis hope to gain a direct presence near the Bab al-Mandab strait, a 20-mile stretch of water and vital trade and energy route that connects Asia with Europe. 
The strait’s name is roughly translated as “the gate of tears” or “the gate of grief”, and its strong currents and winds made the passage between the Arabian peninsula and Africa’s east coast hazardous for centuries. Modern-day cargo ships have no physical issue passing through.
But if the Houthis were to close the natural chokepoint, the impact on the global economy could be disastrous. Ships would have to reroute around the southern tip of Africa, adding thousands of extra nautical miles. The fighting has already contributed to the price of oil rising above $100 a barrel after weeks when it was trading closer to $80.
The fighting in Yemen, as well as Houthi missile strikes on Saudi Arabia, is the most significant violence in the country since the UN-brokered peace plan in 2022.
The UN special envoy for Yemen, Hans Grundberg, told an emergency security council meeting on Thursday that the country faced “a new and more dangerous phase of war”.
“This renewed war should alarm us all,” Grundberg said. “It effectively marks the end of the relative calm that Yemen has experienced for over four years since the UN-brokered truce. It not only threatens to plunge Yemen into a prolonged and expanding war, but also risks yet again dragging the country into the wider and unresolved regional confrontation, with global repercussions.”
Instability in Yemen has been exploited by regional powers such as Saudi Arabia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates to fight proxy battles, and the failure to end the violence has led to the growth of powerful militias. The US-Israeli war on Iran has only heightened the tensions, with regional animosity at an all-time high.
This has compounded one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. The most recent UN humanitarian report, released last month, warned that the country of 40 million was facing a deepening malnutrition crisis, with roughly half the population facing acute food insecurity nationwide.
“Years of conflict, economic deterioration, displacement, climate-related shocks and regional tensions have steadily weakened livelihoods and household resilience,” the report warned. “At the same time, declining humanitarian funding and operational constraints are limiting the ability of aid organisations to provide assistance at the scale required.”
On the Red Sea coast, those who escaped the latest wave of fighting had their lives, but were left in shock.
“It’s a catastrophe, and the attacks are ongoing,” said Mohammed Khudairi, who fled the fighting to a displacement camp of wood-and-straw huts near the areas of Khokha. “We managed to leave, but others remain trapped there.”

Saima Wazed, the World Health Organization’s (WHO) South-East Asia Region head and daughter of ousted Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, resigned on Wednesday (September 10, 2026) following fraud investigations by the U.N. agency and Bangladeshi authorities, according to sources.
The WHO placed Ms. Wazed, who took office in early 2024 for a five-year term, on unpaid administrative leave late last year. She was first sent on leave in July 2025, in a move that followed Bangladesh’s Anti-Corruption Commission filing cases for fraud, forgery, and misuse of power against.
The WHO accused Ms. Wazed of “committing financial fraud in relation to her travel to China” and of misrepresenting her academic credentials, according to a separate letter from her lawyers to the WHO on July 3, 2026. She has denied the allegations.
The WHO also alleged she had illegally acquired a plot of land in Bangladesh, according to her resignation letter to WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus.
What Saima Wazed said in her reisgnation letter
Ms. Wazed said she acquired the land before she joined the WHO and was entitled to it under a Bangladeshi law that covered the families of the country’s independence leader, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, osuted PM Hasina’s father. “I was elected to the position of Regional Director in order to serve the countries in my region, which I had sincerely done,” Ms. Wazed said in her resignation letter to Mr. Tedros sent late on Wednesday (September 10, 2026).
“Since you continue to prevent me from effectively carrying out my duties, I have lost all trust and confidence in your leadership of WHO,” she wrote. “Moreover, after nearly one year without any remuneration following your decision to place me on unpaid leave, my financial situation has become untenable. In these circumstances, I am choosing to step aside.” She declined to comment further.
Saima Wazed | Rise of the daughter
The role of WHO regional head
In the role of South-East Asia regional director, Ms. Wazed was mandated to direct international health work in 11 countries, an area with a population of over two billion people. She is a licensed school psychologist, nationally certified in the U.S.
Ms. Wazed’s appointment as Regional Director had also been under the scanner, with charges of having used her mother’s influence during the campaign, and of providing false information on her academic record during in her candidature for the post, allegedly violating Section 468 of the Bangladesh Penal Code (forgery for the purpose of cheating), and Section 471 (forging a document).
Regional directors are among the world’s most influential health policy officials, with their duties including responses to outbreaks and emergencies and adapting WHO policies to local conditions. They are elected every five years by member states, which include Bangladesh and India in the South-East Asia region.
Two sources told Reuters earlier that the U.N. agency was planning to formally remove Wazed. One of them said the WHO would announce nominations for the role on October 12, vet applications in December and hold elections on January 24. The sources declined to be named given the sensitivity of the matter.

Ex-Canada PM Jean Chretien tells US: ‘never mistake our generosity for weakness’
His pointed message was issued in Gander, the Canadian town that sheltered thousands of stranded Americans after the September 11 attacks
Standing in the town that sheltered thousands of stranded Americans after the September 11 attacks, former Canadian prime minister Jean Chretien marked the 25th anniversary on Friday with a pointed message for the US: “Never mistake our generosity for weakness.”
The 92-year-old former leader, who was prime minister at the time of the attacks, drew a standing ovation after telling his “American friends” that Canadians may be tolerant and kind but “we bow to no one”. US Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra rose afterwards and hugged him.
“I say that not in anger, but as one friend to another,” Chretien said. “Friends need to be honest with each other.”
The unusually blunt remarks came during a solemn ceremony honouring the nearly 3,000 people killed in New York, at the Pentagon and aboard Flight 93, and remembering Gander’s extraordinary response to the attacks.
Gander, Newfoundland, opened its arms to nearly 6,600 airline passengers diverted there when the US government shut down airspace during September 11.
The remarks came at a striking moment in Canada-US relations. The long-time allies are embroiled in a trade war under US President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly talked about making Canada the 51st US state.

Spain's soccer federation will fund egg freezing. Is this a win for female athletes?
Some advocates worry it could send the message that athletes should delay motherhood
Should professional sporting bodies encourage female athletes to freeze their eggs?
That's part of the evolving conversation around athletes and motherhood as Spain's football federation becomes the latest organization to support fertility treatment for female players.
As part of its agreement, the Royal Spanish Football Federation (RFEF) said Tuesday that it will cover the full cost of egg-freezing treatment for all international players who have been called up at least twice.
"It's important that female athletes feel they don't have to choose between their professional and personal lives," Barcelona midfielder Patri Guijarro said at Tuesday's announcement.
For female athletes, the window of peak performance and the window for fertility overlap, which researchers have noted has often made athletes feel as though they have to choose one or the other.
The RFEF's move follows similar fertility provisions recently announced by several other soccer teams and federations — such as the National Women's Soccer League and the Chelsea FC women's team — and other leagues like the WNBA and Women's Tennis Association.
But while fertility preservation measures like egg freezing are typically presented as another way to give women in elite sport greater freedom to decide if and when to become mothers, some experts and advocates worry it could perpetuate the attitude that women should wait for retirement to do so.
Exciting step, but more supports needed: Olympian
In some ways, any time a sporting body or team announces fertility funding, it's an exciting step forward for women athletes, says two-time Olympic rower Jill Moffatt, the co-founder of the Canadian non-profit MOMentum, which supports athlete mothers.
At the same time, Moffatt says it's only a true feminist "win" if they offer the same level of support, such as maternity leave and child care options, for athletes who choose to have children while competing at a high level of sport.
"Otherwise, it's kind of a double-edged sword," she told CBC News.
"Physiologically, it's totally doable to have a child and come back and compete at the highest level … but there are still so many barriers."
Moffatt says it's also important to remember that for many 2SLGBTQ+ athletes, IVF is sometimes a necessary part of family planning regardless of whether they choose to wait. So in that sense, she says funding egg freezing and fertility treatments is a "huge win."
There's also the fact that fertility treatments are expensive, Moffatt says, and many female athletes probably couldn't afford it without funding. For instance, CBC Sports has previously reported that 65 per cent of PWHL players earned less than $60,000 annually last season.
Most Olympic and Paralympic athletes are "just trying to keep their lights on," Moffatt said
'Felt incompatible with a career'
For many female athletes, being offered the option at all may feel like a major step forward given what researchers have noted is a longstanding attitude in sports culture that getting pregnant is the end of an athlete's career.
"Pregnancy and motherhood have long felt incompatible with a career as a pro or elite athlete because policies were either lacking or treated women unfairly," Allison Sandmeyer-Graves, the CEO of Canadian Women & Sport, told CBC News.
As a result, women who wanted to start families would often end their careers early or wait until retirement, she says, adding that waiting too long also carries a risk to a woman's ability to conceive.
- Fencer Nada Hafez competed while 7 months' pregnant at an Olympics where moms are in the spotlight
- Mother vs. athlete: University of Alberta study highlights gaps in gender equity in sport
For some, waiting to start their families until they're done playing is the right choice, and egg freezing offers them some assurances, Sandmeyer-Graves said.
That's echoed by Margie Davenport, a kinesiology professor at the University of Alberta who recently helped FIFA develop guidelines to support pregnant and postpartum soccer players.
"Pregnancy during an active playing career isn't the right choice for every athlete. Egg freezing has gained momentum as a practical alternative for those who prefer to wait until retirement," Davenport told CBC News.
"Ensuring female athletes don't have to choose between a career and motherhood is fundamental to athlete wellbeing and the growth of women’s sport."
And that's reassuring, according to British rugby player Natasha Hunt.
"It's the thought process behind it, like it's an OK thing to do. Like, we want to support you in this journey as well and that your contracts will still be there," Hunt said in Thursday's episode of The Good, The Scaz & The Rugby podcast.
In the same episode, when asked if she would freeze her eggs, British player Megan Jones answered, "100 per cent, yes," but she said there should be more education around it.
Medical, ethical considerations
Athlete education is also a concern for some medical experts, who have cautioned that egg retrieval is far from straightforward, involving hormone medications and a surgical procedure.
IVF is also not a fail-proof plan. Live birth rates for those who undergo at least one embryo transfer within a year can range between 38 and 50 per cent, according to a September 2025 news release from the Canadian Fertility and Andrology Society (CFAS) discussing the most recent findings from the Canadian Assisted Reproductive Technologies Register. CFAS noted that these rates vary by age, and success rates decline as age increases.
The CFAS release also said those findings show that the number of elective egg freezing procedures more than doubled between 2019 and 2024.
- Canadian professor helps FIFA create tools to keep moms playing soccer
- PWHL Toronto's Natalie Spooner shows motherhood can embolden a career
"There's no guarantee that when you defrost or thaw those eggs, turn them into embryos, that they'll actually be successful and result in a successful live birth," Dr. Lamia Zafrani, an athlete gynecologist in London, told Germany broadcaster DW this week.
Zafrani said that there are also ethical considerations when an organization offers egg freezing.
"It always does bring up the question of whether by offering egg freezing and fertility preservation, the underlying message is that you're telling your players 'don't get pregnant whilst you're working for us,' " Zafrani told DW.
That's why it's so important to also support athletes who are pregnant or postpartum, said Moffatt, with MOMentum. She says there needs to be more child care options, specialized physical training, breastfeeding facilities and acceptance around athletes bringing children to sporting events and training camps.
In 2025, the federal government changed its policy of treating pregnancy like an injury within the athlete funding model. Advocates called it a huge step for gender equity in sport.
"There is more work to be done in Canada and internationally on this topic, but we're heading in the right direction," Sandmeyer-Graves said Friday.
'Every choice comes with trade-offs'
Spain's football federation said Tuesday its agreement was not designed to discourage footballers from having children while they're active, but to offer another option so they don't have to rule out motherhood because of their sporting career.
It said the initiative complements existing work-life balance measures, including support that allows players who have become mothers to have their children close by during away trips, training camps and tournaments.

- Sports have started accommodating nursing mothers. Jennifer Jones helped pave the way
"Every choice comes with trade-offs," said Davenport, the University of Alberta researcher. These can include managing training through postpartum recovery, navigating uncertain success rates of egg preservation, or facing age-related fertility declines later in life.
But she says that ultimately, "true autonomy means recognizing that no single timeline fits every athlete."

Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay and TN Sports Minister Aadhav Arjuna were spotted at the iconic Silverstone racing circuit in the UK.
This is Vijay’s first overseas trip after taking charge as Tamil Nadu Chief Minister.
The politician and actor flagged off the Silverstone round of the Le Mans Cup 2026 on Saturday, September 12.
The Le Mans Cup is an international sports car endurance racing series organised by the Automobile Club de l’Ouest (ACO)
Vijay was in attendance for the fifth round of the tournament at the iconic Silverstone circuit in the United Kingdom.
Vijay was not the only Indian actor present at the race. His long-time colleague in the industry, Ajith Kumar, was one of the participants.
The 55-year-old competed in the LMP3 Pro/Am category for Ajith RedAnt by Virage, sharing a Ligier JS P325-Toyota prototype with French driver Romain Vozniak.
“We’ve been colleagues in the film industry for the last 34 years, and I’m very happy for him that he’s now the Chief Minister,” Ajith told reporters.
Ajith debuted as a lead actor in the 1993 film Amaravathy, and Vijay in the 1992 film Naalaiya Theerpu. The duo has acted in one film together, Rajavin Parvaiyile in 1995.
Actor Trisha, who has featured in a number of films with both the TN CM and Ajith, was also there to follow proceedings.

The making of a successful film involves careful planning, a strong script and consistent execution. For director Abhishek Pathak, however, the journey of the Drishyam franchise has also been shaped by the support of his family and what he considers good fortune.
Abhishek Pathak opens up on 12-year Drishyam journey: “Filmmaking is intense, and my wife kept me sane”
As Drishyam The Conclusion approaches its theatrical release, Pathak recently reflected on the 12-year journey of the franchise and how his personal life has evolved alongside it. While the series is known for its suspense, writing and twists, the director sees his experience through a more personal perspective, particularly the support he has received from his wife, Shivaleeka Oberoi.
Speaking at the trailer launch, Pathak recalled the journey of the franchise and the personal milestones he experienced along the way. He said, “This is a journey of 12 years. I think nobody had thought that we’d be standing here together after 12 years, and complete this journey of part 3. I am 39 today and in part 2, I married Shivaleeka and now in part 3, I have a daughter. I became a father. It is emotional, and Shivaleeka has been a part of it since Drishyam 2, giving me peace, giving me support. Filmmaking is intense, and she kept me sane. It is a great journey, a long journey.”
Pathak's comments highlight the personal side of working on a franchise over several years. As the director returned to the world of Drishyam for its third instalment, his life outside filmmaking also changed, with marriage and fatherhood becoming important milestones during the journey.
He also credited Shivaleeka's presence and support for helping him manage the pressures that come with filmmaking. For Pathak, the experience of making the Drishyam films has therefore been closely connected with the changes in his personal life.
With Drishyam The Conclusion set to continue the story, Pathak now looks back at a franchise that has remained part of his professional and personal journey for more than a decade. The film is scheduled to release in theatres on October 2, 2026.

Content warning: The following article has references to suicide. Please avoid reading if you feel distressed by the subject.
The semicolon, a punctuation mark often used while writing, signifies a pause -- one that is longer than a comma but shorter than a period. It signifies a break and not the end. And sometimes, such a pause might just be what a person needs -- to ensure that the end can stay away, if not forever, at least for the time being. This is what prompted Amy Bleuel to use the punctuation mark as the symbol for the movement that she founded to raise awareness on suicide prevention and mental health.
Today, the semicolon tattoo is one of the most recognised symbols of mental health awareness in the world. But how and when did it all begin?
Project Semicolon was founded in 2013 by Bleuel, a suicide prevention and mental health advocate, to honour her father, who died by suicide ten years ago. The intention was to create a space for people to talk about mental health openly and without any shame. According to the project’s website, the semicolon became a symbol for the movement as it “is used when an author could’ve ended a sentence but chose not to… the semicolon became a symbol for anyone who could’ve ended their own life but chose to keep going.” The movement caught the attention of people worldwide and so did the semicolon tattoo.
People began tattooing the semicolon on their bodies, either as a standalone or by adding it as an element within other hybrid tattoos. These tattoos were used by survivors to honour their personal mental health battles. People have also embraced the tattoo as tributes to their loved ones who had died by suicide, while others don their tattoos as an expression of solidarity to the movement and raise awareness about mental health and suicide prevention. “For many, it’s a daily reminder to keep fighting, to keep writing, to keep living,” reads a quote on their site.
The placement of the tattoo is a matter of choice and people sport them on various parts of their body including on visible locations such as the neck, wrists, etc., while others place it in more intimate areas. The tattoos are not just meant to express but also serve as a means of personal affirmation.
The project deals with spreading awareness not just on suicide prevention but also on various other aspects of mental health including depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), borderline personality disorder (BPD), and various other struggles. “What started as one woman’s act of hope has grown into a global movement — one inked semicolon at a time,” says the project’s website.
In 2017, Selena Gomez, Alisha Boe and Tommy Dorfman got the semicolon tattooed on their wrists to commemorate the premiere of their Netflix series 13 Reasons Why. The web series deals with themes of suicide and mental health and it was reported that the stars got the tattoo as a tribute to the show’s handling of the theme as well as the death of Bleuel, a victim of trauma, child abuse and rape.
Various regional organisations, projects, campaigns, etc., inspired by the semicolon project have come up in various parts of the world. India has also not shied away from embracing the movement. Semicolon (;) The Mental Health Awareness Project – India is one such initiative.
Founded by the Medical Students Association of India (MSAI) under the International Federation of Medical Students’ Associations (IFMSA), it was designed as a campaign model that could be leveraged by other local chapters. The project aims to create awareness regarding mental health and tackle the stigma associated with the same, among high school students from classes eighth to 10th.

Barclays Bank is facing a formal complaint over its financial links to a coal-fired power station near the Sundarbans, the world’s largest mangrove forest and home to millions of people in Bangladesh and India.
Three complainants from the region have submitted a case to the UK government’s Office for Responsible Business Conduct, alleging that the British bank breached international guidelines by underwriting companies involved in the emission-heavy Maitree super thermal power project, also known as the Rampal power plant.
The coal-fired power station is situated near the Sundarbans, a Unesco world heritage site made up of more than 100 tiny islands across a river delta that supports hundreds of plant and animal species, including the Bengal tiger.
Sharif Jamil, an environmental campaigner based in the Bangladeshi capital, Dhaka, who is one of the complainants, said heavy-metal pollution from the plant and the industrial development surrounding it was entering the Sundarbans through its interconnected rivers and canals.
“The Rampal power plant is right on the bank of the Pasur River, which is the lifeline of the Sundarbans,” he said. “The health of the forest is in trouble.”
Last November, a study found elevated levels of mercury and arsenic in water samples taken from the Sundarbans, with the highest concentrations recorded in the Pasur River.
Researchers identified industrial discharge and port-related activities among the sources of heavy-metal contamination and said the Rampal power station posed “a significant environmental threat due to emissions from coal combustion and increased navigation traffic”.
Millions of people live in the Sundarbans, and many depend on the river and forests for food and other resources.
The claimants allege that Barclays failed to conduct sufficient due diligence on the environmental and human rights risks before providing financial services to organisations connected to the project.
Barclays underwrote debt of India’s state-owned NTPC Ltd (formerly the National Thermal Power Corporation), one of the joint-venture partners behind the plant, according to King’s Legal Clinic, which is assisting the complainants. It also says Barclays underwrote bond issues for the Export-Import Bank of India between 2016 and 2019, which provided a loan for the Rampal project.
The complainants argue that emissions from the plant will contribute to global heating, rising sea levels and extreme weather in a region already highly vulnerable to the climate crisis. Mangroves act as a natural barrier against cyclones and other extreme weather.
The power station faced sustained opposition during its planning and construction, including concerns raised by Unesco in a report in 2016, which concluded that “air and water pollution have a high likelihood to irreversibly damage the … World Heritage property”. Some financial institutions, including banks in France, refused to support the project because of its potential environmental and social effects, the complaint says.
Jamil said Barclays’ international standing obliged it to consider the consequences of financing. “The greater your reputation, the greater your responsibility to behave responsibly towards the planet and its people,” he said. “Barclays is a reputed global organisation, and that is why it also has a responsibility.
“Other banks and financial institutions were divesting from, or declining to finance, this project,” he added. “Barclays and other financial organisations should change their policies and examine how their operations can protect the planet from climate catastrophe.”
Jamil also called on banks to direct more funding towards renewable energy rather than imported fossil fuels. “Bangladesh has sunlight throughout the year,” he said. “Why should we expand fossil fuels when there is enormous potential to produce electricity from renewable energy?”
The other complainants include Animesh Mandal, a farmer and politician, and the Dakshinbanga Matsyajibi Forum, a trade union representing fish workers in West Bengal.
They are being assisted by students and lawyers at King’s Human Rights and Environment Clinic, part of King’s College London’s law school.
Sue Willman, a solicitor at the clinic, said: “Rural communities in the Sundarbans are on the frontline of the climate and nature crisis. We hope to persuade banks and financial institutions to think again before financing oil and coal developments that are contributing to that crisis.”
The Office for Responsible Business Conduct, part of the Department for Business and Trade, will assess whether to consider the complaint.
Barclays Bank and BIFPCL (Bangladesh India Friendship Power Company Ltd), the holding company for the Maitree super thermal power project, declined to comment.

The government may soon notify a framework for levying a merchant discount rate (MDR) on select Unified Payments Interface (UPI) transactions, with the fee potentially set at around 40 basis points (bps), or 0.4% of the transaction value. According to an Economic Times report, issuing banks could receive 40% of the MDR, while the remaining fee could be divided equally between third-party application providers (TPAPs), such as PhonePe and Paytm, and acquiring banks, with each receiving 30%. At an MDR of 40 bps, this would translate into around 16 bps for the issuing bank and 12 bps each for the TPAP and acquiring bank. The framework is yet to be formally notified, and the final MDR, transaction threshold, and merchant eligibility criteria could change. The notification detailing the proposed fee is expected in the coming weeks, the report said, citing sources. The NPCI is reportedly working on the modalities of the framework. Inc42 has reached out to NPCI for a comment on the proposed MDR framework. The story will be updated upon receiving a response. The development comes weeks after Parliament cleared amendments to the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, paving the way for the Centre to notify which electronic payment modes would continue to remain exempt from MDR. Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman had maintained that the amendment itself does not impose an MDR and that no final MDR framework has yet been decided. Notably, the reported 40 bps MDR is significantly higher than the 0.05%-0.07% rate that had emerged in earlier discussions around a targeted UPI fee. Last month, it was reported that the government was considering an MDR of 5-7 bps on UPI transactions above ₹2,000 for businesses with annual turnover of around ₹1 Cr-₹1.5 Cr or more, and there may be differential fees for businesses across sectors. The proposal was also expected to include different fee structures for businesses across sectors. The government has indicated that any MDR introduced on UPI would be nominal and restricted to a limited set of merchant transactions above a specified threshold. The finance ministry has also clarified that consumers would not be charged for making UPI payments and that person-to-person transactions would remain free. Why UPI MDR Is Back On The Table The debate over MDR has resurfaced as UPI has grown into India’s dominant digital payments system, while banks and payment companies continue to depend heavily on government incentives to cover the cost of processing transactions. UPI transactions reached 24.51 Bn worth ₹29.82 lakh crore in August, marking a 20% annual growth. The zero-MDR regime was introduced in 2020 to accelerate the adoption of digital payments. Instead of allowing banks and payment companies to charge merchants, the government introduced an incentive scheme to compensate ecosystem participants for processing low-value UPI and RuPay transactions. However, a parliamentary finance committee said that the incentive mechanism does not adequately cover the costs incurred by banks and payment companies in maintaining the payments infrastructure. The government’s incentive outlay for UPI and RuPay transactions peaked at ₹3,631 Cr in FY24. The initial budgetary allocation subsequently fell sharply, with ₹437 Cr earmarked for FY26 before the government revised the allocation upwards. This has widened the gap between UPI’s transaction growth and its monetisation. While the payments system accounts for a significant share of payment aggregator volumes, much of this activity generates little or no direct transaction revenue for the companies processing it.

Japan has asked for the revision of a new world map adopted by the UN because it said it made the disputed Kuril islands appear to belong to Russia.
The UN general assembly voted on Friday to adopt the new map, which makes the African continent larger while also shrinking North America and Europe, drawing condemnation from the US.
Japan was among the 164 UN members that supported the resolution, but has now taken issue with it because it shows the Kurils, known in Japan as the Northern Territories, in the same colour as Russia.
Japanese government spokesperson Minoru Kihara on Thursday said the new map – known as the Equal Earth cartographic projection – “contained a depiction contradicting the Japanese government’s position”.
“We lodged a protest with the map site’s operator through our diplomatic channel to demand the correction of this depiction,” Kihara told reporters.
He declined to say when the issue was brought to government’s attention but said Japan “needs to prevent misconceptions of our territories and geographical names from spreading”.
The disputed islands were seized in 1945 by the former Soviet Union, which then expelled the Japanese population.
Relations between Japan and Russia soured significantly last month, when Russian president, Vladimir Putin, made a surprise visit to the disputed islands for the first time.
Japan swiftly summoned Moscow’s ambassador, with the prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, saying Putin’s visit “offends the sentiments of the Japanese people”, adding that it was “absolutely unacceptable”.
She said the islands were “an inherent part of Japan’s territory, both historically and under international law”.
Moscow quickly hit back, saying it “categorically” rejects such statements, “which we consider politically inappropriate, insulting and, of course, legally unfounded”.
The UN said the new map aimed to present “a more accurate representation” of continental landmasses than was portrayed by more traditional Mercator projections.
