Could Andrew Scott make history?
That is the big question concerning the Irish actor’s towering performance in “Elsinore,” which debuted in Telluride before playing the Toronto International Film Festival. Directed by Simon Stone, the film features Scott as Ian Charleson, a Scottish actor whose career has slowed down since featuring in “Chariots of Fire.” The year is 1989, and, when Daniel Day-Lewis walks offstage during a production of “Hamlet” at London’s National Theater, Charleson sees it as an opportunity to show the world what he’s made of as an actor — even as his body is being ravaged by AIDS, and against the advice of his doctor (Olivia Colman), who warns him that the stress could further worsen his health.
As Variety’s Clayton Davis wrote, “The casting is too perfect to be accidental. Scott is himself a celebrated London Hamlet, here playing a man whose Hamlet was his last act of defiance. ‘Elsinore’ is, at its heart, a love letter to actors — to the craft as vocation, to the courage of standing in the light when the body is failing. And a milestone waits inside the role. No openly gay man has ever won the Oscar for best actor, and Scott could very well become the first.”
Popular on Variety
Scott was widely seen as “snubbed” for his embodiment of Richard Rodgers in “Blue Moon” and the haunted Adam in “All of Us Strangers.”
On Saturday, Sept. 12, Scott took the stage at the Royal Alexandra Theatre to roaring applause as part of TIFF’s “In Conversation” series to discuss his much-heralded turn in “Elsinore” and his storied career. The talk was moderated by Keith Bennie, TIFF’s vice president of public programming.
The talk began with Bennie asking Scott, 49, who was sporting a striking purple jumper, about the internet’s obsession with him.
“I don’t have the internet. I never see it,” he joked, before adding, “It’s actually wild: You never know what feral things people [will say].”
“Elsinore” is the first film Scott has ever produced, so he said it “took a huge amount of encouragement and support and vision from so many people” to bring it to fruition. It was also a very personal project for Scott, who is openly gay and has been acting in theater since the ‘90s, including his aforementioned turn as Hamlet in 2017.
“You go through stages with it and the film is so incredibly personal for me, which is the reason why I chose to produce this one,” he explained. “It’s set in the theater and about the representation of gay actors in the ‘90s and it’s about family. So many things that I really relate to.”
Scott made his acting debut as a teenager in “Korea,” an Irish film that premiered at TIFF in 1995. And it was a formative experience for him, since he was given a crash course into how to conduct himself on a film set by watching his co-star, screen veteran Donal Donnelly, who led with authority but treated people with dignity and respect.
“Depressing. No, it was extraordinary. I was 17 and it was the first film I’d ever made,” offered Scott. “I learned how to be on a set because [Donnelly] was incredibly kind and fun with everybody… He wasn’t in any way cruel or anything like that.”
When Scott was a child, he had a speech impediment, which in a roundabout way is how he “fell in love with acting.”
“When I was a kid I had a speech impediment — I had a very strong sort of lisp— so I had to go to allocution lessons at seven or eight,” he shared. “It had a drama section to it where you could improvise in front of the other kids.” Performing poetry and monologues in front of a crowd, however small, “amplified something that was dormant” in him.
At one point during the talk, Bennie shared a scene of Scott’s priest acting alongside Phoebe Waller-Bridge in the second season of “Fleabag,” which became an internet sensation and earned his character the nickname “The Hot Priest.”
“If you had got a script that said, ‘The Hot Priest,’ you’d be like, ‘This is dodgy,’” joked Scott. “It was just called ‘The Priest’ and then the internet took over.”
Scott, however, was immensely proud of “The Hot Priest” craze in the sense that it helped ease some of his own anxieties about whether the audience would accept a gay actor in a role as a woman’s love interest.
“I guess there was a fear that I wouldn’t be able to get cast in those roles. That’s what everybody said,” he confessed. “But I knew, because when I did plays, that the people that were waiting at the stage door, they knew my sexuality and they did not care.”
He continued: “I feel very proud that that was quite a big moment because people were like, ‘The actor is gay. Whoa!’ And it is like this idea that the audience is stupid. We go to see ‘Batman’ and it’s like, ‘Oh my god! He is not a bat?’”
And if you don’t like Scott in those types of roles, that’s on you.
“That’s just prejudice,” said Scott. “And we won’t cater to those people, or I’m certainly not going to.”
About an hour in, the talk swung back to “Elsinore,” a film — and performance — that people will be talking about throughout awards season.
“It’s about how we use our time, and he was enormously fun, attractive, beautiful, amazingly gifted actor,” Scott said of playing Charleson. “And the film is about the support that he got and the courage that he displayed. The reason I was so attracted to it, I think, is because it doesn’t end well for any of us, and quality of time is what he chose… I know what an Olympian absolutely exhausting task that is [to play Hamlet]. I did it 150 times… The idea that he did it when he was so unwell, it always just gets me.”
Scott, who got choked up while discussing the film, also lamented how difficult it was for Charleson to act, or even exist, at a time when gay men, particularly those with HIV/AIDS, were being viciously discriminated against.
“There weren’t any gay actors — for no reason,” he remarked. “That was taken away from them.”

Two days after being placed on a paid leave of absence, Matt Mullenweg says he has been reinstated as CEO of Automattic, according to a Slack message seen by TechCrunch.
Matt Mullenweg reportedly returns as Automattic CEO two days after getting booted
Automattic founder Mullenweg is apparently already back at the helm of Automattic — and is posting about ‘coup’ attempts.
As 404 Media reported on Wednesday, Mullenweg had told staff in Slack that CFO Mark Davies “conspired” with the board of directors, who voted to “put me on a paid leave of absence.” (Mullenweg said he voted against that.) He also told staff that the board had voted for Davies to become interim CEO. Davies, in a separate message, said that Mullenweg would still be a board member, according to 404 Media. An Automattic spokesperson told The Verge that Mullenweg was “currently on leave” from the company and confirmed Davies’ interim appointment.
In the message viewed by TechCrunch, however, Mullenweg wrote that the board is “back in agreement” and that he’s “in control of Automattic.” He added that “A lot happened in the past 48 hours that we need to sort out, and I hope much of it was a misunderstanding, because I have huge respect and regard for those involved.” TechCrunch reports that Davies’ Slack account has been deactivated and that Mullenweg had removed “all” admins from Automattic’s Slack.
404 Media also reported on Mullenweg’s posts about his apparent return, saying he made the posts “late Thursday evening.”
Automattic, which owns companies like Wordpress.com, Tumblr, and Beeper, didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment from The Verge. At 12:20PM ET on Friday, Mullenweg posted on X that “If you don’t have a coup attempt every few years, you’re not hiring strong enough leaders,” adding in a separate post that “I think this was my fifth.” Mullenweg also published a blog post on Friday titled “Major Life Announcement” about making an offer to buy a houseboat.

Since the days immediately following the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks, U.S. President Donald Trump, a native of New York City, has made numerous claims about what he saw that day and his involvement in the recovery efforts.
One such claim Trump has repeatedly made is his assertion that he was at Ground Zero within days of 9/11 and that he sent workers to the recovery effort at the site of the World Trade Center.
In September 2026, multiple X users debated the veracity of the claim. For example, one user (archived) wrote, "There's no proof Trump sent a large group of construction workers to Ground Zero."
Other popular (archived) posts (archived) said there was no evidence Trump, himself, went to Ground Zero and helped with recovery efforts.
Another X post (archived) alternatively claimed, "President Trump is dropping VIDEO PROOF for every Fake News outlet lying to millions that he was nowhere near Ground Zero after 9/11."
(X)
Many Snopes readers searched the site to find out if Trump's claims were true.
A couple of days after the Sept. 11 attacks, Trump told multiple news media outlets that he sent at least 100 workers to Ground Zero to help pull people and bodies out of the rubble, with 125 to 150 more on the way. However, Snopes has never been able to identify any public evidence that crews he hired helped in the immediate recovery of the 9/11 attacks. Since we cannot independently confirm with certainty whether Trump had crews on site somewhere, we are leaving this claim unrated.
Footage of interviews Trump conducted in the immediate days after 9/11 placed him within blocks of Ground Zero. Trump said in those interviews that he visited Ground Zero to encourage the workers he said he brought to assist with clearing rubble at the site. It was not possible to find evidence showing Trump helped clear the pile of debris at Ground Zero, as some posts disputed.
In a phone call with a local news media station immediately after the planes crashed into the Twin Towers, Trump said he watched the towers fall from the window of one of his buildings.
Trump's September 2026 remarks
On Sept. 8, 2026, in a post on Truth Social (archived), Trump continued to maintain that he was at Ground Zero with construction workers after 9/11, clarifying that it was "obviously not on the same day as the collapse, but shortly thereafter":
The Failing New York Magazine wrote a story that I wasn't down at the World Trade Center after the Tragedy of September 11th, because nobody saw me there. Well, I don't think I would be the first thing on anyone's mind but, I was there, obviously not on the same day as the collapse, but shortly thereafter, with a large group of Construction Workers.
He then added he "was there as soon as the Law allowed."
The president was referencing a New York Magazine article disputing his comments about where he was on the day of, and the days following, the attacks.
Trump also made this claim (archived) in a Fox News interview two days prior, in which he added the additional context that he was constructing a new building in New York City. This is the reason, according to Trump at a 9/11 anniversary event on Sept. 8, why he had workers who he could bring to the rubble of the World Trade Center:
I was building a big building in New York and I took the whole crew down there right after this happened and they had no hesitation. Everybody went down with me. We went down as a big group of people. It wasn't too much we could do, I'll be honest.
What Trump told the media in 2001
Trump spoke to the media multiple times a few days after 9/11. On Sept. 13, he told a German news channel, that he had more than 100 men down at the site of the World Trade Center and more than 125 on their way. According to the German-speaking reporter, the interview was conducted a few blocks from Ground Zero.
That same day, NBC News interviewed Trump at what appeared to be the same location as his interview with the German news channel. Trump said he had "hundreds of men inside working right now" and was bringing down another 125.
PBS has a recording of another Trump interview from Sept. 13, in which Trump said he had 100 workers helping to dig people and bodies out of the rubble at the World Trade Center, with another 100 to 150 workers "coming." He told PBS that those workers were "digging out" at the site.
In another interview from that day, Trump told reporters his workers had been at Ground Zero "for about a day and a half." He said they were men from his company and that a couple had gotten hurt while working at the site. He also said he was just down at Ground Zero and was there to support them.
The evidence
When Snopes first researched this claim in 2018, we spoke to Richard Alles, a retired deputy chief with the New York City Fire Department, who later served as director of 9/11 community affairs for the law firm Barasch McGarry Salzman and Penson. Alles said that in all his time he spent at Ground Zero as a New York City Fire Department battalion chief, starting 20 minutes after the buildings collapsed, he never saw a large group of workers whom Trump had hired at the site assisting with search and rescue efforts. "This is the first I'm hearing of it," Alles said via phone call. "There would have been no need for that. Between police, fire and the construction crews, we had it all covered."
Alles added that the construction crews he saw at Ground Zero helping rescue workers were from the trade unions and were not hired by Trump.
John Feal, founder of the 9/11 first responder health advocacy nonprofit the FealGood Foundation, told Snopes at the time that he responded to Ground Zero on Sept. 12, 2001, as a construction demolitions expert and that he didn't see evidence of hundreds of workers hired by Trump at the site.
The Trump Organization was building in New York City in 2001, according to the Skyscraper Center database on skyscrapers. In fact, it finished a series of residential buildings in the city at Trump Place between 1998 and 2004. He was also building the Trump World Tower residential building near the United Nations Headquarters that year.
However, it was not possible to find verifiable information about how many people, either directly employed by Trump or contracted to work on one of the Trump Organization's projects, were working on these buildings and in New York City at the time.
A New York Times fact-check from July 2019 referenced Timothy O'Brien, the author of "TrumpNation: The Art of Being the Donald," who reportedly said the Trump Organization numbered "a little bit over a dozen people" at the time of the attacks, making it impossible to send as many workers to the relief effort as Trump claimed.
Neither the White House nor the Trump Organization responded to Snopes' requests for corroborating evidence in 2018. This lack of response is consistent with past attempts by Politifact, The Washington Post, The New York Times and Politifact again to reach out to the White House and/or the Trump Organization to corroborate evidence of Trump's claims.

In early September 2026, as Repulican U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn campaigned for governor of Tennessee, many people online claimed she announced a plan to bring segregation back to schools in the state if elected.
For example, a Facebook post stated:
BREAKING: Marsha Blackburn has announced that if she wins her bid for governor she will bring segregation back to Tennessee schools with the pilot program being in Chattanooga. "The supreme court will side with President Trump and I on this. The way we see it kids feel more comfortable with other kids that look like them."
(Facebook user, Chattanooga Enquirer)
Snopes readers emailed us to ask whether the claim was true.
The claim originated from an account that was satirical in nature. Blackburn did not say she would bring back school segregation in Tennessee. As such, this claim is labeled satire.
The post came from the Chattanooga Enquirer, a Facebook page that describes itself as a "Satire/Parody" media company. The introduction to the page states: "The one stop shop for Chattanooga's fake but maybe real news."
We searched for the purported quote featured in the post on Google, DuckDuckGo (archived), and Bing, and found no evidence of Blackburn ever making this announcement.
Blackburn has long been an opponent of diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives, and critical race theory in schools. On her Senate website, Blackburn calls CRT "a radical school of thought used by the political left to assign racial significance to objectively neutral concepts like history and mathematics." She adds, "This dangerous agenda insists that America is a racist country and teaches that all individuals are either oppressors or victims."
As Snopes previously reported, CRT looks to the law for answers as to why racial inequality persists even as American founding documents and aspirational ideals vaunt equality, and after the Civil Rights Movement brought about landmark legislation aimed at ending racism de jure.
According to data from the 2023-2024 school year collected by Stanford University, Tennessee is ranked sixth among the most racially segregated public schools in the country.

'It's like a dog set loose on us' - fear over Kenya's crackdown on foreign traders
- Published
For Ndaikech Ali, who has been traversing the streets of the Kenyan capital eking out a living as a tuk-tuk driver for the past nine years, Nairobi's traffic - not xenophobia - has been his biggest concern.
During his time in the East African nation, the Burundian says he has always found Kenyans to be friendly and welcoming - that is until last week, when the president ordered a crackdown on foreigners working as traders or operating small-scale businesses.
"Now they have turned against us," he told the BBC at the Burundian embassy in Nairobi where many have been queuing this week for documents to allow them to travel back home.
"The threats are many… even from children," he said, adding: "It's a like a dog has been set loose upon us. We have been bitten."
President William Ruto made his remarks last week when addressing Kenyan traders gathered at state house - in reference to legislation before parliament that seeks to exclude foreign nationals from petty trade and to mandate the local sourcing of certain materials.
During his speech, he said that all foreign nationals operating small businesses had until 7 September to pack up shop, saying such low-level jobs should be reserved for Kenyans.
Ali, like others, panicked, saying it seemed the president's announcement had been interpreted by some Kenyans as a signal that foreign nationals were no longer welcome in the country.
"We face harassment and can't work," he says. "If our work is stopped, we lose the income that enables us to pay rent and buy food. When those jobs are taken away, the only option left is to return home."
Now he's gone, who will help me pay school fees"
Other Burundians and some other foreign nationals have rushed to border crossing points to leave the country, with reports suggesting that a number have ended up stranded there.
Some couples fear they will be forced to separate - and some families have already been divided.
"I have been here from 2019," said a Burundian man, who identified himself only as Prosper and who has a child with a Kenyan woman.
"When I heard the announcement, it was very painful because when I go, I'm forced to leave my family... and I love my family," he told the BBC.
In Nairobi's low-income neighbourhood of Majengo, Kenyan Grace Wamaitha said her Burundian husband had already gone - leaving the day after the president's 3 September directive.
She is distraught as she has been left trying to feed their five children - and has taken on extra work washing clothes.
"Now he's gone, who will help me pay school fees? I don't know what to do. Let them come back," she told the BBC.
In Nairobi and other major towns, migrants from the region can be found working in barber shops and salons, construction, operating motorbike taxis and street vending, as well as selling clothes, food and household goods.
Some have fled conflicts or economic hardship at home, while others have moved to Kenya in search of better opportunities. Within the East African Community (EAC), a regional bloc made up of eight countries, including Burundi and Kenya, the relative free movement of people is allowed - but employment and long-term residence do require permits.
Kenyan law also recognises the right of refugees to work and operate businesses, although they are also required to obtain the appropriate documentation.
Filmon Eyob, a co-ordinator within Nairobi's Eritrean community, agrees with concerns that the crackdown order will be used as pretext to harass foreigners.
He told the BBC that while many Kenyans had been supportive and welcoming, some Eritreans and Ethiopians had closed their businesses and stayed at home over the last week as a precaution.
The president's remarks also sparked a diplomatic row, with the Burundian foreign affairs minister warning that "hate speech against Burundi" could have repercussions for Kenyans abroad.
The authorities in Kenya have struggled to contain the fallout - and as the matter came to a head, Kenyan foreign affairs official Korir Sing'Oei visited and apologised to Burundians at the embassy this week, assuring them of protection from violence.
Critics argue that Ruto's remarks were a populist move that risked stoking xenophobia, although the government has denied this.
Since then, a series of official statements have sought to clarify the directive.
The government has now given a 90-day window for undocumented foreign nationals running small business to register and comply with local laws. During the process, those undergoing registration will be presumed to be living legally in Kenya.
Yet observers and those affected argue that it did not have to be this way.
Academic Hesbon Owilla told the BBC the president's comments were bound to be misinterpreted, especially by people who did not have the right documentation.
He says that while the proposed policy is good for Kenya and in line with global migration protocols, the communication about it ought to have been more diplomatic.
For those not in the audience, Owilla says people interpreted the president words as saying: "We are kicking these guys out."
The president did not stop at small-scale traders. A day later, he ordered India's Tata Chemicals to leave the country, saying the company had not provided sufficient benefits to the local Maasai community in Kajiado county.
Tata has been mining soda ash for years in Lake Magadi, a vast area often covered by a whitish salt crust. The lake's extreme briny environment sustains algae blooms that attract flamboyances of pink flamingos that thrive in the area.
Mining operations began at the lake in 1911 under a British colonial arrangement that is said to have remained largely intact, despite long-running land and resource disputes pitting the company and its predecessors against community and the government.
Economist Odhiambo Ramogi argues that the move to restrict foreign nationals from businesses is too broad - and could do with finessing.
He points out that Kenya hosts hundreds of thousands of refugees as well as other migrants, mostly from the EAC region, as well as other international investors.
Ramogi says that Ruto's intention seemed to go beyond "just protecting jobs for Kenyans".
The president's remarks have prompted a wave of support for foreign nationals, including by civil society groups and ordinary Kenyans who have criticised his approach.
In the wake of the criticism, Ruto, who is up for re-election next year, has sought to counter the backlash.
"Kenya will remain an open, secure and welcoming country, protecting opportunities for its citizens, safeguarding the rights of all persons lawfully within its borders," a statement by his spokesman said.
"Kenya's commitment to the East African Community of the African continent remains firm."
Ramogi says that in the end, it is Kenya that stands to lose when citizens of neighbouring countries are targeted.
He points out that Kenya earned $56m (£41m) in exports to Burundi last year, adding that the country would still benefit by allowing competition, as "locking out aliens simply means you don't want a competitive economy that gets to grow a lot faster".
"Now, if you got $56m out of a country, why are you worried about a hawker who's just trying to make, say, $200 in a month?
"It absolutely makes no sense what the president has done."
For Nairobi resident Lima Kabura, whose husband is Tanzanian, the president's remarks were just too hasty. She says he should have first established those who were in the country illegally.
"When they are forced out, I'm left with no work, no business and no husband," she said.

Waymo pulls over robotaxi after detecting riders were carrying assault rifle
Waymo does not allow riders to carry weapons in its vehicles
Two minors were arrested last week in San Francisco after a Waymo allegedly detected they were carrying a gun and alerted the police.
On September 3, a Waymo employee was alerted that a gun had been detected in one of its driverless cars in the Outer Richmond neighborhood of San Francisco. The company pulled the driverless car over and alerted police to the presence of the weapon.
Police were dispatched to 40th Avenue just before 4 a.m. and engaged in what SFPD spokesperson Allison Maxie described as a "high-risk vehicle stop," according to SFGATE.
She said that police searched the car and found an "AR-styled assault rifle also known as a ghost gun," and also found "suspected marijuana and mace spray" on the minors.
Both suspects, one male and one female, were arrested and booked into the Juvenile Justice Center, according to SFPD. They will face charges related to the illegal possession of a firearm.
Police have chosen not to release the suspects' identities due to their ages.
Waymo's Rider Rules prohibit carrying a weapon of any type inside its driverless cars. It's not clear exactly how the Waymo detected the firearm, especially one described as a "ghost gun" by the SFPD.
Ghost guns are typically homemade guns, often created using partially 3D-printed parts. They are not registered weapons and don't have serial numbers, and are thus more difficult for law enforcement to track.
The incident wasn't the first time Waymo employees called the cops on their customers. In July, company employees called the San Mateo Police Department to report that two 15-year-old boys were allegedly drinking alcohol and shooting water beads while cruising around in the car, according to SFGATE.
In that case, Waymo reportedly did not alert the riders that the police had been called, and allegedly fed them a false story to explain why the car was pulling over.
The teens "were told the vehicle had issues" before it pulled over, according to San Matteo Police Department spokesperson Jeanine Luna, who spoke to Business Insider about the incident earlier this year.
She impressed that the vehicle's doors were never locked, so the teens could have exited the car at any time before police arrived.
It's unclear if Waymo used a similar tactic to keep the juveniles with the ghost gun from exiting the vehicle.
The Independent has requested comment from the company.
Waymo has been in operation since 2009, when it was launched by Google, and eventually broke off to become its own company in 2016. It began operating in San Diego, Denver, and Tampa earlier this month.

A Chinese rescue team has reached the all-but-obliterated Gyirong border crossing complex for the first time and found “nothing but ruins” as Nepal and China continue their arduous rescue operations in the flood-hit Himalayas.
Surveillance camera footage from the worst-hit Gyirong border crossing complex showed huge torrents of water and debris on Wednesday engulfing buildings and people trying to flee. Only on Friday were rescuers able to reach that area.
State media reported that the Chinese team of 21 rescuers and a search-and-rescue dog crossed mountains and valleys and used ropes to navigate forests and cliffs after roads to the complex, hemmed in by steep Himalayan slopes, were destroyed.
“There was no road … it was all virgin forest and sheer cliffs,” rescue worker Zou Mingqi said. At the complex, “as far as the eye could see, there was nothing but ruins.”
The glacier collapse which unleashed a deadly torrent through Himalayan mountain river systems has killed at least 579 people in Nepal and seven in China’s Tibet. The number of missing in Nepal has nearly doubled to 1,924, officials said on Friday. At least 558 were missing in Tibet’s Gyirong County, Chinese state media said. Among the missing are at least 540 foreigners, many of them Hindu pilgrims from India.
More than 90,000 people have been affected by the disaster, the Red Cross estimated.
Amid the deepening crisis, Nepal has now said it needs foreign help in specialised and technical areas in which it does not have expertise, but not in search and rescue.
Earlier on Friday, Nepal’s foreign ministry had said that Kathmandu could manage the rescue efforts on its own for now and declined foreign involvement.
The areas Nepal is seeking help include opening transport and communication services in places where bridges have been destroyed, identification of dead bodies, DNA testing and storing bodies for longer durations, foreign minister Shisir Khanal said late on Friday.
Asked about that stance of his government, Khanal said there was no need for assistance in general search and rescue which was being done by Nepali rescuers. “We think there is no need for repetition in this,” he said.
India and China, between whom Nepal is wedged, have been requested to supply bailey bridges to reopen transport and communication in an area where about two dozen bridges had been destroyed.
Nepal is continuing to monitor two barrier lakes upstream of the flood zone, with an official warning that flood risks will persist until both lakes fully drain.
Satellite imagery showed the second lake growing larger with no visible outlet, raising concerns that water pressure could still be building.
China’s state-run Xinhua news agency said that the first barrier lake was reducing in size, citing analysis by the water resources ministry. A Chinese government geo-hazards expert warned, however, that the lake may be unstable and that over 100 glacial lakes scattered throughout the area could pose a threat.
In Beijing, a politburo meeting chaired by President Xi Jinping called for stronger monitoring of glacier lakes and landslide risks, and for closer international disaster cooperation, Xinhua reported.
China’s Premier Li Qiang, the country’s No. 2 official, arrived in the area of Gyirong on Thursday afternoon, Xinhua said. The visit suggested Beijing was treating the disaster as a matter of the highest national priority.
In China, strict controls on the flow of information from one of its most sensitive regions are hampering the public’s understanding of events.
The BBC and NY Times have reported videos of the catastrophic floods, widely shared globally, have not appeared on Chinese social media sites.
Chinese state media has carried several broadcasts about the floods and dispatched their own journalists to the area, but reports have focused on the rescue efforts rather than the scale of the devastation. In one broadcast from a relief centre in Tibet, the journalist did not speak to any of the people sitting behind him.
Tibet, brought under Chinese control in the 1950s, is the most sensitive and tightly controlled region in the country.
The Gyirong border port plays a key role in China’s Belt and Road network linking the country to South Asia, with logistics zones and parking lots built there in the past decade.

Elk involved in nearly two-thirds of aggressive encounters in national parks, study finds
Study looked at over 10 years of Parks Canada data on aggressive wildlife encounters
Elk were involved in nearly two-thirds of aggressive wildlife encounters, according to a new study of 25 Canadian national parks.
Researchers analyzed Parks Canada data collected from 2010 to 2023 on aggressive wildlife encounters and what people were doing when they occurred. The study found confrontations happened most often when people were doing quiet, everyday activities like hiking, wildlife watching, sightseeing and strolling in town.
Five animals were examined in the study: elk, mule deer, coyotes, grizzlies and black bears.
Elk were involved with more than 60 per cent of the nearly 3,000 aggressive encounters. They were involved in more than half of the encounters during adventure sports like mountain biking and 80 per cent of encounters at campsites. Elk were also involved in more encounters in town than any other animal.
Study author Shashank Balakrishna says the findings show people don't always recognize which animals can be dangerous.
“Elk are herbivores, and so people tend to believe they aren't as aggressive as a grizzly bear. The results show people are underestimating the power of large herbivores,” he says.
Nick de Ruyter, program director at the Biosphere Institute of the Bow Valley, says the findings don’t surprise him.
Elk spend a lot of time in and around the Town of Banff, he says — in part to stay away from predators.
And because they're used to being around people, de Ruyter says, people can start to see them as tame.
“People get too close. They try to feed them. They try to take photos with them — selfies. And that leads to attacks,” he says.
Eighty per cent of the encounters happened in Banff and Jasper, likely in part because millions of tourists visit the parks every year and there are towns within these two parks, says de Ruyter.
The data groups several types of interactions under “aggressive encounters,” including aggressive displays like stomping, bluff charges and animals chasing people.
Actual attacks made up only 1.6 per cent of encounters.
“The wildlife are actually quite tolerant of people,” de Ruyter says.
Many encounters, such as bluff charges, are actually defensive measures that can signal people are too close.
“So a lot of it comes down to the choices we make. But there should be healthy fear and respect of the wildlife here, because things can go wrong,” he says.
Bears accounted for 27 per cent of aggressive encounters.
Grizzly bear encounters were most commonly associated with low-impact activities, including hiking and walking. De Ruyter says when people are quiet on hiking trails, that leads to more surprise encounters with wildlife.

“Making noise is key,” he says, especially in areas where people can’t see far ahead. Turning a corner quietly, for example, can mean unexpectedly coming across a bear.
Coyotes and mule deer had the least amount of encounters, but when they did become aggressive it was often in town.
De Ruyter says hiking and walking are among the most common activities in the parks, which could be part of the reason why so many encounters happen during these activities.
Balakrishna agrees his study’s results do not mean hiking is more dangerous. He says they don’t have the data on how many people were doing each activity, so they can’t compare risk.
De Ruyter says people should give animals three school bus lengths of space and carry bear spray, even when walking through busy areas of town.
“People shouldn't be scared. They shouldn't be afraid to go out in the mountains, but they should make good choices and be properly prepared,” he says.

The interview Trump doesn’t want you to see
Why ABC won’t air an interview with a Democratic Senate candidate.
Welcome to The Logoff: President Donald Trump’s FCC wants to keep a Democratic Senate candidate off the air.
What’s happening? On Wednesday, late-night host Jimmy Kimmel announced that his upcoming interview with James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Texas, would not air on TV. Instead, he said, “due to circumstances beyond our comprehension,” it would be posted only on YouTube.
According to Kimmel, Trump’s Federal Communications Commission “has threatened me, threatened our show, threatened our network, ABC, our affiliates, our local stations, based on simple, traditional editorial decisions — guest bookings it would seem they don’t like.”
Can Trump do that? It’s unclear — but he can at least make it painful enough for companies that they decide it’s not worth the headache. Kimmel said on Wednesday that his show’s decision was made “out of consideration for our local stations…who would have to deal with this nonsense” if they aired the interview.
Late-night shows like Kimmel’s Jimmy Kimmel Live! have long been considered exempt from something called the equal-time rule, which requires broadcasters to give equal air time for candidates contending for the same office.
In January, however, the Trump administration said that late-night shows needed to comply with the rule; the next month, CBS declined to air an interview with Talarico on its late-night show, The Late Show with Stephen Colbert. (That interview was also posted to YouTube, where it’s since garnered about 9.5 million views.)
What’s the context? This is not Kimmel’s first brush with Trump or the FCC. He was briefly suspended around this time last year after threats from Trump’s FCC chair, and Trump tried again to get him fired earlier this year, with less success.
Last month, ABC and its parent company, Disney, sued the FCC over its attempt to force a review of ABC’s broadcast licenses.
What’s the big picture? This kind of attack on the media is a familiar tactic from competitive authoritarian systems like Hungary, as my colleague Zack Beauchamp explained last year. Trump’s efforts to do the same in the US have often been clumsy or unsuccessful — but in this case, it seems to be working.

Why PLA’s laser-equipped Type 19 vehicle could matter in a Taiwan conflict
Images appear to show amphibious platform adapted with energy weapon and extra sensors for counter-drone defence
Unverified images posted on mainland Chinese social media on August 29 show a new variant of the Type 19 amphibious 8x8 combat vehicle featuring a turret-mounted laser weapon and extra sensors alongside its standard autocannon.
Janes, an open-source defence intelligence provider, reported in 2023 that vehicles from the Type 19 family had entered service with the 73rd Group Army under the Eastern Theatre Command, which includes amphibious brigades expected to play a major role in a potential Taiwan landing operation.
Assuming the new variant retains the base platform’s amphibious capability, it could accompany frontline units in a possible landing operation, providing defence against uncrewed surveillance and loitering munitions.
Timothy Heath, founder of defence consultancy Perceptum and a former senior China analyst at Rand Corporation and for the US military, said it was difficult to know without more technical data whether the modifications affected the Type 19’s amphibious performance, but he believed operating the laser system while afloat “should be possible”.
The added weight could potentially be offset by reducing the crew size or other equipment, although the system would also need to be protected from salt water, he said.
Heath said that if those challenges could be overcome, the laser-based counter-drone system could be “very useful in a Taiwan conflict” in which Taiwanese forces might use drone swarms to target amphibious vehicles coming ashore.
The laser system’s low operating cost could make it particularly useful against such attacks, Heath added.

More than 20 children killed in DR Congo school fire
- Published
At least 24 schoolchildren have died in a stampede as they tried to flee a fire that engulfed two schools in rebel-held Bukavu in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, officials there have said.
Adults are also reported to have died in the fire and there are fears that the death toll could rise further in the densely populated Kadutu commune.
Survivors have been taken to nearby hospitals, and footage of the scene shows children lying on hospital floors in pain.
Some 300 houses have also been destroyed in the fire, the cause of which is unknown.
Rebel‑appointed authorities released a provisional death toll of 24 on Thursday evening, confirming previous reports, but there are fears that more people may have died.
Pictures circulating on social media show young children lying motionless on the ground.
A witness quoted by Reuters news agency said the fire had been put out by afternoon but smoke was still rising from rubble and corrugated metal.
Bukavu, the capital of South Kivu province and one of DR Congo's most crowded hillside cities, was captured by M23 rebels in February last year.
Meanwhile the government in Kinshasa released a statement on X, without specifying numbers of casualties.
"The Ministry of National Education and New Citizenship expressed deep sorrow over the deadly fire," it said.
"With several lives lost and many injured, the toll remains provisional. The minister offered condolences, affirmed solidarity with families, and ordered assessments of affected schools to ensure learning continuity."
The tragedy follows a similar fire in Kinshasa last weekend, where residents died in a stampede at a wedding banquet hall.
In response, the government has ordered strict safety measures and deployed teams nationwide to enforce standards at public gathering places.

Experts say there is no universal clock time that works for everyone. What matters more is when dinner falls in relation to the body’s biological clock and bedtime. An earlier dinner may be beneficial, but there is no fixed 7 p.m. or 8 p.m. cut-off. The gap between dinner and sleep, the quality and composition of the meal, physical activity and individual health needs all play a role.
Insulin sensitivity and glucose tolerance generally decrease as the day progresses, so the body may not handle a heavy meal as well later in the day. However, dinner timing is only one part of the picture. The amount and quality of food, physical activity, sleep and health conditions such as diabetes and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GERD) also affect how the body responds to a meal.
The gap before sleep
“There is no evidence-based ideal dinner time,” said Aafrin Shabbir, medical director, senior consultant and diabetologist, Tambaram Medical Centre and CODE Clinic. The body’s metabolic efficiency is generally better during the daytime, she said, making a smaller and lighter dinner preferable.
She also cautioned against assuming that eating at 10 p.m. is unhealthy for everyone. Someone who sleeps at 1 a.m. has a different biological rhythm from someone who sleeps at 10 p.m. “One rule doesn’t fit all,” she said.
Saravana Bharathy S. P., internal medicine, Dr Mehta’s Hospitals, recommends leaving about two to three hours between dinner and bedtime. This is particularly relevant for people with reflux or digestive discomfort, as lying down soon after a meal can worsen symptoms.
Swathi Padmanaban, consultant, paediatric & adolescent endocrinologist and diabetologist, Rainbow Children’s Hospital, Chennai, said eating dinner earlier is generally better for metabolic health when practical. She advised against making dinner the largest meal of the day, particularly when it is eaten close to bedtime.
Meal timing is linked to the body’s circadian rhythm. The liver, pancreas and gastrointestinal tract have their own biological clocks that work with the brain’s central body clock. As the biological day progresses, insulin sensitivity and glucose tolerance tend to fall, meaning the same meal may cause a greater rise in blood glucose when eaten later.
Late eating
Studies have found that eating dinner at 10 p.m., compared with 6 p.m., led to higher overnight blood glucose and changes in fat metabolism, despite the meals having the same calories and nutrients.
“Late eating may have greater metabolic implications for people living with diabetes, prediabetes and obesity. A carbohydrate-rich meal late at night can cause a larger rise in blood glucose, particularly when physical activity is low,” Dr. Swathi said.
Late, heavy meals can also cause bloating, indigestion and acid reflux and may affect sleep. However, an occasional late dinner is unlikely to carry the same significance as a regular pattern of late-night eating.
Eating after a particular hour does not, by itself, cause obesity or heart disease. Overall calorie intake, food quality, physical activity, sedentary behaviour and sleep also play major roles. “People who regularly eat late may also snack more, sleep less or have irregular work schedules. This makes it difficult to separate the effect of dinner timing from other lifestyle factors,” Dr. Bharathy said.
Healthier dinner timing
For children and adolescents, the focus should be on regular meals, adequate nutrition, appropriate portions, physical activity and good sleep rather than restrictive eating windows.
If a late dinner is unavoidable, a moderate and balanced meal is preferable. Vegetables, protein and fibre can be included, while sugary drinks, sweets and fried or fatty foods should be limited. It is also better to avoid coming home extremely hungry and eating a large, carbohydrate-heavy meal just before bed. If possible, part of the meal can be eaten earlier and the later meal kept smaller. A short walk after dinner may also help with post-meal blood glucose control.
For people living with diabetes, meal timing should be planned around their medication, insulin requirements, blood glucose levels and HbA1c rather than a fixed cut-off.
The practical approach is to eat earlier when possible, leave about two to three hours between dinner and bedtime, keep late meals light and balanced, and maintain regular eating and sleep schedules.

If the midterms were a referendum on whether trans athletes should be barred from women’s sports, or the White House ballroom should be gorgeously renovated, or God should be identified as “nonbinary,” then Republicans would have a clear and confident closing message.
Trump keeps telling voters he doesn’t care much about affordability
The president is engineering a pre-midterms price spike.
Key takeaways
- The cost of living is midterm voters’ top issue.
- The war in Iran has led to the first decline in real wages since 2023.
- Trump could bring gas prices down before Election Day by seeking a ceasefire with Iran, but he’s choosing to prioritize military victory.
- The president is also escalating trade wars, despite their impact on consumer prices.
Unfortunately for the GOP, voters are less concerned with the Christian deity’s preferred pronouns than with their own cost of living. Which is understandable: Diesel fuel prices just hit a record high, mortgage rates are climbing, and groceries keep getting more expensive.
Due partly to these trends, Republicans are poorly positioned to win an argument about inflation — and are only growing more so, as Election Day nears. This was apparent before President Donald Trump convened the first-ever Republican midterm convention in Dallas this week. But the festivities underscored the GOP’s predicament and the many ways that Trump is personally exacerbating it.
Many Republican speakers did address the subject of affordability in Dallas. And the party’s broad narrative is straightforward enough: Democrats created the cost-of-living crisis, Republicans alleviated it by cutting your taxes.
But this is a tough line to sell. Americans might still disdain President Joe Biden’s economic management. Yet they’re far more likely to blame high prices on the current president than the previous one, according to polls.
And not without reason. After all, it was Trump — not Biden — who engineered an oil shock and global trade war. Tellingly, on Wednesday night, all four battleground state Senate candidates — Ken Paxton, Jon Husted, Michael Whatley, and Mike Collins — made no mention of the Iran war or of Trump’s tariffs.
If Republican frontliners are clear-eyed about their party’s liabilities, Trump seems largely indifferent to them. Historically, presidents have often made an effort to limit election-year price increases — and/or, to reduce the salience of their party’s worst issues. Yet Trump has been doing the very opposite.
In recent weeks, the president has escalated his conflict with Iran and his trade war with US allies, driving up Americans’ costs in the process. And he’s been remarkably frank about his refusal to prioritize affordability.
In his remarks to the convention Wednesday, Trump impersonated a disaffected constituent, saying, “You know, I wish you didn’t do the war in Iran. Gasoline’s up, ba ba ba” — before explaining to this critic that preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon took precedence over their energy costs.
Republicans may still weather a midterm backlash. The party remains narrowly favored to retain the Senate, while gerrymandered maps should limit its losses in the House. But if this year’s “blue wave” proves less than tidal, it will be in spite of Trump’s efforts, not because of them.
The GOP’s very simple problem
The Republican Party’s fundamental problem is simple: Voters’ top concern is the cost of living — and American purchasing power has fallen sharply in 2026, as a direct result of the president’s policies.
In virtually every poll, a plurality of voters name “inflation,” “the cost of living,” or “affordability” as their most important issue. And they are not impressed with Trump’s record on that front. In a recent Ipsos survey, 74 percent of respondents said that their cost of living is “off on the wrong track.” Meanwhile, in Nate Silver’s poll tracker, more than 70 percent of Americans disapprove of Trump’s handling of inflation, up from just 41 percent when he took office.
During his first year in office, Trump could have reasonably argued that voters were giving him a bad rap on the economy. After all, real wages — how much Americans earn per hour, adjusted for inflation — actually rose in 2025, even as disapproval of the president’s economic record surged.
But in February 2026, Trump brought nearly three years of real wage growth to a screeching halt: By launching a war with Iran — and thus, triggering its closure of the Strait of Hormuz — Trump triggered the first sustained decline in Americans’ purchasing power since 2022.
According to an estimate from Brown’s Watson School, the Iran war has cost the average US household more than $780 through elevated energy prices.
Politically, this seems to have made a real difference. At the beginning of March, Trump’s net approval rating on inflation was -28, according to Nate Silver’s polling average; as of this writing, it is -45.9.
At this point, there may be little Trump can do to gain broad public trust on the cost of living. But political science research suggests that economic trends in the runup to Election Day can shift votes at the margin. And precisely because this year’s price spike is largely self-inflicted, Trump has an unusual amount of power to increase affordability before Americans head to the polls. All he’d need to do is reach a ceasefire (or, ideally, peace deal) with Iran.
We know Trump could bring down energy costs by pursuing peace because he already has. Throughout 2026, oil prices have consistently fallen whenever the US-Iran war has cooled off — and risen whenever it has intensified.
When Trump signaled an imminent ceasefire deal in early June, the price of an oil barrel swiftly fell, dropping below $75. Once that ceasefire broke down early the next month, oil prices resumed their climb, until Trump paused US strikes on July 25.
Hostilities resumed over the ensuing months. But Tehran appeared to offer Trump a preelection off-ramp on September 1, when Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said that his country would be willing to restore June’s memorandum of understanding — a deal that had temporarily eased restrictions on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
The Iranian regime’s good faith cannot be assumed. And peace negotiations are doubtlessly complex. At the very least, however, Trump had an opportunity to try to reduce fuel prices ahead of November’s elections earlier this month. Embracing a ceasefire would not have prevented the US from resuming attacks after Election Day (Trump is manifestly comfortable with reneging on agreements with Iran). Nevertheless, Trump opted instead to launch a new round of strikes against Iranian military targets and oil tankers, sending crude prices hurtling past $100 a barrel.
Americans have paid a price for Trump’s trade war
The Iran war has been by far the biggest drag on American living standards since Trump took office. But his trade policies certainly haven’t helped.
Back in May, the Dallas Federal Reserve released an analysis of how Trump’s tariffs had impacted consumer prices. In its report, the bank compared America’s core inflation rate to what that rate would have been, if the US charged no tariffs. The two lines diverged sharply after “Liberation Day,” when Trump imposed large tariffs on nearly all of America’s trade partners.
Of course, Trump backed off his most gargantuan Liberation Day tariffs. And in February, the Supreme Court gave Trump a chance to abandon much of his inflationary trade agenda by ruling that the bulk of his tariffs were unconstitutionally enacted. At that point, he could have insisted that his overturned import taxes had been brilliant, but that the courts had left him no choice but to withdraw them (thereby easing price pressures in an election year). Instead, Trump immediately enacted temporary 10 percent across-the-board tariffs with alternative legal authorities. Then, when those were set to expire in late July, he replaced them with nearly identical levies, now legally justified as a means of combatting forced labor abroad.
More recently, Trump escalated commercial tensions with Canada into an all-out trade war. In late August, Trump imposed a 50 percent tariff on $20 billion worth of Canadian imports, declared that Lake Ontario was now “Lake America,” and threatened to extend that levy to Canadian trucks, cars, and auto parts in the new year. Ottawa hit back with up to 50 percent tariffs on $20 billion in US goods. This week, Trump upped the ante again, announcing outright import bans on some Canadian alcohol, dairy, and motorcycle products.
On Wednesday night, Trump signaled that he’s in no rush to reach a compromise with our neighbors to the north, saying that Canada was “dying to make a deal.”
The trade war with Canada is unlikely to have a huge impact on the American economy nationally. But it will be felt in regions heavily integrated with the Canadian economy, including much of Maine, where Republican Sen. Susan Collins is fighting to hold onto her seat.
And the political costs of Trump’s trade actions may be as much optical as economic. When Trump deliberately increases the price of various imported goods by 50 percent, he sends voters a clear message: The GOP’s leader simply does not care very much about lowering the cost of living.
The connection between tariffs and prices is not lost on voters. In a Guardian poll taken earlier this year, seven in 10 Americans said that the Trump’s tariffs had forced them to pay higher prices.
And even Trump understands that his trade agenda is bad for affordability. While he has been enacting new trade restrictions willy-nilly for months, he did pause plans to dramatically raise ground beef tariffs last month, in order to ease meat costs for consumers. Still, Trump has refused to apply the logic of his hamburger policy to broader realms of international commerce.
Crass pandering has its upsides
On one level, Trump’s deprioritization of his party’s short-term political interests might seem noble. As a general matter, we want presidents to put America’s long-term well-being above immediate electoral considerations. If seeking a ceasefire with Tehran would jeopardize American national security — or if allowing imports of Crown Royal whiskey would condemn our grandchildren to Canadian economic tyranny — then it would be bad for Trump to do those things, just to help Susan Collins.
In reality, however, Trump’s war with Iran doesn’t seem to be furthering any of America’s geopolitical goals. Nor has his trade war been a boon to US industry. Whatever Trump is prioritizing over Americans’ purchasing power and Republicans’ midterm odds, it doesn’t seem to be a robust theory of foreign policy or international economics.
To be sure, Trump has not wholly forsworn pandering to voters’ pocketbook concerns. On Wednesday night, the president promised to deliver a $5,000 check to every American adult, if Republicans retain control of Congress in November. But Trump’s audacious giveaway boasts little support on Capitol Hill, in part because high deficits are already putting upward pressure on inflation and interest rates — yet another cost-of-living issue his own policies have exacerbated.
For now, ordinary shoppers are bearing the brunt of Trump’s eccentric and counterproductive priorities. But come November, Republican battleground candidates may also find themselves paying the price.

All eyes on Nepal's young ex-rapper prime minister after flood disaster
He is the former rapper that rose to become Nepal's prime minister with massive gen Z support.
Now Balendra Shah and his new government are grappling with one of the worst disasters the country has seen.
The 36-year-old, popularly known as Balen, is the world's youngest national leader and was elected just six months ago.
His ongoing response to the crisis that has killed at least 1,410 people and left another 5,651 people missing in Nepal and Tibet is being watched closely.
For some his government has not done enough.
Himal Thakur's mother, father, older sister and older brother were working in Timure, Rasuwa district, when the flood hit.
He said he immediately asked the Nepal Army and local authorities for help, but "everyone I tried to ask for help seemed helpless".
"I got no help from anywhere," he told the ABC from Dhanusa district in Nepal.
Days later, his older sister's employer, Machhapuchchhre Bank, secured a helicopter flight so he could search Timure himself.
Three of his family members are still missing, with the body of a man believed to be his brother found recently.
In March, the 23-year-old flew back from Cambodia, where he was working, to vote for Mr Shah's party, the Rastriya Swatantra Party.
He said the government's handling of the flood response made him "regret voting".
"There is a lot more rescue and relief needed in the hill areas, but it hasn't reached there. People haven't received anything there yet. Most of the relief items seem to only reach as far as Nuwakot and not the epicentre of the flood," he said.
The Nepal government was contacted for comment.
Himal Thakur's family was still missing more than two weeks after the flood hit Nepal. (Supplied)
Nepal's prime minister has experience with disaster recovery, using his structural engineering qualifications to help rebuild homes destroyed in the 2015 earthquake that killed nearly 9,000 people.
But this disaster is different, with Nepal's army still rebuilding roads and installing pre-fabricated bridges supplied by India and China to reconnect communities.
Rescue teams and specialist equipment can only get in to many places once access has been restored.
In a frank admission, Bikram Timilsina, Nepal's minister for information and communication, told DW that "on the very first day, we got a bit confused as to how to deal with the crisis".
"[From the] second day onward, we have been putting all our efforts into swift search, rescue and relief works," he said.
Parts of Sabin Shrestha's childhood town Betrawati has been devastated by the floods.
He said the government mobilised the army, police and private helicopters as quickly as they could, but it should have been more open to outside help.
Sabin Shrestha has been broadly happy with the government's flood response. (Supplied)
The Shah government initially believed its own authorities could respond to the disaster, declining offers of assistance from seven countries including China, the US and India, before later accepting them.
"At the end of the day, the question should not be who is providing the help. The question should be whether that help can save lives," Mr Shrestha said.
Coordination between local governments and the central government could have been better, he said, with experienced community-based groups used to find people in remote areas.
Rebuilding communities destroyed by the flood has been estimated to cost billions of dollars. (Reuters: Tyrone Siu)
Despite the scale of the crisis, Mr Shah has not given an address to the nation.
He waited a week to address Nepal's parliament after the flood, but he posted daily to his millions of followers on Facebook, X and Instagram.
He shunned the mainstream media as a hip-hop artist rapping about corruption and inequality in Nepal, then as the independent mayor of Kathmandu and now as prime minister.
But relying on social media to communicate has seemingly not dampened support for his government.
Shah receives 'outpouring' of trust
More than 13 billion rupees ($123 million) has been donated to the prime minister's disaster relief fund so far, something Kathmandu local Toran Pandit said was a sign the public trusted his government.
"His communication was grounded and empathetic — he treated the disaster like a shared national problem rather than just a localised issue, which clearly resonated because people and businesses immediately stepped forward to donate directly to the government's relief fund," he said.
"The way he managed the sheer scale of the situation on the ground, while also pivoting to stand up for Nepal on the global climate stage, really earns my respect. It makes me feel good about backing his team."
Balendra Shah was heavily backed by young people in Nepal. (Reuters: Adnan Abidi, file)
Kathmandu local Sujata Sharma agreed.
"Having to deal with a catastrophic disaster like this within six months of the tenure could have been a disaster in itself," she said.
Professor Krishna Shrestha, global development expert at the University of New South Wales, told the ABC that it was a unique moment in Nepali politics because there was "an outpouring of trust" in the national government.
Sujata Sharma says the government did well considering the scale of the crisis. (Supplied)
"People are not really questioning whether this money will be spent and how it will be spent," he said.
He said the reaction was very different to the 2015 earthquake, because of distrust in the political establishment and deep concerns about corruption.
But not all supporters are happy with Mr Shah's style.
PM skips gen Z vigil
Last Tuesday marked one year since Nepali security forces opened fire on protesters in Kathmandu, killing 76 people.
Young people heavily backed Mr Shah in the first election after the uprising, believing in his anti-establishment and anti-corruption messages.
However, the prime minister did not attend Tuesday's memorial, with other government ministers attending instead.
Pratish Shrestha represented injured protesters at the vigil and said the government could not forget them, or the promises they made about jobs, healthcare and transparency.
"The government is sitting in those chairs because of our blood, sweat and sacrifice," the Kathmandu Post reported him as saying.
"Forgetting us is like cutting off your own roots."
Professor Shrestha said not attending could be a sign of an inexperienced government, but ultimately Mr Shah's response to the floods would define his prime ministership.
"At the moment, it is more gung-ho, this is the action-oriented leadership, regardless of what is happening in the public. I think this can make him isolated and increasingly seen negatively by the public down the track if it's continued," he said.
Mr Shah took to X mark his respects on Tuesday, saying that he hoped the anniversary would "inspire us all to move forward towards building a fair, transparent, and opportunity-filled Nepal".
Several days after the flood, Himal Thakur received a call from a police officer telling him they had found his brother's ID card on a body.
Mr Thakur could not identify the body, and the hospital would not release it because of questions over DNA test results, delaying Mr Thakur's wish to give his brother traditional burial rites.
That was not his only concern.
"There are a lot of helpless people, including me. I have my younger sister, my brother's son and my sister-in-law. I am still young and don't feel grown up myself, so I have no idea how I am going to look after them," he said.
"I can't even expect too much from the government because I'm not sure how many people they can look after. There are so many people who need help."
Translation by Ram Kandel

Early backer Accel India yesterday sold 27 Lakh shares of logistics giant BlackBuck via an open-market transaction for ₹155.5 Cr. As per NSE data, Accel sold the shares at ₹576.05 apiece to rake in the amount. The VC giant offloaded nearly 1.5% of its stake in the logistics giant at a discount of 8.4% to the stock’s last closing price on Friday. The shares that flooded the market were lapped up by asset management company (AMC) Abakkus Investment Managers. Accel, via its affiliate Accel India IV (Mauritius) held a 7.17% stake in the logistics company at the end of June 2026. The block deal comes as investors look to book profits amid a healthy uptick in BlackBuck shares in recent months. While the stock has surged nearly 18% in the past three months, it is down 7.6% on a year-to-date (YTD) basis. The rebound in its stock price has come on the back of its strong financial and operational performance. BlackBuck’s net profit jumped 25% to ₹42.2 Cr in the first quarter (Q1) of the fiscal year 2026-27 (FY27) from ₹33.7 Cr a year earlier. Meanwhile, revenue from operations also zoomed 42% YoY and 10% QoQ to ₹204.2 Cr in the quarter under review. Founded in 2015 by Rajesh Kumar Naidu Yabaji, Chanakya Hridaya and Ramasubramanian Balasubramaniam, BlackBuck operates an online B2B marketplace for inter-city full truck load (FTL) transportation. It also offers telematics solutions and vehicle financing services to truck operators in the country. Backed by the likes of Accel India, Flipkart’s subsidiary Quickroutes and Peak XV Partners, the startup claims to have served 8.83 Lakh customers in Q1 FY27, while monthly transacting customers, using two or more services, rose 20% YoY to 4.6 Lakh. Shares of BlackBuck closed Friday’s trading session 7.46% higher at ₹629.05 on the BSE.

Brics calls for just, equitable energy transition, slams EU carbon border tax
The Brics declaration rejected the European Union’s carbon border adjustment mechanism, describing it as a protectionist hurdle for emerging economies.
Underlining that energy security was essential for economic growth, Brics member states on Saturday declared that while fossil fuels would continue to play a crucial role in emerging and developing nations, energy transitions must be “just, orderly, and equitable.”
In their New Delhi summit declaration, the leaders also launched a sharp critique against unilateral trade-restrictive measures, explicitly rejecting the European Union’s carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM), which they said was a protectionist hurdle for emerging economies.
“We oppose unilateral, punitive, discriminatory and protectionist measures that are not in line with international law, such as carbon border adjustment mechanisms, and express concern that such measures undermine efforts by countries, specifically the developing countries, aimed at addressing the adverse impacts of climate change, increasing adaptive capacity and resilience,” the declaration issued on Saturday said.
Deep Dive
CABM, implemented on January 1, 2026, enforces a carbon pricing policy aimed at equalising carbon costs between domestic and imported goods, effectively placing a pollution tax on certain energy-intensive imports entering the bloc.
Acknowledging growing disasters, including those linked to climate change, the countries reaffirmed their commitment to Brics cooperation to improve national disaster risk reduction systems while mobilising accessible, predictable and adequate financing.
“In this context, we welcome the Brics Guidelines for Disaster Management Early Warning Data Integration and the Brics Voluntary Principles for Climate-Resilient Urban Infrastructure,” the declaration said, acknowledging the role of the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure (CDRI) as an international partnership for supporting member and partner countries in integrating resilience.
“We also underscore the importance of enhancing early warning systems and risk-informed planning to strengthen preparedness and response capacities,” it said.
It also recognised the disproportionate burden climate finance imposes across countries, stating the report “Role of Central Banks towards optimising Sustainable and Green Finance, including Adaptation” looks at making climate finance more bankable.
The Brics grouping further said it remains united in achieving goals under the Paris Agreement.
“This includes its provisions related to mitigation, adaptation, loss and damage and the provision of means of implementation to developing countries, reflecting equity and the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities, in light of different national circumstances. We also recognise that high debt burdens further constrain climate and development investment in many developing countries and call for coordinated international action to enhance debt sustainability, expand fiscal space, and support sustainable development and climate financing,” the statement said, commending the ‘successful’ conclusion of the Brazilian COP30 presidency and expressing support for Ethiopia’s UNFCCC COP32 presidency.
Amid growing global volatility in the energy sector, the declaration called for enhanced energy security—by ensuring energy market stability and maintaining uninterrupted flows of energy from diverse sources, strengthening value chains, and ensuring the resilience and protection of critical energy infrastructure, including cross-border infrastructure.
“We underscore the importance of balanced and diversified energy mixes reflecting national circumstances and recognise that the widest variety of energy sources and technologies, including but not limited to renewable energy, bioenergy, fossil fuels, nuclear energy, hydropower, hydrogen, low-carbon technologies, energy storage technologies, which play an important role in achieving the SDGs and energy security. We underscore the role of all available energy sources, resilient energy supply chains and enhanced cooperation among Brics countries through deliberations in the energy track,” it added.
The declaration further highlighted the potential of the ‘Brics Climate Research Platform’ and the ‘Brics Laboratory for Trade, Climate Change and Sustainable Development’ – for promoting climate action and building resilience in the Brics Member Countries. “We look forward to their further development,” the declaration said.
Li Shuo, Director, China Climate Hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute, said the declaration shows Brics is determined to chart its own course on climate and energy -- one that emphasises the alignment of development and decarbonization rather than treating them as competing priorities.
“The bloc’s explicit rejection of carbon border taxes, alongside its insistence that fossil fuels will remain part of the energy mix for emerging economies, signals that these leading Global South countries intend to define the terms of their own energy transition rather than have them imposed by others,” he said.
