In Summary
- The Live 780NC are the latest headphones in JBL’s premium mid-segment Live series of wireless ANC headphones.
- Featuring a different design from their predecessors as well as some flashy colors, the JBL Live 780NC boast good mainstream sound as well as a number of smart features.
- Priced officially at Rs 15,999 (but available at lower prices), the JBL Live 780NC are one of the best pairs of headphones one can get for about Rs 15,000 in the Indian market.
They let you not only pump up the bass or turn up the treble of the audio playing on them but can also add bass and treble to your voice and the person you are talking to during phone calls. They come with good ANC that adjusts itself to your surroundings and come with very good battery life. Get them in orange, and you can be assured of being the center of attention in every room. All this at a price of USD 199/Rs 15,999. But can these features (and many others) and that price tag help the JBL Live 780NC become the perfect headphones for those who want a lot of sound and smarts, without parting with a truly premium price?
Table of Contents
JBL Live 780NC Looks: Comfortable and delightfully colorful
The JBL Live 780NC can look smart or spectacular depending on the shade you choose. We got the very elegant Black ones, which are at home everywhere, from cafes to campuses to corporate offices, but the Purple, Green, or Orange will definitely turn heads, thanks to their unusually bright shades. They follow the classic over-ear headphone design, with a band connecting two earcups, but look different from their predecessors, the Live 770NC.
The headband of the Live 770NC was of the same thickness throughout, whereas the band of the Live 780NC becomes thinner as it nears the earcups, giving it a sleeker and more contemporary look. There is plenty of cushioning on the earpads as well as the headband. There’s plenty of JBL branding too, which appears on the earcups and headband, but as the lettering is in the same color as the headphones, it does not get overwhelming. The earcups have left and right printed inside them, which is always better than having tiny letters on the frame.
The right earcup has the sliding on/off and connectivity button, as well as a button for switching between ANC and Ambient Aware mode, as well as a Type-C port. The volume controls are on the left earcup. The outer part of the right earcup is also a touch panel. There is no 3.5 mm audio jack, but a Type-C to 3.5 mm cable in the box lets one use the headphones with a device with a 3.5 mm audio jack.
The headphones are mostly made of plastic but have metal hinges, and best of all, fold all the way inwards, making them very easy to bunch up and carry. There is a rather basic cloth bag in the box, which is not as good as a case but should suffice for most of us. At 260 grams, the JBL Live 780NC are not exactly super light (the Sony WH-CH 720N are the bosses there at 192 grams), but not uncomfortably heavy either. We have worn them for 3-4 hours without ever feeling too burdened. All the padding in the ear cushions and headband makes them very comfortable to wear, and the clamping force is just right – tight enough to let us move our head without making the headphones wobble, and loose enough to never make us feel squeezed in the head.
The JBL 780NC have a very solid and substantial feel to them. But they come with no dust or water resistance, so we would advise due caution while using them in the gym or using them for running sessions.
JBL Live 780NC Specs and Features: An impressive feature list
The JBL Live 780NC come with a very good spec and feature lineup. Sound is handled by 40 mm drivers, which deliver the famous mainstream JBL Signature Sound. Also on board are support for high-quality LDAC, adaptive ANC, six microphones (most headphones in this price have four), spatial audio, and a number of smart features, such as ear detection (audio pauses when you remove the headphones) and an AI-trained algorithm for clearer calls.
On the connectivity front, they come with Bluetooth 6.0, multi-point connectivity, and support for Auracast (so one can listen to public broadcasts and announcements wirelessly). They also boast a battery life of 80 hours (without ANC) and support fast charging. There is no charging cable in the box, though one does get a Type-C to 3.5 mm cable and a basic cloth carry bag. On the software side, the headphones work with the JBL Headphones companion app, which gives one access to a number of features as well as detailed equalizers and regular software updates. For their price, the JBL Live 780NC are pretty well stacked in the spec and feature department.
JBL Live 780NC Controls and Interface: Buttons for some, touch for others
Connecting the JBL 780NC is as simple as putting them in pairing mode (just slide the on/off button towards the Bluetooth icon) and selecting them on the other device’s Bluetooth device list. To experience all their features, however, one should also connect them via the JBL Headphones app, which is available for both iOS and Android. While connecting the headphones is simple, the app takes some time to recognize them every time it connects to them, which can be a little irritating.
The JBL Live 780NC controls are a blend of physical buttons and touch, although the touch works only on the right earcup. A single tap on the earcup pauses audio and also resumes playing it; a double tap takes one to the next track; a triple tap takes one to the previous track, while tapping and holding accesses the voice assistant. A double tap can also enable one to take or end a call, while tapping and holding rejects an incoming call. One can customize the touch controls to an extent, and add options to access equalizer settings and spatial audio, although there is no way to access ANC or volumes through touch – those are accessed through buttons on the earcups.
The combination of touch and buttons controls works well enough, once one gets the hang of them – we kept forgetting that touch worked only on the right earcup, and ended up tapping the left one initially, out of habit.
JBL Live 780NC Performance: Super audio, decent ANC and great smart touches
Most users will love the warm and detailed sound that the JBL Live 780NC deliver. While there is an emphasis on bass, it does not overwhelm the vocals. Those who want a sharper sound can tweak the equalizer in the app (move it to ‘Jazz,’ we suggest) to enhance treble, but most users will love the sound of these headphones right out of the box. Enabling spatial audio makes the sound a little more airy, although the absence of head tracking gives one much more of a “sitting in a room with the music” feels. There are three kinds of spatial audio – Movie, Music and Game – and although there is not much difference between Movie and Game, Music is rather different and seems to add slightly more detail to the sound. One can also use the Person-fi feature to let the app personalize a sound signature for it, although we were not too convinced by it.
The app allows one to tweak the sound significantly. LE Audio makes a huge difference to audio quality whenever supported (although turning it on and off requires restarting the app), adding greater detail and depth to sound. One can also choose from six equalizer settings – a relatively plain Studio, a thump-friendly Bass, a rumbling Club, a boosted bass Extreme Bass, a mids-stressing Vocal, and a treble-oriented Jazz. There is also the option to completely come up with one’s own EQ setting under the My EQ option. Most mainstream users will prefer the Bass setting, while purists will like either Studio or Jazz. One can also adjust the balance of sound between the right and left earcups, although we found no reason to do so.
The JBL Live 780NC are perfect for mainstream audio, whether one wants to listen to pop, trance or rock, or watch a film, play games or just lend an ear to podcasts. At their price, they are perhaps the best-sounding wireless ANC headphones out there.
JBL Live 780NC ANC and calls: Super sound over calls, decent sounds of silence
The JBL Live 780NC come with adaptive ANC. You can either specify the level of ANC you want using a slider, or enable Adaptive ANC and let the headphones decide the level. We suggest simply keeping it at maximum. Noise canceling on the headphones is good for their price. Of course, one does not get the kind of ANC that comes on Sony and Bose flagships; the Live 780NC do enough to dull a lot of the traffic sound, kill the hum of the Metro, and can even make a noisy cafe a little quieter.
Call quality is where the Live 780NC shine. Not only do they handle calls very well, with very good levels of clarity, but the app even lets you adjust the tone of the person you are speaking to and your own voice as well. You can actually add more bass or treble to both sides of the conversation on the JBL Live 780NC. The headphones are also able to keep out a fair bit of the ambient noise – we have used them on auto rickshaw rides, with the person we are speaking to not even realizing that we are in the midst of noisy traffic. That AI algorithm for clear calls definitely helps.
JBL Live 780NC Battery life: Charge them once a week only!
JBL claims that the headphones come with 80 hours of battery life without ANC and 50 hours with ANC. We mostly used them with ANC – it does not affect audio quality, apart from making it a little more bass-y – and got a comfortable 40-45 hours of battery life (we admit to hearing them at slightly higher volumes). In practical terms, charging them once easily got us through close to a week of hectic use, where we used them for everything from making calls to listening to music to watching videos, shorts, and reels to playing games. That makes them great daily drivers.
The headphones charge off their USB Type-C port and take about two hours to charge from empty to full. They also come with a fast-charging function that gave us about four hours of audio listening after being charged for five minutes. One can tweak the power settings for the headphones to switch off automatically after 30 minutes, an hour, or two hours, to further conserve power. There is no charging cable in the box, but any Type-C charging cable should work just fine with it.
JBL Live 780NC Review Verdict: In a zone of their own in the Rs 15,000 segment
The headphones are priced at Rs 15,999, but are often available at lower prices (they are available on Amazon India at Rs 14,999 even as this is being written). Their closest competitors are the Sony ULT Wear, which are now available at close to Rs 15,000 but have a very bass-centric sound. The ULT Wear have better ANC than the Live 780NC, but the Live 780NC beat them easily in terms of call handling. offer almost double the battery life and also have a more elegant and foldable design.

Welcome to The Midterms, Actually. Every week I’ll be writing about two things: one big idea or trend I see forming across the 2026 primaries, and one thing I’m hearing from a voice on the ground. You can sign up here to get it in your inbox every week. Let’s get into it.
The GOP midterms strategy is Trump and a prayer
What we learned from the first day of the Republican convention in Dallas.
One big idea: What are Republicans actually running on?
The first-of-its-kind Republican midterms convention began in the same vein as President Donald Trump’s second term: open grift. The president announced a pledge to give every American $5,000 if Republicans win the House and the Senate — part of what he’s calling a new dividend for American voters, and what some Democrats are calling an attempted bribe.
Obviously, there are lots of questions about Trump’s announcement: Who will pay for the $1 trillion-plus dividend? Taxpayers. Could this even happen without congressional approval? Probably not. Why not just vote on it now, while Republicans control Congress? It would likely fail.
But I think the pronouncement — and the GOP convention broadly — is best understood as a proxy for the Republican message in the midterm elections, not a policy roadmap for what Trump would do if Republicans maintained control of the House and Senate.
So what can we actually glean from the GOP’s two-day bonanza in Dallas, and how does the message they were offering on that made-for-TV platform match up with the message they’ve delivered on the campaign trail? I took a close look at the convention speeches on Wednesday and Thursday, dug through our America, Actually reporting focusing on Republican voters and their candidates, and pulled together some trends that help explain the GOP strategy for defying the odds (and the polling) come Election Day.
1. Republicans are mostly in hiding — One reason Trump’s midterm convention sticks out in this year’s landscape: It’s one of the rare places Republicans will campaign out loud. Congressional candidates, even in battleground House districts, have rarely held public events or town halls this year. And as Trump’s unpopularity has continued to grow, driven by rising gas prices and an unpopular war with Iran, it’s not like the GOP has responded by mounting a defense of its leader. They’ve mostly gone AWOL, a result of the electoral pickle the president has put them in.
Trump is undoubtedly still the most powerful figure within the party, particularly among the Republican base, but Trump is also the biggest motivator for the Democratic base, and is increasingly off-putting to independent voters, who backed him in 2024. His approval has sunk to 33 percent in one recent Reuters/Ipsos poll, the lowest of his presidency, and that same poll found Democrats markedly more fired up for the midterms than Republicans — an enthusiasm gap that’s poison for the party in power. The independents who put him over the top have soured as the war drags on: a UMass poll found more than two-thirds disapprove of his handling of Iran nationally, and four in five say the war has driven up their gas and food prices.
So when Trump tells voters at the GOP midterm convention to “pretend that he’s on the ballot” and turn out in November, I think his opponents listen with glee. Democrats are in the position they’re in because of a brewing electoral backlash to Trump — and the reason Republicans are so hard to find on the campaign trail is that they sense that same backlash is brewing, too. Check out what Ted Cruz said on The View this week: “The big open question is, do Republicans show up?” Cruz asked. “If we stay home, there’s a blue wave.”
2. Even Trump is on the defensive — It’s rare to see Trump acknowledge any semblance of failure, but he came close during his speech during the convention’s first night. Trump was clearly on the defensive throughout his remarks: he sought to make the case for his (unpopular) tariff policy, he defended the (deeply unpopular) Iran war but without the usual bluster, and he acknowledged that gas prices may not fall until after Election Day. Last year, he predicted gas prices would soon hit $2 a gallon; this week he’s asking for still more patience after they hit a record $4.15 on Labor Day. From his speech:
“You know, it happens to me all the time. Guys come up, ‘You know, I wish you didn’t do the war in Iran, gasoline’s up, ba, ba, ba.’ And I say, ‘Well, let me ask you…let me ask you one question. Can Iran have a nuclear weapon?’ ‘Absolutely not.’ ‘Well, then I’m right, then I win, okay?’”
But it’s worth remembering that “be patient” is a controversial message even among Republican voters. When our America, Actually team spent a day outside gas stations in Allentown this summer — deep in PA-7, one of the most contested House districts in the country (watch the episode) — we heard a clean split. There were some Republicans willing to eat the higher price in service of Trump’s war:
“Yes, because our president is actually doing something about Iran. He’s not sugarcoating it. It’s something we need to do, and in the long run it’s gonna be better for everybody.”
And there were other Republicans who voted for Trump and are furious: “I voted for him with his promises to the American people…and I think he’s let us down.”
Another put the broken promise plainly: “I blame the president because he indicated to us he’s gonna drop all these costs. I know it can’t happen overnight, but when is it gonna happen? It’s outrageous.”
The message now is to wait until after the election. A lot of the president’s own voters at the pump aren’t sure they can.
3. Notice the candidates who weren’t there — Maybe the most revealing thing about Trump’s convention was the guest list, or more notably, the no-shows. MAGA celebrities who owe their careers to Trump packed the stage, but not a lot of the Republicans who are actually on the ballot in places they must win. Notable absences include candidates like John Sununu in New Hampshire and Susan Collins in Maine, and various congressional candidates from battleground races. And while their political calculus may be obvious — they want to avoid a Dallas-with-Trump photo op that ends up in a challenger’s attack ad — it reflects the “win by hiding” strategy that candidates not named Vivek Ramaswamy seem to be deploying.
Here’s the play in a nutshell: keep enough distance from Trump to maintain credibility and independence, but rely on Trump to raise money, drive up Republican turnout, and savagely attack Democratic opponents.
When conservative activist CJ Pearson came on our show, he insisted the GOP doesn’t have an electability problem at all — voters will see Democrats as too radical on topics like socialism and transgender women in sports, which came up repeatedly in the convention, and Republicans can still find ways to address affordability concerns. “These are 80/20 issues,” he said. ”And so I actually really like our odds here…we’re going to overperform. The Senate, we’re gonna hold onto. The House will be a dogfight, but I like our chances.” He even predicted this exact week, telling me the party would “see a change in his messaging and a reset at the midterm convention in Dallas,” after which “you’ll see those numbers start to change.” Whether Dallas actually delivered that reset — or just a $5,000 bribe and a defensive Trump — is, generously, an open question. And the attendance sheet suggests some of Pearson’s own party’s candidates aren’t waiting around to find out.
4. The JD Vance tightrope — One person who doesn’t have the benefit of keeping distance from Trump is JD Vance, his vice president and the presumed GOP frontrunner for the 2028 presidential nomination. He’s close to right-wing voices who have soured on Trump, and has to worry about voters longer than the president will have to, and the Iran war, tariffs, and Trump’s promises all present conflicts for him. Just last week, he took heat from prominent voices in Trump’s coalition for his refusal to disavow Tucker Carlson, the podcast host and former TV anchor who’s become a vocal critic of the Israeli government and Trump’s second-term agenda.
Looking ahead to his speech tonight, I’ll be watching how carefully he handles Trump’s tariffs, the Iran war, and gas prices. He’s tried to strike a more empathetic note on the economy than Trump, who has described talk of an affordability crisis as a made-up narrative to hurt him politically that — to the extent it was real — was President Joe Biden’s fault anyway. “They caused [it], but we’re fixing it,” the president said Wednesday.
Vance says he won’t “sit down” with Trump to discuss his 2028 plans until after the midterms, but Trump is not the kind of person who seems likely to give his successor a lot of room to run away from his record.
What I’m hearing
This week I talked to Charlotte Matherly, a reporter at the Concord Monitor who has been following the underdiscussed New Hampshire Senate race. New Hampshire is one of the Democrats’ must-win states to take back the Senate, but there’s been some concern that Republican candidate John Sununu — a former New Hampshire senator with a long family legacy in the state — could give Democratic nominee Rep. Chris Pappas deep problems. I talked to Matherly about lessons from the state’s primary and what to expect in the general election.
So, the New Hampshire primary just happened — what were the takeaways? And why has this race gone under the radar?
With the progressive versus moderate conversation happening nationally, that was my biggest question heading into Tuesday. Would we see that progressive wave or ripple or whatever you want to call it here too? Because we did have a progressive candidate [Karishma Manzur] run against Chris Pappas, who really focused on humanitarianism and ending what she saw as US complicity in foreign wars.
Voters who liked her were really passionate about her, but in the end, I think people just wanted to vote for what they know, and [Pappas] was already in Congress. The progressive wave that we’ve seen across the country has not necessarily translated here.
Why do you think New Hampshire has stood apart from the national progressive wave?
To give you context for New Hampshire politics, it’s always kind of different from the national electorate. We’re a true purple state — independents are the largest voting bloc here. But there are some quirks. Like, for the past 20 years, except for a few exceptions, voters tend to send Republicans to the state legislature, but usually vote for Democrats when it comes to Congress or presidential elections. So splitting your ticket is really common here. And I hear from people every time I go out to the polls that someone has switched their party in the past few years, or they fall back and forth. So it’s really hard to tell where the partisan lines fall here.
How has the Republican candidate, John Sununu, handled Donald Trump’s popularity?
Years ago [in 2024], Sununu actually penned an op-ed calling Donald Trump a “loser.” And there’s been some bite from the party about that. But Trump actually ended up endorsing him, and he’s also shared the backing of powerful fundraisers and a lot of conservative organizations hoping to flip the seat red. But still, Sununu is trying to emphasize his independence from the administration. He’s saying he’s not worried about currying favor or anything like that, but he hasn’t really put too many policy differences between himself and Trump.
One example that I can think of is that he said he opposed the [reported $300 billion] included in Trump’s deal with Iran that was earmarked for reconstruction. He had said he didn’t think that the US should provide any money for reconstruction. And so there’s been a few things like that that he has tried to sort of strike out on his own from the president.

A four-year-old child has died in a house fire in central western New South Wales.
Fire crews were called to the home in Woodstock, about 20 kilometres north-east of Cowra just before 3pm today.
They arrived to find the property well alight.

‘Here to do politics on corpses’: Abhijeet Dipke heckled by group of influencers in MP's Balaghat
Dipke visited Adori, Korka and Bondari villages to meet the families of tribal children who allegedly died due to infectious diseases.
Cockroach Janta Party founder Abhijeet Dipke was allegedly heckled by a group of people who appeared to be social media influencers or content creators during his visit to Madhya Pradesh's Balaghat district on Saturday.
Dipke visited Adori, Korka and Bondari villages to meet the families of tribal children who allegedly died due to infectious diseases and to gather information about local healthcare facilities, news agency PTI reported.
A viral video showed a woman 'influencer' sticking a mic in Dipke's face as he was driving away in a car, and asking him if he had come there to "do politics on corpses" and why he was visiting the area so late.
Dipke was heard saying he apologised for visiting the area late.
The woman was also heard saying, "A good road has been constructed here. Can't you see it?"
As the situation escalated, CJP workers accompanying Dipke put him in another car and took him away.
As he left, the woman was heard saying "he ran away, he ran away."
Local journalists said they were surprised to see this group of social media influencers from outside turning up in the remote village, and wondered if they had been sent by someone to disrupt the CJP founder's visit.
Earlier this week, the Jabalpur bench of the Madhya Pradesh High Court sought a response from the state government over the deaths of more than 30 children in the region. The division bench of Acting Chief Justice Vivek Rusia and Justice Pradeep Mittal issued notices to the state Health Department, Women and Child Development Department, Balaghat collector and others while hearing a public interest litigation.
The PIL alleged that children were not receiving adequate treatment and that around 400 children were being treated at a hospital with a capacity of 50 beds.

A Quarter Century of Pain
After 9/11, the U.S. government was over-focused on fighting terrorism, losing sight of other threats. Americans are still living with the consequences.
This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here.
Like most Americans, I spent September 11, 2001, filled with both rage and dread. I wanted the United States to find and kill whoever had planned this attack on my country. I knew little about al-Qaeda, but whoever did this, I thought, must pay. As the shock of that day wore off, I began to wonder, as so many others did in America and around the world, Now what?
Saying this even 25 years later seems uncharitable, but after the attacks of 9/11, many Americans, and their government, panicked. Worse, the United States institutionalized this panic in the form of new priorities, new programs, and new agencies, so that even when the fear subsided, the intemperate policies driven by that fear remained. Over the next quarter century, America would spend trillions of dollars, pass draconian laws, create a behemoth of a new Cabinet department, militarize law enforcement, and embark on two major military campaigns.
These measures were taken because after 9/11, everything became terrorism. Everything, as if we all now agreed that we could push aside all the other trouble in the world because we had finally found the Worst Thing Ever. I say this as a criticism, but I was not exempt from the emotions and the intellectual detours they produced in the moment. And I should have known better: I had spent most of my career studying long-standing problems of security and international relations. Even so, I was one of the millions of Americans and others who believed that the world after 9/11 had changed forever. We were wrong.
In the first days after the attack, the United States acted wisely. Rather than run off on some half-baked crusade—that part would come later—American leaders vowed to bring the terrorists to justice. George W. Bush, in a speech to Congress the week after the attacks, warned that every nation in the world “now has a decision to make. Either you are with us, or you are with the terrorists.” Some people were offended by that, but not me; I cheered the president’s commitment.
As much as I liked Bush’s statements, I was even more impressed by how little else the administration was saying about its plans. Silence can be ominous and intimidating, and I could see its impact on both friends and opponents when I went to the United Kingdom and Russia less than a month after 9/11. (I was researching a book on the Cold War that now seemed less important than current events.) In London, you could almost feel people holding their breath while waiting for the inevitable U.S. strikes in Afghanistan. “So is it tonight, then?” a cabbie asked me and my wife one evening, as if every American knew Bush’s timetable.
The reaction in Moscow was somewhat different. A Russian academic colleague greeted me with condolences, and said: “Now you know how we feel.” He meant the fear that Russians lived with after suffering attacks from Chechen terrorists for years before 9/11. As we strolled through Moscow, we watched uniformed street cops, clearly on heightened alert, as they stopped young men with dark skin (to Russians, an indication of origins in the Caucasus or Central Asia) and asked them for their papers and identification. Russian police are hardly charming even on a good day, and I winced at the obvious profiling. And yet, seeing the local Moscow fuzz push these guys around, I found myself making excuses for the police. I knew what Russia had been through, and I knew that Ground Zero back home was still smoking.
And, frankly, I was blinded by both patriotic pride and righteous anger. Here I was, an American in Russia, commiserating with our former enemies. (Vladimir Putin had been the first to call Bush with an offer to help, a cagey move from the Kremlin leader.) Maybe the world really was different now. Besides, we Americans were already engaging in similar heavy-handed tactics back home.
Still, I started to feel uneasy over the next several months about the strengthening consensus that the hijackers were geniuses and that al-Qaeda was now a significant threat to the entire West. After 9/11, I certainly didn’t doubt that terrorists could inflict massive damage—more than once, I felt nervous walking around Manhattan and London and Moscow in the 2000s—but too many nations, including my own, seemed to be losing all sense of perspective about the enemy.
I recall, for example, informally debating a well-known security scholar in the greenroom after we’d appeared on television together. I said: In the end, all that happened was that 19 men with box cutters hijacked some planes. You and I could have done this with a few classes of our graduate students.
He looked at me as if I’d said that the Green Berets or the 82nd Airborne were just a bunch of wimps.
The deeply flawed assumption that terrorists were 10 feet tall and that 9/11 represented a permanent change in planetary politics drove a frenzy that spread quickly throughout every level of the U.S. government. Not only did everything become terrorism, but every organization also became obsessed with its own role in anti-terrorism. If you worked in national defense and you still cared about nuclear proliferation, the security implications of climate change, Chinese expansionism, or even, say, pandemics—well, those were all worthy issues, of course, but what had you done to stop terrorists lately?
At the Naval War College (where I became the chair of the strategy and policy department shortly after 9/11), we felt this pressure when we started getting calls from Washington that bordered on the ridiculous. After years of ignoring education in regional studies and foreign languages, the Pentagon was now asking us if we could turn some of our students into Middle East experts practically overnight.
We were asked, for example, if we had courses in Arab and Islamic studies; no, we answered, not least because the Navy had always made it difficult to hire scholars who specialize in such things. Well, could the War College perhaps start teaching students Arabic—and maybe Farsi? Again, we reminded the Pentagon that we have the students for only 10 months, and we had no faculty, time, or language labs to do such a thing.
Something deeper, however, was happening in Washington and in other capitals around the world. The shock of 9/11 convinced Americans (and others) that three separate threats—rogue states, nuclear proliferation, and terrorism—were now all the same threat, a single existential danger that had to be eliminated by embarking on war rather than waiting to be struck. America would now reorder the world and stomp out rogue states before they could join forces with terrorists and hand them chemical, biological, or nuclear weapons.
And that meant going to Iraq.
Operation Iraqi Freedom has been relitigated endlessly, and I don’t need to trudge around that track again. As I wrote on that war’s 20th anniversary, I supported the invasion of Iraq; I believed, for many reasons, that removing Saddam Hussein from power was a just cause. I now regret that support because of the way the war was executed.
The Bush administration did not discourage people from seeing a connection between 9/11 and Iraq, but the true link between them was that the occupation of Iraq sprang from the same belief that drove everything after 9/11: The old world was gone, and it was up to the United States and the other allied great powers to shape the new one. As then–U.K. Prime Minister Tony Blair put it while defending the Iraq War in 2004: “This is not a time to err on the side of caution; not a time to weigh the risks to an infinite balance; not a time for the cynicism of the worldly wise who favor playing it long.” The idea that democracies could not be safe in a world of rogue states, terrorists, and unconstrained nuclear proliferation was not new, but 9/11 supercharged this fear, and pushed all other dangers into the shadows.
We are now living with the consequences of this panic and tunnel vision. The same threats that existed before 2001 remain with us, even though American leaders stopped paying attention to them for too long because of the inherently doomed attempt to reduce the threat of terrorism to zero.
First and foremost, we all still live with the only danger that qualifies as existential: nuclear war. (Nuclear terrorism might actually change the global order to the extent that we mistakenly thought 9/11 had, especially if multiple weapons were detonated in major cities. But even that horrible eventuality would not threaten America’s existence or the survival of humanity.) Nuclear weapons, and the means to deliver them, are now in the hands of one of the most dangerous regimes on Earth: North Korea. The United States, meanwhile, has trashed multiple agreements that made the world safer, including one that eliminated an entire class of nuclear arms. India and Pakistan have come perilously close to all-out conflict. Nuclear-armed Russia is perpetrating the largest war in Europe since World War II.
Another threat—one that makes global war more likely—is a direct outcome of 9/11. After the attacks in New York and Virginia, the United States led the way in legitimizing the notion that powerful states should simply squash any possible threats at will, by striking first, striking hard, and letting history sort it out later. (This is also called preventive war; it is an old idea, and rarely a good one.) When the Americans expanded the war against terrorists in Afghanistan to a war against a rogue regime in Iraq in 2003, they were arguing that some situations are simply too dangerous to tolerate, and that therefore states have the right to eradicate them before they ripen into an actual attack.
The Russians, predictably enough, have cynically adopted this concept with gusto as a rationalization for their wars against their neighbors over the past two decades. And now the Trump administration has used this dangerous excuse for its various military adventures around the world, including the war in Iran.
I grieve over one other aspect of the global War on Terror that is still with us. During the Cold War, Americans (mostly) managed to avoid becoming the thing we were fighting against. Western nations defeated the Soviet empire without losing their democracies. But after 9/11, rendition and torture—excuse me, “enhanced interrogations”—and other inhumane practices became policy. The legislature of a free nation granted its government massive, unaccountable powers in the Patriot Act. The horribly named Department of Homeland Security has metastasized into a gigantic boondoggle that weighs in on everything from floods in Vermont to the safe way to fry turkeys. Osama bin Laden has been dead for 15 years, but the damage to civil liberties and the budget to fund more terrible ideas remain.
Americans have for too long resisted the depressing fact that wars, dictatorships, terrorists, and other threats that existed before 2001 cannot be eradicated forever. Acknowledging that reality need not lead to pessimism. If the nuclear-armed nations refrain from destroying the planet—a big if—a strong and vibrant democratic America can survive, and even manage, these and other perils. During the Cold War, Americans learned that the innate strength of their political system and their faith in liberal democracy allowed them to live, and thrive, even in the face of an existentially dangerous enemy. Regaining that self-confidence, and renewing that faith in our principles, are the first steps toward undoing the panic that seized us after 9/11.

BRICS summit 2026 is currently underway in New Delhi with the attendance of several world leaders. Amid several glimpses from the global event online, one has caught netizens' attention, claiming PM Narendra Modi might have gifted his own portrait to Chinese President Xi Jinping. Xi Jinping reached India on Saturday. His attendance at the BRICS Summit in New Delhi is special primarily. It is his first visit to India in seven years, hinting at a major diplomatic thaw after the 2020 clash in the Galwan Valley of Ladakh. A photo of PM Modi and President Xi Jinping has now gone viral. In it, the PM and the Chinese Leader are seen holding a portrait of the former. Quick answers to key questions The viral claim suggested that PM Modi gifted a portrait of himself to China's President Xi Jinping during the BRICS Summit 2026. However, this was proven false as the image dates back to the 2019 Mahabalipuram Summit. Xi Jinping's attendance is significant as it marks his first visit to India in seven years, indicating a potential diplomatic thaw following previous clashes between India and China. The Press Information Bureau clarified that the porcelain memento featuring PM Modi's image was actually gifted to him by Xi Jinping during the 2019 Mahabalipuram Summit, refuting claims of Modi gifting a portrait to Xi. PM Modi proposed a 10-point reform roadmap for global governance, advocating for a shift from a 'pyramid of privilege' to a 'platform of partnership' where all nations have a voice and stake. Yes, PM Modi emphasized that the Global South should transition from being a 'rule-taker' to a 'rule-shaper', actively participating in the formation of global policies and governance. Sharing the picture, a user on X wrote, “Modi gifted Xi Jinping his own portrait. (crying emoji) Self-Love Level: PMO Edition.” However, the picture turns out to be from 2019. It dates back to the 2019 Mahabalipuram Summit when PM Modi and President Xi Jinping exchanged gifts. The Chinese President gifted PM Modi a porcelain memento bearing his picture. Clarifying the same, the official X handle of Press Information Bureau's Fact Check wing wrote, "A video is being shared online claiming that Prime Minister @narendramodi gifted a portrait of himself to Chinese President #XiJinping #PIBFactCheck." “The claim is #FAKE. The porcelain memento featuring PM Narendra Modi's image was gifted by Chinese President Xi Jinping to PM Narendra Modi in #Mamallapuram on 12 October 2019,” it added. Meanwhile, Saturday’s agenda for BRICS 2026 includes a closed-door session on global governance and multilateralism. It is also scheduled to hold a series of bilateral meetings, including with President Xi. The day will conclude with a gala dinner hosted by Modi featuring a “BRICS Symphony” with about 160 artists, mostly Indian dancers and musicians alongside performers from other BRICS countries, according to news agency PTI. Russian President Vladimir Putin, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto, Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi are among the attendees. The summit is of greater significance as it is taking place amid a global impact on the economy due to the Russia-Ukraine war, the West Asia conflict, especially the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, and Trump's trade and tariff policies-related issues. "The current structure of global governance resembles a pyramid: power and decision-making are concentrated at the top, while the lower tiers consist of nations that are affected by these decisions but unable to shape them," Modi said. "Today, the Global South stands in the front row of global crises but in the back row of decision-making. We must transform this 'pyramid of privilege' into a 'platform of partnership' -- one where every nation has a voice, every member has a stake, and the development of humanity lies at the heart of every effort," he added. PM Modi also unveiled a 10-point roadmap for global governance reform under the BRICS framework and advocated for a 'Seafarers' Emergency Support Network' to safeguard sailors from risks in ongoing global and regional crises. New Delhi, Sep 12: President Droupadi Murmu on Saturday met her Iranian counterpart Masoud Pezeshkian during which she reiterated India's commitment to the pursuit of enduring peace in the region and called for conflicts to be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy.
President Murmu's remarks came amid escalating tensions in West Asia in view of fresh US airstrikes on Iranian targets as well as Washington's attempts to inflict economic strain on Tehran through crippling sanctions.
Welcoming President Pezeshkian on his first visit to India, the president expressed appreciation for the support extended by Iran during India's BRICS presidency.
The two leaders discussed the long-standing bonds of friendship between Iran and India, including their strong cultural and people-to-people ties, a statement issued by the Rashtrapati Bhavan said.
The president reiterated India's commitment to the pursuit of enduring peace in the region and called for conflicts to be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy, it said.
The West Asia conflict began in late February this year.
Pezeshkian, who is here to participate in the BRICS Summit, called on President Murmu at the Rashtrapati Bhavan here.

On the rainy morning of August 26, the front courtyard of District Women Hospital in Maharashtra’s Amravati district was crowded with politicians, reporters and bystanders. Amid them stood 30-year-old Swapnil Borde. His bottle-green shirt hung limp with sweat, while his red-rimmed eyes brimmed with tears.
He is the father of one of the three newborns who died after a fire broke out in the four-storey Special Newborn Care Unit and Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU) on the third floor of the maternity hospital around 3.15 a.m. on August 24. Thirty-six babies were rescued and shifted to nearby hospitals, according to Amravati District Collector Ashish Yerekar. Two sustained burn injuries, says Amol Narote, medical superintendent of the government-run super-speciality hospital. Preliminary investigations indicate that a ventilator sparked the fire.
Also Read : Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar fire: 58 rescued, including nine newborns in blaze at hospital
Swapnil’s newborn was of low weight and had breathing issues, so was put on a ventilator two days before the fire.
“Gora bala kala kela. Ek minta pan nahi tambaycha ikde, khup bekar jhala ahe, pan mala ajun majhya mulachi janiv hote (My fair baby was turned black. I don’t want to be here even for a minute, but I still feel the presence of my child here),” says Swapnil, who works as a delivery person.
He adds, “This was the first baby in my family in this generation. It took us four years to conceive him. I took him in my arms only after he died.”
Outside the NICU, the empty fire extinguishers lay on the floor, while the soot-covered room, guarded by the police, continued to be frequented by people. Among them were members of a State-level investigation committee, Amravati MLC Pravin Pote and Achalpur Bharatiya Janata Party MLA Pravin Tayde. Former Leader of the Opposition in the Maharashtra Assembly and Congress leader Vijay Wadettiwar also visited the hospital. The parents of the other two newborns who died in the August 24 fire came from Achalpur and Paratwada, 50 km from the hospital.
Established in 1938, the hospital is one of Amravati’s major government maternity hospitals. It also caters to Wardha, Yavatmal and Washim districts. Primary healthcare centres and sub-district hospitals across Amravati, including Melghat, a tribal-dominated region, refer critical pregnancies here. The hospital was formerly known as Dufferin Hospital, named after Lady Hariot Dufferin, who established the Dufferin Fund in 1884 to provide medical aid to women in India.
Investigation underway
District Civil Surgeon Dr. Vinod Pawar, who is in charge of the maternity hospital, says, “Around 3.15 a.m., my staff in the NICU heard an explosion from the ventilator and saw fire coming out of it. They alerted the fire department and me simultaneously. Our priority was to rescue the babies.”
Dr. Pawar has submitted the fire-audit-related documents to the investigation committee. The police, meanwhile, have registered an accidental death report.
Maharashtra Minister for Public Health and Family Welfare Prakash Abitkar formed a seven-member committee headed by Public Health Commissioner Sanjay Katkar and directed it to submit its report within eight days. He said the committee’s findings would be made public and responsibility fixed.
On August 26, Mr. Katkar and the committee visited the spot and questioned the nurses who were present in the NICU at the time of the incident. The CCTV footage was also handed over to the committee, which comprises officials from the Maharashtra State Electricity Board, AIIMS and the Directorate of Medical Education and Research. It has been tasked with examining ventilator and electrical faults, the fire-audit history and administrative lapses. The report was due on August 31 but has not yet been released.
Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis announced ₹5 lakh in compensation for each family that lost its newborn in the fire and directed that the treatment of injured infants be fully covered by the government.
Of the 36 newborn babies, 11 have been admitted to Dr. Panjabrao Deshmukh Memorial Medical College (PDMMC), 10 to Hope Hospital, eight to Murkey Hospital and two to Parijat Hospital. Five were discharged with their mothers.
Survivors’ accounts
Radhika Yehkade, 19, was the last to deliver her twins before the fire. They were born around 2 a.m. on August 24 and kept in the NICU.
“I had a difficult pregnancy. I was in the hospital the week before my delivery. I am unable to let go of the voices in my head. Nurses shouting, ‘Help,’ people screaming, ‘Fire, fire.’ I am unable to make peace with the fact that my babies’ lives would have lasted only for two hours,” says Radhika, whose twins were admitted to PDMMC.
Radhika’s mother, Phula Shanware, 55, also an eyewitness, adds, “The smoke was dense; the fire brigade reached in time but took almost an hour to take water pipes to the third floor.”
Talking about her daughter, Phula says, “She had a tough pregnancy; we are daily wage earners and have already spent ₹80,000. We have been far from our house in Achalpur for almost 10 days.”
Another woman, Arti Kharale, 27, narrated her story. “When I saw my daughter, she smelt of wet ash. My heart sank when I heard about the fire,” says Arti, who lives in Amravati city. She says this was the second such fire in the hospital. The last, as reported by the media, was in September 2022.
Fifty-three-year-old Asha Dharse’s daughter delivered her baby at PDMMC. Chatting with other women, she says, “In June, I removed my daughter’s name from Dufrin because my cousin said they are negligent. Chutney, bhakri bhetel, pan aulad nahi, navas karava lagto (We will earn food, but not the baby).”
Yogesh Savarkar, 24, is waiting outside the maternity room at PDMMC, where his daughter and wife have been transferred. Recalling the night of the incident, he says he was among the first parents who barged into the room to rescue the infants.
He narrates, “The flames were soaring, wires were sparking, black smoke was coming out of the broken windows, and the equipment was burning. When I entered, I saw three children covered in black powder. One child had burns on his face. We rescued them first.”
Mr. Savarkar is also from Achalpur and came to the maternity hospital on August 17.
Maharashtra’s fire audits
Chief Minister Fadnavis has raised concerns over the hospital’s mandatory fire audit. A fire audit is a systematic inspection of fire safety readiness, assessing electrical load, wiring safety, overloaded circuits, faulty switchboards, and equipment prone to sparking or overheating, such as ventilators, oxygen concentrators and compressors.
According to data from Maharashtra’s Public Health Department, of the 530 government hospitals across the State, 528 have completed fire audits. As many as 442 hospitals have fire safety systems fully installed, while only 372 hospitals hold a fire no-objection certificate (NOC). This means nearly 30% of government hospitals do not have fire NOCs.
In Amravati alone, 18 government hospitals were audited, of which 16 received the NOC. Meanwhile, in Wardha and Gondia districts, 11 hospitals were audited, but none received the NOC. In Beed district in the Marathwada region, 18 hospitals did not receive NOCs.
On August 25, the Public Health Department announced a State-wide fire and electrical safety inspection of all government, private and charitable hospitals. Minister Abitkar had said, “If discrepancies are found in the audit, then they are to be rectified. Every hospital will appoint a nodal officer for fire safety, who will review fire audits, electrical safety, fire-fighting systems, emergency evacuation arrangements, staff training, and mock drills, and submit compliance information to senior levels.”
Initial warning
Records show that the Dufferin Hospital Authority had flagged concerns over the fire safety systems. A letter dated June 29 stated, “The hospital had obtained a fire NOC valid from June 22, 2025, to June 21, 2026. Before this validity period lapses, a registered licensed agency must conduct a fire safety audit, and Form B must be submitted to this office — so the fire NOC renewal proposal can then be forwarded to the Fire Department of Amravati Municipal Corporation.”
A follow-up letter was also written to the Public Works Department on July 17, reminding it to arrange a fire safety audit. “The fire NOC is an essential document for the hospital, and if its validity period lapses, the possibility of legal complications arising during an emergency cannot be ruled out,” the second letter stated, urging immediate action. The letter was marked to Amravati District Collector Ashish Yerekar and health services in the Akola division. Mr. Yerekar has not responded to The Hindu’s query regarding the action taken after receiving this letter.
Meanwhile, hospital staff and patients said this was the second fire incident in the last five years. “We learnt from our mistakes in the 2022 fire. That is why we have been extra careful with fire audits,” says an official from the Amravati maternity hospital. According to hospital authorities, a ventilator in the NICU had also caught fire then, causing minor injuries to two newborns.
The ventilators in both cases were supplied by Schiller Healthcare, which has been called for the investigation. An official said a committee will be set up to create SOPs for the procurement of medical equipment.
Courage under fire
Outside the NICU, the smell of smoke lingered. In the corridor, kaksh-sevikas (nursing attendants) were waiting for their turns to appear before the committee as part of the investigation. Among them was Surekha Dhanvijay, 45, one of the four attendants present in the NICU, who witnessed the fire and called for help. “The moment I heard the explosion, a huge flame burst out. With our bare hands, we tried to douse the fire near the cradle and take a baby out.”
“I have only one regret: that we couldn’t save those three children,” says Kirti Ghanvir, 45, another nursing attendant. Showing her fire burns and blisters, Ms. Ghanvir adds, “I had to feel around in the burning cradles to see if there was a baby. When I found one, I grabbed it.”
In the meantime, they informed others in the hospital, who rushed to help. “Most of us wrapped blankets around ourselves, broke the glass and entered, rescuing babies,” says Lalita Lasbe, 35.
The sevikas say they do not want any appreciation as they consider this part of their jobs, but appeal to the government to increase their salaries. They say they currently get ₹8,000 a month and are hired on contract, so their salaries barely increase.

At least 28 anti-migrant vigilante groups have formed in the UK in the last 18 months, ranging from unauthorised street patrols claiming to protect women and children to groups harassing migrants in France and blocking ports.
From Belfast to the south coast of England, the number of active groups has surged since the summer of 2025, according to analysis by the Guardian, amid widespread concerns over fresh disorder after black-clad vigilantes, many of them wearing balaclavas, blocked roads in Portsmouth and Dover last weekend.
Often arguing that they are filling gaps left by the police or taking action on migration that the government is unable to, the groups range from small-scale community patrols near asylum-seeker accommodation to those attempting to stop migrants crossing the Channel from France.
They include Scots Active, which conducts late-night patrols around Glasgow city centre claiming to protect the public from migrants, sometimes wearing balaclavas and stab-proof vests. It says its activities help ensure the safety of women and girls. It was one of two groups banned from TikTok earlier this year after reportedly sharing footage claiming to expose migrant hotels.
Another is the British Security Project, a self-styled civilian safety group that has described itself as the “tip of the spear in mass deportation under a Rupert Lowe government”. It recruits “visible deterrent patrol” volunteers via its website and social media platforms, and responds to reports from the public about incidents claiming to involve migrants. It aims to “provide 124,000 security personnel to public spaces by 2035”, according to its Facebook page.
When the Guardian contacted the group for comment, a spokesperson said it was neither vigilante nor anti-migrant. “The British Security Project is a developing non-profit community protection organisation committed to lawful, peaceful and accountable volunteer action,” they said. “It has no police or immigration-enforcement powers, does not permit people to be targeted because of their nationality or immigration status, and expressly prohibits vigilantism, intimidation, racism and unlawful discrimination.”
Members of another group, Raise the Colours, made several trips to France in 2025 to try to stop migrants crossing the Channel in small boats. They filmed themselves claiming to have slashed dinghies on French beaches. France subsequently banned 10 members from the country.
Members of far-right Patriot Platform blocked roads near Dover for several hours last Saturday, disrupting traffic to and from the port. Kent police initially said they had received no warning, but later admitted officers had failed to act on calls made on Friday evening.
On Sunday, about 200 black-clad men gathered in Portsmouth after 120 asylum seekers rescued from a dinghy were brought ashore there. They blocked roads and allegedly assaulted several police officers.
The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, urged police on Thursday to curb the activities of such groups, telling senior officers to make full use of their powers.
The rise in vigilante groups is a recent phenomenon, overwhelmingly happening in the last year. Of the 31 active groups the Guardian was able to establish initiation dates for, 28 were set up since last summer, with a spike in August 2025 after Raise the Colours’ flag operation and unrest at an asylum hotel in Epping. Setup dates were taken from online activity on Facebook and Instagram, domain name registrations and media reports.
To classify as anti-migrant vigilantes, the Guardian considers that a group must have taken the law into its own hands in the name of opposing migrants or asylum seekers. Groups limited to more conventional protests and far-right political parties were not included.
In a campaign of intimidation last summer, a vigilante group called the Belfast Nightwatch First Division was involved in targeting dark-skinned males in the city, challenging them to produce identification documents.
Dr Julia Ebner, an expert on extremism at the University of Oxford, said the figures showed a rapid shift in the ways anti-migrant activists were mobilising which was particularly striking.
“At the heart of most vigilante groups is the claim that the authorities are incapable or unwilling to protect a country’s citizens,” she said. “This is a dangerous dynamic, because when trust in authorities is undermined this can quickly translate into justifications of running their own policing operations or even violent campaigns – all supposedly for a good cause.
“Another underlying narrative that is not new but has been amplified across social media is the idea that ‘our’ women and children are threatened by men of migrant backgrounds. There is also a performative aspect of vigilante movements: uniforms, patrols and security equipment can project authority and legitimacy even when the groups themselves are relatively small.
“This can help far-right movements recruit new members and produce visually appealing social media content to increase their public profile and expand their followership.”
 Alex MacKinnon, a researcher at Hope Not Hate, said vigilantism had long been part of far-right activism, but that there had been a dramatic increase in extremists’ grassroots efforts in the last 18 months.
 “While vigilante groups typically purport to protect the wider community, the majority do not properly vet their members, resulting in several being exposed for their violent criminal histories,” he said.
“Furthermore, they regularly engage in intimidatory behaviour, as seen in Patriot Platform’s Dover demonstration. Vigilante groups of this type often promote aggressive anti-migrant agendas, using ‘community protection’ as a cover for racist thuggery.” 
 In response to the Guardian’s analysis, the National Police Chiefs’ Council said it was important for the public to report concerns about crime and safety.
“Police officers are specially trained to respond to a wide range of incidents safely and lawfully,” a spokesperson said. “While we understand people may want to protect their communities, taking enforcement into your own hands can be dangerous, and could compromise a police investigation.”

As diseases loom, CDC's response to measles deaths stirs fears about agency's reliability
The worst measles resurgence in the U.S. in decades keeps growing. Vaccination rates keep falling. Flu, COVID-19, and RSV keep coming back. Against this backdrop, many public health experts are worried about the reliability of health information coming from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
"Red flag. Red alert," says Dr. Demetre Daskalakis, who resigned last year as the director of the National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to protest what he called political interference at the agency.
Daskalakis and other independent public health authorities around the country are alarmed by how the CDC handled two deaths that Pennsylvania state officials recently blamed on measles. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. took the unprecedented step of questioning the deaths, and the CDC removed them from the agency's website.
"When they raise doubt on the adjudication that a state may have made around a death, that is highly problematic," says Daskalakis. "This is dangerous."
Usually, when someone dies from measles, the state where the tragedy happened determines the cause of death and reports the death to the CDC so the agency can alert the public, doctors and health officials around the country. The CDC usually defers to the state's determination.
So Kennedy's public dispute with the state and the CDC's response is concerning for what it may mean for the relationship between states and federal health officials, who have to work closely to protect the public, Daskalakis and others say. That relationship has already become strained under the Trump administration.
"What we have been seeing, that got amplified even more with these measles cases, is a breakdown in the coordination and trust between states and the federal government," says Dr. Anne Zink, a senior fellow at the Yale School of Public Health who previously served as Alaska's chief medical officer and president of the Association for State and Territorial Health Officers. "That to me is a significant concern. These partnerships are critical and essential to making us healthy and well."
Zink and others also worry about whether the public, state and local health officials, doctors and others will be able to trust federal health data about measles as well as other diseases, such as flu, COVID-19 and RSV. Could CDC succumb to pressure to suppress information to minimize concerns about those diseases and the impact of falling immunization rates? Kennedy has long questioned vaccines.
"We need to have good solid evidence-based national data. And I'm obviously concerned that it will happen again for other infectious diseases," says Dr. Georges Benjamin, who heads the American Public Health Association. "If it happens with flu and with COVID, the question is: Who can we rely on for the data on a national level. More people will get sick and more people because they won't know what to do. They won't know who to trust. And that is the problem here."
Many also worry about what this means for the effectiveness of the new CDC director, Dr. Erica Schwartz, who recently took over after a tumultuous year that has left the CDC demoralized and diminished. Many hoped Schultz, a well-respected physician and attorney with solid public health experience, would restore the CDC's morale and credibility by pushing back against political pressure. But many say the way the CDC handled the Pennsylvania measles cases don't bode well for Schultz pushing back against political pressure.
"We are seeing a pretty compromised CDC and a director who is at best facilitating non-scientific behavior and at worst colluding with non-scientific behavior," says Daskalakis.
Others agree.
"What the director should be doing instead of looking into these disease counts is responding to the outbreak itself," says Dr. Debra Houry, who resigned as the CDC's chief medical officer at the same time as Daskalakis for the same reasons. "I haven't heard from her talking about the importance of getting kindergarteners vaccinated when we're seeing declining rates. It's back to school time around the United States. We need her to step up publicly to talk about what can be done."
Neither the CDC nor the Department of Health and Human Services responded to NPR's repeated requests for comment.

England chasing the rainbow with more questions than answers
- Published
It is 2026 and Joe Root is again England Test captain and Kevin Pietersen is back in the fold.
For those two things to be the new normal says plenty about the upheaval in one of the most turbulent summers in English cricket's recent history.
The debate as to whether there should have been alterations to the leadership after the Ashes has become a moot point, because England have nevertheless ended in a post-Bazball era.
Has the lack of change in the spring led to a wasted summer? Try telling any of Jordan Cox, Emilio Gay or Dan Lawrence that the summer has been wasted. Or a resurgent Ollie Robinson. Or Root, who had to rummage around his garage to dig out his old captain's blazer.
Are England a better team in September than they were in June? It is hard to argue that a team that has lost Ben Stokes has improved, though that should take nothing away from all the good things England have done in the 3-0 series sweep of Pakistan.
It is not a criticism of Stokes to say his personality dominated the England team he led. By the end of his reign, England were characterised by what Stokes said and did.
Naturally, England are different under Root, a different personality to Stokes.
Until the third evening of the third Test at Edgbaston, most of those differences seemed positive. There had been a calmness about England's demeanour, perhaps because they had not been tested to that point.
That calmness eroded with every swing of Razaullah's blade. Two hours of chaos frazzled England and exposed old doubts from Root's first spell as captain. The skipper himself felt it necessary to duck off the field. Stokes rarely lost control in such a fashion.
Even after such a bruising session, there were some small positives. Stand-in coach Marcus Trescothick was happy to admit his disappointment at what had transpired, a shift in tone from the Kool Aid messaging of the Bazball boys.
In reality, we are ending the summer with no clear knowledge of how good this England team is, following a pattern of years gone by: the drawn Ashes in 2023, a shock defeat by Sri Lanka at The Oval at the end of 2024 and the failure to win the final Test against India last year.
And that is the ultimate frustration of England's Test performances in the four-plus years that Rob Key has been director of cricket.
When the defining series have rolled around, England have not won them. In between those big challenges there have been more questions than answers. The brass ring always remains just out of reach, always searching for the pot of gold at the end of the rainbow.
- England in better place than start of summer - Root 
  - Published1 hour ago

  - Published3 hours ago
For now, England have a blossoming four-man pace quartet that has drawn comparisons with the famous Ashes winners of 2005.
Robinson has ruled England's summer, taking his 28 wickets at an average of 9.32; the sort of statistics in keeping with Test cricket from before World War I.
With Jofra Archer, Josh Tongue and Gus Atkinson bringing the pace, England have a Swiss army knife of an attack, albeit lacking a left-armer.
Still, England are only one injury away from some inexperienced reserves. Sam Cook, Sonny Baker, Matthew Fisher and Henry Crocombe have four caps between them. Brydon Carse is available, though it remains to be seen if England will take him on tour while the Derby incident is still under investigation. Perhaps the in-form Olly Stone is due a recall.
The challenge for England is to find the right blend to suit the winter. The four seamers could operate in South Africa and the one-off pink-ball 150th anniversary Test in Melbourne, but the two matches in Bangladesh in February will demand a change in formation.
Despite the burning summer, spin has become a redundant weapon. The list of candidates to play in Bangladesh is long because there is no outstanding one among them.
Shoaib Bashir, Jack Leach, Dom Bess, Will Jacks, James Coles, Mason Crane, Liam Patterson-White, Calvin Harrison and Jack Carson may all think they have a shout of being on the plane.
The incumbent is Dan Lawrence, who has not had many opportunities to show the value of his part-time off-breaks.
Lawrence's bowling gives him an advantage when Jacob Bethell returns from a knee injury, probably leaving a choice between Jordan Cox and Emilio Gay for the first Test in South Africa in December.
Both men have made three half-centuries in their first summers as Test batters. Cox is extremely highly rated by the England management, who must decide how much weight to put on Gay's skill as a specialist opener.
The top of the order has emerged as England's biggest batting concern. Ben Duckett made the only century of the summer, yet averages 23 since the beginning of the Ashes.
Gay's average in his six Tests is below 25 and his frustration at his second-innings dismissal against Pakistan came out with a swish of his bat towards the stumps. His running between the wickets is jittery and he is rarely placed in an important position in the field.
Of all the issues around the batting, England need Root to rediscover his best. The captain ends the summer without a hundred for the first time since 2019 and with his lowest average in a home season since the same year.
This time last year, it was full steam ahead in the pursuit of India great Sachin Tendulkar. Now, the 1,643 runs to catch the Little Master look a little further away. The smart money will be on Root to come out of his funk, rather than this being the start of a late-career decline.
Root will meet incoming coach Stephen Fleming in the coming days to plot the route forward.
Along with Key - the great survivor of England's chaotic summer - the trio will look for a way to win the marquee series, to claim the major prizes on offer in the months ahead: in South Africa this winter, the Ashes next summer, in India in early 2028.
And this is where England find themselves yet again, with judgement reserved until biggest challenges.
Still grasping for the brass ring, still chasing the pot of gold.

The Supreme Court on Thursday (September 10, 2026) questioned the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) on how it proposed to determine whether packaged foods were “high” in sugar, salt or fat as part of its proposed front-of-pack warning labels, as it underlined that food safety was a cause of “national interest”.
The FSSAI had last month proposed prominent red warning labels on packaged foods high in added fat, added sugar or salt, marking a regulatory pivot after the top court questioned its reluctance to introduce such warnings.
In an affidavit filed before the court, the food regulator said the labels would take the form of a red hexagonal warning on the front of packages where a product was found to be high in two or more specified nutrients of concern — fat, sugar or salt. The thresholds would be based on those prescribed under the Dietary Guidelines for Indians, 2024, issued by the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition (NIN).
A Bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K. Vinod Chandran, while examining the FSSAI’s affidavit, however, questioned how the regulator would determine the threshold beyond which a packaged food would be classified as “high” in sugar, salt or fat.
“If you ask them to put a label, say high in salt, high in sugar, high in sodium, high in potassium, how will you determine it? Have you laid down any guidelines?” the Bench asked.
Additional Solicitor General Brijender Chahar, appearing for the Centre and the FSSAI, said the regulator was adhering to the guidelines issued by the ICMR-NIN.
The Bench was hearing a public interest litigation petition filed by non-profit organisations 3S and Our Health seeking warning labels on packaged foods to indicate high levels of salt, sugar and saturated fats. On Thursday, it indicated that it would soon pass a detailed order seeking further information from the stakeholders.
“We have done some homework and undertaken some study. We propose to pass an order calling for some further information from you. Study the order and come back with an appropriate further report,” Justice Pardiwala told Mr. Chahar.
‘Take orders seriously’
The top court also asked the regulator to take its directions “seriously”, stressing its concern over the impact of food safety standards on public health, particularly that of growing children.
“We are concerned with the health of people, more particularly growing children. We have taken it up very seriously... We expect one and all to extend cooperation in a cause which is in national interest,” Justice Pardiwala said.
‘Two-phase rollout’
The FSSAI had told the court that it intended to introduce the front-of-pack nutrition labelling (FoPNL) system in two phases to give consumers time to adapt to the new labels and the food industry time to reformulate its products. Under the first phase, the warning would apply to products high in two or more of the three specified nutrients, added fat, added sugar and salt, besides certain sweetened beverages. The second phase would extend it to products high in even one of these nutrients.
The Bench, however, questioned why a product would initially have to be high in more than one nutrient to attract the warning.
“It has to be sugar and salt. Only then will you ask them to put a label?” Justice Pardiwala asked.
Taking the court’s suggestion into account, Mr. Chahar told the Bench that the regulator could consider introducing the warning labels “in one go”, rather than in two phases. This would effectively bring products high in even one of the three nutrients within the warning-label regime from the outset.
Senior advocate Devadatt Kamat, appearing for an intervenor, meanwhile argued that ultra-processed foods could not be placed on the same footing as other packaged foods, citing the example of snacks such as Kurkure on the one hand and eggs or salted cashews on the other. He urged the court to consider a more prominent warning for ultra-processed products.
“Ultra-processed food and packaged food... both cannot be equated,” Mr. Kamat submitted. Pointing out that red and green marks are already used to distinguish non-vegetarian and vegetarian products, respectively, he suggested that a different colour could be prescribed as a warning for ultra-processed foods.
The Bench said it would consider the suggestion and pass an order, which would be uploaded within a day or two.
Earlier, the court had questioned the FSSAI’s reluctance to adopt warning labels for foods high in sugar, salt and saturated fat and asked whether pressure from food manufacturers was influencing the regulator.

The fighting represents the first major test of the mutual defense alliance that was signed between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey last month, adding to a preexisting pact between Islamabad and Riyadh. Pakistani officials worry the Houthi threat is more likely to draw Islamabad into a war than Iranian missile strikes on Saudi energy infrastructure were earlier this year. Throughout 2026, an image circulated online purportedly showing U.S. President Donald Trump's Fordham University transcript featuring a grade point average of 1.28.
The alleged report card suggests Trump got D, C and F grades across five classes.
One Facebook user who shared the supposed university record in January wrote (archived), "Is this a surprise to anyone?"
(Brian Little, accessed via Facebook)
The image also spread on X (archived, archived) and Instagram (archived) throughout the summer of 2026. Snopes readers wrote in asking if the transcript is real.
In short, the report card is fake. In March 2019, Fordham University posted (archived) about the image on X, calling it a "forgery."
The image is a forgery, not an actual Fordham University transcript. Fordham University respects the privacy of its students and alumni, and follows federal law regarding the handling and release of academic records https://t.co/gJ0qfpR4nB pic.twitter.com/CXCQ90kG76
— Fordham University (@FordhamNYC) March 8, 2019
Additionally, the fake document lists an address — 85-15 Wareham Place, Jamaica, New York — for Trump that he reportedly last lived at when he was four years old, meaning he did not live there when he attended Fordham University from 1964 to 1966 (PDF Page 89), aged around 18-20 years old.
It was not possible to find any evidence that Fordham had released an authentic copy of Trump's transcript regarding his years at the school, as of this writing.
Trump's former "fixer" and lawyer Michael Cohen, who testified against Trump in the trial that eventually found the now-president guilty of falsifying business records in connection with payments to a porn star, told Congress in 2019 that Trump asked him to send letters to his former schools that "threatened" them not to release his grades (PDF Page 14).
PBS reported in February 2019 that Fordham University spokesperson Bob Howe said the school had received a letter from Trump's legal team threatening legal action if it released his grades. That same year, Howe also told Snopes, when we previously investigated this claim, that the transcript is fake.
