Cormac McCarthy’s Midlife Crisis
Heading west at 40 transformed his writing—and American literature.
To understand Cormac McCarthy’s midlife crisis, look at America’s landscape. The fierce writer of biblical prose spent most of his first four decades anchored to Tennessee, a child of Appalachia with a lilting drawl and a regional outlook. By the early 1970s, he had published three Faulknerian novels—none of which sold well—and was struggling to finish a fourth book that aimed to chronicle his hometown of Knoxville in the way James Joyce had written about Dublin. McCarthy’s pockets were empty and his second marriage was failing. His then-wife, Annie DeLisle, recalled that on New Year’s Eve 1973, the year he turned 40, he suddenly announced that it was time for a change. As a friend put it, “He just walked off and left everything except his boots and his typewriter.” Pointing his truck west on I-40, McCarthy started driving and spent time in Tucson; Santa Fe; and Juárez, Mexico, before settling in El Paso, where he began researching a new novel called Blood Meridian.
Few life swerves are so productive. The book represented a fresh direction. Instead of another story set in the forests and shambling urban peripheries of Appalachia, Blood Meridian (1985) was an epic Western. It ambitiously set out to align the nation’s past with humankind’s age-old thirst for violence: Wolves cull one another, and so do people. From then on, the fearsome stakes of the West—territorial competition, crime, blood, death—defined McCarthy’s fiction and yielded his strongest work.
His next five novels, including the best sellers All the Pretty Horses (1992) and No Country for Old Men (2005), used desert plains and bleak landscapes to unspool a grim pessimism, shocking readers with stark visions of depravity while preserving the slenderest candlelight of hope: a few good souls carrying the fire. It was as though Appalachia’s dense woods and city fringes had prevented him from seeing the page clearly. Out west, there is nothing but sky.
In Cormac McCarthy: A Legacy Revisited, the first major biography of McCarthy, who died in 2023, Tracy Daugherty depicts his western reorientation as a turning point in his life and work but also looks for continuity. “The desert can be anywhere,” he writes; “the soul’s site of testing”—McCarthy’s lifelong fixation—is not limited to any one place. Although his departure was hurried, the transition took time. McCarthy made laps back to Tennessee during the 1970s and finished his Knoxville novel, Suttree, from his new base. The book was finally published in 1979 and unfairly panned by one critic as a “limited use of an enormous talent.” As for Blood Meridian, although it promised wonders to come, McCarthy’s first Western started off as a cult classic and only later, in the 1990s, began to find success.
Yet once cemented, the relocation was the fulcrum of McCarthy’s life. After the ’70s, he never again lived in Tennessee or made Appalachian culture his subject. He eventually came to be so closely associated with the dusty boots and bleached bones of the West that new readers may be surprised to learn that the first half of his life was spent elsewhere. So why did he leave Knoxville? Daugherty presents a combination of personal failures and artistic imperatives that chased and lured him, respectively. Daugherty’s fascinating biography, which reflects impressive research in the Cormac McCarthy Papers at Texas State University, is very well told and filled with astute judgments about McCarthy’s 12 novels. Although Daugherty declines to elevate one part of his oeuvre over the other, the lesson of the biography—and the work—is clear. The cultural South may have been McCarthy’s home, but the West was his muse.
McCarthy’s father and namesake, Charles McCarthy Sr., represented urban order; he was set on taming the young Cormac’s backwoods waywardness. McCarthy later claimed that his father had beat him savagely during his childhood, afterward calmly sitting back down to finish his supper. Cormac’s artistically inclined mother helplessly watched the abuse. McCarthy Sr. worked as general counsel for the Tennessee Valley Authority, a New Deal agency that displaced tens of thousands of Appalachian families to make way for hydroelectric power. He did so with brisk pragmatism and a clean conscience, infuriating his son. Each man was baffled and hurt as the other rejected his outlook. The tension drives the early pages of Suttree : “The world is run by those willing to take the responsibility for the running of it,” the father in the novel tells his meandering boy.
Siding with the evicted, McCarthy slept on the porch, explored the forests, and caroused with Knoxville’s degenerate class. “Like Shakespeare’s Prince Hal, he liked to go slumming—remaining, just slightly, apart,” Daugherty writes. McCarthy listened and gathered material for his novels as often as he participated in the outlaw revelry. Yet he was no angel: A night with John Sheddan, a local misfit and frequent confederate, could as easily find the two sleeping in a barn or confined to a jail cell for public intoxication as discussing Thomas Hobbes. McCarthy studied physics and engineering at the University of Tennessee but never earned his degree, and began to read Dostoyevsky, Melville, and Faulkner during an uneventful stretch of Air Force service in the 1950s. His first marriage, to Lee Holleman, ended in divorce.
Family and friends offered few durable tethers to home, terrain that lacked lasting fictional appeal too. McCarthy’s early novels, beginning with The Orchard Keeper in 1965, chronicled the types of Appalachian outsiders and scofflaws he liked to run with. They proved off-putting company for readers. The books stood out as much for their desperate circumstances and ghastly subject matter (incest in Outer Dark, from 1968; necrophilia in Child of God five years later) as for their baroque prose and gothic settings. Suttree, the best of these novels and an excellent book, was nevertheless digressive and full of obscure, almost impenetrable writing (“rhomboid and volute shapes of limestone jutted all brindled with mud like great bones washed out”). Critics recognized a rare talent but also a voice struggling to break free of Faulkner’s influence.
As his books misfired, McCarthy lived in an eccentric poverty that has become the stuff of legend. He cut his own hair and cooked canned food on hot plates. Working odd jobs (warehouse attendant in Chicago, garbageman in New Orleans), he recalled scraping by in “cellars on unemployment and welfare.” Without gainsaying these sacrifices, Daugherty calls out some exaggeration and myth building. Both DeLisle and Holleman contributed income; McCarthy’s Random House editor Albert Erskine helped him land fellowships and grants; and his parents, despite his strained relationship with his father, were a ready safety net. Still, between McCarthy’s failed marriages, family tensions, dead-end buddies, and dry artistic well, he had little to keep him in Tennessee as his 30s drew to a close.
A western reinvention allowed McCarthy to continue exploring timeless, elemental themes in a setting that befitted their gravity. In the American imagination, a cowboy’s journey is fraught, and his last breaths are tragic; a hillbilly’s exploits are hapless, and his final moments are merely uncomfortable. We cry for our heroes but wince for our outcasts. McCarthy sensed the difference. For a flailing author, the West also held commercial promise. “I ended up in the Southwest because I knew that nobody had ever written about it,” McCarthy later said. “Besides Coca-Cola, the other thing that is universally known is cowboys and Indians.”
Daugherty bristles at McCarthy’s dismissal of “decades of Southwestern literature”—by Leslie Marmon Silko, Katherine Anne Porter, N. Scott Momaday, and Larry McMurtry, to name just a few—yet the remark reveals a certain canniness: McCarthy cared more about selling books than his austere reputation suggests. It is not the only time Daugherty upends his subject’s ascetic image. In person, McCarthy was courtly and gregarious, a warm conversationalist who liked to sing. One striking scene has him dressed in a new cream suit, dancing into the night on an ocean liner as he twirls and spins his partners.
Blood Meridian proved to be McCarthy’s best novel and a modern masterpiece. Its protagonist is notably a young man who flees Tennessee for the West. The book follows the Glanton gang of scalp hunters in the mid-19th century along the U.S.-Mexico border. In ominous, hyper-violent language, McCarthy displays a nihilism that situates humankind on the raw continuum of predator and prey, river and rock: “The men as they rode turned black in the sun from the blood on their clothes and their faces and then paled slowly in the rising dust until they assumed once more the color of the land through which they passed.” Like an ancient mystic, McCarthy foresaw the endless reenactment of a horrifying cycle of brutality without meaning or purpose, a cursed birthright. “It makes no difference what men think of war,” says his most fearsome character, Judge Holden. “War endures. As well ask men what they think of stone.” To Daugherty, Blood Meridian’s clear-eyed view of American history was as amoral as realpolitik: “Politics as force.”
The Border Trilogy followed—the best-selling All the Pretty Horses leading on to The Crossing (1994) and Cities of the Plain (1998)—adding accessible characters and love stories to at last attract sales and awards. McCarthy’s writing began to shed some of its most ornate flourishes, taking on a stripped-down veneer. (Many of his later books were conceived as screenplays.) Critiques of the works as lightweight fare from the oracular McCarthy overlooked their hidden depths. This arresting insight, for example, comes to the young cowboy John Grady Cole in All the Pretty Horses: “He thought the world’s heart beat at some terrible cost and that the world’s pain and its beauty moved in a relationship of diverging equity and that in this headlong deficit the blood of multitudes might ultimately be exacted for the vision of a single flower.” Daugherty views McCarthy’s evolution in the Westerns as the pairing of a mature style with a genre framework. A similar combination has produced some of the best American movies of the past generation, by filmmakers such as Kathryn Bigelow and the Coen brothers, who directed an Oscar-winning adaptation of No Country for Old Men.
Although he started over, McCarthy could not escape the past. His celebrated 2006 novel, The Road—a sort of postapocalyptic Western—is built on a tender father-son relationship that both reflects McCarthy’s experience as a late-in-life parent and implicitly rejects his own father’s heavy hand. Daugherty quotes wrenching correspondence in which McCarthy and his father tried to reconcile as grown men. “There was and is a strong artistic streak in me that I inherited from my mother’s family and it has caused me a great deal of anguish in my life but an even greater joy,” McCarthy wrote. “I think this was always suspect to you.” Another relationship that echoed in his fiction was one that endured longer than his three marriages combined. McCarthy met Augusta Britt several years after moving out west; they became lovers when she was 17 and he was 43. They remained close for 47 years, but she protested the way he kept using her in his books, including in plotlines that seemed to mirror her life. “Well, baby, that’s what I do,” McCarthy replied. “I’m a writer.”
McCarthy attempted a second reinvention, a turn toward science. By the late 2000s, he was spending much of his time at the Santa Fe Institute, a multidisciplinary research center, where he hobnobbed with physicists, favoring philosophical conversations over writing books. The year before he died, he published a final pair of related novels, The Passenger and Stella Maris, which had been in progress for years; one of the main characters is a mathematics prodigy with a mental illness. In startling new reporting, Daugherty contends that McCarthy’s literary agent assembled the hodgepodge of pages and made the decision to break the mess into two books; McCarthy’s friends told Daugherty they suspected that the ailing writer had not even read the finished product. The result was unconvincing characters, mashups of McCarthy’s many interests, strange psychiatric sessions, and a lack of cohesion.
Maybe we all have only one good pivot in us. Or perhaps it was just too late for McCarthy to change course again. Whatever the case, his turn west in the 1970s reveals not just a man escaping personal failures but a restless writer who sensed that a wide new horizon might require him to expand his vision if he was to find his voice and his audience. The small-town hustles and degradations of Tennessee were ultimately too provincial for such an epoch-spanning talent, which demanded plains, mountains, and an endless expanse of sky to bring out its full potential. After all, deep in the Appalachian woods, you can’t see the buzzards circling.

India's Modi and China's Xi seek to reset ties on BRICS sidelines
It's the latest effort to repair ties strained by a border clash six years ago.
NEW DELHI -- Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping met Saturday on the sidelines of the BRICS summit in New Delhi, the latest effort by the rival neighbors to repair ties strained by a deadly border clash six years ago.
Xi said China has approached relations with India from a “strategic and long-term perspective” and called for the two countries to draw on each other’s strengths, support one another and pursue common development.
He also urged “high-quality cooperation” between the two countries, saying China and India, as major members of the Global South, should promote a more multipolar world and contribute to global peace and stability.
Modi thanked Xi for China’s cooperation in hosting the summit. China will host the summit next year.
The two leaders held talks in China last year during Modi's visit to attend the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, a regional political, economic and security group founded by China.
The summit marks Xi’s first visit to India since 2019 and yet another effort toward a cautious thaw between the rival neighbors, six years after a deadly border clash badly damaged ties.
A military clash in 2020 killed at least 20 Indian soldiers and four Chinese along a grueling frontier in the cold desert region of Ladakh. It turned into a long-running standoff in the rugged mountainous area, where each side has stationed tens of thousands of military personnel backed by artillery, tanks and fighter jets.
India and China have since taken steps to ease tensions, but deep mistrust remains.
The two nuclear-armed powers still dispute some parts of their border, while India’s large trade deficit with China, restrictions on Chinese investment and technology and their competing strategic interests in Asia continue to weigh on relations. India has also significantly expanded military infrastructure along its disputed frontier with China, while Beijing has built roads and defensive positions on its side of the contested border.
Xi’s visit is expected to test whether the recent thaw can translate into a broader stabilization of ties.
Since their 1962 war, the economies of both countries have grown substantially, but China has far outpaced India and runs a large trade surplus with its neighbor. Their growing economic rivalry has added to longstanding territorial and strategic differences.
India has sought to capitalize on China’s rising labor costs and strained ties with the United States and Europe to position itself as an alternative base for foreign manufacturers. New Delhi has also viewed China’s multibillion-dollar Belt and Road Initiative with concern and has strongly opposed it.
At the same time, India’s growing strategic partnership with the U.S. has raised concerns in Beijing, which views the relationship as part of efforts to counter China’s rise.

Top elected official in Pakistan's Balochistan rules out talks with insurgents
The top official in Pakistan's Balochistan province has ruled out negotiations with insurgents
ISLAMABAD -- The top elected official in Pakistan’s southwestern province of Balochistan on Saturday ruled out negotiations with insurgents, indicating that the government will continue operations in which hundreds of militants have been killed in recent months.
Balochistan has long faced a separatist insurgency by ethnic Baloch groups who regularly target security forces and civilians working on development projects. While Pakistan’s government says it has quelled the insurgency, violence has persisted.
Sarfraz Bugti, the chief minister of Balochistan, said in a statement that the “fight against terrorism would continue until the last terrorist is eliminated” in Balochistan. “There will be no negotiations with terrorists, those who have taken up arms against Pakistan and those raising slogans for the country’s disintegration.”
His remarks came as attacks by the Baloch Liberation Army, which has been designated as a foreign terrorist organization by the U.S., have increased. Bugti said the time had come for “major surgery” to eliminate terrorism.
“We are in a state of war,” he said, adding that authorities had never claimed everything in Balochistan was normal. “The security forces are performing their duties under extremely difficult conditions in the province, and all state institutions are working in complete coordination against terrorism.”
Though Pakistan’s largest province, Balochistan is its least populated. Some Balochis have complained about discrimination by the government. There are also deep grievances about enforced disappearances, extrajudicial killings and the exploitation of the abundant natural resources.
Several regional political parties and activists have called in recent years for dialogue with insurgent groups, but BLA and other Baloch groups have not sought talks. No spokesman for the group was immediately available for comment.
Pakistan’s federal government and officials in Balochistan have rejected such calls for dialogue, saying leniency could be considered only for militants who surrender. Some BLA leaders and their associates have surrendered at ceremonies, where they laid down their weapons and were welcomed by local officials.
In 2025, BLA killed 18 paramilitary security forces in one of the deadly coordinated attacks in Balochistan.

Where do Muslim youths fit in India's 'Cockroach' protests?
As protests by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) in Delhi gained momentum this summer, many Muslims urged their children not to participate.
Some mosque announcements cautioned Muslim youths to stay away - not over any clash with the movement’s ideals, but amid fears of harassment, false charges, hounding and intimidation.
For many students, attending protests at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar was a way to show they cared enough about the issues facing the country to show up. But Muslim students in today’s India must always weigh the consequences of their actions.
Other Muslim student activists have spent years languishing in jail, without trial and with little hope of bail. Some have had their homes demolished.
In the eyes of the government, Muslim comes first, and student later. Staying home might look like political apathy from the outside, but inside the community, it is a safety valve, underscoring the limits of what Muslims in India can afford to do.

For a generation of young Indians, the CJP has made it easier to imagine themselves as political actors. The movement - which started out as a joke after appalling remarks by Chief Justice Surya Kant, who compared unemployed youths to “cockroaches” - quickly moved from social media to the streets.
As the protests spread nationwide, they attracted large numbers of young people angry about exam failures, unemployment, and the absence of accountability in a system upon which their futures depend. Thousands marched towards parliament, and on 25 July, Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned.
Political exposure
The warnings to Muslim youths, cautioning them against participation in this countrywide movement, did not stem only from fear. They came from a community with years of experience as to what political exposure can mean.
Protests over the Citizenship Amendment Act, a law that excludes Muslim immigrants and refugees living in India from obtaining citizenship, are part of this same historical memory. The ensuing crackdown culminated in February 2020, when state-orchestrated communal violence in northeastern Delhi killed 53 people, most of them Muslims.
The violence was followed by arrests under anti-terrorism legislation, with some of those arrested still in jail years later without trial.
For communities that have repeatedly experienced police targeting, surveillance and violence after political mobilisation, caution is based on experience. Despite such fears, some Muslims still participated in the CJP protests; among them was Mohammad Junaid, who alleges that he was subsequently harassed by police.
You cannot claim to fight the disease, while telling people living with its symptoms that their suffering is a distraction from the real problem
The CJP movement has made a point of saying that its politics belong to young Indians. Its founder, Abhijeet Dipke, has repeatedly argued that Indian politics has spent too long on Hindu-vs-Muslim issues, and that education and employment should take precedence.
There is a reasonable political frustration behind this argument. A student whose exam has been cancelled should not have to choose a religion before demanding justice.
For Muslims, however, communal politics is not a subject that can simply be put aside so that everyone can get back to talking about education and jobs. It follows them into those areas. It affects how they are spoken about, how their neighbourhoods are policed, and how their political actions are read.
The history behind this is longer than Prime Minister Narendra Modi or the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). Author Vinayak Damodar Savarkar set out the ideological foundations of Hindutva in his 1923 work Essentials of Hindutva, defining the nation through an idea of Hindu cultural belonging that placed Muslims and Christians outside the same conception of national identity.
Modi’s years in power have merely brought an old majoritarian politics deeper into the institutions and everyday life of the country.
Language of incitement
There have been vigilante attacks on Muslims, unlawful demolitions of Muslim homes and businesses, and the expulsion of Bengali-speaking Muslims and Rohingya refugees to Bangladesh. Modi himself made Muslims a central target of his 2024 campaign.
This is the environment in which a Muslim student decides whether a protest is worth attending.
At the same time, the language of incitement coming from the government has continuously shifted. Modi recently revived the term “dimagi Naxal” to refer to an intellectual insurgency, and the BJP quickly turned the phrase into a coordinated meme campaign on social media, targeting CJP protesters, among others.
Muslims know this language well. They have been called infiltrators, terrorists and anti-national long before the introduction of “dimagi Naxal”. This does not necessarily mean that every Hindu sees Muslims as a threat, but it does mean that political parties can build an electoral advantage by making Muslims the group against which the majority is asked to measure its own safety and interests.
In a country where the BJP has won a third consecutive national term by pushing a project based on the systemic extermination of Muslims, these politics cannot be treated as background noise.
That is why blanket statements about “fighting for Indian youth” - while avoiding the word “Muslim”, or refusing to discuss Muslim political prisoners - creates a problem. The CJP can decide not to make Muslims its organising constituency, but it cannot assume that refusing to name Muslims makes communal politics less real.
The success of the CJP thus leaves India with a problem larger than exam leaks. The movement showed that young people can organise, sustain pressure, and make a government act.
A democracy cannot measure the health of its protest culture only by the number of people who turn up. It has to ask who can turn up without calculating how their surname, neighbourhood or religion might affect them after the protests.
The BJP has made communal politics part of everyday life in India. Muslims have lived with its consequences for years: being called infiltrators and security threats, as their neighbourhoods, homes and activities come under increasing scrutiny.
These are not side issues. You cannot claim to fight the disease, while telling people living with its symptoms that their suffering is a distraction from the real problem.
A country can have a constitutional right to protest, while still harbouring a political culture where exercising that right is safer for some than for others. That gap is where democracy is tested. India’s young Muslims know this already. The CJP movement should learn it before it can honestly speak for all.

The cryptocurrency billionaire Christopher Harborne has given £36m to Reform UK, matching a donation from fellow billionaire Ben Delo.
The pledges are jointly the largest donations made to a UK party and are likely to intensify calls for a cap on political donations.
Reform leader, Nigel Farage, said he was “honoured and humbled” by the donations, which come at a time when Reform is facing intense scrutiny regarding its finances.
The Metropolitan police is conducting an inquiry into Reform’s finances, and Farage is facing a parliamentary standards investigation into a £5m gift from Harborne, made before he was first elected an MP in 2024. Reform UK and Farage have denied any wrongdoing.
Farage said: “I am honoured and humbled that Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne have shown such confidence in Reform.
“Both men know that we are the only party that can turn the country around and win the next general election – thanks to their generosity, we are now able to fight that election on a level playing field.”
Harborne said: “There will be a lot of media speculation regarding this donation. So what do I expect in return for my donations? Nothing. No peerage, no policy change, just a party that is ready for government.
“I have already accumulated enough wealth for the rest of my life. I am committed to putting that to work for Britain and humanity as a whole. I want the same as everyone else in Britain: for my children and grandchildren to have the chance to live happy and productive lives here and be rewarded for their hard work.
“At the next general election people will have to vote for the party that they think will best get that done and I’m making a donation very clearly to the party that I believe will do so.”

'A legacy' at 26 - how Hemp has grown at Man City
- Published
Lauren Hemp has already achieved more than most footballers at the age of 26.
The England international made her 200th appearance for Manchester City last Sunday as they began the defence of their Women's Super League title.
She was player of the match as they beat newly promoted Birmingham City 3-1, capping off her milestone appearance in the perfect way.
Hemp is only the fourth player in City's history to reach the landmark of 200 appearances, following Steph Houghton, Keira Walsh and Demi Stokes.
During her eight years at the club, she has grown to become one of Europe's best forwards and helped them lift six major trophies.
It was no surprise City manager Andree Jeglertz said Hemp "already has a legacy" - and there is still plenty of time to build on it.
What impact has Hemp had?
Individual accolades have flooded in during Hemp's time at City.
She scooped up a record fourth Professional Footballers' Association young player of the year award in 2022, has been named in the PFA team of the year three times and has established herself as a key member of Sarina Wiegman's Lionesses.
Hemp has netted 74 goals in 200 appearances and has created more chances from open play than any other player in the WSL's history.
Only striker Khadija Shaw has scored more City goals in the professional era than Hemp, and the England forward is second in the WSL's all-time assist charts.
Against Birmingham, she had more entries in the final third than any team-mate besides Gracie Prior and 16 touches in the opposition box.
In summary, Hemp has proved to be a crucial player for City and starred as they won a domestic double under Jeglertz last season.
"Just give her the ball and something happens!" he said after the victory over Birmingham.
"What I feel is fascinating with Lauren is that if you come and watch one of our training sessions, you see she has the same enjoyment for playing football that she shows in games.
"I really hope she never loses that. She is always kicking a ball, she is never too tired to do anything and she wants to be there. She loves football.
"That shows young players what it's about. They need to love to go to work. It's not just a job, it's an identity.
"What she has done for the club in 200 games... she is still pretty young. She can play many more games here. That's amazing that she has a legacy already."
How is she viewed by fans?
Hemp's City career has also coincided with a successful period for the Lionesses in which she played a key role in helping them win back-to-back European titles.
Having joined from Bristol City as a high-flying teenager in 2018, she has grown up during her time in Manchester.
She was awarded an MBE in 2024 for services to football, and signed a three-year contract extension with City that year.
Last season the club won their first WSL title in a decade, as well as the Women's FA Cup - reward for Hemp's commitment.
Jayne Comer, secretary for the Manchester City supporters club and a season ticket holder for more than 10 years, said Hemp was already considered a "legend".
"She is absolutely loved by us all. She remained fiercely loyal to the club, when, let's face it, she could have signed for any team in the world," Comer told BBC Sport.
"The fact she stayed and gives her all every week means so much to us. We've had the privilege of watching one of the best players in the world.
"Every week she gets us all on our feet. When she gets the ball, it's exciting. You always feel like something spectacular might happen."
Comer, who watched Hemp play live before she joined City, also considered her "one of the greatest players we've ever had".
"She is always one of the first names on the teamsheet for any manager and looks like somebody who loves to play football," she added.
"I remember the very first time I saw Lauren play was when we were away at Bristol and she really caught my attention.
"Even back then, you could see what a talent she was. She just oozed potential. I was really excited to see how she would progress and I have not been disappointed.
"What a player! I count myself lucky every time I see her playing in sky blue."

Alberta separatists expect a win, regardless of numbers that say otherwise, poll suggests
Pollster also finds many support Option 2 for reasons other than full independence
Alberta separatists think they’re going to win a referendum that surveys suggest they are poised to lose by a wide margin, according to exclusive new polling.
And that mismatch of expectations has consequences for what comes next — including the likelihood that Albertans shouldn’t expect this issue to be put to rest with this one vote, say the pollster and a political scientist.
Abacus Data CEO David Coletto presented the results of the new poll, done during the first week of September, to CBC’s West of Centre on Friday.
On Oct. 19, Albertans will vote on a question with two choices: Option 1 is to stay in Canada, while Option 2 supports commencing the legal process to hold a binding referendum on Alberta separation.
That ballot question will be in addition to nine others that focus on constitutional and immigration issues.
Coletto’s poll found 64 per cent of respondents would vote to remain a province in Canada and 24 per cent would vote to start the separation process. Nine per cent were undecided and three per cent said they would skip the question.
But the poll also found that Option 2 supporters have surprisingly high expectations, believing that the separatist option will garner a winning 57 per cent of votes.
Coletto chalks it up to the political bubbles people live in and the natural hopefulness that comes with their strong support of the separatist camp.
Lisa Young, a political science professor at the University of Calgary, says that inflated expectation is worth noting — especially in the context of post-referendum ramifications.
"What he found, I think, should be setting off alarm bells in all of our heads," Young told West of Centre.
"If you do walk into this with the expectation that Option [2] is going to get 57 per cent and the actual outcome is 28 per cent ... the first question is going to be, 'Was this a proper result? Can we trust the outcome?'"
Premier Danielle Smith has said the upcoming referendum will be a gut-check of where Albertans stand, and that the province can hold a vote and move on.
But Young and Coletto don't see it that way.
In the event that the winning side supports remaining in Canada, the poll found many Option 2 voters expect the separatist movement to keep growing. Only six per cent of them said they expect the issue will be settled.
"There seems to be this assumption in the UCP premier's office ... that if you let this group let off steam, it will make the issue go away," Young said.
"This does not simply go away afterward. We're going to live with it one way or another for the next months, if not years."
Who is the typical Option 2 voter?
According to the polling, the typical Option 2 voter is a conservative partisan, somewhat more likely to be a man and tends to be slightly older than the provincial average.
They are more likely to live in small cities or in bedroom communities around Calgary and Edmonton. While rural Alberta contributes more than its share, the communities ringing Alberta's main metropolitan centres provide the most voters.
But the group is more distinguishable by its grievances than its demographics, the poll suggests.
It says Option 2 supporters are far more likely to put being an Albertan ahead of being a Canadian, and have a more favourable view of the United States and Donald Trump. That said, the group is split on whether Alberta should become a U.S. state.
The group also shares near-unanimous agreement that Alberta contributes more to Canada than it gets back, the province’s interests are ignored in Ottawa, and the rest of the country does not respect Alberta, the poll suggests.
Young said she wonders if the separatist camp is adequately reflected among people who were polled.
"I did start thinking back to 2016 in the United States," Young said. "People wouldn't tell a pollster that they were going to vote for Trump because it was seen as sort of socially unacceptable."
Coletto said he's confident his poll factored in as many Option 2 voters as possible, but he also acknowledged this is not a typical election.
"Partisan politics can get divisive. But this is being felt much more deeply and much more emotionally on both sides."
"Whatever side you're on, you've still got to live together no matter what happens going forward."
Do they actually want to leave?
What Option 2 voters hope to get out of a favourable result varies significantly. When asked to identify their main motivation for choosing to commence the process for a binding referendum, only 26 per cent said independence.
The rest are voting for leverage, to send a message or on principle, Coletto said.
"For many Albertans who are inclined to look at Option 2, it's not just a black or white, in and out."
That result aligns with recent messaging from the separatist camp.
“Independence isn't actually on the ballot,” Keith Wilson, with independence group Let Alberta Decide, told West of Centre last month.
“Voting Option 2 sends a message that no, we can do better. We want a more respectful and balanced and fair relationship with Ottawa.”
“Others are prepared to vote for Option 2 when they don't even support independence. And that's why I have some optimism we're going to win on Oct. 19.”
Methodology
Abacus Data surveyed 1,000 Alberta adults online from Sept. 4 to 7, 2026, six weeks before the Oct. 19 referendum. Results are weighted by region, age and gender to census data. A probability sample of this size would carry a margin of error of plus or minus 3.1 points, 19 times out of 20. For subsets, the margin of error is larger.

'It started as a joke, a fantasy' - F1 heads to football-obsessed Madrid
- Published
You could never accuse Formula 1 of shirking a challenge.
Who else would consider competing for the attention of a football-obsessed country, home to the World Cup winners, in a city where a constant stream of the world's most talented players do awe-inspiring things most weeks?
F1 last had a Spanish world champion 20 years ago and there hasn't been a race in Madrid since 1981.
Does F1, which has experienced a huge rise in popularity in other territories around the world, need another track in its crowded European heartland?
This weekend the sport, and Madrid itself, will find out.
Madrilenos know how to make sport great
Real Madrid are considered to be the greatest football club in history.
They have won 15 European Cups and 36 La Liga titles, and then there are the famous Galacticos: the generational set of the world's best players which began with the likes of Zinedine Zidane and Ronaldo and has extended to the modern crop that includes Jude Bellingham and Kylian Mbappe.
Some 75,000 Madridistas roared home Mbappe's majestically deft volley to make it 3-0 after half an hour against Malaga at the end of August, and their city rivals Atletico aren't far adrift of them in La Liga. It's hard to see what else the locals need to sate their sporting needs.
But in both the stunning, newly reconditioned steel spaceship of the Bernabeu, which has lost none of the drama of its frighteningly steep theatrical terracing, or Real Madrid women's atmospheric if less salubrious stadium right next to the new F1 track, will fans be turning their attention to the roar of the engine noise this weekend?
"Yes, [the F1 race] is good for Madrid," says one. "There is pride in our sport, Madrid is an open city with open people and open minds.
"The race can [take] Madrid's [identity] outside of football, and the most we can be seen [by the outside world] is the best.
"But I'm more than excited… I'm curious - I want to see how it goes."
"We've always been dreaming of having something [from F1] closer to home," adds another. "Having it back is great. I've been to Barcelona and the Belgian GP and I think let's see how it goes. Organising tends to be messy in the first year - I don't want to be the guinea pig.
"Let's hope it brings the city more into the spotlight. Madrid has a lot to learn from F1 about how to run a global spectacle; F1 could probably learn the true Spanish way. Barcelona is more international, the drivers and fans coming to Madrid will get more of a taste of Spain."
Welcome to Madring
As the Prado museum demonstrates, Madrid knows its fine art.
The crossing signals resemble birdsong and the Mexican conifers gently sway over the waiting traffic with a backdrop of stunning Palaciosian architecture, which is in contrast to the relatively flat, block layout of the inner city.
This may not have made for the best race experience so instead, organisers plumped for what outsiders may see as an unloved expo area run by the quasi-state owned Ifema organisation next to the city's airport.
"It started as a joke, it was a fantasy," says Luis Garcia Abad, Madring boss and former manager to Spain's only world champion Fernando Alonso, among other Spanish sports stars.
"An F1 grand prix is like a unicorn - you are trying always to see the unicorn but at the end you realise [sometimes] it's impossible.
"The queue of cities trying to organise an F1 GP is huge. They have to choose right - we signed a contract for 10 years.
"Maybe seven or eight years ago we talked about this race. At some point Ifema called me and said 'what are you thinking [about its viability]?' After one morning [here] I said: 'It's possible.'
The new venue may be a world away from the flamenco-inspired boutiques and wine bars of the intimate Salamanca district, but Madrid is relatively diminutive compared to other high-profile capitals, and has high-quality public transport.
As a result, organisers are cutting out many of the car parks and asking fans to leave their own motors at home.
But don't expect Patrick Dempsey, Rafael Nadal and Mbappe to be standing on the platform of Avenida de America to hop on the pink line to the circuit – they will breathe easy at the VIP spaces near to the expansive six-strong VIP area paddock.
Regardless of the journey there, what will fans find?
"It's a real experience, not just to be in Madrid but for F1," says Abad. "Every part of the track has its own personality. Monumental… Turn 12, is huge, amazing.
"We really wanted to have an iconic part of the circuit – more than 30,000 people around one corner."
Ah yes, Monumental. The corner everyone in F1 is talking about when discussing this race.
A 26-degree banked challenge, substantially longer than the one at the Dutch Grand Prix's Zandvoort. Monumental scythes through what will feel like a small town come race day.
It comes complete with a VIP viewing area that could house the King of Spain and his family and sits, appropriately, like a castle on top of the hill. It's a difficult structure to walk up, and in 44C heat, impossible to sit on.
"Luis wanted to think of something recognisable in our circuit. Something iconic," says operations director for Ifema Carlos Jimenez.
Monumental was not the only complex part of a track build, which Jimenez says lends itself to sustainability. Power for the race comes from renewable energy and there is partial use of existing buildings around the site. However, additional construction around the circuit has seen 65m euros of investment, and the track itself cost 85m euros alone.
"There were a lot of challenges," he says. "We started building it in the wettest winter in 20 years in Spain. The rain was torrential. We suffered a lot, and had to stabilise parts of clay which behaves badly with wet conditions. It was very challenging. There are three layers of asphalt here. We learnt from one layer to the next.
"In 2022 it seemed like a little bit of a crazy idea," adds Jimenez. "But Madrid has momentum right now; it's a vibrant city, very well known for football.
"Like a ski resort must have entertainment for apres-ski, a circuit must have good after-race entertainment. Madrid will become in top position - the offer of this city is incredible in terms of gastronomy, a spectacular climate, which is very mild in September. And the party in Madrid is unbeatable."
What could happen in the race?
Make no mistake, Madring is a street circuit: part public roads, part purpose built. And it feels intense to stand on the track, let alone drive it, with the walls on either side appearing to close in on you. And that lack of width, on the eye at least, suggests overtaking will be virtually impossible.
"From a driver's point of view it's quite a harsh circuit," says an excited Abad. "Twenty-two corners, up and down, banking corners - the circuit is adapted to the new [F1] regulations.
"I spoke with Charles Leclerc and he said it was an amazing track, and in the race I believe you will have the opportunity to overtake, but not by free. We're talking about gladiators – the best drivers in the world."
Plenty of drivers have already experienced Madring in anger during a Formula 3 test.
"It's going to be really edgy," says Madrid's own F3 driver Bruno del Pino. "You are always on the limit, the corners are quick and the walls are close. It's like [Saudi GP circuit] Jeddah but with more difficulty.
"With Monumental, you see so much of an angle it never ends. The first time around, you see it going straight up and you feel like you'll fly straight out [of the track].
"It is flat for us because of the downforce so it's not really a corner, but the previous combination of Turns 10 and 11 are high speed and close to the wall - quite a few drivers will kiss the wall."
Britain's F3 driver Freddie Slater goes even further: "A lap of Madrid is so exhilarating, and the adrenaline is pumping - it's an incredible track to drive. It's one of the best tracks on calendar, if not the best.
"It's got character, it's got bumps, uphill and downhill – it's a bit more old-school."
Abad believes it's the spectators who will determine this race's success.
"Not just Madrid needing F1, maybe even F1 needing Madrid," he concludes. "We're investing money to create an experience inside of a city.
"The future of the [F1] championship is something in this direction – we need to take care of customers and spectators. They are our future."

Kimi Antonelli was 10 when his father Marco first realised the boy sitting on his lap, operating the steering and gears, might have an exceptional talent as a racing driver.
The pair were at the Adria circuit in north-east Italy, Marco with his Lamborghini sports car team, Kimi competing in a karting race.
It was the end of the day and Marco, a former driver himself, asked his son: "Do you want to try the Lamborghini?"
Of course he did.
Marco strapped himself and Kimi into the car, belts extended around both. Dad was in charge of the throttle and brake, his son would control the rest.
"I couldn't see the track because he was in front of me with a helmet on," Marco tells BBC Sport. "I could only see beside me the marker panels before each corner - 100m, 50m.
"We started to drive, step by step, faster, faster, faster. In the end, I pushed like I was alone and I arrived at the braking point at the end of the straight, 320km/h, braked very hard and at the limit.
"The car had a lot of oversteer. Kimi controlled the oversteer perfectly, then I went on the throttle, Kimi finished the oversteer, changed gear, and went.
"I said: 'OK, stop, because it has now become dangerous.' But when I saw the video, 10 years old, on my leg, oversteer, everything perfect, I said: 'Maybe he has something special.'"
Now a 19-year-old Kimi is dominating this year's F1 championship in only his second season.
This is the story of a boy his dad says was "born in a garage".
"Kimi from 15 days old was in the garage and heard the sound of the engine and the smell of the exhaust," says Marco, who worked with his wife Veronica on their racing team business.
It was the Christmas holidays when Kimi was about three, and Marco had brought home a simulator he had bought for his guests to try out at the Bologna Motor Show.
"Each evening, Kimi wanted to drive," Marco remembers.
Just like seven years later in the Lamborghini, Kimi would sit on Marco's leg, the controls divided in the same way.
"I remember one night I started to fall asleep because I had been at work very early and we had a crash because I didn't brake when we arrived at the end of the straight," Marco says.
"And Kimi said: 'Dad, dad, no sleep, no sleep. I have to drive.'"
Marco Antonelli did not originally want his son to become a racing driver, because of his own struggles during his career.
"Sometimes you are fast but not in the right position to become a professional driver," he says.
In the 1990s, Marco Antonelli was on the cusp of becoming a works driver in the DTM touring car series, then a huge hit with audiences across Europe.
He tested for Alfa Romeo, but then the team boss left and the opportunity evaporated. Another chance came up with BMW, alongside Roberto Ravaglia and Steve Soper - stars at the time. Again, the same thing happened.
"I suffered a lot for it," Marco says. "And, of course, I was scared that my son [would] relive the same situation. At the beginning, I was very stressed about the passion my son had for motorsport."
Kimi tried a go-kart for the first time when he was five, and immediately showed an awareness of racing lines, braking points and car control.
The Antonellis were what Marco describes as "a normal family". They could not possibly afford to pay for Kimi to take part in all the categories on the way to Formula 1.
Marco decided he could fund Kimi through karting and a year of the basic single-seater category, Formula 4. After that, he figured he might be able to put him in one of his GT cars and become professional that way.
But Kimi immediately started to impress. Whatever category he got into, he was quick, and won.
By the time Kimi was 11, his name was buzzing around motor racing circles. Mercedes heard about him, and their driver academy scout Gwen Lagrue flew to Italy to check him out.
It was a season in which Antonelli had ended up driving a kart with less power than those of his rivals. Marco had told Kimi this would be good for him - he should think not about the result, but about how to improve, always push hard.
"Gwen was impressed about this condition of power and driving in this category that Kimi did," Marco says. "And maybe they understood that Kimi was a different child."
Now Kimi was a member of the Mercedes driver academy, Marco could stop worrying about money, and start focusing on helping his son achieve his full potential.
Mercedes were not the only big names in F1 who had noticed Antonelli's promise.
"When he was in karting, you could already see he was one of the stand-out talents," says four-time world champion Max Verstappen, the only other teenager to win an F1 race.
At 15, Antonelli was ready to move up to cars, and, as a final preparation, did a couple of races in a karting category with gears. On his debut, with minimal pre-event testing, he took pole position. After that, he went to the world final, and stuck it on pole again.
This was the end of 2021, after which Antonelli moved full-time into cars. Through 2022, he swept the board in various championships in Formula 4, and the same happened in Formula Regional in 2023.
1 of 4
By now, Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff was already thinking that Antonelli would be his next F1 driver, potentially a replacement for Lewis Hamilton. With the seven-time champion approaching 40, Wolff was planning on taking control of that generational transition.
So when it came time to negotiate a new contract with Hamilton in 2023, Wolff played hardball. Hamilton wanted to sign for at least two firm years, Wolff only one. In the end, they compromised on a contract for 2024 with an option for 2025.
Hamilton, unimpressed, decided to look at his options, and signed to join Ferrari in 2025, telling Wolff in late January 2024, before the start of that season.
Wolff immediately phoned Marco Antonelli, to tell him the "very big news".
"'We put Kimi in Formula 1,'" Marco remembers Wolff saying. "'What do you think?'
"I said: 'Oh, [it] is a difficult question you ask me. Of course I'm happy that you think about Kimi but are you sure he's ready?'"
Mercedes were at a management away day. Wolff called his senior engineers together to tell them about Hamilton's decision.
"We were reviewing options and trying to come to a fairly rapid conclusion," says trackside engineering director Andrew Shovlin.
"We were all keen to just go with Kimi, which we knew was a bit of a risk. But it was quite exciting and we thought, based on his career to date, he had a good chance of being very good. It seemed like a good challenge."
Antonelli had not even driven an F1 car when Wolff made the call. Mercedes put together a testing programme for him, 20-odd days in cars a couple of years old at tracks all over the world to prepare him for his F1 debut in 2025.
Shovlin and the engineers were immediately impressed.
"It was how rapidly he would get up to speed," Shovlin says. "What you normally see with drivers is they're just incrementally going a little bit quicker, braking a bit later.
"If you compare with other drivers we've seen in an F1 car for the first time, the best I'd ever seen until then was George [Russell]. You suddenly saw someone who was quite similar.
"With Kimi, he took a couple of runs to work out how the car behaved and then he'd be more or less on the limit.
"The other thing you can see is the fidelity of the car control, how they can sit with it right on the edge of breaking away from them on entry to a corner, but they can just control it in that condition.
"Equally, when you looked at the mistakes he was making, they were often errors of judgement or lack of experience. They weren't run-out-of-talent mistakes."
Antonelli made one of these at the 2024 Italian Grand Prix. Wolff decided to give him his first experience of an F1 weekend in first practice at his home race at Monza.
It was a spectacular debut - for both good and bad reasons.
Antonelli set the fastest time on his first lap. Then he went for another. He was flying, miles quicker than anyone up to that point, but then he crashed heavily at the final corner, Parabolica.
"No-one on earth could have got the car around the corner at the speed he was attempting," Shovlin says. "He clearly got into his head that he would try and do something special and it was an error of judgment."
Wolff took Antonelli aside, told him it was OK, and not to worry about it. But the crash had a significant impact on Antonelli.
Wolff was very clear in public about managing expectations of Antonelli going into his debut season.
"I conditioned myself so strong that I said: 'There's going to be moments of brilliance and moments where you want to tear your hair out'," Wolff says.
There were stand-out moments - Antonelli out-qualified Russell at the second race of the season on the high-speed Jeddah street circuit and stuck it on pole for the sprint in Miami.
But the middle part of the season, through Europe, was a disappointment. A change to the rear suspension design made the car nervous and rocked his confidence. His pace was not impressive, and he made too many mistakes.
"We expected more highlights from him," Shovlin says.
Marco Antonelli explains: "Mercedes needed to have a good result after a period that was not like the Hamilton era. And, of course, needed two cars that always take points.
"Kimi felt this necessity. The crash in Monza was very tough for him to forget. It created on him a big pressure."
Wolff said the "moments of brilliance were there" but then there was "a spell of nine races that was really not good".
"Me, personally, I never doubted," says Wolff. "Other people doubted. In the team and externally."
A year on from his practice debut, Antonelli crashed again in Monza practice.
"This was the point where I said: 'Kimi, you've got to turn this around. This is just not good enough'," says Wolff. "He said: 'I know.'"
Marco Antonelli says he and his son talked a lot during this period and that Kimi "understood that everything can change".
"The period was bad but you can see light at the end of the tunnel," he says. "And step by step he started to take confidence."
Once F1 had left Europe in the autumn of last year, there was a shift.
"Suddenly, we felt like we were making really good progress," says Shovlin.
"There were signs towards the end of the year. I'm not saying any of us thought we'd see what we've seen so far this year, but that we had a decent F1 driver."
Antonelli has been rather more than that this year. He has taken the season by storm, and established a consistent supremacy over Russell.
In the best car in the field, Antonelli has taken six poles and six wins in 11 races and heads into the second half of the season, starting at the Dutch Grand Prix this weekend, with a 50-point lead in the championship, and well on course for his first world title. If it had not been for dodgy reliability, he could be even further ahead.
The extent of this turnaround has shocked almost everyone.
"We were all surprised," Wolff says. "My thoughts were always that he needed to make the experience of knowing all the tracks, the pressure of performing on such a high level under the spotlight of the media, the constant public feedback, whether you're doing well or not, the situations everyone wanted to be close to him.
"There wasn't one single defining factor where I would have said that made it difficult for him, but this year, he knew exactly what to expect. What was really nice to see is that the self-confidence, without feeling any entitlement, has shone."
Marco points to his son's "very strong" mentality.
"In F4 and Freca, he started with not good results, and he was able to remake everything and, at the end, work hard and win the championship," he says.
"We talk about F1. I don't know what the spark is in his brain, but Kimi in the past did the same."
Verstappen says: "For me, there was never any doubt that he would make the jump the year after and already be a lot more consistently competitive.
"It's normal in the progression of a driver. In your rookie season, it can be quite tough, but at the moment, of course, he's doing an amazing job."
Kimi pays tribute to his father, describing him as his "rock", while Wolff also praises the driver's "typical Italian family".
"They are caring, they are loving," Wolff says. "Kimi's character, he's gentle, he has empathy, he has charisma, he has the right amount of intelligence for being a racing driver."

Mercedes have been talking to Antonelli about managing his emotions, which have flared at times this season, such as in the sprint in Canada, when the racing between the two Mercedes drivers came close to boiling over.
Shovlin says: "He just says: 'I'm young, I'm Italian, what do you expect?'"
The remark reveals Antonelli's sense of humour, but also a maturity and self-awareness that might not always be expected in someone so young.
Wolff says: "He has all that. He's actually not a typical emotional Italian. He's so clear [in] what he needs to do in a car. I don't see lots of emotion. I see full focus, full concentration. I see, 'OK, this is a problem, let's analyse it, and move on.'
"You see him in a debrief afterwards. You couldn't really say whether there was a bad or a good session. It's all very balanced and stable."
Antonelli took advice on this when he met tennis legend Roger Federer at Wimbledon this summer.
"We chatted about my races," Antonelli says. "About when he used to play, and about life in general.
"About pressure, he just told me to focus on one race at a time, just focus on what you can control, and also to control the emotions, especially the ones that can make you do mistakes."
Federer's words echoed something Marco has always impressed on his son.
"In our family, we use this concept in normal life as well," he says. "We have to live every day our best day. You work hard every day to arrive at the end of the project you have."
Back in February 2024, Wolff followed up his phone call to Marco with a meeting in Milan.
"Toto said: "Of course it will be difficult, but I think after one year of experience, we can do very well with Kimi in F1," Marco says.
"The project was 2025 experience, 2026 start to achieve results. I think we overachieved."

Expressing grave concern over the high prevalence of child marriages resulting in underage pregnancies and deliveries in the State, West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari on Monday (September 7, 2026) said that the State had recorded nearly 60,000 underage institutional deliveries in the first six months of 2026.
Details of underage institutional deliveries from January 1, 2026 to June 30, 2026 had been obtained from the State Health Department, and the numbers were alarming, Mr. Adhikari said.
“As a result of the previous government, we are now number one in two criteria across the country — marriage of girls below 18 years of age, and deliveries before 18 years of age. These numbers are so high that there aren’t enough jails in which to put these people,” the Chief Minister said, addressing media persons at the State Secretariat.
Mr. Adhikari read out the provisions of the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006 and the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012, adding that the law prohibited marriage with a child below 18 years of age. In such cases, “Police action will be initiated and arrests will be made,” he said.
The Chief Minister emphasised that the practice of child marriage could not be allowed to prevail, and the State Health Department would issue a show-cause notice to the offenders, especially the husband, who would have to provide documentary evidence within a month that both he and his ‘wife’ were adults in accordance with the law.
“If he fails to do so, the DGP (Director General of Police), who is sitting right next to me, will take action as per the law,” Mr. Adhikari said. The State government would stop delivering benefits under all Central and State government welfare schemes to these families, he said. Action would be taken against the priest and qazi who solemnised the marriage, and against other family members, he added.
Sharing district-wise details of cases of underage pregnancies, the Chief Minister said 12,847 institutional childbirths by underage girls were recorded in Murshidabad district alone, followed by South 24 Parganas at 4,178.
West Bengal has recorded the highest number of child marriages over the past few years, despite schemes rolled out to keep girls in schools. According to the Sample Registration Survey report published in September 2025, West Bengal recorded 6.3% of females getting married before the age of 18 years, whereas at the national level, 2.1% of females got married before the age of 18 years. Murshidabad remains a hotspot for child marriages. About 55.4% women in the district aged 20 to 24 years said they were married before the age of 18 years, according to the National Family Health Survey-5.
Experts working on the ground, however, say that child marriage is a complex issue involving not only parental or social pressure but also cases of elopement, and minor grooms. They warn that the arrest of husbands may result in placing a strain on already marginalised families, and impact marital relations adversely.

A woman who testified against her own father after her mother was murdered in a notorious mafia killing in Italy is believed to have taken her own life.
Denise Cosco was found critically injured on Sunday and died later in hospital in Rome.
Her mother Lea Garofalo, who was killed in 2009, became a powerful symbol of resistance to the mafia after turning witness for the state against the 'Ndrangheta clan in southern Italy.
Those close to Cosco recall her bravery in speaking out at her father's trial, but also her tremendous struggle in the years that followed.
At 35, she died at the same age her mother was when she was murdered.
Enza Rando, a senator and anti-mafia lawyer who represented Cosco at the murder trial, described her death as "a profound wound for the entire country", and proof that the mafia not only kills, but creates "true monsters in the lives and souls" of those who survive.
Francesca Rispoli, co-president of the anti-mafia organisation Libera, said the death highlighted the struggle experienced by many who break with organised crime.
"The mafia, it's not just something physical. You can leave. You can change your name," she told the BBC. "But there is still a tie, a family tie, that stays… deep inside and is impossible to overcome."
Cosco, like her mother, had lived under state protection with a new name and identity for many years.
But Rispoli said she remained extremely vulnerable and had reconnected with her father, Carlo Cosco, in prison in recent years because, despite everything, she had felt a "hole in her life".
Friends say she struggled with mental health problems and addiction.
"Maybe this is a sign that those trying to lead another life need more support. Not just for one year – maybe their whole life," Rispoli argued, as organised crime groups in Italy – especially the 'Ndrangheta - involve close-knit family networks.
In Cosco's case, both her mother's family and her father were tied to the mafia.
She had always refused to believe her father's story that her mother had abandoned her to start a new life in Australia.
In fact, he had tricked Garofalo to a meeting, then had her strangled, her body dismembered then incinerated.
Several years later, a statement by one of the killers finally allowed police to recover some fragments of bone and a necklace, which Cosco identified.
At a public funeral in 2013, she spoke of her mother's courage in "putting herself on the line… for justice for all".
Her father and three accomplices were already serving life in prison.
At the trial, Cosco described herself as a "proud witness for justice" and said she had taken the difficult choice to testify – speaking from behind a screen – because she wanted "inner freedom to start over" with her life.
Prosecutors have now opened an investigation to determine whether there was any incitement to suicide and her phone has been seized for analysis.
Friends and supporters were due to gather in Milan on Friday evening to remember her near the spot where her mother was abducted.
"Denise's entire life revolved between the two extremes of courage and suffering," Luigi Ciotti, president of Libera wrote, calling that a difficult balance.
"Today, something in that fragile equilibrium was broken forever."

Bill Maher mocks Trump’s bizarre convention pledge of allegiance
‘This really happened this week in America, which used to be a real country,’ Bill Maher said on his show on Friday
Comedian Bill Maher mocked President Donald Trump’s bizarre version of the Pledge of Allegiance, which he had supporters recite during the Republican midterm convention in Dallas on Thursday.
The host of HBO’s Real Time with Bill Maher appeared stunned by the moment during his Friday night monologue.
“This really happened this week in America, which used to be a real country,” Maher, a longtime Trump critic, told the studio audience. “At the convention, he made everybody put their hand up and do a new pledge of allegiance.”
Maher then read aloud the words Trump had instructed supporters to repeat.
“I pledge to the greatest president in the history of the United States that loves us so much he can't even breathe, that I will go out with my family, my friends. I'll do it anyway — I don't care if I'm registered or not. I'm going to try and cheat like hell, like they do,” Maher said.
After finishing the passage, the host threw his hands in the air and said: “I got nothing anymore.”
Trump followed up the pledge Thursday night — the final evening of the first-of-its-kind convention — with a warning to supporters.
“You know what happens if you don't vote? You go to hell, you know that? Okay?” Trump said. “You go to hell, and I don't want that to happen to you.”
Maher has a long record of criticizing Trump on television.
In 2013, responding to Trump’s repeated false claim that Barack Obama was born outside the United States, Maher joked that Trump was the “spawn of his mother having sex with an orangutan.” Trump later sued Maher over the remark.
More recently, Maher has accused Trump of embracing socialism through his interventions in private businesses; denounced him as an “emperor” staging “gladiatorial games,” a reference to the UFC event at the White House; and described Trump’s followers as part of a “cult.”
Trump, for his part, has repeatedly attacked Maher, calling him “highly overrated” and accusing him of having “a terminal case of Trump Derangement Syndrome.”
The two had dinner at the White House in March 2025, after which Maher said the president had been “gracious and measured” and far different from the “crazy” man he sees on television.
Yet, the public insults continued afterward.

- An Intricate Key mould can be found by exploring the Winding Tunnels and destroying rubble piles or defeating certain enemies.
- The Intricate Key Cast can be crafted at level 4 Black Forge, using 5 Bloodgold Ingots.
- Use the cast at a Frost Foundry with Liquid Frost to create the Intricate Key.
The Deep North in Valheim 1.0 is packed with dangerous enemies, freezing conditions, and mysterious dungeons that clearly want you to grind in the game. Among the biggest roadblocks are the massive locked gates of Morkhalla that demand a special item: the Intricate Key. Unfortunately, you cannot simply loot it from any chest; rather, it has a dedicated crafting process. So, check this guide to learn everything about how to craft an Intricate Key in Valheim.
Items Required to Craft an Intricate Key in Valheim
Crafting an Intricate Key in Valheim will require you to have the Cast: Intricate Key alongside the Frost Foundry to use the Cast. Now, this cast is made using two key ingredients: the Intricate Key Mould and Bloodgold. So, here’s how you can get both items:
How to Get Intricate Key Mould in Valheim
The first thing you need to craft an Intricate Key in Valheim is its mould. You won’t be able to craft the key directly without having this item. Here’s what you need to do:
- Head to the Winding Tunnels, an area found beneath the settlements in the Deep North biome.
- Since these areas are full of enemies, make sure you’re equipped with the best weapons and armor in Valheim 1.0.
- Defeating the enemies in Winding Tunnels will give you a chance to obtain the Intricate Key mould.
How to Get Bloodgold in Valheim
Obtaining Bloodgold will be a tough task because you’ll have to defeat one of the most powerful creatures in Valheim. If you’ve explored the Deep North biome, you must have spotted the massive Gammeltroll.
Defeating the Gammeltroll will turn it into a petrified state, and then you can throw Ember Charges on its body to obtain the Petrified Tissue. Put this Petrified Tissue into a Blase Furnace to obtain Bloodgold in Valheim. If you need further help, our linked guide will help you out.
How to Make the Intricate Key
Once you have collected 5 Bloodgold Ingots and the Intricate Key Mould, you’re ready to learn how to craft the Intricate Key in Valheim. Follow the steps below to get the item:
- Combine the ingredients on a Level 4 Black Forge to create the Cast: Intricate Key.
- Take the cast to a Frost Foundry and use Liquid Frost to complete the crafting process.
- Note that Liquid Frost can be obtained by putting ice inside a Frigid Kiln.
- Once the crafting process is complete, the Intricate Key will rise from the Foundry, and you can collect it by pressing ‘E‘ or the interaction key.
How to Use the Intricate Key in Valheim
The Intricate Key isn’t just a collectible item. Its main purpose is to open the locked gates of Morkhalla, located in the Deep North.
While exploring the Deep North, you will come across some settlements that have the passage to the Winding Tunnels. Near them, you can find a tall tower with no gates on the ground. The only way to enter this tower is by using a Grappling Hook in Valheim.
Inside the tower, you will find stairs leading to a basement, where the locked gates to Morkhalla are located. Here, you can use the Intricate Key to open the gates and enter one of the major Deep North dungeons.
And that is all about how to craft an Intricate Key in Valheim. So, have you checked out the best Valheim seeds to have the dream start in the 1.0 update? Tell us in the comments below.

A team of Indian researchers has produced the first comprehensive molecular and functional profile of the venom gland of Stegodyphus sarasinorum, a colonial spider species found across the Indian subcontinent, to identify numerous proteins and small molecules that could serve as promising leads for future drug discovery.
Published in Springer Nature’s peer-reviewed, open-access journal Scientific Reports, the study identifies bioactive compounds associated with anti-cancer, antimicrobial and immune-related functions, while also demonstrating that venom gland extracts can kill cancer cells under laboratory conditions.
The researchers caution, however, that the findings represent an early stage of biomedical research and require extensive validation before any clinical application becomes possible.
Lead researcher A.P. Ajay Kumar of the Department of Zoology at Sree Neelakanta Government Sanskrit College, Pattambi, led the multidisciplinary study.
Unlike most spiders, which are solitary hunters, S. sarasinorum lives in permanent colonies, constructs communal silk nests and captures prey cooperatively. It is among only a small number of permanently social spider species known worldwide, thereby making it an important model for studying both spider behaviour and venom biology.
Although spider venom has long attracted scientific interest for their diverse biological activities, this is the first study to comprehensively analyse the molecular composition of the venom gland of this species using an integrated multi-omics approach, the researchers emphasise.
The research team combined transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics and Confocal Raman Spectroscopy to examine the spider’s venom gland in great detail. Their analysis identified 31 protein components through transcriptomic profiling and 32 proteins through proteomic analysis. In addition, Ultra High-Performance Liquid Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry (UHPLC-MS) detected 81 metabolites, including amino acids, biogenic amines and organic acids to provide a detailed molecular inventory of the venom gland.
To investigate the biological activity of these molecules, the researchers tested venom gland extracts against Dalton’s Lymphoma Ascites (DLA) cancer cells in laboratory experiments. The extracts exhibited dose-dependent cytotoxicity, meaning that higher concentrations destroyed a greater proportion of cancer cells.
The findings suggest that the venom gland contains molecules with anti-cancer potential, the experiments were conducted only in cultured cells. Nonetheless, further studies involving additional cancer models, healthy cells, animals and eventually clinical trials will be required before any therapeutic use can be considered.
Among the most significant discoveries was the identification of several protein families that are already known for their biomedical relevance. These include hemocyanin proteins, which are known to stimulate immune responses and have attracted considerable interest in cancer immunotherapy research. The study also detected U12 and U20 lycotoxins, peptide molecules that can disrupt the membranes of bacteria and cancer cells, making them promising templates for the future development of antimicrobial peptides and targeted anti-cancer compounds.
The experimental work was carried out by research scholar Veena Venugopal, with contributions from collaborators from Calicut University, S.N. College, Nattika, St. Joseph’s College, Devagiri, PSG Institute of Advanced Studies, Coimbatore; GITAM University, Andhra Pradesh; and Ajman University, UAE.
