Anthropologists and community leaders from Nagaland, a remote state in north-eastern India bordering Myanmar, have expressed joy and relief that human remains belonging to their ancestors that had been on display in a British museum for nearly a century are finally being returned.
On Monday, the Pitt Rivers Museum in Oxford announced that 39 pieces of human remains – including parts of skulls, a finger and a piece of skin with hair – belonging to the Naga tribes, will be returned to Nagaland after six years of negotiation between the community and the museum.
For the Nagas, the repatriation is not just about “bones and ancestral remains … It is about memory returning to where it belongs,” the community said in a statement.
“We are at peace,” said A Peihwang Wangsa, an Indigenous Konyak man involved in the repatriation negotiations. “Our forefathers are coming back.”
Wangsa, whose ancestors’ remains are among those being returned, added that the homecoming would be a moment of “mourning and celebration”.
NT Thamlong Phom, a Naga community leader from the Phom sub-tribe, said: “I feel joy, I feel blessed.
“Ever since the announcement was made, my entire community has felt happy,” he said. “Our ancestors’ spirit will have a final resting place.”
Thejao Vihienuo, who is also part of the repatriation discussions and went to Oxford in 2025, said he had been “angry and unhappy” to see the remains of his ancestors, which he said had been “taken in a most dubious manner”.
“It was displayed as if it was a trophy, but they silently spoke of the atrocities the British committed on our people,” he said.
The return caused “mixed feelings”, he said, but added: “We owe it to our ancestors to bring their remains back and put them to peaceful rest. And also to our younger generation to decolonise their minds and show that our children are not inferior to any white man.”
The Nagas are a transnational Indigenous group of tribes living in India’s north-east and parts of Myanmar, once associated with headhunting but now predominantly Christian.
The Pitt Rivers Museum, home to one of the world’s largest ethnological collections, has more than 6,500 Naga objects, 898 of which were on display. Most of the collection was “coercively” acquired by the colonial administrators James Philip Mills and John Henry Hutton.
The human remains were displayed at the museum for 80 years. In 2020, they were put into storage during a revamp aimed at addressing the institution’s colonial past and how exhibiting human remains “reinforced racist and stereotypical thinking” of other cultures.
The museum said in a statement: “Thirty-nine Naga ancestors will soon begin their journey home from Oxford to Nagaland.”
In November, a Naga delegation will visit Oxford for a handover ceremony and the remains are expected to arrive in Nagaland before the end of the year. They will be laid to rest in a traditional community ceremony in the state capital, Kohima.
The repatriation negotiations were led by representatives from all of the Naga tribes.
“It has been a journey of redemption,” said Prof Dolly Kikon, a Naga anthropologist. “This shows that we are no longer victims of colonial violence. We embrace our roles as people who find redemption and healing by giving dignity and honour to a very violent past.”
The negotiations started in 2020, when Kikon wrote to the museum after reading “an article in the Guardian that they were doing an ethical review” of the collection. “They replied within 24 hours,” said Kikon.
That was just the beginning of a lengthy process that soon expanded into a wider community-led campaign.
The Forum for Naga Reconciliation, a community peace group, assembled a team known as Recover, Restore and Decolonise, bringing together Naga volunteers from across the region to work on the repatriation effort.
“They travelled to villages and organised meetings to inform people about the remains,” said Arkotong Longkumer, a Naga anthropologist who worked closely with Kikon to lead the initiative, which he described as “open and transparent”.
“It was an intergenerational journey that brought together students, civil society, tribal leaders and the church,” said Longkumer, who teaches at Edinburgh University.
A Naga delegation, including tribal leaders, visited Oxford in 2025 to officially register a claim to the remains.
“I had never known our ancestral human remains had been taken away like that,” said Wangsa. “I felt angry when I saw them.”
Laura Van Broekhoven, director of the Pitt Rivers Museum and a professor of museum studies and ethics at Oxford University, said the museum was completing paperwork to enable the return of the remains.
“We will then start working towards the ceremonial aspects so we can have everything ready,” she said. “In our experience, handover ceremonies can be very emotional.”

Toothless Spurs blank again as new era turns into a false dawn
- Published
The banner held aloft by a Tottenham Hotspur supporter before kick-off was not so much a plea for action as a cry for help.
"Please Score A Goal" was the message brandished in the direction of the Spurs players as they came out against Everton in search of their first in the Premier League this season.
After another goalless 45 minutes, there was a compelling case for a hasty rewrite asking "Please Have A Shot" as, for all their possession, Roberto de Zerbi's expensively assembled side struggled to get anywhere near Jordan Pickford's goal.
And so it went on in an increasingly angry and frustrated atmosphere inside Tottenham Hotspur Stadium as Spurs' goalless league streak extended to 407 minutes as a stuttering start to what was meant to be brave new era continued.
It was the first time they have failed to score in their opening four league games across all four tiers - and also in four successive Premier League matches since September 2006.
The grim statistic would be bad enough in any circumstances, but it is even worse after Spurs spent in excess of £300m in the summer, much of it designed to give De Zerbi's side an added edge.
Instead, they are a blunt instrument.
This was the first Premier League goalless draw, in the 140th game, at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.
On this evidence, there will be more.
It may seem early days for an apology to the supporters, but De Zerbi felt the need as he said: "I'm sorry to the fans. We are sorry to the fans.
"They were fantastic, especially in the first part of the game because when they see the team is playing well, pushing to find the solution they were inside the pitch with my players. Then the reaction of the fans is normal. We have to say thanks all the time to them."
Everton could have actually made matters worse, but they are also short of attacking threat themselves - luckily for Spurs.
As the second half wore on, the resilient visitors actually missed the game's two best chances through Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall and Brennan Johnson, while the mood became increasingly sour as nerves and anxiety grew.
When £85m summer signing Mateus Fernandes had Spurs' first shot on target after 46 minutes, the stadium rattled to the sound of ironic applause.
There was no irony when they played the ball around at the back with only seven minutes left, and when the final whistle sounded it was just like old times - or at least like last season - as jeers sent De Zerbi's players on their way.
He went through the card in an attempt to change this embarrassing barren sequence in front of goal, playing new signings from Manchester City, Omar Marmoush and Savio, in the attacking positions, with Dominic Solanke handed his first league start of the campaign.
As time went on and the tension mounted, Mohammed Kudus and James Maddison were sent on, but it was another substitute, Lucas Bergvall, who almost snatched victory with a late long-range effort, saved by Everton goalkeeper Pickford after he had gifted the Swede possession and an opportunity.
Watching it all from close quarters was a grim-faced Richarlison, the 29-year-old Brazil striker in dispute with the club over the remaining nine months of his contract.
He was left out of De Zerbi's Premier League squad after a proposed deadline-day return to former club Everton collapsed. A switch back to Brazil with Vasco da Gama has also failed to materialise.
The 'xG' - expected goals - statistic suggests Spurs should have scored three or four goals this season, but their non-penalty xG per shot this season is just 0.066. It gives them an expected conversion rate of 6.6%.
In layman's terms, it means they are not very good when comes to creating an attacking threat.
De Zerbi, never someone to disguise his emotions, grew more animated and irritated as the game went on, marching on to the pitch at the final whistle for an exchange with substitute Mathys Tel.
When any side embarks on the sort of root and branch revolution the Italian presided over this summer, it is inevitable there will be teething problems and time required for understandings and relationships to form.
And the change is understandable after two successive 17th-placed finishes in the Premier League. Indeed, Spurs' last league goal actually came against Everton on the final day of last season, courtesy of Joao Palhinha.
It kept them in the top flight, allowing them to make a fresh start for this campaign.
De Zerbi, who still has much work to do to rid Spurs of the aftershock of two poor seasons, said: "I think in the first 30 minutes we were very, good but we didn't find a goal. I think in that moment we suffer too much with confidence and this is another important part for us at the moment.
"In the second half, I observed many players had a little less confidence and I don't like this. They have to be happy and understand we are in the right way.
"The players are human and they have emotions and they think with their head. My position is to help them and stay focus on the improvement we have to do. If we play 90 minutes like we did in the first 30 minutes, I think we are going to win many games."
Spurs, however, have a toothlessness that must be a concern. It is certainly one for the supporters who watched their players either take too long over chances or, on many occasions, passed on the responsibility.
They also ran into a rugged Everton defence, with Jarrad Branthwaite magnificent as he stepped up his claims for a place in Thomas Tuchel's next England squad after injury troubles.
For Spurs, however, there were few positives as the wait for a first Premier League win - and goal - this season goes on.

New Delhi, Sep 12: Chinese President Xi Jinping on Saturday hailed the BRICS bloc as the world's most influential platform for cooperation among emerging markets and developing countries and called on the grouping to play its "due role" in bringing peace in West Asia.
Addressing the BRICS summit here, Xi said China will work with BRICS members to achieve peace and tranquillity in West Asia and the Gulf region, state-run Xinhua news agency reported.
He said as the situation in West Asia and the Gulf region continues to evolve, the war there has caused serious losses to people across the region and does not serve the common interests of the international community.
He called on the leaders of major emerging economies to play the “due role” in bringing peace to West Asia, urging member states to stand on the right side of history.
He said BRICS countries should oppose the Cold War mentality and called on the member states to oppose violations of other countries' sovereignty and interference in their internal affairs
Xi said the BRICS countries should strengthen cooperation in AI initiative to promote new industrialisation through AI among BRICS countries
He called on BRICS countries to lead global governance in cyberspace, outer space, and the deep sea and amplify the voice of the Global South.
He said that BRICS countries should pioneer in innovative development as well as in maintaining peace and stability, boosting mutual learning among civilisations.
He said the members should focus on improving global governance, noting that the grouping should steer the international order toward greater justice and equity, and work together to build a community with a shared future for humanity.
Xi arrived here early Saturday, marking his first trip to India in seven years.
He was received at the Bharat Mandapam for the 18th BRICS summit by Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
The other leaders attending the summit in New Delhi are Russian President Vladimir Putin, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto, Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed Ali, Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi and Vietnamese Prime Minister Le Minh Hung.
UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres, WTO Director General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, WHO Chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, New Development Bank (NDB) President Dilma Rousseff and Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank Chief Zou Jiayi are also attending the BRICS summit.

The All India Students’ Association (AISA) on Saturday (September 12, 2026) accused an Assistant Proctor of assaulting students amid an ongoing protest over poor food quality at Jamia Millia Islamia’s Jammu and Kashmir Girls’ Hostel. The university denied the allegation and instead said the students had manhandled security personnel. The authorities also said most of the students’ demands had already been accepted.
The protest broke out on Thursday (September 10, 2026) after students complained about the poor quality of food served in the mess, alleging that insects and foreign objects were regularly found in their meals. The students have been demanding an immediate change of the mess vendor, recruitment of female staff, and a written assurance from the administration that no disciplinary action will be taken against those participating in the agitation.
In a statement issued on Saturday (September 12, 2026), AISA accused the university administration of using force against the demonstrating students. The student body claimed that the assistant proctor Maqsood Ahmad Malik manhandled and assaulted a student near the Dean of Students’ Welfare office around 1 a.m. on Friday (September 11, 2026), after the electricity was switched off. It also alleged that several students suffered minor injuries during the commotion.
The students, AISA said, continued their sit-in through the night near Centenary Gate despite the power outage. It also alleged that Gate No. 13 was closed and barricaded with three layers, which it described as an attempt to isolate the protesters.
Rejecting the allegations, university officials said most demands were accepted on day one and accused the students of escalating the situation.
A Jamia Millia Islamia spokesperson said, “Students broke two gates of the girls’ hostel, putting everyone’s security at risk, and manhandled members of the proctorial team.” The university also added that the protesters were not demonstrating at the designated protest site near Gate No. 18.
The university also clarified that lights in parts of the campus are routinely turned off to save energy and the move was unrelated to the protest.

Buddhist monk arrested in suspected $3m embezzlement scandal
- Published
Thai police have arrested a Buddhist monk on suspicion of embezzling 100 million baht ($3m; £2.2m) from his monastery, along with a suspected female accomplice he was filmed having sex with.
Phra Wachirayan Wi, a former abbot at the prominent 14th-Century Wat Phutthaisawan in the ancient capital of Ayutthaya, allegedly pocketed donations meant for the temple on more than 20 occasions over two years.
In Thailand, Buddhist monks take a vow of celibacy and also renounce material possessions. He was defrocked after his arrest. He has yet to comment publicly.
The latest arrests come just over a year after another sex-and-blackmail case involving senior monks rocked Thailand's monastic community.
The 66-year-old was known for creating a highly-coveted coin amulet. Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul reportedly owns some of his creations.
Thailand's Buddhist institution has long been plagued with reports of monks breaking their vow of celibacy, trafficking drugs and committing financial crimes.
In July last year, police opened a hotline for people to report "misbehaving monks" after at least nine monks were found to have had sex with a woman. She then blackmailed them with photos and videos of the acts for nearly $12 million.
Police on Friday said they identified two streams of money linked to donation receipts Phra Wachirayan had issued in the temple's name – one was meant for temple renovations, while the other was payment for amulets and other sacred objects.
"But the money from both streams did not enter the temple's account. Not a single baht," lead police investigator Pattanasak Bupphasuwan told a news conference, according to reports.
Police found cash and gold bars worth more than 100 million baht while raiding Phra Wachirayan's residence on Thursday, with counting going on until late into the night, Thai news outlet The Nation reported.
While examining CCTV footage in the residence, police found a clip of him having sex with a woman on his dining table.
Authorities identified her as 47-year-old Punyavee Rungrueang, who has been arrested on charges of abetting a state official in illegal activities. She has yet to comment publicly.
Many monks in Thailand receive stipends from the government and are therefore considered state officials.
Police seized 35 gold amulets, along with about 1.5kg of gold bars and jewellery, worth an estimated 6.04 million baht, from Punyavee's home.
Police believe Punyavee helped Phra Wachirayan manage his embezzled proceeds, noting that tens of millions of baht circulated through her bank accounts each year, The Bangkok Post reported.
Investigators say they started looking into the case in mid July, after receiving an anonymous tip alleging Phra Wachirayan of misconduct and misuse of temple funds.
Two or three other people could be involved in the case, they say.

Lebanese army detains Bashar Assad's relative on weapons and drugs charges
Lebanese authorities have detained a relative of ousted Syrian President Bashar Assad along with the son of a notorious drug dealer
BEIRUT -- Lebanese authorities have detained a relative of ousted Syrian President Bashar Assad along with the son of a notorious drug dealer in northeast Lebanon on charges of carrying weapons and drugs, officials and the Lebanese army said Saturday.
Suleiman Assad and Ali Zeiter, son of Noah Zeiter, the suspected drug trafficker arrested last year, were detained Friday near the northeastern city of Baalbek, said the two judicial officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media. Suleiman Assad is the son of Hilal Assad, a cousin of the ousted president.
A number of Syrian officials and relatives of Assad have fled from Syria to other countries including Lebanon, after the five-decade Assad family rule came to an end in December 2024, when Islamist rebels seized power. Bashar Assad and his younger brother, Maher, have been living i n Russia.
The Lebanese army said in a statement that it detained three people, including a Syrian citizen who did not have documents proving that he is staying legally in Lebanon.
The army said they had weapons with them along with hashish, a drug that is processed from cannabis that are widely planted in northeast Lebanon. The army did not release the names but the initials of their first and family names matched those of Assad and Zeiter. The army said they were questioned under the supervision of judicial officials.
The arrest of Suleiman Assad comes weeks after Lebanon handed over to Syrian authorities a retired major general who commanded a division in Bashar Assad’s army.

When my eldest son was a little boy, I did something that felt quietly monumental in the moment and slightly ridiculous — I created a Gmail account in his name.
He was 3 years old. Far too young to know what email was, let alone care about it. My BlackBerry (yes, I had a BlackBerry, it was 2010) probably looked more like something he could play games on.
At that stage of life, his interests were vast but often limited to dinosaurs, Duplo, bouncy balls, and snacks. Lots of snacks. There was also him asking "why?" approximately 275 times an hour. But I had the vague sense that childhood moved too quickly and that memories — especially the small ones — had a way of dissolving if you didn't trap them somehow.
I was also pregnant with his twin brothers, so preserving what I could of his "only child" status was important ahead of such a big change. So I opened the account and wrote him his first email.
I wrote down things I didn't want to forget
The plan was simple. Over the years, whenever something happened that I didn't want to forget, I would write to him. When he turned 18, I would hand over the password and let him open the whole archive at once. A digital time capsule, except instead of artifacts, it would contain the messy, funny, sentimental observations of a mother trying to keep up with a growing boy.
I assumed I would write occasionally. It would be fun. Instead, I wrote a lot.
The big moments were easy. The first time he caught a ball. It was at a kid's birthday party at a sports gym. That earned a lengthy email complete with my highly technical analysis of the play ("you ran very fast and didn't drop the ball and everyone started yelling!"). Birthdays, school milestones, and the various phases of childhood enthusiasm — dinosaurs, sharks, Bigfoot, Sesame Street — each found their way into the inbox.
But over time, I discovered that the emails I liked writing the most were about the smaller things. Sometimes they contained only a sentence or two.
One afternoon, I wrote about how the sun hit his hair as I looked back at him in his car seat. It caught the light in a way that made me stop where I was, in the driveway, and just look at him. I pulled out my phone and quickly wrote an email. It was the kind of moment that would normally disappear five seconds later, but writing it down felt like pressing pause.
Another email documented the day he very patiently helped bathe his brothers. I watched as he knelt over the tub with great seriousness, telling them that it was "bath time," repeating instructions until one of them threw a wet face cloth at his head. But he maintained composure throughout his huffing and puffing with frustration.
Those moments never make it into photo albums, but they are the ones that can begin to define a person.
It became kind of like a journal
Over the years, the emails piled up. Some were long and reflective. Others were barely a few sentences typed quickly before I forgot the moment that inspired them. Some included motherly advice that he didn't ask for. Sometimes there were stretches when I didn't write at all. But when I did write, the emails always ended with how much I love him.
The account became a strange journal. Except the audience was a future version of my son.
Every so often, I would wonder what it would feel like when he opened them. Would he read them all? Not read any? Would he laugh? Would he be embarrassed that I kept calling him cute and adorable too much when he was a toddler? Or that I was "that mom" at a football game when he scored a touchdown.
Then, suddenly, 18 arrived.
I gave him the password
Handing over the password felt weirdly ceremonial. It was the end of a project that had been quietly running in the background of our lives for nearly two decades. A teeny act of parenting that required no school forms, no carpools, sports equipment, or doctors' appointments, just the occasional email and the belief that someday it would matter.
When he logged in for the first time, he wasn't opening a typical inbox. He was opening 18 years of moments that might otherwise have vanished: graduations and birthdays, but also the sunlight, the shoelaces, and a thousand other things that seemed ordinary at the time.
Parenthood has a strange relationship with time. When you're in the weeds of it, the days feel so long and chaotic. The lunches to pack, socks to match, and endless reminders to clean bedrooms.
But when you look back, it all compresses into a handful of flashes.
A laugh at the dinner table.
A muddy pair of cleats.
A boy kneeling down to help his brother.
An inside joke.
The email account turned those flashes into something permanent.
Once I realized how meaningful it had become, I did the only logical thing. I created accounts for his younger twin brothers, too. Their inboxes are filling up with the same stories, observations, and evidence that wearing socks outside without shoes will cause holes.
Someday, they'll receive their passwords as well. And it won't just be opening emails. It will be a record of sorts, of a childhood lived alongside their older brother. A childhood full of shared kitchens, backyard games, and the small daily acts of kindness that siblings rarely notice in the moment.
By then, the house will be quieter, the bedrooms cleaner, and the years of noise and motion that once defined them as kids in our family will have softened into memory. But inside those Gmail accounts will be proof that time didn't simply rush past us unnoticed. It was captured, one small moment at a time, as they waited patiently for the day they would look back and see not just who they became as young men, but how deeply they were loved every step of the way.

A decade after her sophomore feature The Love Witch, Anna Biller has returned from a whole other era with another technicolor fever dream of female rage.
In The Face of Horror, the writer/director updates the Kabuki ghost story Yotsuya Kaidan, which she deconstructs for the medieval era with help from stars Kristine Frøseth, Jonah Hauer-King, Ellie Bamber and Bella Heathcote.
The film begins with the knight Edward (Hauer-King) asking Eleanor’s (Frøseth) father for her hand in marriage, which the patriarch rejects over the suitor’s scoundrel, thieving ways. Unable to take “no” for an answer, Edward kills Eleanor’s father, before deceitfully promising her to exact vengeance on his killer and convincing her to marry him so that he can protect her.
As months go by, Edward has grown disgusted with a postpartum Eleanor, instead courting the recently widowed noblewoman Isabel (Heathcote), who devises a plot to kill Eleanor so they can be together. With Edward’s conscience and Eleanor’s livelihood hanging in the balance, the film culminates in a bloody final act filled with ghostly horror and vengeance.
Watch on Deadline
Kristine presents a perfectly subdued performance as the sweet, naive Eleanor, desperate for the love of her own husband, so much so that she’s prepared to go through great lengths to fit his vision of beauty.
As Edward, Hauer-King is a villainous medieval fuckboy with little redeeming qualities. But plagued by the threat of eternal damnation, the actor delivers a tortured portrayal of the weak knight as he struggles to outrun his toxic nature and be redeemed after being haunted for his actions drives him to the point of madness.
Bamber gives a surprise breakout performance as Eleanor’s strong-willed sister Beatrice, whose love for her sister leads to a quest for vengeance that will have audiences cheering, as well as crying.
The final product should be worth the decade-long wait for Biller fans, as she weaves a stunning cinematic ode to Hollywood’s technicolor era and the tragic beauty of the original Kabuki tale, featuring an emotionally volatile narrative with strong operatic performances from its cast that walk the line between camp and Shakespearean drama.
With The Face of Horror, Biller has provided another fix for cinephiles craving some good old-fashioned filmmaking with a contemporary feminist heartbeat.

Is a free VPN worth using? Here's why it could be risky
Free tiers backed by paying subscribers are easier to evaluate than unlimited VPNs that won't explain how they make money.
The old "if it's free, you're the product" line is catchy, but it's too simple for free VPNs. Some reputable providers offer limited free plans because they hope a portion of people who try will eventually pay. Other services rely on advertising, collect more data than privacy-minded users may be comfortable with or aren't clear about how they make money. So a free VPN can be worth using, but the price tag tells you less than the provider behind it and the tradeoffs attached to the free plan.
A virtual private network routes your internet connection through a VPN server before sending traffic on to websites and online services. The VPN app encrypts the connection between your device and that server, while sites you visit generally see the server's public IP address rather than your normal one. That can reduce what your internet provider or Wi-Fi operator learns about the destinations you connect to. Our explanation of how a VPN works goes further into the technical side.
This setup allows you to change your virtual location with a VPN, but it doesn't make you anonymous. Websites can still recognize you through logged-in accounts, cookies, GPS data and other identifiers. Not everyone needs a VPN running all the time, either. What matters here is that using one places a VPN company in a trusted position: you're reducing what one part of the network (your ISP) can see by routing the connection through another.
Why free VPNs can be risky
The pros and cons of a free VPN start with a few obvious compromises, some of which are exacerbated versions of issues inherent to VPNs. Sending traffic through another server can add latency or reduce connection speeds, which is present with any VPN but might be worse on free offerings that impose speed caps. Free VPN plans may offer fewer server locations or impose data limits. Some websites, streaming services and workplace systems block VPN connections, which becomes more of an issue when you have fewer server options for free. These are limitations you must decide whether you're willing to accept.
Privacy practices are harder to judge based on the app itself. The Federal Trade Commission has warned about this tradeoff: a VPN app gets access to internet traffic as it passes through the service, and some free apps make money through advertising or by sharing information with third parties. In other words, hiding some connection information from your ISP doesn't help much if the VPN provider handles that information in malicious ways.
A 2026 NDSS study of Android VPN apps shows why that concern isn't theoretical. Researchers tested 281 popular VPN apps available on the Google Play Store. They found that 29 leaked user traffic outside the VPN tunnel, 61 transmitted some unencrypted data and 76 sent Android Advertising IDs, which can be used for tracking. The study only examined Android apps, so those figures can't be directly applied to VPNs on every platform. They do show that an app saying "connected" doesn't guarantee the connection is being handled securely, though.
In some cases, the problem begins before there's a VPN connection at all. There have been many cases of malware posing as free VPN tools. Having a VPN also doesn't change whether you need antivirus or other malware protection, because these tools do different jobs. A VPN protects the connection between your device and its server. It doesn't stop malicious software from running on your computer or keep you from entering a password on a phishing site.
How to tell if a free VPN is worth using
To evaluate a free VPN, start with its business model. A limited free tier attached to a paid subscription service has an obvious source of funding. The company can restrict the free plan and use it to attract customers without the free version having to generate all of its revenue. Our selection of the best free VPNs for 2026 all come from providers that also sell subscriptions. That's a useful signal, not proof that every freemium VPN is trustworthy.
Next, check whether the provider gives you enough information to verify its claims. Its ownership should be clear, and the privacy policy should spell out what data is collected and how it's used. A recent public security audit carries more weight than simply putting "no logs" on a product page. The Electronic Frontier Foundation's VPN guidance similarly recommends examining data-collection practices, ownership and independent audits instead of relying on marketing claims alone.
The VPN should also explain how it secures the connection. Established protocols such as WireGuard and OpenVPN are widely used, while a provider that won't identify its underlying technology gives you less to evaluate. Features such as a kill switch can help too: if the VPN connection drops, the kill switch blocks internet traffic instead of quietly letting it continue outside the tunnel.
Data caps, smaller server lists and paid-only feature sets are understandable compromises: you know what the free service is withholding and can decide whether you care. If a VPN promises unlimited usage while making its ownership, data practices and/or source of revenue difficult to figure out, the compromise is much harder to see. That's the kind of "free" worth avoiding.

Tamil Nadu recorded nearly 45,000 fewer births in 2025 than the previous year, with the number of births falling by 5.3% from 8.47 lakh in 2024 to 8.02 lakh, pointing to a continuing decline in births in the State.
The decline comes against the backdrop of a long-term fall in fertility in the State. In 2026, five lakh-odd births were recorded so far, according to Civil Registration System data.”
While the decline in births reflects a broader demographic transition, with implications for the workforce and ageing population, experts say greater attention must be paid to education, childcare, social security, elderly care and standard of living.
T. Sundararaman, former executive director, National Health Systems Resource Centre, said the total fertility rate among women of reproductive age fell below the replacement level of 2.1 in Tamil Nadu nearly 20 years ago. “We continued to have a positive population growth rate because of population momentum. We have now moved beyond this phenomenon and a decline in the population is likely to occur,” he said.
S. Irudaya Rajan, chairperson, International Institute for Migration and Development, Thiruvananthapuram, pointed out that Tamil Nadu is better placed compared with Kerala, which has recorded around three lakh births.
“There will be no short-term impact. The State government can focus on creating a productive, healthy population of eight lakh-plus by investing in quality education over the next 20 to 25 years. The focus should be on quality rather than quantity,” he said.
“First of all, there is no need to worry about the low fertility rate or the decline in births,” Padmavathi Srinivasan, independent research consultant in demography, said, adding: “This opens up opportunities to increase and improve the standard of living and enable people to better access the State’s resources. The State government should seize this opportunity and capitalise on low fertility.”
Observing that politicians would worry about what would happen to the State’s labour force, she said, “but this is the time to focus on education and employment opportunities. Tamil Nadu is a prosperous State, but this prosperity needs to translate to better living standards.”
“It would be an injustice if the State focussed on increasing fertility and channelled government funds towards it. Rather, it should focus on the existing population, especially the youth. The State should pay attention to the foundations, such as quality education and the nutritional status of children. There are still pockets of people living in poverty, those who have no access to opportunities and have not benefitted from the State’s economic growth.”
Financial incentives to reverse low fertility rates have never worked, as evidenced in many developed countries, she said, asking: “So, why go down that route, when there are much more pressing issues we need to tackle.”
Professor Rajan said the State government’s “Thaimaman Thanga Mothiram Thittam”, under which one-gram gold rings will be gifted to babies born in government hospitals, is unlikely to help increase births. Increasing maternity leave to women government employees for a third child cannot be considered a meaningful incentive, he believed.
Policies alone will not help much. At best, they may add another 5,000-odd births, he said. “Children are assets, but when you ask couples today, many consider them liabilities. This mindset should change. Increasing the fertility rate is not simple, given factors such as delayed marriages. To motivate young couples to have children, we need out-of-the-box, innovative ideas.”
Priority areas
Professor Sundararaman said increasing longevity means that there will be more people aged 65 or 70 and above. “At the same time, we will have less working age population and a larger elderly population that needs to be cared for. This has already happened in most developed countries that have stronger social security systems and better elderly care,” he said.
“I am less worried about productivity and more concerned about social security and elderly care. We need policies that anticipate these changes,” he added.
Efforts simply to increase childbearing are unlikely to work. What can make a difference is providing child care support for the first two children, he said. “We need to have innovative thinking and creative community-based efforts for elderly care. Our priorities should include elderly care, social security, child care support, good quality primary education and measures that make it easier for working women for childcare. Funds should be better utilised to establish facilities, such as creches for working women,” he added.

If you ask most satellite companies aside from SpaceX, they will tell you the world doesn’t have enough capacity for launching payloads into orbit. This is despite the blistering launch cadence we’ve seen around the world in recent years, led by SpaceX’s Falcon 9 rocket.
Customers in any sector will, of course, usually welcome competition. Theoretically, competition will lead to lower prices and allow the best to rise to the top. It seems like the customers buying launch services were right. SpaceX is dialing back its Falcon 9 launch program, and there is no certainty about when SpaceX’s reusable next-generation super-heavy-lift rocket, Starship, will carry anything to orbit besides the company’s own Starlink satellites.
So it’s no surprise satellite operators are cheering the success of a new launch provider. This was especially the case a few days ago, when Germany’s Isar Aerospace reached orbit for the first time with its Spectrum rocket. The launcher delivered a batch of CubeSats to low-Earth orbit from a spaceport in northern Norway, and Isar tasted success after its first test flight ended in failure last year.
Isar’s success is good news for Europe’s space sector, eager for a new path to orbit alongside the continent’s incumbent launch providers, Arianespace and Avio. Several European companies are running to catch up with Isar, including another German startup, Rocket Factory Augsburg, and Spain’s PLD Space. The Exploration Company, based in Germany and France, is working on a heavy-lift-class rocket engine.
Up early
Halfway around the world from Europe, executives at the Japanese-headquartered satellite company Astroscale were awake at 5 am local time on Sunday to watch the live webcast from Norway as Isar aimed for the stars. Just days earlier, Astroscale announced it had signed a deal with Isar to launch a mission as soon as next year.
This was the second launch contract Astroscale has inked with Isar. The companies announced a contract in March for the Spectrum rocket to launch a different Astroscale satellite. Astroscale signed these agreements with Isar before the company achieved orbit.
Astroscale wasn’t alone in placing early bets on Isar. Government-backed missions from the European Space Agency, the European Union, and the Norwegian and German governments make up the bulk of the company’s launch backlog. Those customers have an interest in helping Isar gain a foothold in the launch market.
But Isar Aerospace could not count Astroscale as part of its captive market, so it was noteworthy that an established company selected an unproven rocket to launch two of its most important missions. Astroscale’s business is focused on satellite servicing and mitigation of space junk, a segment of the market that matches well with rockets the size of Isar’s Spectrum for dedicated rides to orbit.
Another satellite servicing company, US-based Katalyst Space, launched a spacecraft in July in pursuit of a NASA astronomy satellite falling out of orbit. Like Astroscale, Katalyst required a dedicated launch into a unique orbit to reach its target. It chose the seldom-used air-launched Pegasus XL rocket made by Northrop Grumman. Technical problems prevented Katalyst from rescuing NASA’s aging Swift observatory.
One of Astroscale’s missions assigned to launch with Isar Aerospace is ELSA-M, led by Astroscale’s UK division. The ELSA-M spacecraft will capture and deorbit a satellite in Eutelsat’s OneWeb broadband constellation to demonstrate end-of-life servicing. The other is ADRAS-J2, a demonstration mission partially funded by the Japanese space agency that will attempt to grab onto a defunct Japanese rocket in space and remove it from orbit. ADRAS-J2 follows a highly successful demo mission called ADRAS-J that approached and inspected the same Japanese rocket body in 2024.
Both missions are key to proving out Astroscale’s capabilities for what it sees as lucrative business opportunities in the satellite servicing market. Ars spoke with Chris Blackerby, Astroscale’s chief operating officer, this week to discuss the company’s goals in satellite servicing and its appetite for launch services. We present a portion of the interview below.
Nobu Okada, chief executive officer of Astroscale Holdings, center, and Chris Blackerby, group chief operating officer, left, and Nobuhiro Matsuyama, chief financial officer, pose for a photograph during the company’s listing ceremony at the Tokyo Stock Exchange on June 5, 2024.
Ars Technica: You must have been thrilled with the results from Isar’s test flight. What was it like seeing the rocket reach orbit?
Chris Blackerby: It was Sunday morning, 5 am or so Japan time, and I was up watching. They did a fantastic job in everything from the PR side of it, having the chief engineer on there to explain everything. Even just watching them explain through as I was sitting on my couch early in the morning on Sunday, my confidence was growing as I was watching the team explain everything they’d done, all the prep they had taken to get to that point. We’d done a lot of background research. We had teams go out there to do due diligence research at their manufacturing site and talk to a lot of their technical leaders. So we were pretty confident already. Certainly, the launch was incredible. Checking off all the markers, all the milestones, deploying the payloads—it was everything we could have hoped for. Obviously, congratulations to them. But yeah, you’re right. We have two big missions set up on Isar, and we’re excited to see them continue to improve and show success and get to launch with them.
Ars: Astroscale’s business case seems to require dedicated launches. Rideshare doesn’t really work if you’re trying to launch into a very specific orbit and reach a specific satellite for servicing. Is that correct? Why not go for a launch on a proven rocket, like Rocket Lab’s Electron, which you used for your previous mission?
Blackerby: Launch, as you well know, is the big issue around the industry writ large. First of all, to answer the specific question, yeah, you’re right, dedicated launch is pretty essential for us for most of our missions. We could do a rideshare, but it’s much more complicated. So a dedicated launch makes it much better. Then we have to factor in capacity for the payload, and that can answer your second question. Right now, for Rocket Lab current capability, we’ve expanded beyond it. ADRAS-J was smaller, mass-wise, so it could fit into an Electron. ADRAS-J2 and ELSA-M cannot. Of course, they could fit into (Rocket Lab’s) Neutron, but they’re not ready yet.
And when we look around at other options, Stephen, for all of the talk about the ubiquity of launch and the dropping prices and the capacity that’s everywhere, I don’t know. I don’t see it yet. There are not a lot of consistently reliable options that are out there. I don’t think that’s anything that’s too controversial to say. So we had to look for something that fit our budget. It had to fit our capacity in terms of size. It should be dedicated, as you mentioned. So when you get that Venn diagram that throws in all of those various requirements, Isar really fit the bill. And yes, choosing a launch provider that hasn’t proven consistent success yet is definitely a risk. But as I said, we did a lot of checking on them, a lot of due diligence, and we’re very confident what we what we decided.
Ars: The only other proven launch provider in that 1-ton range is Firefly Aerospace, but they’ve had some issues with their Alpha rocket.
Blackerby: That’s exactly right. Our missions are around that area, under a ton, but in the 500 to 700 kilogram area. And yeah, there’s not much. There were a bunch that were out there that were in that area for a while, including Relativity, they were aiming for that, and Astra was in that. There were a few others that were in that range at one time. But everybody is going bigger now, so there’s not a lot. There are still a few small ones out there, but to fit into that dedicated 1-ton class, there’s not a lot. We’re hopeful. We’re thinking about launch vehicles, which we all have to be thinking about, especially with all of the SpaceX news recently, and the uncertainties that have been widely reported about how available rideshares are going to be with SpaceX. We’re just excited to see proof from a lot of different operators. Blue Origin, we saw the big Stoke fundraise recently, so yeah, we’ll see. But you’re right. As far as 500-kilogram to 1-ton class, there are not a lot of options.
King Charles III views a scale replica of Astroscale’s ELSA-M satellite during his visit to the Sustainable Markets Initiative exhibition and reception at Hampton Court Palace on March 12, 2026, in London.
Ars:The ADRAS-J mission appeared to be a huge success for Astroscale. What did you learn, and how did that prepare you for going up to grab that rocket?
Blackerby: It was such an incredible mission. I love talking about it. It was pretty ground-breaking. We are extremely excited and extremely grateful to JAXA (the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency) for driving this, and this is the first step toward proving out an on-orbit servicing capability toward more sustainable use of space and debris removal, which was the foundation of Astroscale. But beyond that, the capabilities to identify, approach, rendezvous with an object in orbit, which is fairly unprecedented from a commercial company, especially a non-communicative one like the ADRAS-J client was, as it will be again for ADRAS-J2.
In terms of what we learned, boy, we need a whole conversation on this. But just building out a mission that needed to approach an unprepared, uncommunicative object, everything that goes into that from the hardware side, from the ConOps (concept of operations) development, making sure that we make it as as safe as possible, so that there is fault identification analysis to say, ‘OK, detect the problem, make sure that the spacecraft knows that when it’s autonomously approaching, as it gets close, it can identify where there’s any kind of anomaly, and it knows we need to try again. Safety is the paramount issue when we’re doing anything like this, approaching an object in orbit. That was key, and all of those learnings from designing, building, manufacturing, launching, operating the satellite. It was everything. We learned so much from that.
The pictures, which you’ve seen, the images that we took from ADRAS-J are so exquisite, and it helped us to build ADRAS-J2. We now know what the client object looks like. We know it’s not rotating. That was a key step. We built ADRAS-J to be able to rotate around the client object in orbit, so that if we had to find that payload adapter as we’re spinning around, we could go in and grab it for ADRAS-J2. What we learned with ADRAS-J is the client object is pretty stably pointing down toward the Earth. We got a very clear image of what the object looks like right now. We know it’s not degraded. We know that there’s a clear path toward grabbing it at the payload adapter. All of those are things that we learned over the development of ADRAS-J that have helped building ADRAS-J2, I won’t say easier because none of this is easy, but easier than it would have been without that kind of capability and that kind of knowledge.
Ars:You have another mission working with JAXA, ISSA-J1, to go rendezvous and inspect two decommissioned Japanese satellites. How is that different than inspecting a rocket body?
Blackerby: ADRAS-J2 is going to an oblong rocket body. It’s not spinning. ISSA-J1 is going to satellites, and it’s going to have to approach something that has a solar array sticking out, so we’re expecting that it could be spinning. So the RPO (rendezvous and proximity operations) is definitely going to be more complex. We need to be able to develop this tech to precisely approach this large piece of debris that likely is not going to be a stable object, and we’re also going to a couple of them with ISSA-J1. A lot of the technical capabilities that we’ve developed by building out all of our missions… they share a common baseline in terms of technology as we think about the guidance, navigation and control, and the visualization and the RPO that’s necessary to do this identification and approach. But there are all these little differences, and that’s why each mission is unique in its own way, and it all builds to this larger dataset of learnings that we’re developing, and all of this is in pursuit of this servicing ecosystem. If we’re going to get to this level of servicing ecosystem for all aspects of security and economics and the sustainability of the space environment, we need to have this large dataset of approaching objects, of identifying objects, and of capturing objects, and so that’s what we’re building out across the board in the portfolio of our missions.
Ars:So you’re crawling before walking or running?
Blackerby: That’s it. Our first mission, ELSA-D, that was definitely a crawl. In that case, we brought our debris with us, and let that go, and then showed we could capture it. That was the first step.
Astroscale’s ADRAS-J spacecraft captured these views of the H-IIA rocket upper stage on July 15, 2024.
Ars:What is the operational use case for the technology Astroscale is developing?
Blackerby: I’m assuming you mean like repeatable, consistent servicing. Every step we take is another step toward that goal. It’s hard for us to give a specific date on that or a timeframe. But the fact is, we’ve got eight, nine missions under manufacturing right now around the world. We have a variety already that are out there. None of them are on the level of, say, a repeatable multi-order service yet. That’s going to come. It’s just a matter of time. The missions that we’re doing now, we’ve taken these incremental steps. ELSA-D, our first mission, was fully internally funded. That was funded by the money that we raised on the equity markets. ADRAS-J, the second mission, that was that was jointly funded with JAXA, so we worked on that together. ELSA-M, we’re working on that together with ESA and the UK Space Agency. With ADRAS-J2, we’re getting toward being revenue-positive with these missions. Our missions going forward, for the most part, are revenue-positive. If we look at that from the perspective of sustainability, not of space, but of our company, economic financial sustainability, we’re already getting to that point. We need to get more toward a commercially repeatable mission, and we’re not there yet. But we’d like to see, by the early part of the next decade, the early 2030s, that we’re going to start seeing a more consistent, commercially viable servicing ecosystem being developed.
Ars:You have a refueling demonstration mission, the Provisioner, under contract with the US Space Force. What business opportunities do you see coming from the US military?
Blackerby: Provisioner is big. We’re really excited about that. That’s launching soon as well, and it’s going to demonstrate the capability of refueling. We think there’s going to be a growing market for that, and the demand signal is coming in from the US. When we think about where that next technology and demand is going to be, refueling is a big one. You’ve seen what some of the other contracts are that are out there. There’s a deorbit-as-a-service study that’s been put out (by the Defense Innovation Unit). There are some life extension mission interests that we see. We see a lot coming out in terms of close-in inspection, making sure that the customer can understand where the threats are, and whether that’s debris or some other kind of threat, they want to be able to have the the capability to do close-in RPO. So we’re excited for all of these kinds of missions that governments are showing an interest in that require a close-in RPO.
To be clear, we’re talking about the capability to identify and station-keep and come in close to an object. This is not about flying by an object and snapping pictures as you go, or getting to within a couple kilometers and taking pictures. We got to within meters of ADRAS-J. That’s the kind of really incredibly exquisite capability that we’re building out. We see that there’s going to be interest in docking, taking pictures, all of that. We’re seeing interest from not just the US government, but from governments and even the commercial sector across all of the regions where we’re located globally.
Stephen Clark is a space reporter at Ars Technica, covering private space companies and the world’s space agencies. Stephen writes about the nexus of technology, science, policy, and business on and off the planet.

What Bush Understood That Trump Doesn’t
The leaders of the American right have embraced the false idea that the United States is at war with Islam.
The current New York City mayor, Zohran Mamdani, has affronted one of his predecessors, Rudy Giuliani, by taking the inflammatory step of deciding to attend the city’s 9/11 commemoration. “It offends me,” Giuliani proclaimed earlier this week on Newsmax.
One might suspect that the nature of Mamdani’s offense lay in his being a politician who is associating himself with a day that Giuliani prefers to associate with Giuliani. But the former mayor proceeded to lay out a much darker rationale. “They’re taking over certain parts of America and certain parts of Europe. They have every desire to take us over. This is not ‘they want to be just another religion,’” he said of Muslims. “Mamdani is a clear, a clear supporter of that. All of the Muslims he supports are murderers!”
Like many of Giuliani’s utterances, this one has no connection to reality. Yet his assertion that Mamdani harbors some secret desire to conquer the United States in the name of Islam, that his religion is the skeleton key to a web of sinister motivations, is now treated on the right as almost banal. A quarter century after 9/11, delirious anti-Muslim bigotry is almost routine in the political rhetoric of many conservatives.
The conventional account of Donald Trump’s political career explains his rise to power as a populist revolt against Republican orthodoxy. The GOP elite had lost touch with their base by endorsing immigration reform, free trade, or forever wars in the Middle East, which created an opening that Trump exploited.
That story is largely true, but it misses an important issue. The President George W. Bush–era Republican Party after 9/11 insisted that the United States was at war not with a religion but with an idea. America opposed radical Islamism, not Islam. We stood for freedom as a universal human principle.
Not all voters on the right accepted this formulation. Some believed that the United States was at war with Islam itself. By 2007, conservative Republicans viewed Islam negatively by a margin of more than 30 points; Democrats, independents, and moderate Republicans all held net-favorable views. Ten years later, nearly 80 percent of Republicans believed that the values of Islam were at odds with American values. One of the most important and ominous notions that Trump has seized upon and legitimized is that Muslims are inherently un-American.
Anti-Muslim sentiment sprang up organically in the immediate aftermath of the 9/11 attacks, but Bush’s forceful defense of pluralism confined it to the rantings of Ann Coulter, Michael Savage, and other fringe reactionaries. After Coulter called on the United States in 2001 to “invade their countries, kill their leaders and convert them to Christianity,” National Review dropped her column. As Bush passed from the scene and was replaced by Barack Obama, some right-wing-outrage entrepreneurs recognized an opportunity to redefine the War on Terror as a war against Islam.
Trump himself was among the first to see the opening. In 2010, a right-wing backlash arose in opposition to a proposal for a Muslim cultural center, modeled on the YMCA or a Jewish community center, in downtown New York. The most hysterical opponents depicted the center, which planned to call itself Park51, as a “victory mosque” celebrating the destruction of the World Trade Center. Other conservatives merely insisted that it was “insensitive” for Muslim Americans to open a center in the general neighborhood of Ground Zero.
Trump inserted himself into the controversy, proposing that he purchase the property to halt construction on the putatively offensive site. In his offer letter (which, naturally, he made public), Trump called it a “very serious, inflammatory, and highly divisive situation that is destined, in my opinion, to only get worse.” David Letterman asked him, “Does this, in fact, suggest that we are officially at war with Muslims?” Trump, who was still in the formative stage of his transition from celebrity to right-wing rabble-rouser, replied, “Well, somebody knocked down the World Trade Center.” He later added, “Somebody’s blowing us up. Somebody’s blowing up buildings, and somebody’s doing lots of bad stuff.”
Trump’s first campaign was pockmarked with undisguised bigotry against Muslims. He falsely claimed that Muslims in New Jersey had cheered the 9/11 attacks en masse, and he called for surveillance of mosques, a database of Muslims in America, and a ban on Muslims entering the United States. He associated the sitting president with Islam by incessantly using his middle name.
He has continued to attack Muslims as disloyal or un-American. He falsely claimed that Representative Ilhan Omar of Minnesota, a Democrat, had praised al-Qaeda, and he demanded that she and Reprepresentative Rashida Tlaib of Michigan, both of whom are U.S. citizens, be sent “back from where they came.” He insinuated that Mamdani has no right to reside in the United States: “A lot of people are saying he’s here illegally.”
The through line connecting these smears is the assumption that Muslims cannot be Americans, even if they arrive legally, even if they are born here. Trump has made this point explicitly and told Sean Hannity in 2016, “Assimilation has been very hard. It’s almost—I won’t say nonexistent, but it gets to be pretty close. And I’m talking about second- and third-generation. They come—they don’t—for some reason, there’s no real assimilation.”
This sort of rhetoric has grown so common that episodes such as the uproar against Mamdani have come to feel like normal politics, rather than paranoia and rank discrimination. The New York Post alone has published at least eight stories (as of press time) hyping the Giuliani-fueled controversy.
Some relatives of 9/11 victims have claimed that Mamdani’s presence at the observance would be a distraction (even though mayoral attendance has been a regular feature throughout its existence). Others have depicted their anger as a protest against Mamdani’s current agenda. “It’s not about his religion or where he came from. It’s about the policies he has today,” one explained. Is it the plan for free buses? The pied-à-terre tax?
That Mamdani wishes to attend the ceremony and has denounced the 9/11 attacks as heinous terrorism ought to serve as satisfactory evidence that, whatever shortcomings he may have, he is not a supporter of al-Qaeda. Indeed, it might well be offensive if Mamdani did not want to attend the ceremony. The New York Post would need to publish phone-book-size editions to convey its full outrage.
The logic of Islamophobia rejects out of hand that it is possible for Mamdani to oppose terrorism. 9/11 was, in this view, a battle in a war against Islam, so he is, by dint of his faith, the enemy. Thus, his desire to commemorate the tragedy, like Muslims’ desire to have a YMCA of their own in New York City, must be understood as revealing hidden malevolence.
If you had asked Bush after 9/11 to imagine a future within his lifetime in which New York had a Muslim mayor who would join the city in mourning the attacks, he’d surely have considered it the ultimate vindication of the ideals he sought to foster. But Republicans have rejected Bush’s understanding of 9/11 and its meaning in favor of Trump’s.
The events of the past decade, and especially the past six months, have clarified that the primary grounds for this repudiation does not seem to be Trump’s abhorrence for wars of choice in the Middle East. It is that Bush denied and suppressed contempt for Muslims, while Trump has honored and nurtured this hatred.

Officials in northern France are investigating whether the derailment of a passenger train on Friday evening was the result of a malicious act.

Local media say 186 passengers were on board the train that was operating between Rouen and Caen in Normandy.
Forty-four people were treated for injuries, including an 18-year-old woman who was airlifted to hospital in a critical condition.
"The train's 'black box' has been seized. Several interviews are scheduled, and a court-appointed expert has been called in," prosecutor Gallois said in a press release.
"The main victim is still in hospital but her life is no longer in danger. The other victims have received care and treatment; they have either been discharged or are about to be."
The Rouen prosecutor's office earlier said the train driver had tested negative for drugs and alcohol.
The train derailed near Cléon, just south of Rouen, shortly before 20:00 (18:00 GMT), and some 140 firefighters and other emergency teams were immediately deployed to the crash scene.
"Suddenly there were a few jolts, and then after about three seconds it got stronger and stronger," Louis, a passenger on the train, told ICI Normandie radio.
"I couldn't stay in my seat anymore. The windows partially shattered, the stones from the track came into the carriage. It was really shocking. I'm still shaking," he added.

Developers are worried about AI. The creator of Claude Code has a response.
On Thursday, Anthropic's Boris Cherny posted an email a developer wrote to him on X. The email was titled: "What to do about slop?" Cherny wrote that he receives emails like this every day and that he tries to respond to as many as possible.
It's no surprise that developers are reaching out to Cherny with their worries. AI has radically changed coding, shifting job descriptions and turning engineers into reviewers. Some engineers love the ease; others call it lonely and tedious.
In the email, the unnamed developer wrote that the shift to AI coding was causing "friction." He broke it down into two views and asked Cherny to broker the dispute.
The first view was a more restrained use of AI tools:
We create code similar to before, accelerated by AI. We may not review all of it, but it should be reviewable. The person submitting the code should be able to explain it. It should be built in such a way to make it as easy to maintain — or easier — than before, by human agents. 
The second view was more permissive. This was the vibe coding position:
We treat the code as a black box. We don't worry about it. We just check the output. 
The developer wrote that many people were incapable of doing option 1 — the more restrained approach — but worried about getting laid off. "A lot of people are just forcing it," they wrote.
Cherny posted his response in full. As for the two options the developer provided, Cherny said there was room for both.
On the "don't worry" approach:
Prototypes and other throw-away code can be treated as totally black box. If you're going to throw it away anyway, and if the blast radius of it breaking is low, it doesn't need to be perfect. 
And, on cautious reviewing:
Production code written by Claude should have a higher bar than if it was written by a human. At Anthropic, we have many guardrails in place to make sure this is happening: lots of lint rules, lots of tests, Claude-driven end to end tests, Claude-powered fuzzers running daily, automated code reviews and security reviews, automated code refactoring, and so on. Without these, you can end up with a mess that is hard to maintain down the line. Luckily, the model makes it increasingly easy to do these well — run a few daily routines, use Claude Code Review, etc. 
The developer's job is to "hold the bar on code quality," Cherny wrote. AI leaders use different terms for this role, such as "mini CEO." It's the developer's job to act like a manager, stopping bad code in its tracks.
If all else fails, Cherny said the developer could be more hands-on with Claude or ask it to rewrite the codebase.
"Or, wait for the next model," he wrote.

Ingebrigtsen pulls out of Ultimate Championship 1,500m, delaying Kerr showdown
BUDAPEST, Sept 12 : Norway's Jakob Ingebrigtsen has withdrawn from Sunday's 1,500 metres at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship, postponing a long-awaited showdown with arch-rival Josh Kerr.
Ingebrigtsen, who won the men's 5,000m title on Friday at the lucrative new event, said he was unwilling to risk racing twice in three days as he continues his comeback from Achilles surgery in February.
The 25-year-old, a two-time Olympic gold medallist, returned to competition only last month after an absence of almost a year due to injury.
"Unfortunately I'm not in a position to go in back-to-back races," Ingebrigtsen said in a video posted on Instagram on Saturday.
"I would love for it to be different, and to be sharper in terms of recovery, but coming from a very difficult last two years with injury problems and Achilles surgery I am forced to be more sensible than I would like to be.
"Ultimately, it is about getting back into racing, getting back to 100 per cent fitness, and thinking about 2027."
Ingebrigtsen, who said he made the decision after a treadmill test on Saturday, added that he had already exceeded expectations simply by returning to elite competition after months of doubt.
He thrilled the sellout crowd on Friday by surging past the field with 100m to go to win the 5,000m.
"Just looking back a short time ago, it is unbelievable that we have been able to get this far in 2026 and be able to be here," he added.
The withdrawal means another delay in the rivalry between Ingebrigtsen and Britain's Kerr, with the pair having not faced each other since 2024.
After returning to competition by winning European 5,000m gold last month, Ingebrigtsen reignited their war of words by criticising athletes who skip major championships, comments seen as directed at Kerr, who opted not to defend his European title.
Kerr, who shattered the world mile record in July, responded last week by welcoming Ingebrigtsen's return to competition, but shrugged off criticism about being very selective with his race schedule.
"I'm a human being at the end of the day. I'm not a robot," Kerr said on a video call with reporters. "I think if you want to have a career that's 10 to 12 years long then you can't (race all the time)."
Sunday's 1,500m final will still feature a stellar field led by Kerr, Olympic champion Cole Hocker, Olympic bronze medallist Yared Nuguse, reigning world champion Isaac Nader and 2022 world champion Jake Wightman.

Family sues daycare over alleged toddler ‘fight club’ at the facility
Surveillance footage allegedly captured an instructor encouraging her own child to attack the victim before shaking the child
A family from Fort Worth, Texas, has filed a lawsuit against a local daycare facility following an incident in which surveillance footage allegedly captured an adult employee instigating a fight involving a 4-year-old boy.
The lawsuit targets Arka Montessori Academy of Risinger, stemming from an April 27 visit by the child’s mother, Heather Harris, who made an unannounced stop at the facility after sensing something was wrong, as reported by ABC affiliate WFAA.
According to the family’s attorney, Russell T. Button, surveillance footage shows a staff member, described as a former employee, encouraging her own son to attack the 4-year-old before shaking the victim and causing him to fall.
“This place looked like a child fight club,” Button told the outlet. “It felt like one. This kid was thrown around like a human rag doll by somebody that was supposed to protect him.”
The lawsuit argues that the facility failed in its duty to protect the child.
Heather Harris told WFAA she felt something was wrong from her son’s demeanor.
She said: ““I knew from his cry, in the look on his face, that something had happened. And from that point on, I said, I need to see the cameras.”
“The trust that I put in this daycare, they failed us,” Richard Harris, the boy's father, told WFAA.
Before enrolling their son, the couple researched multiple facilities, prioritizing cleanliness, educational standards and the presence of 24-7 surveillance cameras.
“Education was big; it was clean,” Richard Harris said. “Arka, we thought we hit gold with Arka.”
Heather Harris added, “Everything that glitters isn’t gold, and that facility was one of them.”
Button said of the lawsuit: “When you speak up, when you bring these things to light, it helps hold everyone accountable, and that makes other daycares take notice. That makes them change their ways, become safer. So, working parents have a place to send their kids."
State records indicate the academy has accumulated 21 deficiencies since January 2024, involving health and safety risks, though a subsequent inspection on August 20, 2026, recorded zero deficiencies.
Prior to the incident, the 4-year-old boy spent his time engaged in sports and practicing Michael Jackson dance moves.
“He’s walking around now with his Michael Jackson glove,” Richard Harris told the outlet. “So, he’s just pretty awesome.”
The Independent has contacted Button, the family’s attorney, and Arka Montessori Academy of Risinger for comment.

The father of two Australian surfers killed in Mexico two years ago testified in court on Tuesday that his life had been turned into hell, as the high-profile trial continued into its second day.
Three men are charged in the killing of Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33, respectively, and their 30-year-old American friend Jack Carter Rhoad, who were on a surfing trip to Mexico’s Pacific coast in April 2024.
Authorities say the three were killed in an attempted robbery, and their bodies were found dumped in a cliff-top shaft with gunshot wounds to their heads.
“It’s hell,” the victims’ father Martin Robinson told the court. “It’s hard for a parent to lose a son, and we lost two sons.”
“It’s not just the loss, but also the potential they had the dreams that lay ahead of them, the places they travelled, and the love they had for others,” he said.
Robinson described the ordeal of having to identify his sons’ bodies: Callum by a tattoo on his forearm, while identifying Jake was more difficult and required photographs.
Rhoad’s mother Page compared the crime to an execution.
“I miss my son every day, and I don’t know if I will ever be able to regain my balance,” she testified. “Carter loved Mexico. He spoke fluent Spanish and loved dancing, Mexican food and its people.”
