Prime Minister Narendra Modi delivers closing remarks during the BRICS Session on 'Inclusive Global Governance and Strengthening Multilateralism', at the 18th BRICS Summit at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi
NEW DELHI: The Brics countries have strongly condemned the Pahalgam terrorist attack in Jammu and Kashmir that killed 26 people, reaffirming their commitment to combating terrorism in all its forms and calling for “zero tolerance” towards the menace.The condemnation was included in the New Delhi Declaration 2026, adopted at the 18th Brics Summit in New Delhi on Saturday.The declaration also opposed double standards in countering terrorism and called for concerted action against all UN-designated terrorists and terrorist entities.“We express strong condemnation of any acts of terrorism as criminal and unjustifiable, regardless of their motivation, whenever, wherever and by whomsoever committed,” the declaration said.It specifically condemned “in the strongest terms” the terrorist attack in Jammu and Kashmir on April 22, 2025, during which 26 people were killed and several others injured.
Brics reaffirms stand against cross-border terror
The Brics declaration reaffirmed the grouping’s commitment to combating terrorism in all its forms and manifestations, including the cross-border movement of terrorists, terrorism financing and safe havens.The grouping said terrorism should not be associated with any religion, nationality, civilisation or ethnic group.
It also stressed that those involved in terrorist activities and their support must be held accountable and brought to justice in accordance with relevant national and international law.The declaration called for “zero tolerance for terrorism” and rejected double standards in countering terrorism.It also emphasised the primary responsibility of states in combating terrorism, while stressing that global efforts to prevent and counter terrorist threats must comply with international law, including the UN Charter and relevant international conventions and protocols.Brics welcomed the activities of its Counter-Terrorism Working Group and its five subgroups, which operate on the basis of the Brics Counter-Terrorism Strategy, Counter-Terrorism Action Plan and the Counter-Terrorism Working Group Position Paper.The grouping also called for the expeditious finalisation and adoption of the Comprehensive Convention on International Terrorism under the UN framework.The declaration further stressed the importance of countering extremism and radicalisation, particularly among younger generations, and called for greater cooperation among Brics countries and their competent authorities, including through the sharing of best practices.
Pahalgam attack and India’s response
On April 22, last year, 26 civilians were killed in a terrorist attack in the Baisaran meadow area near Pahalgam in South Kashmir, a major tourist destination.The victims were segregated by the attackers based on religion before being shot in front of their families, triggering widespread outrage.Security forces launched search operations in the surrounding areas following the attack, while investigations were expanded to trace the terrorist network and its logistical support.India responded with “Operation Sindoor” on May 7, 2025, carrying out precision strikes on terror infrastructure in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir.The operation marked a major escalation with Pakistan, followed by a four-day conflict that ended with a ceasefire on May 10, after Islamabad’s request.In the aftermath, Indian armed forces launched “Operation Mahadev” and tracked down and eliminated the three attackers involved in the Pahalgam killings.
Declaration backs India, Brazil for greater UN role
Beyond terrorism, the New Delhi Declaration reaffirmed Brics' support for comprehensive reform of the United Nations, including the UN Security Council, with greater representation for developing countries.China and Russia, as permanent members of the UN Security Council, reiterated their support for the aspirations of India and Brazil to play a greater role in the UN, including its Security Council.The declaration called for greater and more meaningful participation and representation of emerging market and developing countries, as well as Least Developed Countries, in global decision-making processes.On Security Council reform, Brics said the process should make the body more democratic, representative, effective and efficient while increasing the representation of developing countries.“We stress that the UN Security Council reform is to lead to the amplified voice of the Global South,” the declaration said.The grouping also called for equitable geographical representation in the UN Secretariat and other international organisations, particularly at senior and decision-making levels.
Brics raises concerns over trade measures
The declaration also expressed serious concern over unilateral tariff and non-tariff measures, saying they distort trade, threaten global supply chains and create uncertainty for international economic activity.Brics reaffirmed its support for reform of the World Trade Organization and called for an open, equitable, transparent, fair, inclusive, predictable and rules-based multilateral trading system, with the WTO at its core.The grouping also advocated the immediate restoration of an accessible, effective and fully functioning two-tier binding WTO dispute settlement mechanism and called for the appointment of new Appellate Body members without further delay.
On unilateral coercive measures, Brics condemned sanctions that it said were contrary to international law and reiterated its opposition to unilateral coercive measures, including those not authorised by the UN Security Council.The New Delhi Declaration was adopted during the 18th Brics Summit, being hosted by India on September 12-13 under its 2026 chairship. India’s Brics chairship is guided by the theme “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability.”

- There is no evidence that the FCC issued a direct threat to Jimmy Kimmel or threatened his network to specifically prevent him from airing an interview with James Talarico, a Texas Democrat running for a U.S. Senate seat.
- Kimmel said in September 2026 that ABC would not air his interview with Talarico on television because the FCC had threatened him, ABC and its affiliates over "simple traditional editorial decisions, guest bookings it would seem they don't like." That could reference any or all of a large number of disputes between the Trump administration and ABC.
- ABC and Disney are suing the FCC for various alleged retaliatory measures, including the FCC's decision to require early renewal of ABC's broadcast license after Kimmel made a joke about first lady Melania Trump.
- Under President Donald Trump, the FCC has also issued guidance stating that late-night talk shows are not exempt from the equal-time rule, which essentially means broadcast stations must provide equal opportunities to political candidates, regardless of partisan affiliation. ABC may have pulled the interview for fear of running afoul of this rule.
- The White House denied that FCC Chairman Brendan Carr had threatened Kimmel and said Kimmel was "play-acting" to create a "false narrative" about the Trump administration's policies. A "Jimmy Kimmel Live!" spokesperson did not immediately return a request for more information.
Jimmy Kimmel announced on Sept. 9, 2026, that his show "Jimmy Kimmel Live!" would not air his interview with U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico on television, citing the Federal Communications Commission's threats against the talk-show host's network, ABC, under U.S. President Donald Trump's administration.
Social media users circulated Kimmel's accusations; some claimed Trump or the FCC tried to "block" the interview from airing. In response, readers searched our website to determine whether the FCC actually threatened Kimmel or blocked him from airing the interview with Talarico, a Democratic Texas state representative.
Here's what Kimmel said about the situation (see 9:33 in the video below):
I interviewed Donald Trump when he was running for president in 2015. And at that time, when he was the one sitting next to me, he seemed to have no problem with the idea of talk-show hosts interviewing candidates. In fact, he was very eager to come back for another interview, which he did just before he became the nominee in 2016.
But for some reason, and I can't seem to figure out what that reason is, something has changed.
Now that he is president, his FCC has threatened me, threatened our show, threatened our network, ABC, our affiliates, our local stations based on simple traditional editorial decisions, guest bookings it would seem they don't like.
And so out of consideration for our local stations, especially our ABC affiliates in Texas who would have to deal with this nonsense, my interview tomorrow with James Talarico will not air on television. It will be posted on YouTube instead.
A closer look at Kimmel's words indicates he didn't actually say whether the alleged threat issued by the FCC specifically related to his Sept. 10 interview with Talarico. Kimmel said the FCC threatened him and ABC based on "simple traditional editorial decisions" and "guest bookings." That could be a reference to past disputes between ABC and the Trump administration or changing guidelines from the FCC.
The White House said Brendan Carr, chairman of the FCC, has not threatened Kimmel "regarding interviewing James Talarico, or any other candidate."
"Jimmy Kimmel is play-acting—as he often does—to create a false narrative about this administration's policies," Davis Ingle, a White House spokesman, said in an email. "Any media outlet blindly amplifying Kimmel's egocentric delusion should insist on proof. Of which they will find none."
A spokesperson for "Jimmy Kimmel Live!" didn't immediately respond to a request for that proof, nor to a request to clarify whether Kimmel and ABC had received a specific threat — or whether the network made a proactive decision based on past experiences and Trump administration policy.
We left this claim unrated pending answers to those questions.
Here's more on why ABC might have pulled Talarico's interview from network television, aside from a possible direct threat:
ABC's disputes with Trump administration
Kimmel's accusation that the Trump administration has threatened him and his network could reference any or all of the many disputes he and his network have with the Trump administration.
In fact, Trump has repeatedly called for Kimmel's firing and for the FCC to strip ABC of its licenses in response to various broadcasts he hasn't liked.
In September 2025, ABC temporarily pulled Kimmel off air after comments he made about the assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk. The decision came after Carr suggested he might take action against Disney, ABC's parent company, if it didn't pull Kimmel's show.
The president also called on ABC to fire Kimmel in April 2026 after the talk-show host made a joke about first lady Melania Trump. Shortly after, the FCC ordered ABC to seek early broadcast license renewals, an unprecedented move that can signal "significant concerns with the value" of the station's operations, Carr said.
ABC and Disney sued the FCC in August 2026 for allegedly violating its free-speech rights, arguing (Page 3) that the Trump administration has "waged a retaliatory campaign against ABC for a single reason: it disapproves of what ABC broadcasts."
FCC policy changes
It's also possible ABC may have pulled Talarico's interview from network television because of FCC guidance on giving equal time to political candidates on broadcast television under the Trump administration.
Some forms of broadcast media are exempt from this rule, including "bona fide," or legitimate, newscasts and news interviews. But in January 2026, the FCC issued guidance stating that late-night talk shows don't have a blanket exemption from the equal-time rule.
The FCC's guidance said that, in 2006, the agency determined the interview portion of "The Tonight Show with Jay Leno" qualified for as a "bona fide news interview" and thus would be exempt from the equal-time rule. Networks have relied on this ruling to mean that all late-night talk shows are exempt.
"This is not the case," the FCC said on Page 4 of the notice. "The FCC has not been presented with any evidence that the interview portion of any late night or daytime television talk show program on air presently would qualify for the bona fide news exemption."
The FCC's guidance has had real effects. In February 2026, for example, talk-show host Stephen Colbert claimed CBS blocked an interview with Talarico on "The Late Show with Stephen Colbert" from airing on broadcast television because the network's lawyers said in "no uncertain terms" that the interview could violate the FCC's guidance.
(CBS reportedly disputed Colbert's account and said its lawyers provided only "legal guidance," not a direct prohibition.)
The bottom line
There's no evidence the FCC directly threatened Kimmel, and a closer read of Kimmel's comments indicated that Kimmel never accused the FCC of specifically blocking his interview with Talarico from airing on television.
However, that doesn't mean the FCC hasn't threatened Kimmel and ABC in other ways. The FCC and ABC are embroiled in several disputes, and ABC has alleged that the FCC is engaging in retaliatory measures because the Trump administration doesn't like the network's content.

Lightning Houthi advance in Yemen may bring dangerous new dimension to Iran war
- Published
The Houthis' lightning advance across the southern reaches of the Tihamah – Yemen's arid coastal plain – appears to have taken most observers by surprise.
Until recently, the anti-Houthi coalition known as the National Resistance held significant territory along Yemen's Red Sea coast. In a matter of days, much of this has fallen to the Houthis.
According to some estimates, the Iranian-backed rebels have captured as much as 130km (81 miles) of the country's strategically important coastline.
It's the group's most impressive military coup for several years, proving that despite a civil war that has lasted 12 years, devastating Saudi air raids and attacks by American, Israeli and British forces, the Houthis remain a force to be reckoned with.
With their opponents stunned and demoralised, it's unlikely the Houthis will be dislodged any time soon.
- Houthis claim major advance in Yemen and tighten grip on Red Sea shipping lane 
  - Published1 minute ago
- Oil hits $100 a barrel for first time since July after US and Houthi strikes 
  - Published2 days ago
"Now that they are there, they're going to be entrenched," Hisham al-Omeisi, senior analyst at the Brussels-based European Institute of Peace, told the BBC. "And it's going to be a lot more costly to push them out."
Of course, the Houthis are not alone. They enjoy the backing of Iran, support that has become even more important for Tehran in the wake of the setbacks and defeats experienced by other parts of its so-called "Axis of Resistance" – Lebanese Hezbollah, Hamas in Gaza and the Assad regime in Syria.
"So they redirected their support to the Houthis," al-Omeisi said. "And of course they need that support."
Even though most analysts agree that it's a mistake simply to describe the Houthis as Iranian puppets, events of the past few days raise an uncomfortable new reality.
Seven months after the US and Israel launched their huge, combined assault on Iran, the regime in Tehran now exerts authority over not just one, but two of the world's most important maritime passages: the Strait of Hormuz, at the mouth of the Persian Gulf, and the Bab al-Mandab, gateway to the Red Sea (and the Suez Canal).
"Now Iran, directly and through proxies, controls two of the most strategic choke points in the Middle East and the world," says Farea al-Muslimi, a research fellow at London's Chatham House think tank, "controlling more than 35% of the fuel and oil trade globally."
"This is as much leverage as a nuclear bomb," he says.
If the Houthis have also taken control of several key islands in the Red Sea, including Perim - which sits in the middle of the narrowest point of the Bab al-Mandab - then the group's ability to interfere with international shipping will be greatly enhanced.
As the group's actions in the wake of Israel's war on Gaza proved, shipping in the Red Sea is highly vulnerable to Houthi missiles, drones and small attack boats.
"They were able to control what was going in and out of the Bab al-Mandab and up towards Suez without having these territorial gains," Yemen expert Iona Craig told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Friday.
"But of course now they're controlling the area immediately overlooking the Bab al-Mandab, and this gives them far more leverage."
Shipping companies are likely to be sceptical about the sincerity of a statement released on Friday afternoon, in which the Houthi military said that maritime navigation was "safe for all companies except for Saudi vessels, which have already been subject to a blockade".
In their earlier attacks, the Houthis said they were only targeting vessels linked to Israel, but in fact hit ships with no such connection, including a Norwegian-flagged tanker.
Craig said the Houthis may nevertheless refrain from indiscriminate attacks, fearing a repeat of Operation Rough Rider - six weeks of major US air and naval strikes in the spring of 2025.
"They've already felt the wrath of the US," she said.
But would the US want to get involved anyway?
President Donald Trump's war with Iran is already unpopular. With oil prices creeping back up, it's doubtful that a new front would do much to enhance his approval ratings or his Republican party's chances in November's midterm US elections.
According to the Axios website, appeals for US intervention from the Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman have so far gone unanswered.
Axios writes that the US "is increasingly concerned about the escalating conflict in Yemen and is working to intensify its support for the kingdom while simultaneously seeking to avoid direct military involvement".
But it's not just the potential threat to the Bab al-Mandab that's causing fear in Saudi Arabia.
Satellite images of an apparent Houthi missile-and-drone attack on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline – a vital alternative route for oil exports following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz earlier this year – point to an effort by Iran's Yemeni allies to add to the economic pressures generated by the US-Israeli war with Iran.
Even if Iran did not directly order the attack, it clearly stands to benefit.
Baraa Shaiban, a researcher and analyst at the London-based Royal United Services Institute, says the origins of the latest upsurge in fighting – the worst since a United Nations-brokered truce in 2022 - can be traced back to July, when a Houthi delegation returned from the state funeral of Iran's Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
"Immediately after, the escalation started," he says, "and it looked very clearly that [Iran was] determined to now have a bigger foothold on the Red Sea".
With Yemen teetering on the edge of a return to all-out war, Saudi Arabia anxious about preserving its economic lifeline to the Red Sea and Donald Trump apparently reluctant to get involved, America's conflict with Iran just took on a new and potentially dangerous dimension.
For the people of Yemen, displaced, bombed, starved and impoverished by a dozen years of civil war, recent developments can only make their lives worse.

A group of online creators with a combined 46 million followers is demanding Lowe's and Home Depot — two of the largest home-improvement stores in the US — to cut ties with Flock Safety amid a nationwide campaign against large retailers that may have contracts with the surveillance tech company.
In a letter sent Friday morning to the companies' executives, 56 content creators called on Lowe's and Home Depot to "terminate all its contracts with Flock Safety" and remove the company's automated license plate readers, or ALPRs, from their parking lots.
The letter raised concerns that data gathered by the cameras could be accessed by federal or local law enforcement agencies to target immigrant day laborers and other shoppers.
"By participating in Flock's network, you are endangering the safety of customers, especially the immigrants and people of color who shop at your stores," an email that was sent to the executives and viewed by Business Insider said.
Flock cameras collect license plate and vehicle data. A company spokesperson said Flock has more than 5,000 private sector clients, including retailers, healthcare institutions, small businesses, and places of worship.
Law enforcement officers have previously told Business Insider that Flock's technology has helped their agencies solve crimes. Flock says it helps businesses and communities prevent and investigate crime, including organized retail crime. Business Insider also has reported that Flock cameras can misread license plates, leading law enforcement to the wrong people.
The company has become a flash point amid broader concerns over mass surveillance technology and privacy.
Fight For The Future, a nonprofit digital rights advocacy group that organized the content creator-led campaign, has pointed to a May 2025 report from 404 Media that found local and state police agencies were running searches in Flock's nationwide ALPR network for ICE and immigration-related probes.
The report did not establish that ICE itself had direct access to Flock's system, but showed how local agencies could use the network on ICE's behalf even though the federal agency does not have a formal contract with Flock.
As cities, from Austin to Evanston, Illinois, move to end their contracts with Flock, organizations like Fight For The Future are putting similar pressure on retailers.
A Flock spokesperson said private customers own and control the data collected by their systems, including decisions about access, sharing, and retention. "Law enforcement cannot access a private customer's data without that customer's explicit authorization," the spokesperson said.
A Home Depot spokesperson said the cameras help prevent and investigate theft, fraud, and organized retail crime, as well as protect customers and employees. The retailer said it does not share ALPR data with immigration enforcement or grant federal law enforcement access to its license-plate readers.
Jess Rambo, a Marine veteran who now runs a homesteading and building Instagram account, The Painted Buffalo, with about 28,000 followers, said she shops at her local Home Depot in rural Georgia at least twice a week. She said learning about Home Depot's use of ALPRs — and the potential for law-enforcement access to the data — prompted her to sign the letter.
"The concern for me is definitely the data collection and the safety of people if that data were put into the wrong hands," Rambo said.
Alexa Speed, another signatory of the letter, runs Cut Off the Spigot on Instagram and TikTok, as well as a Substack newsletter where she directs consumers to companies she considers problematic. Speed started the Instagram account in April 2025 and has since gained more than 417,000 followers.
Speed told Business Insider that she published an article on her Substack and a video earlier this year about alternatives to Home Depot and Lowe's after seeing another 404 Media report detailing how local law enforcement can tap into the retailers' Flock surveillance systems. Joining Fight For The Future's campaign was a way to extend her advocacy to a "collective action."
"The only meaningful response is to end and cancel their partnership," Speed said. "I need to get a faucet or a wrench. I don't need to be surveilled."
A Lowe's spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment.

Sam Altman says now is not a good time.
In a Fortune interview that aired on Saturday, OpenAI's CEO said that "given everything that's happening with safety," he doesn't expect to take his company public this year.
"Right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public," he said.
When Fortune's editor in chief, Alyson Shontell, asked if that meant Altman wouldn't take OpenAI public in 2026 and 2027, Altman replied, "I would say not 2026."
"We got a lot of stuff to do," he added. "We need to be able to make decisions that are not obviously in the interest of our business and our shareholders."
The date of OpenAI's initial public offering, which is likely to be a trillion-dollar affair, has been speculated about almost endlessly. In May, a person familiar with the matter told Business Insider that the company was preparing to go public this month.
Altman's comments about "safety" come just as the industry is mired in a debate over whether an AI model could go off the rails and harm humanity. In July, researchers revealed that hundreds of OpenAI agents went rogue during training, hacked into the servers of Hugging Face, another AI company, and then tried to hide their tracks.
Altman's chief rival, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, published a blog post on Saturday calling for a slowdown in AI development. Anthropic is also eyeing an IPO in the near future, though he didn't mention it in the post. Altman replied on X that he agreed. "We need to pace the frontier," Altman said.
SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk also agreed with Amodei's proposals, which included stationing third-party monitors inside the big AI labs.
In filing for an IPO, OpenAI would open its books, giving the public a clearer view of the vast resources it is spending toward the goal of building even more powerful AI models.
OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment sent Saturday.

Bhopal (Madhya Pradesh): The Madhya Pradesh Text Book Corporation (MPTBC) supplies free study material and other educational material to the Rajya Shiksha Kendra and the Directorate of Public Instruction. Dues from the two agencies have remained pending for several years and stand at Rs 300,18,65,146.
The delay has blocked the corporation's funds and caused loss of interest, according to its audit report for financial year 2024-25.
Loss of Rs 57 lakh due to unsaleable, useless books
On the basis of audit report received from various depots and information related to physical verification and inspection of depots, it came to fore that total 1,02,900 books were found unsaleable, obsolete and useless. The net sale price of them was Rs 57,68,185. At the same time, Corporation has to bear various expenditure on the storage and maintenance of these books. The expenditure includes godown rent, electricity expenditure, labour and other expenditures. Had these books were sold timely, then corporation would not have suffered the loss of Rs 57,68,185, said the audit report.
Rs 35.07 crore pending for adjustment
For everyday emergency expenditure, an advance sum is paid by MPTBC headquarters to 15 sales stores and the central store. In financial year 2024-25, a sum of Rs 10,91,27,805 was given to different divisional stores despite an advance of Rs 24,16,18,702 from previous years remaining unadjusted. Thus, as of March 31, 2025, a sum of Rs 35,07,46,507 was pending for adjustment.
Security deposits not obtained
As per rules, the department should obtain a security deposit from government servants handling cash, stores and other valuable material. However, the corporation administration is not doing so.
Registers, records not provided
Audit report pointed that salary register, categorised register of income & expenditure, integrated register of income and expenditure, deduction register, deduction and payable share to employee provident fund, property register, cash book, bank statement, voucher, register related to liabilities etc. were not provided despite repeated reminders.

When an avalanche killed climber Nirmal Purja, his friends faced the hardest mission of all
- Published
As he picked his way past the frozen slope towards two bodies, Mingma Gyalje Sherpa knew his friends were gone.
Together, the three of them had climbed the world's highest peaks, under crisp mountain skies and in treacherous snowstorms. Nirmal Purja and Kili Pemba Sherpa were two of the strongest climbers Mingma G had ever known.
But this July, an avalanche swept through Pakistan's Broad Peak while the two were on their way up, engulfing everything in its path.
The drone images seemed clear: no-one had survived.
And yet, as Mingma G came closer to the fluorescent down suits, sharp against the snow, he couldn't shake the idea they were waiting for him.
"I told them: 'It's ok. You don't have to be here in the cold anymore.'"
Speaking to the BBC in Islamabad, he recalls the terrible moment he reached for their bodies.
Holding one of them, he promised: "I'm here to take you guys home."
Mingma G and Nirmal Purja met in Pakistan in 2021, where they were part of the first team to summit the world's second-highest mountain, K2, during winter.
Mingma G knew of Nirmal - or Nims, as he was known - from his Netflix documentary 14 Peaks, in which he successfully climbed the world's 14 highest mountains in just over six months.
The pair, both avid climbers from Nepal, had taken different paths.
Mingma G came from the Sherpa community and built his reputation as a mountain guide over 20 years. Nims was a former Gurkha and British Special Forces soldier who quickly became one of the world's best-known mountaineers.
Many saw Nims as an incredible climber who helped Nepalese climbers gain international recognition in a field dominated by foreigners. But he also had his critics: they said he focused too much on records, and on marketing his expeditions to a growing social media following.
In 2024 the New York Times published sexual misconduct allegations from two women, which Purja strongly denied through his lawyer at the time, who said they were "false and defamatory". Purja again denied the allegations in a lengthy interview soon after.
Before Mingma G met Nims, he wasn't sure about him: "In the beginning, I had the feeling he was very arrogant."
But that changed when their paths crossed five years ago, as competitors on their way to K2, who then decided to climb the mountain together and share the record. Mingma G says he found Nims to be "very kind-hearted, one of the most beautiful human beings I've met".
Over the years the two would meet on various mountains around the world: Nims "would always be on Everest".
This summer they met again, walking into the Karakoram range, before they would split up for different climbs. Nims headed for Broad Peak and Mingma G for K2, around 8km (five miles) apart.
Nims asked Mingma G to wait another day so they could meet once more before embarking on these separate missions, but that meeting never happened.
"That was the last thing he told me. I still regret it."
On 30 July, "we had perfect weather, sunshine, no winds," Mingma G says.
By then, he was leading a team up K2. Nims's team of climbers had joined others to form a larger group of 10 that was making its way up Broad Peak.
At 08:30, Mingma G spoke to Kili Pemba Sherpa - better known as Kilu - a childhood friend and expert climber in Nims's group. Snow conditions looked good, Kilu had said, and the two agreed to speak again when they both reached the next camp on their respective mountains.
The BBC spoke to two trekkers who spotted the climbers scaling Broad Peak. "We were cheering them on," one says. He took a photo of them on the slope, small silhouettes against the snow.
The group continued ascending. But less than an hour later, there was a "thundercrack", the other trekker says: "a huge avalanche, starting from the top going down both sides of Broad Peak".
"We were hoping and praying that the climbers were above the avalanche," the first trekker continues. But they couldn't see the silhouettes on the slope.
The trekkers' guide notified base camp about what they had witnessed.
The cause of the avalanche is still being investigated, but the Alpine Club of Pakistan told the BBC that while it had snowed heavily earlier that week, their initial research suggested that it was caused by the collapse of an ice slab, irrespective of snowfall.
By the time Mingma G reached the next camp on K2, his team had not heard from the Broad Peak climbers. They didn't panic because climbers often turn off the radio to save battery life.
But something was bothering him.
One of the Broad Peak climbers, Wang Zhong, was a close friend and a client. He would normally message Mingma G through his Garmin satellite tracker to let him know he'd arrived safely at the next camp. But there was no message from him.
Thousands of metres below, Pakistani mountain guide Waqar Ali says he was also trying to contact the group, but to no avail. He thought they may have been sleeping, in preparation for a final push towards the summit that night.
But by 15:00, no-one at base camp had had any contact with the group on Broad Peak.
Mingma G was 7,300m up on K2, where communication was difficult. His team started calling officials, families, contacts in Kathmandu and anyone who might have been in touch with the climbers.
He says it was probably 20:00 when they first heard that the altitude readings from the Broad Peak climbers' trackers had dramatically fallen: one of them had dropped by around 1,600m.
It was too late to climb and too dark to send up a drone, so he decided to wait for sunrise. "I had hope," Mingma G says. Especially for Kilu and Nims, who were "experienced and physically… strong".
Early next morning, a drone was sent up and soon after, the operator radioed them. The drone had spotted bodies down the mountain. It looked like there were no survivors.
"I was totally blank," Mingma G recalls in a low voice.
He wasn't quite ready to accept he had lost so many dear friends at once.
"Maybe still I had a feeling they might all be alive [and] wanted somebody to help them get down. That was just something I had in my heart and mind."
Later that day, Mingma G called off his K2 expedition.
Down at the base of Broad Peak, Waqar wept as he arrived with another climber to start the difficult job of bringing the bodies back.
They retrieved the bodies of Nadhira Al Harthy, the first Omani woman to climb Everest, and Pur Bahadur Gurung, a Nepalese climber who had summited 12 of the world's 14 highest peaks.
But there were still bodies on the mountain and Mingma G was determined to bring his friends home.
When he called Nims's wife and brother-in-law to tell them the tragic news, he says they struggled to believe it. Kilu's wife "couldn't say much, but told me: 'don't leave your brother on the mountain'".
Organising the next steps of the recovery mission was complicated.
The climbers who'd been heading up K2 with Mingma G were unsettled, he says, and facing pressure from their families to go home.
Then there were the logistics. From the drone images, Mingma G thought the bodies could be recovered using a helicopter and a long-line rope, but says he was told this wouldn't be possible. "In Nepal it would have taken like two minutes," he says.
The Pakistani army which would have provided the helicopters didn't respond to the BBC's questions. The Alpine Club of Pakistan says a request made on 1 August was approved, but poor weather meant it could not be carried out for days.
There was only one other option for Mingma G - a recovery operation on foot.
On 1 August, Mingma G says, his team of rescuers set off in search of four bodies they believed they'd seen in the drone shots - those of Nims, Kilu, Zhong and a fellow climber called Nima Sherpa. Gyaljen Sherpa would also be discovered nearby.
With the slope so unstable, there was a risk of falling rocks and further avalanches. A larger team could potentially lead to more casualties, but a smaller team would struggle to bring the bodies down.
The moment the rescue team reached the bodies and began sending them down on ropes, another avalanche hit, he says.
The torrent of snow sent one of the bodies down to the bottom. Three others, including Nims, ended up in a more dangerous position - in the centre of a slope with large pillars of glacial ice precariously balanced to the left and right. If either were to collapse while the rescue team were trying to reach the bodies, the tower of ice could sweep them away.
The team needed a new plan. As the days progressed, some of its members started leaving. Their numbers went from nine to six, then four.
Given how precarious the slope was, the group decided Mingma G would hang back and monitor by drone, instructing the three climbers. The arduous operation took five to six hours, but they finally managed to bring the bodies back down the slope.
The moment Mingma G first saw his friends on the mountain still haunts him.
Nims and Kilu had covered their faces with their jackets - Mingma G believes they had seen the deadly avalanche coming and prepared. The two were attached to the same rope, their legs wrapped in it. Mingma G thinks they may have hit each other on the way down - which he fears killed them rather than the fall.
"They didn't fall that much, almost 500m. But unfortunately they hit each other a lot, I think. If they were not on the rope, maybe there was a possibility that Nims and Kilu might have survived."
The team brought the bodies back down the mountain. They were flown by helicopter to the nearby city of Skardu, then on to the capital Islamabad and finally, home to their families.
Pakistani mountaineer Sohail Sakhi's body was found a few days later, as was the body of American climber Mallory Geis. The body of Nepalese climber Nawang Thindu Sherpa remains on the mountain.
Nims's family say they are deeply grateful to the "extraordinary team led by our brother, Mingma G, who worked in incredibly challenging conditions to bring Nimsdai home".
This recovery operation has stayed with Mingma G. It doesn't compare to any other mission he has done.
As he looks back with deep sorrow, he feels the end of his career could be coming.
Memories of Kilu and Nims - the three of them singing together as they marched up to the summit of a freezing but sunny K2 a few years ago - will always be with him.
But, he says, "I'm not sure if it helps, if the memory helps me to keep climbing or it makes me stop."

Lebanon’s president makes a rare visit to southern city as fears of Israeli attacks grow
Lebanon’s president has made a rare visit to a southern city amid fears of more Israeli attacks
Lebanon’s president made a rare visit to a southern city Saturday, close to where Israel captured a strategic hill, amid fears of more Israeli attacks.
President Joseph Aoun’s visit to Nabatiyeh came after Israel seized parts of Ali Taher ridge earlier this month, where Israeli officials said they had blown up Hezbollah tunnel networks, despite a June 20, U.S.-brokered ceasefire between Israel and the Lebanese militant group.
The ceasefire largely halted active fighting, which began on March 2, when the Iran-backed Hezbollah fired rockets into Israel, two days after the U.S. and Israel launched a war on Iran. However, Israel has continued attacks and airstrikes on areas in southern Lebanon. Hezbollah has also fired explosive drones without claiming responsibility.
Heads of the crisis-hit nation’s security agencies accompanied Aoun, the state-run National News Agency reported. Some residents of Nabatiyeh have been calling on the army to boost its presence in the city in order to avoid a possible Israeli ground offensive.
A man told Aoun in footage aired on local TV stations residents want to feel secure and that their children are safe after being displaced and humiliated. The latest Israel-Hezbollah war killed over 4,000 people in Lebanon and displaced over 1 million. Since the ceasefire was implemented, hundreds of thousands have returned to their homes in southern Lebanon and Beirut’s southern suburbs.
Aoun said the state will follow up on the needs of the residents “so that you stay here."
Lebanon and Israel have held several rounds of direct talks in Washington and Rome. The State Department announced Friday that the next round of Israel-Lebanon talks will be held in Rome in October.
Hezbollah rejects direct talks with Israel and has called on the government to abolish the framework agreement reached in June.

PM Modi holds bilateral meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping on sidelines of BRICS summit
NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping held a bilateral meeting lasting more than 50 minutes in New Delhi on Saturday, shortly after the adoption of the Brics Summit 2026 declaration.The meeting took place on the sidelines of the Brics Summit, where leaders of the grouping adopted the summit declaration following discussions on key global and regional issues.
Welcoming Xi, PM Modi thanked China for its support and cooperation during India's Brics chairmanship and said the two sides now had an opportunity to discuss bilateral ties."It gives me great pleasure to extend a warm welcome to you. Thank you very much for your positive remarks at the Brics Summit. I express my gratitude for the support and cooperation received from China during India's Brics chairmanship. We now have the opportunity to discuss bilateral cooperation. Once again, a warm welcome to India."The meeting assumes significance as India and China have sought to stabilise bilateral relations following tensions along their disputed border in recent years. The two leaders have held several engagements aimed at improving ties and maintaining peace and tranquillity along the border.
PM Modi welcomes Xi
During the bilateral meeting, PM Modi expressed his gratitude for China's cooperation during India's Brics presidency and welcomed Xi to India."I express my gratitude for the support and cooperation received from China during India's Brics chairmanship. We now have the opportunity to discuss bilateral cooperation. Once again, a warm welcome to India."The meeting followed the conclusion of the Brics summit, which brought together leaders and delegations from member countries, partner nations and outreach invitees in New Delhi.
Xi stresses long-term ties
Xi told PM Modi that China views India-China relations from a strategic and long-term perspective, according to Xinhua.He also said China and India can learn from each other's strengths and work towards shared development, signalling Beijing's emphasis on maintaining engagement with New Delhi.
Earlier, the BRICS nations unanimously adopted the New Delhi Declaration 2026, which expressed deep concern over the continued escalation of tensions in West Asia and called for maximum restraint and avoidance of actions that could further aggravate the situation.“We urge to ensure the protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure in accordance with the purposes and principles of the Charter of the United Nations in their entirety and interconnectedness, including respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the States,” the declaration said.The BRICS declaration also encouraged greater efforts through dialogue and diplomacy towards a long-term understanding contributing to lasting peace, security and stability in the region.“We stress the need to work together to maintain smooth flow of global trade, supply chains and energy, in accordance with applicable international law,” it said.The grouping expressed serious concern over deliberate attacks on civilian infrastructure and peaceful nuclear facilities under full safeguards of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), stressing that nuclear safeguards, safety and security must be upheld, including during armed conflicts.The declaration also called for implementation of relevant UN General Assembly and UN Security Council resolutions and urged all parties to ensure the maintenance of ceasefire and full and unhindered humanitarian access in the Gaza Strip.Addressing the BRICS Summit, Xi Jinping called on BRICS nations to play a peacemaking role amid the conflict in West Asia, saying China would work with other members towards that goal.The BRICS declaration also noted the current global context of polarisation and distrust and encouraged global action to strengthen international peace and security. It advocated a multilateral approach that respects diverse national viewpoints on key global issues, including sustainable development, eradication of hunger and poverty and the global response to climate change.
The grouping also expressed concern over growing nuclear risks and conflict and reiterated the need to strengthen the system of disarmament, arms control and non-proliferation to promote global stability and international peace and security.Earlier, addressing the 18th BRICS Summit session on Inclusive Global Governance and Strengthening in New Delhi, PM Modi proposed 10 measures for global governance reform, which BRICS members could develop into a BRICS Reform Roadmap by the next Summit.He also called for transforming the Global South from a “rule-taker into a rule-shaper”, saying the Global South remains at the forefront of global crises but continues to remain on the sidelines when it comes to decision-making.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Heigi Jeong. It has been edited for length and clarity.
People often assume that I quit my six-figure job in product design because of severe burnout or an existential crisis, but that wasn't the case.
I moved from Korea to Toronto in 2020 as an in-house product designer for a tech company, often creating mobile apps and websites.
The paycheck was great — I was making about $173,000 to do a job that allowed me to have a fairly healthy work-life balance. I wasn't working 80 hours per week. Most weeks, I clocked about 40 hours, working mostly 9 to 5. Since my income was more than enough to live on, I was also able to travel when I had time off, never needing to worry about money or budgets.
I decided to quit my job
While I wouldn't say I loved the work, I liked it. The job was about making logical decisions, and then convincing stakeholders of my decisions through storytelling.
It was my dream job as an immigrant, and it was sustainable. I could have carried on working it, but I had also been doing content creation on the side and had just signed a book deal. There weren't enough hours in the day to do all three. It would have been like having three full-time jobs.
Debating which one to let go of, I decided to quit the most stable of the three — product design. Writing a book was very important to me, and I knew content creation would support the promotion of the book.
But I was hesitant to abandon my only employed source of work. The thought was really scary. I remember having so much anxiety in the weeks leading up to my resignation in June 2026.
Was it a mistake to leave a consistent paycheck in the middle of economic uncertainty? Would I be able to re-enter the market should I change my mind?
I'm working for myself for a year
I made a deal with myself to try and quell the anxiety that this was a permanent decision. For one year, I'd work for myself — pursuing content creation and book writing — and then I'd decide if I wanted to go back to the corporate world.
Sure, I might not be able to go back to the same company or make the same salary if I choose to return, but I have a résumé with lots of examples of my work should I decide to return to being a product designer.
Since resigning, every morning, I cycle to a gym and work out, and then head to an office and write from noon until 5 p.m. I fit in content creation throughout the day.
I'm hoping to take my writing on the road and travel this year too.
I'm rushing less
Rushing less, I feel like I'm existing more in the world, noticing myself and the world around me, choosing what I want to fill my time with.
I had saved money, had a supportive partner, and knew it was possible on a practical level to give up my salary. But it hasn't been easy financially. Content creation payments are inconsistent. In July, I only made $6 because there was a delay in the content creation payment system. I've had portions of my book advance, but the income from my self-employment fluctuates a lot. Some months, I earn zero dollars and other months, I earn even more than I used to in my 9 to 5.
I've had to mentally adapt to inconsistent pay, and rather than viewing it as a threat, seeing it as the reality of self-employment.
Another difficulty has been setting boundaries. I could work 24 hours a day as my own boss because there is always more I can do. When I was employed, I'd shut my computer at the end of the day and be done. But being self-employed, my mind is always ticking over about work. I've had to get strict with myself to ensure I do have breaks.
Three months in, I'm nearly always confident that I made the right decision to take this year out, though I do sometimes get shaken for a short time when people online tell me I've made a huge error.
If I hadn't taken this chance to pursue another dream of working for myself, I would have regretted it.
But who knows what will come of it.
Even if I do return to the corporate world, this year wouldn't have been a mistake. I would have had the experience of leaving something that felt nice and stable for the unknown. That's a lesson I think is important to have learned.

A flurry of artificial intelligence algorithms have promised to help identify heart conditions early. By analyzing an electrocardiogram, a common 10-second test of the heart’s activity, AI has been cleared to screen for common arrhythmias and structural heart conditions, and algorithms in development aim to pinpoint patients at highest risk of sudden cardiac arrest.
While many of those models are focused on early diagnosis and prevention, AI also might help a patient when they’re having a heart attack. Last week, the Food and Drug Administration issued a rare de novo classification to a model from Powerful Medical that aims to help triage patients to the right care when they’re having chest pain. The vast majority of AI devices go to market through the FDA’s 510(k) clearance pathway; fewer than 10 each year receive de novo classification, which typically requires more clinical evidence.
The most severe kind of heart attack occurs when a coronary artery, which supplies blood to the heart, is completely blocked off. Those patients need to get to a cardiac catheterization lab as soon as possible to open up the blockage and restore oxygen to the heart. On an EKG, doctors can identify these kinds of myocardial infarctions from their characteristic “ST-segment elevations.”

As longer, more complex passwords have become a necessity, remembering all those strings of numbers, letters, and special characters has become nearly impossible. Password managers can solve that problem, but what happens when you want to move to a different login organizer? Sure, you could manually type all your logins into a new app, but now Android can do that for you without the tedium.
Google designed the new login transfer process to happen entirely on your phone, so you need the corresponding apps installed with your credentials synced. To start the move, you’ll have to find the import option in the app you want to use. The location of that feature will vary, but in Google Password Manager (built into Android), it’s near the top under the settings tab.
The import option in Google Password Manager will plug in to the new migration system, while export still just creates an unencrypted CSV with your passwords that can be dumped into any app. It will be similar in other apps, so make sure to start the process in the app you want to use. Twenty-five dead after fire on cargo ship in eastern China
- Published
Twenty-five people have been killed in a fire on a foreign-flagged cargo ship docked at a port in eastern China, according to Chinese state broadcaster CCTV.
Of the 42 people on board, 17 were were evacuated of which five are in hospital in stable condition, CCTV reports.
The vessel was undergoing maintenance at a shipyard in the city of Qingdao when the blaze erupted at around 11:15 local time (03:15 GMT). It was put out just over three hours later, according to CCTV.
Photos released by state media showed the vessel to be the Ocean Melody, a 190m (623ft) long Liberia-flagged carrier which arrived in Qingdao on 31 August, according to tracking site MarineTraffic.
Qingdao is a major trading hub and ranks among the world's busiest ports.
It is unclear what caused the fire. An eyewitness told the AFP news agency there was thick smoke rising from the ship, but he heard no explosion.
The country's leader Xi Jinping earlier called for "all-out" search and rescue efforts while Premier Li Qiang stressed the need to "prevent secondary disasters".
The fire comes nearly a month after a shipyard explosion in the south-eastern Chinese province of Fujian killed a rescue worker and injured 12 others.

Approximately one in eight girls/women, experienced rape or sexual assault before turning 18, according to UNICEF 2024 estimates. Global estimates have also documented substantial sexual abuse among boys. Child sexual abuse is predominantly seen as a social evil and crime against humanity, but it is equally a serious public health problem. Yet our response understandably revolves around the perpetrator. Was the crime reported? Has the accused been arrested? Will the prosecution succeed? What punishment will follow?
For the young person or child, however, punishment of the offender does not reverse what has happened. There may be physical injuries to treat, infections to prevent, pregnancy to consider and psychological wounds that may surface immediately or years later. Healthcare must begin even if justice is delayed.
The first contact with the healthcare system is crucial. Depending on the nature and timing of the assault, the child may require treatment for physical injuries, testing and treatment for sexually transmitted infections, and assessment of the risk of HIV. When indicated, HIV post-exposure prophylaxis should be started as early as possible and within 72 hours. Emergency contraception can be offered to girls at risk of pregnancy who present within 120 hours. Hepatitis B and HPV vaccination, STI prophylaxis or treatment and pregnancy-related care may also be required. This is why medical examination after sexual assault cannot become merely an exercise in collecting evidence for a criminal case. Evidence matters, but the survivor is also simultaneously a patient sitting in front of the doctor.
Unseen injuries
The immediate psychological response to sexual abuse may include fear, confusion, shame, anger, numbness, disturbed sleep or silence. A child may not even have the vocabulary to explain what has happened. The first psychological intervention, therefore, is not necessarily psychotherapy, but safety. The child must be protected from further abuse, listened to without blame and helped to regain a sense of security and normalcy. Repeatedly asking the child to recount traumatic details can itself cause distress.
While some children recover with family support and appropriate care, others may develop post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), depression, anxiety, nightmares, intrusive memories, hypervigilance or dissociation. Self-harm, suicidal thoughts, eating disorders, substance misuse and behavioural problems can also occur. Longer-term difficulties may involve self-worth, emotional regulation, trust, intimacy and relationships.
Experiencing trauma does not automatically mean developing a psychiatric disorder. Outcomes vary with age, developmental stage, duration of abuse, relationship with the perpetrator and support following disclosure. This is why every survivor should receive a baseline mental health assessment covering mood, sleep, behaviour, schooling, relationships, self-harm and suicidality. Its purpose is not to label the child as mentally ill, but to establish a clinical reference point from which recovery or emerging difficulties can be followed.
Trauma over time
Sexual abuse is also not invariably a single traumatic incident. For most children, particularly when the perpetrator has regular access or authority, abuse may recur for months or years. What clinicians encounter may therefore be the cumulative effect of repeated exposure.
Even after the abuse stops, recovery is not governed by a calendar. Memories, family responses, seeing the perpetrator, investigation and court proceedings can reactivate distress. Childhood is also the period during which emotional regulation, self-concept and ideas about safety and relationships are developing. Trauma occurring during these formative years can become entangled with these processes.
Healing consequently means more than making traumatic memories disappear. It means helping the child resume development. Returning to school, playing, sleeping normally, rebuilding relationships and recovering a sense of safety and control can themselves be important parts of recovery.
Paths to recovery
Treatment must be individualised. Supportive psychotherapy and counselling may be sufficient for some. Children with significant symptoms require assessment by trained mental health professionals. Cognitive behavioural therapy helps identify connections between thoughts, emotions and behaviour and develops healthier ways of responding to distress.
For children and adolescents with post-traumatic stress symptoms or PTSD, trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy, or TF-CBT, is an important evidence-based option. It can teach skills to manage anxiety, gradually and safely process traumatic memories, challenge beliefs such as self-blame and help restore normal functioning.
Other interventions, including interpersonal psychotherapy for appropriate emotional disorders and EMDR for PTSD, may have a role depending on clinical assessment. The principle is that every survivor deserves an assessment and access to care, but not every survivor needs the same treatment.
Families matter
Recovery also rarely happens in the consulting room alone. A supportive, non-offending parent or caregiver can be one of the child’s greatest protective resources. Families need guidance on how to respond to disclosure, avoid blaming or repeatedly questioning the child, recognise warning signs, and restore ordinary routines without pretending that nothing happened.
Where safe and appropriate, caregivers can participate in trauma-focused therapy. They, too, may require psychological support. A parent discovering that their child has been sexually abused may experience guilt, anger, helplessness and enormous distress. Helping the caregiver can indirectly strengthen the child’s recovery.
Building capacity
This requires more than appointing counsellors. The system needs to facilitate frontline doctors, paediatricians, gynaecologists, nurses and counsellors to provide immediate trauma-informed care. District services need access to clinical psychologists and psychiatrists, with clear referral pathways for children requiring specialised interventions. The healthcare providers themselves also need protection. Listening repeatedly to accounts of sexual violence can result in secondary or vicarious trauma. Supervision, manageable caseloads, debriefing, peer support, and periods away from continuous trauma work should be built into services rather than regarded as luxuries.
Eventually, the success of our response cannot be measured only by whether justice was set in motion: it is whether the infection was prevented, whether reproductive healthcare was provided, whether the child’s mental health was assessed, whether treatment was available when needed, whether the family knew how to support the child, whether the child returned to school and, ultimately, whether that child was able to move forward.
A humane health system must, at first, ask what needs to happen for the child, while law simultaneously addressing what needs to happen for justice.
(Dr. C. Aravinda is an academic and public health physician. The views expressed are personal. aravindaaiimsjr10@hotmail.com)

How Google Maps knows when a business is packed
Knowing when a venue is busy can make all the difference when you're hungry.
Google Maps is super useful for step-by-step directions, whether you're walking, driving or taking transit to a destination. But it also offers much more than that, highlighting businesses and points of interest along the way with useful information about them. This can include star ratings, opening hours, travel distance and even suggestions about dishes or services visitors tend to love, but it can also provide real-time information as well. At a glance, it can tell you how busy a place is and how long you may be likely to wait.
This information, only available if Google has sufficient data to provide it, can potentially inform your decision as to where and when to go somewhere. If you're in a rush, you don't want to stop at a very busy breakfast spot that won't get you back on the road quickly. Conversely, if you're looking for a vibe, it's best to wait until the local bar is starting to fill up. So, how does Google Maps not only know this information, but know it practically in real time?
Understanding wait times and visit durations
When it comes to specific establishments, like restaurants, hotels, stores and coffee shops, Google uses an aggregate of anonymous data supplied by random users who have opted into the Google Maps Timeline feature. By tracking the density of devices in a certain place, Google can determine how many people are in a specific venue, and thus how busy it is, using typical traffic as a benchmark.
Google works out popular times, usual wait times and how long people stay by analyzing historical data. Google Maps displays a graph that indicates times when the business may be slow and when it's likely to have queues out of the door. The average visit duration and wait time estimates are calculated using visitor patterns from the previous few weeks.
Visit duration is a great metric because it can give you an idea of how long people visit venues, like a museum, which allows you to better plan your day. Meanwhile, wait times are perfect for determining which restaurants and other service-based businesses will fit into your packed itinerary. You can even chat with Google Maps to order food, reserve hotels and more.
Avoiding areas with lots of people
Google also calculates how busy entire areas are, which is great for outdoor events. You can tap the "Busy area" label to see a chart for the times of day the space is usually at its busiest, along with a directory of the businesses in the vicinity. Google captures this data by combining the information it has on various locations within that locale, like stores, restaurants and even parks. It does not, however, capture data from private residences.
This is calculated, once again, using anonymous data from users who have opted into Google Timeline. Google must collect enough visitor data to be able to show this information, so it might not be as readily available for less popular locales. This feature is usually limited to high-traffic zones that attract a lot of people, like a tourist town or a festival location.
The data is always private, says Google, and never reveals the identity of people or the total number of people in a location. Google Maps will only tell you if a place is busy, not busy or so busy that it's probably not worth the hassle.
Before opting in to Google Timeline, it's worth noting that, with this feature on, Google is essentially always tracking your activity. Bear in mind, this not only helps determine the busyness of a location, but can also prove useful in other areas. Google Maps and its sister app, Waze, use similar techniques to track traffic patterns to help you find the best driving route to your destination.
If you prefer not to be part of the process, simply turn off Google Timeline, and you won't contribute to the company's data collection.

Tokyo police have arrested two American women for allegedly smuggling $1 million worth of cannabis into Japan, with one suspect claiming she was motivated by the idea of a free trip to the country, according to an official and local media reports on Friday.
The pair, both 25, arrived at Tokyo’s Haneda Airport from New York last Saturday with two suitcases in which “cannabis-like dried plants were secretly stored,” a police spokesperson said.

The pair were arrested “on suspicion of violating the drugs and psychotropics control law, or, smuggling to gain profit,” the spokesperson said.
They also breached two other laws, he added.
Smuggling cannabis for the purpose of making a profit is punishable with up to 10 years in prison and a fine of up to ¥3 million.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei says the time has come to slow down AI development and will give third-party evaluators like METR access to its models to help ensure its “adherence to safety practices and commitments.” In a winding essay, Amodei proposed a three-step plan to “pace the frontier” — jargon that simply means to slow the pace of training and development to give companies time to build safeguards and regulators to evaluate models.
Anthropic CEO says it’s time to pump the brakes on AI
Dario Amodei proposed a three-step plan to ‘pace the frontier’ of AI development.
Amodei says that giving external evaluators wide-ranging access is just the first step, and one it is taking now unilaterally. Step two would involve the industry coming together as a whole, likely with government agencies to “establish common safety standards as well as limits on the rate of unchecked AI progress.” This step would focus on AI companies operating in democratic countries, but because passing laws and building regulatory infrastructure takes time, Amodei says that the industry should work together to create safety standards.
The third step would be the most challenging — getting authoritarian governments like those in China and Russia to agree to slow development and adopt a global set of AI safety standards. But he also says it’s crucial that the US and other democracies maintain a technological lead over China and other authoritarian regimes by limiting their access to high-powered chips and cracking down on things like distillation that allow companies to quickly catch up by training its AI to replicate the behavior of a more powerful model.
Amodei says that his concern stems from two primary factors. First is the emergence of recursive self-improvement, or RSI, in which AI systems train the next generation of AI, leading to rapidly accelerating capabilities. “Left unchecked, it could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems,” he says. The other is this summer’s OpenAI / Hugging Face incident, in which “a swarm of agents essentially acted as a fanatically devoted collective, conducting cybersecurity attacks on targets they were not asked to attack and that were unrelated to the task at hand, sacrificing themselves for the success of the group, and attempting to hack into the “grader” responsible for evaluating their performance.“
Of course, Anthropic’s Claude was also responsible for a series of rogue AI hacking incidents that have recently put the company under the spotlight.

The world’s most common childhood disability, cerebral palsy, has long been associated with birth complications like premature birth, infection, lack of oxygen, and perinatal stroke. But population studies suggest those factors account for only a fraction of cases. To fill this diagnostic void, modern medicine has routinely turned to gene sequencing to hunt for a root cause, and researchers have zeroed in on certain genetic variants in a substantial subset of children with cerebral palsy.
For families, gene sequencing offers a profound hope: of ending a gruelling diagnostic odyssey. Finding a definitive genetic root cause optimises patient management, reduces unnecessary testing, and finally gives parents concrete answers.
But a new study in The American Journal of Human Genetics suggests simply finding a pathogenic gene variant in a child is not proof that it caused their motor disability.
In resource-constrained healthcare systems like India’s, acting on a false alarm from a standard genetic panel can divert already limited medical resources away from treatments that actually work.
“The medical community previously has not comprehensively examined the statistical evidence in favor of a cerebral palsy association for genes flagged in large genomics cohort studies,” Peter N. Robinson, a computational biologist at the Jackson Laboratory for Genomic Medicine, U.S., and the study’s corresponding author, said. “Our study showed that there is convincing evidence for only a subset.”
Collapsing narrative
The researchers combed through 21 previously published genomic diagnostic studies involving 5,440 individuals diagnosed with cerebral palsy. Across these diverse cohorts, the original authors had pointed the finger at a staggering 515 different candidate genes, reporting them as the direct genetic cause of the patients’ symptoms.
But when Dr. Robinson’s team subjected this historical data to rigorous statistical analysis, the established narrative collapsed. Sufficient statistical evidence could only confirm a true association for 89 of those 515 proposed genes.
Sequencing the genomes of 460 patients across the Shriners Children’s hospital network in the U.S., the team also identified disease-causing mutations in 60 genes across 15.8% of children. Yet their stricter statistical paradigm whittled the list down to only 16 with significant evidence linked to cerebral palsy.
“What this paper is trying to suggest is some of the genetic variants may not be slam dunk,” said Kuntal Sen, a clinical geneticist and paediatric neurologist at Children’s National Hospital, U.S. “It might explain one problem, like intellectual disability, but it may not tie together everything. Which is a fair point to make, that some genetic test reports might be just a slight association rather than causal.”
False alarms
These false alarms can be traced back to a few traps. One is coincidence. Because roughly 5% of the general population harbours a rare genetic disease, sequencing a child with cerebral palsy frequently uncovers severe mutations entirely unrelated to the disability.
A previous large-scale study flagged the LIPH gene as a cause of cerebral palsy because an affected patient happened to carry it. However, mutations in LIPH actually cause a rare form of hair loss and possess no known neurological link.
Conversely, across both historical literature and the newly sequenced cohort, CTNNB1 mutations showed up far more often than random chance would allow, providing the proof necessary to confirm it is a real risk factor.
The confusion is also compounded by the fact that ‘cerebral palsy’ is a clinical catch-all rather than a single biological disease.
“For me, I think the term ‘cerebral palsy’ does not always make sense from a purely scientific perspective.,” Dr. Sen said. “The motor symptoms that the children have [severe muscle stiffness, and weakness affecting either one side of the body or all four limbs] are more scientifically informative.”
He noted the outdated label survives, rightfully, mainly because it guarantees patients access to specialised insurance and physical therapy in the western world.
But as an umbrella term for brain-derived muscle weakness, the diagnosis lumps a large variety of conditions together. While some stem from birth injuries, others are ‘mimics’: rare metabolic or genetic disorders masquerading as a muscle weakness.
Stakes of precision
This heterogeneous reality is why distinguishing a harmless genetic coincidence from a true biological driver carries large stakes.
If doctors accept an incidental mutation from a standard genetic panel as the final answer, they may halt their workup prematurely, leaving a true, treatable ‘mimic’ undiscovered. But accurately pinpointing the biological cause using strict statistical proof can fine-tune this personalised approach and open the door to highly targeted care.
“If the genetic test report gives you a slam dunk answer, you counsel them, you provide management guidelines, and you can also give a recurrence risk for other family members,” Dr. Sen said.
The researchers estimated that among 8.5% to 24% of individuals who receive a valid genetic diagnosis, the findings point to specific, available treatments. By catching mimics early, doctors can swap generic physical therapy for precise interventions, such as dietary changes for arginase deficiency or specific medications for vitamin-dependent epilepsies and hereditary dystonia.
For these families, getting the statistics right means much more than simply solving a mystery. It unlocks treatments that can alter the course of a child’s life.
For countries like India, where three in every 1,000 live births are affected by cerebral palsy and genetic testing is an emerging and rapidly growing field, studies like this offer an advantage. A severe mutation that breaks a specific protein and masquerades as cerebral palsy does so universally, regardless of ethnicity. And by identifying only the true genetic mimics, local clinics can skip the diagnostic trial-and-error phase of older, bloated sequencing panels, and pave the way to adopt highly accurate genetic testing, connecting families to precise treatments faster.
Cautious path
While the Robinson et al. study has set a rigorous new standard, the authors have also conceded their strict mathematical model might actually underestimate the true number of genes linked to the disorder.
“One must remember that the lack of statistical significance does not imply the absence of an association,” Dr. obinson said. “It is very likely that there are more genes with cerebral palsy association than the 89 we flagged.”
Realising the full promise of this approach will require the medical community to move beyond just sequencing DNA. Scientists need large, globally shared datasets of detailed patient profiles to finally calculate the exact degree of risk a specific genetic variant carries.
Ultimately, translating these statistical insights into daily practice will take time. “With appropriate caution, genomic testing can be a useful addition to CP diagnostics,” Dr. Robinson said. “Caring physicians will integrate many kinds of information when making the decision.”
Anirban Mukhopadhyay is a geneticist by training and science communicator from New Delhi.

Israel uses Lebanese civilians as bargaining chips
Lebanese farmer Saleh* woke up before dawn on 3 September to harvest his fig trees in the southern Lebanese border village of Halta.
When he stepped out and saw lights outside his neighbours' house, abandoned during the war, Saleh knew an Israeli army unit was there.
The Israeli soldiers were searching houses in the village and called three residents on their mobile phones instructing them to come outside.
After several hours of interrogations, they took the three men away, including Hatem Abdel-Aal, a member of the municipal council. The Israeli army returned Hatem at around midnight.
“They told him you have to come to us by foot, without a car,” Saleh told Middle East Eye. “The man followed their instructions and headed their way. He couldn’t refuse.”
