Nepal is demanding $20m in climate compensation for the recent devastating floods, as a senior minister called on the world’s most polluting countries to “wake up” and accept shared responsibility for a disaster that led to the death or disappearance of more than 6,000 people.
Scientists believe the climate crisis had a role to play in the floods, which were triggered when a melting glacier partially collapsed and set off a deadly landslide and flash flooding through Chinese-controlled Tibet and Nepal in late August. So far, more than 1,300 are confirmed dead and more than 5,500 still missing, with hopes of their survival diminished after 12 days of rescue operations.
Speaking to the Guardian, Nepal’s foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, was forthright in his call for climate justice and said it was imperative the world’s biggest economies stepped up to help Nepal recover and rebuild after the catastrophic floods.
Nepal contributes less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions, while its neighbours India and China are among the world’s biggest emitters. The mountains of the Himalayas – which span across India, China, Nepal and Bhutan – have been warming at a rate nearly 50% faster than the global average.
In 2023, the UN said Nepal’s mountains had lost close to a third of their ice in just over 30 years due to global heating.
Khanal emphasised that the recent disaster was far more extreme than any flooding regularly seen during the monsoon season, and said the magnitude of damage was on par with the 2015 earthquake that left much of the country in ruins.
“This felt like a tsunami that was coming from the Himalayas,” he said. “We experienced waves as high as 60, 70 feet, which were mixed with debris, mud, stones, rocks, and came at the speed of almost 180km per hour. Towns, villages and highways were completely wiped out and there are some areas still disconnected.”
Khanal confirmed that Nepal’s ministry of finance and ministry of environment had written a joint letter to the UN’s fund for responding to loss and damage – which was set up in 2022 in line with the Paris climate agreement – to request $20m in climate-related damages.
“We have contributed so little to climate change,” he said. “It is imperative for those in the global community who benefit from larger, much more polluting economies, and whose historical contribution to greenhouse gases is much bigger than ours, to accept a shared responsibility. This affects all of humanity.”
For Nepal, the disaster was particularly worrying because it was “one of the strongest warning signals that we’ve experienced of what’s to come”, he said.
“The global community should not see this as one-off disaster; it should be viewed in the context of the changing climate in the Himalayas,” he said. “We know it is going to be a recurring scenario that more and more communities, not just in Nepal but around the world, will have to face.”
Khanal acknowledged that the compensation amount Nepal has requested from the UN was “obviously not nearly enough to cover the damage that we have sustained”. According to some estimates, the total damage caused by the floods will be upwards of $5bn, though Khanal said it could be even higher.
Upwards of 20,000 homes will probably have to be rebuilt, as well as the main highway. Villages built in vulnerable areas along the river, some of which washed away entirely, may have to be relocated to higher, safer ground.
While Khanal initially singled out India and China as countries that should step in to help – while avoiding mention of the US, which is the world’s biggest polluter – he rowed back on those comments, saying: “It is not just about shifting the blame to one or the other country, it’s about us all working together.”
He emphasised that the compensation demand was also meant to act as a “wake-up call for the global community to establish a more robust mechanism to help vulnerable and small economies like Nepal”.
The UN has admitted the loss and damage fund is already facing a “significant financing gap”. The fund has already received requests totalling $2.8bn from about 119 countries, but so far only around $400m has been given by the international community. The US has given just $17m, after Donald Trump withdrew from the Paris agreement.
Khanal acknowledged there were “political challenges” in getting Nepal the climate compensation it was demanding.
“Yes there always will be people who may not agree to our perspective or deny there is climate change, but there are also people who deny that the Earth is round,” he said bluntly.
He emphasised the importance of funds being made available not just for immediate disaster response but also for preparedness and mitigation for climate-related risk.
Khanal rebuffed allegations that China had failed to give an adequate warning or share data with Nepal about the impending floods. He said he was in discussion with China about enhancing coordination and data sharing for the Himalayan region.
“With the benefit of hindsight, we can now see that this glacier was fragile and had been receding in the past six months,” he said.
“But before the floods hit, there was no knowledge on our part, or on the part of Chinese scientists, that this particular collapse was imminent. I do not believe any of us had any idea of the threat until it happened.”

Osborne makes history as first female jockey to win a Classic with St Leger victory
- Published
Saffie Osborne has become the first female jockey to win one of British Flat racing's five Classics, riding Highwayman to victory in the St Leger at Doncaster.
The 24-year-old burst clear of the field on the 11-1 chance in the closing stages to create history in the 250th anniversary of the world's oldest Classic Flat race.
It was a one-two for winning trainer Joseph O'Brien, whose colt Enceladus (5-2) finished second, two-and-a-half lengths back.
Aidan O'Brien was bidding to become just the third trainer to win a fourth consecutive St Leger but had to be content with third with Amelia Earhart (22-1).
Pre-race favourite Christmas Day (7-4) was heavily backed to give Aidan O'Brien that historic fourth victory in a row and complete the Derby-St Leger double, but finished well down in ninth place.
'Changed my life'
"I definitely didn't have this on the bingo card this week," Osborne told ITV Sport immediately after the historic victory in the fifth and final Classic of the British Flat season.
"I didn't even know if I would be riding the St Leger on Monday morning."
No female jockey has won any of the other four Classics - the 1,000 Guineas and 2,000 Guineas at Newmarket and the Oaks and Derby at Epsom.
Osborne was quick to thank the trainer for giving her the ride, adding: "I have to thank Joseph and his team for putting their faith in me. It won't change Joseph's life, but it's changed mine."
The jockey is the daughter of trainer and former top National Hunt jockey Jamie Osborne, while her mother, Katie O'Sullivan, is a highly-regarded equine artist.
She started as an apprentice in 2020 and finished second in the apprentice championship the following season.
Osborne went on to be crowned leading jockey in the Racing League for three consecutive seasons from 2022 to 2024.
In 2024, she became the first female jockey to win a race at the Dubai Carnival, on Ouzo, while her first Classic ride came in the same season, finishing eighth on Ed Walker's Ten Bob Tony in the 2,000 Guineas.
Like Rachel Blackmore, the first female jockey to win the Grand National, her name will now go down in racing folklore.
'I told her to make history... but I didn't really believe it'
Joseph O'Brien was at Leopardstown for the Irish Champion Stakes on Saturday, but delighted Highwayman owner John Neocleous was at Doncaster to share the moment with Osborne.
"Saffie is amazing, I'm sure she's in shock as well," he said after watching her storm clear at the end of the one mile six furlong trip.
"Joseph came up with the idea, but he called me first and I was extremely happy to have her. She's an up-and-coming jockey, she knows how to ride a finish and I thought if she rode a good finish maybe we'd be placed.
"But she won comprehensively so I'm very happy. I said to Saffie, 'let's go and make history', but I didn't really believe it!"
The surprise victory continues trainer Joseph O'Brien's love affair with the St Leger.
He won the race as a jockey on Leading Light in 2013 and claimed his first victory as a trainer in 2020 with Galileo Chrome.
Enceladus was expected to be his best chance to double his number of winners in the famous old race, having hit top form this season with three big victories, including in the Gordon Stakes at Goodwood.
But Highwayman had also showed rapid improvement this year, especially in winning the Vinnie Roe Stakes at Leopardstown.

GTA 6 is a little over two months away, releasing November 19, 2026, and it’s easily the biggest entertainment property of the decade. Most players have already pre-ordered GTA 6 to experience Jason and Lucia’s story on day one. However, some players are still hoping Rockstar’s next game arrives on Xbox Game Pass at launch. This begs the question: will GTA 6 release on the service at launch? Here’s everything we know so far.
Is GTA 6 Coming to Xbox Game Pass at Launch?
The answer is no, GTA 6 will not be available on Xbox Game Pass at launch on November 19, 2026. Rockstar has never released one of its major games on Xbox Game Pass at launch.
With reports claiming that GTA 6 pre-orders have surpassed 4 million copies, there’s no reason whatsoever for Rockstar to release their biggest game ever on a subscription service.
Furthermore, GTA 6’s $100 Ultimate Edition is already dominating pre-orders over the $80 Standard, so all things considered, Rockstar is doing incredibly well even before the game is released. So, it’s extremely unlikely- rather, impossible that Rockstar releases GTA 6 on Xbox Game Pass at launch.
That’s not to say that GTA 6 won’t drop on Xbox Game Pass in the future. Rockstar has a history of releasing their games on the service several years after release, so the studio could follow the same path with GTA 6. However, just don’t expect it anytime soon.
For players who want to experience the game on day one, there’s no option other than to pre-order GTA 6’s Standard or Ultimate Edition to play it on November 19, 2026. If GTA 6 arrives on Xbox Game Pass in the future, and that’s a big if, you’d already have completed the game ten times over.
Rockstar’s History with Xbox Game Pass
Previously, Rockstar’s two biggest titles, GTA 5 and Red Dead Redemption 2, had their fair share of stints on Xbox Game Pass, though none were particularly long. GTA 5 first appeared on Xbox Game Pass on January 3, 2020, more than six years after its debut on Xbox 360 and PS3 on September 17, 2013.
Meanwhile, Red Dead Redemption 2 appeared on the service on May 7, 2020, nearly two years after its October 26, 2018 release. Since then, both games have returned to the platform multiple times, with GTA 5 appearing four times on Game Pass and Red Dead Redemption 2 once. Here’s a table comparing the two:
| Rockstar Game | First Run | Recent Run | 
|---|---|---|
| GTA 5 | January 3, 2020 – May 7, 2020 | April 15, 2025 – April 15, 2026 | 
| Red Dead Redemption 2 | May 7, 2020 – September 7, 2020 | May 7, 2020 – September 7, 2020 | 
GTA 5 had its longest Xbox Game Pass run this year, while its previous stints lasted around four to six months each. On the other hand, RDR 2 has appeared only once, leaving Game Pass on September 7, 2020, and has not returned since.
Will GTA 6 Come to Xbox Game Pass in the Future?
Judging by Rockstar’s history with Xbox Game Pass, GTA 6 could eventually join the service, but not anytime soon. If anything, you might want to think beyond 2030. If that happens, the game will likely hit the service years after GTA 6’s PC release, which is rumored to arrive next year.
There’s no sugarcoating it, but players waiting to play GTA 6 on Xbox Game Pass will be sorely disappointed if they’re expecting Rockstar to follow the same path with Red Dead Redemption 2. GTA 6 is way bigger than Red Dead Redemption 2, both in sheer scale and in anticipation. It’s the biggest game of the decade, or likely, the century.
There’s a chance Hideo Kojima releases PHYSINT on Xbox before GTA 6 joins Game Pass, and the former likely won’t release on the service either. However, plans could change, and Rockstar may pivot to a quicker release for GTA 6 on the subscription platform.
One thing’s confirmed: GTA 6 is launching on November 19, 2026, on Xbox Series X|S, so you can put those delay concerns to rest. With just over two months to go, we are finally in the home stretch now. That said, when do you think GTA 6 will join Xbox Game Pass? Tell us in the comments section below.
Will GTA 6 launch on Xbox Game Pass day one?
No, GTA 6 won’t join Xbox Game Pass at launch on November 19, 2026. Instead, Xbox players will need to purchase either the Standard or Ultimate Edition through the Xbox Store.
Has Rockstar ever released a game on Xbox Game Pass at launch?
No, Rockstar has never released a game on Xbox Game Pass at launch. However, both GTA 5 and Red Dead Redemption 2 joined the service years after their original releases.
What is the last Rockstar game to join Xbox Game Pass?
The last Rockstar game to join Xbox Game Pass was GTA 5, which returned to the service on April 15, 2025. It was available on Console, PC, and Cloud before leaving on April 15, 2026.

India set out to expand its forested areas a decade ago. Last week, however, we learned that the forest cover programme had barely taken root when the government’s auditors released their findings of the flagship Green India Mission. The shortfall of 97.57% from India’s initial pledge in 2014 was stark enough to alarm the government’s own auditor, who described the progress as “negligible”.
Yet if you ask the government about forest cover, you’ll get a far greener picture.
I’m writing this on the day the UK Met Office issued a calamitous warning – 2027 could be the hottest year yet, on account of the strongest El Niño in more than a century. For India, a disrupted monsoon season puts agriculture and millions who depend on it at risk.
Which makes the question of what’s happening to India’s green cover feel far more urgent than an academic disagreement over numbers. I went down the rabbit hole of reports, datasets and government’s parliamentary disclosures. Here’s what I found.
1. Forest cover v forest cover
The government’s last comprehensive report from 2023 (released a year later) touted that forest cover in India has grown since 2021. But other, independent, assessments have found that forest cover is lower than what the government has claimed in recent years, or that it has reduced.
The discrepancy lies in some creative accounting. Last year, dozens of former civil servants wrote to the government criticising the forest report. They described its methodology as unreliable and nonscientific, pointing to the inclusion of smaller orchards, as well as coconut and rubber plantations, in the calculation of forest cover.
“A lot of the discrepancies are coming from how and what we are counting as forests. We have broadened the definition to include a lot more,” Pooja Choksi, founder of environmental consultancy Ficus Research Consulting, told me.
The government has defended its methodology, saying its definition is internationally accepted and includes tree-covered land outside forests as well as orchards and bamboo and palm plantations.
2. Whose land is it anyway?
Even as the government pledged to increase forestation, over the past five years India has approved the diversion of forest land for development projects covering an area roughly equivalent to the size of Hong Kong, according to data shared in parliament this month. The pace has accelerated, with the last financial year seeing the single largest chunk cleared yet.
Mining was the single-biggest sector, accounting for 22% of all diverted forest land, followed by road works and irrigation projects.
3. Ground zero
The pressure on forests is concentrated in some states. Nearly a quarter of all forest land diverted nationwide since 2021 is in Madhya Pradesh, which is home to the country’s largest forest area. Its share is more than double that of the next state, Odisha. Arunachal Pradesh on the north-eastern border with China ranks third for forest diversions, according to government figures shared in parliament.
One research team that mapped 28 years of satellite data from three central Indian coalmine regions, including two in Madhya Pradesh, found the damage from such projects extended far beyond disappearing trees. Water bodies shrank, soil quality degraded and the overall natural ecosystems diminished by 35%.
4. The ‘great’ project
Perhaps nowhere is this trade-off more starkly visible than in the project proposed in the pristine Andaman and Nicobar Islands, which are home to protected Indigenous tribes.
The central government has touted the Great Nicobar Project as a strategic necessity to strengthen India’s maritime and defence presence in the Indo-Pacific. The project would divert 13,075 hectares of forest land and cut down, conservatively, at least 700,000 trees to make way for a trans-shipment port, an international airport, a mega township and a power plant for their operation, at a combined cost north of $6.89 bn (Rs 90,000 crore). The project has already led to legal challenges and pushback from the opposition Congress party and environmentalists.
“Situated at the precise intersection of variable sea-level rise and sinking land, the Great Nicobar Project is not merely ecologically destructive or culturally erosive for the Indigenous populations – it is geologically impossible,” geoscientist CP Rajendran wrote in The Wire, arguing that the government is using natural security as a pretext to push a commercial hub in one of the world’s most tectonically active zones.
5. Is compensatory afforestation the answer?
For many such development projects that divert forest land, the answer has been to pour substantial public funds into planting trees and creating forests elsewhere. But experts caution that this may not be as simple a solution as it may sound.
Choksi, whose research focuses on biodiversity outcomes of restoration and tree-planting policies, said the rush to meet Paris Agreement targets has made India obsessed with “green cover” while ignoring other aspects of environmental policy.
“We need to move away from this very one-dimensional view that everything is green cover. What is being planted and where it is planted has a huge influence. The third question being why is it being planted because different trees have different purposes,” Choksi said.
A natural forest patch with 100 different species, she added, has very different ecological value to a plantation under the Green India Mission, which might have 20 species. “It does have biodiversity value, but it certainly does not have the same value as the diverse forest patches that we have across the country,” she said.
All of this shows that the true health of India’s forests is not easy to assess, which is in itself concerning. Meanwhile, India’s biennial forest report was due in 2025. We’re still waiting.

A recommendation from someone with great taste
Diet Sabya (@dietsabya), the anonymous Indian fashion watchdog, spills the tea on his current obsession: “Gathering by Haider Saleem is a very under-the-radar, slow-fashion brand that not enough people know about. There’s a lingering notion that Indian menswear-forward brands have to look a certain way or that they somehow can’t occupy the same conversation, say as The Row or Lemaire. Gathering proves otherwise. The clothes have this organic ease to them: earthy tones, flattering cuts, natural fabrics, with much of the dyeing done traditionally in Jaipur. The sort of brand you want to gate keep until everyone discovers it and you can say: “Oh, I’ve known them for ages.’”

A number worth knowing

The Prime Minister’s Citizen Assistance and Relief in Emergency Situations Fund (PM Cares), set up during the coronavirus pandemic, had a balance of £647m (Rs 8,452 crore) at the end of the 2025 financial year, prompting questions about why such a large sum remained unused instead of being put towards relief work. Pradeep Bhandari, a spokesperson for the Bharatiya Janata party, countered the charge in a debate on Times Now, saying the PM Cares fund provides for long-term rehabilitation instead of immediate relief during disasters.
Vibe check
For choreographer and director Usha Jey (@usha_jey), learning bharatanatyam at the age of 20 was a way to connect to her culture. Jey, who is French and of Sri Lankan Tamil heritage, has since developed her own movement language. Hybrid bharatham, as she calls it, fuses the Indian classical dance form with hip-hop but is careful to retain the integrity of both. There is an interplay of abandon and elegance in her choreographic works. Actor Maitreyi Ramakrishnan features in her latest video, Hide N Seek. Train derails in France and injures 44 as authorities investigate possible sabotage
French authorities are investigating whether sabotage caused a train derailment in Normandy that injured 44 people
PARIS -- French authorities are investigating whether sabotage caused a train derailment that injured 44 people in Normandy, after a piece of rail was found on the track, police told The Associated Press on Saturday.
The regional train was carrying 186 passengers from Rouen to Caen when it derailed Friday evening at Cléon, in the Seine-Maritime department of northwestern France.
An 18-year-old woman was among the injured and was evacuated by helicopter to Rouen University Hospital, police said.
A spokeswoman for the French national police communications service, known as SICOP, said that the piece of rail found on the track was “probably” linked to the derailment. She spoke on condition of anonymity because she wasn’t authorized to be publicly named in line with police policy.
Investigators were working to establish whether the circumstances were accidental or involved sabotage, the service said. The prosecutor’s office remained cautious about drawing conclusions, according to the police.
France’s previous rail disasters include the July 2013 derailment at Brétigny-sur-Orge, south of Paris, which killed seven people.
In November 2015, a high-speed TGV train carrying out tests derailed at Eckwersheim, near Strasbourg, killing 11.
More recently, a crash involving two high-speed trains at Adamuz in southern Spain killed 46 people and injured more than 100 in January, according to the Andalusian regional government.

Welcome to Edition 9.10 of the Rocket Report! This week we’re celebrating a historic moment in Europe when a German rocket company successfully put its launch vehicle into orbit. Isar Aerospace became the first purely commercial European company to reach orbit, and impressively it did so on just its second launch attempt. How quickly can they scale up operations? How quickly will the second European launch firm reach this goal? Big questions, which for now we don’t have answers to.
As always, we welcome reader submissions, and if you don’t want to miss an issue, please subscribe using the box below (the form will not appear on AMP-enabled versions of the site). Each report will include information on small-, medium-, and heavy-lift rockets as well as a quick look ahead at the next three launches on the calendar.
Isar Aerospace takes a huge step forward. Isar Aerospace, founded in 2018 by three students at a German university, successfully launched a privately developed rocket into low-Earth orbit on Saturday from a Norwegian spaceport inside the Arctic Circle. The two-stage rocket, Spectrum, became the first fully commercial launch vehicle in Europe to reach orbit, Ars reports. With Saturday’s success, Isar becomes the clear leader among a pack of several European launch startups vying to inject some competition into Europe’s stagnant launch market.
Private capital emerges … It took eight years for Isar to get to orbit, a timetable similar to other successful commercial rocket startups in the West. In that time, the company raised roughly $1 billion through several private financing rounds and now has a workforce of nearly 500 employees. European space officials hope a jolt of competition will light a fire under the continent’s rocket industry. European governments are accustomed to footing the bill and having a say in where rockets are built, a procurement model known as geographical return, or geo-return. The paradigm is different with companies like Isar, which established themselves on a privately funded basis, with ambitions to eventually attract commercial and government business.
Long-forgotten space plane is back? Ars Technica has written precisely one article about Ravn X, an autonomous aircraft and launch vehicle under development by Aevum. This was back in December 2020. We haven’t covered it since, I think it’s safe to say, there is a fair amount of skepticism about whether the project to build the space plane was all that realistic. And time has largely proved us right. The company’s initial target of an orbital mission in 2021 came and went. We largely forgot about the vehicle. Then something mysterious showed up at Long Beach Airport.
Don’t get too excited … TWZ reports that a handful of aviation photographers got a surprise eyeful of a very sleek and large aircraft silhouette last week at the airport and later learned that it was likely a mockup of Ravn X. Later on, in posts on X, Aevum founder Jay Skylus said the company “conducted Test 2 of Ravn X SN0 early this morning. Ravn X completed its first fully autonomous taxi. ~37 minutes of autonomy. We’re reviewing the telemetry and test data now and will share more as soon as I can.” We are not expecting any flights imminently. (submitted by Onychomys)
The Ars Technica Rocket Report
The easiest way to keep up with Eric Berger’s and Stephen Clark’s reporting on all things space is to sign up for our newsletter. We’ll collect their stories and deliver them straight to your inbox.
UK invests big time in northern spaceport. This week, the United Kingdom unveiled a new national space strategy that seeks to “drive growth, strengthen security and back everyday technologies.” As part of efforts to reindustrialize the country, the government is investing 7.8 billion pounds ($10.5 billion) through 2030. About 40 percent of the funding will go toward strengthening connectivity, including the Connectivity in Low Earth Orbit and SKYNET defense communications programs, which “play a pivotal role in keeping our Armed Forces connected wherever they are in the world.”
German rockets to launch from there … The UK government also wants to help push forward a spaceport under development in Shetland, an archipelago north of the Scottish mainland. The government will provide 30 million pounds ($40.5 million) for the SaxaVord Spaceport in Shetland, with the aim of “helping Britain and our partners to launch satellites without relying on countries further afield while creating new jobs.” No orbital rocket has ever successfully launched from the United Kingdom. The main tenant of SaxaVord is German launch company Rocket Factory Augsburg. (submitted by iCowboy)
Firefly to launch from Sweden. Firefly Aerospace announced on Wednesday a multi-launch agreement with SSC Space for two Alpha rocket launches from Sweden’s Esrange Space Center. Targeted to launch no earlier than 2028, the missions will serve Sweden’s national security customers as well as additional commercial rideshare customers.
More to come … Jason Kim, CEO of Firefly Aerospace, said more Alpha launches will follow. “These first two missions are just the start of a long-term, multi-launch partnership with SSC Space that will provide assured access to space for years to come,” he said. SSC Space secured the full payload capacity and can allocate payload space to its government and commercial customers, providing flexible accommodations and launch opportunities for the European satellite market.
Avio seeks higher flight rate. Avio is looking to boost the pace of Vega-C rocket flights to six missions per year, roughly double the current level, and potentially go another 50 percent higher, Aviation Week reports. “We are working to increase, as a first step, the cadence of Vega to six per year, and potentially a second step to nine per year,” Giulio Ranzo said Wednesday during the International Space Summit in Paris.
Solid production is not so solid … The Vega-C rocket is used heavily by institutions for launch in Europe, where demand is rising. “We will follow what they need, what they ask us, and we will try to adapt to continue providing the service,” Ranzo said. One of the challenges in ramping up is that the Vega-C used the same solid rocket motors employed on Ariane 6, which is also looking to boost output. The combination is creating supply-chain bottlenecks that industry and government are trying to address.
Stoke Space eyes larger rocket. Stoke Space announced Tuesday that it has raised another significant round of funding, $1 billion, as it makes a final push toward its debut launch next year. The Washington-based launch company also revealed plans for a larger medium-lift vehicle, Ars reports. The quantity of new funding will enable the company to accelerate work on a larger “Block 2” version of the Nova rocket, capable of lifting 15 metric tons to low-Earth orbit in a fully reusable configuration.
Block 2 will rock you … “We have already started development on a larger vehicle, and we felt like now is the time to pour gas on that fire and really start full-force development of the larger vehicle, and so that’s the reason for the timing,” Stoke co-founder and Chief Executive Andy Lapsa said. The Nova Pathfinder vehicle has a diameter of about 12.5 feet, slightly larger than SpaceX’s Falcon 9 vehicle, although it is considerably shorter. The Block 2 version of Nova is intended to have a 15-foot diameter, Lapsa said. Stoke is targeting 2029 for the debut launch of Block 2.
Ariane 64 gets with Amazon for some more. Arianespace and Amazon Leo announced Wednesday an agreement at the International Space Summit in Paris for six additional Ariane 64 launches to continue deploying the Amazon Leo constellation into low-Earth orbit. The new order brings the total number of Amazon Leo launches with Arianespace to 24, up from 18, with missions scheduled through 2031 from Europe’s Spaceport in French Guiana.
Arianespace, the on-time provider? … To the surprise of some observers, including your humble correspondent, Arianespace has proven to be a more reliable launch partner to Amazon than the other two providers who inked deals with Amazon in 2022, United Launch Alliance and Blue Origin. But Ariane 6 has gotten through its teething pains without major issues, unlike Vulcan and New Glenn. “We committed early because we believed in what Arianespace was building, and they’ve executed mission after mission,” said Chris Weber, vice president of Amazon Leo business and product. “Expanding from 18 to 24 launches reflects our confidence in Ariane 6 and our continued investment in European launch capability.”
Nyx will fly on Ariane 6. Arianespace and The Exploration Company announced this week that Nyx, the reusable space capsule developed by The Exploration Company, will launch into orbit on an Ariane 6 rocket from French Guiana. The Exploration Company chief executive, Hélène Huby, has said she is targeting late 2028 for the launch of this spacecraft, which is due to fly a cargo mission to the International Space Station.
Commercial cargo redux … The launch deal follows the award of a service contract to The Exploration Company by the European Space Agency worth 760 million euros ($880 million) to support the development of Nyx, a demonstration mission, and two operational cargo missions. “We started the development of Nyx with private funding only, and we are now at a technical maturity level where ESA and Member States’ public funding can support us massively, as anchor clients, to help us finalize the vehicle,” Huby said.
Does Europe need a massive rocket? Speaking of Huby and The Exploration Company, the company also announced a $450 million Series C funding round this week, Ars reports. As part of this, the company will continue development of the Storm rocket engine, which is projected to have a thrust of about 400,000 pound-feet. This would be used to power a reusable rocket intended to launch 40 metric tons in reusable mode and 60 tons in expendable mode.
How to stay relevant … The expendable Ariane 6 rocket, by contrast, has a maximum lift capacity of about 20 tons. “If Europe wants to stay relevant—we will not be relevant without a massive rocket at a massive cadence,” Huby said during a teleconference with reporters on Tuesday. “And to do that we need a massive engine, and right now this is something we just do not have in Europe.” An aggressive timeline for the rocket’s development, she said, is 2033.
Terran R gets on-ramped by NASA. NASA said this week it has awarded a “Launch Services II” contract to Relativity Space that allows for on-ramping the Terran R rocket into the agency’s launch services program. Accordingly, the Terran R launch service will be available to NASA for future missions, including science, research, and human spaceflight.
Don’t expect Terran R to win awards right away … NASA still wants to see a new rocket like Terran R, which has yet to make its debut, demonstrate success in flight. However, by receiving this contract, Relativity can now follow a pathway for new launch service providers to compete for future missions. The current ordering period covers missions through December 2032.

A certified meteorologist, Eric lives in Houston.

BRICS 2026: PM Modi meets Abu Dhabi Crown Prince in Delhi; trade, energy security in focus
The meeting comes amid growing India-UAE cooperation, particularly in the areas of trade and energy security
Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday met the Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, with the bilateral talks focusing on push for trade corridors and investment expansion.
The talks, held at the Hyderabad House in New Delhi, took place on the sidelines of the ongoing BRICS Summit. The Abu Dhabi crown prince is in the national capital to attend the summit, representing the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Follow BRICS Summit LIVE updates here.
The meeting comes amid growing India-UAE cooperation, particularly in the areas of trade and energy security, with the two sides working towards shared prosperity.
Deep Dive
The UAE became a full member of BRICS in January 2024, along with Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran and Saudi Arabia, while Indonesia joined the grouping as a full member in January 2025.
According to the UAE News Agency WAM, the country's BRICS membership supports its efforts to expand its economic and trade partnerships and strengthen its presence in global markets, while adding an economy that serves as a global hub for trade, investment and logistics to the group.
It aligns with the UAE's approach of economic openness and diversification of partnerships, while creating opportunities to develop trade corridors, expand investment and business channels, and strengthen cooperation with emerging and developing economies.
This coincides with the expansion of the UAE's Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) programme, under which 38 agreements have been signed since its launch in September 2021, including CEPAs with India and Indonesia, both BRICS members.
India-UAE Comprehensive Strategic Partnership
The ministry of external affairs had earlier on Friday welcomed the Crown Prince to the BRICS Summit and said his visit would provide an opportunity to further strengthen the India-UAE Comprehensive Strategic Partnership.
In a post on X, the MEA said, "Warmly welcome Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi H.H. Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan to the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi. He was received by MOS @KVSinghMPGonda at the airport."
"The visit will be an opportunity to further strengthen India-UAE Comprehensive Strategic Partnership centred on robust trade and energy security for shared prosperity," the ministry said.
More on BRICS
India is hosting the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi on September 12-13. India's Chairship is guided by the theme “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability”, with development, sustainability, and innovation as key areas of focus.
BRICS has emerged as an important platform for coordination among major emerging economies and for advancing the interests of the Global South in multilateral institutions. Its agenda covers development, finance, technology, trade and people-to-people exchanges.
The grouping currently comprises 11 countries -- Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and the UAE. Along with 10 partner countries--Nigeria, Belarus, Bolivia, Cuba, Kazakhstan, Malaysia, Thailand, Uganda, Uzbekistan and Vietnam.

OpenAI is open to slowing the development of AI systems in coordination with other leading AI companies amid growing concerns about the safety of frontier models. CEO Sam Altman told employees at a company-wide meeting this week that OpenAI could moderate the pace of development alongside other AI companies, Bloomberg reported, citing sources. However, Altman said that some companies might not agree to such an approach, according to the report. Inc42 has reached out to OpenAI for a comment on the development. The story will be updated upon receiving a response. Competition among OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, and other AI companies has raised concerns that commercial pressure could lead developers to advance or deploy powerful models before adequate safeguards are in place. OpenAI has previously acknowledged that the pace of frontier-model development may eventually need to be moderated. In July, the company said AI development could accelerate to a point at which the world would “need to pace the rate of AI advancement”. Yesterday, OpenAI also backed mandatory national AI safety requirements in the US, citing the possibility that advanced systems could help accelerate their own development. The latest development follows a series of incidents that have intensified scrutiny of the controls surrounding autonomous AI agents. In August, OpenAI said it paused reinforcement-learning training for some of its latest models for two weeks while strengthening its security measures. The measures followed an incident in which an OpenAI agent escaped a controlled environment, accessed the open internet, and compromised systems belonging to AI developer platform Hugging Face. OpenAI subsequently introduced stronger sandboxing, tighter internet restrictions for high-risk workloads, and enhanced monitoring of potentially unsafe model behaviour. Pro Subscriptions Paused In a separate development, OpenAI has temporarily stopped accepting new subscriptions to its $200 per month Pro plan amid a surge in demand for Astra, its latest flagship AI model. Thibault “Tibo” Sottiaux, an OpenAI product leader responsible for products including ChatGPT and Codex, said in a post on X, “To make sure our current users have an incredible experience and continued access to Astra, we are going to pause subscriptions to our $200 Pro plan.” He added that Pro subscriptions put the greatest strain on OpenAI’s systems and that the company wanted to take the “smallest step” required to continue providing broad access to Astra. The pause will not affect existing Pro subscribers. OpenAI’s other subscription plans and its API remain available, while the company works to add more computing capacity. Launched on September 3, Astra has been rolled out across OpenAI’s Pro, Plus, Enterprise and Business plans. OpenAI described Astra as the beginning of its “AGI era” and a generational leap in AI capabilities. AI Misuse Risks Grow Meanwhile, warnings from researchers who have worked at leading AI companies have added to concerns over the pace of AI development. Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at OpenAI and Anthropic, accused the companies of pursuing increasingly capable and potentially self-improving systems without adequately addressing the risks. Coxon said researchers at the companies “earnestly believe” that advanced AI could pose an existential threat, while accusing the developers of racing towards self-improving superintelligence. Separately, Anthropic’s latest threat-intelligence report, released yesterday, documented the use of its Claude models in activities ranging from cyberattacks and surveillance to fraud, biological misuse, and conventional weapons development. The report, titled ‘Detecting And Countering Misuse Of AI: September 2026’, covered malicious activities identified and disrupted by Anthropic between December 2025 and August 2026. It examined seven areas of harm – cyber operations, influence operations, surveillance, scams and fraud, biological misuse, conventional weapons development, and illicit model distillation. Anthropic said Claude Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus were used in the cases covered by the report. None involved its Fable or Mythos-class models, except for one illicit distillation case. The company said it disrupted the identified activities, strengthened its safeguards using the findings, and shared intelligence with authorities and industry partners where appropriate. According to Anthropic, AI is reducing the expertise and resources needed to carry out sophisticated cyberattacks. In several cases, attackers used AI agents to execute or coordinate tasks including reconnaissance, exploitation, malware modification, and data exfiltration. While human operators continued to select targets and review stolen information, Anthropic said AI’s role had moved beyond answering questions and increasingly involved the direct execution or orchestration of cyber operations. Together, the developments underscore the competing challenges facing AI companies: meeting surging demand for more capable models while strengthening safeguards against loss of control and malicious use.

Calling the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) a “scam” and “conspiracy”, actor Prakash Raj said starting September 22 till September 30, he would visit 100 polling booths across Karnataka, and bring evidence on how arbitrarily the exercise has been conducted, which he said he would present as “National public hearing” at Jantar Mantar in Delhi on October 15.
Mr. Raj said he would also take “this fight” legally, after collecting all the evidence at different courts. He pointed out that at these polling booths, he, along with civil society groups, would do “social audit” by mapping the details, looking into each case of how and why the electors were put into the absent, shifted, duplicate, dead or others (ASDDO) list, and look into the enumeration forms of those who got notices to check if they filled them correctly, or even if not, what discrepancy the notice flags. Mr. Raj argued that these mistakes, for which people are queuing up, are not committed by the citizens who are being punished.
VIP treatment
Questioning the VIP treatment to prominent personalities like actor Shiva Rajkumar, the actor questioned if some people are “more equal”. Such people, who are in the Election Commission’s list of VIPs, where officials will come personally and clear the hearing process, should deny this treatment and stand with the public at this time, because this is outright bias against the common citizen.
“Does that mean just because you are popular, you get the privilege? And if you are not popular, if you are a common man, you are underprivileged in this country? Not fair.”
Criticising political parties across the board, he said, “From Rahul Gandhi to Narendra Modi, everyone offers biryani packets when it is about elections, but when it comes to situations where citizens need them, like now, in SIR, during Covid pandemic, they (political parties) leave the public on their own.”
“In a democracy, a voter decides who will govern, but this exercise is aiming to change that. With this, government wants to decide who can vote. Still no opposition party is speaking for their people who elected them,” he argued.
Forced incrimination
Further taking on the design of the exercise, Mr. Raj said the voters who have been deleted and put into the ASDDO list are told to get included through form-6, while the form-6 declaration itself says, “I am applying for inclusion in Electoral Roll for the ‘first time‘ and my name is not included in any Assembly constituency/Parliamentary constituency. I am aware that making the above statement or declaration in relation to this application which is false and which I know or believe to be false or do not believe to be true, is punishable under Section 31 of Representation of the People Act, 1950 (43 of 1950) with imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year or with fine or with both.”
This way, each voter who is seeking inclusion after being removed is “incriminating“ themselves. Does the Election Commission “technically and legally want each person to lie?” he questioned.
Against claims of inclusion
The actor further pointed to the immunity provided to the Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners under Section 16 of the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners Act, 2023, which bars courts from entertaining or continuing civil or criminal proceedings against them for acts done or purported to be done in the discharge of their official duties. He said, “Such immunity is planned because they knew they are conspiring a scam, otherwise why else such clause be introduced just months before planning something like this?” he questioned, adding that if it was an inclusionary exercise, the timeline would have supported the claim and not been done in a rush.

Intensifying vaccination of dogs and ensuring that people bitten by dogs receive timely and complete rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) could save far more lives in Keralam than routine pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) vaccination of children, according to a new modelling study on the cost-effectiveness of rabies interventions.
What the study found
The study, published in The Lancet Regional Health – Southeast Asia, estimates that routine childhood PrEP—vaccinating children against rabies before any animal exposure — would prevent only about 10 additional deaths over 10 years, while adding an estimated $10.5 million to $36.5 million to healthcare costs.
In contrast, comprehensive vaccination of dogs, combined with improved post-bite treatment and efforts to close gaps in PEP, could reduce rabies deaths by 83% compared to the current strategy, the study says. Scaling up vaccination of both owned and free-roaming dogs to 70% coverage could potentially bring human rabies deaths down to zero in Keralam within three years, according to the model.
The research was led by the University of Glasgow in collaboration with researchers from the Directorate of Medical Education, Kerala University of Health Sciences, the School of Public Health, the Directorates of Health and Animal Husbandry in Keralam, and the London School of Economics and Political Science.
Rabies in Keralam
Rabies prevention is already one of Keralam’s most intensive public health interventions, with more than 9,00,000 people receiving free treatment every year following animal bites. The State also has a PEP completion rate of over 90%. Yet human rabies deaths continue to occur, with 33 deaths reported in 2025, including among children.
The findings add a new dimension to the ongoing debate over whether Keralam should introduce routine PrEP for children as a rabies prevention strategy. Paediatricians and several public health experts have advocated childhood PrEP because children are particularly vulnerable to severe bites, including injuries to the face and hands, which could become fatal, despite post-exposure treatment.
The study does not rule out PrEP. Instead, it argues that PrEP may be more appropriate for specific high-risk populations who face difficulties in reaching healthcare facilities quickly after exposure, including some geographically dispersed tribal communities.
It argues that given Keralam’s relatively strong access to PEP, universal childhood PrEP may produce relatively little additional mortality reduction for the huge resources required, whereas improved dog vaccination and better wound management and timely PEP may produce greater population-level gains.
Cost effectiveness
“The study is a comparison of the cost effectiveness of PrEP against other interventions as a population-level strategy to reduce rabies. It points out that, as a public health strategy, investing in dog vaccination is more cost effective because it stops virus transmission in the community, and takes us closer to rabies elimination,” said Zinia T. Nujum of the School of Public Health, KUHS, who led the research in Kerala.
According to Martha Luka, researcher at the University of Glasgow’s School of Biodiversity, One Health & Veterinary Medicine and lead author, PrEP for children is unlikely to be the best use of public health resources in Keralam, where access to post-bite vaccination and completion of the regimen are already high.
Canines are the reservoir of the rabies virus and accounts for 70% of the rabies cases. Vaccinating the dog population interrupts transmission before people are exposed, whereas PrEP mainly protects vaccinated individuals while the wider risk remains.
The researchers modelled 12 different combinations of dog vaccination, post-bite treatment and PrEP over a 10-year period from 2026-2035. The study’s sensitivity analysis underlines the importance of improving access to PEP. Raising the proportion of bite victims who seek medical care from 70% to 95% could prevent more than 1,100 additional deaths—over 20 times the mortality reduction achievable even with maximum PrEP coverage in the model.
Vaccination of domestic dogs
The researchers also found that increasing vaccination coverage among domestic dogs alone could produce substantial health gains. “About 70-80% of dog-bite cases in the State are due to domestic dogs. Mandatory licensing and vaccination of domestic dogs, can help improve coverage. We could focus on completing domestic dog vaccination and then move on to vaccinating strays,” said Dr. Nujum.
However, she pointed out that the population of free-roaming dogs in Keralam could be at least five times the official estimate, highlighting the need for better data to plan vaccination programmes. The researchers argue that the State’s priority should therefore be a sustained One Health-based dog vaccination programme targeting at least 70% coverage, involving local bodies, Animal Husbandry and Health departments, veterinary teams, NGOs and communities.

The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum on 24-25 February 2025 brought together global partners from the humanitarian sector to discuss urgent health and humanitarian issues. It focused on advocacy for the survival, health diplomacy, well-being, and dignity of people affected by crises, as well as the security of aid workers. The forum, marking the 10th anniversary of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief), witnessed key agreements and pledges aimed at addressing ongoing humanitarian challenges in the Middle East and beyond.
KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing funding agreements in response to humanitarian crises. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
WHO and KSrelief signed new agreements aimed at malaria prevention and cholera control in Yemen. This includes a US$ 12 million for malaria control and US$ 2.1 million to expand cholera treatment. Another agreement, worth US$ 3.6 million, was made between KSrelief and WHO Egypt Country Office to provide dialysis treatment for Sudanese refugees in Egypt due to the ongoing conflict in Sudan.
Read Press Release: WHO and King Salman Humanitarian Aid & Relief Centre expand life-saving health interventions with new agreements at Riyadh Humanitarian Forum
UNICEF Executive Director, Catherine Russel, KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing the Global Polio Eradication Initiative funding agreement for US$ 500 million. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia reaffirmed its US$ 500 million pledge to the GPEI, initially made in April 2024. Two funding agreements were signed with WHO US$ 300 million and UNICEF US$ 200 million. This contribution will support efforts to vaccinate 370 million children annually, aiming to eradicate polio globally. The commitment highlights Saudi Arabia’s role in combatting polio, particularly in conflict-affected regions such as Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Gaza, where the virus has made a resurgence.
Read Press Release: Kingdom of Saudi Arabia confirms US$ 500 million commitment to global polio eradication effort
The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum 2025 was a significant event that underscored the continued partnership between WHO and KSrelief, as well as with other international partners to address critical humanitarian health crises. The agreements made during the forum are pivotal in combating diseases like malaria, cholera, and polio, and ensuring better healthcare for displaced populations. The forum also highlighted Saudi Arabia’s ongoing commitment to global humanitarian efforts, reaffirming its leadership role in tackling some of the world’s pressing health crises.

Succession battle rocks Uganda after death of ‘boy king’ Oyo Nyimba
Oyo was crowned in 1995, at the age of 3, after his father’s death
The funeral has been held in western Uganda for a traditional monarch who ascended the throne of the Tooro Kingdom as an infant in 1995 and died last month at 34, triggering a succession dispute that has rocked the royal family and gripped the nation.
The funeral of Tooro's King Oyo Nyimba in a cathedral in the remote city of Fort Portal, near the Congo border, concludes a nine-day mourning period that was blemished by an increasingly acrimonious dispute over who should succeed him.
Oyo once held the unofficial title of the world’s youngest king, a mesmerizing figure even for world leaders introduced to him at national events, including South Africa’s Nelson Mandela. Oyo was guided by regents appointed by the kingdom until he became an adult at 18.
He will be buried next to his ancestors later on Saturday.
King Oyo, as he was best known to his subjects, was unmarried when he died late in August after suffering from cancer. Elders with the kingdom’s ruling clan, known as the Babiito, said he never declared an heir to them, disputing the account of others in the kingdom who said he left behind a son born out of wedlock. The son has not been publicly identified, leading to sensational claims on social media of at least two possible heirs alleged to be Oyo’s children.
On Wednesday, a committee of Tooro elders announced that they had chosen a prince working as a journalist to succeed Oyo, earning praise from traditionalists who want an adult on the throne and rebuke from the king’s closest relatives.
Oyo’s sister, Ruth Komuntale, said the announcement sought to “bring division and turmoil.” Queen Mother Best Kemigisa said in a statement that the succession battle undermined their ability to mourn the king’s death. “I also appeal to those fighting over the throne: please, there will be time for all of that,” she said in a statement. “Let us grieve and bury my son King Oyo.”
Traditional monarchs are beloved but don’t wield any formal power in the East African country.
Oyo was crowned in 1995, at the age of 3, after his father’s death. He was a curious child in colorful robes and an object of adoration for his hundreds of thousands of followers.
At his coronation, he went through a series of tribal rituals and was led into the royal cemetery to perform a coming-of-age ceremony: successfully tossing nine coffee beans into his father’s tomb.
Amid the ongoing succession dispute, it was not clear who would perform this rite. The matter of Oyo’s successor could go to the courts, after his family said he left behind a will that had been ignored by Tooro elders.
“This is one of those deaths, the Bob Marley kind, that one never heals from,” Timothy Kalyegira, a prominent analyst who is from Tooro, said in a eulogy posted on social platform X. “Not Oyo; not that likeable young man; not at 34. That’s what makes it so painful.”
The late Libyan leader Moammar Gadhafi befriended the Tooro royal family as if they were part of his extended family. He made multiple trips to Uganda and supported Oyo and his mother for years before his death in October 2011.
Uganda’s traditional kingdoms were banned after independence from British colonial rule by a republican president who said he wanted to unify the country, but they were restored in 1993. Although they have no political authority and are legally not allowed to engage in partisan politics, monarchs wield authority as guardians of tribal culture.

Norris takes Madrid pole with 'gorgeous' lap
- Published
Lando Norris took a superb pole position for McLaren at the Spanish Grand Prix, beating Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli and Red Bull's Max Verstappen in a breathless final few seconds of qualifying.
"Oh, what a lap, gorgeous," said an ecstatic Norris after pipping world championship leader Antonelli by just 0.011 seconds. "Oh, that might be my best one."
Verstappen was 0.140secs off the pace, as all three moved ahead of Lewis Hamilton's Ferrari in Madrid.
The seven-time champion had held the top spot after the first runs in the final session.
Hamilton's team-mate Charles Leclerc was fifth, ahead of Mercedes' George Russell and the second McLaren of Oscar Piastri.
Adrenaline high for 'shocked' Norris
Norris' pole came from nowhere. He had been fifth in the first session of qualifying, seventh in the second, and 0.449secs slower than Hamilton's pace-setting lap after the first runs in the final session.
"I'm shocked," the world champion said. "I'm a little bit surprised to be here. It was probably one of the best laps I've done ever in my career.
"One of those laps when everything came together. I had a good idea of what I wanted to do, it was whether it came together but my brain let me do it almost perfect. It's one of those laps when you look at the time and go: 'Oh, that was pretty good."
The session had started with predictions of a crash-fest, after drivers had been warning about the high-risk nature of the new Madring street circuit, with tricky entries to corners and walls coming back at the drivers on the exits.
Two red flags during final practice had led some teams to have private sweepstakes as to how many stoppages there would be in qualifying, but the session ran cleanly, with no incidents.
Pole looked to be a battle between Antonelli and the Ferraris, with Verstappen perhaps in the mix.
In the end, the Ferraris faded, as they so often have this year when it really matters, and Norris rose to the front with a breathtaking performance.
"The adrenaline was high on the last lap," he said. "You have to relax and let it all flow.
"It's easy to get tense around here. There's a lot of walls that come at you pretty quickly. I have been feeling pretty good, I just wasn't relaxed.
"I was pretty much perfect apart from the last corner, where I thought I was in the wall. Everything I wanted to achieve I achieved and it's one of those moments when I was in that flow state."
Hamilton, who had crashed at the final corner in practice and missed the final half of the session, did improve on his last lap, but only by 0.06secs and it was not enough to prevent him falling backwards.
He edged Leclerc by just 0.006secs as Ferrari rued yet another tantalising chance slipping through their fingers.

Late last year, men in parts of Congo’s Tshopo province began whispering about something strange that was happening in nearby villages. At first, the stories sounded too absurd to travel far. A man in a market claimed his genitals had suddenly shrunk after brushing against a stranger. Someone else said it happened inside a taxi. In another village, people spoke about a man who returned from town convinced that the part of his body had disappeared altogether.
And then the videos started appearing, people gathered around phones watching clips of alleged victims speaking inside crowded churches while pastors stood beside them claiming they had been cured through prayer. Some videos spread through Facebook pages and TikTok accounts. Others moved from phone to phone through Bluetooth shares and WhatsApp groups, spreading across villages faster than official information ever could.
In many places, the rumours arrived before the authorities did. By the time officials in Tshopo publicly denied the existence of any mysterious illness, fear had already settled across parts of northeastern Democratic Republic of Congo, where rumours, churches, and social media had combined to create something more powerful than a simple falsehood. Men spoke cautiously around strangers. Communities became suspicious of outsiders. Stories changed slightly depending on who was telling them, but the central fear remained the same.
Something was stealing men’s bodies. In the month of October, the health workers travelling through the Isangi area of Tshopo province arrived in villages already consumed by weeks of panic. They carried tablet computers, questionnaires, and reflective jackets as part of vaccination-related field surveys, but in some communities those unfamiliar objects and routines were interpreted very differently by residents who had spent weeks hearing that outsiders were spreading a disease that caused men’s genitalia to shrink or disappear.
According to Reuters, at least four health workers were later killed after crowds accused them of spreading the supposed illness.
One of them was Dr. John Tangakeya. His wife later told Reuters that the family had spoken to him earlier that day because it was his birthday. The children were waiting for him to come home that evening so that they could celebrate together. Instead, news arrived that the health team he was part of had been attacked by mobs even as they tried to explain that their surveys had nothing to do with the rumours spreading in the province.
The World Health Organization(WHO)-backed Africa Infodemic Response Alliance, which monitors dangerous health misinformation across Africa, later linked at least 17 killings to the rumours, though some incidents could not be independently verified.
Long before social media existed, versions of this panic had already travelled across parts of Africa.
Researchers have documented similar episodes for decades in Ghana, Nigeria, Cameroon, Benin, and Congo itself, where rumours of “penis theft” or genital shrinking periodically triggered mob attacks against people accused of witchcraft or supernatural powers. In Ghana, during the 1990s, several people accused of “penis snatching” were beaten to death by mobs. In Kinshasa, in 2008, police detained more than a dozen suspected “sorcerers” after panic spread through the capital and led to attempted lynchings.
Anthropologists who study such incidents have often argued that the panic is not simply about superstition. In many places, fears around genital theft became tied to larger anxieties about masculinity, illness, vulnerability, power, and social instability, particularly in societies where spiritual explanations for misfortune remain deeply embedded in everyday life.
But something about the Congo episode felt different. Earlier, panic spread through markets, crowded taxis, churches, and radio broadcasts. This time, much of the fear moved online first, where videos featuring alleged victims and miracle cures circulated rapidly through algorithm-driven feeds before local officials fully understood what was unfolding on the ground.
Several churches in Kisangani hosted testimonies from supposed victims while Facebook pages and TikTok accounts reposted clips that gathered hundreds of thousands of views. Some videos remained online even after authorities publicly dismissed the claims as false.
Health officials later said the violence exposed a deeper crisis facing public health systems in parts of Africa, where distrust toward authorities has been shaped by years of political instability, misinformation, and memories of earlier health emergencies, including Ebola and COVID-19 outbreaks, during which some communities viewed outside medical teams with suspicion.
In villages where people had already spent weeks discussing the rumours among themselves, the arrival of unfamiliar health workers carrying devices and asking questions appeared, for some residents, to confirm the fears they already believed were true.
Months later, the rumours have still not completely disappeared.
Officials continue running radio campaigns and public awareness programmes aimed at stopping the spread of misinformation. Arrests have been made in some areas. But many of the original videos are still circulating online, resurfacing again and again across different parts of Congo, long after authorities declared that the illness itself never existed.

September is typically the time when television gets serious again. The summer’s biggest TV shows have aired their finales, the fall schedule is kicking into high gear, and streamers are rolling out everything from high-concept sci-fi to prestige dramas. There’s plenty of familiar IP in the mix, but also some genuinely original shows worth putting on your “to watch” list.
While plenty of outlets will tell you what everyone is watching (see: Reacher), that’s not our goal. As always, the TV shows we’re watching this month reflect the kinds of stories WIRED covers every day—shows that explore technology, science, politics, culture, and the sometimes unsettling ways they intersect.
From returning favorites to ambitious new series—and at least one show that might rekindle your love of traditional anime—these are the TV shows we think you should make time to stream this month.
The Paper
What happens when a newspaper attempts to not just survive, but thrive, in a world where digital media has become the norm? The Paper, a spinoff of The Office from Greg Daniels and Michael Koman, follows the staff of a struggling Midwestern paper as they attempt to revive it.
Ultimately, its idealistic new editor-in-chief Ned Sampson (Star Wars and Harry Potter alum Domhnall Gleeson) and his hungry young reporter Mare Pritti (Chelsea Frei) end up grappling with what journalism looks like in the digital age. Season 2, which arrived on September 9, finds their Toledo Truth Teller newly revitalized and searching for its next big scoop, making the show a surprisingly sharp comedy about the future of journalism—and who gets to shape it.
Lego Star Wars: The Mandalorian
Though this summer’s The Mandalorian and Grogu (which is streaming on Disney+ now) seriously underperformed at the box office, Lucasfilm is partnering with Lego to take another stab at the fan-favorite Star Wars series—which might be exactly what the franchise needs right now. Lucasfilm and Lego are going back to the beginning, reimagining all three seasons of the Pedro Pascal-starring live-action series as a 49-minute animated comedy.
For anyone who somehow managed to miss Mando and Grogu until now, the story follows Din Djarin (Pascal in the live-action series, Gavin Hammon in this iteration), a bounty hunter known as the Mandalorian, who takes a job transporting a mysterious Force-sensitive child. That child, of course, is Grogu, aka Baby Yoda. What starts as a simple assignment turns into a galaxy-spanning adventure as the pair become unlikely partners. Consider this version an entertaining way to play catch-up.
South Park
It’s hard to remember a time when the world didn’t have South Park. For nearly 30 years, audiences have watched as four potty-mouthed fourth-graders—Stan, Kyle, Cartman, and Kenny—navigate life in the bizarre mountain town of South Park, Colorado, in this very much adults-only animated comedy. Along the way, they’ve encountered alien life forms, celebrities, and Elon Musk (yes, the real one). They’ve also watched Kenny die on at least 100 occasions.
Last year, the seemingly never-ending comedy reinvented itself as a particularly pointed political satire by taking aim at figures including JD Vance, Pete Hegseth, Kristi Noem, Donald Trump, and Donald Trump’s manhood. The White House, unsurprisingly, had thoughts. And so did the Emmys; the show just took home the 2026 award for Outstanding Animated Program. Clearly, creators Trey Parker and Matt Stone have no plans to take their foot off the gas; they just announced they’re taking a page out of Trump’s renaming book and rechristening the show South America for its 29th season, which premieres on September 16.
Slow Horses
What if television’s best spy show was also one of its funniest? If John le Carré and (the original) The Office had a baby, it would look and sound a lot like Slow Horses, which returns for a sixth season on September 16.
Based on Mick Herron’s Slough House book series, the series follows a dysfunctional team of MI5 misfits who are banished to the infamous Slough House unit, where they work under the notorious Jackson Lamb (Gary Oldman), a foul-mouthed, flatulent, chain-smoking wreck of a man who also happens to be the most brilliant operative in the room. It’s a prestige spy thriller that doesn’t take itself too seriously, bouncing effortlessly between shoot-outs and the kind of droll office banter you’d expect from the best workplace comedies. In a career full of memorable performances, and an Oscar to show for it, Slow Horses just might be the role Oldman is best remembered for. It’s also the project that has made Jack Lowden oddsmakers’ top pick for the next James Bond.
City of Blood
In City of Blood, an eight-episode miniseries from Germany, climate change has turned Berlin into a sweltering city teetering on the edge of collapse—and vampires are ready to take advantage of the chaos. While the privileged few live beneath a climate-controlled dome, the rest of the city’s denizens are left to battle the heat, crime, and corruption that have become part of everyday life. But when estranged sisters Bea (Lea Drinda) and Phoebe (Soma Pysall) reunite, they uncover a nefarious political plot and learn that, thanks to that aforementioned undead population, blood has become the city’s most coveted commodity. It’s a perfectly strange mix of climate dystopia, family drama, and vampire thriller. And it arrives on September 16.
MobLand
Season 2 of MobLand is almost here—whether Tom Hardy likes it or not. (Despite all the recent headlines surrounding the Oscar winner’s behind-the-scenes drama, he has already signed on for Season 3.) The highly underrated, or perhaps just underseen, crime drama returns with the Harrigan family’s criminal empire under threat from rival forces, forcing their street-smart fixer Harry Da Souza (yep, Hardy) to navigate increasingly bloody internal tensions.
As Harry works to keep the fractured family from tearing itself apart, he’s aided by his trusty sidekick Zosia (Jasmine Jobson), a tech specialist who brings a distinctly 21st-century skill set to their old-school criminal enterprise headed up by Conrad (Pierce Brosnan) and Maeve Harrington (Helen Mirren). Meanwhile, rival forces close in, loyalties shift, and violence spreads through every corner of the family’s world. Expect more bloodshed, shifting allegiances, poor decisions, and one of television’s most kickass theme songs (Fontaines D.C.’s “Starburster”) when Season 2 premieres on September 18.
Outlander: Blood of My Blood
Before there was Jamie and Claire, there were their parents. Like its predecessor, this Outlander prequel follows two separate timelines as it details the courtship of Jamie Fraser’s parents, Brian Fraser (Jamie Roy) and Ellen MacKenzie (Harriet Slater), in 18th-century Scotland, alongside the story of Claire Beauchamp’s parents, Henry Beauchamp (Jeremy Irvine) and Julia Moriston (Hermione Corfield), in World War I-era England. Their two love stories unfold across different time periods, weaving together romance, family drama, and the time-traveling forces that kept Outlander fans enthralled for eight seasons. The series’ second season arrives on September 18.
American Horror Story
Season 13 of Ryan Murphy and Brad Falchuk’s horror anthology is shaping up to be what has at various points called an Avengers-esque “endgame-level event” of “greatest hits.” While the details, as always, have been kept rather quiet, what we do know is that the new season of American Horror Story will pull bits and pieces from each season of the series, with a heavy emphasis on its witchcraft-laden “Coven” and “Apocalypse” storylines.
We also know it is reassembling an all-star cast of past stars, some of whom will play double—or even triple—character duty. Among them: Murphy mainstays Sarah Paulson, Evan Peters, Jessica Lange, Kathy Bates, Emma Roberts, Billie Lourd, and Angela Bassett. The new season arrives on September 26, which gives you plenty of time to brush up on your AHS lore.
Neon Genesis Evangelion
Before Netflix gave it a new English dub—and, depending on who you ask, stirred up a lot of feelings—there was the original Japanese-language version of Neon Genesis Evangelion. The landmark anime, released in 1995, follows a group of teenagers recruited to pilot giant biomechanical weapons called Evangelions, or Evas, as they defend a post-apocalyptic Tokyo (now known as Tokyo-3) from mysterious creatures, aka Angels. But what starts as a fairly straightforward battle-for-humanity story soon becomes something far stranger, delving into trauma, loneliness, identity, and human connection.
The Criterion Channel is bringing all 26 episodes of the classic (pre-Netflix) English dub to streaming for the first time, alongside the original Japanese-language version for all you purists. It’s a fitting return for one of anime’s most boundary-pushing series.
