Trump Will Never Mail the $5,000 Checks
Deconstructing a policy proposal that makes no sense on any level
Donald Trump’s new promise to give a $5,000 check to every adult American citizen if Republicans win the midterm elections may be an effort to answer a variant of an age-old riddle: Can Trump devise a policy so ill-conceived that even Trump’s intelligence is insulted?
Candidates often make inducements part of their campaign pitch. One obvious peculiarity of this plan is that Trump’s party already controls both chambers of Congress. Why, then, should the bonus checks be contingent on voters giving Republicans another two-year majority?
Trump has told reporters that he could distribute the loot without congressional approval. This is untrue. (It’s a facially unconstitutional infringement of Congress’s spending authority.) If it were true, however, it would make his decision to hinge the checks on the election’s outcome even more mysterious. If the choice were his alone, the outcome would seem totally irrelevant.
Under certain economic circumstances, distributing checks to everybody can make sense. In a deeply depressed economy, in which consumer spending is too low to maintain high employment levels, juicing it with a cash infusion can help keep it alive.
However, current circumstances are quite different. Unemployment is low and growth is healthy. The problem is that inflation is running well above target levels. Injecting roughly $1.2 trillion (the one-year cost of the checks) into the economy would likely make inflation worse—more cash would be chasing the same number of goods and services, driving up their price. This, in turn, would probably force the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates to tamp down inflation, which would throw recovery into jeopardy.
J. D. Vance has suggested that the checks could be paid for with tariff revenue. In theory, that would offset the inflationary effect of the new spending. But the tariffs are already in place, meaning that he’s citing a current revenue source to fund a new cost—at a moment when revenue is nowhere near sufficient: The U.S. government is running a deficit of nearly $1.8 trillion.
Trump, for his part, explained to reporters that he intends the checks not as an economic policy but as a treat: “I’m doing it as a reward for people having to put up for five years and four years of a horrible situation caused by Biden … It’s almost a reward for the people having to put up with Biden’s policy.”
When Trump ran in 2024 against Joe Biden’s policies, the “reward” was supposed to be having Trump and his policies in place. Now he seems to be suggesting that Trump’s incredible economy is not enough. This explanation is also impossible to square with his claim that the bonus would be contingent on Republicans winning the midterms. Why do Americans deserve a retroactive bonus for living in Biden’s America only if Republicans win the midterm elections? By Trump’s logic, if we were forced to endure two years of Democrats sharing power, that would make us more, not less, deserving of compensation.
The pretense that these checks have any economic logic has proved too great to bear for at least some Republicans. Senator Ted Cruz of Texas and Florida Governor Ron DeSantis dissented mildly, causing Trump’s advisers to heap them with ridicule. “Ron and Ted—the co-captains of your old high school Math-Lete Team—will nerd out on this while jockeying for 11th place in ’28,” a senior adviser to the White House told Politico Playbook.
In a normal administration, These guys understand high-school-level math is a credential, albeit a minimal one, to opine on economic policy. Only in the Trump era can it be presented as a disqualification.
The actual defense of the policy, obviously, is that it’s never going to happen. Last February, Elon Musk floated a DOGE dividend (which never arrived, in part because DOGE never produced meaningful savings). That year, Trump repeatedly promised tariff-rebate checks, which also never happened.
The Fox News host Laura Ingraham asked Trump why he doesn’t simply send the checks out now. He replied, “Because the Democrats can’t do it. Because for them, it’s negative growth. With us, it’s so positive.” What does this answer mean? Does it mean anything at all? Does Trump even believe it has any meaning, other than constituting a string of sentence fragments conveying the general sentiment Democrats bad; me good?
The actual divide within the party pits the Republicans who think that their voters are dumb enough to fall yet again for Trump’s free-money promise against those who suspect that the ruse has worn thin. Trump has spent his career betting against the intelligence of the American voter. The $5,000-check promise may be the moment he finally underestimated his audience.

Jean Chrétien says ‘we bow to no one’ in fiery 9/11 speech in Gander, N.L.
'Never mistake our kindness for softness,' former PM says
Former Canadian prime minister Jean Chrétien drew thunderous applause on Friday during a fiery and patriotic speech in Gander, N.L., where many had gathered at a sports arena to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, and the legendary humanitarian response as thousands of stranded air travellers had their flights diverted to more than a dozen Canadian airports.
Chrétien was the final speaker during a lengthy and nationally televised event. He began his speech by describing Sept. 11, 2001 "like a nightmare … one that can never be erased." And then recounted how Canadians stepped up, fought side-by-side with U.S. troops in Afghanistan — which drew loud applause.
But then, Chrétien's became the first person to speak on a subject no one else who stepped to the microphone would: the fractured political relationship between Canada and the United States.
"We bow to no one," Chrétien said to an audience that included Pete Hoesktra, the U.S. ambassador to Canada.
"And the more we are insulted or threatened and abused, the more we will stand up for ourselves and stand united."
- We can make a difference in a 'sometimes broken world,' says Gander mayor at 9/11 ceremony
- One woman survived 9/11. Another helped out in Gander. Now they’re as close as sisters
It was a powerful moment in an two-hour event filled with stories of remembrance, honour and sacrifice.
Trade war ongoing
U.S. President Donald Trump initiated a trade war with Canada, and has hurled insults at Prime Minister Mark Carney. Trump has also threatened Canada’s sovereignty by expressing his desire to make Canada’s the 51st U.S. state.
Hoesktra has amplified the rhetoric through his own public comments and by sharing Trump’s social media posts.
Hoesktra avoided the issue of trade and tariffs during his visit to Gander, and praised the longstanding partnership between the two countries. He offered thanks for the kindness and compassion shown to thousands of stranded American travellers in the wake of the terrorist attacks.
"This is to say one more time, thank you," he said, when asked about his visit to the central Newfoundland town. "We’ll get back to the economic issues from, at least our standpoint, when we get past 9/11."
Chrétien, 92, described the U.S. as a "neighbour and our closest friend," and said a massive rally in Ottawa in the days after the 9/11 attacks was "one of the most emotional moments of my life."
Chrétien’s government initiated the process in 2001 to invoke the so-called Article 5, which stipulates that an attack on one member of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) is an attack on all members.
Chrétien also ordered Canadian troops into battle in Afghanistan, fighting alongside U.S. allies, and 158 of those soldiers were killed, including 13 from Newfoundland and Labrador.
"Our friends were hurt, and we were hurting with them," Chrétien said. "I was proud of how we stepped up."
He described the response to 9/11 as "the Canadian way."
But 25 years later, the world has changed, and Canada’s relationship with its powerful southern neighbour has also grown more distant.
So Chrétien concluded his speech — which received no less than three standing ovations — with a strong message "to our American friends."
He said Canada is an open, generous country, and the response to 9/11 in communities such as Gander is an example of this. But he said Canada’s generosity should not be mistaken for weakness.
"Never mistake our tolerance for lack of determination. And never mistake our kindness for softness. We know who we are and we are proud of it," he said.
Chrétien said building a country like Canada, welcoming people from around the globe, and caring for the weakest, "is a sign of strength."
Chrétien said his "honest" message was "from one friend to another," and he called on the U.S. to "respect the friendship" and "be a good neighbour."
He concluded with the following words in French: "Long live the United States and long live Canada."

The iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max are almost here. Announced at Apple’s September 2026 “Sunrise and shine” event alongside the iPhone Duo and other new gear, the two upgraded phones feature the faster A20 Pro processor with more GPU power as well as more neural cores for AI-related tasks, plus some welcome improvements to the camera.
Where to preorder the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max
The faster, better iPhones are almost here, and we’ve got all the details for preordering them.
The phones will arrive on Friday, September 18th, and preordering one is never a bad idea if you want to ensure you get the color and storage capacity configuration you’re seeking. Speaking of, preorders are officially open.
The 6.3-inch iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199 for the 256GB model, and goes all the way up to $2,399 for the version with 2TB of storage. The larger 6.9-inch iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299 for 256GB, with the 2TB model costing $2,499. Both phones are available in four colors: deep black, silver, glacier, and burgundy.
At the time of publication, the only way to preorder an unlocked version of the Pro or Pro Max is directly from Apple. You have some options if you don’t want to pay the full price upfront. Financing through Apple is an option (36 monthly payments with zero percent APR), and the new phones are also eligible for the recently-announced Apple Upgrade program. You can also trade in your existing phone for up to $885 in credit towards the cost of the new phone, with carriers offering additional credits.
The likes of Best Buy and Walmart only have the carrier-locked versions listed at the start of the preorder phase. Best Buy is offering the 18 Pro through Verizon or AT&T, along with the Pro Max tied to Verizon or AT&T. Walmart is offering the 18 Pro through Verizon, AT&T, and T-Mobile, as well as the Pro Max with T-Mobile, Verizon, or AT&T.
Offers from US carriers
- AT&T will offer to cover the cost of an iPhone 18 Pro via billing credits paid back to you over 36 months if you trade in an iPhone 14 or newer. You’ll also need to sign up for the AT&T Extra plan, with slightly lower discounts for less expensive plans. You can find these options on Apple’s checkout page, with the option to pay the $99 difference between the Pro and Pro Max out of pocket.
- T-Mobile is offering the iPhone 18 Pro for free by way of bill credits when you transfer your number or trade in a qualifying phone on the Experience Beyond plan. The credits aren’t as generous as AT&T’s offer if you’re an existing customer already, with only the iPhone 16 and newer covering the cost of a new phone, but it’s very similar if you’re new to T-Mobile.
- The Verizon deal is fairly straightforward. The Simplicity Pro plan, which comes to a total of $80 per month if you’re switching from another carrier, includes a free iPhone 18 Pro, with the option to upgrade your phone after one year. Like other carriers, the “free” phone is paid off to you via monthly bill credits, so you’ll need to stick with the carrier for three years to get the full value.

Yoga and Ayurveda have moved beyond their traditional wellness identity and are increasingly becoming part of India’s global health and diplomatic strategy, with the Centre seeking to expand their footprint through medical tourism, international education, practitioner mobility and trade agreements.
The shift is particularly evident in India’s recent trade diplomacy. The India-Oman Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA), operationalised in June 2026, and the India-New Zealand Free Trade Agreement (FTA) contain dedicated provisions on health-related services and traditional medicine. These include measures to ease licensing, develop standards and facilitate the mobility of AYUSH practitioners and Yoga instructors.
The India-European Union (EU) FTA, signed in January 2026, goes further, allowing AYUSH practitioners to use their Indian qualifications in EU countries where no regulatory framework exists and providing for AYUSH wellness centres and clinics.
Also Read | India partners with WHO to mainstream Ayush globally through agreement on traditional medicine interventions
The agreements represent an attempt to transform AYUSH from being a cultural export to a formalised health and services opportunity.
The India-Oman CEPA contains what the government describes as its first comprehensive commitment on traditional medicine across all modes of supply, while the India-New Zealand FTA has a dedicated ‘health and traditional medicine’ annex covering Ayurveda, Yoga, Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha, Sowa-Rigpa and Homoeopathy.
The New Zealand agreement also provides structured mobility pathways, including a dedicated visa quota for AYUSH practitioners and Yoga instructors. The government said the agreement would institutionalise cooperation in education, training, standards development and wellness services.
Comment | The growing relevance of traditional medicine
Need to convert market access to demand
However, the diplomatic push also raises questions about how far formal recognition and market access will translate into actual international demand.
Experts point to the need for credible standards, evidence, regulation, practitioner quality and patient safety if AYUSH is to establish itself in increasingly regulated global healthcare markets.
Senior officials in the Ministry of Ayush said the Ayush visa, overseas training and exchange programmes were also helping expand the sector.
“Foreign medical arrivals rose from 1.83 lakh in 2020 to 6.44 lakh in 2024, as per our data. Bangladesh, Nepal, Sri Lanka, the United Arab Emirates, the United States, Germany, Russia, Malaysia, Mauritius and Saudi Arabia are among the important markets for AYUSH and Ayurveda treatment. The government does not publish a current consolidated country-wise ranking of AYUSH patients,” an official from the AYUSH Ministry said.
However, the figure of 6.44 lakh refers to overall foreign medical arrivals and not specifically AYUSH patients. The absence of consolidated data makes it difficult to assess AYUSH’s actual share of India’s medical-value-travel market.
The Ayush visa, introduced in 2023, is another component of the strategy. Between January 2023 and December 2025, a total of 3,375 foreign nationals travelled to India on Ayush visas or e-Ayush visas, while another 579 travelled on Ayush attendant visas or e-Ayush attendant visas. Earlier, the Ministry had reported that 1,646 Ayush visas had been issued to nationals of 75 countries between January 2024 and February 2025.
Education is also emerging as another channel of influence. Under the Ayush Fellowship Scheme, 260 students from 32 countries were studying AYUSH in Indian institutions.
The Ministry’s international cooperation programmes also support training, seminars, conferences and knowledge exchange, including Yoga teaching and education overseas.

The rock guitarist whose killing shocked India's north-east
- Published
When Chongtham Vikram Singh finally came home to India's north-eastern state of Manipur, his old friend Dhiren Sadokpam went to the airport to receive him.
It was not the homecoming he had imagined. Vikram arrived in the cargo hold, inside a steel container.
Three days earlier, the 54-year-old musician had been beaten to death outside his home in south-east Delhi.
"Nobody seemed to have the strength to speak," Sadokpam told the BBC. "What could be said?"
Vikram had spent much of his life travelling with his guitars, carrying his music from small stages in Manipur's capital, Imphal, to jazz clubs, classrooms and concert halls in Delhi.
According to police and his family, he had gone downstairs late on Sunday night after a group of men were shouting and drinking outside his apartment building. When he objected to the disturbance, the men allegedly attacked him.
His wife, Joshna Chongtham, said Vikram returned upstairs but was pursued and assaulted outside the family's apartment.
Hours later, after complaining of breathlessness, he was taken to hospital by his 20-year-old son. He died there early in the morning.
Seven men and a juvenile have been arrested in connection with his killing. Police say they are investigating the circumstances of the attack.
The death has prompted an outpouring of grief and anger, and renewed concerns about the discrimination faced by people from India's north-east in Delhi, where members of the community have for years reported racial abuse, harassment and violence.
Police say they have so far found no evidence of a racial motive. But north-eastern groups have held protests and demanded an impartial investigation.
The case has also drawn attention to Vikram himself - a familiar figure in Manipur's music scene who, over four decades of playing and teaching, gathered around him a large circle of students, friends and admirers.
At a press conference two days after his death, his wife Joshna said: "We are not seeking revenge. We are seeking justice. He had a name, a family and a life that mattered."
For most of his 54 years, that life had revolved around music.
Vikram grew up around it. His mother, Chongtham Kamala, was a celebrated singer who lent her voice to Matamgi Manipur, the first feature film made in the Manipuri language.
As a boy, he accompanied her to All India Radio for recordings. Before long, he had auditioned there himself and become a child artist, playing the accordion.
There is an old black-and-white photograph of Vikram from those years. He is kneeling stiffly in front of a microphone with an accordion balanced across his lap. Beside him, another boy sits behind a pair of drums. Both wear the grave expressions of children who have been told that a photograph is being taken.
The boy with the accordion would soon discover guitars - first Hawaiian and Spanish, then electric - and, somewhere along the way, acquire thick black glasses and a splendid moustache.
By the mid-1980s, Imphal had become an unlikely outpost of rock music. The sound travelled there largely on cassette tapes, bringing with it the hard rock and heavy metal being played thousands of miles away.
Young men formed bands and crowded into local halls, working with whatever they could find - modest sound systems, locally made amplifiers, guitars turned up as loud as they would go. They listened, copied, experimented.
Vikram was studying at Don Bosco School then and still playing accordion and Hawaiian guitar. Years later, he remembered how he and his friends would ask the priests for permission to leave school to watch a local band perform.
"Those were sweet and innocent days that actually inspired me to go for rock," he recalled in a 2014 interview, external.
Soon, watching was no longer enough. Vikram took up the electric guitar and began playing in bands himself - first Ultra Vires, then Phoenix and Eastern Dark - becoming part of the generation that was giving Imphal's new rock scene a sound of its own.
It was around this time, in 1987, that Dhiren Sadokpam first met him.
They were setting off from Imphal to study in Shillong, and Sadokpam remembers them waiting at a temporary interstate bus terminal with backpacks, steel luggage boxes and bedding for the long journey.
Vikram was boyish and energetic, he recalls, but mostly kept to himself.
"He would spend long hours in his room, mastering each and every composition that came his way," Sadokpam said.
With each band, Vikram's playing evolved. Ultra Vires became a place to experiment. Phoenix, which would become one of the defining bands of Manipur's early rock scene, brought greater precision and a devoted following that endured long after its heyday.
By the time he joined Eastern Dark, Sadokpam remembers the quiet young man disappearing into the instrument, making its six strings "cry and sing".
In the early 1990s, he spent two years in Calcutta (now Kolkata), where he encountered musicians at the Calcutta School of Music, a century-old institution with a strong tradition of Western classical music, and was drawn more deeply into jazz and classical music. His own playing began to range across styles, from rock and blues to jazz and fusion.
By the 2000s, Vikram had moved to Delhi, where he built a life around performing and teaching music.
In 2010, he reconnected with an old musician friend and formed Fubar Ghetto. The band played jazz, blues, rock and fusion, with improvisation at the centre of it. Their first performance was a charity concert near the Yamuna river.
From there, they worked their way through Delhi's live-music circuit: universities, clubs and cultural festivals, the National School of Drama and, on one occasion, the Czech Embassy.
Vikram never became a major star. Instead, he built the quieter reputation of a working musician - among the people he played with, the students he taught and the musicians he helped along the way.
Since his killing, many of those people have remembered the man who was gentle, generous and largely uninterested in recognition.
Former student guitarist Sachidananda Angom remembered him as "always kind, helpful" and someone who "could really light up a room".
Mame Khan, the Rajasthani folk singer with whom Vikram performed for several years, told The Indian Express, external that Vikram was "a really kind and lovely person" who never picked arguments with anyone.
Sadokpam is careful not to make more of their friendship than it was.
They had met as young men in 1987, lost touch for two decades and found each other again in middle age. In between, Sadokpam followed Vikram's musical life from a distance, as a fan and a friend.
They last met in Delhi in 2019, when Vikram invited him home for dinner.
"Vikram picked up his guitar and played and spoke excitedly about his students," he recalled.
When it was time to leave, Vikram asked him to come again soon. Sadokpam said he promised he would.
"I never made it back."

When the life-simulation game Paralives was released in early access, Danielle Udogaranya’s hand ached at the thought of making new Black hairstyles for it.
It wasn't because she didn't want to create for the game. Udogaranya, better known as Ebonix, has spent over a decade creating custom content for life-simming games with the goal of helping people see themselves on digital screens. Her hesitation stemmed from the physical toll it takes to craft the perfect digital coil, braid, and kink—painstakingly long hours and tedious precision.
“I thought to myself, why am I still having to do this?” Udogaranya, a technical artist who has a degree in psychology, tells WIRED.
Fans of games like The Sims spend time flipping through her sites, downloading custom hair packs inspired by real-life styles not otherwise available in-game. As of now, the Ebonix Patreon has over 115,000 members, and hundreds of both free and paid content items.
The reason behind the demand for custom content in life-simming games is both simple and disappointing: Natural Black hairstyles have been historically underrepresented, and the technology used to make them has been slow to improve.
“With new games coming out now, I'm still seeing the issues, and I'm still seeing the ‘Killmonger locs.’ God forbid we get more than three options,” Udogaranya says, in reference to the stiff, short-dreaded style featured by Michael B. Jordan’s character in Black Panther that became a go-to for many games as well as some other films. Similar examples can be seen in old and new franchises alike, including Tekken 8, Spider-Man 2, Apex Legends, Horizon Zero Dawn, and more. The reason for this Black hair default? Textured hairstyles in games have been reliant on code that was not made for them.
“If you're making straight hair, it’s very easy to taper the ends and then make it cute,” Udogaranya explains. “But when you’re trying to add a black texture on it, it looks like a hot dog.” Thus, immovable, cylindrical “Killmonger locs” are simpler to make than other natural styles.
Black hair in video games has long been a design afterthought—at best—since some of the first Black characters entered the scene. In early 8-bit era games, like SEGA’s Heavyweight Champ, which came out in 1976, Black hairstyles appeared to emphasize minstrel-like stereotypes. During the rise of fighting games in the ’80s and ’90s, where more characters per game were introduced, Black hair was limited because Black player selections were limited. For example, in Street Fighter, there was only one Black character out of the 12 options. When The Sims came out in 2000, the game allowed limited customization, with hair swatches connected to different face options. Though the game allowed for three skin-tone swatches—fair, medium, and dark—natural hairstyle options were virtually nonexistent.
In the decades that followed, 3D animation and customization in gaming continued to flourish, but Black hair has trended toward only a handful of swatches, most of which provided little to minimal movement. However, there have been efforts to tackle this industrywide issue. Dove and Open Source Afro Hair Library launched Code My Crown in 2023, which provides a “complete and free guide for coding textured hair and protective styles in video games,” according to a press release. And, while most of the natural hairstyles in The Sims 4 come from expansion and stuff packs costing around $10 to $40 each, EA has begun to release free downloadable content for players looking to diversify hairstyles. Its latest DLC provides one new natural hairstyle with its pack of six outfits.
Despite these pushes, Udogaranya wanted to make natural hair creation easier and more user-friendly. “After doing some research, and looking at all of the hair tools that are available still to this day, Black hair has just been accommodated in tools that are primarily created for straight hair.”
Udogaranya came across the scholarly paper Curly-Cue: Geometric Methods for Highly Coiled Hair. Published in 2024, it presented new coding techniques to improve both the look and movement of Black hair in 3D animation. With this insight, Udogaranya coded a plug-in for Blender—the free, open-source 3D creation app she normally uses to make custom content.
The Loc & Kinky Strand Generator Tool allows fellow custom content creators to make textured styles that normally could take weeks in under an hour. In just a few clicks, a user can switch from a curl to a coil to a loc. Udogaranya trained her own local AI to assist with automating the processes she did by hand and to fine-tune the code, but no generative AI was used. To use the tool, creators still have to design by hand and can’t type in prompts to generate their styles.
“The whole point of [the Loc & Kinky Strand Generator] tool is that when you do go to draw a strand or apply the actual modifier to a strand, it immediately gives you that kink,” Udogaranya says.
Though the life-sim gaming industry has struggled with diversity, there have been efforts for improvement—in some cases, thanks to Udogaranya herself. In addition to making custom content, she has also served as a gaming consultant for The Sims 4, Life by You, and Love Island: The Game. For other IPs, such as Paralives, Udogaranya notes that there is a shift in interest for Black hair inclusion. Because of this, Udogaranya hopes to eventually make the Blender add-on an independent app and create a licensable version. She tells WIRED that there has been interest from creators for games like Paralives, Roblox, and Second Life, as well as from game developers like Triple-A studios.
The tool is still under development but has been undergoing beta testing. Udogaranya says the test feedback has been “overwhelmingly positive.” Elements of the tool are also patent-pending.
Udogaranya hopes her tool will help eliminate the time, effort, and monetary barriers both content creators and game developers have when it comes to Black hair representation in games. “There’s limitations on the exploration of your identity and self-love and self-worth when the tools that you need are genuinely just missing,” she says. “ I'm ready to get rid of all of that and provide the absolute basic identity identifiers when it comes to games and animation.”

Bulgaria probes explosion at weapon storage site
The facility is run by a Bulgarian arms trader whose facilities have been alleged to be the target of attacks by Russian operatives
Bulgaria is investigating the cause of a fire at a weapons storage facility operated by EMCO, including the possibility of sabotage and a link to a previous blaze at another of the company’s facilities in August, the interior minister said.
No injuries were reported in the fire, which broke out near the village of Tsareva Livada and lit up the night sky, according to videos broadcast locally. The incident came weeks after an explosion and fire at another EMCO weapons depot in western Bulgaria.
Interior Minister Ivan Demerdzhiev told journalists on Saturday that the fire was under control and that an investigation was under way.
“We will review previous cases in which similar fires occurred in the warehouses of this company, as well as at other companies, to look for a possible connection or a similar pattern,” he said.
“We are not ruling out outside interference.”
EMCO later said in a statement that the fire was the result of sabotage, citing more than 10 similar incidents at Bulgarian defence firms since 2011, although it did not identify any suspects.

Bodies from Philippine ferry arrive at port after fire killed at least 35
There were 43 survivors among the 132 people on board
Thirty charred bodies found inside a burned passenger ferry in the western Philippines arrived at a port Saturday for identification after a ship fire killed at least 35 people and left more than 50 others missing earlier this week.
Retrieval operations will continue as more bodies are still inside the MV June Aster, coastguard officials said without providing a count. There were 43 survivors among the 132 people on board.
The ferry sailed from the capital, Manila, and was off the village of Turda some 39km (24 miles) from its destination, the Port of Coron, when the fire was reported on Wednesday evening.
The cause of the blaze has not been determined but a survivor said it may have started from the cargo hold. The survivor recounted hearing a blast, with smoke and fire quickly spreading, fanned by the winds, officials said.
Tents were put up in the Port of Borac in Coron, Palawan province, where body bags will be brought down from a ship that transported them from the burned ferry. The coastguard said the bodies will be turned over to the local government, with police officers assisting in identifying the charred remains.

There are many, many strange things about the stew of conspiracy theories that fall under the umbrella of “9/11 Truth”—the false, often antisemitic worldview purporting that the US government had inside knowledge of or even actively participated in the September 11 attacks. But perhaps the strangest is that the seed of these theories was planted three months before the attacks themselves.
It was June 28, 2001, when Milton William “Bill” Cooper took to the air on his national radio show after watching a news report on CNN. “Supposedly, a CNN reporter found Osama bin Laden, took a television camera crew with him, went into Osama bin Laden's hideout, interviewed him and his top leadership, his top lieutenants and colonels and generals in their hideout,” Cooper told his listeners. “He came out and told everybody, ‘Within three weeks, Osama bin Laden is going to attack the United States and Israel.’”
Cooper had part of the story right—a reporter had indeed just reached the inner sanctum of al Qaeda in the mountains near Kandahar, Afghanistan, but he was actually a correspondent for a Middle Eastern broadcaster. And that reporter, the MBC correspondent Baker Atyani, had actually interviewed al Qaeda’s military chief, Mohammed Atif, not bin Laden. “In the coming weeks, there will be a big surprise; we are going to hit American and Israeli installations,” Atif told Atyani. “The coffin business will increase in the United States.” According to Atyani, bin Laden—who was present for the interview—smiled and nodded.
To Cooper, speaking on the radio that day, the interview represented either a major embarrassment for the US government, which had been hunting bin Laden for years, or it was evidence that the government was lying about the threat from bin Laden.
“Now, don’t you think that’s kind of strange, folks?” Cooper said. “The largest intelligence apparatus in the world, with the biggest budget in the history of the world, has been looking for Osama bin Laden for years and years and years and can't find him. The FBI, also under the leadership of Louis Freeh, has been looking for Osama bin Laden for years and years and years and years and years and many years and can’t find him. Some doofus jerk-off reporter with a camera crew waltzes right into his hideout and interviews him?”
“Now that tells us two things: Either everyone in the intelligence community and all of the intelligence agencies of the United States government are blithering idiots and incompetent fools, including the entire apparatus of the FBI and all of their personnel—or they're lying to us. They're not looking for him at all.”
Cooper went on to say that “the CIA created Osama bin Laden” and that “they're now using him to help bring about world government by making him the big boogeyman because they can't use [Iraqi dictator] Saddam Hussein anymore.”
Cooper argued that the whole threat from bin Laden was a farce—what would now be called a “false flag” operation. “If you believe it, you are one of the stupidest jerks that ever lived on the face of this earth, and whatever’s going to happen they’re going to blame on Osama bin Laden.”
About 10 weeks later, Cooper’s comment would come to be seen as a prophecy.
The events and aftermath of 9/11 altered almost every aspect of American society: from the ever-present security theater of daily life—the 3.4-ounce liquid bottles at airports, the defensive bollards that now dominate so many urban landscapes—to the expansion of the surveillance state, to 20 years of war in Afghanistan, to the backdrop of fear and anxiety that permeates the culture. Few, though, rightly recognize one of the most important and pernicious impacts of 9/11: how it changed our society’s very understanding and relationship to facts and truth.
It’s a story that not many people fully understand, one with roots in the UFO conspiracies of the 1980s and with tentacles that stretch to the National Mall on January 6, 2021—and one that helps in particular to explain the transformation of Alex Jones from a fringe Austin, Texas, talk show host to one of the most important (and disruptive) political forces of the 21st century. This transformation began in the first minutes after the September 11 attacks.
Cooper first came to prominence in the 1980s, among the first of a group who would come to be known as “UFO whistleblowers,” former military or intelligence veterans who purported to have insider knowledge about the government’s cover-up of alien civilizations, captured spacecraft, and recovered alien life-forms. It was the first golden age of modern conspiracism, as trust in government cratered following Vietnam, Watergate, and the revelations of dark assassination plots by the Pike and Church committees; books about cover-ups and urban legends like the Bermuda Triangle and the “Philadelphia Experiment” became bestsellers.
Cooper claimed to have been a naval intelligence officer in the 1970s and said that, as part of his work with a high-ranking admiral, he’d been able to covertly paw through the contents of the admiral’s cabinet of classified material. As Colin Dickey wrote in a review of a Cooper biography, the cabinet became “a repository of secrets known only to Cooper, whose contents seemed to change and evolve over the years, fitting whatever need Cooper’s current conspiracies had.” In early iterations, Cooper hinted it contained the truth about the JFK assassination and the government’s contact with aliens.
In the 1990s, amid the rise of far-right talk shows like that of Rush Limbaugh, Cooper became a national radio figure as well; his shortwave The Hour of the Time focused on a witches’ brew of sinister government conspiracies, alternate histories, warnings about the New World Order and secret societies, and a healthy dose of general-purpose skepticism; Cooper often exhorted his audience, “Wake up, sheeple!” (Much of his conspiracism contained thinly and not-so-thinly veiled antisemitism.)
For a brief period, Cooper was one of the nation’s most famous “UFO-ologists,” but few believed him—he feuded frequently with others in the field. He eventually laid out a grand conspiracy account in his 1991 memoir/fever-dream of a book, Behold a Pale Horse.
Behold a Pale Horse is a wacky piece of writing—there’s almost no other word for it. At one point it quotes the entire text of the Protocols of the Elders of Zion, a fabricated antisemitic screed from the early 1900s that alleged a secret Jewish plot to overthrow Christianity. Cooper’s work was basically QAnon three decades early, outlining a vast global conspiracy, decades-long and all-encompassing, to steal America and our freedoms from real Americans, all to serve some global super elite. The book became an underground bestseller—it still is today—and took off particularly within the militia movement.
This newfound fame coincided with the start of his talk radio career on WWCR, World Wide Christian Radio, in January 1993. With a 100,000-watt signal, he could reach huge swaths of the country from his home in Arizona. And over time, Cooper developed two important—and later infamous—superfans. One was a young Gulf War veteran named Timothy McVeigh, who in the early spring of 1995 journeyed with a companion—their exact identity is disputed—to Arizona to try to talk to Cooper at his home. “The last thing he said before they left in their green Mercury Marquis station wagon with a puke-yellow interior was, ‘Watch Oklahoma City,’” Cooper would later recount. Soon after their meeting, McVeigh attacked the Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building, killing 168 people and injuring nearly 700.
Then there was Alex Jones, a local public-access talk show host in Austin, Texas, who first came onto the national radar for his fundraising work to rebuild the church at the Branch Davidian compound in Waco, Texas. The site had burned down in 1993 at the end of a 51-day siege by the US government, as federal agents tried to arrest the leader of the Branch Davidian cult, David Koresh. In the end, agents in armored vehicles tried to fill the compound with tear gas; the buildings caught fire—it was never clear how the fires started—and most of the Davidians who remained in the compound died in the blaze. There were 75 fatalities, including about two dozen children. The Waco siege was a key flashpoint for the far right in the 1990s.
Jones saw inspiration in Cooper’s model, and Cooper became something of a mentor to the budding radio host, calling in for an interview on Jones’ early shows. Jones’ show on KJFK-FM lasted until 1999—he was even voted “Best of Austin” radio host by a local newspaper, which called him “either Austin’s great exposer of truth or a black helicopter conspiracy nut, depending on your worldview.” But his conspiracism made getting sponsors difficult, and KJFK fired him in December 1999. Jones quickly latched on to a new venture on the expanding internet: Infowars.com.
On September 11, 2001, Cooper was outraged by the attacks and warned of what would come next. “Folks, I can assure you that 72 hours from now, we will be at war. We will be bombing two or maybe three countries … Because that’s how it works. When governments are attacked, they lash out. Thousands of people who had nothing whatsoever to do with what is happening at the World Trade Center and the Pentagon are going to die,” Cooper said. “Nothing will be the same after today.”
Broadcasting that day on Infowars and about 100 syndicated stations, Jones did one better: “I went on the air and said, ‘Those were controlled demolitions,’” he later told Rolling Stone.
In the weeks ahead, Cooper and Jones diverged politically. Cooper had come to see Jones as a copycat, a fearmonger, and a liar. (On September 26, 2001, Cooper’s show was titled simply “Alex Jones—Liar.”)
Amid the aftermath of the September 11 attacks, Jones dove deeper into budding 9/11 conspiracies, and Cooper—who had stopped paying taxes, was drinking heavily, and was engaged in sometimes violent disputes with his neighbors—began prophesying his own death. In November 2001, law enforcement arrived at his Arizona compound to arrest him on an outstanding warrant on suspicion of aggravated assault; Cooper opened fire, shooting one deputy in the head, and was killed in the returning police gunfire.
The field was clear for the rise of Alex Jones.
In the years that followed, Alex Jones became a key force in the spread of 9/11 conspiracies. The movement, which came to be known as “9/11 Truth,” encompassed a host of different theories: that United Airlines Flight 93 had been downed by US fighters; that the Pentagon had been struck by a missile, not a plane; that the World Trade Centers had been brought down by space weapons.
By even the first years after 9/11, the ideas had become so widespread that the government’s 9/11 Commission took pains to document in careful factual detail the impossibility of some of the conspiracies, hoping to avoid the ambiguities that dogged the Warren Commission’s report into the JFK assassination. Popular Mechanics devoted a special issue—later turned into a book, with a foreword by Senator John McCain—to debunking the most popular ones.
But the conspiracies took root in the early internet of the 2000s: Arguably the first viral online documentary, known as Loose Change, took the conspiracies to the broader public, becoming one of the most-watched videos on Google Video and the early era of YouTube. (Jones would even get an “executive producer” credit on one version of the film.) The DVD box promised, “What you will see inside will prove without a shadow of a doubt that everything you know about 9/11 is a complete fabrication.”
The reality is that the film offered no conclusive evidence of government involvement or conspiracy, but would be familiar format-wise to anyone online today in its “We’re-just-asking-questions” tone, cherry-picking quotes and evidence out of context to broadly hand-wave at surely sinister machinations behind the scenes.
9/11 conspiracism found a home politically on both the right, with Jones and his acolytes, and the left in the 2000s, as Democrats protested the documentable lies and mistruths that helped lead the nation into war with Iraq. Documentarian Michael Moore released a blockbuster movie in 2004, Fahrenheit 9/11, a polemic that tied George W. Bush’s administration, Saudi Arabia, and Iraq together in a sinister warmongering and corporate profiteering conspiracy; it became one of the highest-grossing documentaries of all time and won the prestigious Palme d’Or at Cannes.
According to a May 2006 Zogby poll, some 42 percent of Americans believed that the US government and the 9/11 Commission “concealed or refused to investigate critical evidence that contradicts their official explanation of the September 11 attacks” and that “there has been a cover-up.”
I’ve spent much of the past decade writing about 9/11 and have spoken at hundreds of public events; rarely do I make it through an event without an audience question that’s at least conspiracy-adjacent.
Jones, in particular, found conspiracism wildly profitable. As Nicole Hemmer, a Vanderbilt professor who studies the far right, told me, “Because he was a critic of the war in Iraq, he becomes seen by many people outside of the Alex Jones universe as somebody who bridges the left-right divide. Even though he is a far-right figure, he can feast off this credibility that he has as being somebody who is above politics—and that really helps elevate him into, increasingly, a household name.”
Jones became nationally infamous for arguing that later tragedies, like the elementary school shooting at Sandy Hook, were also false-flag operations. In the first Trump term, amid the Covid-19 pandemic, Jones became a fierce voice against government lockdowns, and as the aftermath of the fall 2020 election unfolded, he and his “InfoWars Battle Tank”—an armored truck worth some $300,000—became a ubiquitous presence at Stop the Steal rallies leading up to the protests at the Capitol on January 6. Throughout Donald Trump’s rise and first term, conspiracies loomed large. Trump himself first came to political prominence amid the birtherism movement, and his supporters embraced Pizzagate and the broader QAnon conspiracy.
In recent years, Jones, of course, has suffered a remarkable comedown; his vicious lies finally caught up with him in lawsuits from the families of the victims of the Sandy Hook shooting, and after a lengthy court battle, his InfoWars.com domain has been acquired by The Onion.
But if Jones has lost his most recent battles, it’s hard not to see that his conspiracism has won the broader war. Today, as the nation marks the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks, it’s notable that the anti-government conspiracists have effectively taken over the US government itself—from Health and Human Services secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s Covid and vaccine denialism to President Donald Trump’s own fetid swamp of a social media feed. In news that would make Bill Cooper particularly proud, Trump has even promised to release the government’s files on the truth about UFOs. For the most part, though, we’re still waiting.

Fintech major PhonePe has reportedly shut down its engineering office in the US, winding down a four year-old team. Sources told Times of India that the Bay Area team consisted of seven to eight engineers, who worked directly alongside PhonePe’s main mobile platform and engineering teams based in Bengaluru and other Indian hubs. A source reportedly said that the decision to close the US office was taken after PhonePe concluded that the operation was not producing sufficient results to justify its continuation. “They did not see enough coming out of the US operation to continue running it. Consolidating the work was also a way to cut costs,” a person familiar with the development reportedly said. Inc42 has reached out to the company for a comment on the matter and this story will be updated upon receiving their response. The development comes nearly four years after PhonePe first announced the US office in June 2022. At the time, the fintech major said that the overseas unit would initially employ around 10 engineers and the team would work to build the technology needed to support the company’s next 300 Mn users. The unit was led by Gaurav Lochan, a former Meta engineering executive who joined PhonePe in April 2022 as head of engineering. However, Lochan’s LinkedIn profile shows that he left the fintech unicorn in July 2026. He is currently an adviser at cybersecurity startup Aucert. The shutdown does not necessarily indicate the startup’s broader retreat from overseas expansion. Earlier this week, PhonePe CEO Sameer Nigam reportedly said that the company received its first international licence from the Central Bank of the UAE. The licence will allow PhonePe to acquire merchants, deploy point-of-sale devices and offer foreign-exchange services in the UAE. If the plan materialises, the Gulf nation will become PhonePe’s first overseas market. Back home, on the sidelines of the ongoing Global Fintech Fest (GFF) 2026 in Mumbai, the Walmart-backed fintech major also recently announced a partnership with global card network Visa to launch three cardless payment solutions for consumers and merchants in India. The launches come even as there appears no clarity on PhonePe’s IPO plans. In January this year, the fintech major filed its updated draft red herring prospectus (UDRHP) with SEBI for an public issue, which comprised solely of an offer for sale (OFS) of up to 5.06 Cr equity shares. However, the company later paused its IPO plans in March amid geopolitical tensions in West Asia and volatility in global equity markets. On the financial front, PhonePe’s operating revenue rose 11.5% to ₹7,920.5 Cr in FY26 from ₹7,105 Cr in the previous fiscal year. However, its net loss widened 62% to ₹2,792 Cr from ₹1,727.4 Cr in FY25.

Whatever happened to the measles outbreak that shocked a country this year?
In May, we posted a story about the rapid and devastating spread of measles in Bangladesh. The headline: More than 500 children have died in an outbreak that the world is virtually ignoring. We asked the reporter who covered the story to tell us what has transpired since then.
Over the next week, we'll be looking back at some of our past global health and development stories to see "whatever happened to ..."
There was optimism early on about bringing the measles outbreak in Bangladesh under control.
In April, the country's health minister, Sardar Md. Sakhawat Husain, offered this assessment: "Measles outbreak has somewhat decreased in the country. Once the nationwide vaccination campaign begins on April 20, the situation will improve further."
The goal was to vaccinate 18 million children ages 6 months to 5 years, even if records indicated they'd already been vaccinated. That goal was met and then some, with 18.4 million vaccinations.
Five months later, the outbreak continues apace.
In August, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported that Bangladesh has had more measles cases than any other country from January to June of this year: 57,561.
On the day of Aug. 31, authorities recorded 1,162 suspected cases and 94 confirmed cases in 24 hours.
On September 9, the toll for children who have died from suspected or confirmed measles cases since March 15 passed 1,000, according to the Directorate General of Health Services of Bangladesh.
Why has the virus not been conquered?
It turns out that 18 million vaccinations wasn't enough to reach all the unvaccinated children. Health experts in the country now say that 22.6 million is the true target.
This persistent immunization gap has given the highly contagious virus a continued chance to spread.
"Many children have still not received the measles vaccine, so we cannot go into a relaxed mode," Tajul Abdul Bari told NPR. He is a vaccine expert and former program manager of the government's Expanded Programme on Immunization. "We need to start a new vaccination campaign, potentially covering children from 6 months up to under 10 years of age. We did something similar in 2014."
Dr. Javid Abdelmoneim, president of Médecins Sans Frontières International, told NPR, "The management of a measles outbreak is vaccinating. Vaccinate, vaccinate, vaccinate."
"Measles has a very specific biology. It is highly transmissible. One case of measles can affect 100 others," he added.
Dr Jahangir Alam, the World Health Organization's divisional coordinator for the capital city of Dhaka, said: "Even small gaps in immunization coverage can trigger outbreaks. Every missed child increases the risk."
Indeed, a UNICEF situation report says that 72% of cases are among those with no doses of the two-dose vaccine and 16% of the patients are partially vaccinated.
The toll has been worsened because of the country's widespread malnutrition, which increases the risk of severe illness and death from a measles infection. "Children who are underweight or have two or more medical conditions at the same time suffer more, and their condition worsens," says Colonel Latifa Rahman, director of Mohakhali DNCC Hospital, the hospital in the capital that is now doing nothing but measles care.
Malnutrition can also lessen the immunity conferred by a vaccine.
Next steps
On Aug. 18, Bangladesh announced it will vaccinate another 1.6 million children against measles.
Former Health Services Division Secretary Md Kamruzzaman Chowdhury said official data shows that in some pockets of the country, there are children between 6 months and 5 years who missed out on vaccination. in pockets of the country.
"In light of that, we will administer the 1.6 million vaccines we currently have," he said.
The government is also moving to procure another 2.5 million doses to guard against future shortages, according to Kamruzzaman.
"We will give 1.6 million now and are procuring 2.5 million vaccines for the future. We have spoken with UNICEF about purchasing these vaccines," he added.
So the early forecast of a quick end to the outbreak has been tempered by the reality in Bangladesh.
"There is no scope for unrealistic assurances. Even if the pace of vaccination were doubled, it would still take another two to three months to bring the measles outbreak fully under control," State Minister for Health Dr. M.A. Muhit said on Aug. 19.
The toll on families
As the outbreak continues, thousands of families are being driven into financial distress. Nearly 9 in 10 affected households have borrowed money for treatment and 6 in 10 have exhausted their savings, according to a joint assessment in May and June by the Bangladesh Red Crescent Society and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC).
The assessment covered 2,746 measles-affected households receiving care at 12 government medical colleges and district hospitals.
Sonakshi Dey of the IFRC in Bangladesh said economic hardships continue even if a child has recovered: "Beyond direct medical expenses, caregivers often lose income when they need to stay home to care for a sick child or travel repeatedly to health facilities. For low-income households that depend on daily wages, even a short interruption to work can have serious consequences for household wellbeing and food security."
Families who have lost a child face the heaviest toll of all. Toriqul Islam, whose 10-month-old boy died due to measles on May 9, said in a heavy tone:
"When fate turns against you, this is what happens. I don't know if there is any greater pain in this world.
"Let the government do whatever they want, but all I want is for no one to die."
Ali Asif Shawon is the chief reporter at Dhaka Tribune in Bangladesh, where he covers politics, security, climate change, migration and global health. He can be reached on LinkedIn.

Former Football Association of Maldives (FAM) president Bassam Adeel Jaleel has received a lifetime ban from all football-related activities for misappropriating COVID-19 relief funds for personal use, FIFA announced on Friday.
Jaleel, who had earlier been provisionally suspended while under investigation for alleged money laundering, embezzlement and corruption, has also been ordered to pay a fine of one million Swiss francs (USD 1.23 million).
Jaleel could not be reached for comment. Local media reports that he is serving prison sentences totalling 32 years for depositing FIFA funds into his personal account and using money from FIFA’s COVID-19 Relief Plan to buy an apartment.
Maldivian news outlet Sun Online said he was moved to house arrest last month on the medical board’s recommendation. He had previously been transferred to house arrest in March but was sent back to prison following public outrage.
FIFA said the FAM’s former director of finance and administration, Mohamed Ageel, has also been banned for 10 years. Ageel has been ordered to pay a fine of 100,000 Swiss francs for “facilitating and concealing misuse of FIFA funds, using falsified documentation and failing to cooperate with FIFA’s independent Ethics Committee,” FIFA added.
In a separate case, FIFA has also handed a lifetime ban to former Montserrat Football Association (MFA) president Vincent Cassell, along with a one-million-Swiss-franc fine, for “abuse of position, systemic conflicts of interest, misuse of FIFA and MFA funds and conduct affecting the physical and mental integrity of MFA staff members.”
The MFA’s former general secretary, Tandica Hughes, was banned for 15 years and fined 150,000 Swiss francs for “personally benefiting from and facilitating improper transactions involving FIFA and MFA resources,” FIFA said.
Reuters has contacted both the Maldives and Montserrat FAs for comment on this matter.

Can ego become bigger than love? This question forms the central theme of Main Na Raha Mera, an upcoming romantic musical starring Adhyayan Suman and Divita Rai, who makes her acting debut with the film.
Adhyayan Suman and Divita Rai’s Main Na Raha Mera first look out, teaser to release on September 16

Thank you for joining us for our continuing coverage of the aftermath of Wednesday’s catastrophic flash floods in the Himalayan mountains near the Nepal-Tibet border.
Poor weather has hampered aerial rescue operations in Nepal as the search for thousands of people missing enters its fourth day.
Nepal’s finance minister says his country will need up to $5bn to rebuild after the floods, believed to have been caused by a melting glacier high up in the mountains that set off a deadly cascade of water into the valleys below.
Finance minister Swarnim Wagle told Reuters today those figures are “just an estimate” and that “loss and damage is being assessed”.
Here’s a summary of what we know so far:
Nearly 3,000 people are missing. Nepal’s disaster agency on Saturday said 2,426 people were missing on its side of the border, while China’s Xinhua news agency reports the total number of missing in Tibet is now 554.
The death toll in Nepal has now risen to 626, while China’s Xinhua news agency earlier today reported seven people confirmed dead in Tibet.
More than 3,700 people have been rescued in Nepal so far but at least 93,000 people are estimated to have been affected by the disaster, according to the Red Cross.
At least 777 foreigners are missing, with Nepal’s disaster agency on Friday reporting 517 foreigners unaccounted for – which could include tourists and foreign workers – and Chinese officials putting the number of foreigners missing at 260.
India said it is increasing surveillance of glaciers and glacial lakes in its Himalayan regions bordering Nepal and China.
The deadly floods on the Nepal-Tibet border were believed to have been triggered by a glacial collapse that was detected as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event by geologists. You can read this explainer to find out more about how a collapsing glacier can generate a powerful flood, and whether the climate crisis is contributing to the risk.
Madan Kaushik, state disaster management minister in India’s Himalayan state of Uttarakhand, said: “Since we share a border with Nepal, as a neighbour, and also have a similar geographic situation … we have asked our department to monitor all the glaciers and known glacial lakes in the region.”
Uttarakhand is one of the most ecologically sensitive regions of India, with 1,266 glacial lakes. As glaciers melt, water can accumulate in lakes held back by natural barriers. If those barriers fail, vast volumes of water can be released suddenly, triggering devastating floods.
“We have asked our teams to be vigilant and monitor if a similar situation is emerging anywhere in the state,” Kaushik told AFP.
‘The flood took everything I have’: survivors grieve for relatives and homes swept away in Nepal
The Guardian’s south Asia correspondent Hannah Ellis-Petersen and journalist Gaurav Pokharel report from the Nepalese town of Bidur, where rescue efforts are being coordinated. They spoke to survivors mourning loved ones and confronting the loss of their homes and livelihoods after devastating floods swept through their communities.
Among those caught in the floods was Sangke Dolma Tamang, who described the moment she watched her husband being swept away and returned to find her home and village destroyed:
Sangke Dolma Tamang, 61, had been cheerily cooking snacks in her village of Mailung in the Rasuwa district when the floods came without warning. The whole family ran uphill for safety, but as she grabbed for her husband, he slipped from her grip and was washed into the dark, fast-moving waters.
“Others tried to pull him to safety, but the flood swept him away,” she said, tears rolling down her weathered cheeks. There was, she said, nothing left of her village now. She had spent a night sheltering on higher ground, until an army helicopter arrived and brought to her safety at the barracks. Her son too was missing since the disaster, and she waited anxiously for any news.
“Now I have nothing left to live for,” said Tamang. “The whole house is gone. We couldn’t salvage anything.”
Nepal’s government has appealed for financial help as it faces the daunting task of recovering from the devastating flash floods and braces for the possibility of more flooding.
Entire communities have been swept away, leaving families homeless or sheltering in temporary facilities.
“Multiple bridges have been washed away and major roads disrupted, leaving some of the worst-affected communities extremely difficult to reach,” the Red Cross says.
At least 18 schools have been destroyed and another 20 damaged, leaving about 10,000 school-age children affected, according to the UN Children’s Fund.
The disaster comes just ahead of the anniversary of last year’s 8-9 September mass anti-corruption protests that toppled the government.
Nepal is now led by prime minister Balendra Shah, a 36-year-old rapper turned politician widely known as “Balen”. The former Kathmandu mayor swept March elections on a wave of euphoria calling for political change.
The risk of a lake formed after the glacier collapse bursting near the China-Nepal border where the devastating flood occurred earlier this week has decreased, Chinese authorities said today, as its size appears to have shrunk.
Satellite images from Thursday this morning suggest water in the lake – straddling the China-Nepal border at the confluence of two rivers – has been slowly flowing through, decreasing the reservoir gradually, state broadcaster CCTV reported, citing the water resources ministry.
The ministry said satellite imagery of the surface area of the lake at Purepu Tsangpo river showed it was 99,000 sq metres in size this morning – around the size of 14 football fields combined – having shrunk by 21,000 sq metres compared with images from Thursday.
Experts and authorities have warned of the extremely high risk of secondary disasters in the valley, especially from the lake that was formed by glacier debris, potentially endangering rescue operations downstream.
State-owned engineering and rescue enterprise China Anneng, which has been monitoring the lake since Thursday, dispatched a 15-member team on Friday with reconnaissance drones, portable satellite stations and mobile surveillance cameras to gather more data about the lake.
An overflow from the lake on Friday temporarily halted rescue work before further assessment deemed the risks manageable.

Worldwide, traditional medicine is used by billions of people for their health and well-being. At a signing ceremony in Geneva, the Government of India committed US$ 85 million over 10 years, 2022–2032, to support the programming of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre. India’s 10-year financial contribution will support a cross-sectoral program of work to strengthen the evidence base for traditional medicine by providing data and evidence on traditional medicine policies, practice, products, and public use.
The WHO-India donor agreement is part of a US$ 250 million investment from India in support of the establishment of the WHO Global Centre of Traditional Medicine in 2022, which includes financial support for the workplan of the Centre, interim premises and a new building. This support will scale up WHO’s capacities on traditional medicine across technical divisions and regions in the spirit of global collaboration and solidarity. Part of this substantial contribution from the Government of India will also be included in WHO’s Investment Round to resource WHO’s core work during 2025–2028.
Photo: WHO/Lindsay Mackenzie
“India’s commitment and leadership in expanding the evidence-based contribution of traditional medicine to the health and well-being of all people and the planet, comes at an opportune moment,” said Dr Bruce Aylward, Assistant Director-General of the Universal Health Coverage and Life Course division of WHO. “Traditional medicine, supported within national health systems, can allow us to reach those most often left behind. Integration of traditional practice and knowledge is critical to achieving health for all.”
“The signing of this donor agreement is a major milestone towards achieving the shared vision of Honourable Prime Minister of India Shri Narendra Modi and WHO Director-General Tedros for the development of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre at Jamnagar in India,” said Vice Minister Vaidya Rajesh Kotecha, Secretary of the Ministry of Ayush, Government of India.
“India remains committed to supporting WHO in its work to strengthen traditional medicine systems globally for achieving universal health coverage and serving the entire humanity, especially through this Global Centre in Jamnagar, which would help focus these efforts to benefit all Member States,” said Ambassador Arindam Bagchi, Permanent Representative of India to the UN and other International Organizations in Geneva.
The WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre is is a knowledge hub focusing on five inter-connected areas of work: research and evidence; primary health care and universal health coverage; Indigenous Knowledges and biodiversity; digital health applications; and the biennial WHO Global Traditional Medicine Summit and collaborations. The Centre is led by Dr Shyama Kuruvilla, Director a.i.
The first WHO traditional medicine global summit was held in August 2023 in Gujarat, resulting in the a multistakeholder action agenda, the Gujarat Declaration. The next WHO Global Summit is planned for November 2025, following up on the anticipated launch of the 2025–2034 Global Strategy for Traditional Medicine at the 78th World Health Assembly in May 2025.
India’s support for traditional medicine has been expressed through a variety of long-standing partnerships with WHO. In 2023, India signed a five-year agreement to support the technical work of WHO’s Traditional, Complementary and Integrative Medicine (TCI) unit. The unit is supporting the development of the Member State-requested new WHO traditional medicine global strategy (2025 - 2034), and publishes key benchmark documents, standardized terminologies, and other evidence-informed technical products to support the safe and effective integration of traditional medicine in national health systems.  
The Centre and TCI collaborate closely with teams across WHO to advance WHO’s multisectoral agenda on traditional medicine, including through regular meetings of the WHO Technical Expert Network, coordinated by the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre and TCI, to promote a One WHO approach on traditional medicine across headquarters, regional and country office.

Bhutan has become the first country in the World Health Organization’s South-East Asia Region to eliminate dog-transmitted rabies as a public health problem. The WHO, on Saturday, validated Bhutan’s achievement. The mountain kingdom’s last rabies death was in June 2023.
Rabies burden
Rabies is a viral disease that is almost always fatal if clinical symptoms appear. It is estimated that rabies still claims the lives of approximately 59,000 people each year, with a third of these fatalities occurring in India, where it remains a huge problem with local bodies failing at animal birth control and vaccination programmes.
The disease is endemic throughout the country except for the Andaman and Nicobar and Lakshadweep Islands, and cases are reported from all over the country, the year round. About 96% of the mortality and morbidity is associated with dog bites.The National Rabies Control Programme aims to reduce mortality from rabies among human beings and progressively achieve the target of bringing rabies deaths to zero by 2030.
In a message shared on the WHO website, its Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus congratulated Bhutan ‘which is another step towards our goal to end human deaths from dog-transmitted rabies by 2030.’ He further noted the interventions that made the success possible: “Bhutan’s success shows that the health of humans, animals and the environment we share is inextricably linked. By uniting health workers, veterinarians, and communities, Bhutan has shown that the fight against rabies is won not in silos, but through solidarity across all sectors.”
WHO validation recognises that a country has eliminated dog-transmitted human rabies and consequently through the absence of human deaths from the disease for at least two years, while demonstrating the capacity to prevent transmission from re-emerging. This criterion was set out by the WHO Expert Consultation on Rabies in 2018.
Preventing transmission
Rabies deaths are preventable. A two-pronged strategy is advocated globally- vaccinating dogs to curb the disease at source, and using post exposure prophylaxis (PEP) after a bite. PEP consists of thoroughly washing the bite area with water and soap, administering a full course of human rabies vaccine and, whenever necessary, rabies immunoglobulins.
The WHO attributes the One Health approach, or the firm belief that human and animal health are intrinsically like to ecosystems, to Bhutan’s success story. “Through this approach, Bhutan has prioritised resource allocation, integrated surveillance, and strategic planning,” a WHO statement has recorded. When a suspected rabies case is reported, animal and human health authorities collaborate to identify potential exposures and conduct joint field investigations under the One Health framework.
Nilesh Buddha, Officer-in-Charge, WHO South-East Asia Region, complimented the country: “The dedication of health workers, veterinary professionals and De-suung volunteers known as ‘Guardians of Peace’ helped take dog vaccination, population management and community awareness to every part of the country.”
Sustaining rabies control
A strong collaboration was initiated between the Ministries of Health and the Agriculture and Livestock, together with partners, local governments and communities, united through a One Health approach, Bhutan’s health ministry sources explained. Continued access to PEP, mass dog vaccination, dog population management, community engagement and strengthened surveillance marked the country’s programme.
Bhutan will reportedly continue to maintain the systems that underpin this achievement. Its Nationwide Accelerated Dog Population Management and Rabies Control Programme will be sustained with the same vigour, according to the WHO. Cross-border coordination with adjacent Indian states will be further strengthened to safeguard this success in rabies control.

Huntington’s disease (HD) is an inherited neurological disorder in which nerve cells in parts of the brain gradually break down and die. While there is currently no cure, doctors can treat some of its symptoms and researchers are investigating therapies aimed at slowing or preventing the underlying disease process. Here’s all you need to know about it.
What is Huntington’s disease?
Huntington’s disease is caused by a change in the HTT gene, which carries instructions for producing the huntingtin protein. The abnormal gene contains excessive repetitions of a three-base DNA sequence called CAG (Cytosine, Adenine, and Guanine).
According to information from the National Institutes of Health (NIH), most people have fewer than 27 CAG repeats and are not at risk of developing HD. Those with 27 to 35 repeats are unlikely to develop the disease but may be able to pass an expanded repeat to their children. People with 36 or more repeats may have the disease-causing expansion.
The abnormal huntingtin protein can become malformed and damage brain cells. The basal ganglia, a group of brain structures involved in coordinating movement, and the cortex, which plays a role in thought, perception and memory, are among the areas most affected, according to the NIH’s National Human Genome Research Institute.
HD is an autosomal dominant disorder. This means that a person needs only one copy of the altered gene to develop the disease. Each child of a parent who carries the HD gene has a 50% chance of inheriting it. If a child does not inherit the altered gene, they will not develop HD or pass the gene on to their children.
What are the symptoms?
The symptoms of Huntington’s disease vary from person to person and generally become more severe as the disease progresses. They broadly involve movement, thinking and behaviour or mood.
According to the NIH, one of the most recognisable movement symptoms is chorea — uncontrollable, dance-like movements that can affect the fingers, feet, face or torso. These movements may become worse when a person is nervous or distracted.
Early symptoms can include mild clumsiness, problems with balance or movement, difficulty walking, stiffness or rigid muscles, involuntary shaking or tremors, and dystonia, in which muscles tighten involuntarily and the body can become fixed in unusual positions. Unusual eye movements may also occur early in the disease.
As the condition progresses, people may develop problems with speech, swallowing and eating. Difficulty eating and swallowing can lead to weight loss, choking and lung infections. Other physical symptoms include fatigue, low energy, sleep problems and, in some cases, seizures.
HD also affects cognitive abilities. People may have difficulty concentrating, making decisions, solving problems, judging situations, organising or prioritising tasks, learning or remembering new information, or putting their thoughts into words. These problems can progressively interfere with work, driving and the ability to care for oneself.
Behaviour and mood can change as well. Symptoms may include irritability, mood swings, depression, anger, loss of interest and withdrawal from friends and family. Severe depression, suicidal thoughts and psychosis can occur.
How is it diagnosed?
Doctors diagnose HD by considering a person’s symptoms, family history and neurological examination, supported by laboratory and genetic tests and, where appropriate, brain imaging.
A neurologist may assess reflexes, balance, movement, muscle strength, walking, hearing, thinking, memory and mood. Other specialists, including mental health professionals, genetic counsellors and speech-language therapists, may also be involved in diagnosis and care.
The most accurate way to confirm HD is a genetic test. A blood sample is used to analyse DNA and determine the number of CAG repeats in the HTT gene. The attached NIH material notes that people with 36 or more repeats have the disease-causing expansion, while those with fewer than 26 repeats do not have the condition.
MRI and CT scans can show structural changes in the brain as HD progresses, including shrinkage in affected regions. However, such changes can occur in other conditions and scans can be normal in people with early HD. So, conventional brain imaging is not a replacement for genetic testing to confirm the disease.
Latest research says that a new type of MRI technique could eventually allow researchers to see more than just the shrinkage of the brain and get an indirect picture of the cellular damage caused by HD.
According to The Conversation, researchers used soma and neurite density imaging (Sandi), a diffusion MRI technique, to assess cellular changes in the brains of 56 people with HD and 57 healthy volunteers.
In the basal ganglia of those with HD, the scans showed lower apparent cell-body density, larger cell bodies and more space between cells — changes resembling those seen in postmortem brain tissue.
The measurements were also linked to disease severity and motor performance, and in some striatal regions helped explain up to 63% of observed brain shrinkage. Researchers say Sandi could eventually help track disease progression and assess whether treatments are protecting brain cells, but larger, longer-term studies are needed before it can be used clinically.
What are the treatment options?
According to the U.S. National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke, there is currently no treatment that can stop or reverse HD. Treatment focuses on managing symptoms and improving quality of life.
For chorea, medicines including tetrabenazine, deutetrabenazine and valbenazine can be used to affect the brain signals involved in controlling movement.
Antipsychotic medicines, including risperidone and olanzapine, may help reduce chorea as well as psychiatric symptoms such as severe irritability, unusual thoughts or hallucinations. However, some antipsychotic medicines can worsen movement-related symptoms, so doctors need to monitor patients and adjust treatment where necessary.
Medicines can also be used to treat depression and anxiety. Treatments may have side effects such as tiredness, sleepiness, difficulty concentrating, restlessness or increased activity. Beyond managing symptoms, research is increasingly focused on finding ways to alter the underlying disease.
