In Kolkata as well, reporters of mainstream media outlets were allegedly pushed and shoved after a march on July 24 in solidarity with the Jantar Mantar protest.
Why Were Protesters Angry?
The central allegation against sections of legacy media seemed to be that they had stopped acting as the voice of the people and had instead become the voice of the establishment.
For many of the demonstrators, the resentment did not begin with the July protests.
Television news channels have failed, over the years, to hold the Union government to account over a wide range of issues that affect ordinary citizens’ lives — from examination paper leaks and irregularities in recruitment exams to unemployment, price rise, public health etc. This is precisely the role the media is expected to play as democracy’s fourth pillar. Most television news channels that have ample airtime for communal debates and polarising studio confrontations show far less urgency when the failures of the government directly affect the lives and futures of citizens.
The dissatisfaction was not simply about what television channels were reporting during the protests, but what they had consistently chosen not to report. For a generation facing an increasingly precarious education and employment landscape, the perceived reluctance of mainstream television to question those in power became a source of deep distrust.
Explaining the reasons for the anger against the mainstream media, AISA leader and student face of the Delhi protests Neha Bora said, “The hate that the government peddles comes to our drawing rooms, our WhatsApp groups and our very personal lives, within the four walls of our homes, through the Godi media. The Godi media and the IT cell are single-handedly responsible for the venom that runs through the veins of this country presently. Through systematic targeting and organised campaigns, they have made enemies out of citizens, neighbours and friends.”
Elaborating on how they had failed in their duty, she added, “The government is not a God-like figure. They are there to do a job; they have been elected to serve us. They will have to be questioned. The Godi media has systematically dismantled this idea. We are told not to question the government, criticise its policies or talk about the problems we face. If I say that the answer sheet in the Class 12 examination is not mine, the Godi media and the IT cell are going to call me a Pakistani.”
In May, Doordarshan anchor Ashok Srivastav called Class XII student from Delhi Vedant Srivastava a Pakistani. After receiving unexpectedly low marks in Physics, Vedant had applied for photocopies of his answer sheets through CBSE’s reevaluation process. When the copies arrived, he discovered that the Physics answer sheet uploaded by the Board was not his. He made an X account to post about his grievances.
“The disrespect that the youth has for Godi media stems from this — the recognition that this Godi media and its anchors, who scream at the top of their voices on TV screens, have fractured the democratic, secular fabric of this country,” Neha added.
Asked for her response to ground reporters being heckled, Neha said, “We recognise that there are ground reporters in Godi media who do honest work, and that is why we urged our people not to disrespect them. Our differences need not be expressed through violence. We don’t believe in mobs. But there is no denying that the mainstream media has become a BJP propaganda cell, it seems.”
The protesters’ criticism was also shaped by how they believed the movement itself was being portrayed.
Arnab Goswami, for example, in an apparent bid to discredit the protest and question its legitimacy, mentioned China, US, Bangladesh, Pakistan, BitChat, the deep state, Greta Thunberg, Jeremy Corbyn, and even John Cusack as conspirators behind the CJP protest.
In a podcast hosted by Navika Kumar, lyricist and screenwriter Manoj Muntashir Shukla called protesters anti-nationals.
As clashes broke out between protesters and police on July 20, ANI did not post a single news update throughout the day which mentioned injury to protesters.
In Kolkata, Zee reporter Ayan Ghoshal said while interviewing BJP leader Dilip Ghosh, “For the last 3 days efforts are on in Delhi to break India. PM has shown restraint. We know how Pak or Indonesia curbed students’ protest. Dead bodies were strewn on sreets. But no tough action here. They’re getting encouraged.”
The mainstream media drew criticism on social media for what protesters described as coverage that closely mirrored the official version put forward by the Delhi Police and the government. The channels, on the other hand, maintained that they were reporting developments on the ground.

Rahul Shivshankar, editorial director of CNN News 18, amplified a video where RSS leader Atul Limaye called the CJP protest anti-national and “a weapon against the Constitution”.
It is worth noting that coverage of this kind carries risks beyond the newsroom. Framing a protest movement as anti-national, foreign-funded or a security threat can shape how the protesters are treated on the ground, by the state and by ordinary citizens alike. The Zee reporter’s on-air remarks, for example, were arguably not only biased, but amounted to incitement. Seen against this backdrop, at least some of the heckling and intimidation directed at reporters on the ground could be a reaction to this pattern of coverage.
A Widening Trust Deficit
The outpouring of anger at journalists points to a broader crisis of credibility confronting sections of India’s television news industry.
Alt News’s years of fact-checking work and media-watchdog journalism point to a pattern rather than isolated lapses: In the recent past, large sections of mainstream television media have functioned as an echo chamber for the government. The clearest symptom is the collapse of verification standards and rampant amplification of misinformation. During the India-Pakistan military escalation following the Pahalgam attack, several major channels aired unverified and outright false claims — old and unrelated videos and fabricated visuals presented as live combat coverage.

Further in the past, we documented instances of mainstream media broadcasting misinformation targeting protesters and protest movements. During the 2024 farmers’ movement, Republic, News 18, India TV, Zee News, India Today, Navbharat Times — all ran a doctored video of farmer leader Jagjit Singh Dallewal without any context and amplified the misleading claim that he said Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s popularity graph had skyrocketed after the Ram Mandir inauguration and reached an all-time high.
More examples of such misreporting related the farmers’ protest can be found here and here.
It is worth noting that during the farmers’ movement of 2020–21, too, several mainstream television channels faced sustained criticism over their coverage, including banners at protest sites slamming Godi Media. Farmers accused sections of the media of portraying the agitation as foreign-funded or sympathetic to Khalistani groups rather than engaging with their demands. However, the scale and frequency of confrontations witnessed during the CJP-led protests appear significantly greater than what was seen during the farmers’ movement.

A second, related failure is the normalization of communal debates on prime-time shows. On almost a daily basis, senior journalists anchor panel debates that are structured for conflict, with the hosts allowing and sometimes encouraging inflammatory rhetoric against minorities, because it drives engagement.

The cumulative effect is to cloak hate-mongering as news content night after night. Several prominent channels have faced punitive action in the last few years for peddling communal propaganda on shows hosted by ‘star’ anchors. Related reports by Alt News can be found here, here, here, here and here.
After Operation Sindoor, when several mainstream channels aired unverified and absurd claims, including reports that India had attacked Karachi, the BJP’s official X handle shared a monologue by anchor Sushant Sinha defending the media’s coverage as part of a broader “information war” in national interest.

— BJP (@BJP4India) May 14, 2025
There could be no clearer indicator of the alignment of the mainstream media with the BJP government.
In a functional democracy, the public square is a space that should be open to everyone, equally, without fear, intimidation or violence. Whether that principle still holds in India is increasingly open to question. If sections of society — minorities, independent journalists and critics of the government — cannot live and function without fear of harassment, vilification or even incarceration, the mainstream media has played a significant role in creating and reinforcing that climate. And there appear to be few meaningful avenues for holding these media organisations accountable.
Structural Questions: The Nexus among Media, Corporate Power & the BJP Government
Structural factors help explain this pattern. Both the ownership and revenue models of India’s mainstream media organisations constrain their capacity for critical journalism. Several major outlets — including NDTV, IANS and News18 — are owned by large business conglomerates such as the Adani and Ambani groups, which have close ties to the Union Government.
The journalism produced by these organisations reflects those ties, more often than not. Television news, being capital-intensive, is also heavily dependent on government advertising and large corporate advertisers, who are often reluctant to fund critical journalism.
The incentive to toe the government line shows up not always as an explicit directive but more as a pattern of editorial choices: Aggressive coverage of opposition-ruled states, muted coverage of the same failures under the Union government or in BJP-ruled states; extensive coverage of minor opposition controversies, minimal coverage of major stories embarrassing to the ruling party. See here, here and here.
The closeness between media and corporate power was captured vividly when India Today anchor Rahul Kanwal was filmed tasting food meant for elephants at the Ambanis’ Vantara animal sanctuary, alongside Anant Ambani. For many viewers, the spectacle reinforced the perception of a media establishment more comfortable warming up to power than challenging it.
This was in March 2024. Exactly one year later, Vantara was in the news again. This time, after a South African wildlife coalition urged its government to investigate the transfer of wild animals to the Reliance-owned facility. A handful of Indian outlets reported the concerns, but within days, many of them took down their reports, leaving readers with ‘Error 404’ or ‘Page Not Found’ messages. The reasons for the removals remained unexplained. At least three media houses told Alt News that they had received threatening calls or emails.
In 2018, ABP News managing editor Milind Khandekar and anchor Punya Prasun Bajpai resigned after Bajpai’s show ‘Masterstroke’ fact-checked a claim made during a public interaction involving Prime Minister Modi. Chandramani Kaushik, a farmer from Chhattisgarh, had told Modi her income had doubled after she switched from paddy cultivation to processing custard apple. When ABP interviewed her, she said she had been coached by officials to make the claim. Senior anchor Abhisar Sharma was taken off air days later after e juxtaposed a Modi speech in Lucknow praising Uttar Pradesh’s improved law-and-order record with a shootout in the state on the same day.
Efforts to counter this nexus have had limited success. The Independent and Public-Spirited Media Foundation (IPSMF), set up with funding from Azim Premji and Nandan Nilekani to support independent journalism, has faced funding constraints in recent years and has been the subject of income tax investigations.
These dynamics are reflected in India’s global press freedom rankings, which have declined in the last two decades.
Reporters, like people in every other field of work, must be able to do their job without harassment or fear of violence. And physical retaliation can not become an acceptable response to disliked coverage. Once it is, it can easily be turned against any journalist doing legitimate reporting — not only those seen as compromised. But condemning those attacks should not foreclose an examination of the reasons behind the hostility.
The chants of ‘Godi Media Haye Haye’ were directed not merely at individual reporters standing in front of television cameras, but at institutions that many protesters believe have repeatedly failed to hold those in power accountable. Whether or not that perception is fair, the scenes from Delhi point to a widening gap between a section of India’s youth and parts of the country’s mainstream television news industry — a gap that did not emerge overnight, and is unlikely to close soon.

Family pleads for help amid claims son of Saudi 'oil king' tortured after trip to Australia
The last time Mira Lozi spoke to her husband, Rami Naimi, as a free man was nine years ago, as he was wrapping up a trip to Australia.
"He was extremely happy; he was on a high. Then he just disappeared," Ms Lozi said as she fought back tears. "Our life [has been] completely in a shambles since then."
It was November 2017, and Mr Naimi had been travelling with his father Ali al-Naimi, a former Saudi Arabian oil minister and head of the state oil company, Aramco, who was doing a book tour in Australia after releasing his memoir.
For two decades, Mr Naimi senior was responsible for the policy of the world's largest oil exporter, and was often lauded as the "oil king".
His son was an international businessman and father-of-three, who had settled in London with his family and become a UK resident.
After the book tour, Mr Naimi, then 51, departed Sydney to return home, but never made it to Heathrow Airport.
It took several weeks for his wife to start to piece together what happened after he boarded that flight. She described what she managed to find out as a "horror story".
Ms Lozi said during a routine transit through Dubai Airport, her husband was stopped by border officials, driven to the neighbouring emirate of Abu Dhabi, then flown by private jet to the Saudi Arabian capital Riyadh.
He was then detained at the five-star Ritz-Carlton Hotel during the infamous round-up of 400 of the kingdom's powerful people in a so-called anti-corruption sweep, ordered by Mohammed bin Salman, who had become Saudi Arabia's crown prince — the country's most powerful political role — earlier that year.
The luxury hotel in Riyadh has gained a notorious reputation at the time for the torture and interrogations that took place there.
"The biggest question. Why? Maybe a proxy for his dad, maybe a mis-identification; we have absolutely no idea why Rami was targeted," Ms Lozi said.
"There was the crackdown and he got taken a few days later, but why would he be part of it, if it was anti-corruption? He's not corrupted.
"My husband is not a politician, not a human rights [activist]; he was just an ordinary businessman coming back from Australia."
Claims of interrogation and torture inside five-star hotel
Mr Naimi's family claims he was imprisoned, interrogated, electrocuted and waterboarded by Saudi operatives inside the hotel for the next two months, then released but not allowed to leave the kingdom.
"I was 12 years old and I'm sure you can imagine what it's like to know those kind of things at 12 years old. You have to grow up very quickly," Rami's son Ali Naimi, now aged 21, said.
"It really is something out of a movie. It's shocking and we just want to end this nightmare. It's time to bring my father home."
Over the next nine years, Mr Naimi's loved ones say he has been imprisoned twice, forced to hand over his life savings, tried in secret, and constantly watched by authorities.
Any phone calls they have had with him have been short and monitored.
They say they were advised to keep the ongoing ordeal under the radar to maximise their chances of securing his freedom thorough private and diplomatic channels.
But with no progress, they decided to go public in London this week, with a media and social media campaign alongside their legal team, led by high-profile human rights barrister Caoilfhionn Gallagher KC.
"We simply don't know why Rami was taken, and from 2017 until early 2025 there were no charges whatsoever, no due process, nothing, so this was a completely off grid, non rule-of-law compliant kidnapping," Ms Gallagher said.
"What we can say is Rami's been held for nine years unfairly, unlawfully, and that the charges which have resulted have been unfair, unlawful, in violation of international law."
Charged after seven years
Last year, Saudi officials charged Mr Naimi with exploiting his father's official influence. It was alleged that, acting as agent for a US company in the kingdom, he helped the company secure a contract with Aramco.
It is a charge Mr Naimi strenuously denied. He was tried in a closed court and sentenced to six years behind bars, but has so far been allowed to stay out of prison wearing an electronic tag.
He is living with his father who is now in his 90s, seriously ill and bed-bound. Mr Naimi was also accused of following social media accounts "hostile" to Saudi Arabia and attempting to leave the kingdom without permission.
Those charges are still before the courts.
"He's an honest man and all these allegations against him are completely trumped up and false," Ali said.
"We come from a hard-working background, and he's just an ordinary businessman; he's not part of the Saudi elite, he was not an activist, he's not a politician, and he shouldn't be held against his will just because of who his father is.
"But my grandfather was very respected during his time as minister and as the head of Aramco … we know that he's also done nothing wrong."
The family are concerned that Saudi Arabia, which was long among the world's most secretive countries, is now positioning itself as a luxury tourism destination. They say it is not safe to travel there.
The Saudi Arabian government did not respond to the ABC's questions about Mr Naimi's case.
Speaking out
The decision to go public with the #BRINGRAMIHOME campaign was a difficult one for his loved ones, but they decided it was time after suffering another blow two months ago, when Ms Lozi was diagnosed with cancer.
"I never wanted to launch this campaign, but I'm doing this as a last resort because after nine years of trying quietly to bring my husband home he is still being held against his own will," she said.
"I guess now that I got diagnosed with cancer, I mean, there's not much to lose, right? My kids need their father back … and the world needs to know what happened to Rami. Enough is enough."
They decided not tell Mr Naimi, now 60, about the campaign in case doing so put him in more danger.
"No family should go through this, and any family making a decision like this has got to be supported by their government," Ms Gallagher said.
Mr Naimi is not a British national so he does not qualify for consular assistance from the UK's Foreign Office.
However, Ms Gallagher said the government should "show leadership" on this case because Mr Naimi's wife and three children are British, and London is an international city.
The human rights lawyer has requested meetings with new British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband in the hope they will put pressure on Saudi Arabia to send Mr Naimi home.
"It's entirely a political decision to support a British family in this situation," she said.
"We've seen other families in that situation helped, for example, the Hamas hostages were British family members, but those detained were not British. So they've helped in other situations. Why not here?"
The family's local MP, Joe Powell, has said he would do whatever he could to help.
"I look forward to working with the government to resolve this issue quickly and bring Rami home," he wrote in a social media post after meeting with the Naimi family.
Ms Gallagher's team is also lobbying officials in Malta where he has citizenship, the US where he did business, the European Union, and the United Nations.
A spokesperson for the EU told the ABC its diplomats in Riyadh, London and Brussels had been following Mr Naimi's case and had made contact with his lawyers as well as Maltese authorities.
The spokesperson added that the EU, "underlines the importance of procedural fairness, transparency, and respect for applicable international obligations".
The UN Human Rights office said it was "aware of" Mr Naimi's case, and that "reports of such cases in the region" had been brought to its attention in the past.

Zverev through to third Grand Slam final in a row
- Published
Alexander Zverev beat Karen Khachanov at the US Open to reach a third Grand Slam final in a row and continue his bid for a second major of the year.
The top seed put in a commanding performance to beat the Russian 6-3 7-6 (9-7) 7-6 (8-6).
Germany's Zverev is the favourite in New York after ending his long wait for a Grand Slam title with his French Open triumph in June.
He reached the Wimbledon final in July, losing in four sets to world number one Jannik Sinner.
The 29-year-old will play either eighth seed Ben Shelton or 11th seed Frances Tiafoe in Sunday's showpiece, with the two Americans set to meet in Friday's night session.
"I think it [Sunday] will be incredibly special especially, these two guys are crowd favourites and everyone loves them," said Zverev.
"Tonight will be an epic semi-final and I am looking forward to watching it. Hopefully I can not make their American dream come true."
With Sinner and defending US Open champion Carlos Alcaraz suffering with injuries this year, Zverev has found a consistency that has allowed him to reach all four Grand Slam semi-finals.
He started off the tournament in New York slowly, being taken to five sets in his opening two matches, but has not dropped a set since.
Zverev faced brief moments of pressure against world number 50 Khachanov, saving two set points in the third set, but otherwise remained in control.
"After the second round, at about 3am I was sitting with my team in the locker room and we were laughing at how bad I was playing," Zverev said.
"That sense of humour helped me. I obviously have improved a bit otherwise I would not be in the US Open final."
Zverev won 13 of 15 points behind his first serve and all nine points at the net in the first set as he broke Khachanov to go 5-3 up before serving out the opener.
Khachanov fought back after going a break down early in the second set and forced a tie-break, saving set point with a magnificent backhand to polish off a 22-shot rally.
In a pivotal point of the match, it was Zverev who took the initiative to earn another set point, converting it as he outlasted Khachanov in a draining rally with some magnificent defence from the baseline.
In the third set, both players remained on serve without conceding a single break point to reach another tie-break.
It was Khachanov who settled quickest into the tie-break, opening up a lead and creating two set points - both of which were saved by Zverev.
From there the top seed never looked back, ultimately clinching victory as Khachanov put a forehand long.
After reaching his sixth major final, Zverev stood arms wide in celebration facing his coaching team, before going to the net to shake hands with Khachanov.
Victory means Zverev is into his second US Open final after suffering a heartbreaking five-set loss to Dominic Thiem in 2020.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Russia President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping, Iran President Masoud Pezeshkian (PTI Image)
NEW DELHI: India hosted the 18th Brics Summit in New Delhi on September 12-13, bringing together leaders of the expanded 11-member grouping for discussions on global conflicts, terrorism, trade, energy, technology, climate change and reform of international institutions. India used its 2026 chairship to push a people-centric agenda centred on resilience, innovation, cooperation and sustainability.The summit was marked by high-level bilateral meetings, visible displays of bonhomie among leaders and efforts to bridge differences over the conflicts in West Asia and the Black Sea region. PM Modi held separate meetings with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, while leaders also participated in the Brics Business Forum and other summit engagements.From PM Modi and Putin travelling together by car inside the Bharat Mandapam complex to PM Modi and Xi sharing warm moments and the leaders participating in a gala dinner and cultural engagements, the summit combined diplomacy with symbols of Brics unity.The summit culminated in the adoption of the New Delhi Declaration, a 45-page document containing 140 points that brings together the grouping's positions on terrorism, unilateral military action, West Asia, global governance, trade, sanctions, energy, finance and development.
PM Modi-Xi bilateral: Boundary question and reset in ties
PM Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping held a bilateral meeting on the sidelines of the summit, with both sides stressing the importance of viewing India-China relations from a strategic and long-term perspective.The two leaders committed to seeking a fair, reasonable and mutually acceptable solution to the boundary question. PM Modi stressed that differences should not become disputes and highlighted the importance of mutual respect, mutual sensitivity and mutual interest.The discussions also covered peace and tranquillity along the border, economic relations, trade imbalances, supply chains and people-to-people exchanges. The meeting came as New Delhi and Beijing seek to stabilise bilateral ties while continuing to manage differences over the boundary.The Modi-Xi meeting was one of the summit's most closely watched engagements, given the strategic importance of India-China relations and their simultaneous participation in an expanded Brics framework.
PM Modi-Putin meeting: Ukraine, West Asia and $100 billion trade target
PM Modi held an over 45-minute bilateral meeting with Putin on the eve of the summit, reviewing the India-Russia strategic partnership and discussing regional and global developments.The two leaders discussed the impact of the Russia-Ukraine conflict and the West Asia crisis on maritime trade and the safety and security of Indian seafarers. PM Modi reiterated that dialogue and diplomacy remained the way forward in resolving conflicts and said India was ready to contribute to peace efforts.Five Indian seafarers have died in the Black Sea amid the Russia-Ukraine hostilities, making maritime safety an important concern for New Delhi.The two sides also discussed defence, energy, critical minerals, civil nuclear cooperation, fertilisers, infrastructure, technology and industrial cooperation. India and Russia agreed to work towards taking bilateral trade to $100 billion by 2030.Putin also invited PM Modi to Russia for the 24th India-Russia Annual Summit. The dates will be finalised through diplomatic channels.
Car diplomacy: PM Modi and Putin travel together
After their bilateral meeting, PM Modi and Putin travelled together in the same car inside the Bharat Mandapam complex before attending the Brics Business Forum.The unusual visual quickly became one of the defining moments of the summit, highlighting the close nature of the India-Russia relationship amid continuing geopolitical pressure on Moscow and India's effort to maintain strategic autonomy.PM Modi later highlighted the growing India-Russia economic relationship, including the participation of companies from both countries at the INNOPROM industrial exhibition held at Bharat Mandapam.
PM Modi presented Putin with a Russian translation of the Thirukkural, the classical Tamil work attributed to poet-saint Thiruvalluvar."Two thousand years ago, Thiruvalluvar wrote the Thirukkural. It includes the entire gamut of human life. It has been translated into the Russian language. I am confident that the people-to-people contact will increase with the translation of the Thirukkural into Russian, which will play a big role in strengthening our relations," Modi told Putin.The gift was presented as a cultural bridge between India and Russia and reflected the emphasis placed by India on people-to-people links during its Brics chairship.
PM Modi-Pezeshkian talks: West Asia and regional peace
PM Modi met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on the sidelines of the summit, with the two leaders discussing India-Iran relations, Brics cooperation and the conflict in West Asia.PM Modi reiterated India's position that disputes must be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy and stressed the need for lasting peace and stability in the region.The discussions also covered freedom of navigation and commerce and the safety and well-being of seafarers, issues that have acquired greater importance amid disruption to shipping routes in the region.The meeting followed the leaders' earlier interaction on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation Summit in Bishkek. India also stressed the importance of expanding bilateral trade channels and pursuing a long-term and mutually beneficial relationship with Iran.
PM Modi, Xi, Putin and leaders showcase Brics unity
The summit was accompanied by a series of high-profile visuals showing leaders of the expanded grouping interacting informally.PM Modi was seen greeting Putin and Xi together, holding their hands and sharing smiles. In another visual, Modi walked alongside Putin, Xi and Pezeshkian.PM Modi was also seen holding hands and walking alongside Pezeshkian and other leaders during the Brics Business Forum. The images were widely seen as a demonstration of the grouping's effort to project unity despite differences among members on major geopolitical issues.The presence of leaders from Russia, China, Iran, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Brazil, South Africa and other member states underscored the diversity of interests represented within the expanded grouping.
Gala dinner: Leaders gather for cultural evening
The Brics leaders also attended a gala dinner hosted during the summit, providing an informal setting for interactions between heads of government and state.The cultural programme and dinner formed part of India's effort to showcase its heritage alongside the formal diplomatic agenda. The event brought together leaders who had spent the summit discussing contentious issues ranging from wars and terrorism to trade and global governance.The informal interactions added a softer dimension to a summit otherwise dominated by difficult geopolitical negotiations.
Banyan tree plantation: Symbol of Brics unity
A symbolic tree plantation ceremony was also organised during the summit, with Brics leaders participating in the planting of a Banyan tree.The Banyan tree, known for its extensive roots and interconnected branches, was presented as a symbol of continuity, resilience and interconnectedness. The gesture complemented India's 2026 Brics theme of "Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability".The plantation also reflected India's attempt to connect the summit's diplomatic agenda with sustainability and environmental cooperation.
Brics Business Forum: Trade, investment and technology
The Brics Business Forum brought together heads of state, ministers and business leaders to discuss trade, investment, finance, technology and development.PM Modi highlighted the economic weight of the expanded grouping, saying:"Today, BRICS nations represent 50 per cent of the world's population, 40 per cent of its GDP, and over 25 per cent of global trade. Moreover, while global GDP has grown approximately two-and-a-half-fold over these years, the combined GDP of BRICS nations has expanded nearly four-and-a-half-fold. In other words, the economic strength of BRICS has grown at nearly twice the pace of the rest of the world.""The growing scale, speed, and optimism of BRICS are clearly evident among us. This forum, hosted in India, is the largest BRICS Business Forum to date," the Prime Minister added.Pezeshkian called for Brics to convert its economic potential into practical cooperation through trade, investment and joint financing."We believe that the true strength of BRICS is not confined merely to the size of its members' economies; rather, it becomes more apparent when these capacities are transformed into a network of trade, investment and joint financing – a transition from potential cooperation to operational one," he said.Putin stressed the importance of business-to-business relations and economic partnerships, arguing that they could help create more resilient international economic relations.
Putin attacks trade restrictions, backs new growth platform
At the Business Forum, Putin criticised what he described as attempts by Western competitors to regain their former economic leadership."We have always been told that competition is a sacred cow, something that must not be touched," Putin told a BRICS business forum event. "Yet, unfortunately, today your Western competitors are trying by any means necessary to regain their former leadership.""This competition is sometimes assuming unsightly forms," he said. "They even include direct physical attacks or the destruction of industrial and logistical facilities, pipelines, and so forth."Putin also criticised restrictions on international transport corridors, shipping and trade and called for Brics to contribute to building "a new, sustainable platform for global growth".
India-Russia economic partnership gets push
The summit also provided an opportunity for India and Russia to discuss expanding economic cooperation amid Western sanctions and geopolitical uncertainty.The two countries discussed the Programme for Economic Cooperation 2030 and cooperation in infrastructure, energy, technology, defence, critical minerals and civil nuclear energy.The sides also explored industrial cooperation in railways and tunnelling, the steel value chain and greater access to the Russian market for Indian exporters.India continues to maintain strong energy ties with Russia, while seeking to expand trade beyond traditional sectors.
Brics pushes practical cooperation across sectors
India's 2026 chairship focused heavily on converting Brics into a platform for practical cooperation rather than limiting it to political declarations.More than 350 meetings and high-level engagements were organised across approximately 30 cities during India's chairship. These covered political and security cooperation, economic and financial cooperation, and cultural and people-to-people exchanges.PM Modi said: "It gives me immense pleasure to welcome and greet you all to India. India’s BRICS chairmanship is based on a people-centric and humanity-first approach. Resilience, innovation, cooperation, and sustainability have been our priorities.""Alongside these priorities, we have placed special emphasis on connecting BRICS cooperation with the common people. With this vision in mind, more than 350 meetings were organised. We had the opportunity to welcome your teams to approximately 30 cities..."
Agriculture: Digital farming and climate resilience
Brics countries agreed on new mechanisms to strengthen agricultural cooperation.These include Centres of Excellence on agro-ecology for research and knowledge sharing on natural, organic and regenerative farming, a Brics Network on Digital Agriculture using artificial intelligence, geospatial intelligence, IoT-enabled monitoring and advanced data analytics, and BRICS AGRIN, a voluntary framework covering agricultural inputs, seeds and genetic resources.The initiatives seek to promote climate-resilient farming and greater technology-driven cooperation among member countries.
Health: Lifestyle, traditional medicine and mental health
The Brics Mission for Healthy Lifestyle was launched along with a roadmap for joint cooperation for 2026-2029, focusing on preventive approaches to obesity and other non-communicable diseases.Members also agreed to establish an Expert Working Group on Traditional, Complementary and Integrative Medicine, covering research, evidence generation, academic exchange, quality standards and protection of traditional knowledge.Mental health cooperation was also strengthened through the Brics Training Hub Network and Network of Centres of Excellence, with NIMHANS India as the coordinating centre.
Energy: Smart grids and storage
Brics adopted guiding principles on energy storage and smart grids and launched a Digital Centre of Excellence for Smart Grids and Energy Storage.The initiative will provide a platform for knowledge sharing, capacity building, policy and regulatory cooperation and pilot projects among member countries.The summit also placed emphasis on energy security, diversified energy sources and equitable energy transitions.
MSMEs and startups: New platforms for businesses
India pushed stronger cooperation for micro, small and medium enterprises and startups.The Brics MSME Cooperation Portal will connect MSMEs, technology centres, trade associations, financial institutions and policymakers across member countries.A Brics Incubator Network will connect startups with incubators in other member countries, while the Brics Startup Innovation Fund is intended to support early and growth-stage startups.
Logistics and global supply chains
Brics members agreed on a Logistics Supply-Chain Cooperation Framework aimed at improving resilience, sustainability and connectivity.The grouping also advanced cooperation on global value chains through the GVC Action Plan 2026-2030, including a Technical Council and joint study.The initiatives are intended to reduce vulnerabilities caused by fragmented supply chains, improve connectivity and promote economic diversification.
Urban mobility and climate-resilient infrastructure
The summit also advanced cooperation on sustainable urban development.A Brics Urban Mobility Hub was established as a platform for technical cooperation and knowledge sharing. Members also adopted voluntary principles on climate-resilient urban infrastructure.An Urban Research and Knowledge Network was established to facilitate cross-border research, peer learning and institutional cooperation.
Skilling, youth and sports technology
India also advanced cooperation on skills and employment through BRICS CONNECT, a voluntary network covering capacity building, social security, women's workforce participation, employability and digital public infrastructure.The Brics Youth Cooperation Framework 2026 was adopted to provide greater continuity and structure to youth cooperation.Sports technology cooperation was institutionalised through a working group focusing on technical information, research, institutional experience and best practices.
Science and research cooperation
The Brics Science and Research Repository was welcomed as a structured platform for sharing scientific knowledge among member countries.The initiative is intended to strengthen research collaboration and facilitate greater exchange of scientific information across the expanded grouping.
Brics 2026: A wider and more diverse grouping
Brics currently comprises 11 countries: Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and the UAE.The expansion has significantly widened the grouping's geographical reach across Asia, Africa, the Middle East and Latin America. It has also brought together countries with different political systems, economic priorities and positions on major international conflicts.India's chairship therefore focused not only on expanding cooperation but also on finding consensus among members with competing interests.
New Delhi Declaration: Key outcomes
The summit concluded with the adoption of the New Delhi Declaration 2026, following intensive negotiations among members. The 45-page declaration contains 140 points and represents India's central diplomatic outcome from its 2026 chairship.The declaration addresses terrorism, conflicts, global governance, trade, sanctions, energy, finance, development and the interests of the Global South.
Terrorism: Pahalgam attack explicitly condemned
The declaration strongly condemns terrorism in all its forms and manifestations and calls for "zero tolerance for terrorism".It specifically condemns the April 22, 2025, Pahalgam terrorist attack, in which 26 people were killed. The declaration also condemns cross-border movement of terrorists, terrorism financing and safe havens.Brics reaffirmed that terrorism cannot be associated with any religion, nationality, civilisation or ethnic group and called for those involved in terrorist activities and their support to be held accountable.The grouping also called for progress towards the adoption of the Comprehensive Convention on International Terrorism under the UN framework.
West Asia: Ceasefire, diplomacy and two-state solution
The declaration expresses deep concern over the continuing escalation in West Asia and calls on all parties to exercise maximum restraint.It stresses dialogue, consultation and diplomacy as the means to address conflicts and calls for the protection of civilians and humanitarian assistance.On Gaza, Brics called for the upholding of a ceasefire, unhindered humanitarian aid and an end to forced displacement of Palestinians. It reaffirmed support for a two-state solution based on the internationally recognised 1967 borders.
Unilateral war condemned
The declaration condemns unilateral military action without naming any country.The language assumes significance because Brics includes members with differing positions on the major conflicts in West Asia and the wider international system.The consensus was reached after negotiations continued into the early hours of Saturday, with India working to bridge differences between members and produce a common position.
UN reform and greater Global South representation
Brics reaffirmed its support for comprehensive reform of the United Nations, including the Security Council.The grouping called for greater representation of developing countries in global decision-making and a more democratic, representative and inclusive international system.China and Russia reiterated support for the aspirations of India and Brazil to play a greater role in the UN, including the Security Council.
Trade: Opposition to tariffs and protectionism
The declaration expresses concern over unilateral tariff and non-tariff measures that distort international trade and create uncertainty for businesses and supply chains.Brics reaffirmed support for a rules-based multilateral trading system centred on the World Trade Organization.The grouping also called for the restoration of a fully functioning two-tier binding WTO dispute settlement mechanism.
Brics voiced opposition to unilateral coercive measures that it considers inconsistent with international law and the principles of the UN Charter.The declaration calls for such measures to be eliminated and highlights their impact on international economic relations.The position reflects a longstanding Brics push for a more balanced international economic and political order.
Local currencies and cross-border payments
The declaration supports greater use of local currencies in cross-border payments and trade settlements among Brics countries.Members acknowledged ongoing work on interoperability between payment and messaging systems and efforts to facilitate trade settlements and investment in local currencies.The initiative forms part of the wider Brics effort to strengthen financial resilience and cooperation.
Energy security and transition
The declaration calls for stronger energy security through diversified energy sources, resilient infrastructure and stable markets.It also supports just, orderly, equitable and inclusive energy transitions while recognising the differing circumstances and priorities of member countries.Brics backed cooperation involving renewables, nuclear energy, hydropower, hydrogen, fossil fuels and other low-carbon technologies.
Women and inclusive development
The declaration recognises women as leaders, decision-makers and drivers of economic growth and social transformation.It highlights women's participation in governance, entrepreneurship, employment and peacebuilding and calls for greater financial and digital inclusion.The grouping also emphasised skills development and access to productive and social services.
Tackling organised crime and illicit financial flows
Brics expressed concern over illicit financial flows linked to drug trafficking, firearms trafficking, terrorism financing, human trafficking and organised crime.The grouping called for stronger cooperation between member countries to trace and disrupt criminal proceeds and tackle transnational criminal networks.
The larger message from New Delhi
The New Delhi Declaration combines a strong political message on terrorism, unilateral military action, West Asia and global governance with a broad economic and development agenda.
For India, the outcome represents an effort to demonstrate that the expanded Brics can reach consensus despite major geopolitical differences. The declaration also places India's priorities of resilience, innovation, cooperation and sustainability at the centre of a wider agenda covering trade, technology, energy, health, agriculture, finance and development.The summit therefore ended with two parallel messages: Brics wants a stronger collective voice in global affairs, while India wants that voice translated into practical cooperation that reaches businesses, communities and ordinary people.

Donald Trump and Pete Hegseth used remarks at the memorial ceremony marking the 25th anniversary of 9/11 to defend the US-Israel war on Iran – and suggest the controversial conflict was part of the legacy of the worst terrorist attack in US history.
While such ceremonies on September 11 typically focus on the victims of the 2001 attacks, the US president and his defense secretary each pointed to the war they launched on Iran more than six months ago, with no end in sight.
“We salute every member of the United States military who served in the ‘war on terror’,” Trump said at the Pentagon, which was struck by a hijacked airliner, killing all 64 people onboard and 125 inside the building. “And we salute the service members working right now to ensure the world’s number one sponsor of terror, the Islamic Republic of Iran, will never ever have a nuclear weapon.”
The US president’s decision to stay in Washington has drawn criticism, while his vice‑president, JD Vance, traveled to New York for a memorial at Ground Zero, the site of the World Trade Center’s destruction on 9/11.
Closing out his speech, Trump also tried to draw a direct link between his war on Iran – which is vastly unpopular in the US, according to opinion polls – and the 9/11 terror attacks.
“Today we renew the sacred oath that we first swore in their names a quarter of a century ago. We will never, ever forget,” he said. “That’s why we fight today. We don’t have a choice. There can only be victory. We fight hard. We fight to win.”
Earlier, Hegseth, the US defense secretary, delivered a bellicose speech at the somber memorial. Noting that the Iran war was part of the fight against an “Islamic theocracy that has wished us death for nearly half a century”, he claimed that Iran’s defenses “are gone”, despite evidence to the contrary.
“We’re still sending terrorists where they belong – to hell,” declared Hegseth. “And tankers to the bottom of the ocean where they belong, and we are ensuring that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon. The economic pressure tightens every day.”
Hegseth said at the ceremony: “The struggle against evil continued, and it continues now. It will continue until judgment day. Our only answer here on Earth is eternal vigilance.”
He also claimed the threat extended into US borders, warning that “enemies plot to curb our power and kill our citizens, including from Islamic terrorists abroad and at home”.
Hegseth went on to credit Trump with dismantling Iran’s military capabilities, and closed by calling for a new generation of “strong, brave warriors who will say when it matters most, ‘send me’”.
Separately, during the New York City ceremony, the leader of one group of 9/11 victims’ families pleaded with the Trump administration to hold Saudi Arabia accountable for its alleged support of the terrorists who carried out the attacks.
“It has been one betrayal after another. President Trump can still change that,” said Terry Strada, a widow of one of the victims. “Tell the Saudis to stop lying. Tell them that if they want to be friends with the USA, they cannot continue to deny all of this – all of the pain, all of the destruction that we have all been suffering through.”

Chelsea agree £47.1m move for Monaco's Camara
- Published
Chelsea have agreed a £47.1m deal to sign Monaco midfielder Lamine Camara.
The 22-year-old is set to undergo a medical after Chelsea complete the sale of Enzo Fernandez to Manchester City in a deal that matched the £125m British transfer record.
Chelsea had been reluctant to complete a transfer for Monaco's asking price but they are believed to have dropped their demands when striker Folarin Balogun's move to Everton from the French club came into renewed doubt.
It was expected the Blues would continue with their current midfielder options despite sanctioning Fernandez's exit but an opportunity to sign one of their primary targets at a lower price was taken up.
They had also held talks with Roma's Manu Kone and another unnamed Premier League option.
The signing is not viewed as a like-for-like replacement for Fernandez, with Camara offering a different profile in midfield. However, Chelsea believe the deal will help maintain the strength of new manager Xabi Alonso's squad.
One of the club's aims this summer was to emerge from the transfer window with a stronger squad despite selling Fernandez to a direct rival.
Chelsea believe they have achieved that after signing Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa in a club-record £117m deal, centre-back Maxence Lacroix from Crystal Palace and, most recently, goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez from Aston Villa.
The club have also recruited strikers Emmanuel Emegha and Danny Welbeck, winger Geovany Quenda, midfielders Jordan Henderson and Valentin Barco, as well as full-backs Marco Palestra and Pep Chavarria.
Alonso's side have won all three of their matches this season, beating Fulham and Brighton in the Premier League, and have also reached the third round of the Carabao Cup with victory over Luton Town.

Geneva 17 October 2024 – This afternoon, His Excellency Mr Jérôme Bonnafont, Permanent Representative of France to the United Nations in Geneva, and WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus met in the WHO headquarters for the signing of seven contribution agreements.
The contribution totalling €24 million comes through the Ministry of Europe & Foreign Affairs. It fits in the France–WHO Framework Agreement for 2020 to 2025, which provides both a strategic framework for engagement, aligned with WHO priorities, while providing legal, administrative and financial instruments for operationalizing collaboration.
This latest contribution includes a generous €4.5 million in fully flexible voluntary funds for the Core Voluntary Contributions Account (CVCA).
Additionally, France will support key areas of WHO’s work, addressing some of the most pressing health challenges, including non-communicable diseases (NCDs), urban health labs, One Health, funding for the WHO Contingency Fund for Emergencies (CFE), and several emergencies, such as the WHO response in Gaza, response to cholera outbreaks and mental health support in Ukraine.
France will also continue to support the WHO emergencies centre in Lyon which is playing a crucial role in preparedness and response to epidemics.
Ambassador Jérôme Bonnafont underscored the importance of this collaboration: “France remains deeply committed to supporting the World Health Organization in its efforts to tackle critical global health challenges. These agreements reflect our shared priorities of promoting health equity, responding to emergencies, and strengthening healthcare systems worldwide.”
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of WHO, expressed his gratitude, stating, “We are immensely grateful to the French Government for its steadfast support to WHO, continued partnership and leadership in global health. This contribution will enable us to address key health threats, from non-communicable diseases to emergency response, helping to save lives and protect the most vulnerable populations.”
France is a strong supporter of a fully and flexibly financed WHO, providing leadership and support to the increase of assessed contributions to the Organization. France is also one of the co-hosts to WHO’s first Investment Round towards the mobilization of predictable and flexible resources for WHO’s core work on the Fourteenth General Programme of Work (2025–2028), approved by the World Health Assembly in 2024.
This signing ceremony marks another milestone in the strong and longstanding partnership between WHO and France, reinforcing their joint commitment to a healthier, safer world.

There have been scenes of mayhem across Sydney's west, with a carjacking, collision and stabbing after a motorist drove into oncoming traffic on a busy motorway with two children on board.
Police were called to carry out a welfare check on a 36-year-old driver in Belmore, but began a pursuit after he refused to pull over.
"When the driver allegedly failed to stop as directed, a police pursuit was initiated," NSW Police said in a statement.
"The pursuit continued into Auburn before it was terminated due to the manner of the man's driving."
Police said the man then drove on the wrong side of the M4 Motorway before hitting an oncoming vehicle.
He then got out of the car with the two children and allegedly tried to steal a car.
A 25-year-old man intervened and during a scuffle suffered a stab wound to his hand.
The offender, police allege, then stole the vehicle of a woman who had stopped to help before bundling the two children into her car and speeding off westbound along the M4 Motorway.
He stopped on the Cumberland Highway at Wentworthville and was arrested by an off-duty police officer with help from bystanders.
He was taken to hospital under police guard.
The children suffered minor injuries and were taken to Westmead Children's Hospital as a precaution.
Police are still waiting to interview the man as they piece together what has happened.

In an interview with India Today, former Indian Ambassador to China Ashok Kantha analyzed the state of India-China relations following the meeting between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Xi Jinping on the margins of the BRICS summit in New Delhi. Kantha characterized the diplomatic interaction as an incremental and calibrated process, stating, "we cannot rush into any kind of reset in relations." He emphasized that any continued progress toward normalization remains dependent on maintaining peace and tranquility along the border areas. Kantha highlighted critical structural issues between both nations, including trade deficits, terms of economic engagement, Chinese support to Pakistan during Operation Sindoor, and the mega hydropower project at Medog in Tibet. He noted that summit diplomacy alone cannot serve as a panacea, asserting that India must approach Beijing in a realistic and hard-headed manner while addressing core bilateral disputes through perseverance.
A panel of strategic experts debates the state of bilateral relations between India and China following recent high-level engagements. Brahma Chellaney questions the excessive focus on diplomatic handshakes and argues that New Delhi has steadily lost ground, stating, 'India is moving to normalize relations with Beijing largely on China\'s terms.' He highlights the ballooning trade deficit, ongoing Chinese export controls on critical technologies, and the shift from demanding status quo ante to mere peace and tranquility along the Line of Actual Control. Zorawar Daulet Singh contends that sustained contact and detente remain essential for India to safeguard strategic autonomy, manage border friction, and leverage Asia\'s dominant manufacturing powerhouse amidst global fragmentation. Ross Feingold provides perspective from Taiwan on the regional security implications of a potential Sino-Indian rapprochement. The discussion examines whether structural economic asymmetries and unresolved frontier disputes outweigh high-level bilateral summits.
In an interview with India Today, former NITI Aayog CEO and ex-G20 Sherpa Amitabh Kant analyzed the outcomes of the unanimously adopted BRICS Delhi Declaration. He highlighted that reaching consensus sends a strong message against unilateral tariffs, non-tariff barriers, and coercive secondary economic sanctions, which severely impact India and the Global South. Addressing the absence of specific country names in the declaration, Kant noted that multilateral communiqués traditionally maintain diplomatic phrasing while delivering clear signals regarding unpredictable US trade policies. Furthermore, he emphasized that post-World War II global governance institutions like the United Nations, the Security Council, and the World Trade Organization have become irrelevant for emerging economies, necessitating comprehensive reforms. Addressing China's role, Kant observed, "China weaponizes technology," explaining how Beijing dominates clean energy processing and battery manufacturing. He asserted that China must open up and share manufacturing opportunities with fellow BRICS members to build long-term trust and ensure collective economic growth.
A ground report from Malda district in West Bengal reveals severe inundation caused by swelling waters in the River Ganga and Mahananda. Excess water flowing downstream from Uttar Pradesh and Bihar has completely submerged villages along the riverbanks, including Ratanpur in the Ratua gram panchayat, for over ten days. While National Disaster Response Force teams, civil defence units, and Malda police carry out rescue operations using boats, several families and livestock remain stranded amid severe bank erosion. At the Mahananda Tola Swastha Kendra primary health centre, floodwaters have risen over five feet, leaving outdoor facilities submerged and the power supply completely disconnected. Despite pitch darkness and the threat of venomous snakes entering the building at night, medical officer Dr Arijit Sutradhar and health staff remain stationed round the clock to run emergency services, attending to patients who arrive on local country boats.

Here at WIRED we’ve been trying to make sense of at least two incidents in the AI industry this week: First, the major fight over a million-dollar math problem and whether OpenAI surreptitiously borrowed the work of other researchers to solve the problem first. A day later, an Anthropic researcher—who had previously worked at OpenAI—very publicly quit his job, citing concerns about how both companies were handling AI safety. Another technical staffer at Anthropic said in response that people at the company “really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade.” (Note the exclamation point.)
The internet erupted into a debate about whether these fears are very legitimate, totally overblown, part of a regulatory capture strategy, or self-aggrandizement on the part of the AI labs that make the tech. Or some combination thereof.
One prominent technology and AI researcher, Timnit Gebru, has been especially fiery, posting on X and Bluesky about the overlapping ideas and ideologies that she thinks led us to this bizarro moment. Previously, Gebru was most known for her highly publicized departure from Google. Hired in 2018 to evaluate biases within the company’s fast-advancing AI tools, she and her fellow researchers presented a paper on the potential dangers of probabilistic large language models. Google rejected it. Gebru wasn't at the company much longer. She’s written an upcoming book about her experiences, titled Deep Unlearning: The Rise of AI and the Radicalization of a Tech Idealist (expected to ship early next year).
Gebru has many thoughts on the AI-related events of this past week. While her work is essentially rooted in AI safety, she rejects phrases like “safety and alignment” and thinks those who are warning of our impending doom are trying to distract from the actual harms the tech industry might perpetuate.
LAUREN GOODE: What do you think all the attention on the “math fight” says about the current state of AI?
TIMNIT GEBRU: Well, first I would ask, why are they heavily investing in solving math problems? Why are they choosing certain disciplines? Somehow these subjects, like programming and chess and math, were elevated to mean, OK, you solved this and thereby you’ve solved intelligence. It’s so they can say, “We solved it.”
The story that OpenAI wants you to hear is, this AI did this incredible thing, and it’s super intelligent. That’s why they chose math, this open $1 million question. But if it had gone through the whole process by which the math community vets the significance and novelty of claims and who contributed to them, and we had all waited until the dust settled, we would have gotten a better sense of whether OpenAI was framing this breakthrough accurately.
There’s something called the Leiden Declaration that I think is really good, which warns about what happens if the field of mathematics is used by corporations in this way. Policymakers start to rely on press releases and popular media, when they should be talking to mathematicians themselves. The amount of time it takes now to go from companies claiming an AI breakthrough to Bernie Sanders proposing a bill is really short, and that’s not a good thing.
It’s all just cutthroat right now leading up to their IPOs. Generally, researchers are supposed to be collaborative. When I was at Google, we were collaborating with researchers at Microsoft, at Amazon. You do that all the time. Now, the researchers are all frenetic about the problems they think they’re solving because of their pending IPOs.
How do you interpret the resignation of that Anthropic engineer, who’s saying the companies are reckless and gambling with our lives? On the one hand, you seem to agree that the companies are being reckless; on the other hand, you’ve made clear that you think the “AI will cause the end of civilization” debate is senseless.
My whole career, I’ve been trying to say the same thing from different angles. We wrote our stochastic parrot paper in 2021 for this reason. OpenAI had claimed GPT-2 was too powerful to release. It was so hyped up. And we were saying, you’re asking the wrong questions.
In my book I write, “Can a bridge decide to collapse?” The whole “Oh no, our models went rogue” thing … When a bridge collapses, you don’t analyze whether the bridge was ethical or sentient or why it decided to collapse. You ask, who is the person who built this bridge to be so flimsy? There are permits you have to acquire. There are supposed to be tests. When you ask about the bridge collapsing itself, you’ve lost the thread.
Meanwhile, what’s really existential is AI powering autonomous weapons, killing machines, that are actually being used in warfare. The climate catastrophe is a real thing that could be exacerbated by what these tech companies are building. Bosses are using AI as an excuse to get rid of their pesky workers. This machine-god narrative is, in my opinion, meant to distract us from these. The industry has become a mix of cults, a mix of people who are true believers, just like a preacher who says the end times is coming. The singularity has been coming for decades now.
Take me through, step by step, how “AI extinction” might happen, if it were real. I’m thinking of this post where someone said, Does an angry GPU just show up at my house or something?
I can’t really envision it, but a lot of those scenarios seem to be that you ask the machine to optimize for some other task, and then the machine decides that the way to get to that goal is by killing everyone in the world. Does the AI hypnotize you so that you don’t unplug it? I don’t know! Other people say, well, the AI can infect your machines. Yes—and we already have malware, so…
What about floods and fires? What about a major disruption to the global food supply chain? There are real threats coming to us, like people being able to create and use chemical weapons. [Note: Not long after we spoke, Anthropic revealed that it had blocked several potential malicious attempts by scientists to build biological weapons.]
There’s another element where you’re so privileged that you can’t imagine other things harming you. Like if you’re not worried about police brutality, or floods, or warfare—things that can actually kill you—then you can obsess over the machine-god.
Why are we spending so much time talking about this idea of AI that people have been talking about since the ’40s and ’50s? I have this game I play sometimes where I read quotes to people about artificial intelligence that I’ve gathered in my research, and I ask, What decade was this statement made in? Sometimes people get it right, but a lot of times they do not, because it all sounds the same.

The Justice Ministry plans to launch a pilot program to track sex offenders on parole with GPS devices from as early as fiscal 2027, which begins next April.
Justice Minister Hiroshi Hiraguchi told a news conference Friday that expenses related to the pilot program were included in the ministry’s fiscal 2027 budget request.
Only parolees who consent to participate in the program will be monitored with GPS devices, which are not slated to be attached to parolees’ bodies.
“We are thinking of trying a method that can be handled under the current law,” Hiraguchi said.
The offenders rehabilitation law requires parolees to receive guidance and supervision from probation officers and volunteer probation officers. The system is intended to help prevent recidivism and promote rehabilitation by allowing probation officers to provide guidance if signs of possible reoffending are detected.
Under the program, the ministry is considering providing guidance through interviews and other methods if parolees’ location data indicates behavior potentially linked to crime.
The program will be conducted in a way that places as little burden as possible on parolees. The type of GPS device to be used has yet to be decided.
If the program proves effective, it will be implemented on a full scale.
The second Recidivism Prevention Plan, adopted at a cabinet meeting in 2023, states that the government will “consider measures to enhance the treatment of sex offenders,” citing examples of systems introduced in foreign countries.

Other Windows Laptops to Consider
Dell 14 Plus: This laptop sold for hundreds less throughout 2025. And yet, even at around $1,000, I still find it a really solid deal. I do think the XPS 13 is better in a number of ways, especially the display quality and sleek design. However, the extra ports on the Dell 14 Plus are handy, and some may appreciate the slightly larger screen. It also has an upper hand with twice the storage as the Dell XPS 13 and Surface Laptop 7th Edition.
Surface Laptop 7th Edition: I waited a long time for a Windows machine like this Surface Laptop, which came out in 2024—something that could truly compete with the MacBook Air, and it does. The Snapdragon X2 Elite version of the Surface Laptop is available and should provide extra performance. It’s much more expensive at $1,600, which feels overpriced. It occasionally drops to under $1,400, however, which is closer to what the original model sells for. One caveat: You might come across the Surface Laptop 13, which came out in 2025 and is cheaper. I haven't tested that one, but it lacks some of the features I like in the 7th Edition, such as the 3:2 screen.
Lenovo LOQ 15: For many months, the LOQ 15 (8/10, WIRED Recommended) was one of the only gaming laptops under $1,000 that came with an RTX 5060 graphics card. The price has since risen significantly. Yet, it's still a laptop I recommend, as others have also increased in price. And unlike other cheaper gaming laptops, the LOQ 15 has a higher-quality display that's both bright and colorful.
Alienware 15 Gaming Laptop: Speaking of cheaper gaming laptops, the Alienware 15 falls into many of those same traps. It's thick and chunky, yes, but it also has a lower-quality display than you might expect for the price. But it delivers decent performance, has a nice design, and offers the option of an RTX 5050 graphics card. However, the price has gone up by nearly $600.
Surface Pro 12: Unfortunately, if you're looking for a Windows tablet or 2-in-1, your options are slim. There's a newer Surface Pro 13.8 with one of the Snapdragon X2 chips, which are quite expensive. And the detachable keyboard cover (that you should absolutely buy) doesn't come bundled. That's why, at this point, the smaller (and now cheaper) Surface Pro 12 is what most people should buy.
Asus Zenbook S 16: Windows laptops haven't always been known for being lookers. The Asus Zenbook S 16 undoes that stereotype. This thing is absolutely gorgeous, and not in a way that tries to mimic the MacBook. It has its own aesthetic with its white "ceraluminum" material, and I love it. It's also remarkably thin, has an expansive touchpad, and a sharp OLED display—the complete package. The only problem is that the Zenbook S 16 is quite expensive, and prices haven't dropped as much as I hoped. For a smaller model, check out the Zenbook S 14, which is very similar, except it uses an Intel chip instead.
What to Look For in a Windows Laptop
You'll want to read our extensive guide on How to Choose the Right Laptop, but for the basics, decide what category of laptop you need. Most people should buy a 13-inch or 14-inch laptop, and spending around $750 to $1,000 is a good place to start. At this price, you should expect good battery life, a decent screen, solid performance for basic tasks, and a comfortable keyboard and touchpad. You should also expect at least 16 GB of RAM and 512 GB of storage. Anything more than that gets into premium territory where you're paying for higher specs, more performance, or extra features. If you want a discrete GPU for gaming or creative workflows, you'll need to spend more.
A laptop like the Dell 14 Plus is a great example of what you can get in this price range. You can even find laptops with OLED panels and up to one terabyte of storage, depending on how good the discounts are. I would consider anything under $750 a cheap laptop, and it will come with significant compromises, especially in panel and touchpad quality. Fortunately, laptops that use the Qualcomm Snapdragon X chip get great battery life, even when they fall under $750, such as the HP OmniBook 5 14.
Here's a list of important specs to consider:
CPU: Thanks to the huge variety of good chip options, it's never been trickier to buy a laptop. For thin-and-light laptops, I would recommend one of the following chips:
- Qualcomm Snapdragon X, Snapdragon X Plus, or Snapdragon X Elite
- Qualcomm Snapdragon X2, Snapdragon X2 Plus, or Snapdragon X2 Elite
- Intel Core Ultra 225 V or Core Ultra 7 258V
- Intel Core 5 320, Core Ultra 7 365, or Core Ultra X7 358H
There are many variations of these chips, so you'll undoubtedly run across other strings of numbers, especially on the Intel front. But the above is a good place to start. There’s lots more to say in the world of gaming laptops or content creation devices, so make sure to read our full guide to How to Buy a Gaming Laptop.
GPU: As of now, Intel's Panther Lake X7 or X9 chips have the most powerful integrated graphics. You'll find them in laptops like the Dell XPS 14, which can replicate discrete GPU-level performance like the RTX 4050. Unlike many laptops with discrete GPUs, though, Panther Lake X chips offer great battery life, making them better Windows alternatives to the MacBook Pro.
For discrete options, you'll want one of the latest Nvidia RTX 50-series GPUs, such as the RTX 5060. The biggest leap in performance is between the RTX 5070 and the RTX 5070 Ti, which increases VRAM to 12 GB.
RAM (or memory): Stick with at least 16 GB if you can. Since the Copilot+ designation was introduced in 2024, it has become the new standard. You'll even find laptops as cheap as $600 that have 16 GB of memory. Gamers and content creators should upgrade to 32 GB if possible, though the ongoing memory shortage makes this more expensive. There's been a new surge in 8 GB options, such as the Dell XPS 13, but these should be reserved for only light usage.
Storage: Similar to memory, many laptops have moved to 512 GB as the new standard, and you'll find lots of affordable laptops with that as the base configuration. Upgrading to 1 or 2 terabytes, where possible, will make your life that much easier, especially since many laptops don't offer expandable storage.
Display: Laptops are usually categorized by screen size, with 13-inch, 14-inch, and 16-inch being the most common. Consider size, resolution, refresh rate, and panel type.
Portability: Aside from display size, chassis thickness and weight are the main factors, determining how portable a laptop is to travel with. Other dimensions are important too, but more often than not, that is determined by the screen size.
Ports: Many laptops are limited to USB-C and a headphone jack these days, with some exceptions that include USB-A or HDMI. Make sure your laptop has what you need, or you'll need a USB Hub or laptop docking station to add ports or increase external display support.
Windows 11 vs. Windows 10: What Are the Differences?
If you haven't heard, if you're still on Windows 10, you're no longer getting security updates—at least not without paying extra. If you're wondering what to expect in a new laptop that runs Windows 11, here's a breakdown of the major changes:
Interface: The Start Menu is now centered in the Taskbar and looks a bit different. Visually, it's quite different, but it still functions the same, offering you quick access to applications and documents. Beyond the Start Menu, just about every app will have a different visual flair, with rounded corners and a streamlined aesthetic. While you can still do what you could in Windows 10, things like Settings, Notifications, and System Tray will feel different. You'll also find a new Widgets tray you can activate on the left side of the Taskbar. Unfortunately, you can no longer move the Taskbar to a different side of the screen.
Hardware requirements: This is where most of the frustration around Windows 11 stems from. No one likes being forced to buy new hardware, and while requirements like having at least 4 GB of RAM or 64 GB of storage seem straightforward, the need for a security chip called TPM 2.0 has forced a lot of Windows 10 users to upgrade otherwise good motherboards and CPUs just to move to an operating system they didn't want to begin with.
Performance features: There are tons of new features that help Windows 11 play nicer with accessories and third-party software. One of my favorite examples is HDR support. Windows 11 finally fixes the HDR problem that made using a proper HDR monitor so troublesome, especially in games using Auto HDR. Speaking of games, Windows 11 has features like Game Mode, DirectStorage, and optimizations for windowed games, all of which make for a faster, smoother PC gaming experience.
Is Now a Good Time to Buy?
Laptop prices have been increasing all year, thanks to the memory shortage. In many cases, that means the same laptops cost hundreds of dollars more on any given day. For example, the Dell 14 Plus currently sells for around $1,000, which isn't a terrible price for the configuration. But it was consistently selling for between $650 and $750 for most of 2025. That said, I don't think prices will drop anytime soon. The future of memory pricing is unknown, but many analysts and manufacturers say it will at least last through next year and possibly into 2028.
So yes, there are tons of good options to choose from right now at reasonable prices. All the newest models with the latest chips from Intel, Qualcomm, and AMD are finally out in the wild, along with plenty of good options from 2025. You can always wait for a big sales event like Black Friday, but the savings on specific laptops may not be as big as you might assume. The only significant new hardware we're waiting to see later this year are the new Nvidia RTX Spark laptops. A lot is still unknown about these devices, but they are slated for a fall 2026 release window.
