One company to watch is AST SpaceMobile, a Texas-based firm in the early stages of deploying a network of broadband satellites to beam signals directly to smartphones from low-Earth orbit. SpaceX’s Starlink network already does this, and Amazon is pursuing the direct-to-device connectivity market with its Amazon Leo constellation.
AST officials hinted last month that they are interested in getting into the launch business. The company raised more than $1 billion in a convertible bond sale in July, and AST executives wrote in their most recent quarterly earnings report that they are looking for ways to spend it. The company said it is pursuing an “expanding universe of growth initiatives” to “further vertically integrate our business and mitigate risks associated with third-party launch providers.”
AST’s primary launch providers are SpaceX and Blue Origin. Both are potential competitors in the satellite broadband business. The growth initiatives AST said it was interested in would allow it to “secure additional access to orbit” for its own constellation. AST listed “partnerships and/or acquisitions” as possibilities. A company spokesperson did not respond to questions on the matter.
The balance sheet in AST’s latest quarterly filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission showed the company had approximately $2.3 billion in cash and cash equivalents on hand at the end of June, equal to or more than ULA’s publicly traded subcontractors, Northrop Grumman and L3Harris. That was before AST closed its $1 billion bond sale in July.
There are reasons to question AST’s long-term business outlook, especially as it goes head-to-head against SpaceX and Amazon, two of the most well-capitalized US tech firms. However, vertical integration has served most space companies well, and the same may be true with AST. But there’s a catch. ULA itself is not vertically integrated, with suppliers providing key parts, like engines, payload fairings, and avionics.
AST would surely improve its position with more control of its own access to space. AST already builds its own satellites—each with enormous 2,400-square-foot phased-array antennas—and manages much of its frontend connectivity service, working alongside mobile phone telcos like AT&T and Verizon. T-Mobile is SpaceX’s largest domestic partner on Starlink direct-to-cell.
A buyer for ULA outside of the launch business would also maintain competition in the US launch market. Any sale would have to be approved by the Federal Trade Commission and Department of Justice to ensure it does not substantially reduce competition. Some companies in other sectors are aiming to complete mergers and acquisitions under the Trump administration, which they see as providing a favorable regulatory environment for such transactions.
The launch market would lose a competitor if a company like Blue Origin, with its own heavy-lift rocket, acquired ULA. This would be unwelcome news for the US military as SpaceX prepares for the retirement of its workhorse Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rockets in favor of the newer, more powerful Starship rocket. Starship is unlikely to be certified any time soon for the US government’s most critical national security missions.
The core stage for United Launch Alliance’s fifth Vulcan rocket was raised on its launch platform in May inside a new Amazon-funded integration building at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida. The mission could launch before the end of the month.
The core stage for United Launch Alliance’s fifth Vulcan rocket was raised on its launch platform in May inside a new Amazon-funded integration building at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida. The mission could launch before the end of the month.
Burning down the backlog
United Launch Alliance boasts a substantial order book, a backlog of approximately 80 missions with its Vulcan rocket and the soon-to-retire Atlas V, a number only rivaled by SpaceX.
ULA hopes to resume burning down its backlog in the coming weeks, with the return-to-flight of Vulcan slated for as soon as the end of September. This will be the first of 38 launches Amazon has reserved on the Vulcan rocket and comes as the company faces a bottleneck in launch capacity due to Vulcan’s grounding and the explosion of Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket on the launch pad in May.
The upcoming launch will be ULA’s first under the direction of its new CEO, Mark Peller, who was named to the position last month. Peller replaces Tory Bruno, who retired from ULA last December to take a job overseeing national security business at Blue Origin. Peller is a 36-year veteran of the launch industry, including 20 years at United Launch Alliance, where he led development of the Vulcan rocket from its inception through its certification for US government missions in 2025.
“ULA has a tremendous history of launching some of the nation’s most important national security and exploration missions, and the future is limitless with the new capabilities and performance of our Vulcan rocket,” Peller said in a statement announcing his new role as CEO.
In the near term, this “limitless future” is in the hands of the engineers preparing to return the Vulcan rocket to flight. The next launch of Vulcan will require the thrust from six solid rocket boosters, the most ever on a Vulcan flight to date. That means six data points to show ULA and Northrop have a path to overcoming the booster nozzle problem.
Upon clearing that hurdle, ULA needs a buyer willing to invest in innovation. It would help if the presumed new owner had some skin in the game as an anchor customer for the Vulcan launch vehicle, and more importantly, for what should undoubtedly come next—a reusable rocket.
Stephen Clark is a space reporter at Ars Technica, covering private space companies and the world’s space agencies. Stephen writes about the nexus of technology, science, policy, and business on and off the planet.

Plans for new airport in Damascus sparks outcry over disturbance of thousands of graves
A 2025 investigation identified two suspected grave sites linked to people who died in detention at Mezzeh
Syrian government plans to turn a former military airport in Damascus into a hub for private jets are raising alarm among rights groups and residents who say redevelopment could disturb suspected mass graves and override private land claims.
Syria’s civil aviation authority said last week it was preparing to reclassify Mezzeh military airport for limited civilian use, focused on private and executive aviation, to complement Damascus International Airport, according to a report on Syria's state news agency, SANA. Rubble removal and infrastructure upgrades had already begun, the report said.
The project is emerging as a test of how Syria’s new authorities balance a drive to attract investment and redevelop state assets with two unresolved legacies of Assad’s family rule: the fate of tens of thousands of missing Syrians and property rights clouded by decades of expropriation.
Under ousted ruler Bashar al-Assad and his father Hafez, Mezzeh housed key branches of the powerful Air Force Intelligence Directorate, as well as numerous detention facilities where suspected government opponents were tortured, executed and subjected to enforced disappearance. Parts of the air base were used for presidential and other official flights.
Air Force Intelligence (AFI) documents recently obtained by the Syria Justice and Accountability Centre (SJAC), a U.S.-based Syrian-led human rights group, and shared exclusively with Reuters, show that senior Syrian military officials approved Mezzeh in 2012 as a site for carrying out executions of detainees sentenced to death by military field courts.
One document proposed moving executions from Sednaya — the country's most notorious prison at the time — to Mezzeh because it was a "closed security compound" close to Damascus. Subsequent correspondence discussed a firing range and later a hangar beside the runway as execution sites.
The documents, which underscore the central role of Mezzeh in the Assad-era security system, show officials ordered construction of a platform at the hangar, requested nylon rope and directed that the work be carried out under AFI supervision “in utmost secrecy.”
A 2025 investigation by SJAC identified two suspected grave sites linked to people who died in detention at Mezzeh, where it said more than 1,150 detainees died, some by execution and others from torture or maltreatment.
In a July 2025 letter seen by Reuters, SJAC provided Syria’s National Commission for Missing Persons with the coordinates of the two suspected graves inside the airport, urging authorities to prevent construction or excavation until the sites were investigated.
The commission told SJAC at the time that there were no construction or refurbishment plans for Mezzeh, SJAC told Reuters.
SJAC wrote to the commission again on September 8 after the redevelopment plans emerged, warning that excavation, rubble removal or other works could damage human remains and evidence crucial to identifying victims, according to a second letter seen by Reuters.
SJAC told Reuters it had not yet received a response to its second letter.
Amer Matar, founder of the Syria Prisons Museum, a Germany-based NGO documenting detention facilities including those at Mezzeh, said the planned works showed a lack of respect for Syrian families who still have no answers on the fate of loved ones detained under Assad.
"To construct a business airport on a site that may contain mass graves, without a thorough prior investigation, without site protection, without searching for the missing and their remains, and without preserving evidence, is an act of extreme recklessness and disregard," Matar told Reuters.
The Syrian civil aviation authority, Syria's National Commission for Missing Persons and Syria's defense ministry, which has been operating the airport, did not respond to questions from Reuters about suspected graves and land claims.
SANA cited the civil aviation authority's spokesperson as saying that Mezzeh's refurbishment would take into account the surrounding urban area and relevant legal and social issues, but did not specifically mention the graves or land rights. It is unclear who will develop the airport.
The dispute over the land on which airport facilities were built is decades old.
Under the Assads, private land was regularly expropriated for government projects, often without compensation.
Mezzeh airport was built on land belonging to hundreds of private citizens across 2.76 sq km (1.1 square miles), according to land records from the Moadamiya municipality shared with Reuters.
A former municipal official, who asked not to be named, told Reuters that expropriation decrees retroactively justified the government's use of those lands when the airport was built in 1956, and that compensation had not been paid.
Residents demonstrated in Moadamiya a day after the redevelopment plans were announced. “We welcome investment, but we should be sitting at the table and discussing our share with investors, not the state,” said one protest organiser, who gave his name as Abu Khaled. “We have a documented right to this land.”
The dispute comes as Syria faces calls to address Assad-era property seizures.
On September 2, United Nations land rights experts appealed to Syria's government to suspend and repeal laws they said had enabled systematic property dispossession under Assad, and to either establish mechanisms to return properties to their legitimate owners, or provide adequate compensation.

Canada offered support on Thursday to boost Ukraine’s air defenses and help replenish its drone stocks, as the countries pledged to deepen their alliance during a visit by Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Mark Carney hosted the president of Ukraine in Calgary in the western province of Alberta, where the Canadian prime minister grew up among a large community of people with Ukrainian heritage.
“Canada will always be with you,” Carney assured Zelenskyy.
The leaders signed an agreement to work toward a “hundred-year partnership”.
That deal, to be negotiated over the coming months, aims to codify cooperation in a range of areas, including defense, critical minerals and energy.
“Our two nations have been connected since 1893,” Carney said, referring to a wave of Ukrainians who migrated to the new Canadian nation.
In Alberta, there are an estimated 350,000 Canadians of Ukrainian descent.
“Ukrainians helped build Canada and Canadians will help rebuild Ukraine,” Carney said.
The support announced on Thursday includes C$350m (US$253m) provided through the United States’ Joint Ukraine Multinational Program – Services, Training and Articles Rapid Timeline (Jumpstart) program.
Zelenskyy has emphasized the need for increased air defense as Russia ramps up ballistic missile attacks.
Carney said Canada was also offering C$450m in loan guarantees to enhance the Ukrainian energy supply.
The funds will help repair damaged infrastructure, increase storage capacity and improve power supply to hospitals.
Carney said the goal of the energy support was “to help Ukrainians get through the winter”, a difficult period when the country endures rolling blackouts amid often frigid temperatures.
Canada is moving aggressively to increase its own drone stocks, Carney said, announcing a deal that will see 30% of new Canadian production head to Ukraine.
Zelenskyy told reporters that “these drones will go to Ukraine immediately to [the] battlefield, immediately to our people, our soldiers … to save our children, our families first of all.”
Asked about potential negotiations to ease the fighting, Zelenskyy said he did not anticipate any substantive talks during Russia’s ongoing election period.
But he said he planned to meet Donald Trump in New York City in late September, probably on the sidelines of the UN general assembly, with Washington bidding to revive long-stalled talks to end the war.
“But at the end of September, we will have an opportunity to meet, I think, with the American team in New York,” Zelenskyy said.
“And I think that … I can be more open after the New York meeting with President Trump.”
After the Calgary meeting, Zelenskyy was headed to Banff, a stunning Canadian national park, where he will address a cabinet retreat for Carney’s liberal government.
He then heads to Canada’s largest city, Toronto, and North Bay in northern Ontario.

A cancer survivor hoped to work — then she lost her Medicaid disability coverage
Taya Hailstone has been in remission from childhood Hodgkin lymphoma for five years. But the cancer's lasting damage to her organs and nerves can make basic tasks, like loading a dishwasher, hard.
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
Still, Montana's health department decided last year that Hailstone is no longer eligible for low-cost disability health coverage through Medicaid. The department switched her coverage to the state's Children's Health Insurance Program, another Medicaid program — three months before she aged out.
Before making the decision, the state didn't seek records from the medical team treating Hailstone, according to letters from those doctors reviewed by KFF Health News. Rather, the administrative ruling came after state officials learned the now-19-year-old had stopped receiving Social Security disability payments. She said she did that because she hoped to get healthy enough to work and save some money — beyond what's allowed under the strict income caps tethered to those payments. But her health changes day to day, and she said for now she's still too sick to consistently work.
Hailstone, who lives with her mom, has been able to keep Medicaid coverage while they appeal the case. She said that without Medicaid she can't afford the treatment to manage the aftermath of her cancer.
"It feels like this process was made to make you give up," Hailstone said.
Patients with disabilities have long struggled with administrative hoops, blunders and confusion when trying to qualify for federally subsidized health coverage because of their illness. Now, new federal Medicaid work requirements mean states face the additional task of deciding who qualifies for a medical exemption. That means reviewing medical cases for an even larger swath of Medicaid enrollees.
Attorneys, researchers and advocates who specialize in public aid said disability cases like Hailstone's — though separate from the incoming work requirements — are an indication that states aren't ready to decide who should be exempt from those requirements. As a result, they said, more people will be denied coverage in an opaque process.
"This will be the story of millions of people," said Anthony Wright, who heads Families USA, a national nonprofit that advocates for ways to make healthcare more accessible.
Jon Ebelt, a spokesperson with the Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services, said the state doesn't comment on individual Medicaid cases.
An estimated 18.5 million people will have to meet the new federal requirements, by proving they're working, going to school, or volunteering to keep their Medicaid coverage, according to the Congressional Budget Office. More than 40% of those enrollees live with a chronic health condition, according to KFF.
Some will be excused from those rules if they can prove they're too sick to work.
More than 5 million people are expected to lose Medicaid coverage by 2034 because of the work requirements, according to the CBO.
Work requirements become law
Many Republican policymakers and the Trump administration have touted Medicaid work requirements to preserve coverage for the neediest. Congress made that national policy through last year's One Big Beautiful Bill Act and gave states until January 2027 to implement work-for-coverage rules.
Some states are starting those checks early. Montana began in July. Nebraska initiated work requirements in May.
In the federal law creating the work requirements, Congress allowed states to exempt people who have an illness that qualifies them as "medically frail." Many states created plans for those judgment calls, only to be surprised when federal officials released rules for the requirements that went beyond what Congress outlined, by also requiring enrollees to prove their illness makes it too hard to work.
Families USA and other organizations have argued the new rules force states to set up a patchwork of systems that, together, would be larger and more complicated than the Social Security Administration's own disability review system. Last year, that federal program cost more than $5 billion to administer to roughly 7 million people nationally. For comparison, Wright said, the federal law provided $200 million for states to share as they implement the work requirements. States are paying contractors millions of dollars to prepare often already flawed public aid systems to meet the new standards.
In June, 25 states sued the Trump administration over the medical frailty rules, arguing they're too hard for patients to meet and for states to assess. That case is ongoing.
Hailstone was diagnosed with blood cancer at age 10. Her intestines tore, which led to their partial removal. As a result, her body struggles to process food and she can face severe dehydration. She said lingering side effects from her cancer treatment can leave her mind foggy and cause her hands and feet to swell enough that it's hard to grip a fork or walk across a room.
Cancer dominated nearly half her life. It left mental scars, too.
"Some days you feel fine and then you suddenly crash," Hailstone said.
Hailstone and her mom live in Roundup, a central Montana town of roughly 2,000 people. They regularly make the nearly two-hour round-trip drive to Billings for specialized care. She typically has three medical appointments a week to see her physical and occupational therapists and a mental health counselor.
Hailstone said she's lucky she has her mother's help navigating Medicaid. Her mom, Kyla Hailstone, said that the state hasn't clearly defined how it determined her daughter's disability status and that its appeal process has been slow and dysfunctional.
Taya Hailstone would qualify for Medicaid based on her income if she can't prove her eligibility for disability coverage. But that would mean proving she's too sick to meet the work requirement — putting her in the same position of having to rely on a state review of her illness.
"If I lose this, this is life-changing," Hailstone said.
"Things fall through the cracks"
Hailstone qualified as disabled through the federal government as recently as 2024, about a year before the state said it was dropping her coverage. State officials can do their own medical review to determine whether someone meets the federal definition of a disability to access Medicaid.
"Whether that happens is always a bit of a crapshoot just based on state capacity," said Megan Dishong, deputy director of the Montana Legal Services Association, which helps low-income people navigate public programs. "Things fall through the cracks."
Ebelt said the state health department accepts disability decisions from the Social Security Administration. The state agency can conduct an internal disability determination if a person doesn't have one from the SSA, but Ebelt said it doesn't have to if a person qualifies for coverage another way.
"We are committed to treating every client with respect and helping those who are eligible receive appropriate Medicaid coverage," Ebelt said.
Montana instituted a three-month grace period for the work requirements. State officials won't begin disenrolling people for noncompliance until October.
Pamela Herd, a University of Michigan social policy professor who has studied bureaucratic obstacles to public benefits, said convoluted disability cases are common enough for attorneys to specialize in accessing aid.
"When we've designed public programs in ways that people can't figure out whether they're eligible without consulting lawyers, we've done something wrong," Herd said. "That has huge, huge implications for what's to come."
Montana officials have said they'll automatically review medical records that could help patients qualify for an exemption. Even so, the federal guidelines released in June mean patients will probably still face additional steps to guarantee an exemption.
Meanwhile, already overstretched doctors worry they'll face the burden of judging whether someone's illness qualifies them for a work exemption.
Dishong said that between now and October, Montana officials could offer more clarity on how the process will work. She said she's worried the state will end up "with a slow-roll mess" instead.
"This is a problem that's just starting," Dishong said.
As for Hailstone, she's now reapplying for Social Security disability payments. That aid would limit how much she can work. But it would also guarantee access to Medicaid.

Here's a novel idea for countering the painful side effects of chemotherapy: beforehand, take the hallucinogenic drug found in magic mushrooms.
The study published Thursday in the journal Science involved tests on rats and certain human tissues as researchers looked at using psilocybin to fight a condition called peripheral neuropathy, which affects millions of people around the world.
It is a nerve ailment that hits about three quarters of all people who undergo chemo and commonly causes numbness and tingling, Patrick Dougherty, a co-author of the study, said in a call with reporters.
But a third of that group will develop non-stop, burning pain, said Dougherty, a pain treatment specialist at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center.
The symptoms can lead to trouble walking and other debilitating complications that can last after a person finishes chemotherapy, and even remain with them for life.
And it is not just a quality-of-life issue. This complication also affects a cancer patient's chances of survival because sometimes the side effects are so bad they force doctors to cut back on chemo or stop it altogether.
Protecting nerves
It was almost by accident that these researchers found that psilocybin can help cancer patients.
The team was initially studying how the disease manages to hijack nerve cells in order to grow.
And the researchers were surprised to see the mushroom ingredient -- it was being used to study a brain pathway regeneration concept called neuroplasticity -- actually prevented the emergence of peripheral neuropathy.
Later experiments highlighted psilocybin's role in protecting nerve cells and stimulating inside them the transport of mitochondria, often referred to as a cell's powerhouse.
This is key because chemo destroys the microscopic railroads that allow mitochondria to send energy all the way to the tips of people's hands and feet, killing off nerve endings there.
Psilocybin also seems to act on the brain, preserving electrical activity that chemotherapy thwarts.
In rodents, taking two doses of psilocybin before chemo was enough to prevent the appearance of painful hypersensitivity during as many as six rounds of treatment. And it did this without affecting the animal's immune system or hindering the cancer-fighting action.
Careful with self-medicating
"This is a highly promising finding," said Kristy Townsend, a professor of neurobiology at The Ohio State University who was not involved in the study.
And psilocybin's nerve-protecting quality does not seem to be linked to its hallucinogenic effects because a non-hallucinogenic analogue had the same effect in a lab test, she added.
Before the treatment can be made standard for people, testing will be needed to see if it is safe and effective, said Townsend.
This will be a long, slow process though it should be eased by a boom in medical research on psychedelic substances and a Trump administration executive order in April to speed up research and regulatory reviews, these scientists say.
The MD Anderson Cancer Center plans to launch clinical tests with psilocybin on cancer patients later this year.
Meanwhile it is important for cancer patients to avoid using magic mushrooms on their own as treatment, the researchers warned.
Psilocybin is legal in a few U.S. states.
The drug has an "amplifier" effect and cancer patients who take it without supervision could feel more stressed and anxious than they already are because of their cancer diagnosis, said Gregory Jones, a psychiatrist who took part in the study released Thursday.
"If you put somebody in adversity under these psychedelic substances, you can get much worse," Jones said.

OpenAI has asked members of Congress in recent weeks for clear guidance about whether orchestrating an industry-wide slowdown on frontier AI development would be legal, people close to the company tell WIRED.
Substantive coordination on safety between AI labs may risk running afoul of antitrust law, the people say, which poses a significant obstacle to bringing major tech giants on board with the effort.
Last weekend, OpenAI’s chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, published a blog post arguing that the best path forward for the AI research world includes “coordinating to slow down future development,” which he thinks will be key to ensuring that self-improving AI systems are safe. In the short term, he expects “voluntary slowdowns to become commonplace until shared safety bars are established.”
But some legal scholars say such an effort could conflict with US antitrust laws. Nicholas Felstead, assistant director of the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission and a former AI policy fellow at the Center for Law & AI Risk, argued in a March article that a coordinated pause in AI development may amount to companies restricting output, potentially violating the Sherman Antitrust Act. It would depend “entirely on the precise details of any agreement,” Felstead wrote. “But even if most safety collaborations would ultimately survive antitrust scrutiny, legal uncertainty can act as a powerful deterrent.”
OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment ahead of publication.
There are some early signs that Congress is listening. In July, a bipartisan, bicameral group of lawmakers introduced a bill titled “Collaboration on Adversarial Threats and Security Risks Act,” which would explicitly permit AI labs to coordinate on security and safety work without the risk of violating antitrust statutes. The House version was referred to the Judiciary Committee but has yet to be taken up.
Caleb Knapp, director of government affairs at the nonprofit AI Policy Network, which endorsed the bill, says it would create legal channels for AI labs to work together to address safety and security incidents. Knapp adds that Congress has a “growing appetite to get something done” on AI safety but says enacting anything into law may have to wait until after the upcoming midterm elections.
While some AI executives may have genuine concerns about antitrust, another camp of AI leaders argue those worries are just convenient cover to avoid discussing the real reasons that AI developers may be wary about collaborating, which go far beyond potential legal liabilities.
For one, AI is a massive business, and these companies are fiercely competing to capture a slice of the nascent market for frontier models. Some executives share the Trump administration’s view that staying ahead of China in AI is crucial for national security. Perhaps most importantly, different AI developers have vastly different opinions about the best way to develop safe artificial intelligence, and therefore may be reluctant to work with one another on the issue.
“First step is for industry leaders OpenAI and Anthropic to stop feuding and work on a pacing proposal together,” John Schulman, an OpenAI cofounder who is now chief scientist at the rival AI lab Thinking Machines, wrote in a post on X earlier this week. “They'll cite antitrust, but that's fake—antitrust prohibits certain agreements, but not from jointly developing a proposal.”
Long-simmering fears about the race among AI companies to build and release ever more powerful models erupted into the national spotlight this summer. This week, former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher Jacob Coxon added to the growing alarm when he issued a stark public warning that AI developers were putting humanity at risk. In recent months, a number of security incidents, including OpenAI’s agents hacking Hugging Face, highlighted how the industry’s safeguards have failed to keep pace with the rising capabilities of models. The succession of events has led many lawmakers to make urgent calls for AI regulation.

Everyone knows that when you’re at Olive Garden, you’re family.
But in the 44 years since the casual Italian-American restaurant chain was founded, few have embraced it with the ardor that Braden Sinclair has. In fact, way back in his Little League days, a coach named him “Breadsticks.”
“I had to go to Olive Garden for my birthday, ate too much, missed an entire game,” Sinclair tells WIRED. “One of my coaches decided that because of my initials being B.S., and my number being 11—which he said looked like breadsticks—and then that story, that I had to be called ‘Breadsticks’ for the rest of the season.”
He maintained that close relationship with the chain for many years, until, in 2019, he was rewarded with an almost unfathomable distinction: Sinclair is one of just 50 human beings on the planet to ever secure an Olive Garden Lifetime Pasta Pass.
Unlike the thousands of 13-week Never Ending Pasta Passes that the chain has offered at various intervals since 2014—this summer, a batch of 10,000, priced at $100 apiece, sold out within seconds—Sinclair’s heavy gold card bears no expiration date. It entitles him to as much pasta, toppings, breadsticks, and soup or salad as he cares to eat, for as long as the chain endures and he remains a loyal customer. (No delivery, though, to be clear. A pasta bowl so bottomless demands that one take a seat of honor for the dine-in experience.)
How exactly does Sinclair wield his kingly rights at Olive Garden? All is revealed on his new website, Lifetimepastapass.com, where he crunches the many numbers—both financial and dietary—on his many meals there. And, with a continually updated poll that decides what he should order the next time he drops in, it’s easily the closest you’ll ever get to having the lifetime pass yourself.
Sinclair nabbed his license to feast during a special promotion, when Olive Garden announced that the first 50 people to buy a temporary pasta pass would have the opportunity to upgrade it to the lifetime pass for an extra $400. To this day, Sinclair wonders if his timing was really that good or if the company deliberately selected him to receive the ultimate prize.
“I had sort of a joking relationship with their Instagram for years, just like chatting back and forth,” he explains, adding that it felt a little “weird” and something like “divine intervention” that he won given his coziness with the brand. An Olive Garden vice president of marketing FaceTimed him with the good news, he recalls.
Reactions to the card from Olive Garden employees range from awe to confusion. “They always take it back to the kitchen, show it to people,” Sinclair says. “Managers will come out and ask questions. The other end of the spectrum has been having to kind of prove it's real, which is rare, and I totally understand. Like, if I managed a restaurant and someone came in with a gold card that said I don't need to pay, I would also have questions.”
Now a 33-year-old father of two young kids, Sinclair doesn’t gorge on heaping plates of carbohydrates the way he used to (and, since frequenting Olive Garden makes him more conscientious about the rest of his diet, he’s avoided packing on the pounds). But he says the Lifetime Pasta Pass somewhat justifies his continued fixation on the restaurant, which was a familiar comfort when his family temporarily relocated from Maine to Wisconsin during his childhood. In 2016, he paid homage to the place with a tattoo of its famous rotary cheese grater; the caption reads “SAY WHEN.” He also began collecting vintage T-shirts that the chain had released in the 1980s and 1990s.
This year, Sinclair unveiled the project that brought all of his Olive Garden experiences together in one place. Lifetimepastapass.com documents his “infinite tour of Italy” by showcasing not only his backstory and extensive merch collection but all the data you could ever want about how he has used his rare privilege: number of restaurant visits since 2019 (112), bowls of pasta eaten (152), calories consumed (154,817), meal value ($1,878.87) and total tips ($607.00).
You can also keep tabs on a map of which locations Sinclair has tried—while the South Portland, Maine, restaurant is his home base, he has ventured up and down the Eastern Seaboard. Other charts show his most favored pasta type (rigatoni), sauce (alfredo), and topping (crispy chicken fritta), as well as the monthly frequency of his Olive Garden visits; he dined there nine times in August, the most since he set a personal record of 20 visits in October 2019, shortly after winning the pass.
With a decade of experience in data analytics and visualization, Sinclair saw all this as a fun application of his talents. But he also wanted people to have “skin in the game,” as he puts it—so he built a dashboard where anyone can vote on the combination of ingredients that make up his next pasta order.
“I thought it was just gonna be a joke among my friends,” Sinclair says. “You know, share it on Instagram, so maybe 10 of my friends would go in and vote, and then the next day five, and then the third day no one would care, and it would be over.” Instead, after he shared the project on a couple of subreddits, he was stunned to tally over 700 votes on his next meal. He wound up eating angel hair with spicy alfredo (a new sauce offering) and crispy shrimp fritta.
“A big reason why I wanted to do this is I just kept getting rigatoni with alfredo, five-cheese marinara, and crispy chicken, like on repeat,” Sinclair says. “I was like, ‘I need to branch out.’” His best discovery so far? “I realized that alfredo and meatballs is an insane combination,” he says. “It's so good.”
In some ways, Lifetimepastapass.com is a reflection of Sinclair’s belief that the card comes with great responsibility. Besides tipping diligently, he also skips the refills, aiming to be a “respectful” and “low-impact” diner who doesn’t flaunt his status or make a shift harder for staff. “I see some pictures of people with the [regular] pasta passes who go crazy,” he says. “Bowls full of grated Parmesan just because they can.” Meticulously tracking his own Olive Garden journey toward various virtual “trophies” earned by hitting benchmarks in categories such as “lifetime breadsticks eaten” (he’ll reach the bronze level at 100, gold at 1,000) and “longest streaks of consecutive weeks with at least one visit” seems, by comparison, a kind of reverence for the institution.
If there’s an unexpected downside to the Lifetime Pasta Pass, it may be a certain loneliness at the top. Because Covid-19 hit shortly after people claimed the cards, the promotion has been largely memory-holed, and whatever plans Olive Garden could have had to celebrate or connect the winners were never realized. Sinclair has stumbled upon only a couple of other passholders via social media and has no idea how often others may go to the restaurant these days.
Meanwhile, it’s not always easy to convince your pals to meet up at a restaurant just because you eat there for free. “There's only so many times I can go sit at the Olive Garden by myself,” Sinclair says. “I have some friends who are nice enough to go with me, but oftentimes they’ll just kind of sit there and eat some breadsticks.” And though Sinclair’s wife is an admitted fan of the chain—she’s eaten there with him since their high school days and promised in her wedding vows to go whenever he wants—he finds it “wisest” to seek alternatives whenever they manage a kids-free date night.
The good news is that Sinclair’s 4-year-old is a likely Olive Garden devotee in the making. “I'll probably start bringing my oldest son a little more just because he's obsessed with pasta,” he says. “I think he'll genuinely enjoy it.”
Just not before a Little League game, of course.

Whether Trump's comments amounted to bragging, as some people online claimed, is open to interpretation.
Ahead of the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks, a claim (archived) circulated online that Donald Trump, then a New York City real estate developer, said after the attacks that he now owned the tallest building in downtown Manhattan.
For example, the self-described "pro-democracy" media outlet MeidasTouch wrote in a Facebook post:
In a television interview on the day of the attacks, Trump notably bragged how the destruction of the World Trade Center affected the ranking of his building at 40 Wall Street, claiming it was now the tallest building in downtown Manhattan.
Similar claims about Trump's alleged comments following the 9/11 attacks circulated on X (archived here and here) and Instagram (archived). Snopes readers also contacted us to ask about the claim.
Reminder: Donald Trump's immediate reaction to the 9/11 attacks was to brag that his building was now the tallest in downtown Manhattan after the Twin Towers collapsed. pic.twitter.com/iAkUeGafG9
— Republicans against Trump (@RpsAgainstTrump) September 7, 2026
Trump did tell (time code 2:05, archived) a reporter soon after the 9/11 attacks that 40 Wall Street, which the Trump Organization still owns, was "the tallest" building in downtown Manhattan. As such, we've rated this quote as correctly attributed to Trump.
Whether Trump's comments amounted to bragging, as some people online claimed, is open to interpretation.
Fox 5 New York posted a video of Trump's phone interview with WWOR-TV reporter Alan Marcus on YouTube in 2016. Trump made the claim about owning the tallest building in downtown Manhattan after Marcus asked if 40 Wall Street had sustained any damage during the attacks. The exchange went as follows (time code 01:43 — emphasis ours):
Marcus: Donald, you have one of the landmark buildings down in the financial district, 40 Wall Street, did you have any damage or did you know what's happened down there?
Trump: Well, it was an amazing phone call I made. 40 Wall Street actually was the second-tallest building in downtown Manhattan. And it was, actually before the World Trade Center, was the tallest. And then when they built the World Trade Center, it became known as the second-tallest. And now it's the tallest.
During the 2001 interview, Marcus also asked Trump how he would have handled 9/11 if he were president given that he had considered running for the office the year before (time code 4:14). Trump said he would have taken a "very, very tough line" against "the group of people that did this."
In an interview with Politico in 2016, Marcus reportedly said that Trump's remark about 40 Wall Street was "Donald being Donald." Marcus added, "He is the brand manager of Trump, and he is going to tout that brand, and he does it reflexively."
Trump's claim that 40 Wall Street was the tallest building in downtown Manhattan following the attacks was incorrect. The nearby 952-foot tall 70 Pine Street skyscraper, which was also part of the Manhattan skyline in 2001, is 26 feet taller than 40 Wall Street.
For further reading, Snopes previously investigated whether Trump attacked the National September 11 Memorial & Museum in New York for telling him he would not be allowed to speak at its 25th anniversary commemoration.
Snopes' archives contributed to this report.

Due to a scheduling mishap, I was only able to check out two movies on my second day at the Toronto International Film Festival — but I did manage to get an early look at and some fascinating details on one of my most anticipated films this year.
Laika’s stop-motion fantasy Wildwood looks so smooth
Reviews from TIFF 2026: Julian and Stuffed, along with an early look at Laika’s next animated feature.
Even if you don’t know the name Laika, you probably know the studio’s work; it’s the animation house behind stop-motion hits like ParaNorman, The Boxtrolls, and Kubo and the Two Strings. Over the years Laika’s films have steadily gotten more impressive on both a technical and artistic level. Which brings us to the incredible-looking Wildwood, hitting theaters next month. If you’re unfamiliar, here’s a look:
Some of the crew from Laika was on stage at TIFF to talk about the making of Wildwood, in particular why this film looks more lifelike than the studio’s previous work. There are a few reasons. One has to do with the animation itself, which, as you can see in the trailer, is incredibly smooth in the new film. “We’re in the midst of the evolution of an art form,” Laika’s head of animation Brad Schiff explained. “Because we have digital cameras, we’re able to see what we’re doing; we have what we call frame-grabbers.” This lets Laika’s animators see all of the recently-shot frames as they’re animating, allowing them to track every single movement of a puppet, ensuring everything moves smoothly. “There’s no reason for stuttery animation, other than a stylistic choice,” Schiff said.
The puppets themselves are also more advanced. They utilize an internal “diaphragm” that Laika calls a breather, which the studio first experimented with on its previous film, 2019’s Missing Link. This time, all of the major puppets are outfitted with breathers, and this lets the animators make characters appear to breathe in a lifelike way, so that they seem more human in the final product.
You can see some of that in the trailer above, but I was also able to watch a handful of clips from the film, and — despite Laika stressing that they weren’t final — they looked incredible. One showed a fast and tense bike chase through a bustling version of Portland, where Wildwood takes place. There was a speed and tension to it that felt like a live-action sequence. In the movie, a young girl named Prue loses her little brother in an “impassable wilderness” that’s home to a rich fantasy world. In the clips I saw, she did everything from escaping an ornate mansion filled with guard dogs distracted by their own tails, to soaring above a vast landscape while on the back of a giant bird. Wildwood looked as stylish and detailed as you’d expect from a Laika production, but what impressed me the most was how realistic it all felt in motion.
A few other details for those who love numbers: Wildwood features 233 puppets (36 are just versions of Prue), was brought to life by 49 animators, and took 231 weeks from start to finish. It’s in theaters on October 23rd.
As for the movies I was able to actually catch on day 2 of TIFF, they were both great, but also, could not be more different. One is a sweetly morbid musical, the other a life-affirming family film made with traditional animation. And if you missed my previous TIFF coverage — including films like All of a Sudden and The Only Living Pickpocket in New York — you can check it out right here.
Julián
No theatrical date yet
Julián comes via Irish animation studio Cartoon Saloon, best known for the features Song of the Sea and Wolfwalkers. And it shares much in common with the studio’s previous work, telling the story of a child lost in a world of fantasy. In this case it’s seven-year-old Julián who goes to live with his grandmother in Brooklyn while his dad is on a work trip. Julián is obsessed with ocean life and anything pretty, so when he meets some kids making costumes for an upcoming mermaid parade, joining in becomes his sole focus in life. But his colorful personality often clashes with his more conservative grandmother, and when some boys bully Julián for wearing a mermaid tail, he starts to retreat into himself. Ultimately, Julián is a fairly straightforward tale about being yourself and allowing others to do the same, but it’s told with tremendous style and passion, making it a welcome addition to the studio’s catalog. Plus, the ending is almost guaranteed to make you tear up.
Stuffed
No theatrical date yet
A love story between an eccentric taxidermist and the man who agrees to give up his life in order to fulfill her lifelong dream of stuffing a human. Oh, and also it’s a musical. Stuffed has shades of Sweeney Todd, but despite its macabre premise, it’s much more heartfelt. Barrie (Harry Melling) lives a sad life working at a sandwich factory, collecting obituaries, and caring for his aging mother. But he’s obsessed with being remembered, and when he answers an online ad promising to make him “exceptional,” he meets Araminta (Jodie Comer), whose house is filled with taxidermied animals, but who has also always wanted to take the next step. Their interests, it seems, line up: she wants to stuff a person, he wants to live forever. But as they work together on the weirdo plan, the two become close, complicating the whole killing Barry thing. Stuffed is morbid and occasionally wince-inducing, but it’s also filled with a lot of love and heart, and a not-so-surprising amount of humor.

Between surviving an illness and returning to regular life, lies a journey of a thousand small victories. Physiotherapy helps people take those victories, one step at a time.
There is a moment after a heart attack or stroke that very few people talk about. It is not the moment the ambulance arrives. It is not the moment the doctors say the patient is out of danger. It is the moment when the hospital doors close behind you, you return home, and everyone expects life to slowly return to normal.
But what does ‘normal’ mean?
For someone who has had a stroke, it may mean learning to walk again, using an arm that suddenly feels unfamiliar, finding their balance, or simply getting out of bed without someone holding their hand. For someone who has survived a heart attack, it may mean taking that first walk outside without constantly wondering whether their heart can handle it.
And sometimes, the hardest part is not the physical limitation. It is the fear. “What if it happens again?” That question can stay with a person long after they have left the hospital. This is where physiotherapy becomes much more than a set of exercises.
What rehabilitation entails
We often imagine rehabilitation as someone working hard in a gym, lifting weights or walking on a treadmill. The reality can be much quieter.
For a stroke survivor, the first goal may simply be to sit upright without support. Then to stand. Then to take a few steps. For the family watching, it may seem like very little. For the person doing it, it may feel like climbing a mountain.
A physiotherapist is there for these moments. Not just to count repetitions or measure strength, but to help someone understand that progress does not always have to be dramatic. Sometimes, progress is one extra step. Sometimes, it is standing for ten seconds longer. Sometimes, it is being able to walk to the bathroom without asking for help. And sometimes, it is simply finding the confidence to try.
What patients go through
Imagine being someone who used to walk to work, play with their children, exercise regularly or climb four flights of stairs without giving it a second thought. Then you have a heart attack. Suddenly, your heartbeat becomes something you constantly notice. You begin questioning every sensation. Is this normal? Am I too tired? Is my heart rate too high? Should I stop?
That fear can lead people to become overly cautious and inactive. Cardiac rehabilitation can help break that cycle. With appropriate medical assessment and supervision, patients can gradually return to physical activity, improve their exercise capacity and learn how to manage their cardiovascular health with greater confidence. The physiotherapist’s role is not simply to say, “Push harder.” It is to say: “Let us understand what your body can safely do today—and build from there.”
Not only for the elderly
A stroke or heart attack is often imagined as something that happens late in life, after the age of 60 or so. But when it happens to a younger person, the shock can be enormous. Someone in their 30s or 40s may suddenly find themselves worrying about things they never expected to question. Will I be able to go back to work? Can I take care of my children? Can I travel? Can I exercise again? Can I return to the sport I love?
They may look perfectly healthy from the outside. But inside, they may be dealing with fatigue, weakness, uncertainty and fear about what comes next. That is why rehabilitation cannot simply be based on a person’s age or diagnosis. A younger patient may need to return to a physically demanding job. A sportsperson may want to return to competition. A parent may simply want enough energy to play with their children. Rehabilitation has to fit the life that person wants to return to.
The patient is not a diagnosis. This may be one of the most important things a physiotherapist learns. A medical report might say stroke. It might say heart attack. It might list numbers, test results and medications. But none of those words explain who the patient is. They do not tell you that the patient loves taking their morning walk. They do not tell you that someone has a child waiting at home. They do not tell you that being able to climb the stairs independently means more to that person than almost anything else. Good rehabilitation starts with a simple question: “What do you want to get back to?” The answer may be different for every person. And that answer becomes an important part of the treatment.
Preventive goals
Physiotherapy is also about preventing the next story. Rehabilitation should not only begin after a crisis. Physiotherapists also have an important role in helping people become more physically active, develop healthier movement habits and reduce preventable health risks. Physical activity is an important part of cardiovascular health, but exercise is not a prescription that can simply be copied from one person to another.
The right type, intensity and amount of activity depend on the individual. For someone recovering from a cardiac event, exercise may require appropriate medical guidance and monitoring of symptoms, heart rate, blood pressure and exercise tolerance. For someone recovering from a stroke, rehabilitation may involve improving balance, strength, coordination, walking and everyday functional activities.
The goal is not to push everyone to do more. The goal is to help each person do what is right for them—safely and consistently. The greatest thing a physiotherapist restores is not movement. It is the part of someone’s life they thought was gone forever.
We often say that physiotherapists help people move. But perhaps that does not quite capture the whole story. Physiotherapists help people return to the things that make life feel like life.
(Shanthi Dass is a sports physiotherapist and managing director of Synergy The Clinic, Chennai. synergytheclinic@gmail.com)

The precise composition of ancient Egyptian paints, binders, adhesives, and similar materials used to make artifacts is largely unknown, in part because a full analysis would require taking samples that would damage those valuable artifacts. The development of cutting-edge, non-destructive techniques has been helping to unlock those secrets, aiding conservation efforts.
Most recently, researchers have used mass spectrometry-based proteomics to analyze the glues and adhesives in a broad set of Egyptian artifacts, according to a new paper published in the journal Science Advances. They found plenty of expected sources, such as animal collagens and egg proteins, but also plant proteins, specifically from sesame and drumstick tree (moringa) cereals.
As previously reported, the ancient Egyptians had a highly formalized (and easily recognizable) painting style, and there has been considerable interest in gaining insights into the specific pigments and painting techniques employed. Common pigments included hematite and realgar for red; goethite and orpiment for yellow; Egyptian blue; Egyptian green; carbon-based black; and calcite, gypsum, anhydrite, and huntite for white. (Just last year, Washington State University researchers were able to re-create Egyptian blue by mixing together silicon dioxide, copper, calcium, and sodium carbonate in varying proportions and heating them at very high temperatures akin to those of ancient kilns.)
Many pigments available to ancient Egyptian artists have elemental markers detectable by X-ray fluorescence imaging. Macro-XRF imaging in particular has previously been used (in combination with hyperspectral imaging) to study a Greco-Roman painted funerary portrait from the second century CE, as well as to determine the remnants of color on marble at Delphi in Greece. In 2023, scientists used a portable MA-XRF imaging device to study ancient Egyptian paintings, part of a broader project investigating tomb chapels in the Theban Necropolis.

Platinum-based chemotherapy — in particular cisplatin and carboplatin — are a lifeline for children with certain cancers. These treatments, for instance, transformed the prognosis of hepatoblastoma, a rare cancer of the liver that is the most commonly diagnosed in childhood, from a five-year survival rate of 20% to more than 80% for localized tumors.
However, these medications work by damaging the DNA of cancer cells, and they are also known to cause mutations in the DNA of healthy cells, potentially raising the risk of new cancers later in life. The mutations have been documented in adults, but the picture is less clear when it comes to children. A new study published Thursday in Science sought a clearer understanding of the long-term impact of platinum agents in children treated for hepatoblastoma.
The study looked at children who had received platinum therapy followed by surgery to remove the tumor. The researchers sampled tissues from the liver — both healthy and cancerous — and the patient’s blood, analyzing them through a sophisticated DNA sequencing technique called NanoSeq.
They then compared the sequencing results to those from children who had been treated with different drugs, or had not been treated prior to surgery, as well as to fetal liver tissue. They found that being exposed to platinum agents led to hundreds of mutations in genes (on average 2,200 per liver sample), a burden of mutation usually found in adult livers. In other words, platinum aged the liver cells of treated children, making them look more like adult liver cells.
Mutation load also increased proportionally to platinum exposure: children who received only cisplatin had a smaller number of mutations than those who received both cisplatin and carboplatin. These mutations could increase the likelihood of liver pathologies, or the emergence of secondary tumors, the authors said.
“We found lots of cancer genes but also genes associated with long-term changes in liver metabolism,” said Foad Rouhani, one of the authors of the paper and a professor at King’s College in London. However, he stressed that “by no means does that mean that these cells will definitely become cancerous in time. All we talk about is there was evidence for potential for these cells to eventually cause problems further down the line.”
Liver cells showed many more mutations than blood cells, even though chemotherapy is a systemic treatment. “The platinum is doing something differently to liver cells than other cells. Either it’s been metabolized differently or the liver cells are repairing differently, we don’t really know yet,” said Rouhani. This could mean that the liver was more susceptible to the effects of platinum, or it could be the other way around: The extent of the mutations may explain why that liver got sick in the first place.
In a perspective article, Sanjeev Vasudevan and Donald Williams Parsons, both professors at Baylor College of Medicine in Houston, wrote that the findings “provide strong evidence for conducting survivorship studies of children that have undergone treatment for liver cancer beyond their third decade of life.”
For the study authors, its primary contribution lies in establishing that the damage occurs, so clinicians can monitor these patients more closely during their lifetimes, said Rouhani, and identify issues at an earlier stage.
But there could be a prospective impact on treatment. “If we understand the mechanism, can we then eventually be able to design next-generation chemotherapies which are highly effective at treating the cancer but actually leave the background tissue largely untouched?” said Rouhani.

Bulgaria investigates fire at weapons site that owner calls sabotage
- Published
Bulgaria is investigating the cause of an overnight fire at an ammunition storage site run by a private defence company.
Interior Minister Ivan Demerdzhiev said the authorities "are not ruling out outside interference" in the incident in central Bulgaria. No-one was injured in the blaze that triggered a series of explosions.
EMCO company, whose weapons are used by Ukraine against invading Russian forces, said the fire at its site was sabotage and that human error was "completely ruled out". It did not say who might be responsible.
The latest incident follows last month's fire and blasts at another EMCO ammunition warehouse in the area.
In a statement, EMCO said the storage facility that was burned this time - near the central village of Gorni Varpishta, some 170km (106 miles) east of the capital Sofia - had not been used for months and was inspected just 20 days ago, when full compliance with all regulations was confirmed.
It cited a number of similar incidents at Bulgarian defence firms since 2011, saying that the latest was "no exception to the series of acts of sabotage against the Bulgarian defence industry".
"As the EU and Nato member state most severely affected by such actions, Bulgaria must join the collective effort to prevent and neutralise these attacks," EMCO said.
The firm is run by Bulgarian arms dealer Emilian Gebrev, who Bulgarian prosecutors allege has already been targeted by Russian agents.
This includes a poisoning attempt in 2015 of Gebrev, his son and another company employee - three Russian nationals were later charged in absentia for attempted murder.
Bulgaria is a major weapons supplier to Ukraine, as it continues to repel a full-scale Russian invasion launched in 2022.
And although Sofia has recently halted state-owned arms supplies to Ukraine, Bulgarian private defence companies continue such transfers.
Russia appears to have recently escalated its sabotage campaign across Europe.
Last week, Germany said Russia was responsible for August's drone attack at Leipzig's airport - a claim denied by Moscow as "absurd".
There have also been a number of suspicious fires at defence facilities from Italy to Estonia, with some of the affected countries blaming Russia.

After having a baby last summer, my husband and I realized something: by the time the house was quiet and our baby was asleep, neither of us had much energy left to talk about anything. We weren't fighting often, but little frustrations had a way of lingering because there never seemed to be a "right" time to bring them up. So, we decided to try a new weekly check-in ritual.
We treat it like a physical for our relationship: It's a chance to celebrate what's working, catch small issues before they snowball, and make sure neither of us is quietly carrying resentment.
So far, it's been the single most helpful habit we've adopted as a couple.
We use the same questions every week
Having a structured format works well for us. Instead of wasting time — "What do you want to talk about?" "I don't know, what do you want to talk about?" — we just run down our list, each taking turns to talk or listen. While it took some trial-and-error to find the questions that are most beneficial, here's the set we landed on:
- What made you feel loved this week?
- What's your biggest stressor looking ahead to next week? And what's one thing I can do to support you?
- What's one thing you're really looking forward to this week?
- What would make you feel connected to me this week?
- Is there anything we should talk about now before it becomes a bigger issue?
Each question serves a different purpose.
The first question encourages us to acknowledge each other's efforts
During a busy, stressful week, it can be easy to overlook the little things we both do to care for each other. But my husband and I made a vow never to take each other for granted.
The first question — "What made you feel loved this week?" — offers a natural opportunity for us to express some gratitude. I might let my husband know how much it meant to me that he got up with the baby in the middle of the night. He might thank me for making his morning easier by filling up his water bottle and watching our son while he worked out.
Then, we do some collaborative troubleshooting
I find that naming my stressors out loud can help prevent me from spiraling inside my own head. Plus, when my husband and I share them with each other, we're able to proactively problem-solve together. Better yet, we both have the chance to explain exactly how we'd like to receive support from each other — rather than leaving each other to guess.
So, if I tell him I'm nervous about an interview coming up this week, he could offer some confidence-boosting affirmation, and then I could ask him to rehearse my questions with me the night before so I feel prepared.
We also balance things out with positive anticipation
During our check-in, we're careful not to dwell too much on the potentially anxiety-inducing events coming up. Taking a moment to talk about the things we're looking forward to, whether it's a family walk or a special home-cooked dinner, helps us to feel excited about the week ahead.
We benefit from having an opportunity to express our needs
My husband and I have similar love languages, but we're not mind readers. We can't expect the other person to know exactly what we need from each other. That's precisely why we started asking: "What would make you feel connected to me this week?"
Sometimes, for me, it's often as simple as having breakfast together or getting a text check-in after my therapy appointment.
For him, it might just be an unprompted hug or putting our phones away while we watch something together.
Finally, we tackle any issues before they escalate
If there's one thing we've learned over the last eight years of our relationship, it's that there's a right and wrong time to bring up things that are bothering you. Confronting the other person at the end of a draining workday, or in a moment when one or both of you are already emotionally activated, is unlikely to lead to a productive discussion. That's why we always end our weekly check-ins on this question: Is there anything we should talk about now before it becomes a bigger issue?
This gives us both peace of mind that there's a designated time to air out any concerns, so we don't feel the need to tackle them when we don't have the emotional bandwidth. In my iPhone Notes App, I might jot down something that bugged me — say, when my husband forgot to tell me he was working late — so I don't forget to bring it up. Sometimes, by the time we get to our weekly check-in on Sunday, I'm already over it. But when something is still bothering me, it's super helpful to have a safe space to share it.

The Stunt Driver star Jay Baruchel says Canadians in film industry can 'punch above our weight'
Devon Bostick, Mary Walsh among other Canadians proudly championing homegrown art at TIFF
As tensions between Canada and the U.S. creep into the film industry, Jay Baruchel is more than confident his country can stand toe to toe with its southern neighbour.
"We will be fine," the Ottawa-born actor said on the red carpet Friday ahead of the world premiere of The Stunt Driver at the Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF).
"We have never done anything but punch above our weight, and our record is pretty bloody strong when it comes to that.… We always find a way through."
He's one of a number of Canadian actors sharing their love of the country's film industry and Canada in general on the TIFF red carpet after the festival kicked off Thursday night.
Baruchel, known for films such as BlackBerry and She's Out of My League, is in the driver's seat of the new underdog film, which is based on the true story of stuntman Ken Carter.
Baruchel portrays Carter, known as The Mad Canadian, who attempted to jump over the St. Lawrence River in a rocket-powered car in the 1970s — partially driven by a desire to outdo his American rival Evel Knievel.
The timing of the film's debut during the ongoing trade war between Canada and the U.S. "added an extra sense of urgency … and a vitality" to the film, Baruchel said.
"If you've ever been talked down to, if you've ever been dismissed ... you understand where this comes from," he added, calling the story "an indignant middle finger."
The trade war gained took on a cultural dimension ahead of TIFF when, earlier this month, U.S. President Donald Trump singled out Canada during the announcement of a proposed federal incentive to keep U.S. film productions in the U.S. rather than travelling abroad, stirring up concerns in the Canadian film industry.
- The best-dressed stars at TIFF 2026
- ‘It’s Canada’s turn now’: TIFF market looks to capitalize on U.S. political climate, boost local film
- The U.S. is considering a federal tax incentive for films. How might that affect Canada?
The two film industries have long been close.
"It's been over a hundred years that there's been a very solid bridge built between the entertainers and artists and business people of Canada and the U.S. when it comes to making movies," TIFF CEO Cameron Bailey told CBC News on Thursday, noting that the opening film at TIFF, Being Heumann, is a U.S. production that was shot in Toronto.
At TIFF, Canadian actors and artists say they aren't feeling cowed — but instead feel inspired to champion Canadian art.
"Art can reflect who we are as a country and … who we are as people," Canadian actress Laurence Leboeuf, who plays Carter's wife Gloria in The Stunt Driver, said on the red carpet Friday.
'Canadian renaissance'
Devon Bostick, a Toronto-born actor who co-wrote Closing Night — which also premiered at TIFF — added that he feels "we're part of a Canadian renaissance right now." The film tracks a movie star (Sarah Paulson) as she attempts to connect with her estranged family.
"I live in the States now and from afar I just think Canada's got it going on, and I feel like it's a beacon of light, that what is happening here is thriving and resisting," the Mile End Kicks actor said.
When asked if he had any concerns about the Canadian film industry amid trade tensions, he quipped, "I think I'm not afraid for Canada, I’m afraid for the States."
Mary Walsh, a comedian and actress known for her work with This Hour Has 22 Minutes, echoed those sentiments when she arrived on the red carpet for the upcoming Netflix miniseries Below on Thursday.
"The Canadian film industry is bigger than it's ever been, and it's growing. And the more Mr. Trump threatens to attack us, the more we pull together and become stronger," she said.
Walsh, who hails from St. John's, plays the mayor of a small, shrinking town in Newfoundland in the new horror series.
She said the U.S. upping its aggression against Canada could be the "kick in the arse that the Canadian film industry needed," to back its own artistic works more fully.
"As a country we must support our own … culture, and we do a somewhat good job of that. But at times, you know, Canadians aren't always behind Canadian culture. They've sort of looked to the larger thing to the south, and so I think our eyes are sort of turning back to ourselves.
"If Mr. Trump did only one good thing, only one good thing, it would be that it made us realize that we are a country, and a country worth working together to save and to be."

The National Medical Commission’s plan to create a National Medical Register (NMR), is running into rough weather again as doctors are questioning why medical practitioners are being made to pay a fee and register again for entry into the NMR when their database is already available with respective State Medical Councils.
The question assumes significance as the Ethics and Medical Registration Board (EMRB) of the National Medical Commission (NMC) is moving to amend the Registration of Medical Practitioners and Licence to Practice Medicine Regulations, 2026.
The NMR is envisaged as a single, reliable national database that would make it easier to verify doctors’ qualifications and registration status and facilitate their practice across State boundaries. The system envisages a unique NMR identification number linked to every doctor’s State registration number.
The dispute now is over how this national database would be created -- is it the task of the State Medical Councils to provide the data for the creation of the NMR or should individual doctors have to put in application afresh, pay a fee and then await EMRB’s verification of credentials?
What the law says
Doctors point out that the NMC Act, 2019, already settles this. In Sections 31(1) , 31 (6) and 31 (7), the NMC Act says that the EMRB “shall maintain a National Register” of all licensed medical practitioners.; the State Medical Councils will maintain and update respective State Registers with the EMRB and that it will be the task of EMRB to maintain the National Register and ensure the electronic synchronisation with the State Registers.
“Nowhere in the NMC Act is it stated that it is the responsibility of registered medical practitioners to apply for NMR registration,” points out the Kannur-based doctor and RTI activist, K.V. Babu. Also, in a written reply in the Lok Sabha on August 5, 2025, the Union Health Ministry, quoting the NMC, had said that applying for NMR registration was voluntary.
Doctors therefore argue that the NMR should be populated from the verified data already held by State Medical Councils. “Our data is already with the State Medical Council and it just needs to be handed over to the EMRB. We fail to understand why the NMR database creation should be so complicated and why doctors are being put through the registration and verification formalities all over again,” says the State President of Indian Medical Association, Kerala, M.N. Menon
A registration backlog
The concern raised by doctors is genuine. Applications submitted by several doctors for NMR registration have remained pending before the EMRB for years, raising questions about the practicality of requiring every State-registered doctor to individually apply for national registration. According to the minutes of the NMC’s 17th meeting, fewer than 32,000 registered medical practitioners had applied for NMR registration by December 2025.
The cost angle
The issue also has a financial dimension. Doctors point out that they are already paying a substantial amount as registration and licensing-related charges to State Medical Councils. The registration fee that will be charged in the name of NMR will be another burden on doctors, Dr. Babu says.
Doctors have demanded that the NMC withdraw the proposed draft amendment and ask State Medical Councils to send its database to the EMRB for creating the NMR as well as the unique ID for doctors

Ted Cruz brutally booed on ESPN before Texas college football game: ‘You suck!’
Even some fans standing just behind Ted Cruz — who were visible on camera — joined in
Senator Ted Cruz was mercilessly booed during the Texas Longhorns game on Saturday morning in Austin.
Cruz, a Texas Republican, appeared on ESPN’s “College GameDay” from the stadium to discuss the Protect College Sports Act, which would create federal guidelines for college athletics.
“What we have right now is chaos. There are no rules,” Cruz said, citing student-athlete gambling, repeated transfers, extended eligibility and inadequate compensation as examples.
Shortly after the interview began, however, boos from the crowd at the University of Texas at Austin stadium swelled, at times making it difficult to hear the senator.
At one point, numerous people chanted over and over in unison: “Ted, you suck!” Even some of the young sports enthusiasts standing just behind Cruz — who were visible on camera — joined in.
The Republican, though, continued discussing the proposed legislation despite the crowd’s loud sounds of disapproval. He claimed the bill, which is supported by some Democrats, will have enough votes to pass in the Senate.
Cruz, who mounted an unsuccessful presidential bid in 2016 and has a new book out about Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas, has faced similar public confrontations before.
In 2022, Cruz was booed and flipped off at Yankee Stadium in New York. Later that year, he drew a similar reaction from attendees at the Astros’ World Series victory parade in Houston, where he appeared to duck a beer can.
And in 2024, college football fans circulated a petition to keep Cruz away from Longhorns games, fearing the Republican senator’s attendance would curse their chances of victory. It racked up some 1,500 signatures.
Cruz, an outspoken defender of President Donald Trump, is next up for re-election in 2030.
