OPINION: 25 years on, a nation still mourns
OPINION: 25 years on, a nation still mourns
Yesterday marked a quarter century since the 9-11 terrorist attacks. I still remember — I will always remember —walking the streets of Lower Manhattan through rows of faces in photographs pasted on lampposts and walls with urgent, wrenching words:
"Have you seen my wife?" "Last seen, 8:20 AM, Tuesday." "Have you seen our daughter?" "…our father?" "…my best friend?"
The question marks pierced into you like hooks.
The attacks of September 11, 2001, were attacks on America. But America is made up of the world.
The 2,977 people who were killed that day included people from more than 90 nations -- Canada, India, Great Britain, South Korea, the Dominican Republic and more. That's America.
This week, I remembered a poem dedicated to the 43 members of the Hotel Employees and Restaurant Employees International Union who came to work that morning at Windows on the World restaurant, atop the World Trade Center's North Tower. None of them survived the tower's collapse.
The poem is called 'Alabanza: In Praise of Local 100', by Martín Espada. It reads, in part:
Praise Manhattan from a hundred and seven flights up, like Atlantis glimpsed through the windows of an ancient aquarium.
Praise the great windows where immigrants from the kitchen could squint and almost see their world, hear the chant of nations: Ecuador, México, Republica Dominicana, Haiti, Yemen, Ghana, Bangladesh.
Alabanza. Praise the kitchen in the morning, where the gas burned blue on every stove and exhaust fans fired their diminutive propellers, hands cracked eggs with quick thumbs or sliced open cartons to build an altar of cans.
Alabanza. Praise the busboy's music, the chime-chime of his dishes and silverware in the tub.
Alabanza. Praise the dish-dog, the dishwasher who worked that morning because another dishwasher could not stop coughing, or because he needed overtime to pile the sacks of rice and beans for a family floating away on some Caribbean island plagued by frogs.
Alabanza. Praise the waitress who heard the radio in the kitchen and sang to herself about a man gone. Alabanza.
After the thunder wilder than thunder, after the shudder deep in the glass of the great windows-
Twenty-five years later, we still shudder to think of that day, and pause to praise those we lost in that thunder.

Alien Terrorist Removal Court deports legal US resident to Afghanistan in first-ever case
For the first time, the Justice Department brought a case before a decades-old but until now unused special court to deport a legal US resident to Afghanistan after she conceded to being an "alien terrorist," court records show.
Prosecutors alleged Nazira Haji Zada, 47, originally from Afghanistan, supported a plan by her son and son-in-law to commit an Islamic State-inspired mass shooting on Election Day in 2024, according to court documents. Both men have already been charged and will be deported following their release from prison. Haji Zada's son, Abdullah Haji Zada, 19, was sentenced to 15 years in prison.
Haji Zada was arrested in July at her home in Fort Worth, Texas, and had an initial hearing in late July. Instead of charging Haji Zada in the criminal justice system, leaders at the Justice Department launched the first-ever civil proceedings at the Alien Terrorist Removal Court. The secretive court allows for a lower standard of proof to remove a person from American soil.
Congress created the court in 1996 to make it easier for the DOJ to use classified evidence, that they say poses a risk to national security, to deport people.
In unsealed court filings dated Aug. 20, Haji Zada waived her rights to challenge the detention and agreed to the deportation. Senior U.S. District Judge Joan Ericksen ordered her removal the same day. Haji Zada's admission will not be used in criminal proceedings, and the documents were released to the public on Friday.
Haji Zada's court appointed attorneys, Matthew Farley and Mary Manning Petras, contested the constitutionality of the case in court filings, adding that they weren't permitted to review evidence. The evidence supporting the removal remains classified, the government said in court documents, because it poses a risk to national security.
Haji Zada's attorneys said in a statement that their client's choice to consent to the removal "should not be seen as an endorsement of this court's legitimacy."
"Dragging lawful permanent residents into court but refusing to show them or their attorneys the evidence that will be used against them is a plain violation of due process," the statement said. "We are confident that the Alien Terrorist Removal Court will be struck down as unconstitutional as soon as a judge is asked to address the issue."
Haji Zada came to the U.S. as a lawful permanent resident in 2018. Her husband was employed at the Bagram Air Base, the last major U.S. base in Afghanistan until it was turned over to Afghan forces in 2021, from 2009 to 2016.
As the family "matriarch," U.S. authorities alleged Haji Zada worked to "radicalize" her family and "formally pledged loyalty to ISIS." The government also alleged she and her son-in-law "worked to indoctrinate her children with ISIS ideology and have them pledge loyalty to ISIS."
Prosecutors also said the family allegedly raised funds for the terrorist attack by selling off furniture, computers, a mobile phone, and two vehicles. They added that Haji Zada signed a contract to sell the family's home, and along with other female family members and young male family members, planned to move to an ISIS-controlled location before the attack, which she hid from her "unsuspecting husband." Her son and son-in-law would remain behind to commit the terrorist attack, court documents show.
According to court records, Nasir Ahmad Tawhedi, Haji Zada's son-in-law, admitted that between June 2024 and October 2024, he conspired with at least one other person to purchase two AK-47 rifles, 500 rounds of ammunition and 10 magazines, with the goal of carrying out a mass-casualty attack. Court documents say Tawhedi communicated with an ISIS facilitator about his plan to buy the firearms for the plot on behalf of ISIS, "including asking the individual whether 500 rounds of ammunition would be sufficient."
Tawhedi, 28, pled guilty to two terrorism-related charges.
Attorney General Todd Blanche approved the government application before it went to the judge. In a statement, Blanche said the use of the court shows "how the Department will use every tool at its disposal to protect our country."
"This landmark case, resulting in the prompt removal of this alien terrorist to her country of origin, is a win for national security and the rule of law," Blanche said.

New Delhi: Members of the Brics grouping on Saturday issued a joint statement, calling for de-escalation in West Asia, condemning the 2025 Pahalgam terrorist attack, expressing concern over unilateral tariffs and pushing for reforms to global institutions. The unanimous statement, issued on the first day of the two-day Brics Leadership Summit under India’s presidency, is a diplomatic win for New Delhi after members failed to agree on a joint statement at the grouping’s foreign ministers’ meeting in May. The May meeting ended with India issuing a Chair’s statement and outcome document instead, after differences over the West Asia conflict exposed divergent positions among members. Quick answers to key questions The BRICS joint statement called for de-escalation in West Asia, condemned the Pahalgam terrorist attack, and emphasized the need for dialogue and diplomacy to achieve lasting peace and stability in the region. BRICS members flagged that unilateral tariffs and trade-restrictive actions threaten to disrupt global trade and international supply chains, calling for adherence to WTO rules to maintain an open trading system. India led extensive consultations and negotiations, successfully bridging differences and reconciling divergent positions, especially concerning the Middle East tensions, which resulted in a unanimous joint statement. The BRICS grouping condemned the Pahalgam terrorist attack in the strongest terms and reaffirmed their commitment to combating terrorism in all its forms, emphasizing collective accountability for such acts. Yes, the BRICS joint statement advocated for comprehensive reforms of global governance institutions to better reflect the realities of today's international landscape, particularly to amplify the voice and representation of the Global South. Expressing concern over the continued escalation of the West Asian crisis, the Declaration encouraged efforts – through dialogue and diplomacy – towards a long-term understanding that will contribute to lasting peace, security and stability in the region. It also underscored the need to work together to maintain the smooth flow of global trade, supply chains and energy, in accordance with applicable international law. The group's 11 members include Iran, Saudi Arabia and the UAE who are directly impacted by the conflict triggered by the joint US-Israeli strikes on Tehran on February 28. "Furthermore, we urge to ensure the protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure in accordance with the purposes and principles of the Charter of the United Nations in their entirety and interconnectedness, including respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the states," the member-nations said in the joint statement. It also raised concern over "deliberate attacks on civilian infrastructure and peaceful nuclear facilities under full safeguards of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), in violation of international law and relevant resolutions of the IAEA". "Nuclear safeguards, safety, and security must always be upheld, including in armed conflicts, to protect people and the environment from harm," it added. Brics, initially comprising Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa, expanded in 2024 to include Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, the UAE and Saudi Arabia, with Indonesia joining in 2025. The 11-member group accounts for a half of the world's population, 40% of its gross domestic product and almost a quarter of its exports. The group condemned "in the strongest terms the terrorist attack in Jammu and Kashmir on 22 April 2025, during which 26 people were killed and many more injured", denouncing any acts of terrorism as criminal and unjustifiable, "regardless of their motivation, whenever, wherever and by whomsoever committed". It reaffirmed pledge to combat terrorism in all its forms and manifestations, including the cross-border movement of terrorists, terror financing and safe havens. It also reiterated that terrorism should not be associated with any religion, nationality, civilization or ethnic group and that all those involved in terrorist activities and their support must be held accountable and brought to justice in accordance with relevant national and international law. The group flagged a proliferation of global trade-restrictive actions, whether in the form of tariffs or non-tariff measures, or protectionism under the guise of environmental objectives, stressing that these threaten to further cut global trade and disrupt international supply chains. "We voice serious concerns about the rise of unilateral tariff and non-tariff measures which distort trade and are inconsistent with WTO (World Trade Organization) rules," it said, promising to work together to bolster the global multilateral trade body's responsiveness to trade disruptions. The Brics members supported balanced, inclusive and concrete outcomes that bolster the multilateral trading system and enable it to better address evolving global challenges. It also condemned the imposition of unilateral coercive measures that are contrary to international law. Such measures, including in the form of unilateral economic sanctions and secondary sanctions, have far-reaching negative implications for human rights. These include rights to development, health and food security, of the general population of targeted states. "We call for the elimination of such unlawful measures, which undermine international law and the principles and purposes of the UN Charter," the declaration said. Echoing Prime Minister Narendra Modi's pitch for reforms to international governance systems to reflect today's realities and give Global South its due share in global decision-making and leadership, made at the leaders' summit just a few hours before, the declaration called for inclusive global governance and strengthening multilateralism. The members also pledged to further bolster coordination to make international financial institutions, such as World Banks and the International Monetary Fund, more representative, transparent and accountable. "We reiterate the urgent need to reform the Bretton Woods Institutions (BWI) to make them more agile, effective, credible, inclusive, fit for purpose, unbiased, accountable, and representative, to enhance their legitimacy," it said. The group's members also sought to deepen cooperation in boosting the accessibility of artificial intelligence (AI) resources while ensuring its safety, security, inclusiveness and reliability. "Leveraging AI for economic growth and social good and mitigating potential risks would be essential for promoting a just, fair, equitable and prosperous future of all countries, especially those of Global South," they said in the statement. Brics leaders spoke from their respective national perspectives, but there was a broad convergence on the need to make global governance institutions more representative, inclusive, effective and responsive to today's realities, Sudhakar Dalela, secretary (economic relations) in the ministry of external affairs, said at a press briefing after the leaders' session. The story so far: A rabies vaccine, that could be critical in preventing a fatal infection, has failed a mandatory potency test, after vials bearing the batch number of a genuine Abhayrab consignment were seized from an unlicensed premises in Delhi. The Central Drugs Laboratory (CDL), Kasauli, has declared the samples in question as “Not of Standard Quality” and “misbranded”, setting off an investigation into whether counterfeit vaccine was being manufactured or distributed.
Rabies is almost invariably fatal once clinical symptoms appear, while timely and quality-assured post-exposure vaccination can prevent complications and death. The immediate concern for investigators, therefore, is not only how the questioned vials came to bear the details of a genuine vaccine batch, but whether any person bitten by a potentially rabid animal received a product that lacked the required potency.
The samples, bearing batch number KE25012, were seized on April 22, 2026, during a joint enforcement operation by the Delhi Police Crime Branch and officials of the Delhi Drugs Control Department at an unlicensed residential premises in Mukherjee Nagar, Delhi. Four persons have been arrested in connection with the case, according to the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO).
The laboratory found that the questioned vials failed the prescribed potency test and differed from genuine reference samples in several respects. These included packaging, labelling, artwork, QR-code verification, cap colour and licence details.
Genuine batch or counterfeit? Where is the investigation going?
Indian Immunologicals Ltd. (IIL), which manufactures Abhayrab through its Human Biologicals Institute (HBI), has denied manufacturing the seized vials.
In a statement issued on September 4, the company said the genuine KE25012 batch comprised 83,370 vials, underwent the required testing and was released on November 7, 2025, through its authorised distribution network.
More significantly, IIL said the CDL identified 17 differences between the questioned vials and the genuine retention samples of the same batch submitted by HBI for batch release.
The company has submitted its manufacturing, quality-control, reconciliation and distribution records to CDSCO and has asked authorities to trace the source of the questioned vials and take action against those responsible. The CDL finding establishes that the seized samples were NSQ and misbranded. It does not establish that the genuine KE25012 batch manufactured by IIL was defective. IIL’s position is that its legitimate batch passed the prescribed testing and that the batch number may have been reproduced on unauthorised material.
What are authorities investigating?
Investigators now have to establish who manufactured the questioned vials, where they were stored, how they entered circulation and whether they reached patients through any part of the legitimate or informal medicine supply chain.
A particularly important question is whether anyone was administered the suspect vaccine. If so, authorities may have to determine the nature of the exposure, the treatment received and whether additional medical intervention is required.
The Drugs Controller General of India has asked State and Union Territory drug controllers to maintain strict vigilance over the movement, distribution and availability of Abhayrab bearing batch number KE25012 and to take appropriate regulatory action.
CDSCO has also stated that no part of the concerned genuine batch was exported to another country.
International counterfeit rabies products
The case follows a suspected counterfeit Abhayrab episode involving batch KA24014 in 2025. IIL had reported suspected counterfeit vials to authorities, following which health warnings were issued in some countries over the possibility that travellers to India could have received counterfeit rabies vaccine.
That episode highlighted the international dimension of counterfeit rabies products. Travellers exposed to rabies may begin treatment in one country and complete their vaccination schedule elsewhere. A falsified vaccine can therefore create a public-health concern beyond the country in which it was obtained.
In the present case, however, CDSCO has said no part of the genuine KE25012 batch was exported. The investigation will have to establish whether the questioned vials were entirely domestic and, crucially, whether they entered patient use.
Why rabies vaccine matters?
Rabies is a viral disease that affects the central nervous system and is transmitted mainly through the saliva of infected animals, usually through bites or scratches. Dogs account for up to 99% of human rabies transmission globally. Once clinical symptoms appear, the disease is virtually 100% fatal.
Yet rabies is preventable. Prompt post-exposure prophylaxis involves thorough wound washing, vaccination and, for appropriate severe exposures, rabies immunoglobulin or other recommended biologicals. Quality-assured PEP can prevent the virus from progressing to the nervous system.
This makes the quality of a rabies vaccine particularly consequential. For a person exposed to a potentially rabid animal, the vaccine is not routine preventive medicine; it is a time-sensitive intervention intended to prevent a disease that, once symptomatic, offers virtually no chance of survival.
India’s rabies burden
India continues to bear a substantial share of the global rabies burden. A recent ICMR-National Institute of Epidemiology estimate cited by WHO puts annual human rabies deaths in India at 5,726, alongside an estimated 9.1 million animal bites each year.
Globally, WHO estimates about 59,000 people die of rabies each year, with more than 95% of deaths occurring in Asia and Africa.
The suspected circulation of a misbranded rabies vaccine therefore raises a question that goes beyond counterfeit packaging or regulatory compliance: whether a person who believes they have received life-saving protection has actually received a vaccine capable of providing it.
What happens next?
The Union Health Ministry maintained that the immediate task is to establish the origin and distribution of the questioned KE25012 vials and determine whether any patient received them. Authorities will also have to establish the scale of any unauthorised manufacturing or distribution network.
For IIL, the laboratory comparison, together with its manufacturing and distribution records, will help determine whether the episode concerns a manufacturing-quality failure or the unauthorised use of its product identity and batch details.
For patients and healthcare providers, the case reinforces the importance of obtaining rabies vaccines through licensed hospitals, clinics and pharmacies and reporting suspicious products to drug-control authorities.
With rabies, the margin for error is exceptionally small. A genuine, potent vaccine administered promptly can prevent a fatal disease; a counterfeit product can create the dangerous illusion that protection has been provided.

A rumor that U.S. President Donald Trump claimed in a speech he had saved victims of the 1912 sinking of the RMS Titanic is spreading online.
According to social media posts sharing the claim, Trump said he "saved more people than anybody," told the ship's captain to "turn left," and that "nobody knows icebergs better than [him]." This is despite the fact, of course, that Trump was born in 1946, meaning he was not alive in 1912 when the ship famously sank.
Some users seemed to interpret the claim about the Titanic as true, and readers contacted us to investigate its legitimacy.
We found that Trump made no such assertion, and the rumor is false.
To investigate the rumor's legitimacy, we first used search engines such as DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo. If Trump truly had mentioned assisting rescuers on the Titanic in a speech, journalists with reputable news outlets, such as The Associated Press or Reuters, would have widely reported on it, and those search inquiries would have uncovered such evidence.
That was not the case. We did not find any credible reporting suggesting that Trump had mentioned the Titanic during a recent speech.
Snopes traced the claim as far back as an X post made on the afternoon of Sept. 8, but could not definitively confirm that post as the rumor's origin. However, it neatly aligned with a speech Trump gave earlier that day at a tribute event for the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks, in which he repeated a long-standing claim that he participated in relief efforts. A transcript of that speech included no mention of the Titanic.
Given the timing of those remarks, we concluded that Trump's words about 9/11 in that speech served as inspiration for the fictitious rumor, which we suspect was intended as satirical. However, the earliest account we found that shared the claim did not indicate that in its post. Snopes contacted the X user to confirm our suspicions, but had not heard back by publication.

Police in Thailand have arrested a senior Buddhist monk on suspicion of embezzling $2.8m intended for his monastery, alongside a suspected female accomplice he was filmed having sex with.
The case is the latest scandal to hit the clergy in the Buddhist-majority country, after a sex and extortion case involving senior monks last year prompted public outrage and calls for greater scrutiny of temple finances.
Phra Wachirayan Wi, the 66-year-old abbot of the 14th-century temple Wat Phutthaisawan in the ancient capital of Ayutthaya, was arrested on Thursday on charges including embezzlement and money laundering, according to the lead police investigator Pattanasak Bupphasuwan.
A 47-year-old woman accused of helping convert and conceal the money was also arrested.
Leaked CCTV footage of the pair having sex on a table in the monk’s residence was widely broadcast on Thai media.
In Thailand, Buddhist monks take a vow of celibacy and also renounce material possessions.
Police began investigating Phra Wachirayan in mid-July after receiving an anonymous tip alleging him of misconduct and misuse of temple funds.
Pattanasak, a commander of the police crime suppression division, said investigators identified two streams of money linked to donation receipts issued in the temple’s name.
About 89m baht ($2.7m or £2m) was donated for temple renovations, with another 2.8m baht in payments for Buddhist amulets and other sacred objects, he said.
“But the money from both streams did not enter the temple’s account – not a single baht,” Pattanasak told a news conference on Friday.
He said authorities had seized assets worth about 215m baht, including 16kg (35lb) of gold bars and jewellery and 28 land title deeds.
Police are investigating which are personal property and which belong to the temple.
“We will expand the investigation to identify other people involved and restore public confidence in Buddhism,” said Nattasak Chaowanasai, the commissioner of Thailand’s Central Investigation Bureau.
Wat Phutthaisawan is a prominent royal monastery with a large following that includes government officials, businesspeople, police and military personnel.
The former abbot, also known as Luang Pho Atichot, was well known for making amulets, with the Thai prime minister, Anutin Charnvirakul, reported to be among those who wore his creations.
The abbot was defrocked shortly after his arrest.
Last year, police arrested a woman accused of blackmailing at least 11 monks she had sex with, extorting nearly $12m of monastery funds from them, in a case that shook Thailand.

Did a goat herder's lucky $200 nugget spark a gold rush in western Kenya?
- Published
A goat herder from a remote area of western Kenya has told the BBC his discovery of a golden nugget has sparked a gold rush, overwhelming his small village over the last few weeks.
When people found out that 33-year-old Manasse Lomachar had sold his three grams of gold for 36,000 Kenyan shillings ($280; £205) several weeks ago, he believes this led to thousands of prospectors arrived in Cheporor.
And it is true that what last month was just bushland and rough grazing ground near the village is now scarred by pits, mounds of earth and makeshift mining camps.
It is not clear if was Lomachar's lucky find or other recent discoveries that sparked the excitement. But local authorities estimate that about 10,000 people arrived at the height of the rush.
Even a small amount of the precious metal can transform the futures of these men and women - from Kenya and neighbouring Uganda - many of whose precarious lives rest on an unreliable farming income.
People do sometimes pan for gold in these parts - but rarely find anything significant.
Lomachar's says his discovery came about purely by chance. While he was searching for a missing goat he encountered a group of women panning along a riverbed.
"I joined them, and that's how [the village] realised there was gold in this area," he says.
Farmer and herder Patrick Lokolia, from neighbouring Napawoi village, joined the gold rush hoping to earn some extra money to support his family.
"I have children in school, and paying school fees has been a big problem for me," he tells the BBC wearing an old Chelsea football top and standing amid the mining activity.
Eighteen-year-old Abigael Chelengat says she had never mined before coming to Cheporor from a nearby district, but arrived hoping to find enough gold to pay her school fees and help keep her younger siblings in school.
Behind her hundreds of people work side by side, hacking into the rocky ground with hoes and shovels.
Others carry the earth to a nearby seasonal river, where mostly women crouch in the murky water, washing and sifting mud and sand hoping to detect a tiny trace of the element.
Some of the more experienced miners are deep in holes excavating the earth and drilling at rocks with the same goal.
Hope is kept alive by stories of those for whom the effort has paid off - like Lomachar.
Samuel Kiarie, the deputy commissioner of West Pokot county, says he thinks the rush began after two notable discoveries.
"Young men found what appeared to be a substantial amount of gold. The following day, women made another significant find in the same area," he tells the BBC.
Kiarie explains that women have been finding small quantities of alluvial gold along the same seasonal riverbed for years, typically earning $8-$23 a week.
But the uncovering of larger quantities at the beginning of August is what caught the attention of many people.
Kiarie reckons as rumours spread, the number and size of the discoveries were exaggerated - drawing in ever larger groups of people with little or no mining experience who hoped to replicate the reported early successes.
Since the initial rush, the number of prospectors has gone down to around 2,500 as some have given up the search.
While there is little doubt that some gold has been found in the area, questions remain about the size of the deposit in the earth and its commercial potential.
"I can confirm that small-scale gold traders told us they received an average of about 100 people every day," the deputy commissioner says - though whether the finds were actually gold is not known.
Individual discoveries reportedly range from amounts worth a few hundred Kenyan shillings to one find valued at approximately 78,000 shillings ($600).
West Pokot county borders Uganda, and communities on both sides have long-standing social and family ties.
Mugisha Godfrey, an artisanal miner from Busia in eastern Uganda, travelled to Cheporor after hearing about the discovery from a friend.
He immediately set out for the village spending about 100,000 Ugandan shillings ($27) to get there.
However, the living conditions in Cheporor are not favourable, he says.
"We sleep under the trees, and when morning comes, we continue working. Sometimes we work both day and night," Godfrey tells the BBC.
So far, he has found nothing. But he is not discouraged.
"We can't return unless we find something. Only when we have found what we need can we go back home," he says.
For others, the gold rush has created opportunities without requiring them to dig.
More than 200 businesses have emerged around the site, according to local officials, selling food, water and other essentials to the village's new population.
Irene Ameja travelled from neighbouring Baringo county to cater to the crowds. She sells bottled water, soft drinks, bread, milk and other foodstuffs.
"I am hoping that when I leave, I will have made enough money to continue with my business and expand it," she says.
But the rapid growth of the settlement has also exposed the area's lack of basic services.
"This is a forest and we are in the middle of the mountains," she says. "We don't have clean water to drink or even to bathe."
For women, she adds, the challenges become greater after dark: "You have to find somewhere safe to stay because most of the people sleeping here are men."
Local officials admit the influx has placed enormous pressure on an area with little infrastructure, no piped water and limited sanitation.
Public health officials have been deployed to monitor conditions and help prevent disease outbreaks.
The authorities say they have also increased security patrols amid concerns over sexual violence and the vulnerability of women and girls at the site.
Officials are also worried that children could be drawn into mining activities as schools prepare to reopen in September.
Measures are being put in place to discourage young people from remaining at the site once the new school term begins.
Those still searching are increasingly turning to deeper excavation.
Several truckloads of material have already been transported to nearby Ortum town for processing, with the authorities awaiting the results.
Until then, the size and commercial viability of any mining remain uncertain.
For Lomachar, the answer is not to stop the mining, but to make it more organised.
He wants the government to help local miners establish safer and more effective ways of finding and extracting the gold.
"We would ask the government to help us with things like metal detectors, which could help us find out whether there are other minerals here, so that our community can develop," he says.
He points to the homes nearby as evidence of the area's poverty.
"If you look around, there are hardly any houses with iron-sheet roofs; most are just thatched houses."

Mumbai, September 12, 2026: The special court on Thursday acquitted an absconding man booked in 1989 for dacoity after conducting his trial under the provisions for trial in absentia. The same judge has so far closed several cases after conducting trial even when the accused are still wanted. The same judge is now going to hear the prosecution's plea to conduct the trial against absconding accused in the 26/11 terror attack case in their absence.
Cases From Past Decades Reopened
Special judge Satyanarayan Navander has so far disposed of several cases registered in the 90s and 80s and pending before the court as the accused were absconding. In what is said to be the first of the cases he had, in December last year, acquitted Rajendra Giri, resident of Sakinaka, for having looted a house with valuables worth Rs 3.80 lakh at gunpoint on March 31, 1992.
Similarly, in many such cases, the court appointed a lawyer to defend the absconding accused who had been declared as proclaimed offenders, from the panel of legal aid lawyers to conduct the trial in their absence.
Trial In Absentia Under BNSS
Special judge Navander had in his judgment dated December 18, 2025, said, “as per section 356 of BNSS (deals with proceedings against proclaimed offender) when a person is declared as a proclaimed offender and it is found that, he has absconded to evade trial, and there is no immediate prospect of arresting him, he can be tried as if he is present. The provision of trial in absentia has been thus provided by BNSS, provided the accused is defended by a competent lawyer.”
After Navander, now other courts have also initiated the process to conduct the trial in the cases which are pending because of the absence of the accused. Special judge A. S. Wairagade, dealing with cases of child sexual abuse, also opened around five cases last month which were registered between 1988 to 2003, where accused are still absconding. The court has now framed charges against them to conduct trial in absence of the accused.
More Dormant Cases Taken Up
Similarly, special judge Mahesh Jadhav, too, opened dormant cases pending because the accused are absconding. The special court on September 9 acquitted resident of Thane, Jaspalsingh Chaulansingh, booked for murder charges in August 1986. The court conducted a trial against Chaulansingh while he still remains absconding. Meanwhile, the other accused in the case were acquitted in 1996.

Two men and a teenage boy have been arrested in Portsmouth at a far-right protest against immigration.
Far-right activists have gathered in Portsmouth for a second weekend after a small boat with 140 people seeking asylum on board was intercepted last Sunday while heading towards the city.
They were greeted by counter-protesters as police warned they would not tolerate incitement of fear or violence.
One of the arrested, a 76-year-old man from Southampton, was detained on suspicion of concealing his identity at the Portsmouth protest. Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary had warned that protesters wearing face coverings could be arrested under powers in the Crime and Policing Act.
A 33-year-old man from Portsmouth was also arrested on suspicion of obstructing a highway and a 16-year-old boy, also from Portsmouth, was arrested on suspicion of violent disorder in relation to scenes last Sunday.
Donna Jones, the police and crime commisioner for Hampshire and Isle of Wight, said that they “thankfully didn’t see repeated scenes of Sunday night with assaults on police officers and criminal damage to police vehicles and people’s property” and that “with the exception of a few people, it was peaceful and conducted in accordance with the new law calling for their faces to be uncovered”.
Jones added: “The people of Portsmouth deserve to go about their business without fear and disruption.
“While some may think it was arbitrary to use the new power directing people to remove face coverings, the police ensured it was implemented equally and impartially for everyone involved.
“I will ensure this power is used proportionately in the future for both sides of the spectrum of protesters.”
In Portsmouth city centre, there was a large police presence where demonstrators assembled to march on Saturday.
Some protesters held union flags while some wearing Portsmouth patriot branded clothing gathered outside All Saints Church on Commercial Road.
A man with a megaphone got the crowd chanting “stop the boats”. He said the protest was against “illegal men invading the shores”.
In the neighbouring car park, demonstrators holding Stand Up to Racism (SUTR) and Refugees Welcome banners gathered. Signs included: “RNLI are heroes, no one is illegal” and “stop pretending your racism is patriotism”.
Hundreds of people also gathered in Glasgow for an anti-immigration rally and associated counter-protest.
The Pink Ladies movement organised their event at Glasgow Green, prompting opposing groups, including SUTR, to arrange a counter-protest.
The two groups were contained in separate areas on the eastern side of the park, with the People’s Palace and a heavy police presence between them.
Ch Supt Stevie Dolan warned of a “strong response” if there was any violence after flashpoints at a previous protest in the same park in July.
MSPs Alison Thewliss, a Scottish government minister, and Iris Duane were at the SUTR rally, with the Scottish Trades Union Congress general secretary Roz Foyer.
Prominent figures on the Scottish right, such as Reform UK’s deputy leader in Scotland, Thomas Kerr, and the Reform councillor Audrey Dempsey, attended the Pink Ladies event.
Saturday’s protests came after hundreds of far-right activists descended on Portsmouth last Sunday after a small boat crossing the Channel approached the city. The demonstrators tried to stop those onboard from being processed.
Hampshire police said: “We will support those who want to express their views peacefully and lawfully, but we will not tolerate those whose only aim is to create fear and incite violence.”
The opposing groups were allocated specific locations at which they could gather under protest conditions. Failure to comply with conditions could lead to arrest, police said. The anti-immigration protest marched to Guildhall Square and the counter-protest followed later on the same route.
The incident with the small boat last Sunday is thought to be the first time such a large vessel containing asylum seekers has been brought to Portsmouth and the first time a significant group of anti-migrant protesters have tried to block newly arrived asylum seekers from being processed.
Small boat crossings have fallen by more than 40% compared with the same period last year. While the Home Office has disrupted the smugglers’ business model, their methods appear to have evolved by launching boats – such as the one that arrived on last Sunday – from different parts of the French coast much farther from the UK, making the crossings more dangerous.
Most small boat arrivals are rescued by Border Force and RNLI vessels on the English side of the Channel and brought ashore at Dover. RNLI volunteers and staff have faced abuse from protesters over their rescue work bringing some small boat migrants ashore.
The first man charged over last weekend’s anti-migrant demonstration in Portsmouth appeared in court on Saturday.
Del Leon Somerville, 42, of Paulsgrove in Portsmouth, appeared before the city’s magistrates court charged with violent disorder and assaulting a police constable in the execution of their duty.
Assistant chief constable Tony Rowlinson said Somerville’s arrest was the “first of what we fully anticipate to be a number of arrests” and hoped it would send a “clear warning” to those planning future disruption and disorder.
The government condemned what it described as the “thuggish behaviour” of the protesters last Sunday. “We condemn the intimidating and thuggish behaviour we are seeing tonight,” a government spokesperson said. “The right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but it must never cross a line into disorder.”
The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, met police on Thursday for reassurance they are ready to move quickly in dealing with “far-right groups” seeking to intimidate communities after last weekend’s events in Dover and Portsmouth. Official vehicles were damaged in Portsmouth and a small number of officers were injured, police said. In Dover, crowds of masked men blocked road access to the port in scenes that were condemned by politicians of all parties.
Mahmood said: “These scenes have caused disruption for people and, given that people are dressed in black wearing balaclavas, there is a fear factor and obvious malign intent being communicated to our residents.
“This makes it different from other protests, so we need to make sure we are learning lessons.”

Iraq scrambles to address fallout from alleged militia attack on Saudi oil pipeline
Iran-backed militias deny involvement in strike
Iraq's government was racing Saturday to contain the fallout after local Iran-backed militias were accused of attacking and shuttering a key Saudi pipeline.
Though an umbrella group of Iran-backed militias in Iraq denied their involvement, Iraq's government confirmed the attacks had originated from its territory. The government pledged to investigate and dismissed a military commander.
The country is under mounting pressure to prevent local militias from aiding other Iran proxy groups across the region. The Iraqi government has set a Sept. 30 deadline for non-state groups to disarm, but several of the most powerful militias have said they will not comply.
Pressure to disarm the militias is especially acute as the Iran-backed Houthi rebels make an advance across Yemen’s west coast in a major setback to the Saudi-backed coalition that risks escalating the war in the region. The Houthis on Friday seized an island in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a key shipping lane through which about 12 per cent of global trade passes.
Their virtual control of the strait could send global oil prices — already inflated by the six-month Iran-U.S. war — spiralling. The strait has become a vital commercial lane for Saudi oil ever since the Iran war disrupted shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
Asked about the region on Saturday while speaking to reporters in Dublin, U.S. President Donald Trump said Iran was "probably" responsible for the pipeline attack but tried to calm concerns.
He said his administration has "had discussions" with the Houthis, though he did not specify to which talks he was referring.
"The Houthis called us, and they don't want to fight with us," Trump said. "They would much prefer not having us involved, and they're letting most ships go through."
Iraq to investigate attack on Saudi pipeline
A group of Iran-backed militias in Iraq denied in a statement on Saturday that they were responsible for the attacks on the East-West crude oil pipeline in Saudi Arabia, while praising the Houthis for their "ongoing battlefield victories against Saudi forces."
The group said it would co-operate with the Iraqi government's investigation.
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said earlier Saturday that he'd ordered an investigation into the operations command of Maysan province, along the border with Iran, and dismissed the province's commander.
Saudi Arabia shut down the major, cross-country oil pipeline on Friday, calling it a "precautionary measure" after the pipeline came under drone attack. It blamed the attacks on several drones that came from Iraq but said the kingdom would not retaliate, to give the Iraqi government "an opportunity to take the necessary measures."
Several Arab countries, including Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates, Oman and Egypt, condemned the attack on Saturday, according to the Saudi state news agency.
Built in the 1980s, the East-West pipeline has played an important role in Saudi Arabia's ability to export oil following the disruption of the Strait of Hormuz during the Iran war. By early June, Saudi Arabia had more than doubled oil exports from the Red Sea port at the pipeline's end to more than five million barrels per day, according to the International Energy Agency.
Tehran-backed Iraqi militias have carried out strikes on U.S.-linked targets both inside and outside of Iraq since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28, and have co-ordinated with Yemen's Houthi rebels to attack Saudi Arabia.
Iraq closes border crossings with Iran
In a move possibly linked to the investigation, Iraq closed two key border crossings with Iran, Iraq's state-run news agency reported Saturday.
The report said that Iraqi officials were at the border, investigating previous "violations and infractions" at the crossings.
Valiollah Hayati, the deputy governor of Iran's southwestern Khuzestan province, named the closed crossings as Shalamcheh and Chazabeh. They are among the main official border crossings between Iran and Iraq.
Iranian state media said the measure would halt all passenger and commercial traffic through the two crossings until further notice.
Saudi Arabia and the United States bombed Iranian-backed militias in Iraq in July after blaming them for drone attacks on Saudi oil facilities that had been claimed by the Houthis. Regional officials told The Associated Press that the Houthis helped the Iraqi militias plan and execute the attacks.
Fighting threatens to reignite Yemen’s civil war
The escalating fighting threatens to end a fragile truce that had largely halted Yemen's civil war since 2022. At stake are 40 million people in the Arab world's poorest country. The conflict killed 150,000 and brought many others to the brink of famine.
The surge in fighting in the past week has sent more than 46,000 people fleeing, the United Nations migration agency said Friday.
The Houthis have been at war with Yemen's government since 2014, when the rebels seized much of northern and central Yemen and the capital, Sanaa. Saudi Arabia entered the war the following year on the side of the government.

There isn’t much that we Indians agree on these days. GDP numbers are no exception. Last week, India released glowing GDP numbers for the latest quarter – 7.8% growth – higher than the forecast 7%. It sparked a furore.
Subhash Garg, a former finance secretary under Narendra Modi’s government and now a critic, reframed what Modi called a “herculean feat” as mere smoke and mirrors. According to Garg, the government revised last year’s current-price GDP downwards to inflate this year’s number – he believes the real growth is only 2.6%.
The assertion, made on a television channel, immediately went viral. A flurry of op-eds and hot takes have been published since. Supporters of the government, predictably, rejected the claims. Those who have questions agree on a more fundamental problem: a lack of transparency and statistical credibility in India’s economic data. So why is there no consensus?
Over the past decade, critics say, the government has systematically hollowed out the integrity of its own data infrastructure, weaponising economic data for political gain and creating a trust deficit. Methodologies have been changed, crucial surveys have faced long delays and there have been attempts to suppress inconvenient findings.
In November, the International Monetary Fund rated India’s national accounts data a ‘C’ on a four-point scale, the second-lowest grade. In its report, the IMF said some of the methodologies are outdated, including relying on an old base year, unexplained discrepancies between GDP calculated from the production and expenditure side, as well as a lack of seasonal data.
India’s statistical system once commanded respect, and its data on economic and social indicators was considered rigorous. There might have been disagreements on the quality of estimates but their independence was widely accepted. That trust appears to have eroded in recent years.
“There seems to be a systematic effort by the government to hide the truth,” said R Nagaraj, an economist who taught at the Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, adding that some of the other contested datasets include employment numbers, poverty numbers, health data and consumption data. “Over the last 10 years, the government has changed the methodology for many of these, raising questions. They have apparently also removed critical officials who headed some surveys. All of this adds to the scepticism.”
In one of the most prominent examples, from 2019, a Business Standard journalist revealed that the government had not published an official report showing unemployment at a 45-year high of 6.1%. Two expert members of the National Statistical Commission resigned in protest. The government initially denied it, calling it a draft. The figures were only released months later.
Then there is the census, which for the first time since independence, was delayed in 2021. Economists say relying on outdated demographic data means, among other things, inequitable allocation of welfare entitlements. (The first phase of the latest census finally began in April 2026.)
Nagaraj has witnessed some of this first-hand. He served on a subcommittee in 2014 whose report forms a part of the GDP. “The [numbers] we had discussed in the committee and what came out in the final report were different. So, I had to raise a red flag,” he said. The difference was notable: one figure in the published report had been inflated by 108%.
But government economists reject the ongoing criticism of the GDP numbers. Shamika Ravi, a member of the Economic Advisory Council to the prime minister, described it as a “noisy and very ill-informed debate” arguing that political leanings, not data, are behind the criticism.
The IMF rating was expected, she said. “The IMF rating of ‘C’ is the same rating that China has for its statistics. Several large developing or just developed economies have data issues.” Revisions to its calculations that the government was accused of having manipulated, she added, were precisely the sorts of changes the IMF had recommended.
The sticking point, as some including India’s former chief statistician Pronab Sen have pointed out, is the trustworthiness of the underlying data used.
Complicating this debate is the reality for many Indians. This year, young people have taken to the streets in frustration. Protests, which first began over leaked examination papers, have crystallised into a broader reckoning over systemic failures in education, jobs and the promise of a better future.
Almost 40% of graduates under 25 are unemployed, a recent report by Azim Premji University concluded. An estimated 87 million (8.7 crore) Indians between 15 and 29 are neither working, studying, nor doing skill training, a government thinktank reported last month.
That is why we should care about data quality, economists say. Incorrect data means bad policy. As economist Reetika Khera wrote in her recent book, Freebies or Rights: “Data shines the light to guide policymaking and is important for informed public debates.” As evidence, she points to gaps in basic statistics such as urbanisation and literacy numbers due to the delayed census. The consequences, she argues, are not abstract. Because the government still relies on outdated population numbers to decide who gets food subsidies, she estimates approximately 100 million (10 crore) people who should be covered are being deprived.
The controversy is making waves further ashore. In Sri Lanka, where second-quarter GDP figures are expected, the Daily FT newspaper wrote: “One hopes Sri Lankan policymakers and experts are not watching the theatrics in India with watering mouths and dreaming up smart arguments. Spare us such theatre!”
What else we’re reading about
Lollapalooza | British pop star Olivia Dean is to perform in India for the first time in January when she headlines Lollapalooza 2027 in Mumbai. Limp Bizkit is another headline act at the two-day event. Indian artists on the lineup include Ricky Kej (performing with Stewart Copeland) and Aditya Gadhvi.
The price of gold | Prime Minister Narendra Modi asked Indians once again to refrain from buying gold and travelling abroad. He had first made an appeal to self-reliance in May, in part to conserve India’s declining foreign exchange reserves amid a rise in import prices and global energy shocks.
Census 2027 | The new and expanded questionnaire for the 2027 census is raising concerns, reports Scroll’s Anant Gupta. The questionnaire asks respondents for details about their identity documents, as well as their parents’ religion and place of birth. Several of these questions were part of the controversial National Population Register that has remained in abeyance since 2020 and was controversial due to fears that the data might be used to target minorities through a citizenship registry.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
Singer Prateek Kuhad (@prateekkuhad), whose latest album, Full Moon Chamber, was released in July, shares an indulgent treat: “I’m a big fan of artisanal Indian chocolate makers. I really like Manam, Carra and Naviluna, and there are many others. Although India has been growing cacao [commercially] since the 1960s, its craft bean-to-bar movement is more recent. Even a plain chocolate bar from one of these makers can be remarkably complex and delicious. More people outside India should know about it and try it.”
Count it
A number worth knowing
4,756,000
One-third of the electorate in Delhi, about 4.76 million voters, have been deleted from the draft voting list as the Election Commission carries out a contentious revision of its rolls across states. So far, about 130 million names have been dropped from draft rolls in 30 states and union territories, the Indian Express reported.
Vibe check
Earlier this year, Shakira’s concerts in India was postponed. But Rajasthani folk musicians the Ismail Langa Group (@ismaillanga_official) decided the music had to go on, in their own way. Their mashup of the Colombian star’s Hips Don’t Lie with the traditional folk song called Moruda has got everyone grooving (42m views and counting).
It took two months to pull off, says creative director Jagirdar RV. Most artists in the group, aged between 23 and 60, don’t speak or read English and learned the lyrics by rote. The song choice was simple, he said, because it “has a very nice vibe which matched our vibe”.
It’s been a breakout year for the group, which had a semi-final run on India’s Got Talent and are becoming known for taking folk songs to gen Z audiences on Instagram. They are working on their next English mashup – just not spilling which song, yet.

A food safety officer has become a social media star in India - why?
- Published
The images are hard to ignore.
Cockroaches scurry across kitchen floors. Spider webs cling to walls. Spoiled vegetables rot in corners, while food counters show signs of pest infestation.
One might assume these scenes belong to a struggling restaurant. But the photos are from a members-only club in Mumbai - India's financial capital and the capital of its richest state Maharashtra.
They are among dozens of photos and videos that have gone viral since May, after Maharashtra's Food and Drug Administration (FDA) began a series of inspections at restaurants, cafes and other food businesses across the state.
At the centre of the crackdown is 51-year-old civil servant Tukaram Mundhe, the state's new food commissioner.
Since taking charge in May, Mundhe has overseen thousands of inspections and says food safety laws must be enforced regardless of a business's size, influence or reputation.
His department has suspended the licences of several quick-commerce warehouses and sent notices to Bollywood celebrities for doing advertisements suspected of indirectly promoting restricted products.
"These actions are taken in public health interest. We will continue to take them against violations," Mundhe told the BBC.
The campaign has made Mundhe a recognisable face across India, rare for a civil servant.
Videos of his inspections and press briefings circulate widely on social media, where reels and podcasts have turned him into an unlikely celebrity.
But the spotlight - and the controversy that often comes with it - is nothing new to him.
An officer in the Indian Administrative Service, Mundhe has more than two decades of experience and has been transferred so often that reports say the number exceeds his years in service, though he declines to confirm it.
"I have stopped counting my transfers," he told the BBC.
Admirers see the transfers as evidence of his uncompromising style. Critics argue that this confrontational approach has put him at odds with colleagues and elected representatives.
In the past decade, Mundhe has won praise for his handling of the Covid pandemic outbreak during his time as Nagpur city's municipal commissioner and earlier for his work on water conservation in Maharashtra's drought-prone regions.
"When he was transferred out of Nagpur during the pandemic, thousands showed up outside his home to bid him farewell. It took him an hour just to reach his car," says Shafi Pathan, a journalist who's written Mundhe's biography in the local Marathi language.
But his food-safety crackdown has brought him the most attention yet.
The scale of India's food-safety problem is serious and numbers presented to the parliament in July offer a glimpse of just how widespread the issue is.
Of 223,808 food samples tested across India in 2025 and 2026, nearly one in five, external were found to be "non-conforming" - which means the samples were either unsafe, substandard or mislabelled.
And Mundhe has responded with an unusually aggressive enforcement drive.
By the end of July, his department had carried out more than 3,100 inspections across the state - a number he expects has since crossed 4,000.
Around 300 licences had been suspended and more than 1,000 improvement notices issued. A new complaints portal had also received more than 16,000 complaints in its first three months, Mundhe said.
"Hygiene has always been a problem here," Pawan Agarwal, former chief of India's food regulator, told the BBC. "What Mundhe has done differently is make it visible".
Consumers have responded positively to that visibility, Agarwal says. Unlike in India's conventional system, where food safety cases and consumer complaints can take years to move through regulators and courts, enforcement actions are now playing out in public.
The campaign has also made Mundhe a social media star - he now has more than 3.8 million followers on Instagram.
However, even as consumers welcome the speed and visibility of his actions, many in the food industry are less enthusiastic.
Restaurant associations allege the official has been bypassing a statutory process, while courts have termed some of his actions "high-handed".
Under India's food safety laws, businesses are usually given time to fix violations before regulators suspend or cancel their licences. Regulators can suspend licences immediately only in urgent public health situations but must record their reasons.
"While compliance is non-negotiable, high-handed approaches - like public naming-and-shaming, instant suspensions over minor procedural or rectifiable issues and treating administrative oversights with harsh penal measures - create panic rather than reform," said Niranjan Laxman Shetty, legal chairman of hospitality association Indian Hotel and Restaurant Association.
Responding to the criticism, Mundhe said his raids are lawful and that suspensions are only for extreme cases. However, some businesses have publicly claimed that they've been shut over minor violations, without warning or a chance to improve first.
His actions have also faced legal challenges. In some cases, courts have overturned licence suspensions, ordered compensation for affected businesses and criticised the regulator's approach.
In August, for instance, the Bombay high court ordered, external Mundhe's department to pay 500,000 rupees ($5,291; £3,893) in compensation to a sweets shop whose licence remained suspended even after a reinspection found it 98% compliant with the law.
The court said the regulator's intentions were "laudable" but that it had "gone overboard".
The judges also raised a question - was the regulator applying the same scrutiny to government establishments as it was to private businesses?
Within a day of that criticism, Mundhe's team inspected canteens in the state's high court complex and flagged violations.
For Mundhe, it is proof that the rules apply equally to everyone.
"Had the food business operators or establishment complied with existing regulations, I would not be needed to take those actions," Mundhe told the BBC.
He also insists that they are not trying to shut down businesses but only ensure safety.
"We are not here to close down or suspend every licensee," he said at an event last week. "We are here to ensure food is safe, food is not substandard, it is not misbranded and it is good for consumption."
The restaurant inspections - which dominate social media - are only a part of his work.
Mundhe has enforced bans on using newspapers to wrap food, synthetic dyes and banned analogue paneer - non-dairy cottage cheese substitutes.
Its focus has now shifted to schools. The department has ordered canteens, hostel kitchens and midday meal suppliers to obtain proper licences, and banned the sale of food high in fat, sugar or salt within 50m of schools.
But the bigger question is what happens once Mundhe moves on to his next post.
"The efforts of Mundhe have created a nationwide awareness about food safety, both amongst businesses and consumers, which is desirable - but not sustainable," says Agarwal.
The challenge is to build systems that outlast an individual officer, he adds.
For now, however, the effects are being felt even on the streets.
Yuvraj Yadav, who sells sandwiches in a Mumbai suburb, says he used to wrap them in discarded newspapers, despite concerns that chemicals in the printing ink can leach into food. He recently switched to greaseproof paper after hearing about the ban.
"We started this a few months ago after newspapers were not allowed for packing as it's bad for health," he says.

Overtaking at the Madring? Not a chance, says Verstappen
MADRID, Sept 12 : Max Verstappen rated his chances of overtaking as almost nil in Sunday's Spanish Grand Prix and said he was counting on rivals suffering from higher tyre degradation to get ahead.
The four-time world champion qualified third on Saturday for Red Bull, behind McLaren's Lando Norris on pole position and Mercedes's championship leader Kimi Antonelli.
Asked whether he reckoned he could challenge Norris, Verstappen replied: "It will be tough. I mean, even best case scenario and you're faster, you can't pass. There are no corners where you can pass so you need to rely on people degging (suffering tyre wear) very aggressively.
"The long runs (in practice) were very tough, a lot of deg for everyone, so that will probably be the key point tomorrow. But even with that I need to still figure out a corner where to pass."
Mercedes's title contender George Russell suggested on Friday, half-joking, that thermal degradation might be so extreme - with the signature 'La Monumental' banked curve really 'hurting' the tyres - that a six-stop strategy might be necessary.
Antonelli, 66 points clear of Russell at the top of the standings after 13 rounds, agreed tyre management would be critical at a track with a particularly long pitlane and smooth, high-grip asphalt with fast corners.
"We don't really know how the hard tyre is, how resilient it is, so tomorrow we might have two stops, three stops, we'll see," said the Italian.
"But the key is expecting that first thing is try and manage (the tyres) as much (as possible) without giving up too much time."
Norris missed Friday's second practice after McLaren needed to change his car's gearbox and said he had yet to do many laps with a high fuel load.
"I've got to do my homework, got to see what (teammate) Oscar (Piastri) did yesterday, see what we can prepare for," said the Briton. "I also lost that little indication of what the degradation will be like tomorrow, this chance of high degradation.
"You want certainly a little bit of a feeling of how it degrades, what corners really to save, all those little things, you want those feelings from the car and at the minute I don't have any of them."

Wolves sign former Sunderland winger Traore
- Published
Wolves have signed former Sunderland and Aston Villa winger Bertrand Traore on a one-year deal.
The Burkina Faso international left Sunderland in the spring after 12 appearances in his one season with the Black Cats following his move from Dutch side Ajax.
Traore joined Chelsea as an 18-year-old and made his Premier League and Champions League debuts there before loan spells with Vitesse Arnhem and then Ajax, whom he helped to the Europa League final.
The 31-year-old spent three seasons with Lyon before securing a £17m move to Villa where he scored 10 times in 62 appearances during four seasons.
After four seasons at Villa Park, Traore joined La Liga side Villareal before returning to Ajax for a second stint.
"It's a position we wanted and he's a good player to improve the team, one more option," head coach Cesar Peixoto told the club website., external
"He has the right characteristics I want in this position - good one-versus-one, strong, left-footed to score or assist and fast to attack the space.
"He needs time to get fit because he's been working alone, and he needs time to know our idea of the game, but he is another option to help us fight to get to the Premier League.
"Like we saw on Sunday [Wolves' 2-2 draw at Birmingham], the Championship is very tough, so we need two players in each position to manage the games."

Police freeze HK$30 million in bank account of man who refused to share Mark Six prize
Hong Kong police chief says investigation not directly connected to Food and Environmental Hygiene Department, although suspect is member of staff
Hong Kong police have frozen HK$30 million (US$3.8 million) held in the bank account of a 36-year-old man who was arrested on suspicion of theft after he allegedly refused to split a winning Mark Six jackpot with his colleagues.
The group reportedly included some staff members of the Food and Environmental Hygiene Department (FEHD).
“The case is being investigated by the Western district crime support team. A 36-year-old man was arrested yesterday, and the relevant funds in his bank account have been frozen,” said Commissioner of Police Joe Chow Yat-ming on Saturday.
“Regarding communication with the FEHD, the report was made by another person, so we do not see a direct connection to the department itself.”
The suspect bought the ticket and received the payout into his personal bank account, but refused to split the cash equally among his colleagues, according to the source.

Bollywood has often been associated with established film families and industry connections, but several actors have built successful careers without the advantage of a film lineage. Their journeys have been shaped by varied roles, consistent performances and projects that connected with audiences. From Ali Fazal's Guddu Bhaiya becoming a widely recognised character to Rajkummar Rao finding major commercial success with Stree, these actors have gradually established their positions in Hindi cinema.
From Outsiders to Rs 100 Crores Stars: Ali Fazal, Kartik Aaryan, Rajkummar Rao and others who built their own path
- Ali Fazal
Ali Fazal has followed a diverse career path, moving across independent films, mainstream Bollywood, international projects and streaming platforms. Over the years, he has taken on a range of roles and built a career that spans different formats and genres.
One of his most recognised characters came with Guddu Pandit in Mirzapur. The role turned into an important part of his career and developed a strong following among viewers.
Guddu Bhaiya became a widely discussed pop-culture character, with his hairstyle, fashion and dialogues being referenced by fans. The character's popularity eventually extended beyond the streaming series.
That popularity reached the big screen with Mirzapur The Movie. The film crossed the ₹100 crore mark in India during its opening run, marking a significant theatrical milestone for the franchise. Its performance also demonstrated how the popularity of a streaming character could translate into box-office interest.
For Ali Fazal, the success has further strengthened the connection between his portrayal of Guddu Bhaiya and the audience.
- Kartik Aaryan
Kartik Aaryan's career has developed without the backing of a film family. He gradually built recognition through projects that connected with younger audiences and established a relatable screen presence.
A major turning point came with Bhool Bhulaiyaa 2. By stepping into the franchise, Kartik took on the responsibility of leading a commercial entertainer and emerged as a strong box-office performer.
The success of Bhool Bhulaiyaa 2 significantly changed the scale of his career. It established him as a leading actor capable of carrying a major theatrical franchise.
The Bhool Bhulaiyaa films also gave Kartik a recognisable franchise identity, allowing audiences to associate him with a character and series they were willing to return to theatres for. Following this success, he continued to take on bigger projects and strengthened his position in the commercial space.
- Rajkummar Rao
Rajkummar Rao spent years building his reputation through performance-oriented roles before experiencing a major shift in his commercial journey.
That change came with Stree. The horror-comedy became a major box-office success, with the first instalment crossing the Rs 100 crores mark in India. Its performance showed how a combination of content, memorable characters and positive word of mouth could translate into theatrical success.
The franchise grew further with its subsequent instalment, giving Rajkummar a stronger presence in mainstream cinema.
His journey stands out because his commercial success has remained closely connected to his acting abilities. Rather than moving away from performance-driven stories, Rajkummar has continued to work across different kinds of projects.
The Stree franchise expanded his reach and established him as an actor capable of leading commercially successful films while retaining a focus on performance.
- Ayushmann Khurrana
Ayushmann Khurrana established a distinct position in Bollywood by taking on stories and characters that were often considered unconventional for mainstream Hindi cinema.
Dream Girl became an important commercial success in his career. The film crossed the Rs 100 crores mark and demonstrated that his style of storytelling could attract audiences to theatres.
In the same year, Bala also crossed the Rs 100 crores mark, giving Ayushmann another major commercial success. Together, the films strengthened his position as an actor associated with content-driven entertainers.
His success has been different from that of a conventional commercial star. Ayushmann built his leading-man image around unusual subjects, imperfect characters and stories that addressed themes outside traditional mainstream formulas.
His career has therefore shown that unconventional concepts can also support commercially successful leading actors.
- Pankaj Tripathi
Pankaj Tripathi's rise in Hindi cinema has been gradual. He spent years appearing in supporting and smaller roles before becoming one of the industry's most recognisable character actors.
His performances across films and streaming projects steadily increased his visibility, with audiences developing familiarity with his screen presence.
OMG 2 became an important commercial milestone in this journey. The film collected over Rs 150 crores net in India and crossed Rs 220 crores worldwide, emerging as a major theatrical success.
The performance added another dimension to Pankaj's career, demonstrating that audiences were willing to watch him not only in supporting roles but also in prominent parts of commercially successful films.
From Kaleen Bhaiya in Mirzapur to his role in OMG 2, Pankaj has built a career that reflects the changing definition of a Bollywood star, where character actors can also develop a strong audience following.
- Abhay Verma
Among the newer generation of actors, Abhay Verma's success with Munjya became an important turning point.
The film did not rely on an established superstar to drive its box-office performance. Instead, its momentum grew through audience interest and word of mouth.
Munjya crossed the Rs 100 crores mark in India, eventually collecting over Rs 107 crores net domestically and around Rs 132 crores worldwide.
The film introduced Abhay to a much wider theatrical audience and gave his career a significant boost. For a relatively new actor, the success provided the kind of visibility that can change the course of a career.
Munjya also demonstrated that audiences can respond to fresh faces when the story and character connect with them. For newcomers, the film's performance highlighted the potential of a strong project to create a wider audience base without relying entirely on established star power.
