PM Modi, Xi welcome 'steady progress' in India-China ties at BRICS meet, bat for mutual resolution of border dispute
Xi travelled to India for the first time in seven years to attend the BRICS Summit.
India on Saturday emphasised that peace and tranquillity in the border areas remain the “essential basis” for developing ties with China, as Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Xi Jinping welcomed “steady progress” in bilateral relations during a meeting on the margins of the Brics Summit in New Delhi.
Track live updates on BRICS Summit
Xi travelled to India for the first time in seven years to attend the Brics Summit, setting up the meeting with Modi to take forward the normalisation of bilateral ties amid lingering tensions on the border. The two leaders last met on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation Summit in the Chinese city of Tianjin a year ago.
Deep Dive
‘Peace and tranquillity essential for ties’
Modi emphasised that peace and tranquillity in the border areas “remains an essential basis for the continued development of bilateral relations”, the external affairs ministry said in a readout. He also underlined that both sides should “observe existing agreements and understandings on border-related issues”.
The two leaders “expressed commitment to a fair, reasonable, and mutually acceptable resolution of the boundary question proceeding from the political perspective of their overall bilateral relations and the long-term interests of the two peoples”, the ministry said.
Modi’s comments reiterated India’s stated position that the state of the border will determine the overall course of bilateral ties. The Chinese side, however, has argued that the two sides should place the border dispute in an “appropriate place” while taking forward relations in other spheres such as trade and investment.
Meeting amid border tensions
The two leaders met against the backdrop of fresh tensions between Indian and Chinese troops in the remote Taksing region of Arunachal Pradesh, with reports of face-offs during July and August. The two sides reached an understanding in October 2024 on disengaging troops at “friction points” in the Ladakh sector of the Line of Actual Control (LAC), ending a standoff that lasted more than four years and took ties to a six-decade low.
Modi and Xi welcomed the “steady progress” in India-China relations since their last meeting at Tianjin in August 2025, and reaffirmed that both countries should “take a strategic and long-term perspective of their ties”, the readout said.
“Differences should not become disputes. Prime Minister [Modi] highlighted that both sides must be guided by three mutuals – mutual respect, mutual sensitivity and mutual interest,” the readout said.
Modi and Xi also noted progress in people-to-people ties and underscored the need to promote cultural exchanges, business linkages, and greater mobility between the two countries, the statement added.
In the context of economic and trade relations, they underlined the need to “address each other’s concerns, including structural trade imbalance and supply chain issues, and facilitation of meaningful and predictable market access”, it said.
India continues to have a range of concerns in the economic sphere, including China’s visa curbs for Indian businesspeople, export restrictions on critical machinery and commodities such as fertilisers, and the yawning imbalance in two-way trade. Since Xi’s last visit, India-China trade has grown from about $93 billion in 2019 to $127 billion in 2025, while the trade deficit has risen from $57 billion to almost $100 billion in the same period.
The two leaders further agreed that both sides “must continue to expand common ground on regional and global issues, and in addressing challenges”, the readout said without going into details.
Modi appreciated China's support for India's Brics presidency and its contributions towards the success of the Brics Summit.
Xi, who last visited the Indian capital in 2014, was received at the airport by minister of state for commerce Jitin Prasada. The leaders of India and China have not made any bilateral visits since 2020, when relations plummeted to their lowest point since the 1962 border war because of the face-off in Ladakh. Xi last travelled to India in 2019 for an informal summit with Modi, months before the standoff began.
The talks between Xi and Modi also offered an opportunity to take stock of several rounds of dialogue between the Special Representatives on the border issue, the Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination (WMCC), and senior military commanders. India and China held the first round of talks between military commanders in the eastern sector in Arunachal Pradesh on September 6 and 7.
The issue of a possible “early and substantial harvest” of boundary delimitation and border management has figured in these discussions, though the two sides have not released any details so far.

For 26 days, India watched as Sonam Wangchuk wasted away. His hunger strike, held in solidarity with India’s “Cockroach” youth protest movement, would prove to be one of the most politically consequential fasts held in the country’s modern history.
Many in the country view the gruelling fast, which began on 28 June, as the crucial spark that helped propel the Cockroach movement into one of the most formidable challenges to the government of prime minister, Narendra Modi, in more than a decade.
Abhijit Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach movement, said Wangchuk had “awakened the conscience of an entire nation” through his sacrifice.
The Cockroach movement was launched in May, following the cancellation of a key nationwide exam to enter medical college after a paper was leaked. The cancellation was devastating for the 2 million students who had already sat the exam, a dozen of whom reportedly took their lives.
The movement took its name from comments made by India’s chief justice, Surya Kant, who had compared some unemployed young people to cockroaches and parasites in a court hearing.
Dipke’s demand for education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, to show accountability for the leak by resigning struck a nerve, and anger that had been seething below the surface surged out on to the streets.
The protest ballooned into a nationwide movement. For weeks, deadlock prevailed between the government and Dipke, backed by thousands who flocked to his sit-in protest in Delhi. Eventually, after an unprecedented police crackdown which further influenced public opinion in its favour, the protesters triumphed and Pradhan resigned on 25 July.
The victory was not a foregone conclusion and Dipke has acknowledged the importance of Wangchuck’s fast in determining the outcome. Unlike the students, Wangchuck was a well known and respected figure, recognised for his decades-long efforts to secure educational reforms and environmental protection. Last year, he was arrested in Ladakh on charges of inciting anti-government protests.
The timing was also key: crowds at the Delhi protest site had been thinning before he started his fast on a stage there on 28 June, injecting new energy and momentum into the movement.
Wangchuk had declared he would not end his strike until the government had listened to the demands of India’s protesting youth. He lay outdoors at the Cockroach protest site in the heart of Delhi, day and night, enduring rain, torturous heat and mosquitoes. Already a lean and slight figure, he lost 11kg over the 26 days.
“I felt confined, trapped … like a prison,” he told the Guardian. “The heat and humidity were awful.”
In the aftermath, Wangchuk, a softly-spoken engineer, environmentalist and educationist, remains humble about his role. “I was a known entity and that helped,” he said. His reverence is reserved for the hundreds of thousands of young people in the Cockroach movement, which he says has changed Indian politics for good.
Wangchuk is adamant that the Cockroach movement’s success is far bigger than a single resignation. In an era where dissent is routinely criminalised, young people, he said, had seized back the power of political protest.
“They have stripped away the curtain of fear that existed,” he said. “They are now engaged. They have tasted success in getting results and I expect them to continue.”
The 60-year-old admits the hunger strike took a gruelling toll. By the time he broke his fast on 24 July, he had pushed his body to the limit and was perilously close to organ failure. But as thousands of young people and politicians flocked to his side, his spirit remained unbroken throughout.
The greatest test, he says, came when he was forcibly removed by police from the protest site and taken to hospital against his will. Videos of his frail body being dragged away by burly police went viral and Wangchuk was hailed by young people online as a national hero. When mass protests erupted the following day, Wangchuk’s name was chanted and held aloft on placards.
Wangchuk was not always an obvious figure of anti-government resistance. Born in Ladakh, he rose to international prominence as an engineer and environmentalist, best known for inventing the ice stupor, a unique technique for water storage in human-made glaciers. He became a prominent champion of the rights of Ladakhis and set up his own school and cultural and environmental institution.
He had been a vocal supporter of several prominent policies of Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) but it soon turned to resistance as he accused the BJP of failing the people of Ladakh. Last year, as protests in Ladakh escalated, he was imprisoned by the government for almost six months under draconian anti-terrorist laws.
While his focus has been on rebuilding his body in recent weeks, regaining about 60% of his previous weight, Wangchuk has also continued his call for political reform, albeit without any overt criticism of the Modi government.
In a video message posted before India’s independence day in August, Wangchuk called for a “second independence movement” and urged Indians to choose men and women of “character and substance” to lead the country.
He has urged people to share the names of individuals of integrity who can be trusted and once he has a list, he plans to meet them in Mumbai and Delhi to discuss how elections can be cleansed of those with a criminal background.
“Indians have to trust those at the top,” he said. “At the moment, there is no trust in anything, not in elections, not in exams, not in civil servants. Clean and honest leaders are the first step to a better future.”
He expressed his support for the decision by the Cockroach movement to resist calls to become a political party and instead focus on being a pressure group, championing issues of education. “When we used to talk during the long days of the fast, I used to advise them that being a pressure group is the best way to keep clean and neutral,” he said.
For now, he is back living quietly in Ladakh, finally able to enjoy the one food that lingered on his mind during his hunger strike. “I did dream of apricots,” he said, “but that was just because I was wondering if mine back home had ripened.”

In Summary
- New Apple CEO, John Ternus, announced a range of products at the Surprise and Shine event.
- While most of the focus was on the iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable phone, there was much more to the event than just devices and a CEO debut.
- We bring you eight takeaways that were buried in the buzz around the new devices, which might have escaped your attention.
It might not have surprised too many people – the leaks messed that up – but Apple did a fair bit of shining at its recent Surprise and Shine event. The event, which also marked John Ternus’ debut as Apple CEO at a launch, went on expected lines, with Apple revealing new AirPods, Apple Watches, new iPhone Pros and, of course, the iPhone Duo, which has grabbed the most attention. There was, however, much more to the event than just the launches. Here are our eight biggest takeaways from the day on which the world saw Apple’s new foldable and the CEO on stage:
Table of Contents
New Era? Presentation-wise, Apple is still Cook-ing (Pun intended)
Yes, it was John Ternus who held the reins at Surprise and Shine. But in terms of presentation style, the template that was followed was still from the menu of the preceding chef, Tim Cook. We had multiple speakers, elaborate backdrops, and a similar race through a number of products, leaving the most time for the star of the show (it was the Air last time around, the Duo this time). Yes, in terms of presentation style, Apple remains well ahead of the competition, although we miss the wit and humor of the past; this launch was more from the Cook manual than the Ternus one.
No surprises (Sigh)…
It’s been a while since Apple surprised the Dickens out of us at a launch, but in recent years, the brand’s product announcements have often been leaked out well in advance. And that was pretty much true this time around. From the iPhone Duo to the shades of Burgundy to the fact that there would be no suffix-less iPhone at the event, the leak community got a lot of things right, which, as we have said in the past, takes some of the mystique and surprise out of the event. Mind you, Apple did pull one rabbit out of its hat.
…except for the AirPods 5
There were no suffix-less iPhones at Surprise and Shine, but there sure were suffix-less AirPods. And while most of the noise was about Apple’s first foldable, the AirPods 5 might have emerged as the silent, value-for-money heroes of the show. While most people had been expecting new AirPods Pro with perhaps a camera built into them, Apple brought in a new version of the classic AirPods, complete with better ANC and battery life, even while retaining the “open” fit and, surprise, surprise, the same price tag as its predecessors. Not too many noticed…until the price of the Duo was announced, and suddenly a device with no price increase became the belle of the tech ball.
Hooray, we will now have TWO iPhone launches every year
Surprise and Shine marked the beginning of a new iPhone era, in which Apple will release its iPhones in two tranches over a twelve-month period. While Apple has released iPhones at two different times of the year in the past, the second launch has generally been a relatively low-profile and soft one (of the SE and ‘e’ mainly). That is set to change now. Even if Apple does a soft launch for the iPhone 18, the iPhone Air 2 and the iPhone 18e, rather than a full-fledged event, the fact is that close to half of the iPhone portfolio will be launched in the second half of the year, and the remainder in the first half of the next year. The iPhone schedules just got tweaked.
Apple is getting REALLY serious about AI (no, really, this time)
Two years ago, Apple launched the iPhone 16 series, saying it had been designed from the ground up for Apple’s avatar of AI, Apple Intelligence. However, AI is one area where the Cupertino brand has been found trailing the competition. So it was not surprising that the brand was clearly out to write a new chapter at Surprise and Shine. Every device it announced – iPhones, Apple Watches, AirPods – had a strong element of AI, which different presenters stressed would work wonderfully well, even while preserving the users’ security. Well, we have heard that a few times in the past, but never in such a comprehensive manner. Is Apple finally going to crack the AI puzzle? Based on what we saw, it would be no Surprise if it went on to Shine in that department in the coming months.
Whoop, Whoop, the Apple Watch is now a full-fledged fitness and health device, and is targeting Whoop
It started out trying to be a computer on your wrist, complete with apps, notifications and alerts, but the Apple Watch has of late graduated (or been demoted, depending on your perspective) to being mainly a health and fitness tracking device. And Surprise and Shine saw this trend continuing, with most of the talk about the Apple Watch 4 Ultra and Apple Watch Series 12 revolving around better sensors and measurement. The highlighting of features like Readiness Scores and Health Age seems to indicate that the Cupertino brand now has the screenless Whoop, which popularised these features, in its sights.
The narrative is unmatched, but is now very hardware-driven!
Processors, camera apertures, health sensors, ANC, battery life…these formed the major part of the narrative around Surprise and Shine, showing how Apple’s has shifted from storytelling to specs at its launches in recent times. This might be fine for some, but we do miss the time when an announcer would walk us through nuances of design and amazing (or they called amazing, and often, unbelievable) features on devices.
Yes, Apple remains the lord, master, and commander of product launches, but we prefer tales to tech, and a live presenter on stage to edited videos, no matter how sleekly edited. The fact that the Duo section stood out from the others because of its stress on design and UI only reinforces our belief that Apple might perhaps reconsider going back to its storytelling roots, and leave the specs on the spec sheet, rather than on the speech notes. Everyone else talks specs anyway.
Cosmic orange is out of the Apple cosmos… and Black is back!
This was so typically Apple. After making orange the color of the last twelve months, courtesy of the Cosmic Orange variant of the iPhone 17 Pro series, and making a number of brands come out with orange phones and other devices (JBL even had a pair of headphones in orange), the Cupertino giant pushed the shade out of its color palette. It also brought back the one color that everyone had missed in the Pro series – Black. Henry “Any Color As Long As It Is Black” Ford and AC/DC would approve of the return of the color, and so do we. We are not shedding any tears for orange, although we suspect those orange Pros are going to have great antique value some day.
And one more thing…
Craig Federighi’s hair looks as awesome as ever!

Police say 5 dead, 40 injured in tour bus crash in eastern Switzerland
Police say five people have died and 40 others have been injured in an accident involving a tour bus in eastern Switzerland
GENEVA -- Police say five people have died and 40 others have been injured in an accident involving a tour bus in eastern Switzerland.
The Dutch tour bus overturned Thursday afternoon between the villages of Susch and Zernez in the Alpine canton of Graubuenden, prompting rescuers to rush to the scene.
Three people remained in serious condition at hospital, police said.
Police said the bus had 45 adults on board when it came off the road and overturned.
Prosecutors and police were investigating what led to the accident.

Why is the internet so upset about NVIDIA's DLSS 5?
NVIDIA calls it the biggest graphics breakthrough since ray tracing; critics call it an AI slop filter.
NVIDIA announced DLSS 5 at its GTC conference on March 16, describing the fall release as its most significant graphics breakthrough since real-time ray tracing was launched in 2018. NVIDIA claims DLSS 5 will deliver "photoreal" image quality with AI by repainting a game's lighting and materials in real time, but backlash followed within hours, with gamers and devs accusing the GPU giant of creating and pushing a filter that overwrites games' art direction.
The situation reignited on August 28, when an early leak of NVIDIA's DLSS 5 escaped through an early-access PC copy of NBA 2K27 and modders began forcing it into games that were never meant to run it.
What is DLSS 5, and how is it different from previous versions of DLSS?
Every DLSS release since 2018 has had broadly the same, single job: make games run faster. The original model rendered games at a lower resolution and used AI to reconstruct a sharper image, with later versions adding AI-generated frames between rendered ones. DLSS 4.5 with Dynamic Multi Frame Generation, announced at CES back in January, draws 23 out of every 24 pixels on screen through that combined pipeline, according to NVIDIA. In all those cases, the underlying image belonged to the game's developers; the AI simply produced it more cheaply.
DLSS 5 is much different in that it alters the image itself. NVIDIA says the technology feeds each frame's color and motion vector data into a real-time neural rendering model that "infuses pixels with photoreal lighting and materials," redrawing elements like skin, hair, fabric and lighting while staying anchored to the game's 3D scene and consistent from frame to frame.
The company claims it runs in real time at up to 4K, and CEO Jensen Huang called the technology "the GPT moment for graphics" during NVIDIA March GTC event. Bethesda, Capcom, Ubisoft, Tencent, NetEase and Warner Bros. Games are among the publishers signed up from day one to support it.
So, why are people upset?
NVIDIA's DLSS 5 demonstrations have done most of the damage so far. During the GTC showcase back in March, DLSS 5 was run over Resident Evil Requiem and Starfield, but viewers immediately noticed that characters like Requiem's Leon Kennedy and Grace Ashcroft came out with smoothed, glossy faces that, instead of being photorealistic, looked like a beauty filter, with "yassified" becoming the Internet's term for the effect. The most-liked comment under NVIDIA's reveal video, comparing the output to an AI-generated image, outnumbers the video's own likes, with another user quipping, "We have achieved it, everything looks like a YouTube thumbnail now." Within a day, arguments that gamers are right to be disgusted by NVIDIA's DLSS 5 were everywhere the demos were shared.
Responding to the backlash on its reveal video, an NVIDIA representative wrote that "game developers have full, detailed artistic control" over DLSS 5 to "ensure they maintain their game's unique aesthetic."
The backlash against DLSS 5 extends well beyond aesthetics, though, with several notable artists and developers having questioned NVIDIA's intent with the software. Karla Ortiz, an artist who has worked with Ubisoft and Blizzard, wrote on Bluesky that the technology is "so disrespectful to the intentional art direction of devs," arguing studios that wanted hyperrealism would've built it themselves. Valid points have also been made about convergence: if hundreds of games pass through the same model trained on the same idea of realism, their distinct looks start to blur together. Bethesda responded to early Starfield footage by saying its art teams will tune the effect and that it will be optional for players, while Capcom reportedly wasn't aware(!) its game would appear in the demo at all.
Huang unfortunately made things much, much worse before he made them better, responding that "Well, first of all, they're completely wrong," when asked about the criticism during a GTC Q&A. His argument was that DLSS 5 operates at the geometry level under full developer control rather than as a filter slapped over finished frames.
Since the build leaked in late August, players have injected it into everything from Control to Monster Hunter Rise. Early testers criticized the Control mod's image quality and performance cost, but the same clips impressed enough gamers that TechRadar reported the first signs of the "negative tide turning." DLSS 5 is scheduled to be officially released this fall, with developer-tuned implementations that'll show whether NVIDIA's claims about developer control hold up better than its demos did.

What’s in a school? A Swiss woman's West Bengal initiative offers new meaning
15 years ago, a Swiss woman travelled across India to uncover her true passion for education and social reform. Her work now spans 2 villages and 20,000 lives.
Education, considered one of society's greatest equalisers, became the focal point of a nationwide stir across India recently. Despite being inked into a fundamental right under Article 21A of the Constitution, the topic captured the imagination of the nation, became a common platform for people from diverse backgrounds to rally around, and forced the country to think about the opportunities available to one of its most significant assets — the young.
At a time when real change from the grassroots of India's education sector is demanding the spotlight, HT spoke to someone who came from foreign soil but chose to give her life, finances and time to educating, empowering and uplifting women and children living on a remote island in the Sundarbans of West Bengal.
Sandra Lavie Gojkovic, a young Swiss woman offered all the comfort and convenience one may pray for, chose to live not just for herself but for those less fortunate around her. Travelling across India, mostly by train, exposed her to a very different reality in 2011, and what began as a journey of self-discovery led her to set up the India School Project which has helped boost literacy rates in rural villages, empowered women through vocational training and generated awareness against child marriage, human trafficking and domestic violence.
Also Read I Beyond degrees: A principal’s mission to empower girls
Early hardships, experiences and endeavours
A foreign national with an unfamiliar appearance and no grasp of the local tongue, she set up a school on Sagar Island, where her earliest challenge was persuading families to send their children. "Many parents did not yet understand the importance of regular education. For some families living with very little income, the immediate needs of survival naturally came first," she said in an interview with HT.
Local teachers on her team, who understood the rural community better, proved crucial. "They would literally go from house to house and pick up the children every morning to bring them to school," she said. "I remember thinking at one point, 'This is not going to work.'"
Her team refused to give up, showing the importance of education through the children themselves. Eventually, the tide turned. "Instead of us going from house to house asking parents to send their children, we suddenly had parents queuing up because they wanted their children to attend our school," she said.
Also Read I India’s education spending rises, still lags some BRICS nations
Four projects, one goal
The Primary School Project, one of her earliest initiatives, began by offering core subjects and extra-curricular activities to village students free of cost. It now covers 180 children across five classes, who get a pure vegetarian meal, teacher support and learning material simply for showing up.
A parallel literacy programme, Education Support, addresses the high dropout rate in local schools. Since early 2015, it has partnered with two public schools south of Kolkata to offer 3.5 hours of tutoring. Managed by four teachers and one social worker, it has lifted the annual board exam pass rate from 50% to 100%, as verified by Sandra.
Asked about introducing what may look like foreign concepts to a hyper-traditional community, she said: "Education, protecting children, empowering women, treating people equally and showing compassion are not Western values. They are human values. And many of them have deep roots in Indian culture and philosophy as well. I don't believe in going into a village and telling people that their culture or traditions are wrong. My approach has always been to listen first."
A Swiss mind with an Indian soul
Sandra believes these communities have given her a lot more in return. "You don't simply arrive somewhere and give. You also receive."
Cyclones are a recurring threat. "The communities we work with experience cyclones regularly, and these are not distant environmental events for them — they can completely disrupt people's lives," she said. After one severe cyclone, the school sheltered families "who had lost everything".
Blocks in a broken structure
"When I first arrived in the villages, I saw that there were free government primary schools, so technically, education was available. But in reality, many of the teachers were not consistently present, and the children were often not attending either," she said. Those administrative issues add to the barriers created by poverty and the disproportionate household expectations placed on women.
"Seeing this made me realise that the solution cannot simply be to build more schools or provide access to education. The question is what happens once a child enters that school."
Red tape adds to the burden on India's social welfare sector, in her view, and the constraint is not only a lack of money but how that money is managed and whether there is a long-term vision behind it.
"Social work is often approached through short-term projects: raise money, build something, take a photograph and move on. But real change rarely happens that quickly. Education, in particular, requires years of consistency."

Asked about expanding to other parts of the country, she said: "For me, it is much more important to do something deeply and properly in one place than to spread ourselves too thinly across many locations."
Her ultimate wish is to see a day when her work is no longer required — not because of negligence, but because the issues it addresses have been sufficiently tackled.

Jeremy Thomas, the distinguished British producer of films including Sexy Beast, High-Rise and the multi-Oscar-winning The Last Emperor, has died aged 77.
A representative for Thomas said he died on Friday “peacefully, at his country home in Oxfordshire, surrounded by his family and loved ones”.
Thomas, who started producing feature films in the early 1970s, was known for forging strong creative relationships with acclaimed auteurs, producing a string of films directed by the likes of Nicolas Roeg, David Cronenberg and Bernardo Bertolucci.
The Last Emperor, directed by Bertolucci, was an early triumph for Thomas, winning nine Oscars including best picture. He went on to become a major figure in the British film-making establishment, including a spell as chair of the British Film Institute and winning a Bafta for outstanding British contribution to cinema.
Thomas was held in universally high esteem by the rest of the film industry. Fellow producer Stephen Woolley said that Thomas “was a huge inspiration and a massively undervalued genius and rebel in our industry” and that “I have to thank him for my career”. Mike Downey, former chair of the European film academy said: “Jeremy Thomas was one of the most significant producers of world cinema in the world. The list of the giants of cinema that he curated, encouraged, selflessly supported and believed in, often when others wouldn’t take the risk, was a tribute to his belief in film as an art above all else. Jeremy’s legacy is incalculable and he has left an indelible mark on cinema history.” Trainspotting producer Andrew Macdonald said in a statement to Variety: “He was a hero for me. A rebel with taste.” Luca Guadagnino, director of A Bigger Splash and Queer said: “The canon of his work is unmatched, and some of the greatest movies of the past 50 years have been produced by him. And the level of the partnerships that he established in his career is incredible, from Nagisa Oshima to Bernardo Bertolucci.”
Born in 1949, Thomas’s father, Ralph, was a prolific film director whose work included the popular Doctor in the House series starring Dirk Bogarde, and his uncle Gerald Thomas directed all 30 of the Carry On films. Thomas started out as an assistant editor, working on the Jimmy Cliff thriller The Harder They Come and Ken Loach’s Family Life, before gaining his first producer credit on Mad Dog Morgan in 1976, with Dennis Hopper as the 19th-century Australian outlaw of the title.
Thomas was quickly into his stride, making Bad Timing, Insignificance and Eureka with Roeg, The Shout with Jerzy Skolimowski and Merry Christmas, Mr Lawrence with the Japanese master director Nagisa Oshima. The success of The Last Emperor, which Thomas had to finance independently, consolidated his status as a leading figure in British cinema, and he subsequently concentrated on prestige projects including The Sheltering Sky and Little Buddha (both with Bertolucci) and Naked Lunch (with Cronenberg).
Thomas then suggested to Cronenberg he should direct JG Ballard’s Crash, and the resulting film was enormously controversial, resulting in local authority bans in several areas in the UK. Following this, Thomas’s films included riskier propositions, such as Sexy Beast, directed by Jonathan Glazer, an adaptation of Alexander Trocchi’s Young Adam, by David Mackenzie, and Terry Gilliam’s bizarre corpse comedy Tideland. Later highlights were Jim Jarmusch’s vampire fantasy Only Lovers Left Alive, another Ballard adaptation, High-Rise, directed by Ben Wheatley, and Tale of Tales and Dogman from the Italian director Matteo Garrone.
In 2019 Thomas was the subject of a documentary by Mark Cousins, who accompanied him on his car drive from the UK to the Cannes film festival for another Garrone film, Pinocchio; it screened there in 2021. Thomas also directed one film himself: All the Little Animals, starring Christian Bale, which was released in 1999. His most recent film, Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo, directed by Takashi Miike, is due to premiere at the Toronto film festival on Monday.

Two uniforms, one deadly morning: How this firefighter and former soldier is reflecting on 9/11
Like countless others, Shawn Matheson is looking back 25 years after terror attack
Twenty-five years ago, Shawn Matheson had a foot in two worlds.
As a firefighter with Mississauga Fire and Emergency Services, he and his colleagues watched the collapse of the twin towers in New York City live on television with a deeper appreciation of the horror than most others.
A an officer in the reserves, Matheson knew instinctively where events were headed.
"Like any of us in the fire service, we were trying to figure out just what was all going down and what it meant," Matheson said.
"And I guess my thoughts were sort of switching between the tragedy of what I was seeing unfold on live TV ... as well [as] about being a soldier and what that meant."
Like countless others this week, Matheson has been reflecting on the attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, that resulted in the deaths of nearly 3,000 people — including 24 Canadian citizens.

Being both a firefighter and a soldier has made him keenly aware of the risks and the cost of service, which eventually led him to volunteer for mental health non-profit Wounded Warriors Canada.
As fate would have it, on the day of the attacks a portion of his station was asked to spell off firefighters at a station near Pearson International Airport as the U.S. airspace was closing and aircraft were touching down all across Canada.
The attacks happened on a Tuesday, which also happened to be parade night for his Toronto-based reserve unit, the Governor General's Horse Guards (GGHG).
It was, he said, a surreal feeling.
'Those hours of the unknown'
"It was a very unique day to be putting on our uniform, realizing that in all likelihood, Canada would be going to war," said Matheson, who started out as a full-time armoured soldier in the 1980s and served in Bosnia before becoming a reservist and firefighter.
"In those hours of the unknown, you know, what we realized was, who knows what was going to happen next."
In the weeks after the terrorist attacks, Matheson travelled with fellow firefighters to New York to attend funerals as remains were recovered from the ruins.
"There's some incredible strong connections in the fire community amongst different departments, not only in Canada, but south of the border," he recalled. "So there were firefighters in Mississauga that had friends in the New York Fire Department [and the] surrounding departments around New York City. They played in hockey tournaments together."
While they were at Ground Zero, the remains of six more people were recovered, Matheson said.
The sense of loss was palpable.
Later, as Canada's involvement in the Afghan war became deeper and deadlier, he commanded the GGHG and watched as 14 soldiers from his unit were sent to buttress regular force units fighting in Kandahar.
Luckily, he said, they all returned.
As the 25th anniversary of 9/11 unfolded, Matheson was on a Wounded Warriors fundraising bike ride through Canadian First World War battlefields in Belgium.
He couldn't help but reflect on how support services for both the military and first responders have evolved since the events two and a half decades ago.
Recognition that first responders are affected by the harrowing events they face, Matheson said, is something that was long overdue.
And in many ways, for Matheson, that was the lesson of 9/11.
"They do get exposed to a lot of trauma," said Matheson. "These people on fire rigs and police cars and ambulance buses. they're going to war every day. They don't know at the end of the day, the end of a shift, how things are going to play out in terms of going back home."

When Seher Hashmi speaks about mental health, her words do not stem from textbook theories or clinical observations. They carry the raw truth of a survivor. Having battled severe clinical depression and Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD), and having survived multiple suicide attempts and self-harm, Seher knows the darkest corners of anguish. Today, she is converting her trauma into a movement, traversing thousands of kilometres across India on her Royal Enfield motorcycle to shatter the silence surrounding mental illness.
Her ongoing nationwide campaign, titled ‘Beyond the Horizon – A Ride for Resilience,’ has reached Keralam after completing its north Indian leg. Together with a group of fellow riders, Seher is engaging with youth to transform societal attitudes towards mental health.
Seher’s life began under difficult circumstances. Abandoned by her biological parents at just nine months simply for being their third girl child, she was adopted by renowned social activist Shabnam Hashmi and scientist-writer Gauhar Raza. She is the niece of Safdar Hashmi, the iconic street-theatre activist who was murdered in 1989. Growing up alongside deeply committed parents whose demanding public lives sometimes left little room to process her childhood anxieties, Seher’s struggles gradually worsened into severe mental health challenges.
Path to recovery
Her path to recovery was forged through personal determination, medical intervention, and the empathy of her loved ones. Emerging from that dark space, Seher rebuilt her life as a motivational speaker, fashion stylist, and mental health advocate.
For Seher, every kilometre ridden is a step towards dismantling social stigma. By sharing her own story of survival, she offers young people across the country something far more powerful than advice—proof that resilience is possible, and that no struggle has to be faced alone.
Second journey
This motorcycle odyssey marks her second major awareness journey. Her first expedition took place in 2025, covering over 3,000 kilometres from Delhi to Kashmir and back, reaching thousands of students across 20 cities. Her current campaign—the south Indian leg—was flagged off on August 20, 2026, at the Constitution Club of India in New Delhi by veteran actor Sharmila Tagore. Spanning 55 days, 11 States, and over 7,000 km, the initiative aims at covering 100 venues across schools, colleges, and rural community spaces.
Entering Keralam on September 9, 2026 through Kasaragod, the team will cover nine districts—Kasaragod, Kannur, Kozhikode, Malappuram, Thrissur, Ernakulam, Alappuzha, Kollam, and Thiruvananthapuram—before heading to Kanyakumari on September 18. In Keralam, the campaign is supported by the Yuva Samithi of the Kerala Sastra Sahitya Parishad (KSSP). Glen Basner and Roeg Sutherland opened their global sales playbook at TIFF: The Market. The duo discussed the realities of working in the modern-day independent film business during a conference session at TIFF’s newly-minted market. They also got into the weeds on the dos and don’ts of packaging indie film projects.
Sutherland, CAA’s Co-Head of Media Finance, said that a fast-changing market is nothing new, but the pace of change has accelerated. “It’s cyclical, [but] what is happening now is that things are changing so much quicker than they ever have. Instead of having to reset yourself every six months, you have to reset yourself every two weeks.”
He added: “Things will be uncomfortable, but we work in independent film; everything’s uncomfortable pretty much all the time.”
Watch on Deadline
Sutherland said that when the business is changing super-fast it also creates huge opportunity.
“Studios are not developing the way they used to, which presents an unbelievable opportunity to the independent community. All our talent, be they directors or actors, are desperately looking for great ideas. And those great ideas, for the most part, are not coming out of the traditional routes.”
Basner, CEO of FilmNation Entertainment, talked about challenges around packaging indie film projects, and specifically distributors’ attitude to risk.
“This is my biggest complaint about the independent distribution community right now,” he said. “There’s a very traditional approach to packaging. They’re worried about how much risk they’re taking, and so they know they need to mitigate that by selling their movie to pay television, and specifically to streamers. The only problem is that we’re [then] building movies for the streamer companies. That may work great on streaming, but it’s not the same thing as building a theatrical proposition.”
He continued: “We are trying to evolve to say, ‘how do we make the best possible film so that it can compel people, in an undeniable way, to see it in a movie theater?’ And if they do go and see it, then it’s going to work in home video, it’s going to work on pay TV, it’s going to work on free television.”
To warm applause Basner also sounded an optimistic note about theatrical. “I see all the films that are premiering at festivals like TIFF, and I’m going to have a really busy next four months sitting in a movie theater watching great movies.
“Filmmakers are finding a way, not just to get their films made, but to tell their stories from their own unique perspective… and audiences are responding. I think 2027 is going to be a great year at the theatrical box office.”

At the conclusion of the men’s javelin throw competition at the Indian Athletics final series late on Thursday night in New Delhi, the top of the podium had a couple of expected names.
In first place was Rohit Yadav, who last month became the second best all-time India thrower. Also there was Yash Vir Singh, who recently clinched bronze at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games. Between the two Asian Games-bound throwers, in second place, with a slightly bewildered look on his face – as if he could hardly believe where he was standing - was Tamil Nadu’s Manoj Kumar.
“I just feel so happy that I’m seeing Rohit Yadav sir and Yashvir Singh sir. This was the first time I was even competing with them. Now I am standing along with them,” he tells Sportstar.
To finish second, the 21-year-old had thrown 80.73m in his first attempt of the evening, a personal best. It was also his first throw over 80m: the barrier that marks genuine world-level contenders, much as the 8m mark does in the men’s long jump and the 17m mark does in the men’s triple jump. Manoj is the latest of 20 Indians to have thrown this far, a list headed of course by Olympic gold medallist Neeraj Chopra.
While a steady trickle of Indian throwers have been crossing this barrier in recent years (12 for the first time in the last four years alone), Manoj’s mark was still significant. He’s the first javelin thrower of this caliber from Tamil Nadu, a state far better known for running and jumps than power events like the throws.
That had been something Manoj had often been reminded of when he pursued his passion.
“So many people said I wouldn’t ever achieve anything in the javelin throw. They would laugh at me. There’s no tradition of throwing in Tamil Nadu. They told me I’m wasting my time. Now I can tell them that I made the right choice,” he says
ALSO READ | Tanya, Nirbhay shatter hammer throw National Records as Asian Games-bound athletes give one last test
Not his first choice
Growing up in the village of Kattur Papakuruchi, just outside Tiruchirapalli, Manoj didn’t start off as a javelin thrower either. A student of St. Anthony’s higher secondary school, he took part in athletics with an early interest in pole vault.
“I used to take part in everything – sprinting, jumping. I actually had a lot of speed. But what I really liked was the pole vault. There was a very good pole vaulter in my school and at first I wanted to be like him. I even have a 3m jump at the school level,” he says.
Manoj also played a lot of cricket and although he didn’t know it just yet, both pole vault and cricket would eventually help him in his eventual choice of sport. That was javelin.
“When I was in college, I had a friend, Madheswaran, who was a really good javelin thrower. He wasn’t a national-level thrower but he had thrown 70m in Tamil Nadu. At that time I didn’t really think about whether I had a future in this event. I just thought the javelin throw was interesting. I had already trained as a pole vaulter and cricket so I had some basic strength, speed and a lot of flexibility and that really helped me out,” he says.
Although he started the javelin around the same time Neeraj Chopra created history with his Olympic gold, Manoj says he looked elsewhere for his primary motivation.
“At the time I started the javelin throw, I used to watch a lot of videos. I have a lot of respect for Neeraj Chopra but at that time I actually used to see videos of (World record holder) Jan Zelezny. I felt Neeraj has a lot of power which I didn’t have but I had a lot of speed which was similar to Zelezny,” he remembers.
ALSO READ | After long road to recovery, Avinash Sable confident of defending Asian Games gold
For all his enthusiasm, Manoj still had a major obstacle to clear. For all it’s success in track and field, Tamil Nadu has never had any tradition of top-quality throwing. That meant there were no coaches as well. Initially, Manoj trained under a sprinting coach who also had an interest in the javelin throw.
That meant that, initially at least, his progress was slow. Until 2024, he only had a personal best of 56m at a state-level meet. But that same year, he started training with Santhosh Kumar, a coach who had only just retired from the Indian Army and was training at the Sports Development Authority of Tamil Nadu (SDAT) center in Ariyalur, a town some 75km from Trichy.
Manoj credits Santhosh with his development as an athlete.
“I had interest but I had no way of building on it. I actually believe that my real training happened under Santhosh sir in 2024. Santhosh sir, saw something in me. I hadn’t even thrown 60m when I started training with him and he told me that I could throw much further. He toughened my training and my mindset. He built my speed and technique. He also taught me what to eat and how to respect my sport,” he says.
Near-death experience
Manoj crossed the 60m mark for the first time at the Junior Indian championships in 2024, which despite his modest 11th place finish, he considers amongst the more significant tournaments of his career. It marked a steady improvement in his performance. 2026 though has been his biggest year yet.
He made a throw of 75.18m at the Indian Athletics Series in Pune in June and then improved to 77.82 m at the Indian Athletics Series in Meerut earlier this month.
But his progress hasn’t been all smooth. In 2025 he suffered a severe bout of appendicitis that ruled him out for half the year as he recovered.
“The doctors told me that if I had been brought in just three hours later, I would have suffered sepsis and likely died,” he says.
There has also been the issue that plagues most young Indian athletes – the lack of finances. The son of a farmer, Manoj says he’s always had to keep an eye on his bank account even as he trains and competes. Even the javelin he used in New Delhi was a borrowed one from Madras Christian College in Chennai where he’s currently pursuing his post graduation in public relations.
“Everything costs money and when you are just starting your career you don’t have any,” he says. “I’m lucky because although they don’t understand sports, my parents have always been very supportive. But I don’t have any sponsors and all of this costs money,” he says. Even as he prepared to compete in New Delhi, Manoj says he was calculating his expenses. “Train tickets to Delhi cost 6000 rupees. It’s another 4000 rupees for two days at a hotel and the entrance fee for the competition is 1200 rupees,” he says.
ALSO READ | Asian Games 2026: Annu Rani, Shahnavaz and Nithya dropped from athletics contingent
As such the 50,000 rupees prize money he won in New Delhi will go a long way. “I’ve taken part in five competitions this year and spent close to 50,000 rupees. So with this money, I can take part in another five competitions,” he says.
Manoj is optimistic that things will get easier for him. A couple of months ago, he was inducted to the Indian Army and has started training at the Army Sports Institute in Pune. With just two years of formal training so far, Manoj believes he has a high ceiling for improvement. Standing 5 foot 10 and weighing 76kg, he’s not the biggest thrower but feels he can gain more strength while maintaining his speed.
And while he’s managed to prove more than a few people wrong with his performance in New Delhi on Thursday, he’s looking to do more.
“This is my first major medal in India but I want to be regularly throwing at this level. Right now, I’m just one of many athletes who has thrown 80m. But I have bigger dreams. I want to be able to compete for India at the biggest competitions. I’m happy that I’ve crossed 80m but I’m not satisfied. I know I can throw much more than this,” he says.

The New Mexico Supreme Court on Wednesday fined a defence lawyer $5,000 after he submitted a brief containing fake police testimony and fabricated witness statements generated by OpenAI's ChatGPT. Stephen Aarons, a defence lawyer representing a client in an appeal against a murder conviction, was held in contempt for failing to verify the accuracy of the filing. He said he prepared the brief with the help of the artificial intelligence (AI) programme, Reuters reported. Aarons, a private attorney from Santa Fe, was representing Oscar Renee Sandoval in his appeal. Sandoval had pleaded not guilty to killing the mother of his children but was convicted and sentenced to life in prison last year. Last month, the New Mexico Supreme Court asked Aarons to explain how the fabricated material, which reportedly contained details such as “fictional statements that the shooter was wearing dark pants and a white shirt,” came to be included in his main appeal brief. At a hearing on 21 August, the private attorney told the panel that he uploaded a computer-generated transcript and other case materials to ChatGPT, assuming that the AI chatbot would generate "a bulletproof summary." After hearing his explanation, the judges expressed disbelief that he was not fully aware of AI’s potential to make mistakes. Justice C Shannon Bacon said, "Counsel, do you watch the news? Do you listen to the radio? Do you read anything about what's going on in the world?" and added, "Because the problem with lawyers relying on AI hallucinations is an above-the-fold story every single day.” In a statement, the defence lawyer said that when he agreed to take up the defendant's case last year, he used ChatGPT, OpenAI's chatbot, to summarise the trial proceedings. However, he said he did not understand the degree to which the chatbot could "hallucinate" facts. He said, "I am remorseful but hopeful that the disciplinary board takes into account it was an honest mistake," and added, "It is a lesson learned for all professionals who rely upon this powerful but sometimes unstable technology." Aarons' case comes at a time when courts across the United States are seeing a growing number of cases in which lawyers have been disciplined by both state and federal judges for using AI tools without properly vetting their court documents before submitting them. According to the report, some judges have also faced scrutiny over their own use of AI. Additionally, several lawyers have faced sanctions for submitting briefs containing AI-generated errors, including fake case citations and incorrect references to the law. Aarons’ filing appears to have taken the issue a step further, with fabricated witness testimony included in a criminal appeal. The court said that the filing "contained false testimony from wholly fabricated witnesses," and added that Aarons had “demonstrated a lack of remorse and a lack of concern for his client.” The panel also noted that Aarons will be referred to an attorney disciplinary board for further investigation. The appeal, which is still pending, was assigned to Kim Chavez Cook, a New Mexico public defender, earlier this month. Hong Kong's Tiananmen activists sentenced to up to seven years in prison
- Published
Three Hong Kong activists who organised annual vigils commemorating Beijing's 1989 crackdown on Tiananmen Square protests have been handed prison sentences of up to seven years.
Two of the defendants - Lee Cheuk-yan, 69, and Chow Hang-tung, 41 - were convicted last month of inciting others to subvert state power, under the city's controversial national security law.
A third defendant, Albert Ho, 74, had pleaded guilty in January.
For years, Hong Kong was one of the only places in Chinese territory where people could hold gatherings to mark the Tiananmen Square crackdown - a topic that is highly sensitive and heavily censored in mainland China.
These gatherings were banned by Hong Kong's authorities in 2020, citing Covid-19 policies, but never resumed. That same year, the national security law, which makes illegal a wider range of dissenting acts, officially came into force.
Authorities say the law is necessary to maintain stability, but critics argue it has eroded Hong Kong's autonomy and created a climate of fear.
Lee, Chow and Ho were charged in 2021. They faced up to 10 years in prison after their conviction.
On Friday, the court sentenced Lee to seven years in prison, while Chow was handed seven years and three months. Ho, who pleaded guilty, was sentenced to five years in prison.
According to a court summary in August, Lee and Chow had "incited other persons to organise, plan, commit or participate in acts by unlawful means with a view to subverting the state power", according to a summary on Friday.
Chow told the court in May the law itself was on trial.
Speaking to the BBC before her arrest in 2022, Chow said she was "prepared to be arrested" and "willing to pay the price for fighting for democracy".
The defendants were leaders of the now-disbanded Hong Kong Alliance, a group founded in May 1989 to support students holding pro-democracy rallies.
Weeks later, the Chinese Communist Party sent troops and tanks to crush pro-democracy protests in Beijing's Tiananmen Square. Estimates of the death toll range from a few hundred to many thousands.
Over the next three decades, the Hong Kong Alliance called on authorities to accept responsibility for the crackdown, free dissidents and introduce democratic reform.
The group also held yearly vigils commemorating the Tiananmen Square crackdown. Organisers said some of the gatherings attracted more than 100,000 people, though police had lower estimates of the turnout.
On Friday, the court also handed a HK$1.5m fine ($191,000; £142,000) to the Hong Kong Alliance.
"This sentencing is a triple tragedy: for the activists being unjustly punished; the survivors and victims of the Tiananmen crackdown itself; and the generations of Hongkongers denied the space to discuss one of the most consequential events in modern Chinese history," said Amnesty International's Deputy Regional Director Sarah Brooks.

Modi-Xi meet at BRICS: India, China leaders begin talks amid push to reset ties
Xi’s visit to India, his first in seven years, comes against the backdrop of the prolonged military standoff along the Line of Actual Control (LAC).
Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping began their bilateral meeting on the sidelines of the BRICS Summit in New Delhi on Saturday, as the two countries seek to build on recent efforts to ease tensions and put ties back on a more stable footing.
Xi’s visit to India, his first in seven years, comes against the backdrop of the prolonged military standoff along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) and continuing efforts by New Delhi and Beijing to address outstanding border issues.

Deep Dive
The meeting is expected to provide an opportunity for the two leaders to assess progress in disengagement and de-escalation along the LAC and review the broader trajectory of India-China relations.
Border tensions, normalisation in focus
India and China have been working to normalise ties since reaching an understanding in October 2024 on the disengagement of troops at all “friction points” in the Ladakh sector.
However, the process of de-escalation and the withdrawal of troops to peacetime locations remains incomplete. Fresh tensions have also emerged in the Arunachal Pradesh sector following face-offs between troops during July and August.
Modi and Xi are expected to take stock of several rounds of talks between the two sides, including discussions involving the Special Representatives on the boundary question, the Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination (WMCC) and senior military commanders.
India and China held the first round of military commander-level talks in the eastern sector on September 6 and 7.
Trade imbalance, visa curbs on agenda
The meeting also comes as the two sides seek to address economic irritants. India is expected to raise concerns over China’s visa curbs affecting Indian businesspeople, restrictions on exports of critical machinery and commodities such as fertilisers, and the widening imbalance in bilateral trade.
India-China trade has increased from about $93 billion in 2019 to $127 billion in 2025. Over the same period, India’s trade deficit with China has widened from about $57 billion to nearly $100 billion.

Despite these concerns, there have been signs of a gradual improvement in ties.
The two countries have made progress towards resuming direct flights, reviving the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra and restarting border trade through three designated points.
Xi’s first India visit in seven years
Xi arrived in New Delhi on Saturday to attend the BRICS Summit and was received at the airport by Minister of State for Commerce Jitin Prasada.
External affairs ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said India looked forward to constructive discussions with China as BRICS advances cooperation and contributes to a more balanced, representative and multipolar world.

The Modi-Xi meeting is the latest high-level engagement between the two sides since relations deteriorated sharply after the 2020 Ladakh military standoff.
Xi last visited India in 2019 for an informal summit with Modi, months before the border tensions erupted. The two leaders have not made bilateral visits to each other’s countries since 2020.

'People were trampling me': Philippine ferry fire survivor recalls narrow escape
- Published
Passengers on board a ferry to the Philippines' Palawan province were jolted into chaos on Wednesday night, when a fire broke out on the vessel.
Frantic cries pierced the night sky as hot air filled the boat, recalls Roland Lerma, one of more than 100 passengers aboard the MV June Aster.
Five people have died and 86 people are missing after the fire, which, in a country where shipping accidents are not uncommon, could become one of the deadliest maritime disasters the Philippines has seen.
Families are anxiously awaiting news about their loved ones on board, while survivors like Lerma are coming to terms with their harrowing escape.
Speaking to the BBC from a hospital in Coron, Lerma recalled that as the fire spread and he scrambled to get off the burning boat, he slipped and fell.
"When I was on the floor, people were trampling me," said the 30-year-old.
He started crawling until he could find his footing again, before leaping off the vessel into the sea.
He said he saw children who had also jumped in the water, though he could not make out their faces in the dark.
"When I hit the water, I ditched all my possessions - the clothes I was wearing, phones, bags - so that I could float," he said.
Lerma said he floated on his back for about two hours before rescuers arrived and pulled him and other survivors out of the water.
"It was cold. If the rescue had been delayed, I would have definitely died last night," he said.
Lerma, who works in construction, is from Leyte province. He had travelled to the capital Manila with five of his neighbours, where they boarded the ferry to bring them to work at Coron, a popular tourist spot in Palawan province.
According to the Philippine Coast Guard, the MV June Aster departed Manila's Port of Baseco on Tuesday night at 20:13 local time (12:13 GMT) and was scheduled to arrive at the Coron port at 18:00 on Wednesday.
But the ferry caught fire just 1.2 nautical miles (2.2km) off the coast of Coron's Marcilla village.
The fire was first reported at 18:45 local time on Wednesday night by a staff member of Atienza Shipping Lines, which owns the boat, the Coast Guard said.
The company said in a statement on Thursday that it was co-operating fully with authorities and expressed "profound sadness" about the fire.
Authorities say a survivor had told them the flames had started in the cargo hold after a loud explosion.
The ship had been carrying several motorcycles, an electric car, a forklift, a pick-up van and other goods, the Philippine Coast Guard said.
As the journey was expected to take more than 20 hours, passengers had slept on bunk beds onboard overnight.
Lerma said that two Chileans - a couple who looked like they were in their late 20s or early 30s - had slept in the beds next to his.
Authorities have since confirmed that two Chilean nationals were among the 43 people rescued.
Lerma and two of his neighbours are now in a hospital in Coron. Another person in their group has been taken to a bigger hospital in the neighbouring island of Culion, while two others remain missing, Lerma says.
"I have a couple of bruises and my chest is still hurting," Lerma said. "Last night, I had a hard time breathing. But I am okay now."
Search and rescue operations are ongoing, though authorities say the fire on the MV June Aster has still not been put out and there was visible smoke from the ferry.
A spokesperson for the Philippine Coast Guard said in a local television interview many of the survivors "are still in shock".
Meanwhile, families of the ferry's missing passengers are enduring an agonising wait.
Anelyn Magbanua told the BBC that her husband Marlon was on the ferry. He was returning to Coron after visiting Manila to see two of their children who are studying at the capital.
"He spent a couple of days there. He even sent me their pictures," she said.
She last heard from him while the ferry was passing through a village about two hours from the port in Coron.
Magbanua and her two-year-old son had gone to bed early on Wednesday night expecting Marlon to be home soon.
But she was woken up later that night by a relative who informed her that her husband's ferry had caught fire.
On Thursday she rushed to the hospital when she heard there was a chance her husband might be one of the rescued survivors there.
But officials have since told her that Marlon remains unaccounted for.
"My two-year-old son and I are outside the hospital as we speak. We have nothing but ourselves," she told the BBC over the phone.
"I can't describe what I am feeling right now. I have been crying and praying since last night."

In 2006, Donald Trump was firing people on The Apprentice and Dr. Phil was daytime television's reigning tough-love therapist.
Twenty years later, the former is president of the United States, the latter, his informal UFO ambassador—recently trusted with unreleased government files on unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP) to gauge how the public might handle what's inside.
"Here's what comes in stages. First they acknowledge it, then they confirm it's real, then they tell you where it's from," Dr. Phil said in an August 7 Instagram video discussing UAP disclosure. "And somewhere down that road, maybe, is the big one—the government of the United States standing at a podium and saying out loud, we are not alone."
For most of 2026, a rumor has consumed the world of UFOlogy: President Trump is sitting on a finished speech confirming humanity isn't alone. Whether the “disclosure speech” actually exists is a topic of rabid discussion on X, the r/UFO subreddit, and dozens of extraterrestrial-curious podcasts, but the reasons so many people believe in it are very real. Humans are arguably experiencing the most consequential era for the UFO scene since the ’40s and ’50s, when a mysterious crash outside Roswell, New Mexico, and unexplained radar blips over Washington, DC, birthed decades of legends of little green men and flying-saucers.
There's no doubt that the government has been engaging with the topic. Secretary of State Marco Rubio recently confirmed that Stephen Miller, one of the most powerful figures in the White House, has been handed the UAP portfolio.
Tim Gallaudet, a retired Navy rear admiral who helped run the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration during Trump's first term, testified before Congress about UAP in 2024, and now sits on a UAP Science Advisory Council reporting to the Office of the Director of National Intelligence. He called the increased government interest “a total change in executive-branch transparency from the last 80 years."
But he’s unsure if that would ever culminate in a speech from a sitting president, because they would “have to acknowledge that we're not in control, that we're not the highest level of intelligence on the planet, and that's going to be a very hard thing for any government to admit."
A White House spokesperson tells WIRED via email that “No such speech is planned—rather, the administration continues to release files as they become available, and the public to make up their own minds about the information uncovered.”
For believers, the modern UAP disclosure began in 2017, when a New York Times article revealed a secret Pentagon program quietly investigating UAPs. The Pentagon went on to confirm in 2020 that leaked videos of Navy pilots tracking seemingly impossible objects were real. A 2021 intelligence report conceded the phenomena existed and remained unexplained, and in 2022 the government established an official investigation office. Then, from 2022 to 2025, Congress held yearly public hearings where pilots, military officers, and intelligence veterans (including Gallaudet) testified under oath.
What’s also novel is that UAP disclosure has bipartisan support. Both the House task force on declassifying federal secrets and the House UAP Caucus are made up of legislators from across the aisle.
This year, the drumbeat of government interest turned into a drumroll about a potential Trump speech. In January, filmmaker Mark Christopher Lee claimed a disclosure speech was imminent, pegged to the 79th anniversary of the alleged Roswell crash on July 8. Few took him seriously.
But in February, the president's daughter-in-law, Lara Trump, gave the idea new legs, saying on the Pod Force One podcast she'd heard Trump had a speech ready touching on "some sort of extraterrestrial life." Around the same time, Barack Obama mused in a podcast interview with Brian Tyler Cohen that aliens are “real” before conceding “I haven’t seen them.” Trump then accused his predecessor of disclosing classified information, and announced that he was directing agencies to release their files on "alien and extraterrestrial life."
What followed was bizarre even by this administration's standards. In May, Trump posted an AI-generated image of himself escorting a handcuffed gray alien, and a mysterious loading page appeared on the domain aliens.gov, leading to rampant speculation within the UFO community that the big reveal was coming. But when the White House finally launched aliens.gov late in the month, it ended up being a Star Wars–style website that functioned as an ICE tip line—with aliens being a reference to undocumented people.
The machinery of disclosure kept grinding forward. Since May, the government has released five batches of declassified videos and documents onto the Department of War's website. Detractors say the files lack context and the videos prove little.
Even after the Roswell date passed, rumors about a disclosure speech intensified. In late July, Liberation Times—an independent news website with a record of breaking UAP stories—reported that a speech confirming some UFOs are of non-human origin had been prepared for Trump.
The site’s founder, Christopher Sharp, tells WIRED the story began with a call from a source he deeply trusts.
"They basically said, ‘Look, I'm quite shaken, because it looks like Trump may make some kind of announcement on UAP disclosure’." Another source described the speech itself, he says, alleging it basically reads, “we're not alone, we have captured some of these or retrieved some of these things, they're of non-human origin, and that there is a reverse engineering effort."
Sharp was also told Trump wouldn't deliver it unless unspecified conditions were met.
"If you're the president, you have to be sure that there's firm evidence," he says. "The worst thing you can do is come out with this speech and then whatever you put out could be debunked straight away ... You'll go down in history as a laughingstock."
In August, the rumor hit a fever pitch. Robert Bigelow, the billionaire aerospace mogul who has bankrolled UFO research for decades and once owned Utah's infamous Skinwalker Ranch (a 500-acre plot of land renowned for alleged alien and paranormal activity and later the namesake of a popular History Channel series), told veteran Las Vegas journalist George Knapp that he'd met Trump in the Oval Office months earlier and personally handed him a speech containing a single sentence: "A non-human, intelligent presence has been on Earth for a very long time, using spacecraft and with performances completely beyond our capabilities and our human physics.”
Bigelow said he advised the president to deliver the line casually, on his way to boarding Air Force One—no evidence, no press conference, just confirmation. Trump hasn't said it. Yet.
If the cycle of presidents and UFO disclosure feels familiar, that's because it is. For nearly 80 years, someone has always supposedly been on the verge of revealing the truth, but no president has ever delivered.
"Politicians overpromise," says Greg Eghigian, a professor of history and bioethics at Penn State and author of After the Flying Saucers Came. "The reality is that even presidents are not privy to a lot of classified information that lies within the bowels of the military and intelligence community bureaucracy."
Still, for the believers, the stakes justify the hope.
“Often in the mainstream, when this topic gets brought up, there's a giggle factor. I can tell you who is not giggling about this: senior members of the administration, senior intelligence officials, senior members of the military, senior members of Congress,” says Jordan Flowers, executive director of the Disclosure Foundation, a nonprofit that advocates for UAP transparency. “When the door closes, no one ever says, ‘Oh, this is all made up, isn't it?’ No. The door closes and they say, ‘We know there's something happening here, we know this is serious, what do we do about it?’"
But that discourse still hasn’t been confirmed, at least in a meaningful way to the general public.
"A speech from the President of the United States confirming the existence of things in our airspace that we do not understand would unequivocally contribute to the public taking this issue seriously," says Flowers.
Eghigian, however, isn't so sure a Trump pronouncement would settle anything, particularly from "this president, who has a long history of not telling the truth."
If the past is any indicator, this could be another nothingburger.
“Unless something radically different happens, which I know a lot of people are counting on, what we could probably expect is that this will eventually die down,” he says, citing an 80-year history of “intense moments where societies are really focused on the subject, and then all of a sudden interest wanes, and then all of a sudden it appears again."
Right now, interest is arguably at anall-timee high. Few politicians enjoy a public spectacle as much as Trump, and what spectacle could be bigger than news that transcends our planet, and potentially our galaxy. Maybe the rumor just becomes another footnote on presidents and UFO lore. Or maybe it becomes the most important proclamation in human history, delivered by a reality TV star, with a talk show shrink by his side.

A probe has been ordered by Bhopal Police Commissioner Sanjay Kumar, a day after at least four MBBS intern doctors suffered injuries due to water cannons that were used against them during their protest in the campus of government-run Gandhi Medical College (GMC) to demand a hike in their stipend.
On Monday (September 7, 2026), hundreds of interns of the GMC, Bhopal, protested at their campus over their longstanding demand that their stipend be increased from the current ₹14,437 to ₹30,000. However, as they planned a march to the Chief Minister’s residence, the police used water cannons on the protestors, visuals of which appeared on the internet.
The protestors also alleged that as they continued their march later in the day, the police also resorted to baton charge on them near the campus. The march was stopped less than 2 kilometres from the CM house, prompting them to launch a sit-in at the site.
The sit-in in Bhopal’s Kamla Park area continued through the night and on Tuesday (September 8) even as they boycotted the OPD and routine operation theatre (OT) services, while emergency services remained operational. Services were also interrupted at Gwalior’s Gajra Raja Medical College in support of the protest.
Four interns injured in the police action
Speaking to The Hindu, Siddhartha Kumar Rai, undergraduate student wing president of the Junior Doctors’ Association (JDA), Madhya Pradesh, said that at least four interns got seriously injured in the police action, including one person suffering a broken arm and another an eye injury.
“It was a completely peaceful protest inside the campus but still the interns who perform 36-hour-long duties and contribute the most in handling the heavy patient load at government hospitals were treated like goons by the police. They even targeted the girl interns who were standing on the side,” he said.
Meanwhile, various other doctors’ bodies in the State have also come out in support of the interns’ protest while condemning the police action.
Mr. Rai said that if a written assurance was not given by Tuesday night, the JDA and various other bodies will boycott medical services across the State from Wednesday (September 9).
Dr. Kavita N. Singh, Dean and CEO, GMC, Bhopal, also slammed the use of force in a letter to Commissioner Kumar while seeking an inquiry into the matter and action against responsible officers.
“Water cannon was used and lathicharge was done on the intern students at the emergency gate in which two students were injured.
Taking such action against intern students on the hospital campus without prior notice is completely inappropriate,” she wrote.
In an order, Mr. Kumar said that the matter was brought to attention by Deputy Chief Minister and Health Minister Rajendra Shukla and that Deputy Commissioner of Police (DCP), Zone 2, Vikas Sahwal has been appointed to conduct an “impartial investigation of the whole incident”.
“It has been brought to the notice by Shri Rajendra Shukla, Deputy Chief Minister, that during the protest of intern doctors in Bhopal on September 7, 2026, the police sprayed water using water cannon near the gate of Hamidia Hospital, due to which some doctors were injured,” the order read.
Mr. Rai also claimed that Madhya Pradesh ranked 28th in the country in the amount of stipend given to MBBS interns, after the Uttar Pradesh increasing the amount from ₹12,000 to ₹25,000 in August.
“But in terms of MBBS fee at government colleges, we are at the third position with about ₹1.15 lakh. How is this fair,” he asked.
Meanwhile, Mr. Shukla also held a meeting with senior officials and the management of the GMC to discuss the issue and interns’ demand and said that a resolution will be reached soon.
“I am aware of the issue raised by intern doctors in Bhopal regarding an increase in stipends. The expectations and problems of young doctors in the state are being taken seriously. I am in constant touch with representatives of the intern doctors on this matter,” he wrote on X.
“Our effort is to engage in positive discussions with all parties and arrive at an appropriate and practical solution to this issue. Young doctors play a vital role in strengthening the health services of the state, and the government is sensitive to their rightful expectations. Following discussions and necessary deliberations, appropriate and necessary decisions will be taken in this regard,” he added.
