The footpath in front of the Rajiv Gandhi University of Health Sciences (RGUHS) campus in Jayanagar IV ‘T’ Block, which till recently was a picture of neglect, now looks not only squeaky clean but is all embellished with fresh paint and rangoli, thanks to the efforts of medical students.
In a special drive, the RGUHS students cleared garbage and debris from the footpath, taken away vehicles abandoned there, and beautified the area with paint and rangoli.
For years, the footpath was in an unusable state. An abandoned bus shelter had become an additional eyesore, while the area around it had also become a place for undesirable activities. The situation was further worsened by people using the compound wall as a public urination spot.
This issue was brought to the attention of Bhagawan B.C., Vice Chancellor of RGUHS. The University’s Sports Department and NSS wing recently got into action, while discussions were held with BBMP officials and traffic police authorities to find a practical solution. Various options were weighed for a month.
Finally, in a drive jointly taken up, the damaged pathway was completely renovated, the surroundings were cleaned and beautified with pots, the walls along the pathway were given a fresh coat of paint and rangoli designs drawn.
The neighbourhood appears impressed with the effort of the students. “I commute to work every day and take the bus in front of RGUHS. Previously, the area was unbearable due to people urinating there, making it impossible to wait for a bus. The footpath was broken, and garbage was strewn everywhere. But the students have transformed the place,” said Deepa, a private company employee.
Speaking to The Hindu, Dr. Bhagawan said, “Clean and safe footpaths are not merely a civic necessity, but they are an important part of public health. RGUHS believes it is our responsibility to ensure a clean, safe and accessible environment around our campuses.”

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese president Xi Jinping on Saturday reaffirmed the need to take a “strategic and long term perspective” of India-China ties, while stressing border peace, adherence to existing agreements and a “fair, reasonable, and mutually acceptable” resolution of the boundary question, the ministry of external affairs (MEA) said.The two leaders met in New Delhi on the sidelines of the Brics Summit and “welcomed the steady progress in India-China bilateral relations” since their last meeting in Tianjin in August 2025.“Differences should not become disputes,” PM Modi said, stressing that both sides must be guided by three principles — “mutual respect, mutual sensitivity and mutual interest”.Also read: Reset in India-China ties? PM Modi offers 'opportunity' to Xi during bilateral talksAccording to the MEA, PM Modi emphasised that “peace and tranquility in the border areas remains an essential basis for the continued development of bilateral relations”. He also underlined the need for both countries to observe existing agreements and understandings on border-related issues.The two leaders “expressed commitment” to a “fair, reasonable, and mutually acceptable resolution of the boundary question”, with the process to proceed from the political perspective of their overall bilateral relationship and the long-term interests of the two peoples, the MEA said.
The meeting also covered efforts to expand people-to-people ties. Both sides “underscored the need to further promote cultural exchanges, business linkages and greater mobility” between India and China.On economic and trade relations, the leaders agreed on the need to address each other’s concerns, including the “structural trade imbalance and supply chain issues”, while facilitating “meaningful and predictable market access”.
The discussions also extended to regional and global issues, with the two leaders agreeing that India and China should “continue to expand common ground” in addressing shared challenges.The MEA said PM Modi appreciated China’s support for India’s Brics chairship and its contribution to the success of the Brics Summit 2026.The meeting comes as New Delhi and Beijing work to consolidate the progress made in bilateral ties since the military standoff along the Line of Actual Control.

In Summary
- The Redmi Turbo 5 sees the Redmi brand return to a higher price point. It had earlier released the K series in this segment.
- The Redmi Turbo 5 follows Redmi’s classic formula of offering very good specs at surprisingly affordable prices. Its highlights are a powerful chip and a large Silicon Carbon battery.
- Priced at Rs 41,999, the Redmi Turbo 5 is one of the best options for those looking for something close to a budget flagship in an era of rapidly rising prices.
Redmi is mainly known for its budget-friendly devices, mostly in the mid- and lower-mid segment. It has occasionally released slightly more expensive devices, most notably in its K series, but has then gone back to the comfort of the Redmis and Redmi Notes. Now, as phone prices get on an upward-heading escalator, Redmi is getting back into the higher price zone with the Redmi Turbo 5. It comes with a starting price of Rs. 41,999, and while that may seem a bit on the premium side for a Redmi smartphone, it brings an equally premium spec sheet to the table. But can it help Redmi stretch beyond Note-land? Let’s find out!
Table of Contents
Redmi Turbo 5 design and appearance: Classy, yet not-so-loud appearance
The Redmi Turbo 5 does not come with a radically new design – it looks very similar to its cousin, the Poco X8 Pro. And that is a good thing. The phone has all the design elements that make up a trendy smartphone in today’s day and age – a tall, display dominated front which is surrounded by razor thin bezels, a flat back with two circular camera rings jutting out just a little parked on the top left side, and has those flat sides that have become an essential part of a modern day smartphone’s anatomy.
While not out of the box, the Turbo 5 still has a few distinct design touches that catch attention, the kind that are not obvious or scream for attention, but do not get lost completely either. The right side of the back comes with a thick vertical strip filled with very dainty checkered patterns, and the cameras seem like two independent lenses stacked together, but there is a subtle capsule outline encasing them. The two camera lenses also have LED rings inside them, which is a nice conversation starter.
We received the Turbo White variant of the smartphone, which has a red Redmi logo near the base of the back. The cameras and the power/lock button also come with a very distinct red accent. These subtle touches make the design of the Redmi Turbo 5 give it a personality of sorts, making it stand out in the crowd. The back comes with a matte finish, which keeps smudges and scratches at bay and keeps the phone relatively clean. The metallic frame (a pleasant surprise at this price) is home to a handful of features as well. The top carries an infrared port while the base holds a SIM card tray, a USB Type-C port, and a speaker grille. The left side is bare while the right one bears the volume rocker and the power lock button.
Although relatively light for the size of the battery it carries (more about that later), the phone is not exactly light. It weighs 204 grams, and you can feel the weight in hand and even when the phone is in your pocket. At 157.5 mm, the Redmi Turbo 5 falls somewhere between large (160 mm and above) and compact phones (153 mm and below). It is 75.2 mm wide and, at 8.18 mm, is impressively slim, again considering the size of its battery. It is quite a sturdy phone with Gorilla Glass 7i protection on its front and back, and with IP68 and IP69K ratings for dust and water resistance, which means it can easily survive a fall in the water.
At first glance, the Redmi Turbo 5 might seem routine, but give it more attention, and little details start to pop up, and you start appreciating it for its classy, yet not-so-loud appearance.
Redmi Turbo 5 Specs: Ticks a surprising number of boxes
At a time when brands are cutting spec corners, the Redmi Turbo 5 ticks a surprising number of boxes. The phone is powered by a MediaTek Dimensity 8500 Ultra processor, which is considered to be in the budget flagship zone, and is paired with 8 GB and 12 GB RAM options and 256 GB of storage. What’s more, the 12 GB RAM variant comes with LPDDR5X RAM, and the storage on both variants is UFS 4.1. On paper, this is a very powerful setup for the price, which can not only run your everyday smartphone tasks but even handle high-end gaming.
The phone comes with a 6.59-inch AMOLED full HD+ (2756 x 1268) display with 120 Hz refresh rate and a peak brightness of 3500 nits, which can actually cover as much as 25 per cent of the display, instead of being isolated to a tiny section. Photography is handled by a dual camera setup on the back comprising a 50 megapixel Sony IMX882 main sensor with OIS, and an 8 megapixel ultrawide sensor, while a 20 megapixel sensor on the front handles selfies.
The Turbo 5 also packs in some very impressive battery numbers – it brings a sizable 7540 mAh Silicon Carbon battery (a rarity at this price, actually at any price) with support for 100W charging and 27W reverse charging. Also on board are stereo speakers, an in-display fingerprint scanner, and an IR blaster. Like all Redmi devices, the Turbo 5 also runs on Android 16 topped with Xiaomi’s HyperOS 3. Xiaomi promises four years of software and six years of security updates.
In sheer spec terms, this is one of the best specced devices out there in its segment. Some might find the display a little small, but the power of that processor and the RAM and storage options will attract gamers on a budget.
Redmi Turbo 5 Performance: A smooth, powerful operator
The Redmi Turbo 5’s speedy processor+ RAM+ storage set up, reflects in its performance as well. The phone sails smoothly through everyday duties. It moves from app to app smoothly, handles multi-tasking without a hiccup, keeps going through intense social media scrolls, and binge sessions on OTT. The phone can also handle high-end games like Call of Duty and BGMI at 120 fps for long-ish sessions. Although it does get warm while going through power-hungry tasks, the temperature comes down quickly enough.
The AMOLED display with a 120 Hz refresh rate does not disappoint. It delivers a very rich contrast with vibrant colors and is bright enough not to dull down against a very harsh sun either. The 120 Hz refresh rate kept scrolling through social media breezy. The in-display fingerprint scanner works smoothly as well. This, combined with the loud and clear stereo speakers, makes the phone a multimedia master. We did not face any call drops or connectivity issues with the phone either.
Redmi Turbo 5 Cameras: One sensor show (censor the others)
Cameras are not the forte of the Redmi Turbo 5. There are three sensors on the phone, but all the photography weight rests on the 50-megapixel main sensor’s shoulders. This performs well in daylight conditions, capturing a good amount of detail and producing sharp images, so much so that the photos look decent even after a little zoom-in. The colors seem slightly more vibrant than reality but never to a point of looking unnatural. The details do take a very marginal hit in low light, but the presence of OIS helps, and Night mode on the device also improves results a fair bit. A number of other modes are built right into the native camera app, which offer a lot of scope for creative photography.
The 8-megapixel ultrawide sensor is capable of capturing a wider area, but it does not really do an impressive job. The colors remain nice and vibrant, but the details take a nose dive, resulting in images that look noisier, especially when compared to the main sensor. Matters only get worse as the light dims down. The sensor is usable and will allow you to take some quick snaps for social media in good light conditions, but do not pin your photography hopes on it. The 20-megapixel sensor on the front delivers social media-ready snaps but has the tendency to smooth out skin texture even with no ‘beauty mode’ on. The colors also lean towards being a little oversaturated, but you can get good casual snaps, and video calls are handled well.
The main camera supports 4K video at 60 fps, but the other two cameras are limited to 1080p at 60 fps. The video performance of the main camera sensor is good in daylight and even in low-light conditions, but the others miss the mark a bit. Overall, the 50-megapixel camera is the star of the Redmi Turbo 5’s camera show, while the other two are just supporting staff.
Redmi Turbo 5 software and UI: Very nice HyperOS, but loaded with third-party apps
The Redmi Turbo 5 runs on HyperOS 3. Now, HyperOS has been one of the most intuitive, simple, and functional Android skins since its MIUI days, and while that still largely remains true, the phone comes loaded with a plethora of third-party apps. This really makes the experience feel very cluttered and might even seem overwhelming to those new to the UI. Most of these third-party apps can be uninstalled, thankfully.
That said, features like Xiaomi Interconnectivity that not only allow you to connect your smartphone with other HyperOS products but with other gadgets as well, letting you create a hybrid ecosystem, give HyperOS its productivity edge. Top this with add-ons like Hyper Island (similar to Dynamic Island on the iPhone), and AI features like AI Translate, writing assist, call transcription, and a range of customizations, and HyperOS comes across as a very functionality-forward UI. The LED rings around the camera sensors that light up when you get notifications or calls were actually very handy, even while being a nice party trick as well.
Redmi Turbo 5 Battery: Lasts for days, gets charged in a jiffy
The phone’s massive 7540 mAh battery can see you through even the heaviest work days. Emails, messaging, gaming, photography- we did all of that and more with the smartphone, and it still had some juice left even after a day. If you are someone who does not push their device as much, the phone would easily see off more than two days on a single charge. It comes with 100W fast charging support with a 100W brick in the box, which means you get a fully charged phone in slightly over an hour, while the phone goes from 0-50 percent in about 30 minutes. This makes the Redmi Turbo 5 a device that will not only last for day(s) but will also get charged in a jiffy. The reverse charging feature is quite handy too and charges our TWS at a very decent speed.
Redmi Turbo 5 Price: Typically Redmi!
The Redmi Turbo 5 is available in two RAM variants – 8 GB and 12 GB, while the storage remains 256 GB for both options. Although the phone was initially launched at Rs 37,999, this price has since been revised, given rising costs of inputs. The 8 GB/ 256 GB version of the phone is now priced at Rs. 41,999, while the 12 GB/ 256 GB version is priced at Rs. 46,999.
It might have a much higher starting price than the Redmi Note series, but the Redmi Turbo 5 brings a solid spec sheet to the table at a price tag that is typically Redmi. While there are other devices in its price range, at the time of writing, none quite match its price-to-spec equation.
Perhaps the one that comes closest is its own cousin, the Poco X8 Pro, which comes with a similar processor and a similarly sized display at Rs 39,999, but has a smaller battery. Devices like the OnePlus Nord 6 come with a comparable Qualcomm Snapdragon 8s Gen 4 chip, but are more expensive at Rs 46,999, while the recently launched Vivo S2 brings a sleeker design and bigger display to the table at Rs 39,999 but loses out in terms of processor muscle.
Redmi Turbo 5 Review Verdict: A phone that does everything well
It might come with a higher price tag, but the Redmi Turbo 5 is a typical Redmi smartphone in more than one aspect. It delivers a very consistent performance across multiple segments, making it one of the most reliable and powerful options at its price point (typical Redmi!). Its gaming and general performance are both quite smooth; the main camera delivers good snaps, its battery is perhaps its biggest USP, and the display combined with the stereo speakers make it an entertainment master. The price tag is a little higher than some might expect, but the Redmi Turbo 5 is a device for those who are looking for a very good everyday phone that does almost everything well.
- Smart design, sturdy build
- Gorgeous display
- Very good speakers
- Long battery that charges swiftly too
- Good gaming and multimedia performance
- Smooth overall performance
- Ultrawide camera is average
- Bloatware in UI

Brics agrees to establish AGRIN, continue work on grain trading platform
The declaration also backed continued work on establishing a Brics Grain Exchange, with members agreeing to discuss its functioning and subsequent development.
Brics countries have agreed to establish a collaborative, non-binding and farmer-centric Brics AGRIN (Agro-Inputs, Genetic Resources, and Information Network), as well as to continue work on a Brics-focused grain trading platform, according to the New Delhi Declaration adopted by the grouping on Saturday.
The declaration said AGRIN would draw on national, regional, and international practices and focus on cooperation on agro-inputs, genetic resources, and agricultural information. The leaders have welcomed the launch of a Global Forum on Farmers’ Rights in Seed Systems to address shared challenges, promote effective policies and facilitate the documentation and exchange of traditional knowledge on agriculture and seed systems.
The declaration also backed continued work on establishing a Brics Grain Exchange, with members agreeing to discuss its functioning and subsequent development. The platform could eventually be expanded beyond grains to “other agricultural products and commodities,” the declaration said.
Deep Dive
The push comes against the backdrop of concerns over “acute food price volatility” and abrupt supply crises, including fertiliser shortages. BRICS leaders said the grouping’s position as a major force in global food production gave it a “critical role in enhancing agricultural productivity and sustainability” and ensuring global food security and nutrition.
Brics has 11 members—Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and the United Arab Emirates—and 10 partners—Belarus, Bolivia, Kazakhstan, Cuba, Malaysia, Nigeria, Thailand, Uganda, Uzbekistan and Vietnam.
The declaration called for greater coordination to improve food availability, accessibility, stability and affordability, as well as access to agricultural and food-production inputs. It specifically backed measures to strengthen countries’ ability to respond to supply disruptions, including national food reserve systems and “drought resilient and climate adaptive seed systems”.
The declaration separately welcomed the creation of a Brics Network of Centres of Excellence on Agroecology and Regenerative Agriculture for Climate Resilience and Productivity, as well as a Brics Network on Digital Agriculture covering agroforestry, fisheries and aquaculture.
On global trade, Brics leaders reaffirmed their commitment to agriculture negotiations at the WTO and said they would work towards a “fair, balanced and development-oriented” agricultural trading system. They noted that changing policies and regulations increasingly affect agricultural production and trade, food security and the livelihoods of smallholders and family farmers.
The declaration also recognised family farmers, smallholders, pastoralists, small-scale fishers, aquaculture producers, indigenous peoples, local communities, women and youth as “essential stakeholders” in agriculture and food systems.

The ghazal album ‘Lovestruck’ has been released as a nine-track collection exploring different emotions associated with love, including passion, tenderness, longing and melancholy. The album combines traditional Indian musical influences with contemporary arrangements and is accompanied by visuals shot across picturesque locations in India.
Talat Aziz, Anup Jalota, Shaan and others come together for nine-track Ghazal album ‘Lovestruck’
The music features an acoustic soundscape incorporating instruments such as sitar, tabla, harmonium, violin and guitar. The compositions aim to retain the traditional character of ghazals while presenting the genre through a contemporary musical approach. The songs are built around themes of love, separation, longing and devotion.
Produced by Sheeba Lateef and directed by Altamash Abbas, ‘Lovestruck’ features a lineup of playback singers and ghazal performers, including Talat Aziz, Anup Jalota, Shaan, Mahalakshmi Iyer, Shahid Mallya, Jaspinder Narula, Jaswinder Singh, Prithvi Gandharv and Niti D Jain.
The album's compositions have been arranged by Prem Murti, while the poetry has been penned by Kashif Raza, Sheeba Lateef, Altamash Abbas and Faraz Faani. Together, the team has brought together traditional ghazal elements with modern musical arrangements.
The album's first single, ‘Ujaalo'n Mein’, featuring vocals by Talat Aziz, was released on August 21. It was followed by Anup Jalota's ‘Besabab Tark E Talluq’ on August 25. The third track, ‘Sirf Tumse’, sung by Shahid Mallya, was released on September 1.
Speaking about the launch of the third single, Sheeba Lateef, producer of ‘Lovestruck’ and Managing Director of Trio Set of Three Arts, shared her vision for the album. She said, “This album is surely going to bring the true nostalgia of ghazals back to listeners and viewers, and it will create history as all these renowned singers have absolutely nailed their performances. Our music director Prem Murti has done a wonderful job, and the entire camera and production teams have executed an extraordinary vision. I congratulate the entire team of Lovestruck, including my fellow Trio partners—Chairman Altamash Abbas and Chief Patron Kashif Raza.”
With its nine tracks, ‘Lovestruck’ brings together established voices from the ghazal and playback music space while attempting to present the genre through a mix of traditional instrumentation and contemporary arrangements.

ESDS Software Solution extended its post-listing surge into a sixth consecutive trading session today, with its shares touching the upper circuit once again and climbing to more than four times their IPO price. The rally underscores strong investor appetite for the enterprise cloud and AI infrastructure play. Shares of the enterprise cloud and AI company jumped 10% to touch an intraday high of ₹1,740.40 on the NSE. However, the stock subsequently pared some of its gains and was trading 9.7% higher at ₹1,735 as of 14:00 IST. At its intraday high, ESDS was trading 305.7% above its IPO issue price of ₹429 per share. On the BSE, ESDS shares remained locked at the 10% upper circuit of ₹1,716.35. At this price, the stock was up 300.1% from the issue price, while the company’s market capitalisation stood at ₹20,117.5 Cr (about $xx Bn). ESDS made its stock market debut on September 4, listing at ₹757 on the NSE, a premium of 76.5% over its issue price. On the BSE, the shares listed at ₹746.30, nearly 74% above the issue price. The stock subsequently hit its 20% upper circuit at ₹908.40 on the NSE and ₹895.55 on the BSE on the listing day. It has continued to hit its upper circuit in every trading session since then. After being locked at the 20% upper circuit for three consecutive sessions, the stock’s circuit filter was reduced to 10%. The rally has also drawn regulatory scrutiny. The BSE sought a clarification from ESDS earlier this week over the sharp movement in its share price. The company said it was unaware of any undisclosed information that could explain the surge. “The company is not aware of any specific reason for the significant movement in the price of its security,” ESDS said, adding that the movement in its share price and trading volumes was consistent with the activity typically observed in a newly listed security. ESDS’ ₹720 Cr IPO, comprising entirely a fresh issue of shares, was subscribed 135.88X during its three-day bidding period. Ahead of the IPO, ESDS raised ₹216 Cr from anchor investors by allotting 50.3 Lakh shares to 19 entities at ₹429 apiece. The anchor investors included Motilal Oswal Mutual Fund, Bandhan Mutual Fund, Quant Mutual Fund, ITI Mutual Fund, and JM Flexicap Fund, among others. Founded in 2005, Nashik-based ESDS provides cloud computing, data centre, managed services, and AI-led digital solutions to government and enterprise customers. The company plans to deploy ₹576 Cr from the net IPO proceeds towards purchasing and installing cloud computing equipment and other infrastructure at its data centres in Airoli, Bengaluru, Mohali, and Nashik. A portion of the proceeds will be used for general corporate purposes. On the financial front, ESDS’ consolidated net profit more than doubled to ₹120.8 Cr in FY26 from ₹55.6 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Its operating revenue increased 30.7% to ₹472.2 Cr from ₹361.3 Cr in FY25.

The trip from Yokohama to Tohoku and back began at 4:40 a.m. at a local bus stop — where we lined up with a surprisingly large crowd and some early-rising mosquitoes — and ended aboard a reserved-seat green car that pulled into Yokohama Station, having freed us from battling for space on the last leg of our long train journey.
In between, my 11-year-old son and I were on a five-day trip that took us to the cities of Sendai and Ishinomaki in Japan’s northeast region. The catch: We could ride only local trains, a constraint of Japan Railway’s Seishun 18 ticket, which can be used during set periods every spring, summer and winter.
The ticket, which debuted in 1982, holds legendary status among rail-travel fans (while seishun means “youth,” there is no age limit). But a host of rule changes deployed in 2024 took the wind out of its pantographs. I planned this journey to put the revamped version to the test, convinced I could make it worthwhile despite the objectively worse conditions.

Mumbai has seen a surge in H1N1 (swine flu) cases over the last three months, as the number of cases have jumped to 441 this year from 62 during same period last year. This marks a 612% rise, while for malaria the cases have seen a 20% rise.
According to Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC)’s monsoon data for June, July, and August, 441 cases of H1N1, and 4,485 malaria cases were recorded between June and August as compared to 3,733 last year.
To curb the surge of swine flu, BMC has been screening suspected H1N1 patients, and prescribing Oseltamivir. Further, surveys are being conducted in the affected regions, where the H1N1 positive cases have been located.
The BMC said suspected H1N1 patients are being screened and treated with oseltamivir wherever required. Close contacts of infected patients are being monitored for 10 days, while door-to-door surveys are being conducted in affected areas. BMC also clarified that they have prepared ventilators, PPE kits, reserved beds and medicines to manage patients for hospitalisation.’
Mumbai’s E-ward, K-West ward, G-South ward, F-South ward, and H-West ward have so far recorded the highest cases of malaria. To combat the vector-borne disease, BMC has increased the field-level monitoring in most affected areas. They have surveyed 52,197 potential breeding sites for malaria control. Anopheles mosquito breeding sites were detected at 8,055 locations, along with 12,55,469 potential mosquito breeding sites for dengue control, and Aedes mosquito breeding at 27,352 areas.
Decline in monsoon related illnesses.
Mumbai saw a decline in dengue cases,leptospirosis cases, COVID-19 cases, Chikungunya, and Gastroenteritis. According to BMC data, COVID-19 cases dropped drastically by 77% this year, as 151 cases were recorded compared to last year’s 668. For dengue the fall has been by 20% — 1,563 patients recorded this year in June, July, and August. For chikungunya, cases have dropped from 370 to 46, a decrease of 87%.
Leptospirosis cases declined by 37% — from 406 to 255, while gastroenteritis cases dropped from 2,197 to 1,954, this year.

Trump Loses the Other Strait
The Houthi advance is bad news for the U.S., and even worse news for Saudi Arabia.
As recently as last week, the Iran war appeared to be turning slightly in America’s favor. The Houthis—the Yemen-based militia that is Iran’s most formidable remaining ally in the Middle East—were under pressure from their local rivals, and the Saudi air force was pounding them with air strikes. The president of Yemen’s internationally recognized government issued a triumphant statement declaring that the Houthis’ miscalculations “will open the door to their complete collapse.” With their Houthi partners wounded, Iran’s leaders would have one more reason to back down and agree to Donald Trump’s terms.
Yesterday morning, those delusions drifted away like smoke as Houthi forces broke through their enemies’ defenses and seized the towns and islands around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, one of the most important maritime choke points in the world.
That loss leaves Trump, who had been hoping to win back control of the Strait of Hormuz from Iran, with a bitter surprise. His enemies now control both of the two important straits in the Middle East, through which a combined total of about a third of the world’s oil shipments pass every day.
It also underscores a stubborn fact: For all the setbacks suffered by Iran’s “Axis of Resistance” over the past year or two, its forces retain an ideological fervor and an esprit de corps that is sorely lacking on the other side. The Gulf states’ failure to work together against the Houthis has been catastrophic, and it echoes Trump’s own failure to devise a plausible or coordinated strategy against Iran.
Although the Houthis already had the ability to threaten shipping in the Red Sea, the capture of the Bab el-Mandeb “means you can literally sit on the coast and fire at passing ships,” April Longley Alley, a Yemen expert at the Washington Institute on Near East Policy and the former political adviser to the United Nations special envoy for Yemen, told me. “It makes it easier and cheaper, and it solidifies, from a military and political point of view, that they have a stranglehold on the strait.”
The United States might not be able to do much about this, even if the Pentagon launches a new round of air strikes on the Houthis. (The Saudi leader, Crown Prince Mohammad bin Salman, called Trump twice yesterday urging him to strike the Houthis, Axios reported.) Bombs and missiles would achieve little without a ground force to take advantage of them, and America’s Yemeni allies are now battered and divided. The Trump administration waged a seven-week war against the group last year, and although it succeeded in killing some Houthi commanders, it did not dislodge the group or alter its ability to wage war, as Trump had promised.
The Houthi advance is even worse news for Saudi Arabia. For many years, the Saudis have been struggling to tamp down the Houthi threat on its border. Now the Houthis have inherited a great deal of Saudi and Emirati supplies left behind by the official Yemeni government’s retreating forces. A video circulated yesterday of Mohammad Ali al-Houthi, one of the group’s top commanders and a cousin of its supreme leader, Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, riding though Mokha in an Emirati armored vehicle.
The mess that Saudi Arabia faces in Yemen is partly of its own making. The Houthis were born three decades ago in reaction to Saudi meddling in Yemen’s religious and political sphere. In December, tensions between the Saudi and Emirati leadership led Riyadh to demand that the Emiratis—their nominal allies—withdraw from Yemen, leaving the Saudis in charge of a patchwork of militias with divided loyalties. The various Yemeni factions continued to squabble among themselves even as their Houthi enemies were at the gates.
“There was no coordination between commanders, between the intelligence and the drones, between the coast guard and the army—nothing,” Farea Al-Muslimi, a Yemen specialist at the think tank Chatham House, told me.
The Houthis have clearly benefited from the Gulf’s disunity. “Last time the Houthis made a breakthrough at Marib in 2022, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia were able to jointly support a devastatingly effective Yemeni-government counterattack,” Michael Knights, the head of research at the consultancy Horizon Engage, told me.
The Houthis, meanwhile, were disciplined and focused. “They sacrificed hundreds if not thousands of fighters,” a member of Yemen’s officially recognized government, who asked not to be identified for fear of repercussions, told me. “Our bullshit activists were putting out fake news about victories, while the Houthis were working in silence.”
With the momentum on their side, the Houthis could now go on to seize more terrain in other parts of Yemen, including Marib province, where much of Yemen’s oil is located. They could also extend their power bloodlessly, by cutting deals with tribal and regional leaders in the south and east. All of this would further consolidate their power and strengthen their Iranian patrons.
The Houthi victories have already put into doubt the value of the Mecca Alliance, the mutual-defense pact formed in August by Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Turkey. Islamabad and Ankara have shown no inclination to help the Saudis, despite a rash of recent Houthi strikes on targets in southern Saudi Arabia.
Iran’s vaunted Axis of Resistance is not a bulletproof covenant either. The Houthis were absent earlier this year when the United States and Israel started bombing Iran.
But unlike their enemies, the Houthis and the Iranians have a deep ideological bond, one that their soldiers willingly die for. And the Houthis do not need to win every battle. As long as they can sink an occasional oil tanker, they will hold a whip hand over their Saudi neighbors, and over the rest of the world too.

- The claim that attendees of the 2026 Republican National Convention in Dallas, Texas, caused an outage of popular gay dating app Grindr circulated online in September 2026.
- The rumor stems from incident reports shared on social media, taken from a third-party service called Downdetector during the time of the event. However, the incidents were not isolated to Dallas, and Grindr itself did not report any major outages connected to the event.
- A spokesperson for Grindr told Snopes, "Grindr has not experienced recent outages. Third party sources that often make these claims rely on unreliable data such as self-reporting, while Grindr reports outages directly on its status page." The status page showed no outages in August or September 2026.
- While some users may have had trouble with the service on Sept. 9 and 10, 2026, including in and around the area where the RNC was being held, we were unable to independently verify that the reported errors were authentic or that they were caused specifically by RNC attendees.
With high-stakes midterms looming in November 2026, the Republican National Convention took place in Dallas, Texas, on Sept. 9 and 10, 2026. Rumors spread that the convention's attendees were causing an outage of the popular gay dating app Grindr.
People on social media sites shared a purported screenshot that showed a map depicting hotspots of Grindr outages across the country, with the brightest spot focused on Dallas.
The popularity of the rumor led many Snopes readers to reach out via email and social media, asking if the claim was true.
We weren't able to independently verify claims of Grindr outages in Dallas, so we've left this claim unrated. The screenshots appeared to be taken from Downdetector, a third-party service that tracks outages of popular services, and did not show signs of fabrication or misleading editing.
According to Downdetector, users did report incidents at the time and location in question, but the incidents reported on Sept. 9 and 10 were not limited to Dallas or even Texas. There was also no way to confirm that the reports reflected real issues with the app, as Downdetector does not require users to submit any proof.
Grindr itself did not report any outages during that time.
A spokesperson for Grindr told Snopes via email: "Grindr has not experienced recent outages. Third party sources that often make these claims rely on unreliable data such as self-reporting, while Grindr reports outages directly on its status page."
The company's status page showed no outages or incidents in August or September 2026.
Downdetector tracks data for the prior 24 hours and does not archive its history.
Snopes first checked Downdetector's page for Grindr on Sept. 10, 2026. It showed a spike of reported outages on Sept. 9 around 8:49 p.m., with the highest number of reports clocked at 460.
Grindr outage report on Sept. 10, 2026. (Downdetector)
When we checked Downdetector on Sept. 11, the past 24 hours showed a peak of only 73 reports around 3:18 p.m. on Sept. 10.
Grindr outage report on Sept. 11, 2026. (Downdetector)
The incident heat map provided by Downdetector, which we first checked on Sept. 10, showed the highest concentration of outages in Dallas and Austin, Texas, but also indicated reports were being submitted in other major cities like New York, Boston and Chicago.
Grindr outage map on Sept. 10, 2026. (Downdetector)
A look at the same map one day later showed lower concentrations of reports of problems in the same cities.
(Grindr outage map on Sept. 11, 2026. (Downdetector))
The page explains that Downdetector "calculates a baseline volume of typical problem reports for each service monitored" based on an average over six months, and "only reports an incident when the number of problem reports is significantly higher than the baseline."
Further, Downdetector allows users reporting the issues to comment on the page. During the period of Snopes' review for this claim, multiple comments on Grindr's Downdetector page referenced the RNC with comments like, "Convention in Dallas, as always." There was no indication those comments came from people genuinely experiencing connection issues in Dallas.
So while it appeared that some users may have had trouble with the service on Sept. 9 and 10, 2026, including in and around the area where the RNC was being held, there was not enough evidence to conclude without a doubt that the reported errors were entirely authentic or that they were indeed caused specifically by attendees at the RNC.
We reached out to Ookla, the parent company of Downdetector, for further comment and will update this article if we hear back.
For further reading, we've investigated similar claims about Grindr, such as rumors of alleged Grindr outages near Charlie Kirk's memorial in September 2025.

Japan’s Digital Agency said Friday that about 246,000 sets of personal information, including the names and addresses of government employees, may have been leaked due to unauthorized access to a network system operated by the agency.
So far, no secondary damage, such as the misuse of the possibly leaked personal information, has been confirmed.
The information also included email addresses and phone numbers, but not My Number personal identification numbers or bank account information.
On June 25, the agency detected suspicious access to a large number of files on the server from an account of system maintenance and operation staff. It then began investigating the incident and found on July 9 that there had been unauthorized access from an external third party.
The agency said in a statement that it is deeply sorry for causing problems and anxiety to those concerned.

Record heatwaves in France set to make champagne stronger
- Published
Champagne lovers may find themselves getting tipsy more quickly after French producers have been given the go-ahead to raise the alcohol content in a bottle of bubbly for the first time following this summer's record heatwave.
Winemakers can temporarily produce champagne with an alcohol content of up to 15% - above the 13% cap, industry officials have said.
The extreme heat and drought produced grapes with exceptionally higher sugar levels. Yeast converts sugar into alcohol during fermentation.
France's Champagne region also saw its earliest-ever harvest due to the weather, something that could become the norm "in 10 to 15 years" because of climate change, according to the Comite Champagne industry association.
- How will extreme weather affect our food? 
  - Published24 August
- France links sharp rise in drownings to heatwaves 
  - Published23 August
The temporary increase in champagne's alcohol content is only expected to affect a small number of wines, a spokeswoman for the Comite Champagne told the BBC.
During the second fermentation process, which gives champagne its bubbles, "a very small number of wines from this harvest could have slightly exceeded the regulatory limit of 13%, reaching around 13.1% or 13.2%".
"Therefore a decision was made to exceptionally and temporarily increase the regulatory limit to 15% - only for this year," she said.
The first grapes were cut in early August and the harvest expanded by the middle of the month, "the earliest ever recorded in Champagne", the association said.
"The 2026 growing season will be remembered as one of the most unusual in Champagne's history, marked by severe spring frosts of historic intensity, an exceptionally early flowering period and five heatwaves throughout the summer." it added.
Speaking in the Times newspaper, Stéphane Vignon, a producer in Verzenay said: "The Mediterranean climate is moving north. This is year one of a new cycle. It's unlikely to be every year, but it will happen again".
Higher-strength champagne is unlikely to be an obvious selling point, warned Jane Anson, a wine columnist and author based in Bordeaux.
She told the Times: "Today people increasingly prefer lower-alcohol
"The battle between what consumers want and what nature provides must be very stressful for producers."
The 2026 vintage is unlikely to hit shelves until 2028 as champagne must age for at least 15 months.
Maxime Toubart, co-chair of the Comite Champagne, told the AFP news agency that the likelihood of hotter weather in the future means "this unusual harvest will probably become the norm in 10 to 15 years".
France has been one of Europe's worst-hit countries during this year's extreme weather, sparking huge wildfires.
Climate change is driving up global average temperatures, making heatwaves more frequent and intense.
It has been felt acutely in Europe, which is the fastest warming continent, heating up twice as fast as the global average, according to the Copernicus climate service., external

US secretary of state Marco Rubio gave new clarity on the approach toward combating drug trafficking in Latin American waters, saying the Trump administration was focused on working with allied countries and aligning with their laws but insisting the military will “still blow up ships if need be.”
The public acknowledgment of a shift in US strategy comes a year after Washington began a campaign of unilateral deadly strikes against those it calls “narco-terrorists” operating boats in international waters.
Late Wednesday, US Southern Command announced the latest such strike in the Caribbean Sea, saying it killed three people. That brought the number of people who have been killed in boat strikes by the US military to at least 230 in 69 strikes.
Still, the Trump administration is focused on building agreements for joint operations with allied countries in the region, including Colombia and Ecuador, that comply with their laws in their waters.
“I think its an incredible advance for the first time to have countries that are willing to participate in these efforts in their territorial waters,” Rubio told reporters on a trip to the Ecuadorian capital, Quito.
“The important point is that these routes are being disrupted. These routes are being ended,” he added.
He said the decision is “a strike-by-strike or operation-by-operation determination” that depends on the threat and location of the boat.
Recent US interdictions in Latin American waters are unlike the Trump administration’s initial strikes on alleged drug-trafficking boats that began in September 2025. People onboard floating refueling stations said to be supporting drug trafficking have been removed and transferred to Ecuadorian authorities. Then the US military blows up the vessels.
The shift comes after a series of strikes on boats over the year on people the Trump administration accused of being “narco-terrorists” without providing evidence.
Rubio’s comments came during a three-nation tour of South America aimed at boosting security cooperation with conservative leaders who have cozied up to Donald Trump.

The US government launched at least three previously unreported investigations into trading on the prediction market Polymarket, according to documents obtained by WIRED through a Freedom of Information Act request.
Voting records from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the federal agency that regulates prediction markets, shed new light on how the government approaches these investigations. In early May, CFTC chairman Michael Selig approved an order allowing the agency’s enforcement division to launch a private investigation into potential insider trading on Polymarket event contracts related to pardons issued by former president Joseph Biden. The order granted permission to take testimony, obtain subpoenas, administer oaths, and require the production of documents in the course of the investigation.
The documents obtained by WIRED did not specify which trades were under suspicion, but the order came several weeks after an NPR report on a suspicious Polymarket trader who netted over $300,000 on pardon-related markets in the final days of the Biden administration. The trader correctly wagered that the former president would issue preemptive pardons to a number of prominent MAGA critics, including former US representatives Liz Cheney and Adam Kinzinger, and US senator Adam Schiff.
At the end of May, Selig approved another investigation order. This time, the topic was “Iran event contracts” on Polymarket. As with the Biden pardon documents, the investigation order did not provide details, but it came two weeks after 60 Minutes aired a report on a network of suspicious Polymarket accounts that made $2.4 million on Iran-related trades, with a 98 percent win rate.
“If these investigations are being prompted solely by press reports of potential violations of the Commodities Exchange Act, that’s a significant sign of weakness in this regulatory scheme,” says Joseph Konizeski, a former chief trial attorney in the CFTC’s division of enforcement. The agency has come under fire in the second Trump era for its perceived friendliness to the prediction market industry.
In July, Selig greenlit a third investigation, this time focused on suspected insider trading on Google-themed Polymarket event contracts. In an email exchange included in the documents obtained by WIRED, Paul Hayeck, the acting director of the CFTC’s department of enforcement, noted that the investigation would focus on “additional individuals who may have engaged in insider trading related to Google’s 2025 Year in Search Ranking.” Hayeck wrote that the Southern District of New York is conducting a “parallel investigation.” He specified that the CFTC's investigation would be separate from the ongoing case against Michele Spagnuolo, a Google engineer accused of insider trading.
SDNY declined to comment. Google declined to comment. It pointed WIRED to a statement it released in June noting that Spagnuolo was no longer with the company. The CFTC did not respond to requests for comment and questions about the status of the investigations.
“While we do not comment on specific investigations, we regularly refer matters to law enforcement and support ongoing investigations as part of our commitment to protecting the integrity of our markets,” Olivia Chalos, deputy chief legal officer at Polymarket, told WIRED in an email.
The CFTC is also reportedly investigating Polymarket itself. The company, which had its flagship platform banned from the United States in 2022, was permitted to launch a US-regulated version with a narrower set of markets in late 2025. It recently underwent a fundraising round led by Donald Trump Jr.’s venture capital firm, 1789 Capital, which valued the company at $21 billion.
The CFTC has also launched investigations into potential insider trading on Kalshi, Polymarket’s archrival, in the past. According to The New York Times, Kalshi has referred at least 32 cases to the agency. The CFTC fined former US representative George Santos $35,000 for his behavior related to a Kalshi contract about whether he would attend Trump’s 2026 State of the Union address.
Kalshi issued its first-ever lifetime ban to Santos for violating its rules on market manipulation for the same behavior, and also fined him just over $71,000. Santos was not criminally charged.
So far, two arrests have been made stemming from Polymarket insider trading investigations. In April, federal authorities arrested a US special forces officer who prosecutors say used classified information to make more than $400,000 in profits on event contracts related to the capture of former Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro. And in May, Spagnuolo, who allegedly made over $1.2 million on insider trades, was arrested while traveling to New York. In both cases, the CFTC filed civil charges, and the Department of Justice filed criminal fraud charges. Both men are fighting back by arguing that Polymarket trades are a form of betting and not subject to commodities law.
It’s unclear if the Department of Justice has launched parallel investigations into the Iran War or Biden pardon contracts. The DOJ did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
A former CFTC staffer tells WIRED that parallel criminal investigations are likely, “given the significance of the matters.”

Good morning. Chelsea Cirruzzo here. Today we remember 25 years since the 9/11 terrorist attacks. While I was too young to have many recollections of the attack, I did grow up in New York and vividly remember the impact it had on the people around me. So, I always take the time each year to reflect.
Today, we’ve published a First Opinion essay by a thoracic surgeon in New York City who treats first responders still facing extraordinary health challenges after being exposed to the toxic aftermath of ground zero. I hope you spend time with it, too.
Trump’s $500 Obamacare promise
President Trump has promised to send $500 refund checks to nearly 1 million Americans on Affordable Care Act plans, who also happen to live mostly in swing states, with checks arriving ahead of the midterms.
The checks will only go out to people who don’t receive federal subsidies for their insurance plans — after Republicans declined to extend enhanced ACA premiums that expired at the end of last year.
The White House said the money will help “Americans most exposed to the higher costs imposed by the Biden administration’s gross mismanagement of Obamacare.”
People are eligible for the $500 if they live in one of the 30 states that use the federal government’s ACA marketplace, such as Ohio and Florida. It’s unclear whether only people with current coverage qualify, or whether people who had plans in the past may also get checks.
My colleagues Bob Herman and Tara Bannow have more on the unclear legality of the move.
Can AI catch a heart attack? The FDA thinks so
A number of artificial intelligence algorithms have promised to help identify and treat heart conditions early, but how about when a patient is actively having a heart attack? Last week, the Food and Drug Administration issued a rare de novo classification to an algorithm from Powerful Medical that aims to help triage patients to the right care when they’re having chest pain. The vast majority of AI devices go to market through the FDA’s 510(k) clearance pathway; fewer than 10 each year receive de novo classification, which typically requires more clinical evidence.
Here’s how the new algorithm, Queen of Hearts, works: It can detect patterns indicating a patient is experiencing the most severe kind of heart attack, when a coronary artery, which supplies blood to the heart, is completely blocked off. In doing so, it can help doctors make sure a patient gets treatment as soon as possible to open up the blockage and restore oxygen to the heart.
My colleague Katie Palmer has more on what it means for patients and doctors if we can more quickly detect these ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction patterns with an EKG.
A valuable childhood cancer treatment with long-term implications
A platinum-based treatment for children with certain cancers can be a lifeline, but it can also cause healthy cells to mutate, potentially increasing the risk of new cancers later in life, my colleague Annalisa Merelli reports.
That’s according to a new study published Thursday in Science, seeking a clearer understanding of the long-term impact of platinum agents in children treated for hepatoblastoma, a rare cancer of the liver that is most commonly diagnosed in childhood.
The study looked at children who had received platinum therapy followed by surgery to remove the tumor. Researchers sampled both healthy and cancerous liver tissue and blood from the patients and compared the results to samples from children given different treatments.
What they found were hundreds of mutations in the samples exposed to platinum, usually found in adult livers. In other words, platinum aged the liver cells of treated children, making them look more like adult liver cells.
Read on for what this means for long-term monitoring and treatment.
Sorry to burst your (bouncy castle) bubble
What kid doesn’t love getting to carom around in a bouncy castle? But the inflated structures could be the source of skin infections, an investigation into a large outbreak of community-acquired methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus — more commonly known as MRSA — in eastern Ireland reveals.
About four dozen children who attended a community party in August 2025 later developed skin and soft tissue lesions and abscesses caused by the bacterium, Irish public health officials reported Thursday in the online journal Eurosurveillance.
The event, attended by about 120 adults and children, featured three bouncy castles. Many of the kids reportedly spent considerable time — hours, even — playing in them. About a quarter of the cases had symptoms beyond skin lesions, such as fever, nausea, or vomiting. Four of the infected kids were admitted to the hospital, though all recovered. Uganda's King Oyo buried amid calls for unity over his successor
- Published
Uganda's King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, once the world's youngest reigning monarch, was buried on Saturday, days after a row broke out over who would succeed him.
Oyo, 34, who had ruled the traditional kingdom of Tooro in western Uganda since the age of three, died last month while undergoing cancer treatment in the US.
Tooro is one of Uganda's traditional kingdoms. They were abolished in 1967 but restored in the 1990s under President Museveni. Their monarchs are recognised as cultural leaders rather than political rulers.
Thousands of mourners lined the streets as the king's casket was transported to the royal tombs in Fort Portal where a private ceremony took place.
Oyo was just a toddler when he was named as Tooro's king and, according to Guinness World Records, was the world's youngest monarch while he reigned.
TV news presenter Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, 56, who was named as the next monarch by clan elders, reportedly cast nine coffee beans into Oyo's grave, a ritual signifying the end of one reign and the start of another.
But days earlier, Oyo's family rejected Kijanangoma, the late monarch's cousin, as Tooro's new king.
Oyo's sister, Princess Ruth Komuntale, said the late king had left a will, written in 2022, naming his young son as his successor.
The boy's identity has never been disclosed.
Meanwhile, his mother, Queen Best Kemigisa, said royal guards had been withdrawn from the palace and soldiers deployed. This, she said, restricted the royal family's movement and their ability to receive visitors, describing it as "house arrest".
On Saturday, the Archbishop of the Church of Uganda, Stephen Kazimba Mugalu, urged unity.
"Words spoken in grief can cause pain, division and conflict. It can even destroy the legacy of the king we are mourning," he told mourners.
Uganda's President Yoweri Museveni also called for the matter to be resolved "and to favour unity over division".
The clan overseeing the succession defended its choice of Kijanangoma.
Omusuuga Charles Karumasi, head of the Babiito royal clan, said: "We have done everything in observance of the culture and traditions of Tooro. We must all preserve peace and serenity."

Time for a digital divorce? Trade war puts spotlight on Canada's relationship with U.S. big tech
Experts say Canada can reduce its reliance on U.S. tech, but there's a difficult road ahead
Trade and political tensions between Canada and the United States have raised concerns about Canada's digital sovereignty, but what does that term mean, and how can Canada promote it?
While it may sound like jargon, experts say digital sovereignty can be defined simply.
It's about regulation, Vass Bednar, managing director of independent public policy think-tank the Canadian Shield Institute, told CBC Radio's Just Asking.
"Fundamentally, our digital sovereignty is our ability to regulate digital environments using the tools that we have," she said, including regulation of algorithms that influence what information we see online.
It's also about choice and the law, according to Michael Geist, Canada Research Chair in internet and e-commerce law at the University of Ottawa.
"It's fundamentally about both the ability to make Canadian choices … so we have alternatives to some of the larger — predominately U.S. — players, and also ensuring that Canadian law applies," he told CBC Manitoba's Information Radio last week.
- Google updates maps to show Lake America in the U.S. — but Canadians are now seeing it, too
- 'Lake America' change highlights Canada's reliance on U.S. tech
The federal government also has a definition.
"Digital sovereignty means Canada stays in control of its own digital future — including its data, technology and essential online services — instead of relying on foreign companies, foreign systems or foreign laws," a government webpage reads.
"Think of it like this: Just as we want our homes, money and identities protected in Canada, we want the same protection for our digital information and services."
A mid-August X post from the U.S. Trade Representative account said a potential trade deal between Canada and the U.S. would include "digital trade alignment," which prompted expert concerns and speculation about digital sovereignty. Only days later, talks between the two countries fell apart at the last minute, reportedly over American insistence that U.S. streaming companies be exempt from Canadian content rules.
After talks broke down, President Donald Trump signed an executive order that Lake Ontario be renamed Lake America. Google and Apple Maps quickly implemented the change for American users, but some Canadians reported seeing it on their maps.
So, how American is our tech?
Right now, Canada doesn't have many alternatives to American technology companies and digital platforms.
"We are heavily dependent on the American big tech companies when it comes to our Canadian businesses and the public sector," said Shion Guha, assistant professor in information and computer science at the University of Toronto, on Just Asking.
The federal government also uses the Microsoft Office and Microsoft 365 platforms. In January, Shared Services Canada, which is responsible for providing IT services to the government, renewed its agreement with Microsoft in a deal worth $940 million over seven years.
Guha was part of a study on the federal government's AI Register which found that Microsoft was the single biggest supplier of systems, accounting for 42 of 409.
"An American big tech company is very heavily intertwined, not just with things like email or OneDrive … or Microsoft Office, but also in the types of predictive analytics and other types of AI products that the federal government has currently acquired," Guha said.
"This type of dependence on one big tech company is generally not a good thing for any kind of sovereignty."
There is precedent for switching, Bednar said, noting, "France has been a little bit ahead of the curve here."
- Canada ready to further distance itself from U.S. on military procurement
- Why isn't Canada blocking the Welland Canal? Other trade war questions answered
France's Interministerial Directorate for Digital Affairs announced in April that it will remove Microsoft's Windows operating system from government computers. Open-source software Linux will replace it.
The French government also developed Tchap, an instant messaging application, and mandated its use for public sector employees, citing security and privacy concerns. The French government says over 600,000 public sector employees use the app.
What can Canadians do?
But if getting the Canadian government to switch platforms could be difficult, getting Canadians to change everything from their credit cards to their cloud storage to their social media and instant messaging platforms and more could be even harder.
Gander Social launched in July, marketing itself as a nicer, Canadian alternative to U.S. social media platforms. The company posted on Facebook last week, saying it's approaching 50,000 users, though Bednar pointed out that Prime Minister Mark Carney isn't among them.
But having Canadian options doesn't mean Canadians will want them, Guha said.
"There is a certain amount of inertia in getting Canadians to switch to things, because convenience usually rules over most things," he said.
"Just because we can, or do, have Canadian alternatives — and they may provide better features, they may be good for us — doesn't mean that we can overcome the social inertia to get people to switch."
But it is one way ordinary Canadians can promote digital sovereignty, Bednar said. Though she also acknowledged it's going to require more "institutional imagination in Canada" to move forward.
Staying sovereign in the AI age
The Canadian government released its National AI Strategy in June. In it, the government pledges to develop a home-grown supercomputer, as well as "sovereign cloud, AI, cyber and quantum initiatives."
Geist said the government should take an approach that balances building Canadian AI programs with access to foreign ones.
"If a single government gets to determine whether or not you have access to those frontier models, they're really determining whether or not you've got the very best tools to counter things like cybersecurity threats," he said.
- AnalysisCanada wants sovereign AI data centres. What does that actually mean?
- Want to build a data centre in Canada? These are the federal government's new expectations
Guha said the federal government has also started referring to the data centres that help power AI and other services as "critical infrastructure."
The federal government's five principles for data centre construction, released earlier this month, require projects to "strengthen Canada's long-term digital resilience, security and compute capacity." They also say that the facilities must follow Canadian laws on cybersecurity and data protection.
"If we don't make the rules here, we will have to follow someone else's,” AI Minister Evan Solomon said at a news conference announcing the principles, which arrive amid concerns about the U.S. government using its laws to access Canadian data.
Bednar said Canada's current effort to assert its sovereignty against the U.S. is different from those of the past because of how much more of our lives exist digitally.
"Digital ... is the infrastructure of our economy," she said.
"It is just as, if not arguably more, important than manufacturing, automobiles, aluminum, steel — take your pick."

Five minutes to steal a Renoir: Why museum thefts are becoming bolder across Europe
- Published
When thieves broke into a French museum earlier this week and stole four paintings by the impressionist artist Pierre-Auguste Renoir, worth millions of euros, not everyone was surprised.
Just last month, the European policing agency (Europol) had warned that museum thefts across Europe were growing increasingly brazen.
And just days before the Renoir heist, internationally known art detective Arthur Brand predicted to the BBC that more high-profile burglaries were likely - particularly in the wake of the successful robbery at the Louvre in Paris last October.
The audacious crime in one of the world's most famous museums stunned France, and the stolen jewellery worth €88m (£75m) has still not been recovered, nearly a year on.
"We will see more of this," says Brand, "because if you are able to hit the Louvre, thieves all around the world are watching that, thinking, 'Wow' - and then they think, 'Don't we have a local museum with gold and silver?'".
Within hours of the Louvre burglary, thieves had raided coins from a smaller museum in France. Since then, criminals have stolen a diamond necklace in Vienna, Bronze Age artefacts in Spain, and art from two Italian museums - and that's only what the BBC has written about.
The heist at the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer is the latest, and detectives are still working to track down the remaining multi-million-pound paintings - two of which were quickly recovered after thieves dropped them in the museum garden.
Europol tells the BBC the number of museum theft cases reported to them across Europe began to increase about two years ago.
Its recent report says both the methods and targets of thefts are changing - with a rise in more forceful tactics, and, as in the Louvre case, a focus on high-value items such as precious metals and gemstones.
Both Brand and Ibrahim Bulut, a museum security expert from a Belgian security consulting firm, believe many thefts that followed the Louvre burglary are copycats.
"Every museum in the world is stressing now," Brand says. "In every museum there have been meetings with the security officer or with the police."
From tiaras to Bronze Age rings: Stolen museum treasures
1 of 10
The Association for Research into Crimes against Art (ARCA) says the recent thefts show "a repeated preference for small, portable, immediately accessible objects and for attacks designed to be completed in minutes".
Data provided to the BBC by ARCA shows recorded museum thefts in France spiked in 2024, and rose again slightly in 2025.
However, numbers go up and down over time, with more thefts recorded in 2015 than a decade later.
These crimes threaten what many consider invaluable artefacts of historical and cultural value enjoyed by the public - although some people argue they steal "from the rich, who cares?" Brand says.
Others point out the colonial history behind many treasures in European museums, with art historians highlighting the French crown jewels stolen from the Louvre contained emeralds, diamonds, sapphires and pearls which are not native to France.
Why are museums being targeted?
Museums are vulnerable and easy to burgle, Brand says, compared with well-secured jewellery shops and banks - which these days hold less cash.
Directors historically "never have enough money for security" or prefer to spend it on the next exhibition, and museums are often housed in old buildings that are difficult to protect, he adds.
For example, the Denis Diderot Maison des Lumières (House of Enlightenment) - burgled hours after the Louvre - is housed in two 18th-Century mansions in Langres.
"We therefore have to reconcile modern security requirements with the need to preserve historic buildings and comply with France's heritage regulations," local mayor Théo Caviezel explains.
Museums are also open public spaces that have less access control and perpetrators can come in as visitors, says Kumar Sokka, CEO of Acre Security which works with some museums in Europe.
And even if a museum is secured well, thieves could still come in armed, Brand says, adding that it would be impractical to put police in galleries.
Many of these burglaries are over in minutes and the thieves have long gone by the time police show up - the Renoir case happened within five minutes.
Heists used to depend on deception, but burglaries are now becoming increasingly violent, Europol's report last month, external points out. Offenders are using tools such as sledgehammers, axes, crowbars and, in some instances, explosives, to get inside.
In the Louvre, the thieves used a mechanical lift to gain access, cut through the window with power tools and then threatened guards, who left, before forcing their way inside displays and grabbing the jewels. In the Renoir case, the perpetrators used an electric knife to cut through a fence before sawing through structures holding the paintings' frames in place.
The increased aggression creates new security concerns.
"An armed incident during opening hours, like the one we experienced, creates a situation in which the immediate priority is to keep our audience and staff safe," says Lilli Hollein, the director of the Museum of Applied Arts (MAK) in Vienna, which was burgled last month.
What is being stolen is also changing. While paintings are still taken, they're harder to sell, so about 10 years ago, thieves began shifting to goods that are easier to get rid of, Brand says.
Now precious metals, gemstones, and culturally significant artefacts including Chinese porcelain are increasingly targeted, according to Europol's report.
"Precious metals can be easily melted down, leaving no trace for law enforcement, and facilitating illicit sales during the fencing process," it says. "Precious stones in jewellery, on the other hand, can be easily removed and sold further."
Meanwhile, Chinese porcelain is likely to be easily sold on the art market because of high demand, Europol says.
After a theft, police generally have between four and six days to catch the thieves, according to Brand, who works with investigators by calling informants and receiving tips from the public or even ex-partners of perpetrators.
But while suspects may be arrested, jewels or precious metals might not be found - such as with the Louvre case.
On the other hand, Brand believes the Renoir paintings stolen this week - two of which were dropped by the thieves on their way out - "will probably be recovered" because "no one will want to buy" them and "it is likely, then, that the thieves have no idea what to do with them".
Christopher A Marinello, the boss of Art Recovery International that recovers stolen art, says only 5-10% of stolen art is ever recovered, making thefts from small museums like this week's "extra painful".
Tuesday's heist is another example of "Europe's museums under siege", he adds.
So how can museums be protected?
After its theft in October, Maison des Lumières launched a security audit carried out by police officers appointed by France's cultural ministry, mayor Caviezel says.
Some recommendations are already being implemented, such as enhanced video surveillance, while other structural improvements are in the process of being developed.
MAK in Vienna also increased its security to prevent "copycat offenders and to provide our audience with visible security", its director says. Entry is through a metal detector, and bags must be put in the cloakroom or in lockers, and there are more security guards.
Experts say the trick is to create physical barriers that will delay thieves so there is time for the police to arrive, or to make any theft take so long that it would deter would-be offenders from attempting it.
"Security is about buying time", says Bulut. "The objective is not to make the theft theoretically impossible, but to make removal difficult, noisy, detectable and above all, time-consuming, because to be very honest, thefts can always happen, it's the timing that you're concerned about."
Brand says a delay could be building an extra, heavy door anchored into the ground, thickening the glass on display cases or using a fog machine.
Sokka says it's critical to have integrated systems - so for example if an alarm goes off, you could shut down the facility, or lock down all high net worth paintings.
However, security measures are expensive. Mayor Caviezel, whose small French city hosts two museums and collections, says finding the money is "one of our main challenges".
"A small city can be entrusted with collections of national importance without having the financial resources of a major Parisian institution."
Bulut, who sits on the International Committee for Museum Security board, says it's not all about expensive gadgets. It could also be training guards to spot suspicious people who may be casing a museum and ask them if they need help, which may deter them from returning.
Museums are investing: Sokka says his company has seen an uptick in seismic offerings, that can detect vibration such as drilling in walls, in the past 18 months.
Museum heists are not increasing everywhere in Europe. In Sweden, major museum thefts began to decline around a decade ago and have not changed significantly in recent years, said Peg Magnusson, Sweden's representative for a Unesco convention to combat illicit trafficking of cultural property. However, other worrying cultural artefact targets have emerged.
The challenge for museums now is increasing security while also staying open to the public.
"A museum cannot be a fortress," Hollein says. "We want to be open institutions; at the same time, we are facing new challenges and attacks against museums that will require new standards."
