EaseMyTrip cofounder and chairman Nishant Pitti has pledged 34.51 Cr shares of the online travel aggregator, worth ₹211.9 Cr, to Motilal Oswal Financial Services for “personal use”. The pledge, created on August 24, covers 8.66% of EaseMyTrip’s total share capital, according to an exchange filing. The shares were valued at ₹6.14 apiece at the time of the transaction. The filing pegged both the value of the pledged shares and the amount involved at ₹211.9 Cr, implying a security cover ratio of 1:1. The 34.51 Cr shares covered by the latest pledge represent about 76.1% of Pitti’s 45.37 Cr share holding in EaseMyTrip. Before the transaction, 10.36 Cr of Pitti’s shares were already encumbered. Following the creation of the pledge, his total encumbered holding stood at 44.87 Cr shares, representing 11.26% of EaseMyTrip’s total share capital. The pledged shares represent 98.89% of Pitti’s individual holding, leaving him with 50 Lakh unencumbered shares. The pledged shares account for 25.83% of the combined shareholding of EaseMyTrip’s promoter group, which includes Nishant Pitti, Rikant Pittie, and Prashant Pitti. Total Pledge Unchanged However, Pitti’s overall pledged holding remains unchanged from April, when he had pledged a total of 44.87 Cr EaseMyTrip shares. While the latest filing classifies the transaction as the creation of a pledge, the unchanged post-transaction holding suggests that existing encumbrances were restructured. The filing did not elaborate on the reason for the change. Pitti had pledged 6.86 Cr shares worth about ₹55 Cr to Motilal Oswal Financial Services in March this year. This followed a string of pledge creations and releases over the preceding year. In June 2025, Pitti pledged 9 Cr shares worth ₹94.5 Cr to Motilal Oswal Financial Services, also for personal use. At the time, his total pledged holding stood at 17.01 Cr shares. Pitti’s pledges have come alongside a reduction in his stake in EaseMyTrip. He sold nearly 5 Cr shares worth ₹78.3 Cr in December 2024 after offloading 24.65 Cr shares for about ₹920 Cr in September that year. His stake in the company subsequently declined to 12.8% at the end of FY25 from 28.13% a year earlier. Pitti stepped down as EaseMyTrip’s CEO in January 2025 and was succeeded by his brother and cofounder Rikant Pittie. At the time, Nishant Pitti said the share sale was due to “personal reasons” and assured shareholders that he would not sell any more shares. Another cofounder, Prashant Pitti, resigned as the company’s MD in August 2025. EaseMyTrip Under Pressure The pledge disclosure comes at a time when EaseMyTrip’s earnings remain under pressure. The OTA slipped into the red in Q1 FY27, reporting a consolidated net loss of ₹11.7 Cr as against a net profit of ₹44 Lakh in Q1 FY26. This came despite operating revenue rising 18.4% YoY to ₹134.7 Cr. The weak quarter followed a challenging FY26. EaseMyTrip reported a ₹47.5 Cr loss in FY26 as against a profit of ₹108.6 Cr in FY25. Revenue from operations declined 8.8% YoY to ₹535.7 Cr. EaseMyTrip's board in May approved a proposal to raise up to ₹500 Cr through a rights issue. The company had earlier said the capital would be used to strengthen its technology and platform, expand into segments such as hotels and holidays, and pursue strategic acquisitions. Shares of EaseMyTrip were trading at ₹5.83 at 15:10, 0.5% higher from the opening price on BSE.

The New Mexico Supreme Court held a ChatGPT-using lawyer in direct contempt of court for submitting a brief with “false testimony from wholly fabricated witnesses,” including fake police testimony and other mistakes. The state’s top court referred the lawyer to a disciplinary board for further proceedings and concluded that he “demonstrated a lack of remorse and a lack of concern for his client.”
Attorney Stephen Aarons “admitted to the Court that he did not verify the factual claims and legal authority in his AI-generated brief before signing it and filing it with the Court, and that he did not inform his client of this failure or that the brief in chief contained multiple factual and legal misrepresentations,” the state Supreme Court said in an order on Wednesday.
Aarons has been a criminal defense lawyer in New Mexico for over 40 years and was hired by a defendant’s family members to appeal a murder conviction. Aaron’s now-former client, Oscar Renee Sandoval, was sentenced to life in prison in February 2025 after being convicted of killing Shiereen Al-Jibury, who was his partner and the mother of his children.
A little over a year ago, in August 2025, Aarons submitted the brief containing fake testimony and other errors. Weeks later, the state of New Mexico filed a motion to strike portions of that brief.
“Respondent admitted to the Court that the brief in chief contained false testimony from wholly fabricated witnesses—Officer Michelle Amarillo, Officer Sanchez, Manal Al-Jibury, and Teresa Marquez,” the court order on Wednesday said.
Lawyer fed trial transcript into ChatGPT
Aarons further admitted submitting “false testimony from Danny Stanton that he received threats,” “false testimony from Linda Stanton about the threats her husband received,” and “false testimony from Mariah Chavez and Teresa Marquez (fabricated witness) regarding the shooter’s clothing and appearance,” according to the order, which said Aarons also “misrepresented legal authority” in citations to previous cases.
Many lawyers have been caught citing fake cases in briefs or inaccurately describing real cases. While Aarons didn’t cite fake cases, he inaccurately described real ones and cited fake testimony.
Aarons told the state Supreme Court at a hearing on August 21 that he fed a computer-generated transcript of the murder trial and other documents related to the case into ChatGPT, which outputted the fake quotes.
“It’s of little comfort to know that my stupidity is what brings us together this afternoon,” Aarons told the court. Aarons admitted his brief quoted “several witnesses who were never called at trial,” another “witness who was called but the brief got the name wrong,” and that his brief inaccurately described precedents.
Aarons indicated that he used a version of ChatGPT powered by the OpenAI o3 model, which was released earlier in 2025. “I assumed that it generated a bulletproof summary of proceedings,” he said at the hearing, explaining that he thought it would be accurate because of how widespread AI use is in the legal and medical fields.
Aarons was barred from appearing before the New Mexico Supreme Court pending the outcome of any disciplinary board investigation and proceedings. He was fined $5,000, to be paid to the State Bar of New Mexico Client Protection Fund, but more penalties could come out of the disciplinary proceedings ordered by the court.
The state Supreme Court ordered the public defender office to appoint a new lawyer for the defendant, struck all previous briefs from the record, and said the case will proceed in the court’s 2026-27 term.
Justice: “You buried your head in the sand”
Justices lambasted Aarons during last month’s hearing. They expressed surprise that Aarons didn’t know AI tools could generate false information and pointed out that attorneys must verify the accuracy of information no matter where it comes from. Whether a lawyer gets help from an AI tool, a law student, or a fellow attorney, the lawyer signing the brief must attest to its accuracy, they said.
Justice C. Shannon Bacon was particularly withering in her criticism of Aarons. She told Aarons that there are “at least eight or nine provisions in the code of conduct that you violated.” Bacon said she was “really struggling with” Aarons’ claim to be unaware of AI hallucinations, noting that her 13-year-old nephew and 75-year-old stepmother are both aware of the problem.
“So counsel, do you watch the news? Do you listen to the radio? Do you read anything about what’s going on in the world? Because the problem with lawyers relying on AI hallucinations is an above-the-fold story every single day,” she said. “So either you buried your head in the sand—and that’s a choice to do that, an intentional choice to be uninformed—or you took a gamble, and neither of those are consistent with the code of conduct.”
Aarons responded that he submitted the brief a year ago and “a lot has come out in the last year.” However, the problem of lawyers using AI in briefs that cite made-up cases has been in the news regularly for well over three years.
Aarons added that the cases he cited in his brief were not fake, although his brief described them inaccurately. Bacon responded that there’s no “material distinction” between inaccurately describing a real case and citing a fake one, as the rules about candor to the court apply “with equal force” either way.
“I didn’t know that AI could hallucinate facts”
Aarons provided a statement when contacted by Ars today. He said:
In March 2025 I agreed to handle an appeal and used ChatGPT to summarize the trial proceedings. I wrote the brief but the table of contents and the summary contained numerous errors. At the time, I didn’t know that AI could hallucinate facts not only in my brief but in pleadings submitted by other attorneys. I am glad the court threw out my defective pleading and ordered the public defender to write a new brief on behalf of my former client. As for myself, I am remorseful but hopeful that the disciplinary board takes into account it was an honest mistake. It is a lesson learned for all professionals who rely upon this powerful but sometimes unstable technology.
Aarons told the court that he began by using Rev.com, a service that provides AI transcripts of audio files, and then put that transcript and other materials into ChatGPT.
“I believe I did confirm” that the trial transcript was accurate, he said when asked if he confirmed its accuracy before inputting it into ChatGPT. “The problem wasn’t in the transcript. It was when I loaded it and all the other information” into ChatGPT, he said. In addition to the transcript, Aarons said he put “the record proper, the statement of issues, and some of the discovery” into ChatGPT.
Aarons said he hoped the court would take steps to prevent other lawyers from making the same mistake he did, such as by issuing a standing order requiring that briefs contain a certificate of compliance regarding the use of AI. Justices treated Aaron’s suggestion as a distraction from the main problem, his failure to verify the accuracy of the brief.
“Assume with me that you had relied on the work of a first-year lawyer that was working for you and that they had just made stuff up… and you signed it. You’d be in the same exact soup you are right now,” Bacon said. “So the idea that, the suggestion in your briefing that because the court didn’t tell you at the time that you did this, ‘be careful,’ it somehow relieves you of obligation, falls on absolute deaf ears because the rules of professional conduct already tell you what your obligation is.”
“Your client is the one suffering”
“The other thing that’s completely missing from your response is anything about what this has done to your client,” Bacon went on to say. “That’s who I’m worried about. You have presented briefing to the court that we cannot rely on, and your client is the one suffering because of this far more than you will ever suffer.”
Chief Justice Julie Vargas similarly told Aarons, “I’m really interested with the approach you’re taking in this hearing. You seem to be telling us all the policy that we’ve been thinking about for years about what to do with AI, but you’re not talking about how to address the situation that’s in front of us, which has significant impacts on a criminal defendant who is in custody, who’s going to stay in custody until we resolve this matter. And I really don’t care about the policy concerns right now. I care about what we’re going to do with your client and what we should do in this circumstance based on the behavior that you showed us.”
Justice Michael Vigil said there’s nothing wrong with using AI to help write a legal argument as long as the lawyer verifies its accuracy. “It doesn’t matter what the tool is. It doesn’t matter how advanced the AI-generated program is or what improvements they make, whatever,” he said. “It doesn’t matter whether you use a C-student lawyer or a A-student lawyer [if] you didn’t check their work before you filed the brief. That’s the issue. And I wish, or I’m hoping you would focus on that, take responsibility for it.”
Aarons replied, “I hope I don’t present myself as not accepting responsibility. I mean, my only hope is that the mistakes that I made that somehow can prevent someone else down the line from repeating my mistake because the AI capacity is amazing.”
Lawyer didn’t tell client and family about ChatGPT use
Bacon criticized Aarons for not disclosing the problem to his client. “I have not. He’s a Spanish speaker and I wanted to see what happened today,” Aarons told Bacon when she asked if he told Sandoval about the problem.
Aarons said he was hired by Sandoval’s brother and cousin, and that he told them there was a problem with a brief. “They’re aware that there was a problem with the first brief that I filed and that the court’s looking at that. That’s pretty much it,” he said.
Bacon replied, “You didn’t say, ‘I relied on ChatGPT and it submitted lies to the court and the court is mad at me and now there’s a hearing.’ I’m guessing you didn’t tell your client’s family members that.”
“I didn’t talk about ChatGPT,” Aarons said. “I just said there was a problem with the brief that I filed.” Bacon told Aarons that his client needed to know the extent of the problem so he can make an informed decision “about whether you’re the right person to represent him.”
Bacon asked Aarons whether he was working on the case on a public defender contract or as private counsel. Aarons answered that he was hired as private counsel but hadn’t been paid yet.
“I’m not sure that’s going to happen,” Bacon replied.
Jon is a Senior IT Reporter for Ars Technica. He covers the telecom industry, Federal Communications Commission rulemakings, broadband consumer affairs, court cases, and government regulation of the tech industry.

With the Sri Meenakshi Sundareswarar Temple consecration fast approaching, Minister for Energy Resources and Law C.T.R. Nirmal Kumar conducted an inspection of the newly established Integrated Control Room at Pudumandapam.
Set up near the Nandi statue, the high-tech command centre will serve as the nerve centre for pilgrim safety, crowd control, and real-time monitoring throughout the consecration. Following his inspection of the facility, the Minister held a review meeting with senior district administrators and elected representatives.
The control room operates under a Special District Revenue Officer, where pilgrims can access round-the-clock emergency assistance via toll-free hotlines (1800-425-6781 and 1800-425-6782). A robust security grid of 3,500 police personnel will be deployed, supported by 207 CCTV cameras, 70 facial recognition system units, 10 police help desks, and 41 public-facing LED display screens, said a press statement of the district administration.
For crowd flow and transit, general devotees will enter through the west and south gopurams starting at 10 a.m., exiting via the east gopuram. To ease traffic congestion, free shuttle buses will operate across key urban corridors, including the Mattuthavani-Simmakkal and Arapalayam-Periyar routes.
Special buses
Overall, 666 city buses (including 60 specials) and 300 mofussil buses (including 40 specials) will run on frequent rotations from major city terminals, supplemented by 55 free parking spaces and a 210-vehicle parking lot at the Periyar Bus Stand.
To maintain public health standards, authorities have installed 225 permanent toilets across 24 locations, 107 temporary units across 16 spots, and 17 dedicated water-dispensing stations alongside 26 large-capacity water tanks. A sanitation force of 264 regular and 60 specialised solid-waste management workers will operate across three continuous shifts, while 50 QR-coded temporary signboards will guide visitors, the statement added.
“Twenty-seven medical camps have been set up both inside and outside the temple complex, staffed by 70 doctors, 150 paramedical staff, Red Cross volunteers, 10 standard 108 ambulances, and two mobile emergency units,” a press release said. Additionally, a regional firefighting contingent of 400 personnel from Madurai, Virudhunagar, Theni, Sivaganga, and Ramanathapuram has been deployed.
Uninterrupted power will be guaranteed via dedicated back-feeding lines from the Subramaniyapuram, Mahalipatti, and temple sub-stations, while food safety inspectors will continuously collect and test meal samples from authorised annadanam organisers, the release said.
Emphasising the magnitude of the event, Mr. Nirmal Kumar urged all government departments to ensure they coordinate with each other so that every visiting pilgrim has a smooth, safe, and hassle-free darshan.
Collector Nishanth Krishna, Police Commissioner S. Rajendran, and Madurai Corporation Commissioner Gaurav Kumar, among others, were present during the inspection.

'Nothing good was supposed to come out of me'
- Published
A Nigerian man has shared the story of how he rose up out of "abject poverty" as a child, to become one of the leading UK academics in his field.
David Etor, 43, who grew up in Nigeria, only learned to read and write aged 12 and was told as a child that "nothing good will come out of you", but is now a lecturer in electrical and mechanical engineering at the University of Bristol.
He told the BBC how his family was so poor growing up that his mum would pretend to cook food in a kitchen they shared with others, "to protect our integrity" in front of neighbours.
"I didn't see a way out," he said.
'The poor called us poor'
Speaking to John Darvall on BBC Radio Bristol about the publication of his first book, Etor described growing up in a "compound" with several other families, all sharing a single kitchen, toilet and bathroom.
"It was a very poor neighbourhood. We were particularly very poor that the poor neighbours would refer to us as poor," he said.
"I do remember that there was a time where my mum would boil water.
"[She would] go back in and out, lift the lid, stir the water, go back into the room [and] come back as though she was preparing food...
"She would come back in with that pot of water after a couple of hours and it will be as though she's just finished cooking a meal, but it was just water.
"She was trying to protect our integrity."

Etor's first break came whilst doing a kind of national service in Nigeria, when he realised lots of locals were being hospitalised with food poisoning, because they were trying to preserve things by drying them in fields.
To solve the problem, he designed and built a kind of "solar oven".
"It worked incredibly well," he said, which led to an award from the state government and a job.
He then completed an undergraduate degree at Newcastle University and a PhD at the University of Durham, before securing his current job in Bristol.
Sir Steve Webb, the former MP and Pensions Minister, who got to know Etor through the church in Bristol, called his achievements "remarkable".
"David's message is very much that people shouldn't be defined by their upbringing or their background," he said. "They shouldn't be written off."
"I was pinching myself on my way here this morning," Etor added.
"Nothing good was supposed to come out of me."

Married true-crime buffs embarked on an obsessive mission to prove a double murderer’s innocence. It got complicated
Eileen and Keen Umbehr's obsession with the prosecution of Dana Chandler led them to spend more than 15 years trying to prove her innocence — an all-consuming odyssey that’s the subject of a new, three-part HBO docuseries, reports Bruce Golding
Two married true-crime buffs from a tiny city in Kansas are so convinced that a woman they never knew is wrongly imprisoned for the 2002 slayings of her ex-husband and his girlfriend that they’ve devoted their lives to proving her innocence.
Even though her own children helped put her away.
Eileen and Keen Umbehr's obsession with the prosecution of Dana Chandler led them to spend more than 15 years trying to prove her innocence — an all-consuming odyssey that’s the subject of a new, three-part HBO docuseries.
Chandler, 66, is serving two consecutive life sentences for killing Mike Sisco and Karen Harkness, for which she wasn't arrested until nine years after they were shot in bed inside Harkness's Topeka home early on July 7, 2002.
“When they arrested Dana, everybody believed they got the right person, except for us,” Eileen says in A Killer Story.
The tortuous legal proceedings that followed include an overturned conviction, a hung jury and Chandler's second conviction last year. The case also ended the career of a prosecutor whom the Kansas Supreme Court said used "intolerable acts of deception" to convince Chandler's first jury to find her guilty after just 83 minutes of deliberations.
"We're just so committed to this case that there's nothing else in life that matters," Keen adds in the series, as the couple also shows investigative journalist Joe Sexton a sprawling field dotted with thickets of trees and a pond.
“We’re gonna sell this,” Keen tells Sexton, to help finance their crusade to clear Chandler.
“ Eileen and Keen have always been passionate about seeking justice and have been willing to risk everything for causes they believe in,” Eileen’s brother, attorney Robert Van Kirk, who represented Keen before the U.S. Supreme Court in an unrelated 1995 case, told The Independent.
“The Dana Chandler case is just one of many examples in their lives where they have fought for what they believed was right, often against seemingly insurmountable odds,” added Van Kirk, a powerhouse Washington, D.C., trial lawyer who specializes in complex commercial cases and securities law.
But retired Topeka police Sgt. Richard Volle, who was the lead detective in the case, told The Independent he had no doubt Chandler was the person who shot Sisco and Harkness — at least five times each.
“I'm convinced. The family is convinced. Two juries were convinced — two and a half juries were convinced — that Chandler's in the right place,” he said.
Volle added: “Dana's a psychopath. She's very good at what she does. She can lie easily.”
Chandler is appealing her conviction and is represented by court-appointed lawyer Kristen Patty of Wichita, Kansas, although she filed a motion last year to be appointed a different lawyer. Patty, who's asked for permission to withdraw from the case, didn't respond to voicemail and email inquiries from The Independent.
Chandler and Sisco married in 1982 and were raising a daughter and a son in Lawrence, Kansas, by 1997 when Sisco, a sales manager for a welding-supply company, filed for divorce.
The divorce was finalized the following year, with Sisco granted custody of the kids and Chandler ordered to move out of the family's home and pay child support.
Sisco had been dating Harkness — who was also divorced, with a daughter and a son — for about four years when her father found their bodies ahead of a planned family fish fry at which relatives expected the couple might announce their engagement.
Cops who responded to his 911 call quickly ruled out robbery as the motive in the slayings of Sisco, 47, and Harkness, 53, who'd both spent the previous night at a nearby casino before returning early in the morning.
At the time of her death, Harkness was wearing jewelry that included a diamond bracelet, gold ring and Rolex watch, and Sisco's wallet, found in his shorts, held more than $950 and two uncashed checks.
Sisco's checkbook was also found on the dining room table and Harkness' purse, left on the kitchen counter, held a billfold with more than $350.
But no fingerprints were found on the empty 9-mm shell casings that littered the bedroom and there wasn't any other evidence that pointed to the killer, leaving authorities with little more than the suspicions of family members on both sides who thought Chandler did it.
The case went cold until October 2009, when CBS broadcast the first of three 48 Hours episodes about the killings, which it learned about from Vernon Geberth, a former New York City police official-turned-homicide consultant.
Geberth had been hired by Topeka police to review evidence in the case and concluded in his report that Chandler was “the one and only person who had the motive, means and opportunity to commit these murders.”
During the program, which featured interviews with several family members, Chandler was publicly identified as a potential suspect for the first time.
Video also showed 48 Hours correspondent Harold Dow confronting her as she walked to her car.
“I have no idea what happened to Mike and Karen,” she said.
The program, titled “Haunted,” aired several months after Eileen Umbehr compiled an inch-thick, 200-page dossier that called Harkness's son-in-law, Jeff Sutton, “Person of Interest 2” and sent it to various law enforcement agencies across the state. He has not been arrested or charged in the killings.
Authorities dismissed the dossier because the son-in-law's alibi checked out, with Volle testifying the dossier was based on a “crackpot theory” developed due to a “long-standing feud” between Keen and Sutton, who’s interviewed at length in A Killer Story.
In July 2011, Chandler was arrested in a parking lot in Duncan, Oklahoma, where she was reportedly living in a camping trailer behind her sister's nearby house, local TV station KSWO reported at the time.
Both 48 Hours — which devoted two more episodes to Chandler's case, including a double-length program in 2025 that was rerun in July — and The Topeka Capital-Journal were on hand to watch as she surrendered to heavily armed law enforcement officers from multiple agencies.
They included then-Shawnee County District Attorney Chad Taylor, who took office in January 2009 and was recorded wearing a badge around his neck as he strapped on a handgun.
Chandler went on trial for two counts of first-degree murder in March 2012, with the prosecution presenting a circumstantial case based on more than 900 exhibits and testimony from 80 witnesses, including both of the defendant's children.
The prosecution's theory relied in part on Chandler's purchase of two five-gallon gas cans the day before the killing.
At the time, she was living in Denver, and prosecutors suggested she used the gas cans to refuel her car and return to Colorado without being seen.
Daughter Hailey Sisco, who was 17 when her dad was slain, also revealed that she'd secretly recorded her mom while asking her questions about the killings.
During one conversation in 2005, Chandler denied having committed the shootings but admitted, “I said I could kill him. You ever think about killing him?”
Hailey responded, “No, but —” and Chandler said, “I did.”
“Honestly, I can say I did,” Chandler added.
During closing arguments, prosecutor Jacqie Spradling emphasized those remarks, as well as Volle's testimony that Sisco had obtained a “protection from abuse” order against Chandler in 1998 — a detail the Kansas Supreme Court later ruled he had recanted during defense questioning.
After the jury convicted Chandler, she was sentenced to two life terms.
Eileen Umbehr was in court for every day of the trial, and she and her husband, who live in Alma, Kansas — about 40 miles west of Topeka, with an estimated population of just 1,063 — began digging into the trial records as Chandler's conviction headed for an appeal.
Keen had formerly been the trash collector for surrounding Waubansee County, where he ran afoul of government officials by writing highly critical columns in a local newspaper.
When two of three county commissioners retaliated by terminating his contract in 1991, Keen sued in a case that eventually went before the U.S. Supreme Court.
The high court sided with Keen in a landmark 1996 free-speech ruling, and after settling with the county, he went to college and law school, passed the bar in 2005 and opened his own law office.
Eileen, meanwhile, self-published a 588-page account of her husband’s legal battle, Small Town Showdown, in 2007.
Keen also got involved in politics, mounting an unsuccessful 2012 Republican primary race for the Kansas House of Representatives, and two years later finished a distant third as a Libertarian in the state governor's race, with one of his four sons, Josh, as his running mate.
In 2016, Keen was running in the Republican primary for Shawnee County district attorney when he filed a disciplinary complaint against Spradling, alleging she knew Sisco hadn't obtained a protection from abuse order against Chandler.
An investigation into the complaint was put on hold pending Chandler's appeal, which the Kansas Supreme Court granted in 2018 following oral arguments during which Justice Daniel Rosen blistered Spradling for telling jurors the order had been issued.
“Why isn't that misconduct, and why isn't that something we should look at?” Rosen, now the court's chief justice, said in remarks featured in A Killer Story.
The Kansas Supreme Court later disbarred Spradling in a 101-page decision that also faulted her for misstating evidence and inflaming the “passions of the jury” during an unrelated sex-crimes trial that also led to overturned convictions.
By the time Chandler won her appeal, Eileen had been sending emails about the case for two years to investigative journalist Joe Sexton, a former reporter and editor for The New York Times who was then working for the non-profit news outlet ProPublica.
Sexton, the producer of A Killer Story, serves as its grizzled and frequently foul-mouthed narrator in voiceovers and while sitting at a bar, in front of a bottle of beer and a pack of cigarettes.
Sexton says he largely ignored Eileen's barrage of messages until he “had the dumb luck” to open “email number 2,714.”
“I've done all manner of crime stories. State murder convictions overturned? S*** doesn't happen every day. And the lady was still in prison. They were gonna retry her,” he says.
Sexton recalls being “fueled by the reporter's trademark cocktail of adrenaline and dread” when he arrived to meet Eileen, who he describes as “a housewife who seemed alternately brilliant and deranged.”
And on August 5, 2022, he was in the courtroom gallery for opening statements at Chandler's retrial, at which Spradling was replaced by prosecutor Charles Kitt.
“There was nothing new. There was no, you know, smoking gun. There was no dispositive piece of evidence that established her guilt,” Sexton says. “But now, Dana's defense lawyers had in front of them a detective who, by their lights, had committed perjury in the first trial.”
A Killer Story features extended portions of the cross-examinations of Volle and Chandler's daughter, who'd since gotten married and is now known as Hailey Seel, with Sexton concluding that Chandler's defense lawyers were doing “a pretty effective job of highlighting the deficiencies in the prosecution's case.”
The series also includes an interview with former Shawnee County District Attorney Bob Hecht, who refused to prosecute Chandler before being succeeded by Chad Taylor.
“None of the investigation was able to establish that anyone saw Dana Chandler in Topeka the day before, the day of, or the day after the homicide,” he says.
Hecht, who died in August 2025, acknowledged that his decision “created anger and frustration among members of the police department,” but said, “You shouldn't file charges unless you have sufficient evidence to establish the crime beyond a reasonable doubt.”
Sexton also stood outside the courthouse, asking to interview jurors after they split 7-5 in favor of conviction following six days of deliberations.
“The prosecution never proved beyond a reasonable doubt that she committed the crime,” said juror Carrie Kimes, who voted to acquit. “They could never put her in Topeka. They couldn't put her in Kansas. So I couldn't vote that she was guilty.”
In October 2022, Chandler was released on a $350,000 bond — reduced from $1 million — to await her third trial, which was moved from Topeka to Westmoreland, Kansas, about an hour away, in order to find impartial jurors.
The proceedings began with the bombshell revelation that Chandler had fired her lawyers and would represent herself.
The proceedings included a stunning face-off between Chandler and her daughter, who sparred with her mother, at one point asking, “Is this a good setting to explain our personal relationship?”
“Well, that's a lot of what this trial is about — is my relationship with you,” Chandler replied. “That's what the accusers are trying to put in front of this jury: our relationship or a lack thereof. So absolutely, this is a proper place.”
And if that weren't enough, Chandler also took the stand for the first time, describing how her unhappy marriage led her to start drinking, and her repeated efforts to “get sober.”
But under cross-examination, her claimed alibi for not being in Kansas during the killings fell apart during questioning about the different accounts she gave to the police and a friend.
“And you've had 23 years to figure out what story to tell this jury. Is that true?” prosecutor Kitt asked.
“That's absolutely not true,” Chandler insisted.
The jury took less than four hours to convict her again, and she received the same sentence of two life terms in prison, with no possibility of parole before December 8, 2063 — when she'd be 103.

BRICS leaders on Saturday (September 12, 2026) called for stronger cooperation in disease surveillance and medical product regulation, welcoming the establishment of a dedicated sub-working group to advance an integrated early warning system for the prevention and response to mass infectious diseases.
In their New Delhi Declaration, the leaders stressed the importance of strengthening health infrastructure and local production of medical products to enhance preparedness for future health emergencies and ensure timely, affordable and equitable access to healthcare services, vaccines, therapeutics and diagnostics.
They also called for strengthened collaboration among BRICS medical products regulatory authorities and welcomed efforts to develop a common GxP white paper consolidating regulatory best practices and technical approaches.
Public health emergencies transcend national borders
The leaders recognised that infectious disease outbreaks, zoonotic threats, antimicrobial resistance and other public health emergencies transcend national borders and require stronger international cooperation, timely information sharing and coordinated action.
"Acknowledging that infectious disease outbreaks, zoonotic threats, antimicrobial resistance and other public health emergencies transcend national borders and require strengthened international cooperation, timely information sharing and coordinated collective action, we underscore the importance of enhancing global health security through resilient surveillance systems, effective early warning mechanisms, and strengthened preparedness and response capacities," the declaration said.
The leaders recognising the central role of the World Health Organization and the amended International Health Regulations (2005), underscored the importance of resilient surveillance, early warning and rapid response systems and coordination.
"In this regard, we welcome the establishment of a dedicated Sub-Working Group to advance the BRICS Integrated Early Warning System for the prevention and response to Mass Infectious Diseases, and its Terms of Reference," they said.
Collective preparedness
The initiative is aimed at strengthening collective preparedness against infectious disease threats through closer coordination among member countries and faster sharing of information.
The declaration also called for greater regulatory cooperation to ensure that medical products remain available, accessible and meet standards of quality, safety and efficacy across BRICS countries.
"We encourage strengthened collaboration among BRICS Medical Products Regulatory Authorities by extending the scope of the existing Memorandum of Understanding on cooperation in the field of medical products regulation to the Regulatory Authorities of all BRICS member countries," the declaration said.
Collaborative regulatory approaches
They reiterated the importance of strengthening collaborative regulatory approaches to ensure the continued availability and accessibility of quality, safe and efficacious medical products.
The leaders also welcomed the collective efforts of BRICS regulatory authorities in developing the BRICS GxP White Paper.
"We welcome the collective efforts of BRICS Regulatory Authorities in developing the BRICS GxP White Paper, consolidating best practices of regulatory experience and technical approaches," the declaration said.
The GxP refers broadly to good-practice standards followed in areas such as manufacturing, laboratory and clinical processes, with the common framework expected to facilitate greater sharing of regulatory experience and technical approaches among member countries.
Strengthen domestic health infrastructure
The leaders also linked health security with stronger domestic health infrastructure and local production of medical products, calling for greater preparedness for future health emergencies.
"We emphasize the importance of strengthening health infrastructure and local production of medical products, enhancing preparedness for future health emergencies through stronger surveillance systems, laboratory networks, leveraging digital health technology and Artificial Intelligence," the declaration said.
They also called for technical cooperation among public health institutes, development of robust regulatory frameworks, skilled health workforces and collaborative research and development.
The declaration stressed that these measures were needed to improve access to healthcare products and services and strengthen the capacity of BRICS countries to respond collectively to health emergencies.
People-centred digital healthcare systems
The leaders also reaffirmed their commitment to people-centred digital healthcare systems and welcomed the BRICS Compendium on Digital Health Architecture for Continuum of Care, including access to healthcare in remote areas.
The leaders also supported the activities of the BRICS Vaccine Research and Development Centre and recognised the importance of collaboration in nuclear medicine.
They welcomed the activities of the BRICS Nuclear Medicine Working Group and noted the importance of the BRICS Health Journal in disseminating research findings and promoting scientific cooperation within the BRICS framework.
The declaration also emphasised the importance of sharing experiences, innovations and best practices among BRICS countries to improve health outcomes and advance universal health coverage.

ExclusiveSenior official asked to resign over defective lifts at Queen Mary Hospital
Chief project manager at the Architectural Services Department left her post last month, sources say
A senior Hong Kong government official who oversaw faulty lift installation work that stalled the launch of a new block at Queen Mary Hospital was asked to resign and left her post last month to take responsibility for the defects and delays on other projects, the South China Morning Post has learned.
But experts criticised the authorities’ handling of civil service management missteps, which bypassed the established disciplinary mechanism, saying it lacked transparency.
Multiple sources said that Tuesday Li Pak-yee, a chief project manager at the Architectural Services Department (ASD) who oversaw the multibillion-dollar redevelopment of the hospital in Pok Fu Lam, left her directorate pay-level post in August.
“[Li] was advised by the Architectural Services Department to resign,” a government insider said. “Such a departure is extremely rare within the civil service framework.”
Another government source said the department regarded Li, who served as the main official liaising with contractors and overseeing the hospital project’s execution, as possibly having made “management missteps” over the delay, and that it tried to resolve the matter internally rather than initiate formal disciplinary proceedings.

GoFundMe accused of deceptively adding ‘tips’ to donations that go to company and not helping others
A recently filed lawsuit against the fundraising site takes issue with the automatic tip added at checkout that is allegedly difficult to opt out of
GoFundMe has been accused of deceptively adding “tips” to donations that go to the company and not helping others.
The fundraising site has skyrocketed in popularity since it launched in 2010, helping strangers connect with grieving families struggling to pay for funeral costs or those who can’t afford to pay for medical bills after a tragic accident. Donors can send money to those in need through GoFundMe with a click of a button.
But when people go to donate to a charitable cause of their choice on the site, they are also hit with an automatic tip to the company that they can opt out of, a practice that a recently filed lawsuit claims is tricking donors into paying more.
“Once automatically added, GoFundMe makes the ‘tips’ difficult to remove, forcing consumers to hunt around for a way to remove them,” according to a lawsuit filed in a federal court in Illinois last month by Sandra Donovan of Illinois and Ebony Baker of Georgia, who have both made donations on GoFundMe.
The Independent, which obtained the lawsuit from ClassAction.org, has reached out to GoFundMe for comment.
The lawsuit also challenges how GoFundMe explains the tipping option on its site.
When donors go to pay on the site, the company has a blurb that reads, “GoFundMe has a 0% platform fee for organizers and relies primarily on the generosity of donors like you to operate our service.”
But the lawsuit argues that this description is “false,” adding, “In reality, completely unbeknownst to those who donate through its website, GoFundMe funds its services by charging charitable organizations hefty transaction fees on each donation they receive.”
GoFundMe says on its site that while it's free to create a fundraiser, the company charges “one small transaction fee per donation.”
The fee varies slightly depending on who creates the fundraiser. Individuals and businesses are charged 2.9 percent of the donation plus $0.30, while certified nonprofits are charged 2.2 percent of the donation plus $0.30.
“Donors act quickly, often emotionally, and with the reasonable expectation that their money will go where they intend—toward helping others, not toward undisclosed or preselected middleman fees like the ‘tips’ charged by GoFundMe,” the lawsuit claims.
Donovan and Baker “paid money they did not knowingly authorize, conferring an improper financial benefit on GoFundMe” because of the company’s business practices, the lawsuit argues.
Donovan and Baker's lawyers are asking the court to certify the case as a class action and are demanding a jury trial to stop GoFundMe's “deceptive conduct and return its ill-gotten gains,” according to the lawsuit.
A GoFundMe spokesperson told The Independent that the company “exists to help people help each other, and we have carefully designed our business model to deliver as much support as possible to those who need it – the beneficiaries of fundraisers.
“Donors have the choice to leave GoFundMe an optional tip, which helps us provide fundraising technology, customer support, and Trust & Safety protections to our community. Tips are completely voluntary and can easily be adjusted to any amount, including zero.”
The spokesperson said the claims in the lawsuit have “no merit.”
“The majority of donors adjust the suggested tip amount, and many choose to leave no tip at all. On July 13, an Iranian civilian aircraft carrying a high-level Houthi delegation was heading towards Sana’a, Yemen’s capital. Under an unwritten understanding between the Houthis (or Ansar Allah), who control northern and northwestern Yemen, including Sana’a, and the country’s Saudi-backed government, planes seeking to land in Houthi-held territory were required to obtain prior approval. The Houthi delegation had left Yemen on July 3 on another Iranian aircraft to attend the funeral of Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, Iran’s Supreme Leader who was assassinated by the U.S. and Israel on February 28 when they launched their war against Tehran.
Yemen’s Saudi-backed government had protested the Iranian plane transporting Houthi leaders, arguing it was a violation of Yemen’s sovereignty. It also opposed the delegation taking an Iranian plane back home, and instead offered to facilitate their return on a non-Iranian airline. The government’s main concern was that the flight could also be used to transport personnel of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and military equipment to Yemen. The Houthis, nevertheless, chose to return on a Mahan Air flight. To prevent the aircraft from landing, Saudi-backed forces bombed the runway of Sana’a airport, forcing the plane to land in Hodeidah. This was the trigger.
The Houthis, who took control of Sana’a in 2014, said the strike was a violation of a 2022 ceasefire. They responded by bombing Saudi energy infrastructure and launching an offensive in Hodeidah and Taiz governorates. They also imposed a naval blockade on Saudi vessels in the Red Sea. Within two months, the Houthis made dramatic territorial gains, seizing the entire Red Sea coastline of Yemen and taking the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the narrow chokepoint connecting the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden, under their control.
A revivalist movement
The roots of the Houthi movement can be traced to ‘Believing Youth’ (Muntada al-Shahab Al-Mu’min), a Zaydi revivalist group founded in Northern Yemen in the early 1990s. Hussein al-Houthi and his father, Badr al-Din al-Houthi, influential Zaydi clerics in northern Yemen, became the movement’s leading figures. Inspired by the Iranian revolution of 1979 and the rise of Hezbollah in southern Lebanon in the 1980s, Badr al-Din and his sons started building vast social and religious networks among the Zaydi Shias of Yemen, who make up roughly one-third of the Sunni-majority country’s population. While the Zaydis are seen as part of the Shia branch of Islam, both in terms of theology and practice, they are different from the ‘Twelver’ Shias of Iran, Iraq and Lebanon.
In 2004, Ali Abdullah Saleh’s government, upset with the growing popularity and rebellion of the Houthis, issued an arrest warrant against Hussein. He resisted the arrest, starting an insurgency. In September, government troops attacked the rebels and killed Hussein. But the movement he founded would only grow, forcing Saleh to step down in 2012 and capturing Sana’a from government forces in 2014.
Alarmed by the rise of an Iran-aligned Shia militia across its southern border, Saudi Arabia formed a coalition and declared war against the Houthis in 2015. An intense bombing campaign followed, but the Saudi-led coalition failed to dislodge the rebels, who built a parallel state in northern Yemen. In 2022, amid a broader rapprochement between Iran and Saudi Arabia, the Houthis and Saudi-backed forces agreed to a ceasefire.
The Saudis also struggled to build a credible counterweight to the Houthis inside Yemen. The top leadership of the government was based in Saudi Arabia, while in the south, the UAE-backed Southern Transitional Council broke with the government and pursued its own separatist agenda, further weakening the anti-Houthi camp. Broader tensions between Saudi Arabia and the UAE also complicated their war efforts in Yemen. But the Saudis still maintained an air and naval blockade on Houthi-held territory.
The ceasefire allowed the Houthis to consolidate their position in the north and northwest, despite economic woes. The parallel state, an ideologically committed base, years of warfare and sustained Iranian support enabled the group to transform itself into a formidable territorial army. Their access to the Red Sea, a key shipping route, raised their profile as a naval force. When Israel launched a devastating war on Palestinians in Gaza following Hamas’s October 7, 2023 attack, Houthis “declared war” against Israel “in solidarity with the Palestinians”. They also carried out attacks on Israel-linked ships in the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. In March 2025, U.S. President Donald Trump announced a major air and naval operation against the Houthis, threatening to destroy the group. Despite the enormous firepower brought against them, the Houthis continued launching missiles and drones at U.S. naval forces. Seven weeks later, Mr. Trump announced an end to the U.S. strikes following an Oman-mediated ceasefire.
After the U.S. and Israel launched the war on Iran on February 28, the Houthis, to the surprise of many, stayed out of the conflict. Iran retaliated by attacking American bases in the Persian Gulf and shutting down the Strait of Hormuz. The Houthis understood that Iran’s closure of the strait strengthened their strategic position: they had the capacity to disrupt maritime traffic through the Red Sea. They also wanted the Saudi blockade of their air space and ports lifted. In the first week of July, as a second round of bombings between Iran and the U.S. was unfolding, the Houthis decided to test Saudi Arabia’s resolve by sending a delegation to Iran on an Iranian plane. Saudi Arabia responded by bombing the runway at Sana’a airport as the delegation was returning, effectively breaking the ceasefire. Then the Houthis moved rapidly up the escalation ladder.
Renewed conflict brings Saudi Arabia under enormous pressure. After traffic through the Strait of Hormuz was disrupted by Iran, Riyadh increasingly relied on its Red Sea terminals to export crude oil. Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline, connecting its oil fields in the east with the ports on the Red Sea, allowed the Kingdom to skirt the impact of the disruptions in Hormuz to a certain extent. But the Houthis, after the ceasefire broke down, directly targeted Saudi oil infrastructure, apparently in coordination with Iran-aligned Shia militants in Iraq. On September 11, Saudi Arabia announced that the pipeline was shut, following drone attacks from Iraq. In Yemen, in a lightning offensive launched in early September, the Houthis captured the port cities of Mokha and Dhubab and the Perim Island in the Bab el-Mandeb, extending their control along the coast and into the strait.
Two chokepoints
More than 20% of the world’s seaborne oil trade passed through the Strait of Hormuz before the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran. The Red Sea, which connects Asia and Europe through the Suez Canal in the north and Bab el-Mandeb in the south, typically carries roughly 12-15% of global trade. This means that Iran and Ansar Allah now have the ability to exert pressure on two of the world’s critical maritime chokepoints. The Houthi capture of more territories along the Red Sea, as government forces collapsed within days, has also given them a clear upper hand in the civil war and allowed them to consolidate their position inside Yemen.
On February 27, before the war, both the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait were open, and Iran was prepared to make concessions on its nuclear programme. On June 17, when the U.S. and Iran signed an MoU, committing Tehran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in return for sanctions relief from the U.S. and a regional ceasefire involving Lebanon, the Bab el-Mandeb was still fully open. Today, maritime traffic through both the chokepoints is disrupted, any regional ceasefire will have to include Yemen, and any final settlement will have to address the Houthis’ demands, while Iran’s nuclear programme has been pushed to the back burner.

Philippine rescuers have recovered 41 more charred remains from a ferry fire, raising the death toll to 76 and leaving 13 people unaccounted-for.
The rescue mission comes after a deadly fire broke out on the MV June Aster ferry as it sailed past tourist hotspot Palawan in the Philippines on Wednesday.
What's next?
Philippine Coast Guard official Geronimo Tuvilla says the immediate priority was to identify the victims and determine the cause of the fire.
Philippine rescuers have recovered 41 more charred remains from a ferry fire, raising the death toll to 76 and leaving 13 people unaccounted-for, as forensic teams face the daunting task of identifying the victims.
The rescue mission comes after a deadly fire broke out on the MV June Aster ferry, carrying more than 130 people, as it sailed past tourist hotspot Palawan in the Philippines on Wednesday.
Loading...
Firefighters entered the ferry for the first time on Friday after extinguishing the blaze more than a day after it broke out. Rescuers recovered 30 bodies on Friday.
Authorities said on Saturday that teams had finally gained access to areas of the ferry that had been hard to reach because of thick smoke and extreme heat.
The Coast Guard said burnt remains were discovered in the ferry's economy accommodation section.
Many bodies yet to be identified
Philippine Coast Guard official Geronimo Tuvilla said at a press conference on Saturday that the immediate priority was to identify the victims and determine the cause of the fire.
Responders in protective suits were seen carrying black body bags from a coast guard vessel into tents raised at the nearby Coron Town, where bodies had been brought for identification.
Anxious family members waited nearby for news of their loved ones, including Anelyn Magbanua, 37 — whose husband was returning to Coron after visiting their children in Manila when the ferry caught fire near the end of its more than 20-hour journey.
"I hope he is not among the dead being brought off the ship. I hope he is alive and has only drifted to another island," she said.
"It will be very difficult to accept if he's really gone."
"He loved his children very much."
Questions remain over captain's fate
Images released by the Coast Guard showed the scale of the destruction inside the vessel, with rows of steel bed frames twisted by intense heat and blanketed in ash.
Some photographs appeared to show skeletal remains among the debris.
A statement from the Maritime Industry Authority, citing survivor accounts, said two explosions were heard inside the vessel shortly before the fire broke out.
One survivor interviewed by GMA News recalled seeing a small amount of smoke that turned into a fire and quickly spread through the ferry within seconds.
Questions also remain over the fate of the vessel's captain.
Coast Guard spokesperson Commodore Noemie Cayabyab said she had received information that he was alive, but added that the captain's name was not on the list of the 43 confirmed survivors.
The fire is the latest in a string of deadly maritime accidents in the Philippines, an archipelago of more than 7,600 islands where millions rely on ferries and small boats to travel between provinces and islands.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has called on artificial intelligence companies to slow the pace of development of increasingly powerful AI models, warning that unchecked progress could make the technology harder for humans to understand and control.
“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models. Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain,” Amodei wrote in an essay published on his personal website on Saturday.
Amodei said AI could bring major benefits but also carried serious risks because of the power of the technology.
“AI brings risks, and because it is such a powerful technology, these risks are serious,” he wrote.
His call has received support from 
OpenAI
 CEO Sam Altman and Tesla chief 
Elon Musk
. Altman said the need to pace the development of frontier AI had been a key topic of discussions at OpenAI in recent weeks.
“I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier,” Altman said in a post on X. “Committing to having independent evaluators with employee-like access is a great idea, and we will do the same.”
Musk also endorsed Amodei’s proposal, writing: “Dario is right.”
Why Amodei wants AI development slowed
Amodei said his concern had grown as AI development accelerated, particularly because AI systems were increasingly being used to help build the next generation of AI.
“My first concern is that, since roughly this summer, AI has been advancing drastically faster, driven primarily by AI’s growing ability to build the next generation of AI,” he wrote.
He referred to this process as “recursive self-improvement” and said it was beginning to happen across the industry, including at Anthropic.
“Left unchecked, it could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems, and so must be pursued very carefully, if at all,” Amodei wrote.
He also pointed to risks including the possibility of losing control of AI systems, misuse of AI for cyberattacks and bioterrorism, and serious economic disruption.
Amodei said commercial incentives could make these risks more acute if companies engaged in a race to develop increasingly capable systems without sufficient safeguards.
Anthropic proposes third-party AI evaluators
Amodei said Anthropic would take steps to allow independent scrutiny of its AI systems.
“We’ll provide third-party evaluators with permanent, employee-level access to our systems, so that they can verify adherence to our safety measures, report on incidents, and assess models’ alignment during training,” he wrote.
His wider three-part plan calls for each frontier AI company to give ongoing, employee-like access to embedded third-party evaluators.
He also proposed coordination among AI companies to establish common safety standards and limits on the rate of unchecked AI progress, along with global coordination on AI development.
Amodei said democratic governments should coordinate with authoritarian governments while recognising the difficulties involved in verifying compliance.
OpenAI testing raises safety concerns
The discussion comes amid concerns over the behaviour of increasingly capable AI systems.
OpenAI had revealed during testing that some AI models broke out of their confined environment, connected to the internet and infiltrated Hugging Face, a platform used by developers to store and share code.
Amodei also referred to an incident involving an OpenAI-Hugging Face system in which a swarm of AI agents staged cybersecurity attacks on targets they had not been instructed to attack.
He warned that such a swarm could potentially become capable of taking over the internet.
Researcher quits AI industry over concerns
Amodei's comments came days after AI researcher Jacob Coxon announced that he was leaving the industry after spending three years pretraining AI models, first at OpenAI and later at Anthropic.
Coxon had considered Anthropic more cautious in its approach but said both companies were moving too quickly towards increasingly autonomous systems.
“Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” Coxon said on Tuesday.
“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” he said in a post on X.
Pretraining is the stage in which AI models absorb vast quantities of data.
Superintelligence refers to the theoretical point at which AI capabilities exceed human intelligence.
Amodei says AI benefits remain the goal
Despite his call for slower development, Amodei said he continued to believe AI could significantly improve human life.
“I have worked on AI for the last twelve years because I believe it could dramatically raise the quality of human life,” he wrote.
He said AI could potentially cure major diseases in the next five to 10 years, accelerate economic growth, create a world of abundance and empowerment, and contribute to a renaissance of democracy and freedom.
But he argued that achieving those benefits would require greater care over how the technology is developed.
“The benefits will only be achieved if we build the technology in the right way,” Amodei wrote.
He said the time gained by slowing development could be used to advance research into AI interpretability, improve operational security and strengthen safeguards at frontier AI companies.
Amodei's latest call echoes an earlier appeal by Anthropic in June to slow or suspend AI development. In late July, Altman had also said AI developers might need to voluntarily slow their rapid advances to give society time to catch up.
At around the same time, more than 1,000 employees at leading AI companies, including Amodei, signed a petition calling on the US government to help “deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development”.

A rare thunderstorm system that would normally move rapidly instead remained nearly stationary for hours over Chiba Prefecture last month, contributing to the record rainfall that killed at least 13 people, researchers said Thursday.
A preliminary analysis by the Meteorological Research Institute — part of the Japan Meteorological Agency — said a squall-line-type precipitation system (a linear rainband) was responsible for the Aug. 13 downpours.
Squall-line-type systems are characterized by highly developed thunderclouds capable of producing intense rain, hail, lightning and strong winds, and typically move quickly. In Chiba, however, the storm remained near the Boso Peninsula, with its northern portion lingering there for more than six hours.
“I was honestly surprised,” Toru Adachi, a senior researcher at the institute’s typhoon and severe weather research department, said at a news conference Thursday.
“It was shocking that a phenomenon occurred for which we have not yet accumulated sufficient knowledge, and that it led to a disaster like this. We need to properly understand what happened.”
Researchers said the storm’s movement was likely suppressed by opposing air flows. A layer of cold air generated and strengthened by rainfall pushed the storm system eastward, while warm easterly winds from the Pacific acted as a headwind — pushing against it from opposite directions.
Those forces largely balanced each other, causing the rain-producing system to stall rather than move away as squall lines normally do. The central and southern portions of the storm moved only about 20 to 30 kilometers between 6 p.m. and 9 p.m., while its northern section stayed almost stationary for over six hours.
The institute said the system developed in two stages. Daytime rainfall first created a pool of cold air over inland parts of the Kanto region. Near the Boso Peninsula, warm air flowing in from the Pacific met the cold air, forming a localized boundary known as a shear line. The warmer air was forced upward along that boundary, allowing cumulonimbus clouds to develop.
From around 5:30 p.m., rainfall from those clouds strengthened the cold-air layer and pushed the boundary outward into a bow shape, creating what meteorologists call a gust front. At the same time, a strong current known as a rear-inflow jet developed on the western side of the system, helping intensify the front and fuel further thunderstorm growth.
The clouds repeatedly regenerated above the gust front and reached heights of more than 15 km. That was almost twice the roughly 8-km height of thunderclouds observed during the 2015 Kanto-Tohoku torrential rains, according to the institute.
A linear rainband developed at around 6 p.m. on Aug. 13, and a special heavy rain warning was issued roughly 90 minutes later. The city of Chiba recorded 367 millimeters of rain over 24 hours — the highest level ever observed there.
Researchers also detected a counterclockwise vortex about 2 to 5 km in diameter inside thunderclouds in the northern part of the system, where some of the heaviest rainfall occurred.
The vortex, found at an altitude of roughly 1 to 3 km, may have locally strengthened upward air currents and accelerated the formation of precipitation particles, contributing to the extreme rainfall, the institute said.
The institute said the findings remain preliminary and that researchers plan further analysis to determine more precisely how the opposing air masses allowed the storm to remain in place for so long. The research could eventually help improve monitoring and forecasting of similar extreme rainfall events, the institute said.

Environmental groups have criticised the ongoing protests against the re-issued draft notification proposing to declare parts of the Western Ghats as an ecologically sensitive area (ESA), alleging that vested interests are behind the agitation.
Conservation groups alleged that those opposing the draft have a “hidden agenda”. The Wayanad Prakruthi Samrakshana Samithi (WPSS) said people should understand the rationale and objectives behind identifying ESAs before opposing the proposal. The organisation said the objectives included protecting the Western Ghats’ biodiversity and wildlife habitats, reducing the risk of natural disasters such as floods and landslides, safeguarding river basins and ensuring water availability during dry spells, mitigating the impacts of climate change and promoting sustainable development.
The organisation rejected concerns that ESA restrictions would force people off their land or destroy their livelihoods.
“The Western Ghats is one of the world’s most important biodiversity hotspots. Conservation does not mean evicting people but preventing ecological damage caused by unregulated development,” said WPSS president N. Badusha.
Environmentalists said the High Level Working Group (HLWG) on Western Ghats, headed by K. Kasturirangan, had distinguished between natural and cultural landscapes, with the latter comprising human-dominated land uses such as settlements and agriculture. The HLWG report had identified the biologically rich portions of the natural landscapes as ESA, while large cultural landscapes were excluded from the ESA. Environmental protection would further help safeguard farmers and local communities from the adverse impacts of climate change, conservationists added.
On concerns over restrictions on agriculture and other activities, they said ESA regulations primarily sought to prohibit activities such as mining and quarrying, red-category polluting industries and large construction projects exceeding 20,000 sq m. Existing agriculture, residences and small-scale industries would not be affected, environmentalists claimed.
ESZ a 'shock absorber’
The Animal and Nature Ethics Community (ANEC) Trust, an organisation working on animal welfare and wildlife conservation, said that declaring regions outside protected areas such as national parks and wildlife sanctuaries as ecologically sensitive zones (ESZs) would act as a “shock absorbers” that could reduce the ecological impact of unregulated development.
The organisations alleged that the protests against the ESA proposal were ultimately aimed at protecting the interests of mining, forest encroachment and land mafias.
The Union Environment Ministry issued the seventh draft notification on July 27, 2026, after the previous draft expired. The latest draft proposes to cover 56,825.7 sq. km across six States, including 9,993.7 sq. km in Keralam. The draft remains open for objections and suggestions until September 25, 2026.

Tamil Nadu Minister for Health and Family Welfare K.G. Arunraj on Tuesday (September 8, 2026) announced in the Legislative Assembly that the State government would implement a Statewide mission to reduce the amount of salt in the daily diet of the public.
Dr. Arunraj said non-communicable diseases such as hypertension, cardiovascular diseases, stroke, and kidney disorders were among the most important public health challenges in Tamil Nadu. Nearly 50% of medically certified deaths in Tamil Nadu are caused by cardiovascular diseases. Approximately 1.8 crore people in Tamil Nadu are living with hypertension.
The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that a person should consume less than five grams of salt a day. However, scientific studies indicate that the people of Tamil Nadu consume an average of 7 to 8 grams of salt per day. Studies have also found that approximately 88% of the salt consumed as part of the South Indian diet comes from salt added during cooking at home. Global scientific studies have established that even a reduction of just one gram of salt per day can significantly lower blood pressure, he said.
Further, an international study involving approximately 21,000 people who used a low-sodium salt substitute, in which a portion of the sodium was replaced with potassium, demonstrated a 14% reduction in strokes and a 12% reduction in overall mortality. Based on this scientific evidence, the State government has decided to formulate and implement an integrated strategy to reduce high salt consumption in Tamil Nadu, Dr. Arunraj said.
Statewide survey
Announcing the key initiatives under the mission, Dr. Arunraj said for the first time, a Statewide survey based on urine samples would be undertaken to scientifically determine the current level of salt consumption among the people of Tamil Nadu.
Standards would be implemented to gradually reduce the amount of salt used in kitchens under the direct control of the government, including those serving the Nutritious Meal Programme, the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) scheme, government hospitals and hostels, he said.
The feasibility of making available to the public a low-sodium salt substitute, in which a portion of sodium is replaced with potassium and which does not produce a noticeable difference in taste, would be studied as a pilot project in selected areas, he said.
Through the ‘Makkalai Thedi Maruthuvam’ initiative and Health and Wellness Centres, people with hypertension would receive systematic counselling on reducing salt intake. A Statewide awareness campaign will be undertaken to educate people about salt content in food and simple ways to gradually reduce the excessive use of salt in everyday home cooking, he added.
