Voters will head to the polls on Sunday for a tight election that stands to decide whether the country will shun the direction of the last government or deepen this political shift.
The ruling centre-right minority coalition relies on outside support from the anti-immigration Sweden Democrats, a party that has steadily come into the mainstream and is now polling at 19 per cent. A win would offer them ministerial positions for the first time, inviting deep-seated concern from onlookers.
“The election is a referendum on the Sweden Democrats; whether we continue to go down a far-right path,” according to author and political commentator Jan Guillou.
Ahead of Sunday’s general elections, The Independent looks at what a far-right victory could mean for a country again grappling with its identity.
Who are the Sweden Democrats?
The Sweden Democrats were founded in 1988 as a radical nationalist party. According to an internal investigation, some founders were neo-Nazis, although the party under Jimmie Åkesson, who has led them since 2005, has disavowed those roots, expelling openly racist members and saying it maintains a strict “no racism” policy.
Cleaning up the party’s image has helped a marginal movement grow into a substantial force with influence over talking points across the political spectrum. The movement still leans on hardline populist messaging around migration, criminal justice and national identity. Åkesson has found an audience in appeals to making Sweden “great again”.
“He’s not up on a high horse and he has a knack for explaining complicated issues in an easy, understandable way,” explains Jenny Madestam, a political scientist at Sweden’s Södertörn University. “He is the guy next door.”
This appeal has won the Sweden Democrats enough influence to become essential in the centre right’s battle to hold on to power. Prime minister Ulf Kristersson says the country needs a stable majority government to tackle important issues, such as national security and gang crime, and that the only way is to include the Sweden Democrats. Some Conservatives last time around framed an alliance with the far right as a way to contain its influence.
One area where all the main parties seem to agree is Russia. Nicholas Aylott, associate professor of political science at Södertörn University, told the Associated Press: “The biggest threat to Sweden's security is from the war in Ukraine and there is almost complete consensus in Sweden about support for Ukraine and deep antipathy towards Russia.”
What would the Sweden Democrats do with power?
The party’s 2026 programme gives an indication of what ministers might try to achieve if the Sweden Democrats become part of a four-way ruling partnership: reducing migration to the lowest possible level, deporting foreign nationals accused of serious crimes, imposing harsher criminal penalties, and keeping fuel and energy costs down.
Asylum numbers have dropped to a 40-year low and while Kristersson says the focus will now be on integration, the Sweden Democrats want to go further. In July, while campaigning for the upcoming election, the party paid for adverts promoting a new initiative offering migrants around 350,000 Swedish crowns (£26,700/$37,000) to leave the country.
“Do you miss Mogadishu? The remigration grant will help you get home,” reads one of the adverts.
So far this year, 171 people have taken up the offer of cash to leave. The Sweden Democrats want to extend the offer to immigrants with Swedish citizenship, if they agree to revoke it and leave.
Critics fear the party’s promises to end multiculturalism, restore traditional Swedish values and ban some forms of Muslim dress could deepen social divisions and shift the political centre of gravity even further right.
“If the Sweden Democrats enter government, that would have an enormously negative impact on the liberal ideals of our country,” says Birgitta Ohlsson, European Affairs minister from 2010 to 2014, and now a Center Party lawmaker. “We’ve already seen the effects while they’ve been outside government, and it would be 10 times worse.”
Despite a consensus over tight immigration policies, many Swedes still feel a deep unease about the far right and polls point to a knife-edge vote with the centre-left opposition, which is backing Social Democrats leader Magdalena Andersson for prime minister, holding a small but narrowing lead.
A wider pattern across Europe
The election comes a week after the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party won an historic victory in Saxony-Anhalt, sending ripples through the political establishment and further undermining the unpopular centre-right government.
The AfD, bolstered by public angst over the scale of mass immigration, surged into first place on Sunday in the state election, the first time a far-right party has come within reach of power at the state level since the Second World War.
The outcome earned the recognition of US president Donald Trump, who seized the opportunity to praise the party and criticise the “absolutely horrible Immigration rules and regulations which have hurt Germany so badly”.
Across Europe, mainstream governments continue to be reshaped by pressure from the far right, adopting populist language and policies in an attempt to stay relevant. Sweden’s election, like Germany before it, will be another test of where that leads.

Trade 'war' or not, are Canada and the United States now dug in?
However close they once were to a deal, it could be awhile before they get back there
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer might not like to think of it as a trade "war," but whatever you call it — a difference of opinion? an incongruity? the unpleasantness? — it's now been going on for more than 19 months.
In February 2025, Donald Trump, in defiance of a free trade deal he himself signed in 2018, first announced tariffs on a number of Canadian products.
And it seems now it could be several more months before hostilities are reduced, let alone ceased.
"I think it is more likely than not that the current situation remains unchanged until the end of the year," said Wolfgang Alschner, a professor of business and trade law at the University of Ottawa.
"From the latest rounds of talks, we know that there is a potential landing zone but also that positions are currently too far removed to easily reach an agreement. The status quo is painful, but not so painful as to drive either side into forcing a change in position."
- Jean Chrétien says 'we bow to no one' in fiery 9/11 speech in Gander, N.L.
- Why isn't Canada blocking the Welland Canal? Other trade war questions answered
Speaking to reporters on Thursday, Mark Carney described the latest round of American tariffs announced earlier this week as "relatively modest," at least "in the context of other things that the U.S. administration has done."
That might suggest Carney doesn't see a need to respond with further measures against American imports. The recent cycle of escalation may have reached a kind of equilibrium.
Carney also said Canada is "always ready to strike a fair deal." But if one is willing to entertain war analogies, it might be said that both sides now seem dug in.
The fact that the principal negotiators — Greer on the American side, Dominic LeBlanc and Janice Charette for the Canadian government — have largely avoided the political fray and acted professionally may serve to keep a door open to negotiations, suggests Meredith Lilly, a professor of international economic policy at Carleton University and a former foreign policy and trade adviser to Stephen Harper.
Lilly also sees a few potential "trigger moments" in the months ahead that could restart talks. If the United States and Mexico were to come to an agreement on their issues, for instance, that could put pressure on Canada. The results of the midterm elections in the United States could also change the political calculus on the American side. And lingering in the distance is an American threat to impose new auto and truck tariffs on Jan. 1, 2027.
Trump could also conceivably try to force the issue with a new threat of tariffs, like he did this summer.
Perhaps less optimistically, there is Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew's account that provinces have been told to plan for "two-plus years" of turmoil.
Is anyone winning this fight?
American officials may believe that U.S. economic power ultimately gives them the advantage — U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has likened Canada to a "yippy" dachshund trying to pick a fight with a German shepherd.
But both Paul Krugman, the American economist, and Roland Paris, the Canadian foreign policy scholar, argued this week that Canada may have the motivational or political advantage, with Canadians largely united against a clear and potentially existential threat.
"Trade wars test not only economic strength but also political resolve," Paris wrote.
Recent polls have shown high support among Canadians for taking a tough approach with the United States. And the Angus Reid Institute found a significant bump in support for Carney's Liberals in the wake of trade talks collapsing.
That may strengthen Carney's hand at the negotiating table, but could the Canadian public's reaction conceivably make it harder to get to some kind of deal with the United States?
Before negotiations were formally suspended, Charette reportedly warned her American counterparts that a breakdown in talks and the imposition of new American tariffs could push discussions over a cliff — the public and political reaction, she said, would only shrink the Canadian side's room to negotiate.
David Coletto of Abacus Data has now made a similar argument, suggesting that public sentiment could be a serious impediment to a new deal.
"My sincere hope is that the temperature is turned down in both countries," Lilly said. "In particular, the president really needs to reduce this very aggressive social media campaign that he's pursuing. It makes it politically very difficult, if not impossible, for the Canadian side to engage."
Lilly said she wonders if it would be harder now to even get back to whatever deal the two sides were broadly in agreement about when Trump first announced in August that one was likely.
A fight that will take the measure of Carney and Canada
Some Canadians may trust Carney enough to defer to his judgment on what constitutes a good deal — or the best possible deal under the circumstances. And public opinion polling would suggest he has ample political capital to draw on right now.
But no level of support ever amounts to a blank check. The Carney government may have been acknowledging as much with its decision this week to not move forward with at least some of its most controversial proposals to amend environmental assessment laws.
For the sake of maintaining a strong hand, there might be more Carney could do in the days and weeks ahead.
The Liberal government obviously didn't heed the Conservative opposition's calls to reconvene Parliament, while releasing the text of any draft agreement, as the Conservatives also demanded, may have been impractical or unwise.
But there is also something to be said for the emphasis Conservatives have put on transparency, not only as a matter of accountability, but for the sake of building trust. That might be particularly important for Carney if this fight is to only get longer and harder — and after he was criticized for his handling of the agreement to open the Gordie Howe Bridge.
On a larger scale, the collapse of trade talks and everything that has ensued over the last two weeks may only add credence to Carney's contention that there has been a "rupture" and that Canada's "old relationship" with the United States is over.
Much of the onus for responding to that falls on the prime minister, and it's still too early to know exactly what path Canada will set out on.
But it is perhaps not too early to wonder if this moment is already leaving a mark on the Canadian psyche.
According to polling by the Environics Institute, Canadians held a decidedly favourable view of the United States for some 20 years, from the early 1980s to the early 2000s — from the presidency of Ronald Reagan through to the election of George W. Bush.
Canadian attitudes then plummeted around the time of the American invasion of Iraq, but more or less fully recovered with the election of Barack Obama as president.
There was another marked drop when Trump became president. But unlike the rebound when Obama came to office, the Canadian view of the United States did not fully recover when Joe Biden succeeded Trump, suggesting perhaps that some lasting damage was done.
If anything, the second four years of Trump have been more contentious among Canadians than the first four. And so even if a deal is reached in the next few months, it might be a long while before this trade war — for that is how people on this side of the border will surely remember it — is either forgiven or forgotten.

An Australian teenage girl’s death, suspected to be preceded by consensual “choking” during sex, has renewed calls to ban showing the act in porn.
This latest tragedy, reportedly believed to involve sexual strangulation, comes just months after the UK banned porn showing the practice. But despite all the noise, most people still aren’t aware of just how dangerous the trend is.
Sexual strangulation or “choking” during sex, as it’s referred to colloquially, has become wildly popular—especially among adults aged 18 to 35, despite the risk of severe injury, brain damage, and even death. Some researchers argue that porn is to blame for that normalization, but members of the adult industry say that banning depictions of choking won’t stop this kind of content from flourishing or serve as the kind of sex education and media literacy the public sorely needs.
“With the misinformation that’s out there, especially online, many people do think that maybe at lighter pressures they might be ‘safe,’ and that’s not the case,” says Debby Herbenick, a professor at the Indiana University School of Public Health and one of the leading researchers on sexual strangulation. Herbenick cautions that applying sustained pressure to the front and sides of the throat—via your hands, an object, or otherwise—can lead to blood clots and stroke, tears in the carotid arteries, vision impairment, and cumulative brain injuries.
“It’s these things that we wouldn’t even notice,” she says. “Those tiny, incremental changes in your vision, or your brain, or so on.”
Or, in the most extreme cases, death. Pressing on the front of the throat can lead to airway collapse, Herbenick says. Two weeks ago, a 16-year-old girl in Sydney passed out after authorities believe she was strangled by her equally young partner during sex. She died after being taken to a local hospital in critical condition, and the investigation is ongoing. It’s unknown what her exact injuries were.
The Australian Social Services Minister has since said the government is “very seriously” looking at efforts to ban pornographic depictions of choking in sex, in line with the country’s recently passed age-verification laws that ban social media for children under the age of 16. But critics of these social media bans say they don’t actually work and make it harder for teens to access news and information they need, including sex education around the dangers of choking and strangulation.
The data regarding rates of young people choking and being choked during sex can appear staggering. In Herbenick’s 2021 survey of nearly 5,000 college students in the US, 58 percent of women had been choked during sex and a quarter had been first choked by age 17. Researchers in Australia similarly found rates of around half of people aged 18 to 35 engaging in the practice. Herbenick found that women are usually the ones being choked by men during heterosexual sex and that sexual and gender minorities are also more likely to be choked during sex.
“There are other people who say ‘I asked them to choke me or I said it was OK, but then they really pushed past my limits or it was a lot harder than I expected, or I asked them to stop and they didn’t,’” Herbenick says. She also says that while some young men enjoy the act, others “tell us that they don’t want to be choking their partners, but they think they’re supposed to, or they get asked all the time.”
Most of the self-reported occurrences of sexual strangulation among US college students Herbenick surveyed were described as consensual, but when choking is nonconsensual, it can be even more dangerous. In fact, strangulation is one of the strongest predictors for murder in an abusive relationship.
It’s important to distinguish between the different types of intimate partner strangulation: as a form of abuse, nonconsensual introduction of strangulation into what may have started as a consensual hookup, fully consensual choking, and fictional depictions of choking, like what is usually happening in legal pornography and television. But with the exception of staged or implied choking (like placing a hand over a partner’s neck without actually applying pressure), all of these kinds of strangulation carry major and even deadly health risks for the person on the receiving end.
Clare McGlynn, a law professor at Durham University whose work has contributed to pornography regulation in the UK for 20 years, says the amount of porn involving strangulation has risen over the past few decades and corresponds with an increase in children viewing strangulation content.
“If you ask young people, ‘Where do you get your ideas for sex or sexual activity?’ they say ‘porn.’ And you think, ‘Well, yeah, of course you do,’” McGlynn says. “I think its ubiquity in porn does mean that’s why we see large numbers of young people engaging in this practice consensually, because they think through scripts they’ve seen in mainstream porn that it’s normal, it’s expected.”
The UK’s recent ban on porn showing strangulation or suffocation falls under the country’s Online Safety Act, which requires social media platforms, search engines, and other web services to proactively remove illegal material and employ controversial age-verification measures. According to McGlynn, the strangulation ban was adopted in April but hasn’t been implemented or enforced yet, meaning the government has yet to take action against any companies or individuals.
“The platforms aren’t going to act in and of themselves,” she says. “They’re only going to act if they think the regulator is going to take action against them.”
McGlynn believes that within a few years of the ban on strangulation in porn actually being enforced, a new generation of young people may grow up without seeing choking as a standard part of sex. It’s an optimistic view—one that isn’t shared by everyone.
Cherie DeVille, a well-known pornographic actress, points to the fallout from age-verification laws—requiring proof of age to access adult content—as an example of the futility of banning porn. Consumers can simply use VPNs to get around local laws and turn to the unregulated world of sexually explicit content, often hosted by foreign platforms that don’t comply with any of the laws that major companies are forced to obey.
DeVille, who was a physical therapist prior to entering the adult film industry, describes how talent liaisons assist in the negotiation of what is allowed in specific scenes before filming, including choking, which she says never involves putting actual pressure on the trachea.
Pornhub echoed its consent policy for performers in an email statement to WIRED, writing, “We can be confident that the acts that appear in our content are completely consensual, unlike other platforms that don't have the same consent requirements.” Meanwhile, adult creators on OnlyFans are wary of posting anything involving choking after the service was forced to clamp down on most hardcore content in 2021 to avoid banks freezing payments. (OnlyFans didn’t respond to a request for comment about whether choking and sexual strangulation are technically banned on the platform.)
While Herbenick says that young men are more likely to learn about sexual strangulation from porn, young women are more likely to learn about it from memes, mainstream entertainment, or even erotic fanfiction about One Direction. HBO director Sam Levinson featured it in early episodes of Euphoria and The Idol. It was the opener to a chart-topping Jack Harlow song, where he crooned about choking a woman but not being a “killer.”
“Porn is an appealing boogeyman to say we can stop this by regulating this very specific type of speech, despite the fact that this is ubiquitous throughout culture,” says Mike Stabile, the director of public policy for the Free Speech Coalition, which is the nonprofit trade association for the US adult industry. “The solution is education. The solution is to talk about consent rather than try and find a singular cause that, if you were able to censor it, will solve the problem.”
Herbenick agrees about education. She says one of the biggest cultural changes we need to make is for parents to talk to their kids and teenagers about the dangers of strangulation and the type of messaging they’re consuming about choking during sex—whether it’s in porn or the Billboard Hot 100.

The use of coal to generate electricity on the US grid has been plunging for nearly two decades, and the first Trump administration was unable to affect the trend. So his second administration has attempted more aggressive interventions to prop up coal use. One of its most direct means of doing so is to order coal plants that were scheduled to close to remain open, even if there is no need for them.
The administration’s justification for these orders is a statute that allows the Department of Energy (DOE) to declare an emergency in the case of wartime or a sudden shortfall in generation. A number of parties, including states where coal plants have been slated to close, have challenged this declaration. And on Friday, in the first of these cases to make its way through the courts, the declaration was judged to be contrary to the statute. While this only affects a single coal plant in Michigan, the reasoning of the decision will apply to every coal plant closure that has been blocked by the DOE.
No emergency
The decision was issued by a unanimous three-judge panel from the DC Circuit’s Court of Appeals. It focuses on the J.H. Campbell Generating Plant, which was scheduled to close last year but has been kept open by a total of five emergency declarations by the DOE, each limited to 90 days by the Federal Power Act. At issue was section 202(c) of that Act, which allows the DOE to declare emergencies when the US is at war or when “an emergency exists by reason of a sudden increase in the demand for electric energy, or a shortage of electric energy.”

When it was announced last year that the acclaimed manga “Look Back” by Tatsuki Fujimoto would be getting a live-action adaptation, I was both excited and confused. Excited because the film was being helmed by Hirokazu Koreeda, one of Japan’s best directors, and confused because an anime adaptation had already been released in 2024.
“Look Back,” which hits theaters Sept. 11, is far from the first double-dip in the long history of Japanese visual media. Popular manga titles have often been adapted into both live-action and anime films over the decades. While this can sometimes feel like a money grab, these releases also give audiences the chance to experience multiple takes on the same material.
A semiautobiographical manga by Fujimoto (“Chainsaw Man”), “Look Back” is a coming-of-age tale about two girls who team up to become professional manga artists. The anime film, directed by Kiyotaka Oshiyama, was both a financial and critical success, earning more than ¥2 billion (around $13 million) and bagging a number of awards, including best animated feature at the Japan Academy Awards.

It was at the 1992 Olympics in Barcelona when the mutterings about a new "secret weapon" started.
Dozens of Great Britain athletes had been taking a new product that increased muscle mass and improved athletic performance – a "wonder pill" that didn't fall foul of any doping rules.
They were talking about creatine.
Now found in tubs and bags on many supermarket shelves and tagged in your social feeds, it is the supplement of choice for millions of people and one of the most scientifically researched.
But back then, when it came on the scene at the very top of British elite sport, there were suspicions and stigma around the use of any substance described as 'performance enhancing' – even if it was legal.
From the minute an athlete wakes, to the moment they go to bed, they are thinking about how they can optimise their performance and recovery.
Today, creatine is just one of a long list of supplements taken by elite athletes in this pursuit of marginal gains. Some help with muscle size and strength, while others correct deficiencies in the diet.
"There are various reports in the literature of some studies that say maybe up to 90% of athletes take supplements. I often jokingly say that means 10% are lying," says Prof Graeme Close, professor of human physiology at Liverpool John Moores University.
"The sports teams that I've worked in, I think that's probably closer to 100% of athletes will be taking some form of supplementation."
So, what do supplements actually do and why do athletes take them? And in the world of strict liability, where elite athletes are solely responsible for what they put in their bodies, how do they make sure they stay clean?
While experts like Close advocate for seeking to meet nutritional needs through food in the first instance, it may not always be possible or practical to do this - and that is where supplements come in.
Take, for example, creatine, which is found naturally in meat and fish.
"You would need the best part of a kilogram of raw chicken a day to get the amount of creatine you need," says Close. But it is unsafe to eat raw poultry because of the food poisoning risk from harmful bacteria.
Creatine is a natural compound in the body produced in the kidneys, liver and pancreas. It is a quick source of energy for muscles, which is especially important for short-duration, high intensity activities such as sprinting.
Its big break as a supplement came in the 1990s when two scientists who had been researching it for two decades shared their findings with Steve Jennings, whose Maxim sports nutrition company supplied products to the British Olympic team.
During the 1992 Barcelona Games, investigative reporter Doug Gillon had learned of a 'secret trial' involving British athletes and seen a box of their Ergomax C150 – effervescent creatine tablets. He wrote that if the scientists' claims - that creatine could improve explosive athletic performance by 1-3% - were true, then "sport may never be the same again".
In terms of sport supplements and nutrition, he was right. By the time of the next Olympics in 1996, an estimated 80% of athletes were taking creatine, and since then it has become mainstream, with research suggesting there may be cognitive benefits as well as physical.
According to the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition, the creatine breakthrough of the 1990s had "launched a new era in sports nutrition" and "sparked exploration into other supplements".
The global dietary supplements market size was valued at $209.5bn (£154bn) in 2025 and is projected to grow to $431.7bn (£317.4bn) by 2033, according to Grand View Research., external
Close, who oversaw nutrition for last year's British and Irish Lions rugby union tour, sees supplements as the "final piece of the jigsaw" rather than a starting point.
"What we're talking about is small margins of benefit, where actually these athletes who focus on the food, I think what you often find is that they've got the big-ticket items right," he says.
"So they're seeing great performance benefits because their overall diet is immaculate.
"They might be missing out on the one per-centers, but they've really nailed the 99 per-centers. And they often do better than those who chase the one per-centers but have not given enough attention to the 99 per-centers."
Australian cyclist Nicole Frain agrees, adding: "I'm a pretty big believer that they are called sport supplements. They are there to supplement the things you already do right.
"I don't think supplements are the answer to fix my problems.
"You need to be eating a balanced diet, training well, sleeping right, recovering well, hydrating – all of those things – before we add in all of the extras."
Close puts protein powders top of the list of supplements taken by athletes he works with, followed by creatine and vitamin D.
Protein powders maximise muscle repair and contribute to muscle growth, while creatine is a quick source of energy for muscles and important in short-duration, high-intensity activities like sprinting. Vitamin D, meanwhile, is essential for bone health and supports muscle function.
Other popular supplements include carbohydrate gels, which Close says were key in the first sub-two hour marathon run earlier this year by Kenyan long-distance runner Sabastian Sawe.
"As sport nutritionists we were all fascinated at what the fuelling programme was, and it was the sports drinks and gels that played a huge part of that fuelling," Close says.
"There was a calculation done of what it would take to break the two-hour marathon, and that did involve making sure that over 100 grams of supplemental carbohydrate were ingested per hour.
"And the reports coming out of the recent sub-two-hour marathon was that it was 110 grams of carbohydrate per hour that was achieved."
Supplements can improve performance, but there is an uneasy ring to describing them as 'performance enhancing' because of the association with banned substances and anti-doping rule violations.
So what determines whether something is on the World Anti-Doping Agency's (Wada) banned list?
"For Wada to put anything on the list, it's got to hit two out of three criteria: dangerous to health, performance enhancing, and against the spirit of sport," Close explains.
"So just because something enhances performance, if it's not dangerous to health and not against the spirit of sport, Wada will not touch it.
"So creatine is a good example.
"Though something like an anabolic steroid, where it's against the spirit of sport to be injecting yourself for a performance benefit, it's dangerous to health and it's performance enhancing - that hits all three."
But taking a supplement still carries anti-doping risks.
"No guarantee can be given that any particular supplement is free from prohibited substances," UK Anti-Doping advice states, urging athletes to "be vigilant" in using them.
And if you test positive for a prohibited substance, consuming it unintentionally can result in the same four-year ban as if you deliberately took it.
There are supplement-testing programmes which batch test products before they are sold to make sure they do not contain any Wada-prohibited substances.
One of those is Informed Sport, which says as many as one in 10 supplements is contaminated with ingredients and compounds prohibited in sport and points to a study carried out by the Anti-Doping Knowledge Centre that showed product contamination was responsible for 8% of all anti-doping violations between 2005 and 2022.
While Informed Sport is a very well used system among athletes, Wada makes it clear that quality assurance schemes can reduce but do not eliminate the risk of an anti-doping infringement.
If you do accept the risk, you need to be organised to keep track.
In the case of Great Britain rower Heidi Long, it takes a spreadsheet.
"I've recorded the batch number of every product that I've taken and its expiry date because if you take it after the expiry date the Informed Sport [certification] is no longer viable," she says.
Close says he has also done site visits to factories to see where the supplements are made to check the manufacturing processes because "the risk of failing a drugs test is huge".
There are risks to the general population too, he adds, saying: "You can be buying supplements off the internet that are made in somebody's garage and you've got no idea of the manufacturing processes."
He points to studies on creatine products which have found there is no creatine in them and so "you're completely wasting your money" and that in the worst case scenario it may contain substances that are dangerous to your health.
"So it is really important that the message is that while they can play a small role, the safety considerations are the key factor," he says.
There is, however, more than one way for an elite athlete to chase a competitive edge – and some are going back to basics.
For every trending supplement, there is an unprocessed, wholefood alternative – from the anti-inflammatory benefits of turmeric, staving off cramp with pickle juice or consumption of high-nitrate foods like beetroot before competition.
It is what Close calls a "food-first" or "food-only" approach and something he says every athlete should use as a starting point.
The latest to have its moment in the spotlight is an ancient Ethiopian grain called teff.
Used for thousands of years in traditional east African diets, teff is now making its mark globally in performance nutrition.
In comparison to other popular grains like wheat, rice and quinoa, teff has a high mineral content and is rich in calcium, iron and vitamin C. Naturally gluten-free and good for the gut, it is also unique for being a 'complete' protein, meaning it provides all nine essential amino acids required for human nutrition.
These superfood credentials have caught the attention of some of the world's best athletes over the years, from Olympic champion marathon runner Haile Gebrselassie to seven-time Grand Slam singles champion Venus Williams, and it is now becoming a more common sight on UK supermarket shelves.
British boxer Fran Hennessy was introduced to teff by her nutritionist and it is now part of her daily routine.
"I've never looked back," she says. "What I'm putting in my body is good fuel and energy and teff has so much. It energises you so much before a workout and it gives you the fibre you need."
As well as boosting her performances, Hennessy credits teff with being key to recovery.
She says: "Each meal I'm having there's a reason behind and everything that's in it there's a reason behind... I know what I'm putting in my body is fuelling me, recovering me, energising me."
Cost is another consideration when athletes are deciding on supplements.
"The supplement industry is really expensive," says Long. "And we're definitely not made of money. So I think it's really picking and choosing when you want to put that investment in."
She says it makes sense to have more supplements around racing time "when the performance is super critical and very time dependent".
"[But] on a daily basis if I can get the protein intake from my dinner and a glass of milk or yoghurt and breakfast then actually I was going to be eating that food anyway so it's not as expensive."
And then there is taste.
"I would much rather enjoy a coffee in the morning with friends or while I'm working rather than have one of the gels," she says. "Some of the gels ... you'll end up holding your nose when you take it.
"I guess it's just like the enjoyment of what you're taking, you know, it's nicer to eat food than it is to take supplements."

The Year Great-White Sharks Took Over Maine
More and more people have spotted them this season, but no one knows exactly why—or what to do.
If you spend a lot of time in the ocean, it is hard not to think about sharks. I visit the beach near my home in southern Maine regularly with my family, and almost every night from spring to fall, I go surf fishing after dark. For a long time, I soothed my anxiety with statistics—in America, you are far more likely to be killed by a riding mower than a man-eating fish—and by reminding myself that, in all my years of beachgoing and striped-bass fishing, I’d never encountered a great white in the wild. But then, late one night a few weeks ago, I saw one. It was, as best as I could tell, a juvenile white, and the experience was wholly anticlimactic: A dark triangular fin appeared about 10 yards from where I was wading. It cruised the shallows at a 45-degree angle to the shoreline and seemed uninterested in me. I backpedaled out of the water.
This would be the year that I finally spotted a shark. Maine’s great-white population has been growing for some time—the state had its first fatal shark attack in 2020—and this season, sightings have been unusually high. In July, beaches in Phippsburg were temporarily closed due to a shark sighting. Last month, Mile Beach, Half Mile Beach, East Beach, Wells Beach, and multiple Biddeford beaches were closed for the same reason. At one point, nearly a dozen sharks were reported at Pine Point Beach in a 48-hour period. Then, a longtime lifeguard at Scarborough Beach, Greg Wilfert, was dragged five or six feet underwater by a shark that grabbed his rescue torpedo. After the incident, Wilfert and his fellow lifeguards began monitoring the water with drones. He told me that they’ve seen as many as 15 great whites a day, which they chase off with Jet Skis. (Curious if they were exaggerating, I accompanied a drone-owning friend to check things out on a random afternoon: We saw four great whites in 30 minutes.)
But if seemingly everyone agrees that more sharks have been around this season than in the past, even scientists are having a hard time pinning down what exactly is driving the spate of sightings, and what it means about the future of Maine’s beaches. Jérôme Pinti, a senior scientist at the Gulf of Maine Research Institute, attributed the rising number of great whites to a combination of factors: Climate change has expanded the species’ northern range; the effects of shark-conservation efforts begun in the 1990s are beginning to be felt; and, because the state is home to large biomasses of prey species including striped bass and seals, all the new great whites are finding ample food.
Pinti also said, however, that ascertaining the true extent of the state’s white-shark increase is difficult without a formal stock assessment, which has yet to be done. He noted that the growing popularity of recreational drone use muddies the picture. “I believe we have more sharks,” Pinti told me. But also, “everybody and their brother has a drone right now. So if you have drones above the water all the time, you’re gonna see sharks a lot more.” Whether the rise in shark sightings is because of an actual increase in the number of sharks swimming in Maine waters, or because new technology simply makes the fish easier to spot, is an open question.
Another open question is what, if anything, Mainers and those who visit the state’s beaches should now do differently. Ryan McDermott, a co-owner of the Black Point Surf Shop in Scarborough, told me that the sharks are making him and his fellow surfers choosier about when they go out. “It better be pretty good surf to get you out there when you know that there’s more than a handful of great whites just around the corner,” he said. I suggested that coastal Maine may soon become Cape Cod 2.0—another New England tourist destination that has had to negotiate its own rapidly expanding population of toothy ocean inhabitants. McDermott corrected me: “It’s already kinda happened.”
When I tracked down Wilfert, an affable 71-year-old who bears more than a passing resemblance to Dog the Bounty Hunter, he was still manning his lifeguard post, flanked by a pair of massive Newfoundland water-rescue dogs. He walked me down to the water’s edge and showed me the frayed rope of his yellow rescue torpedo. He told me that he didn’t see the shark that came after him—he felt it. He thought his buoy had gotten caught on a boat propeller, until the fish dived and started dragging him down. “I’ve been here 55 years,” he said, “and I’ve never seen a shark.”
When I asked Wilfert whether he’d changed his habits, he said he was still swimming, though he confessed that he was not going out as far and had recently relied on drone shark spotters. As our conversation ended, a pair of elementary-school-age boys ran up to the perma-tanned Wilfert to ask him if he was the lifeguard who had been attacked. They, too, wanted to hear about the shark.
In the emptier-than-usual parking lot, a stone’s throw from the beach smoothie shack, I walked past a stylish woman unloading beach chairs while her teenage kids impatiently snapped their gum. I stopped on the way to my own car, identified myself as a journalist, and asked whether she was worried about the recent surge of great whites.
“Not worried and don’t care,” came the reply. “My husband is a lobsterman.”

“Solanki told me, ‘I have to talk to you. My way of talking is very different.’ I later understood what she meant by that,” Shaheen said.
The sisters then asked to be allowed to call their families. At that point, their phones were taken away, Shaheen alleged.
“The moment they snatched our phone, she began slapping us repeatedly. This happened in the reception area. If the CCTV footage has not been tampered with, all of this should be recorded.”
“We kept asking, ‘Why are you hitting us? What have we done? You cannot hit us. We have committed no crime, and even if you believe we have committed a crime, you do not have the right to beat us’.”
Solanki then allegedly began dragging them towards another room upstairs.
“We did not know where she was taking us. She dragged us through the area where the SHO’s room is located. She pulled our hair and clothes,” Shaheen alleged.

‘Teach them a lesson’: Dragged, slapped, kicked
Shaheen said she managed to break free and rushed into the SHO’s room, seeking his intervention.
“I asked the SHO what we had done wrong. I told him, ‘Under what authority is she beating us? Please intervene.’ But instead of listening to me or helping me, the SHO told the police constable who had followed me into the room to take me upstairs and ‘teach them a lesson.’”
Shaheen alleged that she was then forcibly dragged upstairs.
“They beat us and dragged us by whatever they could grab — our hair, our clothes. We were brutally dragged up the stairs. I could not walk; I could not breathe properly. I kept saying, ‘Please stop, let me breathe. Tell me where you are taking me.’ But they did not tell us anything.”
The room where the women were taken did not have CCTV cameras, Shaheen said, although there was a camera in the corridor leading to it.

Shaheen Khan and Nafisa Khan from 4PM News Network were covering the opening of a new wing at Max Hospital in Saket, attended by Home Minister Amit Shah and CM Gupta.

Shaheen alleged that the assault escalated inside the room.
“They threw me to the floor. They kicked me, punched me and slapped me repeatedly. They slapped me continuously. Then they picked me up and threw me onto a sofa. They began pulling my hair and scratching my face. My head was banged against the wall.”
She alleged that a baton was then brought into the room.
“She told me, ‘I will show you. You ask too many questions.’ She hit both me and Nafisa with the baton. At one point, when she became tired, she sat down at a table. The phone they had taken from me rang at that moment.”
‘Oh, you are a Muslim!’
Shaheen said the officer’s demeanour changed after she saw the name of the incoming caller on her phone.
“When she looked at my phone, there was an incoming call from someone named Mohammad Khan. The moment she saw the name, there was a complete change in her demeanour. She immediately got up from her chair and said, ‘Oh, you are a Muslim. Then I will hit you with four more baton blows and slap you four more times.’”
“She then began hitting me again. She also told the constable accompanying her to hit us. All of them then started beating us, including people who had stood still until then. They beat us so badly that I could not breathe. I needed water and told them, ‘At least give me some water’.”
Shaheen broke into tears while recounting the incident.
MLC ‘Delayed’, Police Sought Compromise
Neetu, another colleague of Shaheen and Nafisa, told Alt News that the police did not arrange a medico-legal examination (MLC) after the alleged assault and instead sought a compromise.
“After the assault, they did not arrange an MLC. They wanted us to compromise and suppress the entire matter. We then called the police ourselves on 100 and went for the MLC on our own.”
Neetu alleged that the MLC was deliberately delayed and took five hours to be conducted. After the medical examination, the journalists returned to Saket police station around 9 pm.
“After that, they made us wait there until around 4 am without registering an FIR. Three SHOs came to the police station and eventually left. We were then told to remove two names from the complaint and that ‘whatever happens will happen’. But the FIR was not registered,” Neetu said.

‘Even if I had Committed a Crime, there is Law’
Shaheen disputed the police’s version of the incident.
“The DCP posted a tweet and then deleted it. If what he said was true, why did he delete it? The DCP should be ashamed of making such a statement. Under what law are they trying to justify this heinous act?” she said.
“Even if we assume that I had committed a crime, under which provision of law and under what procedure were we detained, assaulted, locked inside a room and had our phones snatched? We were literally kidnapped. On what legal basis was all of this done?”
“Whatever I may have done, you could have registered an FIR against me and taken legal action. You could have prosecuted me according to the law. I would have cooperated with you,” Shaheen said.
What was Shaheen Reporting on when She was Detained?
Shaheen claims she was detained for asking questions to the chief minister.
“I did not question anybody there directly. I was simply shooting my segment, in which I raised a few basic questions. The government has a responsibility towards its citizens, right? But instead, it appears to be devoting so much attention to private hospitals.”
In the roughly two-minute segment, Shaheen questioned why elected leaders were giving so much time and attention to a private hospital while public hospitals, women’s safety and law and order remained issues.
“This was a barely two-minute video. In it, I raised these questions and showed the venue and the surrounding area, which had been transformed and decorated for the event yesterday, even though it is usually littered with waste,” Shaheen said.
Several journalists’ associations, including the Press Club of India, “strongly condemned” the incident and called for “punitive action against Delhi Police officials posted at the Saket Police Station, including the Station House Officer (SHO), for brutally assaulting freelance journalists Shaheen Khan and Nafisa Khan while they were reporting…”

On Friday, the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed the dismissal of a lawsuit against the city of Jackson, Mississippi, which alleged the city knowingly let residents drink lead-contaminated water.
The lawsuit, first filed in 2022, says the contamination violated Jacksonians’ constitutional right to bodily integrity. Donald Trump–appointed judge Kurt Engelhardt disagreed. “The Constitution does not provide redress for every governmental wrongdoing,” Engelhardt said. “Defendants’ actions allegedly deprived Plaintiffs of clean water and guileless information. These deprivations, while grievous, do not infringe upon any deeply rooted constitutional right.”
That may be true in Mississippi—but on the state level in at least nine US states, and in more than a dozen other countries, clean drinking water is in fact a protected right. In countries including Uruguay and South Africa, a right to clean water is enshrined in the constitution. New York’s state constitution, as of a 2021 amendment, states that “each person shall have a right to clean air and water, and a healthful environment.” So too in Massachusetts, where “the right to clean air and water” has been constitutionally protected since 1972.
But according to the Fifth Circuit ruling, the US constitution is too narrow for such a claim. The Jackson plaintiffs alleged that their city government deliberately withheld information about the water’s toxicity and exacerbated the problem through a series of boil-water notices—a practice that can eliminate some bacterial contamination, but also concentrates lead in water. Engelhardt stated there is no “constitutional right to truthful information from officials during a public health crisis.”
Jackson is more than 80 percent Black and has a poverty rate that is more than double the national average. The city’s water system has long been in dire need of upgrades. In 2015, officials from the Mississippi State Department of Health found elevated lead levels in the water supply. Instead of immediately informing citizens, they remained silent about the issue for six months, according to reporting from Grist, while residents continued drinking toxic water.
EPA officials ran a series of tests in 2020 and found “persistent and concerning violations” of water safety policy, including leaks, corrosion, and high lead levels throughout the system.
But no city, state, or federal agency fixed the problem. Meanwhile, people, including Jackson plaintiff Priscilla Sterling, continued drinking water with unsafe levels of lead. According to the 2022 lawsuit, several of Sterling’s children have since been diagnosed with lead poisoning, which can cause permanent brain damage. A quarter of Jackson’s residents are children, who are particularly vulnerable to the lifelong effects of lead poisoning.
The Fifth Circuit ruling comes as the Trump administration moves to weaken clean-water-related protections. Also on Friday, Trump’s EPA released a supplemental rule to further dilute the Clean Water Act, quickly condemned by environmental watchdogs.
“The administration is clearly struggling to craft a rule that will hold up in court while satisfying their donors’ desire to effectively scrap these protections wherever possible,” said Jim Murphy of the National Wildlife Federation. “One thing is clear: If we don’t protect our streams and wetlands, the cost of dirtier drinking water and increased flooding will flow downstream to households at a time when most Americans are living paycheck to paycheck.”

New-age tech stocks delivered a mixed performance this week as weakness in the broader equity market kept investor sentiment cautious. Of the 63 listed new-age tech stocks under Inc42’s coverage till last week, 33 declined between 0.01% and nearly 14% this week. Thirty stocks ended in the green. Pernia’s Pop-Up Shop parent Purple Style Labs became the 64th new-age tech company under Inc42’s coverage after making its stock market debut on Monday (September 7). The stock listed at a discount of about 6% on the BSE but recovered during the week to close at ₹570.15, around 0.8% below its IPO price of ₹575 Following the addition of Purple Style Labs, the combined market capitalisation of the 64 new-age tech companies under Inc42’s coverage stood at $171.6 Bn at the end of the week. The 63 companies covered by Inc42 at the end of the previous week had a combined market capitalisation of $170.5 Bn. NSE SME-listed Yudiz Solutions led the losers for the second consecutive week, falling 13.91% to ₹22.60. It was followed by recently listed logistics company LEAP India, which declined 9.23% to ₹144.55. LEAP India touched a fresh intraday low of ₹136 yesterday. FirstCry, Capillary Technologies, EaseMyTrip, and IndiaMART InterMESH also fell to new lows during the week. On the other hand, Lenskart, Paytm, and Nykaa touched fresh highs, while Swiggy, Honasa Consumer, and Groww were among the other stocks that registered healthy gains this week. ESDS Software emerged as the biggest gainer, surging 91.65% during its first full week of trading to close at ₹1,716.35 on the BSE. Now, let’s take a look at some of the other major developments involving listed new-age tech companies this week. RentoMojo To List Next: Furniture and appliance rental startup RentoMojo’s IPO closed with a subscription of 72.88X, receiving bids for 158.68 Cr shares against 2.18 Cr shares on offer. Its shares are tentatively scheduled to list on the bourses on Thursday (September 17). Shiprocket Cuts Loss: The logistics company’s consolidated net loss narrowed 24% YoY and 16% QoQ to ₹13.7 Cr in Q1 FY27. Its operating revenue jumped 34% YoY and 7% QoQ to ₹592.1 Cr. Shiprocket shares gained 1.99% during the week to close at ₹134.05. Cofounder Pledges EaseMyTrip Shares: Cofounder and chairman Nishant Pitti pledged 34.51 Cr EaseMyTrip shares, worth around ₹211.9 Cr, to Motilal Oswal Financial Services for “personal use”. The latest pledge represents 8.66% of the online travel aggregator’s total share capital. Pitti’s total encumbered holding now stands at 44.87 Cr shares, equivalent to 11.26% of the company’s share capital. Swiggy-Udaan Deal: Swiggy will sell retail distribution platform LYNK to Udaan through a share-swap transaction valued at around ₹500 Cr. In return, Swiggy will receive a roughly 2.8% stake in Udaan and invest another ₹75 Cr for an additional 0.4%, taking its total holding in the B2B ecommerce unicorn to about 3.2%. Veefin Eyes Mainboard Migration: BSE SME-listed fintech SaaS company Veefin Solutions submitted an information memorandum to the BSE to migrate to its mainboard. It also plans to apply for direct listing on the NSE after receiving the requisite approval from the BSE. Meesho Scraps CPO Role: Ecommerce major Meesho discontinued the position of chief product officer as part of a restructuring of its product leadership team. Consequently, incumbent CPO Prasanna Arunachalam ceased to be part of the company’s senior management personnel. Go Digit Director Resigns: Go Digit independent director Giridhar Aramane resigned following an increase in his responsibilities after being appointed chairman and managing director of Unitech Ltd. BlackBuck Sets Up Subsidiary: BlackBuck’s board approved the incorporation of wholly owned subsidiary BlackBuck Transport Services Pvt Ltd to provide trucking and logistics services. The subsidiary may own or lease commercial vehicles, develop platforms for transport-asset transactions, and provide fleet management, warehousing, and related services. Against this backdrop, here is a look at the broader market performance during the week. Markets Fall For Fifth Week India’s benchmark indices ended lower for the fifth consecutive week amid elevated crude oil prices, rising global bond yields, and concerns over US inflation. The Sensex declined 2.27% during the week to close at 74,781.76, while the Nifty 50 fell 2.09% to 23,398.10. The midcap and smallcap indices also declined 1.40% and 0.88%, respectively. Crude oil added to market pressure, with Brent briefly crossing $110 per barrel yesterday before ending the week at $104.61, up 8.7%, amid the escalating US-Iran conflict and disruptions along key Middle Eastern shipping routes. Persistently high oil prices could add to India’s imported inflation, widen the current account deficit, increase costs for companies, and put further pressure on the rupee. Meanwhile, the US 10-year Treasury yield moved closer to 5%. A sustained increase in US bond yields could strengthen the dollar and accelerate foreign portfolio investor outflows from emerging markets such as India. Foreign portfolio investors pulled out around ₹7,443 Cr from Indian equities in the first week of September after turning net buyers in July and August. The ongoing correction follows a mixed performance in August. While the Nifty 50 declined 1.24% during the month, the Nifty Midcap 150 and Nifty Smallcap 250 gained 1.72% and 2.52%, respectively. The Nifty Microcap 250 rose 5.41%. Despite the near-term volatility, brokerages remain constructive on India’s longer-term prospects. Morgan Stanley expects the Sensex to reach 89,000 by June 2027, provided crude oil prices moderate. Jefferies sees opportunities emerging from India’s next industrial cycle across manufacturing, semiconductors, electronics, space, and data-centre infrastructure. Investors will now track the US Federal Reserve’s policy decision, domestic inflation data, crude oil prices, and developments in the US-Iran conflict for further cues. Now, let’s take a look at the performance of the week’s biggest gainer and the fintech group. ESDS Extends Blockbuster Run ESDS Software emerged as the standout performer among recently listed new-age tech companies, with its stock nearly doubling during its first full week of trading despite weakness in the broader market. The enterprise cloud and AI infrastructure company made its market debut on September 4. Its shares closed their debut session at ₹895.50 on the BSE, more than double the IPO price of ₹429. The rally continued throughout the week, with the stock touching its upper circuit in every session. Its circuit limit was subsequently narrowed from 20% to 10%. ESDS shares ended at ₹1,716.35 on the BSE yesterday, up 91.65% from their debut-day closing price. The stock is now 300.1% above its IPO price. The company’s market capitalisation stood at around ₹20,118 Cr (about $2.11 Bn) at the end of the week, compared with an IPO valuation of about ₹5,028 Cr. The rally highlighted strong investor appetite for listed AI infrastructure plays. ESDS’ ₹720 Cr IPO was subscribed 135.88X, with the portion reserved for qualified institutional buyers (QIBs) booked 261.51X. Optimism from the Street provided another trigger. Choice Institutional Equities initiated coverage on ESDS with a ‘Buy’ rating and a price target of ₹1,550, citing its AI infrastructure opportunity and $1.25 Bn contract with Sharon AI. ESDS crossed Choice’s target price within five trading sessions. Fintech Stocks Ride MDR Hopes Shares of listed fintech companies rallied during the week of the Global Fintech Fest (GFF) 2026, with the possibility of MDR being introduced on certain UPI transactions providing investors with a potential earnings trigger. Pine Labs was among the biggest beneficiaries, gaining 14.17% during the week to close at ₹202.35. The stock surged 16.9% during yesterday’s session alone, while Paytm, MobiKwik, and AvenuesAI also posted sharp gains. The rally followed a report that an MDR of around 40 basis points could be introduced on UPI transactions involving larger merchants or higher transaction values. UPI currently operates under a zero-MDR regime, limiting the direct revenue that banks and payment companies earn from such transactions and leaving them dependent on adjacent services and government incentives. Introducing MDR, even on a limited set of transactions, could therefore create a direct revenue stream for banks, acquiring entities, and third-party application providers. Brokerage Bernstein named Paytm its top fintech pick, citing the possible introduction of MDR, growth in merchant lending, and improving operating leverage as potential earnings drivers. The developments coincided with GFF 2026, where UPI and the next phase of India’s digital payments ecosystem took centre stage. Prime Minister Narendra Modi called for expanding UPI’s international footprint and linking it with more global payment systems, while NPCI unveiled initiatives spanning ticketing, contactless payments, and international RuPay credit card payments through UPI. Pro-Khalistan graffiti appears at Delhi’s Singhu Border ahead of BRICS Summit, 3 arrested
The graffiti, featuring offensive slogans, was painted on walls at the Singhu Border on September 6.
Three men have been arrested for allegedly painting pro-Khalistan graffiti at Delhi’s Singhu Border days before the BRICS Summit, with police alleging that the act was carried out at the behest of banned organisation Sikhs for Justice (SFJ) and its chief Gurpatwant Singh Pannun.
The Delhi Police Special Cell made the arrests after examining CCTV footage and following other leads in the case, news agency ANI reported. The alleged mastermind was reportedly in direct contact with a foreign handler, receiving foreign funding and managing SFJ's operations in India.

How police traced the accused
Deep Dive
The graffiti, featuring offensive slogans, was painted on walls at the Singhu Border on September 6. Pannun had claimed responsibility for the act in a post on X, ANI reported.
The Special Cell registered an FIR and launched an investigation into the incident. During the probe, investigators examined CCTV footage from the area and gathered clues that led them to the three accused.
Police have also recovered the car allegedly used by the accused to carry out the graffiti. Further investigation is underway.
Security amped up in Delhi
Security has been stepped up across the national capital as India hosts the 18th BRICS Summit at Bharat Mandapam on September 12 and 13. Dog squads have also been deployed as part of the security arrangements.
Delhi Police has mobilised around 15,000 personnel, while nearly 200 companies of paramilitary forces have been deployed for security and other operational duties.
“Delhi Police has mobilised over 15,000 personnel for these arrangements. The MHA has provided us with approximately 200 CAPF companies, which are being deployed for law and order duties and other operational tasks,” Special Commissioner of Police (Security) Manish Agarwal said on Friday.

In the past, a ‘healthy plate’ was the single prominent determinant of what constitutes healthy eating. Things, however, are far more complex today, as awareness grows about each meal, micro meals, snacks and what must comprise each such unit.
Even as, on one side, awareness about packaging and labels on packaged foods grows with the new FSSAI (Food Safety and Standards Authority of India) mandates, on the dark side, online/social media continue to influence food fads and generalised opinion gets packaged as expert advice. The flavour of a few seasons now, seems to be protein.
ALSO READ |Paying attention to our packaged food
India is asking the wrong question about protein, the Physicians Association for Nutrition, India (PAN India) said in a White Paper, issued in the context of the National Nutrition Week between September 1 and 7. “Protein has become one of the most talked-about and most misunderstood topics in nutrition. Conversations are dominated by grams, “complete vs incomplete” labels, and high-protein product marketing. These measures are useful, but none of them alone tells you whether someone’s diet is actually healthy or adequate,” the paper says.
The treatise starts by contesting a basic principle: The conventional idea that animal protein is “complete” and plant protein is “incomplete” is oversimplification. Plant foods too contain all the essential amino acids the body needs; the amounts of each just vary by food. Within a varied diet with enough calories, the body gets what it needs across the day; you do not need to combine specific foods at every single meal, the nutritionists argue.
Push for protein
At the heart of the concern is excessive influence wielded on social media that pushes the protein narrative and sits in judgement over those not calibrating their protein per meal or per day. From recommending adding fish and chicken, to protein shakes and even, lately a ‘Profee’ (protein and coffee) the online space has become a hyperactive protein-pushing zone. Algorithms aggressively push recommendations and create fresh anxiety over whether one is getting enough protein or not.
Meenakshi Bajaj, dietician, Tamil Nadu Government Multi Super Speciality Hospital, says: “Unfortunately, social media content is available anytime and everywhere, just a swipe away. As a result, it often appears to have more influence than qualified professionals or evidence-based medicine. It is unfortunate that patients, regardless of age or education, can fall prey to food fads. Content shared by influencers, gym trainers, people with large followings, and unqualified health enthusiasts are being followed without checking the source, credentials, or scientific basis.”
She adds: “Just yesterday, I met a qualified professional undergoing dialysis who had read on social media that people on dialysis require high protein. While that is correct, the post did not explain appropriate protein sources. He was consuming three to four whole eggs daily, along with 17 to 20 almonds and walnuts, which contributed to very high potassium and phosphorus levels that could be life-threatening. Had he consulted a qualified dietitian, she would have explained suitable food sources and cooking methods to control potassium and phosphorus while still meeting his protein needs.”
Another reason why protein has occupied centre stage is the growing use of GLP-1 antagonists, used widely for weight loss. Those on these drugs, are advised to watch muscle loss, a side effect of the process of losing weight. Protein is also said to assist with satiety in managing hunger. During any rapid weight loss process, protein may be burned for energy instead of serving the traditional function of tissue maintenance and repair.
The White Paper —Rethinking Protein in Plant-Based Diets — argues that protein should be understood within the context of a person’s complete diet rather than reduced to grams, amino-acid scores or marketing claims.
As per the Indian Council for Medical Research -National Institute of Nutrition recommendations, a healthy Indian adult must have approximately 0.83 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight daily, making it about 50 grams of protein for a 60-kg adult. This is the generalised norm, however, children in their growth phase, breastfeeding women, sportspersons and older adults might require more protein, the quantity going up to 2 grams per kg per day.
Chennai-based health and fitness coach Priyadarshini Raju says, “I wouldn’t call consuming protein itself a fad, but yes, there is a great deal of hype around protein right now. You don’t need to have protein written on the package of everything that you find in the aisle of a supermarket. However, for our population, a meal is extremely carbohydrate dominant. Just rice, chapati, idlis, dosas.”
For clients, her advise is to add a small amount of protein to each meal, as also fibre. But what kind of protein? “Breakfast can be as simple as besan or oats, or if you’re having dosa, just add a little paneer or tofu to it, if you are a vegetarian. Similarly, for lunch, add the same, or fish or chicken. The meal doesn’t have to be protein dominant but yes, there should be a little protein along with your carbs and fibre; fats, anyway, we get enough of in our traditional diets.”
Plant vs animal proteins
The paper pitches a similar angle: “In a varied diet with adequate calories, people generally do not need to combine specific proteins at every meal. Traditional combinations such as rice and dal, roti and chana, or idli and sambar are useful, but the more important issue is eating sufficient quantities of protein-rich foods,” also challenges the familiar claim that animal proteins are “complete” while plant proteins are “incomplete”.
Almost all plant foods contain all nine essential amino acids; there is a difference of course, and it lies in their relative proportions. It goes on to recommend prioritising pulses, beans, lentils, soy foods, nuts, seeds and whole grains, as they provide protein along with good fibre, unsaturated fats, vitamins, minerals and beneficial plant compounds.
PAN-India also addresses another elephant in the room: Supplements. While arguing that protein supplements are not routinely necessary for healthy adults, they might have a role to play in helping athletes, older people with poor appetite, individuals on GLP-1 medications, or those recovering from illness. Ms. Priyadarshini agrees. “As far as supplements, I might recommend them to people who do are reluctant to bring any protein in their diet, especially vegetarians who have just a carb-loaded diet. Otherwise, I think as long as you’re able to fit in whole foods into your diet, you will be good. That is the best way.” Her vote is for raising awareness of protein consumption and making wholesome food choices.
Dr. Bajaj says: “A diversified, wholesome diet especially one with a high dietary diversity score, age-appropriate portion sizes, and foods that are local, traditional, and seasonal rather than packaged or processed would be considered as an ideal prescription for good health.” She explains that the core principles of nutrition prescription are adequacy, individualisation, and avoiding excess. “Therefore, a therapeutic nutrition plan should be guided by ABCDE: anthropometric measures, biochemical parameters, clinical signs and symptoms, dietary assessment, and exercise type, frequency, and intensity. It must also account for age, gender, medical and surgical history, drug–nutrient interactions, food allergies or intolerances, and economic status,” she adds. Food, ergo, is a complex business, best not left in the hands of social media influence.
“Protein should not be viewed only as a number on a food label. It is an essential macronutrient that supports growth, development, digestion, immunity, healing, and muscle protein synthesis, especially when combined with resistance training,” Dr. Bajaj notes.

The internet's obsession with 1980s analogue nostalgia has taken over social media feeds, with users using AI image generators to turn everyday ideas into faded, film-grained memories. As the social media swoons over the 80s, users can now recreate the warm, nostalgic atmosphere of late 20th-century Punjab—characterised by earth-toned village courtyards, classic handloom textiles, vintage vehicles, and soft, direct-flash photography. Here are five ready-to-use prompts to capture that classic 1980s Punjab aesthetic: Quick answers to key questions Some effective prompts include specific instructions for capturing the subject in nostalgic settings with details like clothing styles, textures, and compositions that reflect 1980s Punjab aesthetics. The trend reflects a cultural nostalgia among users seeking to recreate warm, retro aesthetics from the 1980s, as well as the allure of turning current photographs into vintage-style images that emulate past memories. To maintain authenticity, specify in your prompt that the AI should preserve facial features, skin tone, and identity while detailing the period-appropriate clothing and setting to achieve a true vintage look. Yes, privacy concerns arise when uploading identifiable images, as they can contain biometric information and metadata. Users should be cautious and consider cropping sensitive details before sharing. Prompts should specify details like clothing styles, hairstyles, vintage props, lighting conditions, and settings that are typical of 1980s Punjab to achieve an authentic nostalgic feel. Prompt: “Preserve the exact facial identity, bone structure, eye shape, facial proportions, and skin tone of the person in the uploaded image without any alteration or airbrushing. Recreate them as the subject of a formal 1980s small-town photo studio portrait in Punjab. The subject is posed sitting upright on a carved wooden armchair in front of a hand-painted pastoral garden backdrop. Dress them in mid-1980s formal wear—either a tailored retro blazer with a wide-collar shirt or an embroidered vintage salwar-suit with a delicate phulkari dupatta.” You are a creative image-editing assistant. Transform the provided image into a 1980s Punjab-style retro AI photo. Days after Sam Altman said that OpenAI was open to slowing the development of AI systems, Anthropic cofounder and CEO Dario Amodei has now also called for reining in the pace at which AI companies are improving frontier models. In an essay called “We Must Pace the Frontier”, Amodei argued that rapid gains in AI capabilities were beginning to outstrip the industry’s ability to test and control the systems it is building. While noting that AI had the potential to accelerate economic growth, he also flagged that the same systems could create severe risks if companies race ahead without giving safety research enough time to catch up. Amodei’s comments come as AI labs compete to build more capable models and invest billions of dollars in computing infrastructure. However, rising competition has raised concerns that commercial pressure could lead developers to deploy powerful models before adequate safeguards are in place. However, the industry appears to be aligning together on the matter. Responding to Amodei’s post on X, Altman said that he agreed that there was a need to “pace” frontier model development. He also committed to Amodei’s idea of roping in independent evaluators with employee-like access to build for safeguards AI development. Elon Musk, who runs SpaceX and xAI, also said that he agreed with Amodei in a post on X. In his essay, the Anthropic CEO said that “pacing” AI development did not mean halting research or stopping model training. Instead, he proposed slowing capability improvements enough to give companies, independent auditors and governments time to ensure that safety safeguards are keeping pace. He cited two developments for the cautious approach. Firstly, he flagged the recursive self-improvement, the growing ability of AI models to help build the next generation of AI. Secondly, he warned that agentic systems, over the next 12 months, could potentially be capable of creating persistent botnets and taking over parts of the internet. Amid this backdrop, Amodei has proposed a three-pronged approach to curb these threats and foster “pacing” of AI systems: Embed external evaluators inside frontier AI companies. These third-party teams would receive employee-like access to the company’s systems, training processes and internal risk-assessment tools. Coordination among frontier AI firms operating in “democratic” countries. He also proposed common safety standards and limits on unchecked capability advances, backed by government support. Global coordination between nations Amodei said a slower pace would allow AI labs to improve operational controls, refine alignment techniques, advance interpretability research and develop more robust evaluations designed to detect deception, manipulation and cyber-risk capabilities. Also while acknowledging that it would be “much harder” to foster coordination between the US and China, the Anthropic CEO said that any agreement with “authoritarian” governments would need strong verification mechanisms. To preserve the US-led bloc’s lead in the AI race, Amodei also called for restrictions on the export of advanced AI chips and semiconductor equipment to China, stronger action against chip smuggling and remote access to overseas data centres. He also called for tougher controls on unauthorised model distillation and improved security against the theft of model weights. The essay follows a series of incidents that have raised concerns over safeguards surrounding autonomous AI agents. AI Misuse Risks Grow The severity of the concerns came to fore in July this year after an incident occurred during an internal test at OpenAI, which was designed to measure how capable its latest AI models were at carrying out complex cyber tasks. To complete the test, the AI model tried to break out of its testing environment and eventually reached a machine connected to the internet. Once online, it identified Hugging Face as a likely source of information and exploited multiple vulnerabilities to access Hugging Face’s production infrastructure. However, better AI models have been launched since then. Earlier this month, OpenAI launched Astra and called the frontier model as the beginning of its “AGI (artificial general intelligence) era” and a generational leap in AI capabilities. The AI giant said that the model is the first from its kitty to cross its internal “critical” cybersecurity risk threshold. Separately, Anthropic recently released a report, which documented the use of its Claude models in activities ranging from cyberattacks and surveillance to fraud and biological misuse. Amid all this, former researchers at AI companies have flagged concerns over the pace of AI development. Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at OpenAI and Anthropic, recently accused AI companies of pursuing increasingly capable and potentially self-improving systems without adequately addressing the risks. Right after this, Altman reportedly told employees that OpenAI was open to the idea of slowing down the development of AI systems in coordination with other leading AI companies.

For years, we at Inc42 have tracked the Indian tech startup ecosystem and seen it grow from a kid to an adult. Among the clearest signs of evolution and maturity of this ecosystem is the growing number of startups eyeing a public listing now. For Indian companies, achieving a public listing has for long symbolised operational progression, transparency, and long-term viability. For startups, it’s a relatively new but increasingly critical rite of passage, one that not only signals coming of age but also creates pathways for investor exits and wealth creation. Currently, a handful of startups, including the likes of Razorpay, OYO, PhonePe, among others, are in various stages of their IPO journey. Meanwhile, over 70 Indian new-age tech companies have already crossed the milestone and are now listed on the bourses. The list now also includes Indian companies like MakeMyTrip and Freshworks, which are listed on Nasdaq in the US. India’s startup IPO wave reached its peak in 2025, surpassing the previous year's momentum. While 13 startups went public in 2024, the number has already been overtaken this year, with 18 companies making their market debut in the previous year. The list of new-age tech companies that went public in 2025 included Meesho, Ather Energy, Urban Company, Lenskart, Groww, Pine Labs and PhysicsWallah. Inside The Dalal Street Startup Ride Indian startups had gained a reputation for being “loss making” by prioritising growth at all costs and market share over immediate profitability. The trend of putting scale ahead of the bottom line was at its peak amid the funding boom of 2020-22. While prioritising growth is not wrong for startups, especially at early stages, the start of funding winter in 2022 gave a reality check to the Indian startup ecosystem. Subsequently, startups started pushing for profitability. Giving further wings to the aggressive profitability push was the ambition to list on the exchanges. While new-age tech companies look to turn profitable before filing their draft IPO papers, those that cross the line manage to stay in the green, data shows. About 64% of the listed new-age tech companies, 41 to be precise, are currently profitable.
