Anthropic said Thursday it has blocked efforts by bad actors to use its artificial intelligence models for malicious activity such as cyberattacks, surveillance, and research that could have led to biological weapons.
As AI models grow more powerful, elaborate cyberattacks no longer require sophisticated skills and even lone individuals can create threats that would not have been possible even a year ago, Anthropic said. The company said it has added stronger safeguards in its latest models to restrict biological research that could also be used to make weapons.
“The cases we share here aren’t typical misuse, but rather examples of the most notable and novel threat activity we’ve identified to date,” Anthropic said in its third report since March 2025 describing AI misuse. The report includes snippets of the malicious code and AI prompts Anthropic said it found, and urges governments and AI competitors to identify and prevent similar abuse.
“We’re publishing this work because we believe we have a responsibility to disclose malicious misuse of our services. As models become increasingly capable, their risks will increase, unless AI developers and society’s defenders act to make them safer,” the company said.
The lengthy report by the AI startup, which is planning an initial public offering this fall, was published two days after one of its researchers announced he's resigning over concerns that Anthropic and its competitors are not acting responsibly in AI development. He echoed concerns raised inside and outside of the industry about the technology’s potential to elude human control.
Between December 2025 and August 2026, researchers at Anthropic found misuse by actors ranging from spyware vendors and “politically motivated individuals” to state-sponsored groups spreading propaganda.
Among the findings in the company's report are unnamed actors attempting to use its models for research that could have led to biological weapons. In one instance, Anthropic said its systems blocked a request for Claude’s assistance in authoring a grant application for scientific funding.
“The work discussed in the application involved gain-of-function research (that is, research that genetically alters an organism to create a new or enhanced biological property) on the chikungunya virus. This gain of function research was aimed at the virus’ transmissibility and immune evasion properties,” the report said.
Chikungunya is a mosquito-borne virus that causes debilitating symptoms such as severe pain and fever. The request involved a grant proposal for research seeking to enhance mutations to make the virus progressively more harmful. While such research could “certainly” be used to develop better vaccines and treatments, Anthropic said, “it could also be used to make the pathogen more dangerous.”
None of the cases Anthropic included in its report were found to be using its newer, more powerful Claude Fable or Mythos-class models, with the exception of one illicit distillation case that Anthropic described as “an industrial-scale, covert campaign to extract a model’s capabilities and replicate them in another model without authorization.”
Anthropic said its older models, such as Claude Opus 4 and Claude Sonnet 4.5, from 2025, “were well below the threshold where they could meaningfully assist a sophisticated user in carrying out dangerous biological research.”
“As a result, safeguards on these models were less stringent, directed mostly at preventing access to content that might uplift novices in recreating known bioweapons,” the report said. “But for today’s models — which are capable of assisting in a range of complex scientific research tasks — the evidence is no longer certain, and we cannot make that same assurance.”
Because of this, Anthropic has applied “stronger safeguards that restrict access to a wide range of dual-use biological research queries” in its more recent models, such as Claude Fable 5, the report said.
As companies introduce increasingly powerful AI models, experts have called on governments to regulate the technology, rather than relying on the industry to police itself.
John Thickstun, an assistant professor of computer science at Cornell University, said it is an uncomfortable position for companies like Anthropic and OpenAI to be in when they are expected to determine what is safe vs. unsafe behaviour and make "value judgments at societal scale without any kind of democratic or deliberative oversight.”
Anthropic also found groups that created hundreds of social media accounts that look like they belong to ordinary people and then posted material amplifying the same political view over the course of a week. The company outlined nine such cases it found, originating in Russia, Iran, Turkey and across the Persian Gulf, South Asia, Africa and Europe.
While social media companies can detect influence operations on their platforms once posts are circulating, “we may see it on Claude while the operation is still being built.”
Anthropic released this report after one of its researchers, Jacob Coxon, announced he's resigning amid fears the company and its chief rival OpenAI “are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Coxon's post warned that some of his colleagues now believe AI could threaten human life by the end of the decade.
But Anthropic said it has blocked each of the malicious activities it identified, used the experience to strengthen safeguards and shared information with government authorities and industry partners.
“We hope that the findings in this report will help other developers recognize similar patterns on their own platforms, give governments and civil society a clearer view of how emerging threats take shape, and strengthen collective defenses,” Anthropic said.

Why Houthi military gains in Yemen may further increase gas prices
DUBAI, United Arab Emirates - A tenuous years-long truce in Yemen unraveled further this week as Iran-backed Houthi fighters pushed out Saudi-backed Yemeni forces along a key stretch of Red Sea coastline.
Statements by the Houthis and a rival Yemeni commander, who's cited by The Associated Press, said Friday the Iran-backed group had taken control of the port city of Mokha, just north of the Bab al-Mandeb waterway.
The fighting in Yemen, and the Houthis' targeting of Saudi oil carriers around that waterway, coincided this week with another exchange of fire in the Persian Gulf between the United States and Iran.
As a result, the price of Brent crude—a global metric for oil prices—shot up to nearly $110 a barrel. The London-based research firm Capital Economics says the fighting on both sides of the Arabian Peninsula raises the risk of even further energy price hikes in the coming weeks.
AAA says gasoline prices in the United States are up by 34% from last year at this time, averaging $4.28 a gallon now. Diesel, used for farming and trucks, is up by 61%.
Data from maritime analytics firm Kpler, and cited by multiple news outlets, shows Saudi Arabia exported just 3.2 million barrels a day last month, its lowest level in more than a decade.
While higher oil prices help Gulf Arab producers like Saudi Arabia offset the sharp fall in their energy exports, they still face growing budget deficits, in part due to attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
Now, Saudi oil tankers run a gauntlet to bypass the Houthi attacks in the southwestern Bab al-Mandeb shipping corridor, squeezing one of the world's biggest oil producers.
Saudi Arabia is also a key stabilizer of energy prices in OPEC, but with its exports curtailed by the two conflicts and other Gulf Arab producers struggling to get oil and gas out, countries around the world are digging into emergency oil reserves to plug the gap, leading to higher prices.
Saudi Arabia had been re-routing its crude through an east-west pipeline leading to the Red Sea as a fallback measure to keep oil flowing following the closure by Iran of the Strait of Hormuz in response to the U.S.-Israeli war.
The Houthi attacks on shipping have forced Saudi Arabia to use a much longer and costlier route through the Suez Canal to the Mediterranean Sea and around Africa in order to reach buyers in Asia.
The Houthi takeover of the Yemeni port city of Mokha comes just days after the group fired missiles and drones at four regions of southwestern Saudi Arabia. The group says the attacks were in response to dozens of Saudi airstrikes on Yemen, including one that killed civilians at a prison.
The Saudi Energy Ministry said the Houthis struck Saudi oil facilities, sparking fires that halted operations on Tuesday. Saudi Arabia said more than 70 people were wounded in the attacks.
The renewed fighting in Yemen comes 11 years after Saudi Arabia first led a coalition of Arab countries into war in Yemen to roll back a Houthi takeover of the capital, Sanaa, and reinstall Yemen's government to power. More than a decade later, the Houthis still control Sanaa.
The deadly fighting in recent days for control of Mokha and other areas of Yemen's western coast has displaced at least 18,500 people, according to the United Nations' International Organization of Migration.
It says families are fleeing with nothing and arriving at humanitarian sites that already lack emergency food stocks and shelter supplies.

French police probe if sabotage derailed train and injured 44
A fragment of rail was found on the track, with the possibility of a malicious act that resulted in 44 people injured
Investigators suspect that a train derailment in northwest France which injured 44, one gravely, was the result of sabotage, a police source said on Saturday.
A fragment of rail was found on the track, with the possibility of a malicious act being treated as the main line of inquiry as a result, the source said.
Carrying 186 passengers, the train was running between the Normandy cities of Rouen and Caen when it derailed around 7.45pm local time on Friday close to Renault’s factory in the town of Cleon.
Authorities activated a mass-casualty response plan, with 130 firefighters, five medical teams and 80 vehicles drafted in.
An AFP photographer saw a mass of railway staff working around the train on Saturday morning.
Rouen prosecutor Sebastien Gallois said 44 people were injured including an 18-year-old woman evacuated “in a critical condition”, while tests for drugs and alcohol on the train driver had come back negative.

New system, same problems - Alonso not happy with 'soft' Chelsea
- Published
It was a familiar story for the Premier League's top scorers.
Chelsea's entertaining 2-2 draw with Hull on Saturday means the Blues have now found the net 10 times this season - but they have also conceded two or more goals in each of their opening four league matches for the first time in 11 years.
Only Crystal Palace and Ipswich Town have conceded more than Chelsea's nine goals in the top flight so far this season.
The issue predates manager Xabi Alonso's arrival. Chelsea are now without a clean sheet in 20 league matches stretching back to January, their longest such run for 65 years.
Alonso still appears to be experimenting. This week alone, he changed shape in three successive matches - from the defeat at Arsenal to the 6-3 Carabao Cup win over Leeds in midweek and again against Hull.
Yet it was Hull who looked more likely to find a winner. No wonder there was a subdued mood at Stamford Bridge.
Alonso summed up the feeling afterwards, saying his side needed to be "competing better" and avoid being "soft" in duels.
There were also individual errors.
Jorrel Hato misjudged a cross before Hull scored their equaliser, while Mohamed Belloumi's second goal came after Chelsea failed to clear a corner.
Despite an early goal from Morgan Rogers and a second-half equaliser from Joao Pedro, with Cole Palmer involved in both strikes, Chelsea had to settle for a point.
Hull boss Sergej Jakirovic even described Chelsea goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez as the "man of the match" after the Argentine denied Oli McBurnie, Mohamed-Ali Cho and Lucas Herrington.
Asked about Chelsea's defensive issues, former defender and BBC pundit Ashley Williams said: "Chelsea are all over the place in transitions. When they lose the ball, they are wide open. The goals they conceded are just basic errors.
"Both individually and as a defensive unit, they are so far off it and are shipping goals. They are not going to achieve what they want this season defending like that."
'We got what we deserved'
With Rogers, Palmer and Joao Pedro in fine form offensively this season, the Blues know they need to find solutions defensively.
Alonso said: "We had one or two good chances to get the winner, but you're still open. Not happy. We can do better. We got what we deserved.
"We need to be more solid and be more controlled. [We have] new players and new staff. This is the process. In a few months I'm sure we'll be able to control better."
However, he said his decision to switch to a back four was not a solution to recent defensive issues, explaining: "It's about the profile of the players.
"You can say it was back three or four, so it's about the choice of the players, their qualities, where they play better.
"Today we played with Malo [Gusto], he was playing in good positions, trying to find him and on the right linking with other players, so it wasn't that much of a change for me."
It was a "tactical" decision to take Hato off at half-time, he continued, before going into more detail about what it will take to fix Chelsea's issues.
"It's all maybe entertaining, but I hope that one day you say it was a boring game and we win and we don't give these entertaining moments," Alonso added. "But for sure it kind of repeats some patterns that we are making.
"It will take time or it will take moments to fix them when we get the lead and you still need to be competing and not to give the chance so easily for them to come back. Especially in the first goal, we can do much better.
"It was too soft to give them this hope because until then we were controlling, we were creating chances, but that momentum that we had changed the mood and the score of the game and it's something that we need to be talking [about], we address and we will get better, but it's having an impact on our performances at the moment."
There will be concerns going into the trip to Brentford on Friday, the last match before the three-week international break, given that the Bees are known to be dangerous at set-pieces.
It's not just set-pieces, though. Chelsea have conceded the majority of the goals from open play, which is something Alonso acknowledged.
"Overall, I think that we are attacking better than defending in every part," he continued.
"We know that it's a big topic and a big theme for us. For sure it's just four games, but the dynamic in terms of conceding, I don't like it and we need to do much better. Open play, set-pieces, long balls, this toughness, this competitive sense, we can do better."
Some players, like Malo Gusto, have been criticised by supporters, and his substitution was celebrated by his own fans inside Stamford Bridge.
Meanwhile, with Moises Caicedo out injured, Chelsea have looked short of quality and numbers in the middle of the park.
Monaco pulled the plug on Chelsea's £47m deal to sign midfielder Lamine Camara on deadline day, having made attempts to sign Roma's Manu Kone and Fulham's Sander Berge as alternative options.
Key defensive signing Maxence Lacroix was left out on Saturday but none of the defensive options have excelled this season, although their attack remain in blistering form.
It will be on Alonso to fix these problems on the training pitch with no more opportunities to sign players until the January transfer window.

Yemen’s rampant Houthi forces have captured a strategic island in the Bab al-Mandab strait, expanding their control of the narrow waterway, one of the world’s vital shipping routes.
The Iran-aligned Houthis took control of the volcanic island after forces allied to the UN-backed, Aden-based government left in the latest of a dramatic series of reverses along Yemen’s west coast in recent days, including the loss of the port city of Mocha on Thursday.
Saudi Arabia, which supports and bankrolls the official Yemen government, mounted air raids on Houthi positions in Mocha on Friday.
The Bab al-Mandab strait links Asia to Europe via the Red Sea and Suez canal. Perim island, also known as Mayun, divides the waterway in two, close to its narrowest point. The United Arab Emirates, a former Saudi ally in the anti-Houthi coalition, had been building an airbase on the island before ending its active involvement in the conflict in January.
Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab to export its crude since Iran has been targeting vessels in the strait of Hormuz. About 12% of the world’s goods are typically shipped through the strait.
Full Houthi control of shipping in the strait, alongside Iranian control of the strait of Hormuz, would strengthen the chokeholds of anti-western forces over global energy shipments. Oil prices have risen to more than $100 a barrel as the fighting in Yemen has escalated.
Iran hailed the Houthi advances in an official statement on Friday, its first extended comment on the renewed fighting inside Yemen. Iran and the Houthis have been allied since the Houthis rose to power inside Yemen in 2014.
British diplomatic sources said they did not at present expect Donald Trump to sanction any US bombing of Houthi positions in Yemen, despite requests to do so from Saudi Arabia. The pace of the Houthi advance, and political divisions in the Yemen governorates not controlled by the Houthis, have left western capitals fearful that even the Yemen government capital, Aden, could fall to the Houthis. The UK effectively treated Yemen as a British protectorate until 1967.
The surge in fighting in the past week had sent more than 46,000 people fleeing, and “overnight, large numbers of people were reportedly seen leaving Mocha with their belongings”, the UN migration agency said on Friday.
The Houthi progress down the Red Sea coast from the port of Hodeidah also strengthens Iran’s hand in trying to reach an agreement with other Gulf states on future control of the strait of Hormuz, the central dispute between the US and Iran. Iran has reached an agreement on temporary approved routes with Oman, the country sharing the southern coast of the Hormuz strait. The proposed deal is supposed to be discussed at a meeting of Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) foreign ministers in the Omani coastal city of Salalah on Monday.
The deal, including a temporary approved route for shipping largely under Iranian control, would – if agreed by the GCC – put pressure on the US to lift its highly effective blockade of Iranian oil ports, which is severely damaging the Iranian economy.
The US struck a surprise ceasefire deal with the Houthis in May 2025 after the cost of a bombing campaign escalated, and Houthis gave private assurances that they would not attack US shipping in the Red Sea. The Houthi leadership this week continued to give similar assurances to all shipping except Saudi Arabian oil tankers.
On 14 August Saudi Arabia assembled a 14-country international maritime naval coalition to protect freedom of navigation in the Bab al-Mandab strait and the Gulf of Aden. The coalition, including Bahrain, Pakistan, Somalia, Djibouti, Turkey and Egypt, has so far been invisible, though Riyadh would argue that such a coalition of the willing takes time to assemble.
Recriminations are under way over the fall of Mocha, with the role of Maj Gen Tareq Saleh, the leader of the National Resistance Forces that retreated from the city, under scrutiny. He said the retreat was necessary to regroup his forces.
On her Facebook page, the Yemeni 2011 Nobel peace prize winner, Tawakkol Karman, called on Yemen’s president, Rashad al-Alimi, to dismiss Saleh and to refer him for investigation and trial of charges of conspiracy and high treason.
Saudi Arabia is facing a familiar dilemma: whether to reach a negotiated settlement with the Houthis on the future of Yemen or to try to push the highly stretched Houthi forces back.
Although the Houthis operate independently of Tehran’s instructions, it is hugely to Iran’s advantage for them to be fighting Saudi Arabia, as the Saudis are more likely in turn to put pressure on Washington to relent over Iran.
There is also concern in western capitals about the use of western weaponry by the Saudis in Yemen, and whether their activity complies with international humanitarian law, including whether the Saudi strikes can truly be seen as acts of self-defence.

An inter-island ferry carrying 45 people, including crew, has sunk north of Vanuatu during rough weather conditions.
Seven people have been rescued, while a further 38 people remain unaccounted-for.
What's next?
Search efforts continue via land and sea, with communities on the coast of Ambae Islands told to look out for and help possible survivors.
Vanuatu authorities have been searching for survivors after an inter-island ferry carrying 34 passengers and 11 crew members sank in critical weather conditions on Friday.
Seven people have been rescued, with an estimated 38 people still unaccounted-for, as boats and a flying doctor plane search for more survivors 24 hours after the vessel sank in the north of the country.
Police told national broadcaster VBCTC that MV Matui sank in rough seas on Friday while sailing between the islands of Ambae and Santo.
Police said one survivor made it to shore on the island of Santo, where a diver took him to the local community for help.
A video showing the man, named Jefferson, covered in a blanket and being offered a cup of hot tea has been shared widely on social media.
"We floated to Ambae but the tide was too strong … I swam … until I ended up here (Santo),"
he said.

There were also calls for communities on the coast of the Ambae Islands to keep an eye out and help possible survivors as the search continues.
Former foreign minister Matai Seremaiah, who was aboard the vessel LC Mahalia, rescued a number of survivors.
He posted on Facebook that two additional survivors had been spotted by a plane, though darkness made retrieval difficult.
Flying Doctor Mark Turnbull used his plane to drop life jackets and helped locate survivors for rescue vessels.

"We rescued two people today," he told ABC News.

My partner and I have always enjoyed going to live events, festivals, and concerts. The city we live in has so many nearby events that it is basically impossible to be bored.
Now that we have a child, we don't just seek out kid-focused events; we still go see the bands and performers we enjoy — even if they happen in the evening.
We often choose to keep our toddler out later than most other parents to enjoy these events. Some people may feel differently, but I have no regrets about bringing our daughter along to enjoy a fun night out with her parents.
I've always been an extrovert
I didn't suddenly stop enjoying concerts and evening events out of the house around fun people. I may even crave and appreciate them more now.
Over the years, I've been told "life is never boring around you," asked "how do you always know what fun stuff is going on?" and, most recently, jokingly crowned "the queen of local events" by a friend. I didn't think I was doing anything much differently than others for the first few years, but I have finally come to own these truths. There are so many vibrant activities to enjoy out in the community.
It's hard to find other parents like us
At times, it's been isolating to not have parent friends who like going out as much as we do, or much at all. I get why many don't want to go to a concert that starts at 8 p.m. because they don't want to miss their kid's bedtime or secure childcare. That's just not something we let hold us back.
We're always open to company, but it's been hard to find. Rarely, some friends will also bring their kids to a fun late-evening event, but mostly we've just made peace with our toddler exploring the world with us in a nontraditional manner.
Our toddler seems to like being out on the town
At a year old, our daughter was a regular at our local art crawls and art museum's after-hours DJ parties and even got her first few autographs. She bops with joy (while wearing protective headphones) at almost every concert we attend, and still occasionally stays up past 9 p.m., or later, if the situation warrants it.
By the time she turned 3, the big-name concerts that we took our daughter to included Tyler Rich (her first headphone autograph!), Uncle Kracker, Keith Urban (she was up way past 11 p.m. that night, she didn't sleep like we had expected her to), Dasha/Jordan Davis (up way past 11 p.m. again), Jelly Roll, and Gwen Stefani.
A third of the time, she is busy dancing her heart out, another third she is befriending whoever is behind us or next to us (or any nearby dogs), and therest of the time, she might fall asleep, need a potty break or diaper change, want another snack, or get a little too antsy so we'll walk her around a little bit to reset.
No, our toddler isn't invited to every concert we attend. She was not invited to see Kesha or Pitbull when I went out for a girls' night. Nor did she see Brooks & Dunn. For that one, we split a babysitter and carpooled with friends. But she has come to basically all other big evening events with us.
This year, our threenager has enjoyed seeing Jo Dee Messina, Alana Springsteen, Fitz and the Tantrums, Fake Happy (a Paramore tribute band), Teddy Swims, and Miranda Lambert. Up next, we're taking her to see Brad Paisley.
For us, this is the logical choice
In parent math, the choice about whether to bring my child to concerts is pretty clear.
How can I accurately estimate when the openers will finish and when the main artist will play? It's hard, I've tried.
How crazy will the traffic and parking be around the concert? Sometimes friends or prior experiences can help guesstimate, but that could always be wrong. That's not ideal when you have a sitter waiting back at home.
Also, do I want to ask around for a babysitter and pay them $15 to $20, or more, per hour? Do I want to go to the concert so badly that I'd add $100 or more to the cost, prepare the house, have backup plans for various worst-case scenarios, and make sure we're monitoring our phones constantly through (probably) loud music? It's pretty unlikely.
Does our daughter enjoy music and people? An enthusiastic yes. So that's the option I'm picking.
After living through years of COVID protocols during our engagement and the formative years of our marriage, it's so joyful to appreciate music and energetic events in a crowd of friendly people and to watch our daughter learn to do the same. 
It's OK if sleep schedules are a little off sometimes — for us, it's worth it. And, luckily, my pediatric sleep consultant said that what we're doing is fine. Thank goodness.

The difficult teenage years are sometimes characterized as a wasteland, but more resemble a forest for the interdependent trio at the sinking heart of Jannis Lenz‘s “Oasis,” the German-born, Austrian-trained filmmaker’s creepy, controlled debut feature. Retreating to the woods surrounding their German hometown, three ostracized high-schoolers create an arcane shared reality that provides them with comfort, support and the opportunity to explore boundaries in a uniquely non-judgmental way. But Lenz’s steady, sorrowful film radiates ambivalence about whether that’s a good thing or whether, in finding each other, these kids will be lost to the world. That’s the thing about forests; you can lose sight of them for the trees.
Lukas (Florian Geißelmann) is a quiet boy: sensitive, artistic, keeps to himself. Basically, all the descriptors that, after the fact, people use to describe a school shooter, apply to him, right down to a rarely seen, perfectly delinquent lop-sided smile. Yet he is not actively unpopular, despite the significant teenage handicap of having a father, Martin (Godehard Giese) — Lukas’ sole parent since the not-too-long-ago death of his mother — who is a teacher at his school. It is only when Lukas befriends big, wounded Andi (Anton Petzold) the son of a soldier recently posted to the base nearby, that he sees his small store of social capital start to dwindle. It doesn’t bother him too much initially, he can always rely instead on his best friend, Maya (a breakout Mathilda Smidt) who lives, apparently un-parented, in a big, airy house nearby and attends a specialist music school. Maya’s vocal exercises, as her class practise their plosives and sibilants, open the film on an appropriately strange, rhythmic note.
Popular on Variety
Cinematographer Alexander Dirninger (who also co-wrote the elegantly spare screenplay with Lenz) observes the slow-building action with such cool, detached dispassion that it always takes some time to understand the behavior we’re watching. This habit of withholding — that does get a little wearing during a stretched-out middle third — is unsurprising, given that Lenz apprenticed with some of the major figures from the school of severe Austrian formalism (his movie could be glibly summarized as “Michael Haneke goes to High School.”) It’s a few scenes before we realize, for example, that when Lukas methodically cuts the shoulder pads out of his dead mother’s blouses and tapes them around his torso, he is not acting on some dysfunctional grieving instinct. He’s constructing a homemade flak vest, for when he meets up with Andi in the woods to shoot paintball guns at each other. His taped-up tee is not exactly Kevlar. Lukas comes home with a livid, baseball-sized bruise blossoming on his shoulder.
After that first paintball-gun chase, Lukas and Andi sit in a field smoking cigarettes and barely talking, letting the whomp-whomp from the nearby wind turbines fill the companionable silence — the sound design, by Nora Czamler and Benedikt Palier (who also provides the disquieting, echoey score) is particularly superb. But there is a lot going unspoken here. That very day a video has started to circulate on social media, of Andi being cruelly humiliated by his classmates. In the coming days, he reacts to the mounting taunting with occasional defensive outbursts, that inevitably bring him to the attention of the school authorities.
Lukas, likely afraid of being targeted himself, rarely intervenes (“Why don’t you ever do anything?” Andi will later shout at him). But he does introduce Andi to Maya and somehow, the three of them gel, gently coaxing each other into more and more peculiar, unsavory, sex-adjacent-but-never-actually-sexual games of touching and biting and bruising. Less of an outlet for their inarticulate feelings of shame and anger, these rituals become an inlet, leading them deeper into (possibly unhealthy, but who’s to say?) emotional co-dependence, while estranging them further from their peers.
Martin is alarmed by his son’s surly withdrawal from their amicable father-son dinners and impromptu Guitar Hero sessions. But then all of the adults involved — Martin, the principal, the school staff and the concerned parents of Lukas and Andi’s classmates — believe they know their kids’ best interests, while only having the vaguest notion of what really interests their kids. Lenz’s film draws a faint parallel between the group dynamics among the teens and those among their purported guardians, as though the instinct to make yourself more integral to the herd by picking on its most vulnerable member is one that does not lessen with age, it simply metastasizes into a more sophisticated variant.
In an effort to sway his sympathies away from Andi, the school counselor (Britta Hammelstein) tells Lukas “Sometimes the victim role is a personal choice” which is an insane statement for a therapy professional to make. But no matter, like all efforts to separate them, it only brings the threesome closer together, and toward ever more intimate acts of mutual masochism and self-harm. Are these games a valuable pressure-valve that can defuse antisocial behavior or are they an early stage of escalation to actual, non-consensual, outward-directed violence? Are they an exorcism or are they practise? As Lenz’s taut, self-contained narrative releases some of its rigor in a rather underwhelmingly open-ended final act, it does give one to wonder what happens to this little club’s arcane rites and secret ceremonies when the safe, accepting space that fostered them turns out to be less oasis than mirage.

If you want to bring your music everywhere, the humble Bluetooth speaker is your best bet. You’ll lose some audio quality compared to bookshelf speakers, but these days, Bluetooth speakers sound pretty great, and let you blast the tunes wherever you go—the backyard, the beach, and beyond.
Since they first appeared on the audio scene back in 2010, the team at WIRED has reviewed hundreds of Bluetooth speakers at every price range. My top pick for most use cases remains the portable, durable, and affordable JBL Flip 7 ($150), but I’ve got specialized recommendations for nearly every use case and budget. From outdoor parties, beach days and poolside fun, to at-home listening in every room, these are the best speakers for everything you do.
Don’t forget to check out WIRED’s other audio guides, including the Best Soundbars, Best Wireless Earbuds, and Best Computer Speakers.
Updated September 2026: I’ve added the LG xboom Stage 501 and JBL Go 5 to my recommendations, refreshed the Honorable Mentions list, and updated pricing and copy with the most up to date information.
How I Test Bluetooth Speakers
WIRED’s audio experts have spent countless hours listening to, carrying, charging, dropping, and dunking Bluetooth speakers. I’ve been testing audio equipment for more than 20 years and remember the excitement surrounding the launch of the industry-changing Jawbone Jambox way back in 2010. It helped take wireless speakers mainstream and kick-started an entire industry. Since then, I’ve lost count of the number of Bluetooth speakers I’ve tested, but looking around my office today, I count at least 20 cluttering up the place.
Every speaker gets extensive listening with a wide mix of music, podcasts, and recordings of varying quality, including basic Spotify streams and high-resolution lossless audio from Qobuz and Tidal. This guide focuses on portable, battery-powered speakers, so there are inevitable compromises in sound compared to hi-fi speakers, but the difference between the best and worst is still remarkable.
Where possible, I compare similarly priced and sized speakers directly. A $50 speaker does not need to compete with a $500 one, but it does need to outperform the alternatives you might realistically buy instead.
I also test portability, controls, apps, Bluetooth reliability, useful extras, and battery life against manufacturers’ claims. The latter takes increasingly ridiculous amounts of time these days, especially with many speakers breaching the 50 hour mark.
And if a brand says its speaker is built for the beach, backyard, or pool, I test that too. Admittedly, WIRED doesn’t get as many pool days as it would like, but there’s always the bath.
What Should I Look for in a Bluetooth Speaker?
That entirely depends on what you plan to use it for. The best advice we have is to start with how and where you’d like to listen to music and work backwards to a specific model from there. Speakers include tiny keychains, larger boomboxes, and everything in between. We select speakers based largely on how they perform in their specialty, whether that’s audio quality, durability, or some other particular niche.
As far as durability, we look for speakers with solid IP ratings for dust and water resistance and tend to prefer long battery life; batteries with larger capacities tend to still work well even after a few years of degradation.

Honorable Mentions

Soundboks Mix for $799: The 21.4-pound Soundboks Mix is tremendously loud, with a 10-inch woofer, 1.2-inch tweeter, and 40-hour replaceable battery. IP65 protection, sturdy handles, and rubberized tennis-ball style corners make it particularly well suited to outdoor parties. It’s expensive and heavy compared to the new breed of party speakers from brands like LG and Sony, but it is superb at what it does.
JBL Charge 6 for $150: It’s just too big to be our absolute favorite Bluetooth speaker, but it was a close run thing between two superb JBL options. The great sound and portability of the Flip 7 won out, but the 40 watts from the Charge 6 deliver more bass and scale, while maintaining detail. Battery life stretches to 24 hours, and you also get IP68 protection, Auracast, app EQ, USB-C lossless playback, and reverse charging. Currently on sale too, making it a real bargain at $150.
Bose SoundLink Plus for $269: Sitting neatly between Bose’s little Flex and chunky Max, the Bose SoundLink Plus weighs 3.37 pounds but produces surprisingly substantial sound, with excellent detail, robust bass, and plenty of power without any rawness at volume. IP67 protection is solid, the 20-hour battery is replaceable, and it can also charge your phone over USB-C. There’s multipoint Bluetooth, app EQ, stereo pairing, and aptX Adaptive for Android too. It takes an irritating five hours to recharge, however. Bose could do with a refresh soon, as the competition has caught up with them.
Sonos Roam 2 for $179: The Sonos Roam 2 is a superb little speaker and if the hugely versatile Sonos Play didn’t exist, it would be one of my top picks. It lacks a bit of punch and scale compared to the larger option, but can still be connected over Wi-Fi or Bluetooth, so it remains ideal at home, in the garden, or out and about. IP67 protection means beach sand and bathroom splashes aren’t a concern. Battery life is a meager 10 hours, though, and it costs considerably more than similarly sized Bluetooth-only rivals, but if you’re a Sonos fan, you won’t be disappointed.
Ultimate Ears Megaboom 4 for $200: If you don’t mind something a bit large, the 9-inch tall Megaboom 4 is one of the best outdoor speakers you can get, according to former WIRED writer Ryan Waniata. It blasts sound in 360-degrees, with enough bass in every direction to please most listeners. It’s also IP67 dust and waterproof, and it floats, making it especially suited to pool and beach days. Like other Ultimate Ears speakers, you can pair multiple Megaboom 4s together through the app and adjust settings like EQ.
Beats Pill for $150: Remember the Beats Pill? WIRED loved the revived 2024 model when it launched, and it remains an excellent choice if you’re wedded to Apple’s ecosystem. You get one-touch pairing, Find My support, and a friction-free setup Apple does so well. Android gets similarly easy pairing and Find My Device support too. Sound is unmistakably Beats, with crisp treble, impressive clarity, and a whole pile of bass, although there’s still no EQ adjustability (you need to use your streaming service’s settings) to tame some occasional brightness. The 24-hour battery, IP67 protection, reverse USB-C charging, lossless playback over USB-C, and stereo pairing keep it competitive, especially since it’s often on sale.

Washington Spirit sign Luvanga - but is it a record deal?
- Published
Tanzanian striker Clara Luvanga has joined the Washington Spirit from Saudi Arabian club Al-Nassr in a deal believed to be one of the most costly in the history of women's football.
The fee paid by the National Women's Soccer League side has not been officially disclosed.
Some are reporting it to be $2.3m, external (about £1.7m), which would make Luvanga the most expensive female footballer in history.
BBC Sport has not been able to verify this figure, although a well-placed source said they believed it ranked in the top five most expensive signings in the women's game.
The Spirit declined to comment on the fee involved when contacted by BBC Sport.
Luvanga, 21, has signed a contract running to the end of the 2029 NWSL season.
If the reported record figure is correct, it would mean the fee passes the £1.4m that London City Lionesses are said to have paid to Paris St-Germain for Grace Geyoro last year.
However, the Geyoro fee has been disputed, further illustrating how transfer figures in the women's game are often kept private.
With her move, Luvanga becomes the first Tanzanian player in NWSL history.
Luvanga won the Saudi Women's Premier League in all three of her seasons with Al-Nassr, as well as the Saudi Women's Cup, Saudi Women's Super Cup and West Asian Football Federation (WAFF) Women's Clubs Championship.
She also claimed the league's golden boot last season after scoring 24 goals in 14 appearances.
The Washington Spirit are owned by Michele Kang, who also owns London City Lionesses.
London City made a series of high-profile signings during the summer transfer window, including two-time Ballon d'Or winner Alexia Putellas who arrived from Barcelona on a three-year deal.
Luvanga made her senior international debut for Tanzania in 2024. Before joining Al-Nassr in 2023, she played for DUX Logrono in Spain, having developed through the youth system at Tanzanian club Yanga Princess.
When discussing her new club, Luvanga said: "I am very excited to join the Washington Spirit and to take on this new challenge in the NWSL.
"I know I am arriving with the season already under way, but I'm really excited to play in a new league and a new country."
Spirit sporting director James Hocken said: "Clara adds an exciting new dimension to our attack as we head toward the play-offs.
"Despite her young age, she has demonstrated the ability to score goals in different ways and has the profile to be very successful in this league."
Inspired by Ronaldo, dancing her way to the top - analysis
Luvanga's rise from Tanzania to one of the world's most competitive women's football leagues has been remarkably rapid.
She began her career with Yanga Princess in her native country before her big international breakthrough came in August 2023, when she joined Spanish side DUX Logrono. But Spain was only a brief stop on her career journey.
By October of that year, Luvanga headed for Saudi Arabia to join Al-Nassr, a move that would prove transformative for her career.
Over three seasons in the Middle East, she helped Al-Nassr win the Saudi Women's Premier League title each time, establishing herself as one of the division's most prolific forwards.
Her time at Al-Nassr also provided an opportunity to meet one of football's biggest stars, Cristiano Ronaldo, who plays for Al-Nassr's men's team. Luvanga has spoken about modelling aspects of her own career on the Portuguese forward.
"The focus and determination that he has, when you look at his life, I wish to live like that," she told BBC Sport Africa in 2025.
There is another side to the Tanzanian forward that goes beyond the goals.
Her former team-mate at Al-Nassr, goalkeeper Sara Khalid Al-Dossary, described Luvanga to BBC Sport Africa as a great player and colleague but also revealed another of her talents: she is a great dancer.
Now Luvanga is taking both her football and her personality to the United States.
Her move to the Washington Spirit makes her the first Tanzanian woman to play in the NWSL, another significant milestone in the internationalisation of Tanzanian women's football.
She will also enter a dressing room containing a sizeable African contingent, with the Washington Spirit's roster now featuring seven African internationals.
For all her success at club level, Luvanga has not enjoyed the same impact in Tanzania colours at senior international level. Her 12 goals for Tanzania have come at youth level — 10 for the U-17 side and two for the U-20 team, while fitness problems have limited her involvement around the past two Women's Africa Cup of Nations campaigns.

Mumbai final: Manoj Jarange announces march, indefinite fast at Azad Maidan
Manoj Jarange has announced a Maratha march from Antarwali Sarati to Mumbai from September 15. He said the agitation will remain peaceful but continue until the community gets reservation.
Maratha reservation activist Manoj Jarange has announced a fresh escalation in the agitation, saying members of the community will march from Antarwali Sarati in Jalna to Mumbai from September 15. Jarange said he will begin an indefinite hunger strike at Azad Maidan in Mumbai on September 19.
Speaking after a decisive meeting of the Maratha community at Antarwali Sarati, Jarange asked those present whether they wanted to continue the agitation there or march to Mumbai. After the gathering backed the Mumbai march, he declared, “Mumbai final”.
Jarange said the march will begin at 11 am on September 15 and that his fast will continue during the journey. He said the group could take two to four days to reach Mumbai and vowed not to return from the city without securing reservation for the Maratha community.
MARCH ROUTE ANNOUNCED
Jarange said the proposed route will include stops at Patoda in Beed district, Shrigonda in Ahilyanagar district, Hadapsar in Pune district and Khopoli in Raigad district. Khopoli has currently been identified as the final halt before Mumbai.
He appealed to Maratha community members in Patoda, Shrigonda, Pune city, Hadapsar, Khopoli and surrounding areas to prepare for the march. Those unable to travel to Mumbai were asked to join the agitation at different points along the route and extend their support.
CALL FOR PEACEFUL PROTEST
Jarange urged supporters to keep the agitation completely peaceful and specifically appealed against arson and stone-pelting. He also appealed to the police and the Home Department not to stop protesters by putting up barricades.
He said that if protesters are stopped, they should sit peacefully at the spot and continue their agitation. Jarange stressed that the protest should remain peaceful from Antarwali Sarati to Mumbai and during the return journey after securing reservation.
Jarange also made a strong appeal to the community, saying that if the blood of any Maratha protester is shed, Maharashtra should be shut down within 10 minutes. He also called for peaceful sit-ins at the taluka level in such a situation.
GOVERNMENT STILL HAS TIME, SAYS JARANGE
Jarange said the government still has time to meet the community’s demands before the protesters reach Mumbai. He urged Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis to announce the implementation of the Maratha community’s demands.
He said that if the government wants to hold talks, it can meet the protesters on their way to Mumbai or come to Azad Maidan for discussions.
Jarange also warned the BJP politically, saying that if Marathas were prevented from reaching Mumbai, it should be understood that their votes had moved away from the party. At the same time, he said he hoped Fadnavis would not stop the protesters.
Jarange urged supporters to arrange dry food and medical camps along the route. He also appealed to those unable to travel to Mumbai to spend at least a day along the march route to show solidarity.
ED ACTION CLAIM
During his address, Jarange also alleged that the government had given the names of people close to him to the Enforcement Directorate in an attempt to stop the agitation. He said that if his associates were being investigated, an application would also be made to the ED seeking an investigation into people close to Fadnavis.
Jarange became emotional while addressing the gathering and appealed to the Maratha community to stand firmly with the community and its youth rather than political leaders. He also urged voters to defeat leaders who do not attend meetings of the community.
Jarange reiterated that the agitation would not be withdrawn without reservation and that the protest in Mumbai would continue peacefully.

Games may be life with all the hard bits removed, but they provide a way to study why people make the choices they make. Traditional games are usually played against a static background: the rewards per outcome are constant. That limits their relevance to behavior because, in real life, the rewards and consequences of strategic choices are ever changing. Now, researchers have used a mathematical model to study a series of games that include evolving strategies and randomly varying returns.
A bit of history
Perhaps the most famous game-theory contest is the prisoner’s dilemma. In the prisoner’s dilemma, a pair of thieves have been captured and are being separately interrogated by the police. If both clam up, they will be punished for a lesser crime. If one prisoner makes a deal (defects) then that prisoner gets to go free and the other gets a heavier sentence. If both make a deal, they both get an in-between punishment.
The person running the game can start it with different rewards for cooperating and defecting to explore how the optimum strategy varies with reward and risk, which the players can figure out by varying the strategies across multiple rounds. Depending on the balance between the reward for staying silent (cooperating) and betrayal, the game stabilizes with everyone betraying everyone. In this simple situation, everyone loses.
Similar dynamics can be found in games of chicken, rock-paper-scissors, and more. The evolution of strategies can lead to stable populations, bistable populations (where the population flips between two stable strategies), or limit cycles, where the population shifts continuously among multiple strategies.
There is also a rich history of changing a game as it is played. Usually, these are within-game variations. For instance, you can set a limit on the amount of reward available, so strategies evolve to take into account increasingly limited resources as the number of rounds goes up. In other words, most of this older work studied situations where the player’s behavior in the current round changed the resources or rewards available for the next round.

The Chinese president, Xi Jinping, has received a red-carpet welcome in India for a summit of Brics developing nations, as regional rivals Beijing and Delhi make a public display of thawing relations while quietly competing to lead at a time of shaky US global dominance.
As Xi stepped off the plane, he was walked past an honour guard of Indian soldiers and traditional dancers in colourful dresses.
The Russian president, Vladimir Putin, and Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, had already been welcomed by the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, who is hosting one of the group’s most closely watched gatherings since its inception.
The summit marks Xi’s first visit to India in seven years and is seen as the biggest step towards reconciliation after a deadly 2020 military clash along the disputed Himalayan border, in which 20 Indian and four Chinese soldiers were killed.
Ties between the nuclear-armed Asian giants have been warming recently, with flights and high-level contacts gradually being restored. China was “willing” to work with India to properly manage differences and be “good neighbours and friends”, China’s foreign ministry said on Friday.
Leaders and diplomats have been convening in India for the annual gathering of the Brics grouping, named after five of its earliest members – Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa – that was conceived as a counterweight to western dominance.
This summit comes as wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, along with rising US-China tensions, test the bloc’s ability to find common ground.
Since its inception in 2009, Brics has expanded as a forum for major emerging economies to include Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The group now rivals the US-dominated G7 forum of advanced economies, accounting for half of the global population.
But its growth has also created new fractures and disunity – Iran was bombing Saudi Arabia and the UAE earlier this year, and Brics foreign ministers failed to agree on a joint statement when they met in Delhi in May.
Reuters reported on Saturday that India’s summit would result in a generic joint declaration that would show unity by condemning unilateral war, but was unlikely to name any single country.
Jiang Shixue, vice-president of the expert committee of the China thinktank Council for BRICs cooperation (China), said the 11 members “cannot speak with one voice on many issues”.
“The only solution is to continuously strengthen political consensus,” he told the South China Morning Post.
Beijing and Delhi have differing views on the role of the group.
China has sought to expand Brics power as a counterweight to the US under Donald Trump’s leadership, which has launched global tariff and trade wars and retreated from multilateral institutions such as the UN, which afforded it international credibility.
India has taken a more cautious approach, seeing Brics as a bridge between the west and the developing world.
Chietigj Bajpaee, a senior research fellow for South Asia in the Asia-Pacific programme at Chatham House, said this week that Delhi had found it hard to maintain its policy of “strategic hedging” during such a disruptive US presidency.
“India’s position can appear out of sync in a forum whose membership includes countries with more overtly anti-western agendas, including China, Russia and Iran. And two other Brics countries, South Africa and Brazil, have suffered high-profile diplomatic disputes with the US,” he wrote.
“The challenge for Delhi is that it wishes to promote this worldview in a way that is non-western but not explicitly anti-western.”
Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

Story so far: The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) has stepped up action against food companies using “100%” claims on their products, saying such claims can give consumers an impression of absolute purity or completeness that may not match what is actually inside the packet.
The move comes as food regulators are paying closer attention to how products are labelled and advertised. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has also asked food businesses to stop using “100%” claims on food labels, packaging and promotional material.
The key question is: can a company claim “100%” when the product does not actually contain 100% of that ingredient? The CCPA’s orders offer some clues.
What has the CCPA found?
In June 2026, the CCPA imposed a ₹1 lakh penalty each on Mrs. Bectors Food Specialities, which markets English Oven products, and Storia Foods and Beverages for misleading “100%” claims. The companies were also directed to stop using the claims on their packaging, websites and digital platforms.
In the case of Mrs. Bectors, one of its bread products was marketed as “100% Atta Bread” and “100% Whole Wheat Bread”. The company, however, admitted that the bread contained 87% whole wheat flour.
Mrs. Bectors argued that “100% Atta” was meant to convey that wheat flour was the only grain used in the bread. The CCPA did not accept this explanation. It said that “100%” is an exact numerical expression and should not be used loosely or approximately.
The Authority also took into account the use of “Zero Maida” alongside “100% Whole Wheat Bread”. Taken together, these claims could give consumers the impression that the bread was entirely made from whole wheat flour.
What about ‘100% Juice’?
The Storia case involved a similar concern, but with beverages.
Storia marketed one of its products as “100% Tender Coconut Water” and “100% Natural Tender Coconut Water”. However, the ingredient declaration listed water and 9.6% coconut water concentrate, followed by the words “Equivalent to 100% Coconut Water” and “Reconstituted”.
The CCPA found the prominent “100% Tender Coconut Water” claim misleading because an ordinary consumer could understand it to mean that the product was entirely natural tender coconut water.
The CCPA raised a similar concern over Storia’s fruit beverages marketed as “100% Juice”. These products contained water as well as specified quantities of fruit pulp or juice concentrates.
For example, the pomegranate variant contained water, 4% pomegranate juice concentrate and 10% apple juice concentrate. The mango variant contained water, 16% mango pulp and 12.5% apple juice concentrate.
Can the fine print save a claim?
The CCPA’s orders suggest that putting the correct information in the fine print may not be enough if the prominent claim creates a misleading impression.
Consumers typically see the front of a packet before reading its detailed ingredient list. The CCPA has therefore looked at the overall impression created by the packaging and advertising, rather than assuming that a detailed ingredient declaration automatically corrects a prominent claim.
This approach was also seen in the case of McVitie’s Wholewheat Marie biscuits.
The biscuits contained 19.5% whole wheat flour, while refined wheat flour accounted for 52%. The CCPA found that the prominent use of the word “Wholewheat”, along with wheat imagery on the packaging, could lead consumers to believe that the biscuits were predominantly made from whole wheat.
Pladis India, the manufacturer, argued that “Wholewheat” was part of its registered trademark and pointed to a disclaimer on the packaging.
The CCPA, however, said that being a registered trademark does not put a company outside consumer-protection laws. Nor, it held, can a disclaimer necessarily cancel out a prominent representation that may mislead consumers.
What is the FSSAI’s stand on ‘100%’?
The FSSAI too has taken note of a noticeable surge in the use of the term “100%” across food product labels and promotional platforms.
In May 2025, it advised Food Business Operators (FBOs) not to use “100%” on food labels, packaging or promotional material. It said the expression was not defined under the existing food regulations and could create a false impression of absolute purity or superiority.
The FSSAI had earlier taken a more specific position on packaged juice products. In June 2024, it directed food businesses to remove “100% Fruit Juice” claims from labels and advertisements where the juice was made by reconstituting concentrate.
The FSSAI’s action primarily deals with food safety, standards and labelling requirements. The CCPA, on the other hand, looks at whether companies are misleading consumers through their advertisements or product claims.
Under Section 21 of the Consumer Protection Act, the CCPA can order a false or misleading advertisement to be discontinued or modified. It can also impose a penalty of up to ₹10 lakh on a manufacturer, which can rise to ₹50 lakh for every subsequent contravention.
What does this mean for food companies and consumers?
The recent orders show that the ingredient list is not the only thing that matters. The CCPA can also look at how a product is presented on its packaging and in advertisements.
For companies, this means that product names, claims, images and disclaimers may all be considered when assessing whether it could mislead consumers.
For consumers, the front of a packet may not always give the complete picture. The ingredient list can help show what the product actually contains.

Business sentiment among large Japanese companies turned positive in the July-September quarter thanks to stronger semiconductor-related demand and more customers at hotels and restaurants, government data showed Friday.
The business survey index for large companies stood at plus 5.3, compared with minus 0.5 in the previous three months, according to the data released by the Finance Ministry and the Cabinet Office.
The index is calculated by subtracting the percentage of companies reporting deteriorating business conditions over the preceding three months from that of those reporting improved conditions.
The impact of the war in Iran had eased from the April-June quarter, a Finance Ministry official said. Citing the recent rise in crude oil prices, however, the official said, “We’ll continue to closely monitor corporate activities.”
The index for large manufacturers stood at plus 7.6. The production machinery manufacturing sector posted an index reading of plus 23.4 on increased demand for semiconductor manufacturing equipment.
The information and communications equipment manufacturing sector had a reading of plus 19.9, thanks to growing demand tied to artificial intelligence data centers.
The index for large nonmanufacturers was at plus 4.2. The service sector, including hotels and restaurants, posted a reading of plus 7.6, while finance and insurance companies recorded a reading of plus 3.4 as higher lending rates improved earnings.
The index for midsize companies was at plus 0.8, while that for small companies was at minus 10.9.
Companies across all sizes and industries expect to report higher sales and profits for fiscal 2026 from the previous year. Capital investment is projected to increase 11%.

Quick Answer
One UI 9 focuses on control, privacy, and usability with customizable Quick Settings, a redesigned media player, per-app network blocking, unified call history, network speed indicators, PIN-protected shutdown, bypass charging, and dual-camera video recording.
One UI 9 is Samsung’s latest update based on Android 17, which was launched with the Galaxy Z Fold8 and Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra. As for its slab phones, the One UI 9 update is still in beta for the Galaxy S26 series and was recently made available in the US, India, and South Korea for older models like the Galaxy S25 series, Galaxy Z Fold7, Z Flip7, and even the Galaxy S24 series. Samsung has already confirmed that the One UI 9 stable update will soon reach the Galaxy S26 series, but the exact date isn’t confirmed as of yet. One UI 9c isn’t a massive overhaul but is focusing heavily on privacy, aesthetics, and usability. Here are the top new features of One UI 9 that you will get on eligible One UI 9 phones.

Here is the complete list of Samsung devices that are slated to receive the Android 17 One UI 9 update:

| Rugged devices | Galaxy XCover7, Galaxy XCover7 Pro, Galaxy Tab Active5, Galaxy Tab Active5 Pro | 
New One UI 9 features
While we await the One UI 9 Android 17 stable update on our phones, here are the new features that you should know about:
Highly customizable Quick Settings panel
Samsung has tweaked the Quick Settings panel a lot after the One UI 8 update. Now with One UI 9, the company will take things further and introduce a highly customizable Quick Settings panel. While at first glance, you will notice a familiar Samsung identity, the visual tweaks make it more ergonomic and pleasing to the eye. Samsung introduced thicker, more tactile sliders for volume and brightness, making them easier to adjust quickly with your thumb. Additionally, the dark mode toggles and volume settings have also been undocked from these sliders, which gives the interface a much cleaner and less cramped look.
However, you will notice that with One UI 9, you will be able to resize the brightness and volume sliders to a compact 2×1 grid size. This is fantastic for those who want to get more quick setting toggles on a single page. You also get dedicated new toggles for accessibility features such as “Select to speak,” which reads aloud what is displayed on your screen.
Redesigned media player
The media player Quick Settings tile has also been refreshed. Noticeably, the album and podcast get new circular toggles for play/pause, rewind, and skip. The visualizer waveform on playback now dynamically extracts hues and colors from your currently playing album art. This gives your lockscreen a visual overhaul and a rich look.
Network restriction controls
Let us face it. We have been in this situation so many times where we download an offline game, a calculator app, or even a flashlight tool, and are suddenly bombarded with full-screen ads. These ads not only waste a lot of time, but sometimes they are so intrusive that you cannot close them, or they force you to purchase the pro version. One UI 9 fixes this and introduces a feature that power users have been begging for.
Network Restriction Controls is the new setting that is buried within the main Settings app; you now have a master kill-switch to block specific applications from connecting to the internet entirely. This is a massive win for privacy and data management. If an app does not strictly need an external internet connection to function, you can cut its Wi-Fi and mobile data access with a single turn of a toggle. This will stop ad-filled apps from quietly phoning home with your personal data in the background.
A unified phone app
Calling is no longer limited to standard cellular calls. You now make calls on WhatsApp, Google Meet, or message family members on Viber. But the problem with all this is that all of your call logs are scattered across various apps. WhatsApp calls will be available in its app, Google Meet’s call history is available in its app, and so on. You have to switch between apps just to view the call history.
One UI 9 fixes this issue and introduces a unified phone app. It fixes the headache by merging all of your calling applications into one centralized feed inside the Samsung Phone app. Now, when you open your dialer, your WhatsApp calls, Google Meet calls, and standard carrier calls all live in one neatly organized timeline.
Status bar enhancements
If you are someone who loves keeping a close eye on the device’s performance, then One UI 9 brings a highly requested feature: a native network speed indicator in the status bar. While this has been a staple on many Chinese smartphone brands, Samsung models will finally get a built-in way to see real-time download and upload speeds. It is an incredibly useful diagnostic tool to quickly see if your Wi-Fi is acting up or if you are getting the correct speed with it or not.
Note that you still need to make use of the Good Lock “Quickstar” module to enable it. But it is well worth the two minutes if you want to keep an eye on your internet speed. Plus, Samsung has also adjusted the size of the status bar pill area, basically the area that shows background activities like active calls or screen recordings. The pill is noticeably larger now, which allows it to display more content.
Everyday usability and multitasking tweaks
When it comes to multitasking, Samsung has always been the king. The One UI 9 update brings a few quality-of-life improvements that only help get things done much easier.
- Browser Windows in Recents menu: After using Google Chrome for years, I ditched it for Samsung Internet Browser as my default. One UI 9 brings a massive usability bump, as you can now configure individual browser tabs to show up as separate cards in your phone’s Recent Apps menu. This way, you don’t have to open the Samsung Internet Browser app just to close these tabs. You can do that from the Recent Apps menu.
- Mandatory PIN for shutdown: Smartphone theft is a real concern. Just the other day during a stroll around Hyde Park, my phone was almost snatched by a thief. While my phone was not stolen, thieves, when they get their hands on a phone they usually turn it off to stop tracking immediately. One UI 9 adds a crucial security layer, and you now you need to enter your PIN, password, or biometric data before the phone lets you restart or power off your phone.
- Clearer Routines: For those who use Samsung Routines to automate their device, they will be happy to know that Samsung has finally added plain-English explanation text for all the presets. You no longer have to guess what a specific routine means.
- Floating Bars return: Throughout various first-party apps, Samsung has brought back floating action bars. This gives you a cleaner gesture area at the bottom of your screen, good for those who customize their home screen.
- Bypass Charging: Mobile gamers are getting a new Bypass Charging feature. With this, the phone will route the power directly to the processor rather than charging the battery. This will reduce heat and protect your battery in the long-term.
- Dual Vertical Video: Samsung’s Camera app is packed with features, but One UI 9 adds some more elements to it, especially tailored for social media creators. You can now record vertical video using both the front and back camera simultaneously. The phone will record the footage in a 1:1 square aspect ratio.
Final thoughts
One UI 9, based on Android 17, may not be the biggest visual overhaul update that you might be expecting, but that was already done with the One UI 8 update. Now, with the latest update, Samsung is aiming to give users more control. It is a mature, polished, and thoughtful update that makes every Galaxy device a little bit more intuitive. More details will come about the update after the stable update is pushed.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian met the Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, who represents the United Arab Emirates, on the sidelines of the BRICS Summit in New Delhi. The meeting is a diplomatic coup of sorts as the two sides have been at odds during the ongoing US-Iran War. Iran’s official news agency IRNA released video footage of the meeting, but provided no details about the discussions between the two sides. The two leaders discussed a number of regional and international issues, along with the importance of supporting de-escalation efforts, reducing tensions, and achieving stability in the region, as well as enhancing opportunities for peace and development for its peoples, according to people familiar with the developments. Quick answers to key questions Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and UAE Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed discussed regional issues, emphasizing de-escalation efforts and stability in the Middle East amidst the US-Iran conflict. The BRICS Summit offers a platform for Iran and the UAE to address their differing interests amidst ongoing conflicts, fostering diplomatic discussions aimed at reducing tensions and promoting regional stability. India facilitated intensive negotiations among BRICS nations, particularly between Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, to achieve a consensus on a joint statement despite their competing geopolitical interests. The New Delhi Declaration represents a crucial diplomatic breakthrough, urging members to address international conflicts and advocating for reforms in global governance, particularly in the context of the ongoing US-Iran war. Yes, ongoing support for de-escalation efforts is essential for maintaining stability in the region, especially given the complexities of the US-Iran war and differing interests of member countries. The BRICS Summit, hosted by India as chair this year, came at a challenging moment for India, as the grouping navigates the fallout from the US-Iran war and the wider crisis in the Middle East. For New Delhi, the challenge was to strike a delicate diplomatic balance. The expanded BRICS includes Iran as well as the UAE and Saudi Arabia, countries with differing interests and positions on the regional conflict in Middle East due to US-Iran war. At the same time, India maintains important strategic and economic relationships with the United States and the Gulf countries. On Saturday evening, Prime Minister Narendra Modi confirmed the adoption of the New Delhi Declaration after the first day of the two-day summit hosted by India at Bharat Mandapam. The declaration is seen as a significant diplomatic breakthrough as its leaders began summit hoping to bridge divisions between members Iran and the United Arab Emirates over the Gulf conflict, which is being held as the United States and Iran resume tit-for-tat strikes in their six-month-old war. In its declaration, the BRICS bloc also called for the implementation of the relevant UNGA and UNSC Resolutions and urge all parties to ensure the maintenance of ceasefire and full and unhindered humanitarian access in the Gaza Strip. The joint declaration did not name any country but condemned unilateral aggression by any country. Both Iran and the UAE approved the New Delhi declaration. During his address to the BRICS Summit the Iranian President had urged the BRICS forum to take practical measures to counter unilateral and inhumane sanctions. Pezeshkian said BRICS must be a voice for justice. "BRICS members have a responsibility to stand against the normalization of attacks on civilian infrastructure and peaceful nuclear facilities, because any action against these sites constitutes a direct threat to international peace and security.
