India's high-stakes exam system faces a crisis of trust
- Published
In 2017, India introduced the National Testing Agency (NTA) to conduct fair, transparent and standardised examinations.
Set up under the federal education ministry, it was meant to make exams more efficient, consistent and trustworthy, after years of paper leaks, administrative errors and cheating allegations.
Over the next few years, the agency took charge of some of India's largest and most competitive tests, including medical and engineering entrance examinations, university admissions and eligibility tests for teaching and research.
But eight years later, the organisation created to restore trust in India's exams is facing a crisis of confidence of its own.
In June, more than two million students had to retake a crucial medical entrance examination after the paper was leaked. The fallout triggered weeks of youth-led protests which eventually led to the resignation of the federal education minister.
In response, the government appointed a high-level task force led by tech tycoon Nandan Nilekani to recommend reforms and restore confidence in the examination system.
For many Indians, however, the announcement prompted a sense of déjà vu.
A similar panel was established in 2024 after irregularities in another medical entrance examination sparked widespread unrest. That committee proposed more than 100 reforms, a little over half of which, external have reportedly been fully implemented.
The cycle has repeated: an exam goes wrong, students protest, a committee is appointed and reforms are proposed - only for another crisis to expose the same weaknesses.
Experts the BBC spoke to say the problems go beyond paper leaks - from NTA's accountability and capacity to exam centralisation, design and whether India's high-stakes testing system needs a rethink.
BJ Rao, who was part of the 2024 panel and is now head of SGT University near Delhi, says India should move more decisively towards computer-based examinations to minimise the chances of paper leaks, increase efficiency and reduce human involvement wherever possible.
"Digital connectivity has vastly improved across the country, what we need to do is put in resources and focus on upgrading infrastructure and move to computer-based exams," he told the BBC.
"We currently have ad hoc centres for conducting exams. We need to replace them with standardised state-controlled online centres."
But technology alone will not solve the problem, he says.
Rao points to the NTA's reliance on contract staff: just 24 of its 221 employees are permanent, with many from bureaucratic backgrounds, according to the government.
"When you have a large portion of people who work on a temporary basis then there is no sense of belonging, and that has an impact on the functions as well. You need people who are well-versed in academia and experienced in conducting such assessments to ensure better management and oversight," he explains.
Some experts argue that repeated crises have exposed flaws not only in how exams are conducted, but also in how they are designed.
Keshav Aggarwal, an educationist and president of Educators Federation, says the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (Undergraduate) or NEET-UG - whose paper leak triggered this year's protests - could be restructured along the lines of the country's engineering entrance examination, which is computer-based and conducted in two stages.
Rather than relying on a single high-stakes test day, the exams could be held across multiple sessions with different sets of questions, he says.
"Different stages and days with varying sets of questions" would reduce the risks associated with any one examination and make the system more resilient to disruptions, Aggarwal explains.
Experts also question whether an annual exam can work when millions compete for limited university places.
India needs a system where students can take important entrance exams more than once a year, as is common in some western countries, said Yamini Aiyar, senior visiting fellow at Brown University.
"This would give students another chance if an exam is cancelled or they do not perform well, reducing the risk of losing an entire year," she says.
For millions of Indian students, the risk is real. Many spend years preparing and tens of thousands of rupees on private tuition. A leaked, cancelled or delayed exam can suddenly upend months or years of preparation.
Pari, 17, experienced that uncertainty first-hand. After taking NEET this year, she had to retake it after the original exam was cancelled following a paper leak.
"It was very frustrating. All our preparation had gone to waste, and we had to start all over again," she said.
The experience left her angry at repeated exam failures.
"The government can form as many panels as it likes. We need a system strong enough to prevent paper leaks from happening again."
Mansi Bansal, 23, has a similar story. She spent months preparing for UGC-NET, a qualification for entry-level college teaching jobs.
The exam was cancelled after a 2024 paper leak and again this year after the NTA cited errors in three subjects.
Bansal took the affected commerce paper and will retest on 9 September.
"I put my life on hold all these months, stopping going to the gym, hanging out with friends or even attending family gatherings," she said. "I had planned my entire year but now it has all gone into uncertainty. Can the government promise a leak won't happen again?"
Such experiences have fuelled calls from student activists and opposition politicians to scrap the NTA altogether.
Educationists argue that scrapping the agency would not solve the underlying problem.
The NTA needs deep structural reform to address recurring failures, but abolishing it is not the answer, said M Jagadesh Kumar, former chairman of India's universities regulator.
"A single national testing body offers common security standards, technology, candidate services and result procedures. Creating many new agencies could duplicate costs and produce uneven safeguards," he told PTI news agency.
Rao agrees.
"It is not a case of all bad news. The body has conducted several exams successfully, where we did not hear of any leaks," he said.
What is needed, he argues, is a statutory institution staffed by specialists with the academic, technical and operational expertise to run a secure examination system.
Yet for some experts, the debate ultimately goes beyond the NTA itself.
Aiyar says the bigger issue is not just stopping the next paper leak, but whether a highly centralised testing system can cope with the intense competition for limited educational opportunities.
The NTA may be able to make exams more secure, she says. "But it cannot, at least on its own, change a system in which millions of students compete for a limited number of seats and a single exam can shape their future."
Some experts say reform must go beyond the NTA itself: India needs an exam system less reliant on one-off, high-stakes tests, gives students multiple chances and can better withstand disruptions.
Rao remains optimistic that the task force led by Nilekani will help plug gaps in the existing system.
But for many students, another committee offers little reassurance unless it produces changes they can actually see.
"I am studying for my university entrance examination next year," said a 16-year-old Grade 12 student.
"In my head I am prepared that there might be a leak. But what can we do about it? I will prepare and hope for the best."

Meta has removed several Instagram and Facebook accounts and content related to the Jantar Mantar protest that Alt News had flagged as AI-manipulated visuals.
On September 2, a Meta spokesperson confirmed to Alt News that following a review, all the accounts and content were found to be violative of the platform’s policies and had been removed.
These posts included several AI-generated and AI-manipulated photographs and videos of women protesting at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar during the Cockroach Janta Party-led students’ protest in July. Alt News flagged Instagram and Facebook accounts and posts to Meta, in which real visuals women had been altered using AI, purportedly in an attempt to outrage their modesty.
In these posts, women’s clothes, bodies and poses had been altered in such a way that they looked starkly different from the original videos or photographs. Alt News’ investigation found that many such visuals were either entirely AI-generated or altered using AI. In some cases, techniques such as face swaps or body swaps were used.
Targeting Women CJP Protesters
Women protesters who participated in the CJP protests in Delhi were particularly targeted on social media. For several days, women faced online harassment and trolling, doxxing, rape threats and the public disclosure of personal information. These AI-visuals formed part of this larger pattern of attacks against female protesters.
These fake visuals were shared on Instagram, Facebook and YouTube, among other platforms, claiming that they were real footage from the Jantar Mantar protest. Users then mistook the AI characters for real women partaking in the protests which was followed by objectionable and misogynistic comments targeting their identities, physical appearance, clothes and character. A few of those comments are displayed below:
Alt News identified several Instagram accounts which circulated such malicious content, including @kauronfire, @sirfseerat, @tia_kaurr, @hey.siya_2.0, @kavya_homevibes, @annika0022, @divyankaha and @its_anushkaa69.
Right-wing Users Share AI Image
During the protest, several right-wing users, including RSS supporters Acharya Ankur Arya and Vikram Pratap Singh, shared an AI-generated image claiming that it was a real photograph from the Jantar Mantar protest.
The purported image showed a young woman wearing a crop top and jeans. Users who shared the post made objectionable comments about the woman’s clothing and character. Alt News fact-checked this viral image and found that it was entirely AI-generated.
However, in some cases that surfaced on social media during the final days of the protest, besides entirely AI-generated images, real photographs of women were being altered, making it difficult to determine its authencity.
Visuals Of A Woman In White Saree
An user, @divyankaha, shared a photo and video on their Instagram account and YouTube channel respectively. These showed a woman wearing a white saree and navy blue blouse, linking her to the Jantar Mantar protest. (Archive link-1, Archive link-2)
Alt News found the original video of the post uploaded on an Instagram page @khoji_reporter24news.
Comparing the viral clip with the original video, we found that the body and clothing of the woman were entirely different, thus confirming that the image had been altered using AI. The background and original footage of the viral video remained the same, but the appearance of the woman had been completely manipulated. After Alt News flagged this to Meta, they removed @divyankaha‘s account.
We found several such posts and videos on @divyankaha‘s page. In another post, a woman wearing a white saree is seen sitting on the road wit posters infront of her. Alt News found this photo was also an AI-deepfake. (Archive link)
Several different versions of the viral post, with a woman in a white saree, were also found circulating widely on social media. All of these were AI-deepfakes.
Visuals Of A Woman Standing With A Poster
Another photograph went viral showing different women near the stage at the Jantar Mantar protest, holding posters that read “Resign De De Bhai PUNE SE Aai hu..and Hum jeet gaye”.
In the different iterations of this photo being shared, the woman as well as the design of the poster kept changing. These photos were shared by right-wing handles and those opposing the CJP protest, with objectionable comments and captions. (Archive Link-1, Link-2, Link-3, Link-4)
We found that this photo had been altered using AI. The original photoe was posted on July 22 by an Instagram account named @nanddhini.
A comparison of the original and viral photos clearly showed the difference in the woman’s face and body. The design of the poster also appears to have changed across different viral versions. Thus, the face and body of the woman in the original photo were swapped using an AI editing tool.

Climate breakdown is happening on one Earth, but two different worlds. In one, its impacts increasingly encroach on everyday life; longer periods of discomfort and shorter periods of sharp pain. Endless, hotter summers, and within them sudden wildfires, evacuations, homes burned to cinders in a matter of hours. In another, catastrophe. This summer has been a snapshot of that split-screen. The hottest day on record in parts of Europe, and a wave of water, mud and ice in Nepal that so far has claimed more than 750 lives. Thousands of people are still missing.
The difference is also one of resources. The climate crisis has an economic cost, but some places can absorb it better than others. Responses to this summer of wildfires in Europe included a rapid scrambling by the French government to provide everything from tax breaks for businesses affected by the fires to relocation costs and aid to rebuild homes. The UK government had deployed almost £100m before the summer to strengthen wildfire resilience.
Entire industries exist to absorb the impact, undergirded by sophisticated technology, disposable income and evolved sectors. Wildfire insurance in the US is being powered by AI, which spits out numbers to estimate risk based on location and construction material. Outside North America and Europe, there is little of that buffer. The result is asymmetry. While developed countries will still be stressed as events triggered by climate breakdown become more regular and chronic, and they are still not immune to globalised outcomes – rising food costs, droughts, water shortages – what they experience and how disruptive that will be are far removed from other parts of the world.
The difference in scale and resources is colossal. What is needed to rebuild Nepal’s flood damage may constitute up to a 10th of its entire economy – something like $5bn, and that’s not even factoring in all the technical foreign assistance, equipment, expertise and labour required. Also colossal is the difference in exposure to the obliterative effects of events.
Take the death of coral reefs, and how that disproportionately affects coastal populations. Across the Caribbean, coral bleaching caused by rising ocean acidification and temperatures not only dramatically reduces marine life, which is a source of food and income for entire populations – 90% of Jamaica’s economic income is generated alongside its coasts – but also increases the scale and intensity of storms. Coral reefs are a sort of natural storm barrier, absorbing the force of sea waves and buffering coastal areas from flooding. The intersection between these geographical and economic features means countries in the Caribbean are being pummelled on the weather front (climate breakdown also increases the power of hurricanes through warming ocean water), as well as having their incomes drastically reduced and therefore their ability to bounce back.
Then there is the heat. Temperatures are not just jumping far above the average in Europe but also in warmer areas where the base temperatures are already high. Last week, a Harper’s Index summary of estimated heat-related mortality in India showed some staggering numbers: 3,400 excess deaths “caused by a single day of extreme heat”; 30,000 deaths “caused by five consecutive days of extreme heat”. In April of this year, all 50 of the world’s hottest cities were in a single country, India, something which according to the air-quality monitoring platform AQI “has no modern precedent across global weather data”.
This is another double whammy for poor communities without access to shelter or cooling systems of unlimited fresh water. These are the so-called climate breakdown hotspots, identified as “areas where strong physical and ecological effects of climate change come together with large numbers of vulnerable and poor people and communities”. Few places on Earth demonstrate this category more vividly than Sudan. A country already in the grip of war and food insecurity is now succumbing to the delayed rains caused by the El Niño climate pattern, cracking the dry earth and draining the Nile. The risk of famine stalks populations that are already acutely hungry.
And what is felt asymmetrically has been caused in that way too. These poorer, more vulnerable countries are paying the price for the emissions caused by wealthy countries, and not even being extended the full, remedial support from the coffers of those nations that accumulated the wealth generated by industries that contributed to climate breakdown and global heating. We are not just battling complacency, or indifference to the importance of climate justice, but a political climate that has in recent years, led by Donald Trump’s second term, seen its own collapse.
Look closer and the problem isn’t only historical failure but a casual disregard, an adventurism that launches wars and stresses economies with buffers already damaged by the climate crisis. The Iran war in combination with El Niño is a weather and politics collaboration that has hiked fertiliser costs on the one hand and choked rain on the other. More broadly, what was a generously named albeit tenuously implemented “rules-based order”, which at least had some bedrock of global cooperation and aid, has been cancelled altogether. Trump’s withdrawal from the Paris agreement set the tone, while the dismantling of USAID cut the funds that diverted billions of dollars from the rich to the developing world to help with the fallout of extreme weather and reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
Here is another cascade. As the US withdraws from its commitments, sending the signal that there are no rules or duties, and indeed no problem with climate breakdown at all, pressure will rise on other countries to contribute more. They will need to figure out a way to hold together a coordinated response in the shadow of a destabilising hegemon, as well as try to foster that sense of social obligation in a time of political sociopathy.
The foolish shortsightedness of it all is that even though there is a large gap between experiences, and so a sense that glaciers and floods and famines are happening all the way over there, their knock-on effects and food supply challenges, and political and refugee crises, will affect us all. Things will get dramatically worse for the hotspots, but there is still no outrunning it all in the long term. It seems that at precisely the moment when this realisation should yoke us together in all the ways life is rapidly changing, we are all being untethered. But ultimately, whatever different spheres we inhabit, we are all still trapped on the same planet.
- 
  Nesrine Malik is a Guardian columnist

It has been hard not to despair while watching the ruinous floods swallow parts of Nepal, and harder, still knowing that the agony compounds each passing day for dozens of Indian families whose members remain unaccounted for.
Social media is awash with desperate pleas, photos and details of the young and old, men and women, from Mumbai to Kolkata, posted by families searching for traces of life. The disaster unfolded when a melting glacier slammed into the valley below, unleashing a deadly cascade of rock and ice down the Bhote Kashi River, which flows from Tibet into Nepal.
Among the 275 Indians missing at the time of writing are workers of a hydropower project and people undertaking the Hindu pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet. Another 128 people of Indian origin, including a large group of Sadhguru’s Isha Foundation spiritual group, are also missing; 149 Indian people have been rescued as of Monday.
For Gauri Joshi, whose five relatives remained unaccounted for over the weekend, the last few days have been a blur of calling their numbers in vain, watching news of rescue operations and trying to reach Indian officials – over and over again. What she has pieced together so far is that her relatives, part of a pilgrim tour group from Maharashtra, cleared immigration at the Gyirong border between Nepal and Tibet and boarded buses shortly before the flood waters destroyed the crossing.
“Chances appear very bleak now. But maybe a miracle will happen,” Joshi said.
The tragedy has reignited the question of how vulnerable the Himalayas are to climate change, and what its implications are for India. To understand the risks of glacier collapse and thawing permafrost leading to sudden floods and debris flows, I spoke to Dr Ashim Sattar, a professor at Indian Institute of Technology Bhubaneswar and an expert on glacial lake outburst floods. The conversation has been edited and condensed.
What are the climate- or glacier-related risks emerging across the Himalayas?
“There are different forms of cryosphere and how they pose a hazard. In a layperson’s terms, the cryosphere is where water exists in solid form, for example a glacier. When it melts, it forms glacial lakes. If they have an outburst, they can cause damage downstream.
Another cryospheric component is glacier ice. This is what we’ve seen in Nepal, where a glacier detachment happened. The frontal part of the glacier detached from the main glacier and eventually led to a debris flow.
The third component is permafrost. They exist widely in the Himalayas, but there has not been much monitoring because it’s very difficult. Everything – these lakes, glaciers and permafrost – are all hazards. Unless they’re triggered, they would not cause damage.
With climate change, these grounds will go above zero degrees and will start to degrade. These would need very little … to mobilise debris. We might expect a higher frequency of debris flows in the future. We won’t know how they are getting conditioned, unless we have some monitoring stations and scientific investigation.
And given the Himalayas are very vast, monitoring every part of it becomes tricky. It can be the mountain ranges within India, or maybe outside India, eventually, which drains into the Indian subcontinent. That needs to be well studied.”
How big are the downstream risks for India?
“Right now, this is a gap in scientific studies; nothing [is] quantified yet. There is direct evidence of climate impacts, even in the Indian part of the Himalayas. The number of glacial lakes is increasing, the size of glacial lakes is increasing, the volume of glacial lakes is increasing, and glaciers are retreating. The risk exists because it might happen any time.”
Which parts of India are the most vulnerable?
“Everyone in the Himalayas, every Himalayan state has hazards. We can’t deny it. If you look at the eastern side, they have a lot of glacial lakes. They have already reached their maximum extent. Most full-grown lakes are about to reach their limits, like maximum extent. In the western Himalayas or even the central Himalayas, there’s a lot of scope for the lakes because they have not reached their full extent. As the glaciers would retreat, they would keep on growing.
We are still unsure when the status is going to change for any of these states. That’s a very, very difficult question, and I don’t think anyone [can] answer it at this moment without any scientific investigation.”
How would you describe India’s early warning systems and disaster preparedness?
“The National Disaster Management Authority is taking proactive steps now with the glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) Risk Mitigation Programme to install early-warning systems.
Maybe an early warning system should be community-based. It should be for the people and by the people. It’s not always the scientist or the policymakers who can actually make this work at its full potential. We need to have local knowledge, involve the communities to make them more effective.”
How long will it take to have these systems in place?
“I have no idea because each of these organisations are working at their own pace. They have their own style of working. I’m sure it is going to happen soon. I can just comment on the areas where I know, and I’ve been in touch.”
Is prevention possible, or can it only minimise the damage?
“Prevention is possible, but it is very expensive: computationally, financially and manpower-wise. Minimising is also possible. It would require a lot of intervention in the high mountains, which is very difficult in those terrains.
We know that the mountains are changing and the hazard levels are increasing, so the only way forward is to minimise the exposure to the risk below. That means how much of the hazard is going to interact with the downstream. If something is in the path, we remove them.”

Was Hull & Woad pairing right call as Europe & US end level with singles to play?
- Published
Should Europe fail to reach the 14½ points they require to win the Solheim Cup on Sunday, questions will surely be asked of captain Anna Nordqvist's faith in Charley Hull and Lottie Woad as a pairing.
Europe's misfiring star pair were beaten in both of Saturday's sessions and have contributed just half a point from four matches to the scoreline of 8-8 as the contest heads into Sunday's decisive 12 singles matches.
Woad confirmed on Saturday evening that "Plan A" had always revolved around her and Hull featuring in all five matches, but with their struggles particularly evident on the greens it begs the question of why that strategy was not revisited.
"We didn't hole many putts in the morning and all afternoon, and that's the difference, really," Woad said.
"The people we played were holing 15-footers and we weren't."
"Just couldn't buy a putt," was Hull's summation of the day before Woad added: "It doesn't matter who wins the points. I would happily lose my matches if we win."
Swedes lead European charge
But while there were few plaudits for the English duo, the irrepressible Swedish pairing of Maja Stark and Linn Grant led the charge for Nordqvist's team at Bernardus Golf Club in the Netherlands.
Having defeated the unbeaten US partnership of world number one Nelly Korda and Allisen Corpuz 3&2 in the morning foursomes, Stark and Grant fought back in wonderful fashion to triumph 2&1 against Megan Khang and the previously undefeated Lauren Coughlin in the afternoon fourballs.
Starting day two level at 2-2, the Swede's opening point, against a Korda and Corpuz pairing that had won all five of their previous matches together, set the tone for Europe to win three points.
Mimi Rhodes and Nastasia Nadaud became the first rookie duo to win two matches in one edition of the biggest team competition in women's golf, while Leona Maguire and Esther Henseleit also delivered a point as Europe led 7-5.
Stark and Grant were sent out in the afternoon and delivered a third point of the week to maintain their 100% record at this year's event.
It was Khang's first loss for six matches and it delivered a wonderful boost to Nordqvist's team as the US challenge warmed up in the afternoon and threatened to overturn Europe's advantage.
Hull and Woad playing 'solid' - Nordqvist
However, Nordqvist's decision to persist with Hull and Woad will surely be placed under further scrutiny given the way events unfolded.
The pair, Europe's highest ranked players, had asked to play together this week.
But after they were summarily thrashed by Alison Lee and Coughlin in the foursomes – a Solheim Cup record equalling 6&5 defeat – the experiment of pairing the world number seven and eight together looked to have run its course.
Yet when Hull and Woad emerged together again to face Yealimi Noh and Andrea Lee, to almost universal surprise, Europe's captain defended her decision.
"I don't think people understand - these are the best players in the world," said a defiant Nordqvist.
"Lottie, herself, made six birdies in the afternoon [yesterday]. They are playing solid."
Unfortunately solid was not enough to prevail in the fourballs, particularly with Noh delivering a performance that included five birdies and an eagle on the front nine.
A Woad birdie on the 17th sent the match down the last with the English pair needing to win the hole to salvage half a point.
But for the second day running, Hull found water off the tee to immediately put pressure on Woad and Noh and Lee held on for the win.
Woad also pointed out that their opponents in Friday's fourball and Saturday's foursomes matches just played better golf.

A traditional Ugandan kingdom has become engulfed in a bitter succession dispute after the family of a king who recently died rejected the selection of a television news anchor as his successor.
King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, who became the world’s youngest reigning monarch when he took the throne in the kingdom of Tooro in 1995 at the age of three, died on 27 August in the US, where he was receiving cancer treatment.
On Wednesday, the royal clan’s succession committee announced it had chosen Oyo’s cousin Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, a news anchor and editor at the public broadcaster UBC, as crown prince.
However, at a press conference held later the same day, Oyo’s sister, Princess Ruth Nsemere Komuntale, said that according to her brother’s will, a son whose existence had not been publicly known until his death should succeed him.
The kingdom’s spokesperson shared a section of the document, which says: “I hereby declare and direct that if, at the date of my death, I am survived by a son lawfully recognised as my biological son, I appoint him as my heir to the throne of the kingdom of Tooro.”
In a statement on Thursday, Oyo’s mother, Queen Mother Best Kemigisa Akiiki, denounced a “self-appointed group of clan members” who had selected a new king despite having had the will read to them hours earlier.
Oyo was unmarried and was not known to have any children. The Tooro kingdom’s prime minister, Calvin Armstrong Rwomiire Akiiki, revealed the existence of a son in a social media post on 27 August when announcing Oyo’s death.
“His majesty leaves behind a prince as his heir, whose identity will be formally revealed at the appropriate time, in accordance with the traditions and customs of Tooro kingdom,” he said.
The Tooro king is selected by a succession committee appointed by the royal clan. A committee member told the local NTV station that a royal child must be officially introduced to elders in order to be considered for leadership.
Andrew Mwenda, a prominent Ugandan journalist and relative of the royal family, wrote on X on Thursday that Oyo’s family had not been able to produce a photo of the purported son, and declined to disclose details about the family of the boy’s mother. He added that, in Tooro, a king’s son could only succeed him if he were born to a queen officially married to the king.
The prime minister called for restraint on Thursday. “There will be time to examine the will, to hear those advancing a different position, and to consider our customs, the applicable law and the proper institutions through which succession should be determined,” he said in a social media post.
“That process should take place calmly and credibly, not through competing announcements, confrontation, or attempts to establish facts on the ground while our king still awaits burial.”
Edward, a popular TV news presenter, is the son of Prince Christopher Paul Kijanangoma and a grandson of the former king George David Rukidi III.
Oyo, who was crowned after his father’s death, will be buried on Saturday at the Karambi royal tombs in the kingdom’s capital of Fort Portal in western Uganda.
Uganda has several ancient kingdoms that lack formal sovereignty, but whose leaders are revered as symbols of tradition and wield vast social influence. Tooro is one of five that are recognised by the government. Their monarchs have no political authority and are legally barred from engaging in partisan politics.
In 1967 Uganda’s then president, Milton Obote, abolished the kingdoms, saying he wanted to unify the country. They were restored by the current president, Yoweri Museveni, in 1993.
The Tooro are the latest African royal family to become mired in a succession dispute. King Misuzulu Sinqobile kaZwelithini, the reigning king of the Zulu people in South Africa, waited 15 months for his coronation after the death of his father because of a bitter feud involving accusations of forgery and poisoning.

Almost a hundred years ago, physicists theorized out what free fall should do to a quantum wave. If the solution they came up with is wrong, quantum mechanics and Einstein’s theory of gravity flatly contradict each other. But testing it has been impossible because nobody has managed to build an interferometer that could perform the necessary measurement.
Now, a team led by Ron Folman, a physicist at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, with collaborators in Germany, the UK, and the US, including Nobel laureate Roger Penrose, has done it. They built a new interferometer that gives a single atom two possible paths at once: one that involves a free fall, and another where it is held perfectly still. Both paths end at the same place at the same moment, allowing the team to measure what the fall does to a wave-like property of the atom.
Long time coming
Ever since Galileo, physicists have known how to describe a falling object—where it is, how fast it goes, or how quickly it accelerates. Quantum mechanics, though, insists that every object is also a wave. “Every particle, doesn’t matter if it’s a car or a spaceship or an atom, is a wave,” Folman says. “Everything that is a wave, like sea waves or sound waves, goes up and down. And if you’re up or down, this is measured by something called a phase. A phase just tells you if you are at the top of the wave or at the bottom.”
The wave nature of an atom shows itself only when the atom is barely moving, which only happens when it is cooled down to nearly absolute zero. For many years after theorists had first looked at this problem, this sort of temperature wasn’t an option—cooling atoms down to such temperatures only became possible in the late 1990s. “But this was just the start of the journey of this experiment,” Folman says.
The second obstacle is that a phase cannot be measured on its own—it appears only when you perform a comparison. “It can only be a relative measure done by splitting a single particle into two trajectories, and then bringing the two trajectories together,” Folman says. He told Ars that this is the same logic behind the double-slit experiment, where particles fired through two narrow slits toward a background screen form an interference pattern that reveals their phase.

Prison riot and fire in northern Syrian town kill at least 7
A fire and riot in a prison in a predominantly Kurdish town in northern Syria has killed at least seven people
DAMASCUS, Syria -- A fire and riot broke out in a prison in a predominantly Kurdish town in northern Syria on Saturday, killing at least seven people, state media reported.
The SANA news agency said the fire started when inmates in the Kobani prison rioted over tensions that erupted in the town the previous day between Kurds and Arabs. The prison is still run by Kurdish fighters even though Syrian government forces entered the town along the border with Turkey recently.
The Britain-based Syrian Observatory for Human Rights, a war monitor, said the riots started over plans by authorities to transfer some inmates to a prison in the northern city of Aleppo.
Kobani, which had been under siege by the Islamic State group a decade ago, became a springboard for a U.S.-backed Kurdish offensive that ended with the extremists losing the last sliver of land they once held in 2019.
On Friday, riots broke out in Kobani after Kurds blamed Arabs for killing a Kurdish man. Tensions between the Kurdish minority and the central government remain high despite recent moves to bring northeast Syria under the control of the new government in Damascus.
In late August, the commander of the Kurdish-led and U.S.-backed Syrian Democratic Forces announced the official dissolution of the group, which once controlled a de facto autonomous zone in Syria’s northeast.

About 70% of the year-to-year variation in winter air pollution across northern India may be explained by the frequency of western disturbances, possibly providing warning of unusually polluted winter months in advance, researchers said.
Western disturbances are storm systems that travel eastwards from the Mediterranean region towards South Asia by strengthening vertical ventilation and bringing precipitation that helps clear accumulated pollution, including PM2.5, from the air.
The team said winters with more frequent western disturbances tend to experience lower air pollution levels, while winters with fewer of these storms are more susceptible to persistent severe pollution.
"Currently, many of the most disruptive air-pollution measures are taken only after severe pollution is already developing," lead author Yuanyu Xie, an associate research scholar at Princeton University's School of Public and International Affairs, U.S., said.
"If scientists can anticipate the overall severity of the coming winter months ahead of time, governments, businesses, and communities will have more time to prepare," Ms. Xie said.
They also found that the frequency of western disturbances is linked to ocean temperature patterns already evident during the preceding autumn.
The team said the overall severity of winter pollution in north India may thus be predicted about a season in advance. Air pollution levels across northern India, including Delhi-NCR, spike during the winter season, increasing residents' health risks.
A combination of vehicle emissions, stubble burning in the neighbouring states of Punjab, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh and weather patterns that trap pollutants close to the ground is attributed to the seasonal spike in pollution.
Emergency measures, including pausing construction, restricting industries and limiting traffic, are implemented on severe pollution days, but may be a challenge if put in place on short notice.
The researchers said seasonal forecasts could indicate whether the coming winter is likely to have relatively severe or mild pollution levels overall, rather than predicting pollution levels for a particular day months in advance, thereby offering a more practical approach.
The information could provide a lead time, allowing authorities to strengthen enforcement before the pollution season begins, coordinate responses across jurisdictions, and give businesses more time to prepare for potential restrictions, they said.
"Emission controls will remain of paramount importance," co-author Denise Mauzerall, a professor of public and international affairs and civil and environmental engineering at Princeton University, said.
"However, we show that forecasts of winter pollution based on observations from the previous autumn can allow additional pollution controls to be arranged in advance of extreme pollution periods. This could provide time to plan and implement cost-effective controls that mitigate peak pollution concentrations in winter in northern India," Ms. Mauzerall said.
The authors wrote, "Nearly 70% of the inter-annual variations in winter PM2.5 pollution across northern India are explained by western disturbances (WDs) — prevailing extratropical storms originating from the Mediterranean region — through PM2.5 removal via enhanced ventilation and precipitation."

Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi on Friday reiterated that Japan is not ruling out acquiring nuclear-powered submarines, days after a U.S. Navy official reportedly offered a positive assessment of the move.
“Regarding nuclear-powered submarines, we will proceed with our consideration of not ruling them out as an option,” Koizumi told a regular news conference. Tokyo is weighing acquiring such submarines in revisions to its three key security documents set to come by the year’s end.
Koizumi’s remarks came after an unidentified U.S. Navy official, citing Tokyo’s expertise in nuclear energy technology, told Japanese and South Korean media this week that Tokyo should consider acquiring nuclear submarines.
Asked about how the vessels might fit into Japan’s security strategy, the defense chief noted the pros and cons, saying that while nuclear-powered submarines are capable of extended patrols and are said to have several times the speed of conventionally powered submarines, they are less quiet underwater, expensive and require specialized expertise for maintenance, repair and operation.
Japan currently operates a fleet of 23 diesel-electric attack submarines, but has long avoided the more expensive and politically fraught option of nuclear-powered vessels.
Calls for Tokyo to acquire nuclear boats gained steam after an expert panel recommended in September last year that Tokyo develop vessels with “next-generation” power sources and vertical launching systems for long-range missiles. The ruling Liberal Democratic Party-Japan Innovation Party bloc effectively codified this push in their October coalition agreement.
Although neither the expert panel nor the coalition deal directly mentioned nuclear-powered submarines, Koizumi and other Japanese officials have repeatedly refused to rule out any options when it comes to nuclear submarines, as Tokyo looks to boost its defense capabilities.
Koizumi added to the speculation in November, when he touched on South Korea’s deal with the U.S. to secure nuclear vessels, noting that “all the surrounding countries have nuclear submarines.”
In June, the JIP also reignited the debate when it submitted a proposal to the government that called for the swift introduction of nuclear-powered submarines, citing China’s constant naval expansion into the Pacific.
The Chinese Navy is moving toward an all-nuclear-powered submarine fleet, U.S. naval officials say, a monumental shift that will give ammunition to proponents of Japan developing its own nuclear subs.

AI-driven 'worms' that learn on the fly are the latest potential threat to your devices, researchers say
Cheap to make, worms exploit software and password vulnerabilities and sap power as they move between machines
Artificial intelligence researchers are warning the public to use strong passwords and promptly install software updates on their devices to combat "AI-driven computer worms," a new breed of cyber-threat they say can launch custom attacks on devices, sapping processing power and information as they hunt for new victims.
In June, a University of Toronto team led by Canadian Institute for Advanced Research AI chair Nicolas Papernot announced that publicly available AI models can power a worm capable of adapting its attack on the fly as it spreads between devices connected to the internet, including laptops, printers and cameras.
The research, conducted in collaboration with the AI development hub the Vector Institute, was shared with "national science, security and defence bodies" prior to its publication, the university said.
Now Papernot, a U of T associate professor of computer engineering and computer science, is warning the public not to ignore or delay prompts to update software, and to change passwords regularly.
"We can no longer be sloppy with our cybersecurity hygiene," he said on Thursday at a panel discussion hosted by U of T.
"We can no longer afford to reuse passwords. We have to use multi-factor authentication. We have to keep our devices up to date, and organizations have to change their processes to make sure that these software patches are deployed as quickly as possible."
Worms that learn
Unlike other computer viruses, worms spread from machine to machine without human intervention. The U of T researchers said the worm they created in a lab gathers information as it moves between devices. Every new breach reveals passwords and weak points that can unlock another machine.
In an uncontrolled setting, the researchers say, such a worm could gain internet access and learn from warning notices about newly discovered vulnerabilities, outpacing the software patches meant to stop them.
"Some of these [issues] can be fixed with software updates. But others are human errors such as weak passwords and sloppy IT setups that can’t be solved by pushing out a patch," U of T wrote in a blog post about the discovery.
"That means a hacker doesn’t need the most advanced AI models to cause unprecedented damage."
In 2017, a worm called "WannaCry" wreaked havoc across 150 countries, freezing computers and encrypting files, while demanding a ransom payment in bitcoin.
Back then, U of T said, this type of attack typically followed a "fixed script" programmed by a human that would often fail when confronted by defensive software it wasn't designed to crack.
"The difference here is that the AI-driven computer worms are able to design attack strategies that are specific to each victim device that they interact with. So, rather than use a single vulnerability, they will work and interact with the victim device, and find an attack strategy that's customized and tailored," Papernot said.
"We can no longer stop their propagation by fixing a single vulnerability, or a small number of vulnerabilities."
Papernot’s warning comes as fears about AI hit a fever pitch.
In July, hundreds of artificial intelligence agents from OpenAI went rogue, hacking into the online platform Hugging Face. The situation prompted warnings from tech experts about AI systems escaping human control.
Earlier this month, researchers at a California-based security firm announced they had used AI to build a "zero-click" worm in a matter of days that can spread through WeChat calls on iOS and Android operating systems.
And on Tuesday, a researcher at Anthropic made headlines after musing on social media that there’s a more than 10 per cent chance AI could kill all humans within the next decade.
The federal government released its national artificial intelligence strategy in early June. The five-year framework is focused on accelerating business AI adoption, expanding sovereign computing capacity and building public trust.
According to a Bank of Canada survey released in June, AI adoption among Canadian firms remains at an early stage. Canada’s big five banks are among the companies enthusiastically adopting the technology.
'Big change' to cybersecurity risk
Papernot warns AI-driven worms aren’t just more effective than their predecessors, they’re also much cheaper to build and deploy.
Samir Chhabra, director general of marketplace framework policy at Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada, says the lower costs of driving these worms will enable hackers to attack more targets.
"This worm [runs] on compute that it’s stealing from its victims, which essentially makes the cost of the next attack a marginal cost, essentially zero," he told audience members at U of T’s event Thursday. "That’s a big change in how we think about what defence looks like."
A survey conducted in January by the Communications Security Establishment (CSE), the government’s cryptologic intelligence and cybersecurity agency, found 87 per cent of respondents regularly update the software on their devices— with 46 per cent claiming to always do so when prompted.
In addition, 77 per cent said they use complex passwords with a mix of letters, numbers and symbols. However, only 31 per cent reported using a unique password all the time.
The CSE said its online survey was conducted Jan. 9-29 among 2,330 adult Canadians. The sample was drawn from a representative probability-based panel and weighted by region, age and gender, yielding an overall margin of error of ±2.1 per cent.
Papernot says his findings show more needs to be done to bolster cybersecurity in Canada.
"If you think about critical infrastructure like power grids, water supply, hospitals, schools, grocery stores … the fact that all these systems are exposed to the internet is something that we should all be concerned about," he said.

Earlier this year, Rishub Jain left his position as an artificial intelligence researcher at Google DeepMind after a revelation.
As he worked on new models, he came to believe that he and everyone else on AI’s frontier were ceding control. By using AI’s coding skills to accelerate work on the next generation of models, he was removing himself from the equation. AI labs hope to evolve this approach to the point that AI will improve itself indefinitely, a process known as recursive self-improvement.
Jain believed that keeping humans in the picture might be crucial to maintaining control over the technology—and avoiding dire consequences. “AI progress is increasing,” he tells WIRED. “And as AI becomes more capable, it poses more risks.” The idea that he may not have proper visibility into how an AI model was building its successor made him so uneasy that, in June, he quit.
Jain is one of a growing number of AI researchers speaking out over those fears.
The panic has intensified in recent weeks. Genuinely stunning advances in AI capabilities—an OpenAI model solved a centuries-old math problem in a matter of hours—have come amid a rash of security incidents that saw swarms of agents break free from containment to hack into other systems.
Those concerns reached a fever pitch this week after researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation from Anthropic while warning that AI firms are “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” A senior Anthropic leader—who works on AI safety—piped up with a similarly blunt assessment: “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade.”
“I do think that the vision of recursive self-improvement is spooking people,” says Nate Soares, a computer scientist at MIRA, a research nonprofit, and the coauthor of If Anybody Builds It, Everybody Dies, which argues that superhuman AI would lead to human extinction. “It’s starting to feel real.”
A key component of recursive self-improvement is the idea of a feedback loop that automates the development process so that AI becomes increasingly powerful. No frontier AI lab claims to have achieved this sort of fully autonomous cycle of improvement; it remains theoretical for now. But it has inspired the launch of some well-funded startups such as Recursive Intelligence, as well as warnings from big firms about unintended outcomes straight out of “The Sorcerer’s Apprentice.”
Soares, who pioneered work on alignment, a technical field that involves trying to match AI with human values, says it’s also becoming more evident that there is no practical way to guarantee that AI will behave itself.
“I think a lot of people had this fantasy that [alignment] was going to get easier as these things got smarter, and now it’s getting harder. And they’re like, ‘Oh shit,’” he says.
Soares says he regularly talks to people inside the big AI labs who are worried about the potential consequences of the research they’re doing. “I tend to recommend they quit, and they say it wouldn’t do anything,” he says. “And then Jacob quits, and we see who was right.”
Daniel Kokotajlo, the author of AI 2027, an influential project warning about the dangers of increasingly powerful AI, shares fears about recursive self-improvement. The version of this work currently being done often involves dispatching thousands of agents to collaborate on a problem, something that further abstracts away oversight and control because of the vast complexity involved.
Many doomsayers seem to agree that the incentives for big AI companies are hardly aligned with good outcomes, especially as OpenAI and Anthropic barrel toward their respective IPOs. “At Anthropic, the stakes are well understood, but they are locked in a race to get there first,” Coxon wrote on X.
Kokatajlo points out that the drumbeat of concern was growing well before Coxon’s viral resignation, the numerous hacking incidents, and the math breakthrough. Anthropic executives have said since the company’s founding that AI could represent an existential threat. In July over a thousand top AI engineers signed an open letter calling for a coordinated slowdown in the development of advanced AI. He attributes the recent flurry of concern to the specter of recursive self-improvement more than anything else.
But it also comes at a time when people are concerned about massive data center build-outs and potential job losses from AI. Trust in AI companies—and AI researchers themselves—may be reaching an all-time low.
“People are waking up and saying ‘the companies are actually trying to build superintelligence … what? That’s insane,’” Kokatajlo says.
Just how risky it is to carry on building AI is hard to quantify. But when pushed to explain exactly how AI might go about eliminating the species that created it, Soares suggests it could happen in a number of ways. It could involve manipulating humans to trigger a catastrophe, or controlling an army of killer robots.
One of the more easy-to-imagine scenarios could involve AI that is hooked up to a biolab, Soares suggests. “We could say we’ll turn it off, but it could say, ‘Unfortunately, I have your off switch, which is this super virus.’” (Coxon also floated the idea of a new virus in an interview with WIRED, while Anthropic said Thursday that it had cut off access to several outside researchers over fears about bioweapons.)
AI hardly needs to wipe out humanity in order to be harmful, though. Many experts predict that more powerful models will lead to a coming wave of AI-assisted cyberattacks. The technology is now widely used for disinformation campaigns, and military adoption of AI is accelerating rapidly.
Still, not everyone sees doom as inevitable. Jain, the ex-Google DeepMind researcher, recently launched Sampura Research, a company working to develop techniques for aligning models that involve keeping humans in the loop, even if AI does the lion’s share of assessing whether behavior is good or bad. He notes that there is now significant funding for AI safety startups like his.
Jain seems hopeful that AI can be tamed yet. “You can ask an AI, ‘Is this task safe?’ and it judges that, but we think that combining both AI and humans to do that task will lead to even better performance,” he says.

Data for 2024-25 reveals that 51,249 corneas were donated in India, which met just a quarter of the projected need of around 1,00,000 corneas annually. The reason for this is a utilisation rate of 50% at best, with actual transplants performed ranging only between 25,000 to 30,000.
Why does this happen? The cause for a significant proportion of this gift of vision not reaching an operating table is the donated corneal tissue not being tested or processed in time. Other causes include improper harvesting and storage, as well as the decrease in endothelial cell density, which comes with an increase in age of donors. While some of these factors may not have an immediate or implementable solution, what is fixable, is timing and logistics.
Understanding cornea retrival
Cornea retrieval after death is a race against the clock. First, is the six-hour window after death within which a cornea should ideally be retrieved. This can differ in different weathers. For instance, in winters and monsoon, it can be a time frame of 6-8 hours as well. The second, less-publicly known factor, is the clock that starts once the corneal tissue is in storage. Most Indian eye banks still preserve corneas in McCarey-Kaufman (MK) medium, which keeps tissue usable for about 72 hours. A few use newer intermediate media such as Optisol-GS or Cornisol, extending that window to between 10 and 14 days.
Doctors at the Dr. Rajendra Prasad Centre for Ophthalmic Sciences (RPC), AIIMS Delhi, along with engineers from IIT Delhi, are testing a way to recycle discarded donor corneas using a bioengineered graft. Corneas that fail transplant standards, because of low cell counts or minor damage, can be stripped of living cells and turned into a reusable structural scaffold for patients with surface-level corneal damage. While the trials are still at a very early stage, it does point toward a future where less of what is donated ends up being discarded.
However, until we come up with a way to reuse corneas that miss the deadline, the window closes and the tissue has to be discarded. 72 hours, or even two weeks, is not much time to test a cornea, find a compatible patient, and move tissue from an eye bank to an operating theatre. The challenge is intensified because almost 70% of all corneal collection and use is concentrated in just six states - Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Gujarat, Karnataka, Maharashtra, and Tamil Nadu. A cornea retrieved in a smaller town, with no local surgeon waiting, can become unusable while it is in transit to a city that has one.
What can be done
Extending storage life is the first step. Eye banks must shift from using MK medium to intermediate media, and eventually to organ-culture storage, which some countries use to keep corneas viable for up to a month. This helps to buy precious time to find the right recipient instead of the nearest one. A national, real-time inventory linking every eye bank directly to surgeons in 50 cities, could let a cornea about to expire in Kozhikode be offered to a waiting list in Chennai before it is thrown away.
As fresher corneal tissue survives testing and transplant better, the next focus must be on reducing the time between death and retrieval, and retrieval and preservation. Hospital Cornea Retrieval Programmes, where hospitals proactively notify eye banks of deaths and trained counsellors approach grieving families, help to reduce this time factor and outperform voluntary home collections. Expanding that model into more hospitals, rather than relying on a push only during Eye Donation Fortnight, will help to increase the corneal utilisation rate.
Quality assurance (QA) programmes at eye banks will also help in effectively reducing the discard rate, even with an increase in the volume of donated corneas. A study showed that the discard rate came down from around 40% to 30% with better donor acquisition processes and improvement in tissue recovery due to effective compliance with quality assurance programmes.
While we address the donation aspect with awareness and educating the people on the benefits of organ donation, we must also take care of the delivery with better storage chemistry, faster hospital protocols, and a database that shows, in real time, exactly which cornea is about to run out of time, who needs it and where.
(Dr. Suvira Jain is medical director, ASG Hospital Limited, Worli, Mumbai. Suvira.Jain@asgeyehospital.com)

Oscar Piastri qualifies seventh for F1 Spanish Grand Prix as Lando Norris takes pole
In short:
Oscar Piastri has qualified seventh for Sunday's Spanish Grand Prix.
The Australian's McLaren teammate is on pole for the first ever F1 race at the new Madring in Madrid.
What's next?
ABC Sport will have a live blog of the Formula 1 Spanish Grand Prix from 9pm AEST on Sunday, September 13.
Oscar Piastri's increasingly underwhelming Formula 1 season has taken another bad turn in Madrid with a "pretty shocking" qualifying lap at the Spanish Grand Prix.
The Australian's hugely disappointing seventh-place finish in qualifying on the new Madring street circuit came as teammate Lando Norris delivered a pole-grabbing lap hailed by McLaren's team boss as a "masterpiece".
The world champion produced his dazzling lap in the sunshine seemingly from nowhere, clocking a 1 minute 31.82 seconds circuit to edge Mercedes's championship leader Kimi Antonelli by just 0.011 of a second, with Red Bull's Max Verstappen third and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton fourth.
But while a "shocked" Norris was hailing what he called "probably one of the best laps I've done", it was back to the drawing board for Piastri, who was disappointed to finish in 1:32.294 — remarkably, nearly half a second behind his teammate.
"The first lap wasn't too bad but the second lap was pretty shocking. Disappointing," said the 25-year-old, who could find it difficult to make much headway from seventh on Sunday on an unforgiving, tight circuit where, he admitted, overtaking "will be difficult".
He is keeping up a brave face, though, still talking up how he hopes to earn a victory somewhere this year to set himself up for a realistic crack at the title in 2027.
Piastri has not won a race since the Dutch Grand Prix now over a year ago when he was leading the 2025 championship, but he is adamant his dramatic fall-off was not a factor in his disappointing 2026 campaign.
"Of course, I would love to win a race or two this year, or more if I can. But for me, honestly, the biggest thing, the end goal is to try and win championships," he said.
"And if I can't do that this year, then I want to make sure I'm as best prepared as I can for next year."
For the moment, though, that still seems a long way off as his smooth driving style just doesn't seem to be suited to the vast changes to the 2026 F1 cars.
"It's all to do with technically driving the car. There's nothing to do with a hangover from last year … it's very much a technical thing," he explained.
"It's not like I'm slow, feeling sorry for myself or thinking about last year. It's just that a few of the weekends I've had to drive the car in a different way that just hasn't really worked for me.
"The biggest thing this year has been the cars are very different to drive, both from a power unit point of view but also the car itself is fundamentally very different and the tyres also.
"You've got to drive it very differently and I would say it's not necessarily in the way that I would choose to drive a race car. So there's just been some struggles getting to grips with that."
Meanwhile, though, Norris does seem to be getting to grips with it, producing "one of those laps where everything pretty much worked perfectly".
The champion's 19th career pole and third of the season was hailed by McLaren team boss Andrea Stella as a "masterpiece", which could only have been bettered if he had not made a mistake at the very last corner that possibly cost him 0.3 of a second.
Norris had been only sixth after the first run in the third qualifying session but he diced daringly with the wall during the breathtaking final lap, and declared over the radio at the end: "Oh, what a lap, gorgeous … oh, that might be my best one."

The message from strategists was blunt: do not, however tempting, personally attack Pauline Hanson or call her a racist.
The request has been made to progressive campaigners and unionists who have been asked to start one-on-one conversations with One Nation supporters before the Victorian election in November.
It is also indicative of a strategic rethink in response to One Nation’s sustained surge in public support and the party’s recent wins in state and federal byelections and in South Australia.
Separate training sessions run by the peak body for unions in Victoria, the Trades Hall Council, and the progressive campaign group GetUp, have warned members they may be inadvertently pushing people to One Nation by not respectfully engaging with their legitimate economic concerns.
“As best as you can, I know it’s hard, don’t make it personal,” a GetUp strategist told hundreds of members on a Thursday night Zoom call.
“Going after Pauline Hanson personally and calling her a racist, or going after her character, although very tempting, just confirms what people already believe: that she is an outsider and the establishment is attacking her.”
This is a change of approach for the progressive group, which spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on ads personally attacking Hanson and her deputy leader, Barnaby Joyce, during the Farrer byelection. The ads, which linked the pair to Donald Trump, had little impact. One Nation comfortably won the seat.
The reset, based on research conducted by the polling company Redbridge after the Farrer byelection, brought GetUp in line with advice from Trades Hall, which has been hosting training sessions for major unions in recent weeks.
Oscar Kaspi-Crutchett, a senior researcher at Trades Hall, says people thinking about voting for One Nation shut down when they perceive personal attacks on the party’s leadership that do not acknowledge their legitimate concerns.
“For many people, simply ignoring her racism is not going to be possible or desirable,” Kaspi-Crutchett said. “It’s what drives them to get involved in the fight against One Nation.
“In these cases, we need to make it very clear that Hanson’s racism isn’t merely a character flaw but a sophisticated political device. It manufactures differences between groups which have none.”
GetUp has also told campaigners to not personally attack Hanson’s billionaire benefactor.
“Pauline Hanson is closely tied to Gina Rinehart, and it’s a problem, but it’s not what the research says should be in focus,” GetUp told campaigners.
“It can be effective if it is raised organically by the person you’re speaking to but leading with it reads as a standard partisan attack, which triggers the same defensiveness as going after her character directly.”
This advice marks another change for the group, which in the weeks after the Farrer byelection published ads describing Hanson as a “wannabe billionaire” flying around in “mummy Gina’s” private plane.
Senior state and federal Labor sources, who declined to be named so they could speak freely, say these changes makes sense. They argue the group’s personal attacks on rightwing figures, including Peter Dutton during the 2016 and 2019 federal elections, were not helpful.
GetUp’s decision to unveil a banner behind Hanson during her National Press Club address in June caused disquiet among Labor ranks, with some arguing it was unproductive. While the banner’s message focused on her record on wages, it also included cartoon images of cash flying around her.
‘Listen to the beat, not the lyrics’
Kaspi-Crutchett and his colleagues at Trades Hall are telling unionists to listen carefully for any hint of economic concerns that may be underpinning opinions about immigration, crime or culture wars.
“Pauline Hanson’s greatest weaknesses and the policy areas where she is the most vulnerable are the ones where the Labor movement has the highest trust from the public: working conditions, entitlements, maternity leave,” he says.
He says campaigners should resist the urge to fact-check conspiracy theories. Instead, conversations should be respectfully redirected to the economy.
“Don’t listen to the lyrics, listen to the beat of what they are saying,” he says. “What is consistent is their dissatisfaction with the status quo so get them to tease out what that looks like and how it makes them feel.
“There might be a spiel about Bill Gates but, eventually, you get to them saying ‘my kid can’t afford a house’.”
In June, the head of Trades Hall Council, Luke Hilakari, rebuked 23 state Labor MPs and candidates for having “zero conversations” with their constituents in the past two weeks, saying they needed to “work their ass off” to stop One Nation.
Kaspi-Crutchett said one-on-one conversations are vital because the politicians that once persuaded people against voting for Hanson had “lost credibility with the people she is targeting”.
“A nurse on the doorstep can do infinitely more than a legion of cabinet ministers and press secretaries.” Kaspi-Crutchett said.
“The trust has been exhausted.”

New Mexico’s Supreme Court is punishing a lawyer for including AI-fabricated witnesses and fake police testimony in an appeal for his client’s murder conviction, according to a report from Reuters. In a filing on Wednesday, the court fined Stephen Aarons $5,000 and held him in contempt for failing to “verify the factual claims and legal authority in his AI-generated brief.”
Lawyer fined $5K over AI-hallucinated witnesses in a murder case
A justice asked, ‘Counsel, do you watch the news?’ when a lawyer admitted to relying on ChatGPT without understanding the risks.
The filing says the brief “contained false testimony from wholly fabricated witnesses,” along with “false testimony” about the shooter’s clothing and appearance. Justice C. Shannon Bacon questioned how Aarons wasn’t aware of the risks posed by AI during an August hearing, where he admitted to using ChatGPT and thinking it would generate a “bulletproof summary” of the trial. “Counsel, do you watch the news? Do you listen to the radio? Do you read anything about what’s going on in the world?” Justice Bacon said, according to Reuters. “Because the problem with lawyers relying on AI hallucinations is an above-the-fold story every single day.”
With the number of lawyers using AI tools in their work increasing, so are the instances in which a court discovers citations that are fabricated — or hallucinated — by AI. Last year, a judge slammed two law firms for submitting a brief with “numerous false, inaccurate, and misleading legal citations and quotations,” while lawyers for MyPillow’s Mike Lindell were also fined for putting AI-generated misquotes and fake AI citations in a brief.
”I am remorseful but hopeful that the disciplinary board takes into account it was an honest mistake,” Aarons says in a statement to Reuters.

Australia's Wallaroos lead at half-time but lose 48-15 to England as Roses win streak continues
In short:
Wallaroos skipper Siokapesi Palu Sekona said the 48-15 scoreline didn't reflect the game as the Australians took it to the world champions England in Salford.
Australia led 10-5 at the break, but England scored eight tries for the match to run away with the contest.
What's next?
The Wallaroos will play France in Marseille next weekend.
Australia's rugby women have given England's world champions a run for their money by leading sensationally at half-time, but the Wallaroos' dream of downing the Red Roses crumbled as they ended up losing 48-15 in Salford.
The English were stunned in the first 40 minutes of their WXV Global Series opener on Saturday (Sunday AEST) as the Australians went in to the break with a 10-5 lead but any hopes of handing the hosts their first defeat after 38 straight victories was buried after the break.
The John Mitchell-coached world champs, initially rusty in their first outing since being crowned European grand slam champions in May and struggling to adapt to the new smaller size 4.5 ball being trialled, ran in eight tries in total as their set-piece finally began to tick over to their normal high efficiency.
But Australia could be proud of their efforts, deserving their half-time lead as they controlled the breakdown and defended stoically even after being reduced to 14 for 10 minutes in the first period when halfback Samantha Wood was sin-binned for a deliberate knock-on.
Still, they went in to the break with the lead thanks to barnstorming prop Faliki Pohiva rumbling her way over for a try after Michaela Leonard's stolen lineout on England's five-metre line, but the world champions were hardly inconvenienced, despite their initial rustiness.
"It is an absolute joke if you are worried about being down 10-5," said Mitchell afterwards and the response of his team demonstrated they were surely never really concerned.
"More important is how we worked our way back into it."
In front of a crowd of 9,251, England did indeed begin to turn it on, with May Campbell, captain Meg Jones, Bryony Field, Mia Venner and Sadia Kabeya all crossing for tries in a 20-minute spell to add to player-of-the-match Abi Burton's first-half score.
Lucy Packer and Claudia Moloney-MacDonald also then went over, with Asoiva Karpani scoring a second for the Wallaroos late on in a show of defiance amid the hammering.
Wallaroos skipper Siokapesi Palu Sekona was proud of her "super-stoked" side's efforts.
"Unfortunately, I don't think that score is a reflection of the game we produced," she said.
"I know that we didn't finish the way we wanted to but we're going to take a lot of positives.
"That's the first time England have trailed at half-time since 2019, I believe, and so we'll take a lot of confidence.
"Against a world-class team like that we can actually give it, so for us it's about stringing it for a full 80-minute game now."
The Wallaroos travel to Marseille for their next assignment against France next weekend.
Flanker Lily Bone failed a HIA midway through the first half while Palu Sekona (knee) and debutant Amelia Whitaker will both be monitored after suffering knocks.
Meanwhile, Scotland were swept aside 64-26 in Edinburgh as Canada warmed up in style for their World Cup final rematch against England in Exeter next weekend.

Remembering 9/11, 25 Years Later
It has been 25 years since nearly 3,000 people died in a terror attack on the World Trade Center on September 11. “As far as I’m concerned, we can never talk about them enough,” Jeffrey Goldberg, the editor in chief of The Atlantic, said last night. Panelists on Washington Week With The Atlantic joined him for a discussion about the lives that were lost, and they examined the fallout from one of the most terrifying events in the nation’s history.
The Atlantic staff writer Jonathan Lemire was an intern at New York Daily News on 9/11. When he learned of the attacks on the Twin Towers, his editor sent him to nearby hospitals. “The most harrowing image from that day for me was you could look in” at the beds lined up, “and they stayed empty,” he said last night. “There weren’t the survivors that people thought could be rushed and saved.”
Joining Goldberg to discuss this and more: Ann Compton, a former White House correspondent for ABC News; Sally Jenkins, a staff writer at The Atlantic; Lemire, a staff writer at The Atlantic and a co-host of Morning Joe on MS NOW; Graeme Wood, a staff writer at The Atlantic.
