American football is coming to Australia - can it succeed?
- Published
An oval ball, in September, in Melbourne usually means just one thing - the business end of the Australian rules football (AFL) season.
But on Friday, at the unsportingly early time of 7am, 100,000 people will begin filing into the Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG) for a very un-Australian sporting spectacle - American football.
The LA Rams take on the San Francisco 49ers in their opening National Football League (NFL) fixture, the first time the country has hosted a meaningful, non-exhibition regular season game.
The match sold out months ago, with more than half the crowd expected to be people living outside the state of Victoria. On the official ticket resale site, a restricted view seat is priced at more than A$650 (£350/US$470).
"Walking down the street, it's AFL finals week and you wouldn't even know," says Thomas McMillan, host of the NFL podcast Any Given Sunday Australia.
"It's all NFL everywhere. There are bars that are nothing but 49ers bars or Rams bars. We have a Ram Tram getting around the district. When you're in Melbourne and AFL isn't visible, it shows how big this is at the moment."
Kickoff at 10.35am local time on Friday may not be typical for local fans, but meets the demands of prime time US television schedules and their advertisers.
The league held its first international match in 2007, and over the past two decades the overseas matches have become a long-term strategy to attract supporters and their dollars.
Nine games outside the US are scheduled for the upcoming season, including three in London. But Melbourne is the furthest that players and US-based fans will have to travel.
"Obviously there are question marks when you hear you are playing in Australia," 49ers running back Christian McCaffrey told a press conference this week.
"But it has been so cool… the food's incredible, the coffee's great."
That caffeine reference was perhaps as much to the time zone, as nod to the city's famous café culture.
Melbourne is a mind-warping 17 hours ahead of California where both teams are based, and much of the pre-match attention has been on the two teams and their contrasting approaches to trying to "beat" the jet lag.
For the 49ers, who arrived late last week, their players have had time to get over the long journey, adjust to the time zone, acclimatise and practice at a nearby stadium.
Controversially, the LA Rams are taking things to the other extreme, planning to arrive on Thursday morning local time on a charted Qantas A380 superjumbo, play on Friday, and get back to the US west coast shortly afterwards, in theory to prepare for their next match with minimum disruption to the player's body clocks.
"Definitely it's a gamble," says McMillan. "If they don't quite get things right after the 16-hour flight, you still might have that jet lag, even though you're trying to avoid it."
"And not everyone can sleep on planes," says his co-host Danny Webb. "Whether you're in first class, business class, whatever it is, you're still on a plane."
"And", adds McMillan: "And they're six foot six most of them, so it's going to be even tighter seats".
Despite it technically being a "home" game for the Rams, who bid for NFL marketing rights in Australia under the leagues Global Markets programme, this all means it is the San Francisco 49ers that have more of a presence around Melbourne this week.
And while most practice sessions have been behind closed doors, there have been player appearances at a rally for fans and an AFL match, while ex-stars turned up at that most Australian of traditions, the weekly fundraising "sausage sizzle" at the country's most high-profile hardware chain.
American sports journalist Dontay Atkinson predicts this fan engagement will be reflected inside the stadium and that the MCG will be "heavily red" (the 49ers colour), accusing the Rams of doing "exactly jack squat to sell the NFL brand or connect with Australians".
Writing on X he added: "Fly in, fly out, no contact. I'm sure the Aussies feel great about that snub."
McMillan says he can understand the approach by the Rams, who are seen as contenders for the 2027 Superbowl.
"They're looking at this as a game they need to win," he says.
"We do feel a bit snubbed, and feel the 49ers are doing the right thing,
"But it is their job, so that's where the Rams coaching staff has gone 'nah, we're taking this approach'.
"I just worry that they have missed the boat of ingraining themselves as the Australian team. It leaves it open for others, and the 49ers have really jumped on that."
The LA Rams insist there has been no snub, though speaking to the BBC, the club's Head of International Stephanie Cheng dodged the question of whether she would have preferred her players to have been in town this week.
"It's really a culmination of more than four years of work," she said. "It's not just about game week. We have long term rights."
Cheng says the Rams are the only NFL team with a membership programme for Australian fans, and that it has sent coaches into schools and communities to promote "flag football" – the non-contact version of the sport which will feature in the LA 2028 Olympics.
She also points to regular earlier visits by star players including running back Kyren Williams in March. This week its cheerleaders have visited US military bases in Australia before coming to Melbourne, and the franchise has installed a 22-yard floating football field on Melbourne's Yarra River serving as a fan zone.
"From day one, when we've come to Australia, there's been incredible enthusiasm," Cheng said.
While no Australian players will be on the field on Friday, there are dozens playing US college football and a handful in the NFL.
Most are punters, kicking specialists tapped up after showing their prowess playing AFL or rugby league.
But it is the success of Jordan Mailata, an offensive left tackle with the Philadelphia Eagles, who in 2025 became the first Australian to play in, and win, a Superbowl that was a "major turning point in Australia's fandom of the NFL " says Webb.
"Seeing an Australian in what we'd called a skilled position and then winning a Superbowl. It doesn't get better than that".
Friday's game is the first of three matches in Melbourne to be held over four years, under a contract between the NFL and the state of Victoria.
The league's preference, says Gerrit Meier, managing director and head of NFL International, is to have annual games in Australia similar, to the way the game has grown in the UK.
"We're working off the hypothesis that we need to make a commitment to a market," he told Reuters.

Most people associate heart disease with men, and generally elderly men. This, however, is far from the real picture. Heart disease is a serious health problem in women as well, but still remains underdiagnosed and sub-optimally managed in our country. One of the main reasons for this is that in many cases, women may not have the ‘classic’ symptoms of a heart attack. This can result in symptoms being overlooked or misdiagnosed as acidity, stress, tiredness or other minor health issues.
Warning signs in women
Chest pain or pressure is common in women, but they can also get other, more subtle, symptoms. These may occur suddenly or slowly.
The following signs should be watched out for:
- Unusual shortness of breath, even without much exertion
- Abnormally excessive fatigue
- Nausea, vomiting, dizziness or sweating
- Back pain or discomfort in the back, jaw, neck, shoulders or arms
- A sense of pressure, weight or unease in the chest
Sometimes, both women and healthcare providers may ignore these symptoms or dismiss them as fatigue or digestive issues, particularly when there is no severe chest pain. But continued or atypical symptoms should never be left to self-diagnosis.
Understanding heart disease in women
The risks of heart disease can vary for women of different ages. High blood pressure, diabetes, obesity and high cholesterol contribute to the risk. Heart health can also be impacted by smoking, inactivity, poor diet and chronic stress. Some conditions that can occur during pregnancy are also likely to be factors in heart risk, and should be discussed with a doctor, including high blood pressure and diabetes during pregnancy. Hormonal changes may also play a role. Once women reach menopause, the risk of cardiovascular disease rises, as there is less protective oestrogen in the body.
Also, coronary artery disease is not always obstructive: a normal angiogram does not necessarily exclude heart disease. as women have a higher incidence of microvascular angina, and so, it is important to not stop evaluations.
What is also of great concern is that women might not seek medical treatment if symptoms are atypical. During a heart attack this delay can be fatal, as every minute counts.
Steps to make a difference
Protecting your heart health does not always mean making big changes in your lifestyle. Simple daily practices and regular health checkups can make a big difference.
These are some steps that women can take:
Know your numbers: Be aware of blood pressure, blood sugar and cholesterol—especially if there is a family history of heart disease.
Diet : Follow a balanced, nutritious diet, preferably a Mediterranean/DASH diet.
Be physically active: Walk, exercise or do something you enjoy regularly, to help maintain your heart health.
Stop smoking completely: This protects the heart and the rest of the body as well
Do not ignore unusual symptoms: Sudden difficulty in breathing, sudden weakness, chest discomfort or pain in the jaw, back or arms should be promptly evaluated.
Women don’t always experience noticeable symptoms when they have a heart disease. Sometimes, symptoms may not be obvious. For women to own their heart health, it is crucial to be aware of these symptoms, understand their risk factors, and seek timely medical attention. Women’s heart health should be also given increased importance in healthcare settings because their symptoms may be less apparent at times, and early detection and prompt medical intervention can make a huge difference.
(Dr. Saurabh Juneja is director & head, CTVS, cardiac sciences, ISIC Multispeciality Hospital. dr.juneja@gmail.com)

Last month, a team of scientists published a high-profile paper describing how they’d taught an AI model to help produce brand-new, deadly viruses. The AI—a “genome-language model” trained on DNA sequences—had designed multiple new genomes that scientists then synthesized into functional viruses. And some of those viruses were capable of killing bacteria in a dish.
News of AI-made viruses went over poorly. The loudest reaction to the study (which had been released as a preprint about a year ago) was fear. Now that AI can design viruses that go after bacteria, perhaps someone could use the technology to manufacture pathogens that harm people—sparking a major outbreak, even a devastating pandemic. This potential threat evoked some of the same concerns that politicians, researchers, and tech leaders (including Bill Gates) have raised. And these fears are only gaining traction: On Thursday, Anthropic released a report that sparked a round of doom-laden headlines, detailing several instances in which the company banned accounts that were using its LLM, Claude, for what could have been reputable research efforts—or efforts to develop biological weapons.
AI, which has repeatedly proved itself capable of exceeding user expectations and bypassing guardrails, is a formidable force; many fears about its potential biological threat stem from its relentless pace of development and the possibility that it could make independent breakthroughs, exceeding researchers’ own understanding, especially if AIs eventually achieve recursive self-improvement—that is, models designing newer and smarter models. Kevin Esvelt, a biologist at MIT and a co-founder of Secure Bio, a biosecurity nonprofit, told me that although he thinks the probability of an AI-driven pandemic remains quite low, the consequences of such a catastrophe would be so large that “it’s very important that we drive that probability down as low as we can.”
But many other biologists, especially infectious-disease experts and virologists, told me that the threat of a pandemic need not loom particularly large on the list of AI-made threats. To the scientists most familiar with the minutiae of growing, modifying, and testing viruses in a lab, and the havoc they can wreak in the real world, the viruses that have already arisen through evolution, or will soon enough, still present much more immediate perils. In other words, humans should be investing aggressively in pandemic preparation, but not because of AI.
To be clear, viruses made with the help of AI could pose some threat. The experts I spoke with agreed that, in the wrong hands, AI could be used to speed infectious destruction, to a degree. To create the bacterium-killing virus, scientists led by a group at Stanford University and the Arc Institute fed the AI model, called Evo, only viral genomes that attack bacteria. Those genomes are much simpler and smaller than ones coding for viruses that go after humans. In theory, though, with a similar technique, researchers could train AI on the genomes of viruses that infect humans, with the aim of manufacturing novel pathogens. Or perhaps—as some people worry is likelier, easier, and more dangerous—users could ask AI to adjust specific traits of viruses known to cause disease, until those pathogens can skirt available vaccines.
Scientists have long been able to manipulate viral genetics without AI. This kind of “gain of function” research has stirred its own political and scientific controversy—especially in discussions about the origins of COVID-19—and the Trump administration has restricted federal funding for it. But current AI models have the capacity to “put a supreme battery in the back of the things that people were already doing,” Brandon Ogbunu, an evolutionary biologist and infectious-diseases modeler at Yale University, told me. Tom Inglesby, the director of the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security, worries about bad actors using AI to surmount some of the limits of their own technical expertise. Ideally, models powerful enough to suggest new viral genomes should be subject to strict, formal review, Inglesby said; perhaps they could even be limited to training on only certain types of benign data. (For instance, the team that built Evo trained it only on viruses that kill bacteria, and withheld any data about viruses that can harm more complex life forms, including humans.) Esvelt advocates for restricting access to certain models entirely.
Other researchers, however, including the virologists I spoke with, pointed out that another set of safeguards is already in place: how little we humans—the creators and users of AI—understand about pathogenic viruses. For AI to map out more effective pathogens, people must be able to feed it data on what makes viruses highly transmissible, dangerous, and able to circumvent immune safeguards.
But these concepts are complex and murky enough that the chasm AI would need to cross is wide; researchers lack much of the basic knowledge they’d need to train an AI properly on such topics. “Right now, the data is junk going in,” Seema Lakdawala, a virologist at Emory University, told me. Generations of virologists have not come up with firm answers to key questions about what makes certain viruses better at causing diseases than others, or why some people are more susceptible to particular infections than others. Even expert virologists may struggle to ask AI the best prompts to guide it in useful directions.
In her own research on viral transmission, Lakdawala hasn’t found LLMs such as Claude and ChatGPT particularly helpful or correct, she told me, even when she’s asked it questions far simpler than “How do I make a pandemic virus?” (for example, basic questions about the flu-virus genome). Brian Hie, the lead researcher on the team that designed Evo, told me he’s also unconvinced “that AI would even be the method of choice for someone trying to make a dangerous pathogen.” It does not know enough about pathogens, because we don’t know enough about pathogens.
Esvelt, at MIT, argues that AI might not need to understand viruses perfectly, or even that well, to stumble across a dangerous iteration of one. AIs might also improve rapidly enough to make more sense of the existing data than human researchers ever have. But no matter how good AIs get, they so far have no way to build and test new pathogens, Gigi Gronvall, a health-security expert at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, told me. Even a very motivated human—whether they wanted to spark a pandemic for a government or terrorist organization, or for their own ends—would still have to pick through AI-generated possibilities, successfully synthesize them, assess them for enhanced (or at least sufficient) transmissibility and virulence, produce a sufficient quantity to do serious damage, and then release that payload of new virus into the world. All of that requires substantial skill in the lab, as well as expensive equipment and lab animals. It’s not impossible, but it certainly isn’t easy, either.
The practice of building new viruses in a laboratory is fickle: “Even if I give two experienced scientists the same protocol, they’re going to do it differently, and the results could come out differently,” Linsey Marr, a viral-transmission researcher at Virginia Tech, told me. Tinkering with viruses the old-fashioned way has also taught researchers that many hypotheses about what should make a virus more contagious or dangerous don’t pan out. Researchers cannot simply tune up a virus’s transmissibility or virulence like a dial; such changes can come with serious costs, including rendering the entire pathogen nonfunctional—incapable of infecting or hurting a person at all.
Evolution is already a master at tinkering with life forms and building upon their most successful—or dangerous—traits. Viruses are constantly trying out new versions of themselves and aren’t limited by human expectations about what “dangerous” agents of disease look like. Evolving pathogens also need no assistance from malevolent actors to start epidemics; in nature, where species constantly mingle, new outbreaks begin all the time. And nature has an elegant way of dealing with mistakes: Unviable iterations of life simply never come to exist at all. As good as AI is getting, “I can’t look anyone in the eye and say that process is any more harmful than what nature is already operating,” Ogbunu, the Yale evolutionary biologist, said.
The virologists I spoke with did agree that AI models should be monitored and regulated, but were wary of limitations that would hinder AI’s ability to speed the development of new vaccines, shore up viral surveillance, boost epidemiological modeling, or otherwise benefit public-health and infectious-disease research. (Even the types of bacterium-killing viruses that caused such an uproar could be deployed against antibiotic-resistant infections.)
Worries about killer viruses are already interfering with such lines of research. Among the examples of potential threats in Anthropic’s report were gain-of-function work on chikungunya virus and research about how flu viruses adapt to mammals—projects that could have been malicious or, in theory, could improve therapeutics or outbreak detection, respectively. (The company said in the report that it couldn’t confirm whether the queries represented the pursuit of knowledge for the public good or attempts at bioterrorism, and had erred on the side of caution.) Lakdawala and Marr told me that, recently, when they have asked Claude or ChatGPT about, say, genetic quirks in the flu-virus genome or using UV light to inactivate viruses, the AI flagged or halted their conversations. “It happens to me almost daily,” Marr said. (An OpenAI spokesperson wrote over email that “today’s models are specifically trained to withhold biological information that could enable harm” and that researchers “pursuing legitimate biological and life sciences work” can apply to its Trusted Access for Cyber program, which requires proof of identification. Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment.)
Lakdawala and Marr are now trying to develop their own framework to help AI models distinguish legitimate scientific pursuits from nefarious ones. Both say that it’s difficult: What would the criteria be? Who would be the final arbiters of those criteria and of ambiguous cases? And none of those guardrails would address the most extreme concerns about viruses created by AI—that a self-improving intelligence might eventually be able to deliberately design, manufacture, and release a pathogen. For now, though, AI is still a tool. We’re still in charge of the questions we ask it, the data we feed it, and the fate of any virus that it might suggest we create.

New Delhi, Sep 12: Chinese President Xi Jinping landed in the national capital on Saturday for a two-day trip to attend the BRICS Summit, marking his first visit to India in seven years.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi will host him for bilateral talks on Saturday evening with a focus on boosting trade and investment ties.
President Xi's visit to New Delhi follows a series of recent high-level exchanges, including the Special Representative dialogue in Beijing between National Security Advisor Ajit Doval and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, even as concerns linger over aggressive Chinese military posturing along the Arunachal Pradesh sector.
The Chinese leader is accompanied by a high-level delegation comprising government officials and top business leaders.
Both sides have rolled out a series of confidence-building measures over the past year to repair ties frayed by the more than four-and-a-half-year military standoff in eastern Ladakh.

Presidential pardon for controversial Sri Lankan monk overturned
- Published
Sri Lanka's Supreme Court has overturned a presidential pardon granted to a hardline Buddhist monk and ordered him to serve the remainder of a six-year prison sentence for intimidating the wife of a missing political cartoonist.
Galagodaatte Gnanasara was sentenced in 2018 for contempt of court and intimidating Sanya Eknaligoda, the wife of Prageeth Eknaligoda who disappeared in 2010.
The monk had interrupted a court hearing to speak in support of military intelligence officials who were accused of abducting the cartoonist.
Gnanasara served less than a year of that sentence because he received a pardon from Maithripala Sirisena, who was the country's president at the time.
In his cartoons, Prageeth Eknaligoda depicted issues of media freedom, political power and social disadvantage.
His work was critical of the former president Mahinda Rajapaksa, a nationalist credited with the defeat of the Tamil separatist rebels in 2009 after a bloody civil war.
Eknaligoda went missing in 2010 and has not been seen since. His wife has led a campaign to trace his whereabouts, and accuses the authorities of not doing enough to investigate his disappearance.
Gnanasara, who leads the Bodu Bala Sena (BBS) or "Buddhist Power Force", was a supporter of Rajapaksa and his brother Gotobaya, who also later served as president.
In 2025, he received a separate nine-month prison term for insulting Islam and inciting religious hatred.
Sri Lanka rarely convicts Buddhist monks, and it is almost unheard of for one to receive a custodial sentence.

North Korea fired “multiple” ballistic missiles toward its eastern coast on Saturday, the South Korean military said, a day after the South concluded trilateral military drills with the U.S. and Japan.
The South Korean military said it was analyzing the firing and sharing information with the U.S. and Japan, the Yonhap news agency reported. The missiles flew about 250 kilometers.
The U.S. Pacific Command said it was aware of the launches and was “consulting closely” with allies and partners. “The United States remains committed to the defense of the U.S. homeland and our allies in the region,” it added.
Nuclear-armed North Korea labeled the Freedom Edge maritime drills by South Korea, the United States and Japan a “threat” and claimed that Washington “is perpetrating air espionage and other anti-DPRK military provocations one after another.” DRPK is the acronym for North Korea’s formal name.
Last month, Pyongyang fired off a barrage of around 10 short-range ballistic missiles, hours after U.S. President Donald Trump claimed he would meet North Korean leader Kim Jong Un later this year.
But North Korea has poured cold water on the idea of talks, with Pyongyang saying that the Trump administration has “fully reconfirmed its invariable hostile policy to wantonly violate the sovereignty, political system and security interests of the DPRK.”
Experts say Trump will face an uphill battle in rekindling his relationship with Kim. The North Korean has also hinted at an openness to talks — but only on his terms: recognizing his country as a nuclear power and ending what Pyongyang says is a “hostile” U.S. policy toward the pariah state.

For years, drugmakers have offered free meals, samples, gifts, and speaking fees to physicians, a widely studied issue due to concerns such largesse may unduly influence prescribing habits.
But to what extent have interactions between doctors and pharmaceutical representatives changed behaviors over time?
A new analysis attempts to provide some answers. A group of researchers surveyed 283 physicians who were among more than 1,300 medical students and residents queried in 2011. They compared the responses to an updated effort that was undertaken two years ago, and the results suggest the topic is likely to remain contentious.

Royal family rift after popular TV news presenter chosen to succeed Ugandan king
- Published
A bitter succession dispute has erupted in one of Uganda's traditional kingdoms, days before the burial of its late king, who until his death had been the world's youngest reigning monarch.
King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, who ruled the Tooro Kingdom for more than three decades, was undergoing cancer treatment in the US when he died last month aged 34.
Royal clan elders have named popular TV news presenter Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, 56, as the next monarch, but this has been rejected by Oyo's close family.
His sister, Princess Ruth Komuntale, said the late king had left a will written in 2022 naming his young son, whose identity has never been disclosed, as his successor.
"My brother did leave behind an heir to the throne, and that was very clearly stated," she said, accusing those behind the announcement on Wednesday night of creating "confusion and turmoil" while the family was still grieving.
Meanwhile the late king's mother, Queen Best Kemigisa, has said royal guards have been withdrawn from the palace and soldiers deployed, restricting the royal family's movement and their ability to receive visitors, describing the situation as "house arrest".
She appealed to the army's leadership and President Yoweri Museveni to allow the family to mourn and bury Oyo in peace on Saturday.
"I appeal to those fighting over the throne: please, there will be time for all of that," she said. "Let us grieve and bury my son King Oyo."
Thousands of mourners are expected to attend the burial at the royal tombs near the palace in Fort Portal in western Uganda.
His body was returned to Uganda from the US on Friday, and preparations for the funeral are under way.
Tooro is one of Uganda's traditional kingdoms. Its monarch has no formal political authority but remains an important cultural figure in western Uganda.
Uganda abolished its traditional kingdoms in 1967, but they were restored in the 1990s under President Museveni. Their monarchs are recognised as cultural leaders rather than political rulers.
The existence of Oyo's son was first publicly revealed in the days after the king's death by President Museveni, who said he had been told about the young boy by the queen mother.
No other details have officially been disclosed, and he had not previously been presented as Oyo's heir.
The disagreement has exposed the complicated way in which succession works in Tooro.
Unlike Britain's monarchy, where the crown passes according to an established line of succession, Tooro's monarch is chosen from the Babiito, the royal dynastic clan.
At a press conference in the kingdom's capital of Fort Portal, the royal clan's succession committee announced Kijanangoma, Oyo's cousin and a news presenter at the state-run broadcaster UBC, as monarch.
The clan elders said they had the customary authority to choose a suitable prince to become "the Omukama" - the local title for the king of Tooro.
The succession panel said it had carried out "due diligence, consultation and adequate consideration" before selecting Kijanangoma, with 19 members signing the resolution.
Kijanangoma is the son of Prince Christopher Paul Kijanangoma and a grandson of former Tooro king George David Rukidi III.
Another royal, UK-based Prince George Desmond Kamurasi, was initially considered for the throne but declined, citing other responsibilities, according to the succession committee.
It is not yet clear when the enthronement will take place, but the committee said it would be conducted in accordance with the traditions and customs of the Tooro kingdom.
Oyo's family quickly called a press conference to denounce the announcement, insisting the late king's written wishes should be respected.
Princess Komuntale said Oyo had left "very strict instructions" on his succession, naming his son as first in line and also setting out alternatives if the boy could not take the throne - a position backed by her aunt, senior royal Princess Elizabeth Bagaaya.
But clan representatives said that reports of Oyo having a son were not sufficient because the child had not been formally presented to the royal clan as dictated by Tooro tradition.
One committee member told Uganda's NTV station that a royal child must be formally introduced to elders and then must undergo ceremonies and others preparations if they were to be considered for future leadership.
Culture Minister Henry Tumukunde has stepped in to say he will be overseeing mediation efforts, with an outcome expected after consultations with President Museveni and cultural leaders.

Madhuri, also known as Mahadevi, returned to the Nandani Math in Kolhapur more than a year after she had been relocated to the Vantara animal rescue centre in Jamnagar, Gujarat.
As Madhuri travelled through Pune, residents gathered to welcome her, showering flowers on the vehicle carrying the elephant. In Kolhapur, hundreds of people gathered outside the Math to give Madhuri a grand welcome and celebrate her return home.
We fully understand the deep sentiments surrounding Madhuri in Kolhapur. Following discussions with the Government of Maharashtra, its officers, stakeholders and members of the community, Vantara stated on 06 August 2025 that it respected those sentiments and would abide by the directions of the competent authorities, as per the press release.
The elephant had been shifted to Vantara on 28 July 2025 following directions from a High-Powered Committee (HPC). The decision had subsequently been upheld by both the Bombay High Court and the Supreme Court. Madhuri’s relocation had come amid protests and a prolonged legal dispute over where she should be housed.
Following an inspection of the proposed facility in Kolhapur, the HPC gave clearance for Madhuri to return to the Nandani Math on 9 September 2026, more than a year after her relocation.
Vantara said it had not intended to hurt religious sentiments and had acted only on court orders. "We recognise and respect the sentiments of the devotees, the leadership of the Jain Math, and the wider community who have expressed their concerns and attachment to Madhuri's presence in Kolhapur," it said.
“At no stage did Vantara initiate or recommend the relocation, nor was there any intent to interfere with religious practice or sentiment," the statement reads.
Vantara said it will also help set up a new elephant care centre for Madhuri in Kolhapur’s Nandani area. This new place will follow animal care rules and expert advice.
“The proposed facility will be developed in accordance with the established animal welfare guidelines, after consultation with experts from the High-Powered Committee and consensus of the Math, while aligned to international best practices in elephant care," Vantara had said in its statement.
Madhuri, a 36-year-old elephant, had lived at a Jain monastery in Kolhapur since 1992 and was loved by the local community. In 2023, PETA complained that she was sick and badly treated.
A court-appointed team confirmed her health issues, such as arthritis and mental stress. Based on this, the Bombay High Court and the Supreme Court ordered her to move to Vantara in July.
This upset many in Maharashtra, especially the Jain community, who said Madhuri was part of their faith. People protested, called for a boycott of Jio, used hashtags, and wrote letters.

'You're not alone in the darkness': Gambia president urges calm after violent blackout protests
- Published
The Gambia's President Adama Barrow has urged citizens to remain calm over prolonged power cuts, saying the country is not alone in facing an electricity crisis that has affected several parts of West Africa.
His comments follow protests on Monday night in the capital Banjul and surrounding areas over blackouts that residents say have sometimes lasted up to 48 hours.
"When you lie down in the heat and the dark, believe that you are not alone in that darkness," Barrow said, pledging to boost power supplies by next month.
The Gambia supplements its own generation with imported electricity, including supplies from Guinea and neighbouring Senegal.
The tiny West African country has endured persistent blackouts since June, with outages becoming longer and more frequent during the current hot season as soaring temperatures drive up electricity demand.
Frustration boiled over on Monday night, when protesters took to the streets in Banjul and surrounding areas, burning tyres and blocking roads over the prolonged power cuts.
Police used tear gas to disperse crowds in Westfield area as they moved towards the headquarters of the national electricity company, Nawec, with some chanting. "Barrow must go".
Protesters also gathered outside the vice-president's residence in Farato, where banners at an office of Barrow's ruling National People's Party were damaged.
The unrest comes just months before a presidential election expected in December, in which Barrow is seeking a controversial third term.
In a televised address on Tuesday night, Barrow acknowledged the hardship caused by the blackouts but warned protesters against damaging public infrastructure, saying it would only worsen the disruption and divert money towards repairs.
"Let us not destroy in a moment of anger what we suffered so long to gain," he said.
The president admitted there had been shortcomings in the government's planning, power generation and maintenance systems, calling the resulting outages "a national security issue" and an "emergency".
"I know that the fans have stopped turning, children work in the dark, mothers throw away stale food, and the heat is unbearable by day and by night," the president, promising that supplies would improve by the end of October.
He said a new 24-megawatt generating unit was being installed at the Brikama power station and would be commissioned by the end of next month.
A contract has also been awarded for a 50MW solar power plant in Soma, although no completion date was given.
"For a system of our size, this is considerable power, enough to make a big difference in your homes," Barrow added.
The president visited facilities for the national energy utility on Tuesday morning and promised that The Gambia would receive new generators this week.
Gallo Saidy, the Nawec chief, also appealed for patience, saying reduced electricity imports from the regional grid had contributed to the shortages.
He said lower rainfall this year had reduced the electricity available through the regional network.
"We are aware of the frustration and constraints that the Gambian people have," he said. "We are just asking The Gambian people to give us a little bit of time and patience."
Nawec had warned in August that unusually high temperatures had driven a surge in electricity demand, while a technical problem had also affected a major generating unit supplying imported power.

Standing on the roof of her hostel at the National Institute of Sports in Patiala, wushu player Divyanshi Choudhary recorded a video on her Instagram social media profile. The last few posts the 18-year-old had made were all about the excitement she felt as she counted down the days to the Asian Games. She had posted pictures of her kit laid out on her bed, scenes from the send off ceremony of the Indian team in New Delhi a couple of days ago.
In her latest video though, Divyanshi was dejected and teary eyed.
She had just learned that she had been dropped from the squad in the women’s 60kg category and replaced by Roshibina Devi Naorem, whom she had earlier beaten in the selection trials for the Games in Nagoya. Teary-eyed, she alleged she was being unfairly treated.
“I’m tired of this... I have been mentally harassed so much. Since June, July, they have been after me because she (Roshibina) wanted to go. Given that I beat her, why is it a problem for her now,” Divyanshi said in a video message. “I beat her, it’s my right to go there (Japan). She has been knocking at different doors...it’s abuse of power,” Divyanshi said.
Speaking to Sportstar, Divyanshi’s father Sunil said that Divyanshi was only informed of the decision that she was being dropped from the team on Friday morning, that no reason was given for her removal and alleged that the plan was actually to inform when she reached the airport that she would not be flying out with the team. He also questioned the selection of Roshibina Devi – a world medallist, two-time Asian medallist and Arjuna awardee in Divyanshi’s place.
“Divyanshi beat Roshibina in the semifinals of the trials. If the federation had to send someone, they should have sent the individual who Divyanshi beat in the final,” Sunil said.
The allegations were disputed by the Wushu Federation of India. Speaking to Sportstar, Federation president Jitender Bajwa said that the Divyanshi’s name was not removed from the team by them but by the Sports Authority of India (SAI) after it was discovered that she was hiding a knee injury.
“Divyanshi joined the national camp which was organised by SAI a month back. She was carrying a knee injury and was trying to hide it by avoiding training. When SAI eventually found out about this, the replaced her name,” Bajwa said.
Divyanshi’s father Sunil admitted that she had got an injury but stated it was being treated. “After she got an injury, we got Divyanshi checked by a doctor. She had an injury to her ACL (Anterior Cruiciate ligament). The doctor said it could be treated by rehabilitation,” he said.
This too was disputed by Bajwa.
“It was not our call to remove Divyanshi’s name. The coaches in the camp had recommended that Divyanshi be checked for an injury because she was not training. Eventually, the coaches informed SAI which arranged for a medical test which showed she was carrying a knee injury. They couldn’t carry an injured athlete to the Asian Games so they had to remove her name,” he said.
Bajwa added that Divyanshi had been replaced by Roshibina – who had been beaten in the semifinals of the trials and not the finalists -- not because they favoured her but because the losing finalists had also suffered an injury.
“The losing finalist, Himanshi of Chandigarh, suffered a fracture to her jaw which is why her name was not included. Instead the coaches had already recommended the name of Roshibina Devi as the replacement player for Divyanshi,” he said.
Bajwa added that the federation too was disappointed in Divyanshi missing out on the Asian Games. “She is a very talented athlete. She performed very well at the trials. It is bad luck that she will not be going to the Asian Games,” he said.

Uganda’s King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, long the world’s youngest monarch, has been buried among the tombs of his royal forebears as his Tooro kingdom looked to put a bitter succession battle behind it.
Oyo’s appointed successor, the news anchor Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, cast nine coffee berries into the grave at the Karambi Royal Tombs, marking the formal handover of power in the western Ugandan kingdom.
Oyo made global headlines in 1995 when he took the throne at the age of three. Images of the toddler king wearing a crown and royal robes sparked curiosity and adoration around the world.
He died last month at 34 in the United States, where he was receiving treatment for cancer.
Uganda is led by an elected head of state but retains several kingdoms that pre-date the British colonial era and are regarded as bulwarks of traditional identity and heritage.
At a church service before the burial, Oyo, who became a UN goodwill ambassador championing the fight against HIV and Aids, was eulogised as a reserved but jovial young man.
“Although he became king and carried responsibilities far beyond what most people ever experience, he never completely lost the young boy who loved to have fun,” said his sister, Ruth Komuntale.
Royal guards clad in orange shawls then led the hearse carrying Oyo’s casket through the streets of the kingdom’s capital, Fort Portal, to the royal tombs, as thousands of mourners joined the procession on foot.
The burial, which was held 31 years to the day after Oyo’s coronation, followed days of bickering within the notoriously fractious royal family.
A committee consisting of members of the royal clan announced on Wednesday it had chosen Oyo’s cousin, Kijanangoma, a news anchor and editor at state broadcaster UBC, as king.
But the late king’s immediate family said his hitherto unknown son should succeed him, as called for in his will. Oyo never married and was not known to have any children until the kingdom’s prime minister said in the statement announcing his death that he had a son.
Supporters of Kijanangoma’s succession say Oyo’s family has not been able to produce basic information about the purported son.
A source with knowledge of crisis talks over the matter said Ugandan authorities had successfully pushed through Kijanangoma’s succession on Friday. A government spokesperson could not be reached for comment.
The archbishop of the Church of Uganda, Stephen Kaziimba Mugalu, called for unity.
“Words spoken in grief can cause pain, division and conflict,” he told mourners. “It can even destroy the legacy of the king we are mourning.“
Oyo himself took the throne after a protracted succession battle that finished in court.
In addition to his ceremonial responsibilities and campaigning against HIV and Aids, Oyo cultivated close ties with former Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi, whom he named a special adviser to the monarch. Gaddafi donated money towards refurbishment of the royal palace.
The 56-year-old Kijanangoma, who maintained a lower profile as the succession battle played out, has been described by fellow Ugandan journalists as quiet and humble.
Besides the throne, the new king will inherit a considerable royal estate including swathes of land and sizeable cash payouts from the central government.

Donald Trump has said he would “love” to see a united Ireland and that it “may as well happen now”.
The US president appeared to endorse the push for constitutional change on the island at the start of a two-day visit to Ireland on Saturday. The unexpected intervention prompted a swift rebuttal from the UK government and Northern Ireland’s unionist leaders.
“I don’t want to cause any problems, but I will tell you, I’d love to see it unified,” Trump told reporters at joint press conference with the taoiseach, Micheál Martin, in Dublin. “I think it would be a great feather in everybody’s cap if that happened. You know what? The way I look at it, it’s going to happen eventually. It may as well happen now.”
The unification of Northern Ireland with the republic of Ireland would be “fantastic”, Trump said. “The UK will have something to say about it, obviously. But I think it would be a great thing. I mean, how can it be bad?”
The intervention jolted his hosts and came two weeks after Andy Burnham said a referendum on unification was “off the table”, which angered Sinn Féin and other Irish nationalists.
Speaking later on Saturday, Trump acknowledged that his comments on unification, made in response to a reporter’s question, would be controversial. “No matter what you say or how you say it, there’s no good answer,” he said. “I gave a nice answer, I think. We’ll worry about it tomorrow.” Unification, he added, would be a “very cool thing”.
A Downing Street spokesperson said the prime minister still believed there was not the required support for unification to trigger a referendum, as set out in the Good Friday agreement.
Gavin Robinson, the Democratic Unionist party (DUP) leader, said Northern Ireland’s constitutional future would be decided by its people, not by commentary in London, Dublin or Washington.
“Northern Ireland is part of the United Kingdom because that is the settled democratic will of its people. I am confident Northern Ireland will continue to choose the UK and the security it offers. As unionists we are not interested in the destruction of our country by joining with the Irish republic.”
Colum Eastwood, an MP and former leader of the Social Democratic and Labour party (SDLP), and frequent critic of Trump, posted a clip of the president’s remarks on social media and wrote: “Always liked him.”
The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, said: “President Trump is shooting from the hip as usual, just like he did with Greenland and Canada becoming the 51st state. This sort of loose talk about the future of democratic countries is deeply unhelpful and creates unnecessary tension.”
Trump’s comments strayed from predecessors who sought to keep the White House neutral on Ireland’s constitutional future, but the off-the-cuff nature of the remarks suggested there was no change in US policy.
Trump’s unofficial visit is centred on golf – he flew on Saturday afternoon to his resort in Doonbeg, County Clare, which is hosting the Irish Open – but started with a courtesy call in Dublin to Áras an Uachtaráin, the official residence and workplace of the Irish president, Catherine Connolly.
Before her election to the ceremonial post last year, Connolly called Trump a bully and criticised his policies in Gaza and Iran. Their brief encounter, behind closed doors, appeared to go smoothly despite a coded critique of White House policies.
Connolly said in a statement afterwards that she “conveyed the strong view of the Irish people that the normalisation of war and genocide can never be accepted” and stressed the importance of the United Nations – an organisation Trump has disparaged. Trump said they had a wide-ranging discussion, including about energy and water, and that Connolly was “terrific”.
Trump held a separate meeting with Martin at the Phoenix Park, where he told the press that Iran would seek peace after the US midterm elections and repeated his claim that his war had prevented Tehran obtaining a nuclear weapon.
Asked about protests against his visit – a large crowd was expected in central Dublin, 5 miles away, as well as at Doonbeg – the president said he had not seen any protests.
Addressing guests as at the US ambassador’s residence, Trump assailed US Democrats as extremists and criticised Europe’s approach to immigration.
He lauded US-Irish relations but reiterated a complaint about the American pharma giants in Ireland. “You took all our medical companies, we’ve got to get a couple of them back. You fleeced us but that’s OK. There’s a lot of room to go around and our relationship with you is fantastic.”
As he left Dublin a crowd at the Garden of Remembrance waved banners and chanted: “Donald Trump, can you hear? We don’t want you here.”
Trump is expected to stay overnight in Doonbeg and present the Irish Open trophy before returning to Washington on Sunday.

Srinagar, Sep 12: Srinagar Lok Sabha Member of Parliament, Aga Ruhullah Mehdi, expressed solidarity with the protesting veterinary interns at the Sher-e-Kashmir University of Agricultural Sciences and Technology - Kashmir (SKUAST-K), Shuhama campus.

India calls for local currency trade among BRICS to enhance economic resilience
External Affairs Minister Jaishankar emphasized self-reliance amid global economic challenges.
India on Friday urged Brics nations to create a predictable business environment, build resilient supply chains and link their payment systems to allow trade in local currencies, as Russia proposed a Brics grain exchange to strengthen food security across the bloc.
Delivering the keynote address at the Brics Business Forum, external affairs minister S Jaishankar said India’s chairship was focused on resilience, innovation, cooperation and sustainability. “We meet at a time when [the] global political and economic order is under churn. Volatility, uncertainty, and complexity have become defining features of the world around us. We are witnessing the economic consequences of geopolitical conflicts, of pandemics, and of climate-related disruptions,” he said.
Jaishankar called for “greater self-reliance” within Brics to strengthen economic security. “The objective is to strengthen our ability to absorb shocks while remaining connected and competitive,” he said, listing genuine market practices, dependable logistics, a predictable business environment, diversified commercial relationships and transparent trade and investment as priorities. Energy systems capable of coping with disruption, and transition pathways suited to different national circumstances, were also needed, he added, citing digital public infrastructure (DPI), artificial intelligence, fintech and advanced manufacturing as areas of major opportunity.

I don’t know about you, but whenever I go to see my primary care doctor, my mental health isn’t usually at the top of my list of things to talk about. But it should be. In fact, experts say that all of us could benefit from more candid conversations with our doctors about our mental health.
How — and why — to tell your doctor you’re feeling depressed
Your doctor can be your mental health ally. Here’s how to talk about it.
(This story discusses mental health issues and suicide. If you or someone you know is struggling or in crisis, help is available. You are not alone. You can call the national 988 hotline for support.)
For years, the United States has been trying to figure out “parity” for mental health care — to have it treated and paid for like any other medical need, not something that is carved out and separate. A big part of that has been pushing primary care doctors and OB/GYNs to do more screenings, to make your mental state a part of your well-being that you discuss with your doctor the same as your blood pressure or any physical ailment.
But that is easier said than done. A lot of people may not even realize that their depression or anxiety or stress is something they should talk about with their primary care doctor. Others might fear being judged, and for good reason — national policymakers warn there continues to be a stigma toward mental health conditions among doctors.
About one in three Americans say they have never been asked about their mental health by a doctor, which is unsettling considering that the nation has been going through a collective mental health crisis for several years. Men are significantly less likely to be asked about their mental health than women — perhaps a reflection of a culture that expects men to “tough it out” when it comes to their feelings. But those attitudes come with a price: Men are diagnosed with depression at half the rate as women, but die by suicide much more frequently.
Much of the burden for starting these conversations should fall on your doctor to be more curious and accommodating during annual exams. But you don’t have to wait to be asked to bring it up. Regularly talking to your provider about your mental health is the best way to get ahead of any problems and get treated if you need to be. In honor of Suicide Prevention Month, I reached out to a handful of doctors who have studied why it’s sometimes so hard for patients and doctors to talk about depression, anxiety, and stress — and learned some novel strategies for how you can take charge, push through any stigma, and start having more honest talks with your doctor about your state of mind. Here’s what you should know.
Know the relevant symptoms before you talk to your doctor
One of the tricky things about depression or any serious mental health problem is that it isn’t always easy to identify when you’re the one experiencing it. “Patients need to recognize their distress…as potentially emanating from depression,” Dr. Richard Kravitz, a general medicine professor at UC Davis who has studied depression screening in primary care, told me.
There is a checklist of sorts that you can go through on your own to understand whether you’re just having a tough couple of days or there’s something more serious at work, said Dr. Maria Garcia, an internal medicine physician at UC San Francisco. You might be feeling down or unmotivated or have a lack of energy, or be more agitated, angry, or irritable than usual. Sometimes there are less obvious signs, like trouble with money or problems at work.
Symptoms of depression
Here are some of the possible signs of depression, according to the Mayo Clinic. If you or someone you know is struggling or in crisis, help is available. You can call the national 988 hotline for support.
- Feeling sad or hopeless or like you are a burden to others
- Feeling more irritable and angry than usual, losing your temper more easily
- Losing interest in most or all normal day-to-day activities and hobbies
- Sleep problems, whether you are sleeping too little or too much
- Feeling less energetic than usual
- Changes in appetite — whether you are eating less and losing weight or eating more and gaining weight
- Concentration and memory problems
- Unexplained physical symptoms
“If you’re not getting enjoyment from your normal hobbies or talking to the people that you would normally really enjoy talking to, if you find yourself isolating from people that you normally really enjoy spending time with, I think those are certainly triggers,” she said. Consider the duration of your symptoms, too: “If it’s every day for a couple of weeks, that definitely isn’t normal.”
And oftentimes, depression symptoms can mirror symptoms of other ailments or problems, like a lack of sleep, low appetite, or physical aches and pains. This is one reason why it is so important to talk with your doctor about it, Garcia said. Is that fatigue a result of depression — or is it a problem with your thyroid? Your primary care physician is best positioned to help you figure that out. One of the benefits of a long-term relationship with a physician is that they may be able to help you recognize symptoms of depression even if they aren’t obvious to you.
It’s hard to be that self-aware; I’m certainly not all the time. But the more you pay attention to your mood and how it’s affecting your life, the more you can tell your doctor about what’s really going on. You don’t have to know all the fancy clinical terms, said Paul Duberstein, a clinical psychologist and professor of health behavior, society, and policy at the Rutgers School of Public Health. “The language that people are most comfortable using are words like stress or frustrated or impatient or something like that,” Duberstein told me. “Those are the kinds of things we really do want to incentivize and encourage people to talk to their doctors about.”
How to bring up your mental health with your doctor
Okay, you feel like something might be off and you have a doctor’s appointment coming up. What do you do?
You might not have to do anything. These days, you are likely to be given a depression screening by your physician’s office before you ever arrive (usually as part of your pre-visit paperwork). Garcia said it’s important to be honest and to be thorough when answering those questions, as that will tell your doctor that your mental health should be a focus for your upcoming visit.
Our political wellness landscape has shifted: new leaders, shady science, contradictory advice, broken trust, and overwhelming systems. How is anyone supposed to make sense of it all? Vox’s senior correspondent Dylan Scott has been on the health beat for a long time, and every week, he’ll wade into sticky debates, answer fair questions, and contextualize what’s happening in American healthcare policy. Sign up here.
But if you aren’t proactively screened for depression and you have some of the symptoms described above or you just have a hunch that something might be wrong, try to alert your doctor in advance that your mental health is something you want to talk about. If that’s not possible, tell your doctor early on in the appointment that your mental state is something you want to discuss. Garcia said that, rightly or wrongly, doctors can sometimes be reluctant to dive deep into a discussion about mental health late into a visit; they only have so much time with individual patients, and they might balk at trying to squeeze in a mental health discussion at the end. The conversation is more likely to be productive if you proactively start it before your physician is sidetracked with your blood sugar.
During this conversation, you can ask for a depression screening outright. Doctors have become adept at recognizing code words; if you say your mood has been off, they may pick up the signal that you may be experiencing mental health struggles. But there is a good argument for being very direct about how you’re feeling, Kravitz said.
“My advice…is just simply to say to the doctor, ‘I’ve been feeling down’ or ‘I’ve been feeling irritable’ or ‘I’ve been losing sleep’ or ‘Something’s wrong and I don’t know what it is. Do you think it might be depression?’ Just ask,” Kravitz said. If you aren’t sure if it’s a mental or physical issue, tell them that. Activate your doctor’s curiosity, Kravitz told me. Get them invested in figuring out what’s going on with you.
Once the conversation starts, your doctor is likely to ask how long you have been experiencing symptoms and how they are affecting your day-to-day function. When that happens, you should be as thorough and truthful as possible.
“Is it affecting your ability to take care of your family? Is it affecting your ability to go to work, get up in the morning, cook dinner, get out of the house, go grocery shopping?” Garcia said. “Those things are really helpful because then we can tailor the treatments for the amount of functional impairment.”
Talk to your doctor about your sleep, too, Duberstein said. Not only is it an important indicator of your physical health, but it will also tell your doctor something about your mental well-being. And it doesn’t require any special emotional vocabulary: You probably know if you’re sleeping well or not.
“If you think about major depression as a collection of, say, nine symptoms and you ask, ‘Well, what symptoms appear first? Is it the depressed mood? Or the difficulty concentrating?’ The first thing that appears typically is sleep,” Duberstein told me. “Disrupted sleep is something that I think people do feel comfortable talking with their doctor about.”
How to talk to your doctor about a treatment plan
If you have a productive conversation with your doctor and they recognize symptoms of depression, they’ll want to establish a treatment plan. This has historically been another barrier to honest conversations between doctors and patients about mental health: Patients don’t want to be prescribed antidepressants or referred to therapy, so they don’t bring it up.
But ignoring your symptoms is, of course, not the solution. Instead, use your appointment as an opportunity to ask all of your questions to make sure that you are fully comfortable with the doctor’s proposed treatment plan and can get on the road to better mental health.
Many Americans have doubts about antidepressants, which have been egged on by high-profile figures like US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. If you’re hesitant to take meds, you should tell your provider about the things that you’ve heard that give you pause, the negative experiences people have shared, or whatever major questions or concerns you have. They can help you understand the very real trade-offs that come with taking an antidepressant, Kravitz said. Your doctor can also debunk some of the misconceptions that make people hesitant to take these drugs even when they are struggling.
“The duration of therapy sometimes surprises people. But no, it doesn’t mean that you’ll have to be on it forever. No, most people don’t have serious withdrawal symptoms. Those can usually be managed by careful tapering if necessary and so on,” Kravitz said. He said you can ask your doctor outright: “What can I expect to happen over time? How long will I need to be on this?”
If you’d rather not go on medication immediately, that’s totally valid. Your doctor may instead be able to help you find a therapist with a referral, Duberstein said. Therapists have historically been hard to find in the US — but one positive outcome of the pandemic was the proliferation of online mental health services.
“I think it’s important for the public to know that one of the major barriers to getting into psychotherapy or even seeing a therapist — like getting into your car, driving, finding a bus, finding a subway, whatever — that those barriers are gone,” he told me. “Because you could see a therapist online now in all 50 states.”
The goal is that you leave your doctor’s office feeling heard and feeling on-board with the approach, even if you still have some trepidation (which is very common). And if you don’t feel comfortable talking to your doctor about these issues, that may be a sign you need to find a new provider whom you feel you can trust with those sensitive discussions, Duberstein said.
The point is, your doctor should be your ally in pursuing whatever treatment you need for whatever ails for your mental health. Nobody has to go through it alone.

It is unclear whether TMZ's photos of Matthews with an enlarged chin and jawline and bulging muscles are authentic, meaning not generated or edited using artificial intelligence software. However, Matthews later told the outlet his look in the pictures was a result of prosthetics for an ad campaign, not plastic surgery.
In early September 2026, alleged photos circulated online purportedly showing former NFL linebacker Clay Matthews after extensive plastic surgery.
One X user who shared the images, which showed Matthews with an enlarged chin and jawline, bulging arm and leg muscles and loading bags into a car, wrote (archived): "TRENDING: Packers legend Clay Matthews was spotted out grabbing groceries, looking VERY different after getting some work done. An absolutely shocking transformation."
(X)
The pictures, originally published by celebrity magazine TMZ, also circulated on Facebook, Instagram and Reddit, where social media users discussed whether they were real.
It is unclear whether TMZ's images of Matthews are authentic, meaning not generated or edited using artificial intelligence software. Pangram, a highly regarded artificial intelligence detector, determined that several images from TMZ's gallery were "fully AI." Such tools are fallible though and should not be entirely relied upon for answers to media's authenticity.
Regardless, TMZ's images do not show Matthews after plastic surgery. Therefore, we rate this claim false.
The outlet reported on Sept. 9, 2026 (archived), that Matthews had prosthetics fitted for an ad campaign for a sports betting platform that created the look seen in TMZ's pictures. That sports betting platform sponsored that TMZ article. It was not possible to independently confirm whether the outlet's images of Matthews were staged as part of the platform's advertising campaign. Snopes contacted TMZ to ask about the authenticity of its images and await a reply.
The TMZ article features a video of Matthews saying it took four hours to fit the prosthetics, which another video (archived) posted to the former Green Bay Packers linebacker's Facebook page shows also included his calves. The sports betting platform Matthews advertised for when he wore the prosthetics also posted a video on X (archived) that shows them being fitted to the former NFL star's face.
Given that Matthews did wear the prosthetics in question, it is likely that TMZ's images of him are authentic.
The prosthetics' cartoonishly enlarged jawline and muscles played on the "looksmaxxing" trend that the Merriam-Webster dictionary defines as "efforts, sometimes extreme, young men take to look more attractive."

New 108 ambulance fleet to hit Keralam roads by month-end: Health Minister
Thiruvananthapuram, A new fleet of 108 ambulances will hit the roads across Keralam by the end of this month, Health Minister K Muraleedharan said on Saturday.
As many as 335 ambulances are being deployed across the state and are currently being fitted with essential life-saving equipment in Thiruvananthapuram.
The new fleet is expected to replace the ageing fleet of 108 ambulances.
Speaking to reporters, Muraleedharan said the ambulances would be released once the final clearance was received.
He said the state government had completed all procedures related to their registration.
"In any case, it will be rolled out on the roads this month itself. There is no doubt about that," he said.
The minister alleged that lapses on the part of the agency operating the ambulance service had caused delays in releasing the vehicles.
He also said some drivers' associations were protesting against the agency and that the matter had to be resolved between the two sides.
"One thing has been made clear: strict action will be taken by the government against anyone who blocks vehicles carrying patients. Protests should not be staged by stopping 108 ambulances. The government will put mechanisms in place to ensure they remain operational," he said.
Muraleedharan said the government had no role in resolving disputes between 108 ambulance drivers and the company operating the service.
The ambulance drivers' associations have announced a protest from September 17 against the operating agency over issues related to the disbursement of salary bonuses.
The minister said a recent incident was reported in which a driver was unavailable to operate a 108 ambulance, and an alternative arrangement had to be made.
"None of this means any organisation will be allowed to disrupt the operation of 108 ambulances, regardless of which party they belong to," he said.
The 108 ambulance service is operated under the supervision of the Kerala Medical Services Corporation Limited .
The new fleet comprises 315 basic life support ambulances, 14 advanced life support units equipped with ventilators and six specialised neonatal ambulances for newborn care, officials said.
The ambulance service is available by dialling 108 across Keralam.

Thousands of patients in India are diagnosed with melanoma, a type of skin cancer, each year. While melanoma is far less common here than in Western populations, it is far from rare and the way it presents in our patient population makes it uniquely difficult to detect early. Too many patients come to us when the disease is already advanced, precisely at a time when treatment options have never been more powerful or more personalised. This contrast between available therapies and the stage at which patients are diagnosed defines one of the most pressing challenges in melanoma care in India today.
Why melanoma gets missed
The warning signs most people associate with skin cancer come from research developed for fairer-skinned populations, where melanoma tends to appear on sun-exposed areas as an irregular or darkening mole. That picture does not reflect what clinicians see in India.
Melanoma here, most commonly presents on the soles of the feet or beneath the nails, sites that are rarely examined and even more rarely associated with cancer. This condition is called acral lentiginous melanoma, a subtype that accounts for 35 to 60% of cases in dark-skinned individuals. Such lesions are frequently mistaken for bruises, fungal infections, or diabetic ulcers, and by the time a biopsy is taken, the disease has often progressed.
Mucosal melanomas, a rare type of cancer that starts in the mucous membranes, are highly aggressive with a very low chance of recovery and produce few early warning signs. Most are diagnosed only after spread has occurred.
Any pigmented lesion that changes or persists, wherever it appears on the body, deserves investigation rather than reassurance.
A decade of transformation
When I began my oncology career, managing advanced melanoma meant offering patients limited and rarely durable options. That has fortunately changed significantly.
The foundational shift came from James Allison and Tasuku Honjo, whose discoveries on CTLA-4 and PD-1 earned them the 2018 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Their research established the principle of immune-checkpoint blockade: rather than attacking a tumour directly, we can sometimes release the biological brakes that stop the patient’s own immune system from doing so. The results can be extraordinary. Former U.S. President Jimmy Carter was diagnosed at 91 with melanoma that had spread to his liver and brain. Surgical resection of liver disease, stereotactic radiation for the brain, and immunotherapy with the checkpoint inhibitor pembrolizumab produced a durable remission, and he lived to 100.
Precision medicine has reshaped the approach in parallel. Some melanomas carry specific mutations, particularly in the BRAF pathway, that can be directly targeted with molecularly designed therapies. This is where next-generation sequencing, or NGS, becomes critical. In simple terms, it reads the genetic blueprint of a patient’s tumour and identifies the alterations that should guide treatment, turning what was once a single clinical decision into a detailed, individualised process.
The melanoma story is not over; it is only becoming more exciting. TIL therapy takes tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes, expands them in the laboratory, and reinfuses them in far greater numbers, a step toward truly personalised cellular treatment. In August 2026, intismeran, a personalised mRNA vaccine built from the patient’s own tumour sequence, was combined with pembrolizumab in high-risk melanoma patients after surgery. The results were striking: a significant reduction in recurrence compared with pembrolizumab alone, making it the first positive late-stage trial of a personalised mRNA cancer vaccine, though survival data remain pending.
What still needs to change
All of these advances deliver their best results when treatment begins early. The more sophisticated our therapies become, the more clearly we see that they work best before the disease has spread. In India, awareness and referral gaps continue to push diagnosis toward advanced stages.
Recalibrating public health messaging to reflect how melanoma actually presents in Indian patients is a start. Faster pathways from primary care to specialist centres matter equally. More fundamentally, India needs a national melanoma registry, stronger epidemiological and genomic data, more clinical trials in Indian patients, and deeper international collaboration. The advances of the past decade are genuinely extraordinary. Whether they reach the patients who need them comes down to one thing: a diagnosis early enough to act on.
(Prof. Jyoti Bajpai is director – medical precision immuno-oncology, Apollo Hospitals, Mumbai & Western Zone. drjyoti_ba@apollohospitals.com)

“‘Does Trump cheat?’ I can’t cheat”: President on Secret Service stopping him from cheating at golf
‘It’s not that I wouldn’t cheat,’ Trump told business leaders gathered in Dublin on Saturday
President Donald Trump said the Secret Service agents assigned to protect him make it impossible for him to cheat at golf.
The Republican president made the remark Saturday during an address at the U.S. Embassy in Dublin, before attending the Irish Open, a professional golf tournament.
“I was with the head of the biggest company in the world and we’re playing golf and we have, you know, like all these things going around and we had hundreds of Secret Service all over the course,” Trump told business leaders gathered at the ambassador’s residence.
“In fact, they said, ‘Does Trump cheat?’ I can’t cheat,” he said. “You have 250 Secret Service agents running down.”
“It’s not that I wouldn’t cheat,” the 80-year-old president said, drawing laughter from the crowd. “But you can’t move the ball. I don’t know if they play or not but they know you’re not supposed to be moving the ball around, okay?”
Trump, an avid golfer, has long faced accusations that he bends the rules on the course.
Sportswriter Rick Reilly devoted a 2019 book to the subject titled Commander in Cheat: How Golf Explains Trump.
“Trump doesn’t just cheat at golf,” Reilly wrote in the book. “He throws it, boots it, and moves it. He lies about his lies. He fudges and foozles and fluffs. At Winged Foot, where Trump is a member, the caddies got so used to seeing him kick his ball back onto the fairway they came up with a nickname for him: ‘Pele.’”
Lindsey Graham, Trump’s longtime ally and the late South Carolina senator, also reportedly suggested that Trump did not always follow the rules.
“Some people say you may outdrive him, but you’re not going to outdrive his caddy. It is what it is,” Graham said during a 2022 grand jury appearance in Georgia, according to testimony transcripts obtained by The New York Times.
Trump, for his part, has denied cheating at golf.
In 2016, after former boxer Oscar De La Hoya accused him of foul play, Trump replied: “Not only didn't I cheat, I didn't play with him…I have never played a round of golf with this guy.”
“He's absolutely lying,” Trump added. “Golf is an important thing and I felt I had to say something.”

Queiroz returns as Ghana head coach
- Published
Carlos Queiroz has been reappointed as head coach of Ghana's men's national team.
The 73-year-old, who had two spells as assistant manager at Manchester United under Sir Alex Ferguson, took charge of the Black Stars in April and led the side to the last 32 at this year's Fifa World Cup, where they were beaten 1-0 by Colombia.
Queiroz appeared to announce his own departure on social media shortly after that defeat, but the Ghana Football Association (GFA) has decided to re-engage him for another spell in charge following internal discussions.
The GFA has not announced the length of his new deal but said he will prepare the team for "a successful new phase on the international stage".
"The GFA believes Queiroz's extensive international experience, technical expertise and knowledge of the Black Stars position him strongly to lead the team into this next chapter," a statement added.
Queiroz has previously led Iran, Portugal and Egypt at major tournaments and has had stints in charge of South Africa, Colombia and Qatar.
Further details on his mandate will be announced by the GFA in due course.
Queiroz said the chance to continue in the role gave him "immense pride and honour".
"Serving Ghana is far more than coaching a football team," he added in a post on Instagram.
"It is a privilege, a responsibility and a mission to honour one of Africa's greatest football nations and its incredible and passionate football people.
"Our ambition is clear: improve every day, unite the nation, make Ghana stronger and fight for every victory with passion, humility and pride. The mission continues."
Queiroz will begin his second spell in charge of the West Africans with qualifiers for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations, which begin later this month.
The Black Stars are yet to announce the dates and venues for their first two fixtures in Group C, where they have been drawn alongside Ivory Coast, The Gambia and Somalia.

20 December 2024 was a crucial moment for Luxembourg in supporting WHO and strengthening global public health, to make progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals in 2025–2028. A Strategic Partnership Framework (SPF) with the Ministry of Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Affairs was signed amounting to €46.5 million – the largest-ever agreement WHO has had with Luxembourg. Furthermore, the first-ever multiyear agreement with the Ministry of Health and Social Safety €1 million was launched, as the country’s first voluntary contribution to WHO.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General greets with Luxembourg's Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety and Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. © MAE Luxembourg
“From now till 2028, this contribution will help finance priority areas in Luxembourg’s collaboration with WHO” said Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety during the bilateral meeting, “notably for sanitary crisis preparedness and response and the fight against health inequalities, with a special focus on gender.”
The amount of €46.5 million contains fully flexible and thematic funding, and allocations for the Universal Health Coverage Partnership, tropical disease research and polio eradication. The fully flexible funding enables WHO to allocate the money to the areas of highest need.
“By signing two new partnership agreements, we have reaffirmed Luxembourg's continued support for the WHO and its mission,” said Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. “This reflects our strong commitment to promoting global health and multilateralism. We launch these agreements with WHO because we believe the best way to avoid is to prevent.”
To support the achievement of WHO’s priorities, the strategic partnership framework with Luxembourg includes support for WHO’s core work to develop, deliver and implement high-quality technical products – the guidelines, norms and standards on which many countries rely.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General, remarked how symbolic it was that the agreements were signed on the International Day of Solidarity. They are “a strong statement of solidarity by Luxembourg, not just with WHO, but with the people of the world”, said Dr Tedros.
Xavier Bettel, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus and Martine Deprez at the signing ceremony. © MAE Luxembourg
WHO and Luxembourg continue their historical strategic partnership, collaborating to fulfill a shared mission to promote, provide and protect health.
