Searchlight Pictures boss Matthew Greenfield broke down how YouTube has become fertile ground for finding new stories and filmmakers. The Searchlight Pictures boss also spoke about the battle with familiarity and the need for original ideas to get people into movie theaters in the streaming age.
After Obsession and Backrooms, studios and producers are scouring YouTube for the next big property originating on the Google-owned video sharing platform.
“YouTube is an incredible resource, and we’re always looking for new storytellers,” Greenfield said.
“One of the things that’s super exciting about [YouTube] is that it used to be that we would find, collectively in the industry, new talent from short films, from first features, from short stories. But all of those had to go through gatekeepers in one form or another.
Watch on Deadline
“With YouTube, obviously, people can go direct and find and build their own audience. And we can find things that wouldn’t have come through the standard [avenues]. So, for sure, it’s an exciting place to find new talent.”
Greenfield was speaking at TIFF: The Market, the Toronto Film Festival’s shiny new film and TV market, which also has a conference strand to take the temperature of the industry.
The Searchlight exec talked about there being a battle with familiarity that needs to be waged to get people into theaters. “Familiarity is the challenge that we have to battle against,” he said. “How do we tell stories that feel new, that feel fresh, that feel interesting, that feel worthy of a theatrical experience?”
He continued: “Everybody has to decide every time they go to a movie: should I pay X dollars, make a real effort, get out of the house, travel, pay to see a movie in the theater, which is a great experience if you’re seeing something you love. Or, should I stay at home and watch everything that has ever been made in the history of human culture?”
Greenfield was speaking at a live recording of industry podcast The Town.

Benn defies concerns to make weight for Garcia bout
- Published
Conor Benn and Ryan Garcia both comfortably made the welterweight limit for their WBC title fight despite concerns at how they would fare on the scales.
Briton Benn, 29, weighed in at 10st 6lb (66kg) for Saturday's bout - half a pound heavier than the champion.
The official weigh-in took place behind closed doors at the UFC Apex on Friday, in front of about 50 members of the media, before a ceremonial event later in the day which will be open to the public.
Garcia has won 25 of his 28 professional contests, including 20 knockout victories, with two defeats and one no-contest. Benn has 25 wins - 14 by knockout - and one loss, and is fighting for his first world title.
American Garcia, 28, won the WBC belt with a dominant points victory over Mario Barrios in February and is making his first defence against Benn.
- Eggs, insults & a champion with a fake beard - Garcia and Benn face off 
  - Published18 hours ago
- Why Nigel Benn can't walk away from Conor 
  - Published22 hours ago
- Benn does not deserve world title shot - Garcia 
  - Published1 day ago
How did they look?
Much of the build-up this week has centred on how Benn would cope with returning to the 10st 7lb welterweight limit for the first time in more than four years.
His two fights against Chris Eubank Jr were both at middleweight, with Benn weighing 11st 2lb (71kg) for the first and 11st 5lb (72kg) for the rematch. For his win over Regis Prograis in April, Benn weighed 10st 10lb (69kg).
He has already said he will vacate the title and move back up in weight if he beats Garcia.
Benn had looked increasingly gaunt and drawn during fight week and told BBC Sport the cut had taken him to the "pits of hell".
But Benn smiled as his weight was announced and looked in good shape, surprising several observers who had expected the effects of the cut to be far more visible.
A handful of undercard fighters weighed in after Benn while Garcia was still nowhere to be seen, prompting questions about whether the Californian was having difficulties making the limit.
Garcia has had problems on the scales before. He weighed more than three pounds over the light-welterweight limit before his fight against Devin Haney in 2024.
There was no such drama this time. Garcia sprinted towards the scales about 10 minutes after Benn and also looked at ease as he comfortably made weight.
Why does the weight matter?
The weight is particularly significant because of the contrasting styles.
Benn relies heavily on aggression, explosiveness and sustained pressure, while Garcia is a fast and dangerous counter-puncher who is comfortable catching opponents as they come forward.
Any draining effects of the cut could therefore leave Benn more vulnerable to Garcia's speed and powerful left hook, while also raising questions over whether the Briton can maintain his usual intensity over 12 rounds.
With no rehydration clause in place, Benn said he could weigh as much as 12st 7lb (80kg) by the time he steps into the ring on Saturday.
He is still an underdog against Garcia - a fighter with greater amateur pedigree and a more accomplished professional resume - but Benn's size and physical pressure could become one of his biggest advantages.

Rockstar Games’ best-selling Grand Theft Auto series wasn’t often accused of political sensitivity during its legendary run from the late 1990s through the early 2010s.
In fact, parents and activists denounced the franchise for exposing children to a seedy world of sex, violence, crude humor, and wanton crime. Elon Musk even claimed that he couldn’t get into the last installment, GTA V, because he was mortified to play as a character who shoots police officers.
But times (and moral panics) change. In the 13 years that fans have waited for Grand Theft Auto VI—finally out on November 19—the American right-wing grievance machine has drifted from fears of impressionable kids turning to a life of larceny to concerns that they will grow up “woke.” And despite knowing very little about the forthcoming game, the agitators of the latter movement have decided it must amount to a stealth campaign to poison the youth with depictions of gender equality, LGBTQ acceptance, and racial diversity. (Rockstar did not immediately return a request for comment.)
Since the height of Gamergate in 2014, an angst-ridden subset of male gamers have maintained a paranoid vigil against what they see as the creeping influence of women and LGBTQ developers in the gaming world. Between the feverish anticipation for GTA VI and the various delays of its release date, they’ve had ample opportunity to foment a preemptive backlash to what is sure to be a massive hit, not unlike the failed furor over supposedly “woke” elements of Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey.
“GTA 6 is a humiliation ritual for all male gamers,” an X user with the handle @Wokenessisevil complained on Tuesday, sharing a clip of the game’s two lead characters, Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, who are in a relationship that evolves based on the player’s choices. In the scene, Lucia, the series’ first mandatory female protagonist, asks Jason to pick an outfit for her and expresses mild annoyance when he seems more or less indifferent to the options she presents.
It’s an exchange that could have been lifted from any sitcom of the past 50 years, yet it seems to have fueled a reactionary narrative about the game’s male protagonist being subjugated to a nefarious feminist agenda. Another X user recently claimed, contrary to the clip’s bog-standard depiction of a heterosexual couple, that Jason has a “gay vibe,” since no straight man would know what sequins are or use the word “cocktails,” as he does in the clip.
“The script is definitely written by a woman who has no clue what a man thinks or how he talks,” they wrote. “Jason is written as a caricature, much like what a delusional woman thinks a ‘man’ should be.”
Similarly, a gaming YouTuber seethed that Rockstar was appealing to women and gay men by showing Jason shirtless in another scene. “Gone are the days of edgy based masculine GTA games,” he wrote on X. “I could be wrong but right now it’s looking like it will be a woke fest.”
While multiple leaks and a 27-minute “extended look” preview on Netflix have revealed key details of the game, and Rockstar creatives declared their intent to realistically portray the diversity of the Miami-inspired setting and bring a fleshed-out female character into the spotlight, would-be detractors are still straining a bit for reasons to pronounce it dead on arrival. One YouTuber has convinced himself that it will subliminally brainwash players with “bisexual lighting.”
Other men have simply defaulted to rank sexism, griping that Lucia’s breasts are too small because of “they/thems” working at Rockstar or posting jokes such as: “female lead in GTA 6? i thought the whole point of GTA was to be able to drive.” An AI enthusiast used an image generator to replace a woman of color in a crop top on the game’s cover with a white blonde in a bikini.
While each new snippet of content has become grist for more manufactured outrage, the tantrums over the ideological trajectory of GTA began long ago. In 2022, for its remastered version of GTA V, Rockstar removed a number of gags and non-playable characters that critics had described as transphobic, leading to complaints from some fans.
The following year, after the game publisher released a trailer for GTA VI, trolls floated the groundless theory that the Lucia character was a transgender woman. Last month, when former video game executive Mark Kern, known for his crusades against “woke” content, deemed Lucia attractive, his followers disagreed in openly racist and misogynistic replies.
Much of this ire is aimed directly at the Rockstar team, who have been blasted for allegedly embracing “identity politics,” reportedly making efforts to avoid punching down against marginalized groups in the game’s storyline, and allowing women to contribute in any way to the franchise. A photo of female staff at the company’s studio in Scotland, shared on social media in 2019 to commemorate International Women’s Day, has circulated widely with sneering comments about how they likely ruined GTA VI.
Yet a few prominent streamers on the right, including Zack Hoyt (better known as Asmongold) and white nationalist Nick Fuentes, have taken a wait-and-see approach, declining to bash the game before checking it out for themselves. Fuentes went so far as to mock those bemoaning its creative direction. “Just go outside, touch grass,” he told one viewer who brought up the topic in his live chat.
If any of these gamers entertain fantasies of an actual boycott or commercial failure, they are bound to be disappointed. According to one estimate of preorders from a third-party data analytics firm, Rockstar has already sold 5.28 million copies of GTA VI, taking in more than $500 million in revenue. Though it is likely the most expensive game ever made, with a budget somewhere north of a billion dollars, the studio stands to easily recoup that cost, possibly by the day it comes out.
That might call for a moment of reflection from the culture warriors—or so you’d think. It’s awfully difficult, it seems, to admit that you’re so out of touch with the mainstream and have no control over the popularity of various media. They will no doubt have their objections to other aspects of the game, but once GTA VI starts breaking records, there won’t be any point in continuing the crusade. By then, the next fake controversy will be on the horizon.

Harleen Deol is raring to go for the newest opportunity in her career: Women’s Caribbean Premier League (WCPL).
The India international became the fifth Indian to join the ongoing edition after a last-minute move saw her sign for defending champion Barbados Tridents.
She’ll share the dressing room with pace-bowling all-rounder Pooja Vastrakar and big-hitter Kiran Navgire. Meanwhile, wicketkeeper-batter Yastika Bhatia and pace ace Shikha Pandey have been drafted by the Trinbago Knight Riders.
“It’s been amazing. I’ve just attended one practice session, and then we went on a cruise for a team bonding activity. That was a really nice experience,” Harleen, for whom this is a maiden international franchise stint, told reporters on Friday.
The 28-year-old has been part of the Women’s Premier League since its inaugural edition in 2023, representing Gujarat Giants for three seasons. Most recently, she played for the UP Warriorz. She has amassed 653 runs in 28 innings overall, striking at 116.19.
“Shashank Shekhar Tapikar (Cricket Operations, Barbados Tridents) sir had approached me and asked whether I wanted to play in WCPL. I said ‘why not’. It’d be a different experience, different wickets, and different people. Franchise cricket is a bit different but it’s good for learning,” the 28-year-old batter revealed.
Harleen was part of India’s 2025 ODI World Cup-winning squad and travelled to England for the historic first-ever women’s Test at Lord’s, although she didn’t feature in the four-day fixture.
However, the Punjab player did not make the T20 World Cup 2026, Asia Cup, and the Asian Games squads. The last time she played a T20I for India was last December. Moreover, she was also left out of the India A squads for the ongoing multi-format home series against the visiting Australians after captaining One-Day A squad during the England tour in May. India won the 50-over leg 2-1, with Harleen registering a half century in the opening fixture too.
Missing out on action with the Indian setup, at A or senior level, doesn’t bother her.
“I don’t think a lot about these things. Wherever I am, it’s the same cricket that is to be played. I just want to play and enjoy, and give my best wherever I’m playing,” she explained.
“I don’t think as a player you change a lot in your technique. Yes, you can watch someone and learn something from them. But I don’t think you can change your technique through this method. I have not changed too much,” she said when asked whether she would use this WCPL stint to better her T20 game.
“If we talk about internationals, it’s not that I haven’t done well in T20Is. It’s about the combinations that fit in.”
For now, Harleen wants to bank on a tried and tested mantra during her stay in the Caribbean: going with the flow.
“ Ye sab plan karte karte banda fass jata hai (You get stuck as soon as you start planning what you want to achieve). I’m someone who takes it one day at a time. If you think too much ahead, it can disappoint you. In T20 cricket, I’m focussing on my process and not the result.”

A "Black Swan" investor says to guard against disasters — but take risks too.
Mark Spitznagel has built his career on protecting his clients' portfolios against extreme, rare, and unpredictable events known as "black swans" or "tail risks."
Yet the Universa Investments founder and chief told Business Insider over coffee in London this month that simply preparing for the worst isn't a winning strategy in life.
Not taking enough risks can be the "biggest mistake someone makes," Spitznagel said. "You need to be exposed, you need to bet your beliefs."
His career advice mirrors what he says Universa offers to clients: a tail hedge that not only stops them from blowing up, but allows them to be more bullish in their bets.
Spitznagel also warned against obsessing over the power of compounding money over time.
In his 20s, Warren Buffett famously felt like he was paying $300,000 for a haircut. The legendary investor firmly believed that's how much he could make over time if he invested the money instead of handing it to his barber.
Spitznagel said that mindset can be a "curse" because people have to live their lives: "What's the point of compounding if you're not around to see it?"
Stay in the game
The veteran trader, who ran a hedge fund with "The Black Swan" author Nassim Taleb before starting Universa in 2007, recommended people focus on "mitigating the big losses, not the little ones."
"It's not just that it kills you, but it goes down so much, it takes forever to crawl out," he said.
He gave the example of an investor taking a 50% loss on a position, then having to make a 100% gain just to break even.
Spitznagel championed the "Kelly criterion," a mathematical formula that can help investors correctly size their bets so they avoid catastrophic losses.
He said it's more applicable for people to "think about their life from a Kelly standpoint, rather than just a tail-hedging standpoint."
"You can't let your losses take you out of the game," he said.
Humans and goats
Writing has been one of the most common uses for AI tools like ChatGPT, but Spitznagel said he still expects the "ability to express yourself and write" to remain valuable.
The Universa boss said he employs "some of the brightest mathematicians and programmers" on the planet, and they're on the "bleeding edge" of using AI tools.
But AI will "never replace basic human judgment," he said. "There will always be an important place for that."
Asked to name the best investment he's ever made, Spitznagel pointed to his goat farm in Northport, Michigan.
He said that running a farm is "better than anything: yachts, planes, sports teams." He emphasized the satisfaction he gets from "making something tangible," and the pride he feels in producing goat milk and cheese.
Spitznagel also said that farming grounds him and connects him to his family, and he enjoys adapting to the different seasons and thinking in very long timeframes.
"That's the easiest answer in the world," he said. "It's not even close."

Fears that modern electronic devices may harm children are nothing new. Gadgets with screens of any size have long been allegedly melting, rotting, and/or corrupting the brains of youths for decades. However, a medical case report published this week offers a new and alarming way our digital doodads may cause physical harm.
In BMJ Case Reports, two UK doctors, Mara Znagoveanu and Edward Artley, report the case of a boy who came to an emergency department with alarming marks on his abdomen. The marks were described as being in a patch about 15 centimeters (six inches) wide, made of flat, reddish-brown “interlacing lines forming irregular circles and a lace-like morphology.” A picture of the marks is here.
Mysterious marks
The boy, whom they described only as being in “mid-childhood,” was not in any pain, and the rash was not warm to the touch or tender. He and his parents said they couldn’t think of any recent injuries or trauma that might explain the marks. He was otherwise healthy, hadn’t recently been ill, and had no systemic symptoms, such as fever or fatigue. Everything about the boy’s health, growth, and medical history looked normal.
Nurses in the emergency department initially described it as “spontaneous bruising.” A physical exam yielded no insights; there were no other skin abnormalities, abdominal tenderness, or signs of organ trouble. They did a chest X-ray, searching for an explanation. It revealed a small patch of whiteness over his left lung, indicating cells or fluid, such as pus or blood.
As the doctors were taking blood for further testing, the boy told them that he did have one injury: About a week prior, around when the marks appeared, he was play-fighting with his siblings and got pushed into a chair. He said he didn’t mention it before because he didn’t want his siblings to get in trouble.
The new information pointed the doctors to the idea of an underlying traumatic injury. They did a computed tomography (CT) scan, looking for internal abdominal injuries. But they found none, besides the small blip in his lungs that the X-ray showed—which could have just been incidental from a minor infection.

Xi tells Modi China and India bear ‘significant responsibilities’ as Global South powers
Leaders meet on sidelines of Brics summit in New Delhi; Indian statement says they reaffirmed that ‘differences should not become disputes’
Chinese President Xi Jinping told Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday that China and India, as the world’s most populous nations and key members of the Global South, bore “significant responsibilities” in an international landscape “fraught with turbulence and change”.
Xi said that although the countries had different national circumstances, “there is ample scope for us to learn from each other’s strengths, offer mutual support, achieve shared success and pursue common development”.
“Over the past two years, Prime Minister Modi and I have met twice, guiding the relationship from a ‘fresh start’ to a ‘new level of advancement’,” Xi said, according to a readout from Xinhua.
“Institutional exchanges between the two countries have gradually resumed, the list of cooperative initiatives has steadily expanded, and the volume of bilateral trade has hit a new high. This situation was hard-won and deserves to be cherished.”
On the border issue, Xi said that both sides should maintain peace and tranquillity in boundary areas and commit to “parallel development and mutual promotion of bilateral relations and border issues”.
The two sides have sparred repeatedly along their ill-defined border, including the 2020 Galwan Valley clash in which at least 20 Indian and four Chinese soldiers were killed.
Even the length of the border is not agreed upon, with India recording it at around 2,160-miles (3,476 km) while China puts it at less than half that.

How to properly clean and sanitize your secondhand tech finds
Finding a great secondhand item is exciting, but make sure you properly clean it up before giving it a second life.
Isn't it great when you score a secondhand piece of tech that still has life in it? It might be a vintage record player, a smartphone that's still usable, or a cool SLR camera to enhance your photography hobby. This not only saves you money, but extending the life of a product that would otherwise go unused is also great for the environment. As with anything you buy secondhand, it's important to clean and sanitize these items.
While used tech might look clean and the seller may assure you that they've thoroughly cleaned it all, it's always best to do the job yourself. Secondhand gadgets can harbor all types of nasty surprises, from bugs to caked-on gunk you can't see. So before you put any new-to-you items to good use, give them more than just a surface-level wipe down.
Basic tech cleaning tips
After bringing an item home, make sure it's unplugged and turned off. Use a soft microfiber cloth to wipe it down. This removes dirt and fingerprints, which is especially important for cleaning screens. Don't use any other type of cloth that could scratch screens or delicate surfaces.
While you can use a little mild detergent and warm water, avoid liquid cleaners that contain chlorine, peroxides, solvents or ammonia. These can damage internal components or protective applications like the coating on a screen. You can find special tech cleaning solutions from brands like Whoosh! for screens and Tech2Clean, which are safe to use on any surface. I have used both and they work great. There are also specialized monitor wipes for screens like those on TVs, cameras or phones.
For something that has small crevices, like a laptop or keyboard, first turn it over and give it a light shake to release any loose debris. Then, use compressed air to remove trapped dust from within areas like ports and vents. For tech like turntables that has intricate needles, you can buy special cleaning kits and brushes, or use a small brush with soft bristles.
Cleaning all types of devices thoroughly
To remove caked-on gunk, use a soft cotton swab with a few tiny drops of alcohol. (There's conflicting advice about using alcohol, but generally, using a tiny amount of isopropyl alcohol on a soft swab should be fine). However, it's important to use gentle strokes while cleaning. This is especially important for gadgets like earbuds, which can trap dirt and grime inside the acoustic vents. You'll want to thoroughly clean the rubber ear tips as well. Let the item air dry completely in a safe area before you turn it back on.
Don't forget to wipe down all surfaces, including the back, sides and underside. It's worth cleaning accessories like protective cases for a pair of headphones or a camera, as well as chargers and cables if you aren't going to safely recycle them.
Smartwatches in particular can gather a lot of nastiness on the underside if someone wore the device 24/7. Removable fabric bands for a smartwatch or fitness tracker can potentially go into the washing machine on a gentle cycle. Ideally, purchase a new band since they're usually swappable; you can find cheap third-party options to help the wearable feel like new.
Sanitize your gear and always keep it clean
If you want to take an extra step for smaller gadgets, you can buy a portable UV sanitizer from brands like Phonesoap or Homedics. These use ultraviolet light to kill bacteria and viruses, and rose in popularity during the COVID-19 pandemic.
They're designed primarily for phones, which can be 10 times dirtier than a toilet seat (consider how you have yours with you 24/7, touch the screen after contacting many surfaces, and often plop your phone on random surfaces). However, you can also toss in compact items like earbuds, smartwatches, or even keys and credit cards.
While every gadget's second life should start with a deep clean, these tips are still essential for maintaining all your electronics. It's important to keep a consistent cleaning regimen for your gear. You should do a deep clean of your laptop every 3-6 months, your phone every week (with daily wipe downs), earbuds at least once a month and a TV screen or monitor every two to four weeks.

Fintech company stocks — Paytm, Pine Labs, Mobikwik and AvenuesAI — rallied today amid reports suggesting that the merchant discount rate (MDR) fees on UPI transactions could soon be notified. Pine Labs’ stock surged the most, jumping 16.9% to close the day at ₹202.35 on the BSE. Mobikwik climbed just over 8% to close at ₹209.80, while AvenuesAI jumped 6.1% to ₹16.31. Meanwhile, shares of Paytm ended today’s trading session 3.9% higher at ₹1,806.25. The stock jumped as much as 5.2% during intraday trade to touch a fresh all-time high of ₹1,829.50. The rally came after reports earlier in the day suggested that MDR fees on UPI payments are likely to be set at around 40 basis points (bps), or 0.4%, of the transaction value. This comes around a month after the Centre amended the Payment and Settlement Systems Act (PSSA), 2007, to remove a blanket prohibition barring banks and system providers from charging fees on UPI payments. MDR is likely to be charged on P2M transactions only and exclude P2P transactions, with a turnover-based threshold to ensure that only merchants with an annual turnover of around ₹1 Cr-₹1.5 Cr or more. There may be differential fees for businesses across sectors, as was earlier reported. Third-party application providers (TPAPs) – UPI apps – would receive roughly 30% of the MDR, or 12 bps of the transaction value, as per an Economic Times report earlier today. The proposal would unlock a revenue stream of around ₹5,000-10,000 Cr for payments platforms like the four aforementioned companies, brokerage Jefferies had said earlier in a research note. It must be noted that the brokerage firm had estimated a slightly lower MDR of 15-30 bps on transactions above ₹2,000 in its calculations. “Assuming 25% CAGR in value of P2M over FY26-28, we estimate the revenue pool could be about ₹5,000-10,000 Cr in FY28 (estimated),” said Jefferies. As a result, Paytm’s FY28 EBITDA and profit could grow around 15-35% while Pine Labs’ FY28 EBIT and profit could jump 9-23% in this scenario, per the brokerage’s estimates. Another brokerage, Bernstein, had previously projected that Paytm could add ₹1,320 Cr to its EBITDA in the case of 35 bps MDR on a subset of UPI transactions. “We estimate MDR will apply to~50% of transaction value and that Paytm can realise ~3-4bps of incremental net payments margin, translating into ₹2,200 Cr of incremental EBITDA by FY30 (estimated),” it noted. However, Jefferies had raised a question around slippage between the notified MDR rate and the earned take-rate in the event that competition to onboard merchants intensified among payments platforms.

One rural hospital offers hope amid nationwide rural maternity ward closures
When Nikki Johnson heard Mayo Clinic Health System was closing its labor and delivery unit at her local clinic in Fairmont, Minnesota, she was shocked. It was 2024, and she was 33 weeks pregnant. Instead of giving birth in her small rural town, she was suddenly faced with having to drive to Mayo's Mankato clinic about an hour away when she went into labor.
"I asked the doctor, so what happens if I go into labor and it goes pretty fast and I have to pull over on the side of the road on the way to Mankato?" Johnson recalled. "I was like, that would be terrifying. Giving birth is scary to begin with."
Johnson's experience isn't unique. Labor and delivery units have been closing across the state and the nation in recent years. The latest data from the University of Minnesota Rural Health Research Center shows that in 2010, 56% of U.S. counties had at least one hospital with obstetrics services. 14 years later, that dropped by 9% — almost 300 counties had lost hospital-based obstetrics services and rural areas had been hardest hit.
Labor and delivery units require 24/7 staffing since births can happen at any time. That makes it expensive. Rural hospitals see more low-income patients on Medicaid, which offers lower reimbursement, and they see fewer births, so labor and delivery units rarely pay for themselves. They tend to have fewer resources for simulation training and telemedicine support.
Katy Kozhimannil, co-director of the Rural Health Research Center, said when rural units close, it can make giving birth more dangerous.
"Certainly in rural areas, for every hospital that closes its obstetric unit or closes entirely, the nearest place to give birth gets further and further away, and that distance is associated with poor outcomes for moms and for babies," Kozhimannil explained.
She said many pregnant people are forced to give birth in under-resourced rural emergency rooms, in ambulances, or even on the side of the road, leading to more instances of pre-term birth and infant mortality.
Bucking the trend
However, there's one rural hospital birthing center that is thriving, and its success could offer a template for others. Minnesota's United Hospital District runs a small critical access hospital and three clinics in rural counties. Johnson gave birth to her daughter Sylvie at the hospital. It's located in Blue Earth, Minnesota. 3,000 people live in the town and the hospital is the only one in the county.
"We're the last one here," said United Hospital District CEO Richard Ash. "If we're not doing OB, there's a big desert here, and there's a lot of people that are going to either have to move or take the risk."
Ash said during much of his time leading the hospital, about 50 babies a year were born at the facility in Blue Earth. However, since 2020 there's been an increase every year and in 2025, they delivered 178 babies. He said the hospital's on track to follow suit this year.
Ash says has United Health District implemented a few different tactics to remain open. It joined Headwaters, a clinically integrated network of rural hospitals in Minnesota. That gave the hospital more negotiating power in purchasing supplies and allowed them to lower other costs. The hospital is also able to offset financial losses in labor and delivery by providing other services, like outpatient surgery, that bring in more money.
UHD's Chief Medical Officer Aaron Johnson said cross training is also crucial to balancing the hospital's budget.
"The biggest thing, I think, that allows us to keep our head above water, is that people can do multiple things," Johnson said. "If our labor and delivery staff were just L&D nurses it wouldn't work. There's no way it would work."
Building close relationships with patients is key
Maija Whitefeather Manning and her husband chose to give birth to both their sons in Blue Earth instead of other larger hospital system affiliates nearby because of the rave reviews she heard from her colleagues.
"I mean, we live in a world of technology, right?" Whitefeather Manning said. "And you can look at reviews, and you can read all these things. But also, when you live in a small community, what people say is true and has a lot of weight."
Both Whitefeather Manning and Johnson said they feel heard and understood at the Blue Earth hospital. They also recalled little homey touches that stood out: seasonally-inspired baby hats crocheted by church volunteers in town; the gift basket the hospital sent them home with; and a special multi-course meal for the new parents during their last night at the hospital.
"They gave us a little menu, it was like, steak or chicken breast and dessert and a bottle of sparkling grape juice," Johnson said jokingly that was not the sort of thing she'd come to expect with hospital care. "Like they are not setting up a little romantic meal for you and your husband."
Kozhimannil, co-director of the Rural Health Research Center said the hospital's strategy is a textbook example of what some rural hospitals are doing in order to succeed. And staying open and building capacity to serve more patients is crucial to improving the delivery of health care in rural areas.
For many of those who work at United Hospital District, the commitment to keeping the labor and delivery unit open feels personal.
"I mean for us, these are our neighbors," chief medical officer Aaron Johnson said. "These are our family members. These are the people that we go to church with, go to school with, go to football games with. We want to provide the best care for them."

On food labelling and misleading claims, weight loss drugs, climate change, rabies, cancer care, and more
(In the weekly Health Matters newsletter, Ramya Kannan writes about getting to good health, and staying there. You can subscribe here to get the newsletter in your inbox.)
This past week, as with the previous week, the nation continues to be concerned with food labelling. With the Supreme Court bringing up the packaged food labelling issue up again, a couple of weeks ago, it has been surely and firmly dragged into the public platform. There has been a great deal of interest in the Food Safety and Standards Association of India’s recommendations on front-of-pack labels, and debate about the merits of the case.
What are these standards that FSSAI promises to hold the packaged food in India up to? We took a long,hard look.
For an idea of what the whole FSSAI submission on labelling was, initially, check out this conversation between Zubeda Hamid and I; we also indicate trends worldwide, in Sunday’s Health Wrap video. While appreciable that some standards have come to play in this entirely unregulated sector, there are questions about the caveats in the proposed recommendations. FSSAI has proposed that the warning initially apply to products high in two or more of the three “nutrients of concern” — added sugar, added saturated fat and salt — as well as specified highly sweetened beverages. Activists find the “two or more” classification problematic.
For a more detailed explanation on what the Red hexagon on your snack pack means, read what Bindu Shajan Perappadan wrote. FSSAI has proposed a two-phase rollout. In the first phase, products high in at least two of the three nutrients would carry the red hexagon, along with specified highly sweetened beverages. In the second phase, the warning would extend to products high in any one of the three nutrients. However, FSSAI has not specified a firm timeline for moving to the second phase. The FSSAI proposal refers to added sugar and added saturated fat, rather than total sugar and total fat. The plan is to exempt single-ingredient foods and products inherently rich in these nutrients, including ghee, edible oil, jaggery and honey.
Meanwhile, Soibam Rocky Singh explains why the Central Consumer Protection Authority is cracking down on ‘100%’ claims on food products. Such claims can give consumers an impression of absolute purity or completeness that may not match what is actually inside the packet. The FSSAI has also asked food businesses to stop using “100%” claims on food labels, packaging and promotional material.
Here, Prabalika M. Borah examines the hype behind Proffee: protien+coffee, and here are the highlights of an ICMR-NIN study which shows that Vitamin D3 outperforms D2 in supporting muscles and heart.
Close on the nutrition topic is weight loss drugs. A recent study showed that GLP-1 weight loss drugs are effective even at low starter doses, with lower side effects. Yet another study in the United States showed that more children under 12 in U.S. are being prescribed weight-loss drugs. Prescriptions for GLP-1 weight-loss drugs among children under 12 in the U.S. have risen more than 300-fold since 2019.
Here is a supervised experiment of a fitness coaching putting himself through a GLP 1 course, recording minute observations through the course. Arvind Ashok writes: ‘I’m a fitness coach. I tried a GLP-1 drug for three weeks’, issuing a statutory warning to readers not to attempt the same at home without a prescription.
Climate change will also never be further than a beck and call away. It has dominated headlines periodically, and likely will be even more frequent in future. Jacob Koshy writes: Global warming will exceed limit, UN says in a report that maps path to get back below danger zone. UNEP’s detailed ‘overshoot, peak and decline’ pathway seeks to hold the peak as low as possible and then bring temperatures back down below the 1.5°C limit; report terms it ‘best remaining option’.
Yet another new study highlights the life-saving role of air conditioning, but indicates that it comes at a cost. Do check this story out, for the details: Keeping cool saves thousands of lives yearly, but at a cost of worsening global warming, experts say.
On the rabies front, there was some exciting news in the region. I record how Bhutan leads South-East Asia in eliminating rabies as public health problem. The WHO also validated Bhutan’s claim and explained that this was achieved through conscious of deployment of the One Health approach, affording some key lessons for neighbour India too.
Meanwhile, Authorities are probing ‘counterfeit’ rabies vaccine, and the counterfeit ‘Abhayrab’ rabies vaccine batch remains under investigation. Why is this important? With rabies, the margin for error is exceptionally small. A genuine, potent vaccine administered promptly can prevent a fatal disease; a counterfeit product can create the dangerous illusion that protection has been provided.
On dogs, segueing into cancer, we had an interesting article this week on whether dogs can sniff cancer? Bengaluru-based startup Dognosis is using AI to analyse dogs’ brain activity, respiration and body language, turning their reaction to scent into data. Click on the link to learn more.

Ever since Denis Villeneuve’s forthcoming James Bond film was announced, the million-dollar question has been: Who will take on the role of the iconic spy? Now, former 007 Pierce Brosnan is offering his thoughts.
In a recent interview with The Times, the actor, who played the character in four films from 1995 to 2002, said that “there are lots of good hats in the ring” and “lots of great actors” being considered. “I see it. I follow it. They could probably just go left-field and pick someone that none of us know about.”
When it comes to names, Brosnan remained neutral: “I wouldn’t pick anyone,” he continued. “My wife told me not to say anything and I’ve said too much. Because once I say something it goes [everywhere] and I get hanged.”
Popular on Variety
Brosnan also explained that he hasn’t revisited his own Bond films since their release. “I have no desire to see myself in Bond,” he said. “I’m just a member of the audience now awaiting the next Bond and wishing him well.”
This isn’t the first time the actor has waded into the Bond waters — back in Aug. 2025, while speaking with the Radio Times, Brosnan joked that he’d return as a senior citizen Bond.
“I don’t think anyone wants to see a craggy, 72-year-old Bond, but if Villeneuve had something up his sleeve I would look at it in a heartbeat,” Brosnan said. “Why not? It’s great entertainment. It could be lots of laughs. Bald caps, prosthetics… who knows?”
Variety previously reported that Amazon MGM Studios enlisted casting director Nina Gold to find the new secret agent. Her credits include the Netflix series “The Crown,” five films in the Star Wars franchise, “Les Misérables,” “The Martian” and “Conclave.” In 2025, she was nominated for an Oscar for her work on “Hamnet.”
	While the final casting for the film has not been confirmed, Callum Turner, Jacob Elordi, Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Harris Dickinson and Jack Lowden have all been reported as among those in the final running.

The Supreme Court on Thursday (September 10, 2026) refused to entertain a PIL raising concerns over the government-run nationwide human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination campaign for adolescent girls to prevent cervical cancer.
A Bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana said whenever there is a case of incorrect vaccination, ordinary rules of compensation will apply.
"Would you like to withdraw? Do you want us to comment something?" the Bench observed.
"Don't ask us to make harsh observations. If petitioner members are doctors, it's a very very serious issue. It's a question of health of millions of our daughters. And you want to derail this," it said.
The top court orally said that the PIL was filed with an ulterior motive and lacked bonafide.
The lawyer appearing for the petitioner said that he was only pressing on adverse events and compensation, nothing on HPV.
"I am not at all anti-vaccine. My first contention is the way it is being implemented. Second, there is no adverse event mechanism. Whenever there is an adverse event, it must be monitored. There should also be a compensation scheme," the lawyer said.
When the apex court refused to entertain the plea, the counsel withdrew the plea and the matter was dismissed as withdrawn.
The top court was hearing a plea filed by the Universal Health Organisation challenging the manner in which the government-backed HPV vaccination programme is being implemented.
The plea alleged that it violates constitutional guarantees of informed consent, bodily autonomy, transparency and accountability.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi launched the nationwide HPV vaccination campaign for 14-year-old girls from Ajmer in Rajasthan on February 28.
A single-dose Gardasil 4 vaccine, a quadrivalent HPV vaccine, is being used under the campaign. The injection provides protection against HPV types 16 and 18, which are responsible for cervical cancer, as well as types 6 and 11.

Delhi is welcoming several of the world's most prominent leaders this weekend as the BRICS Summit takes place in the capital. Amid the high-profile gathering, Delhi has also recorded a noticeable improvement in air quality. At around 4 pm on September 12, Delhi's lowest AQI reading was recorded at 62, putting it in the moderate category, according to AQI.in. The improvement in air quality comes as Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and other BRICS leaders arrive in Delhi for the two-day summit. Quick answers to key questions The improvement in Delhi's air quality, with an AQI of 62, was primarily due to recent rainfall and overcast skies from an active monsoon, which helped wash away suspended pollutants. Rainfall enhances air quality by capturing dust and pollutants as raindrops fall, reducing the concentration of airborne particles in urban settings. The BRICS Summit focused on global trade, energy security, conflict prevention, and the need for reform in global governance and financial institutions. The BRICS Summit coincided with a period of unusually clean air for Delhi, influenced by favorable weather conditions, which helped create a more agreeable environment for the high-profile gathering. The New Delhi Declaration emphasizes collective efforts for global governance reform, conflict prevention, and the rejection of unilateral economic sanctions, reflecting a commitment to cooperation among BRICS nations. The change is notable because the capital had recorded comparatively higher pollution levels earlier this week. Delhi's official AQI was 133 on September 10, which was also in the moderate category. The reading had risen further to 155 during the early hours of Friday, September 11. The capital has experienced rainfall and overcast skies in recent days as an active monsoon spell continues to influence the region. The India Meteorological Department (IMD) had predicted generally cloudy conditions accompanied by moderate rain in Delhi on September 12. The wet weather is also expected to persist over the coming days. Rainfall can provide a temporary boost to air quality by washing some suspended pollutants out of the atmosphere. As raindrops move towards the ground, they can capture dust and other pollution particles present in the air. Changes in wind patterns and atmospheric conditions can further aid the dispersion of pollutants, preventing them from accumulating near the surface. The ongoing weather conditions are also linked to a broader monsoon system. A low-pressure area over the northwest and west-central Bay of Bengal is influencing rainfall across several parts of northern and central India, including Delhi. For the BRICS Summit, the timing could hardly have been better. Whether by coincidence or good fortune, the two-day event has arrived during a relatively cleaner window for the capital as leaders gather to discuss global issues. India is hosting the BRICS Summit this year at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi on September 12-13. The conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine, along with global trade turbulence and energy security, are expected to dominate the two-day meeting of the 11-nation bloc. The BRICS grouping on Saturday adopted a joint declaration with consensus, Prime Minister Narendra Modi said. Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced the adoption of the declaration at the end of the opening day's deliberations at the two-day India-hosted summit. Prime Minister Modi was seen shaking hands with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the conclusion of the inaugural session at the summit.
