Apple’s first foldable, the iPhone Duo, could give the stagnant foldable market a much-needed push. It may not reinvent the category, but Apple’s reach, software focus, and mainstream appeal could make foldables far more popular.
September is here and so are the new iPhones. This year at Apple’s Surprise and Shine event, the Cupertino tech giant came with a number of changes, not just in terms of devices but in terms of management too. There was a new CEO – it was John Ternus’ first event as CEO – as well as new Apple Watches, AirPods and, of course, new iPhones too.
The Duo dominates the new iPhones
Even though Apple showcases a number of products during its September event, it is mainly the iPhones that the world waits for. And even in iPhones, it is usually the Pro and Pro Max iPhones that make the headlines (barring the odd occasion when the Air popped up). The plain iPhones are usually pushed to the sidelines and launched as the more “economical”, “affordable” iPhones whose price tags and generally minor upgrades in specs and design are the only things that get them any attention.
For the longest time, we have been feeling for the plain iPhones because they are quite capable and bring in big sales numbers (especially in markets like India, where they are bestsellers) and yet do not get the hype they deserve. Well, this time around, the iPhone Pro and the Pro Max got the taste of this bitter medicine. The two smartphones had to fold (pun intended) and give up all their headline space for the more expensive, exclusive, and most different iPhone since the inception of the original iPhone: the iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable iPhone.
With the iPhone Duo, Apple has finally marked its official entry in the world of foldables. It comes with a starting price of Rs. 299,900 in India ($1,999 in the US), which has naturally inspired a tsunami of reinvented kidney jokes and all sorts of comparisons about all that you can buy for that price. It has also got many competing brands scoffing at Apple’s very late attempt at foldables, calling the Duo a “copy”. While some of the criticism and cynicism around the Duo is valid, we think a foldable phone from Apple is just what the foldable market needed to make foldables mainstream. Not because the Duo is an out-of-the-tech-world, never-seen-before, and extraordinary folding smartphone (hey, we haven’t reviewed it yet), but for much simpler reasons.
Ghost of foldables past: A story mainly of Samsung
Samsung is considered by many to be the modern foldable phone pioneer. It was the trailblazer that was responsible for actually bringing in foldable phones that not only landed on the tech moon but also managed to stick around for seven2 years – Samsung’s first Galaxy Fold arrived in 2019, followed by the Galaxy Z Flip in 2020. The brand did not really have a working blueprint that they could have used back then to have perfected their foldables and technology around it, but it enjoyed an early mover’s advantage in the segment and managed to create a very strong reputation for itself. They built a strong rapport with the consumers that none of the other brands could develop, even after launching just as good, just as powerful foldable smartphones.
Following Samsung’s start, many leading tech brands have been surfing the foldable wave for a while now. The OG flip phone master, Motorola; the Android originator Google; the flagship killer OnePlus; the Chinese Apple, Xiaomi; Vivo, Oppo, and others have created foldables with their own touches and twists. Huawei has gone one step further and has launched a tri-fold – a smartphone that folds twice. But even after all this effort, none of them could really be a standout foldable smartphone brand. Only Samsung did.
But in spite of Samsung’s consistency and the efforts of other brands, foldable smartphones have not become mainstream. They have never really made impressive numbers or become popular/common devices. Yes, most of them come with premium price tags, but even those that are relatively affordable – mostly flips or budget foldables (yes, there are some) – have not gained the kind of traction that had been expected. The foldable revolution that many had predicted seemed to have stalled, and apart from a few devices (mainly from Samsung), growth was largely limited.
Apple and the tech snowball effect… could it come to foldables?
Now Apple has stepped into the foldable ring, and while there are many contenders in it already, we think the Cupertino tech giant might get the buzz around foldables going. It has been quite a trend setter in the tech world, and is identified with premium innovation. Features, functions, and devices that existed long before Apple “reinvented” them suddenly became popular once they started shipping with an Apple logo and Apple’s own unique take on them. They not only became mainstream but also often became a common sight on products from other brands as well. Touchscreen phones, apps and app stores, music stores, portrait mode, notches (Dynamic Island), are just some of the products that Apple did not invent, but made a part of
everyday technology.
Of course, every time this happens, the Internet is flooded with techies pointing out how the particular feature or product has been around for years and how Apple is not really innovating or, rather, thinking differently (Apple’s very tagline). Despite all the chatter and gossip around this topic, somehow the feature picks up momentum, and soon enough the world gets interested in knowing how it works and then owning a device that lets them use it. This initiates a snowball effect of sorts, which leads to that feature or device becoming extremely popular.
We will keep it simple: quite often, it basically takes an Apple device or feature to grab mainstream attention. It happened with GUI, MP3 players, ultra-portable notebooks, touchscreen phones, tablets, TWS, smartwatches, and we think it could happen with foldables too. The Duo has the potential to put the seemingly jammed foldable wheels in motion.
It is important to remember that it is not like whatever Apple does just becomes a hit automatically. The brand has a loyal following, but it has released many features, devices, and functions that did not strike a chord with consumers and have faded away. The Apple Vision Pro, HomePod, iPhone Mini and iPhone Plus, the Touch Bar on the Mac…Apple’s failure list is quite long. It may be one of the most successful tech brands in history, but Apple is no tech Midas – there is no real guarantee that the iPhone Duo would be an absolute hit. The stakes are quite high for the Duo, especially given its price tag (which is even higher in India).
It has got the hype, but what would make the Duo click?
Unlike Samsung, Apple has not had to reinvent the foldable wheel. It has had time to read, research, develop, try, and make mistakes, and fix them all, even while observing the efforts of other tech brands. And while the Duo’s design and specs, and indeed, many of its features, are nothing we have not seen before, these are not areas where Apple differentiates itself from the regular crowd. The iPhone Duo needs to bring Apple’s attention to detail when it comes to user experience, and software tuned exactly to suit the needs and capabilities of the device it supports.
We have not yet had the pleasure (or pain) to experience the device but so far, from the looks and the videos on the Internet, we can tell you there are a few things we love about the iPhone Duo – the TouchID on the side (yes, we actually love it), the vertical tool bar for easy access, the matte display layer which makes the crease largely invisible, and yes, of course, the animation that blurs out the side/front screen when the phone is being opened or folded. But it’s not all pink skies and red roses. We are not very convinced by the asymmetrical shape of the device, the insanely high price tag, and, well, even the name. Duo? Really, Apple? We are also really curious about how Apple has worked on apps for the cover display as well as the inner ones.
But these are early days. The iPhone Duo is more than a month away, and we are sure Apple will fine-tune it even further before releasing it. In the meantime, we expect the kidney jokes to continue and even gather momentum, but on the flip side, curiosity will also grow, as we are sure more will be revealed about the device and its features and functions.
The iPhone Duo has generated more buzz about the foldables in a few months than other players in the field got in years, but it is all going to boil down to how well and how differently it works from other foldables. Given the interest levels around it, it might just prove to be the elixir that foldables need.

LG denies accusations of smart TVs continuously recording its users
The company said that user privacy is a “fundamental principle” of its products.
After an unsettling report that accused LG's smart TVs of spying on its users, the company has responded by saying that "some recent media coverage may have contributed to misconceptions about how LG smart TVs work." To address the claims made in a lengthy video published on Gamers Nexus, LG said that its "smart TVs do not continuously record or transmit user's conversations."
LG released a comprehensive statement a few days after the 135-minute long video from Gamers Nexus was published, which claimed the Korean electronics company's smart TVs can capture audio recordings even when the TV is asleep or unplugged from the network, as well as collecting sensitive data like IP addresses, geographic locations, names of nearby WiFi networks and devices connected to those networks even if they're not connected to the TV. The report was conducted by Gamers Nexus alongside Level1 Techs and independent cybersecurity researchers.
Following the report, LG denied these claims in statements to news outlets, but the company put out a much longer response on its website. Beyond clarifying that its smart TVs don't "continuously listen to, record, or store conversations in the home," LG added that its "speech-to-text processing begins only if a user activates a voice interaction through a supported wake-word feature or by pressing the voice button on the remote control," and that voice data wasn't stored for later upload after a TV is disconnected from the internet. LG also explained that some features like "Automatic Content Recognition," voice recognition and interest-based advertising are optional features that are turned off by default.
On top of claims of recording conversations, the Gamers Nexus' report noted that there are business-to-business benefits of collecting all of that data, but also a risk of exposure to potential exploits or security vulnerabilities. In response to this, LG said that "no connected product is ever completely immune from security vulnerabilities, which is why ongoing monitoring, testing and improvement remain important throughout the product lifecycle."

The bodies of passengers killed in a ferry fire off the Philippines arrived at a port near the resort town of Coron, Palawan, on Saturday morning, as the country’s coast guard warned the death toll of 35 would grow.
Tents were being set up to receive 30 bodies brought from the M/V June Aster, which ran aground near the tourist hotspot after a fire erupted on Wednesday evening and tore through the vessel “in seconds”.
Coast guard spokesperson Noemie Cayabyab told a Saturday press conference the remains would be turned over to police forensic investigators for “proper disposition and identification” before allowing local authorities to inform family members.
“Currently, we are focused on the retrieval, and after that we will proceed with the investigation,” she said, confirming the bodies had been found in the ship’s economy accommodation area.
Police investigators were seen arriving at the port shortly after the press conference ended.
Asked how many bodies remained aboard the ship, she said authorities would provide an update later in the day.
Cayabyab told AFP on Friday evening that the first transfer had been capped at 30 bodies because of the capacity of the patrol vessel transporting them and that additional cadavers remained on the ferry.
Five others had been confirmed dead in the immediate wake of the fire.
Photos released by the coast guard showed rows of body bags being placed into a small ship alongside men in hazmat suits. Thirty passengers and 13 crew have so far been rescued, while 54 people remain unaccounted for.
On Friday, Cayabyab had told a radio station the fire had begun in the cargo hold, then tore through the ship within seconds.
“From the time that they heard the loud explosion, the appearance of smoke, and then fire. It spread very quickly,” she said of survivors’ accounts.
“Everything happened in seconds,” she said, adding that those who made it off the ship had not even had time to put on lifejackets.
Myra Cabilan said she had flown to Coron to find her missing brother, 40-year-old Rammel Gonzaga, who had taken the ferry from Manila on a business trip with his brother-in-law.
“His wife had just given birth a month ago. He was so happy he was given a daughter,” Cabilan said, fighting back tears.
“At dawn, I still believed he survived. But he’s still missing. I have lost hope.”
Hundreds of people desperate for news about the incident have taken to leaving comments on the Facebook page of a local mayor, searching for relatives, friends and even a dog.
The ferry’s manifest listed 134 crew and passengers, but two had not boarded, according to the coast guard. The ferry was also carrying goods, an electric vehicle, a pickup truck, and motorcycles.
The archipelago nation of 116 million has a long history of disasters involving the inter-island ferries that ply its seas.
Many rely on cheap and poorly regulated boats and ships for transport between the country’s more than 7,000 islands, despite regular accidents.
On Thursday, the company that owns the M/V June Aster, Atienza Interisland Ferries Inc, said it was fully cooperating with the investigation.

Amid war and sanctions, many Iranians are losing their jobs and struggling to get by
ISTANBUL — Rasoul had a plan for the worst-case scenario. A 42-year-old engineer in Tehran with a steady job at a tech company, he often reassured his wife about their financial security. If times ever got truly tough, he would tell her, he could always drive for Snapp—Iran's local ride-sharing equivalent to Uber.
Then the war hit, and the worst-case scenario arrived.
Since the United States and Israel attacked Iran over six months ago, ordinary Iranians have borne the brunt of a collapsing economy. Inflation has skyrocketed, driving up the costs of gas, food, and rent. Livelihoods across the country are unraveling, forcing many to borrow just to survive and put major life milestones on hold.
While the official unemployment rate in Iran sits at 9%, independent analysts say the true figure is significantly higher. The desperation for work is palpable: Jobvision, a prominent Iranian job-seeking portal, reported a 50% spike in resume submissions in late April alone.
Even state-sanctioned labor leaders acknowledge the depth of the crisis. In May, Alireza Mahjoob, head of Iran's Workers House—the country's primary labor organization—admitted on state television that joblessness was far worse than anticipated.
"We don't know how much it will afflict our already fragile working class, leaving us all helpless and powerless," Mahjoob said.
Disrupted Networks and Shut Down Transit
For Rasoul, the decline was swift. In January, during a brutal government crackdown on protests, Iranian authorities severely restricted internet access to cut off communication with the outside world.
Because his company depended on worldwide networks that were cut off by the regime, the disruptions severely damaged his company's delivery services.
"The company's situation got really bad," Rasoul said. "They were losing customers one by one."
By mid-February, he was laid off, triggering a period of severe depression. Like all Iranians interviewed for this report, he spoke on the condition that his full name be withheld out of fear of government retribution.
Desperate to pay his bills, Rasoul reluctantly turned to his backup plan and began driving for Snapp at night.
"I remember being extremely anxious—accepting a ride, waiting, having the passenger get in, and so on," he recalled.
The strategy failed. The U.S. and Israel launched a war against Iran at the end of February, and ever-tighter US sanctions and a naval blockade of the Strait of Hormuz led to rising fuel prices, and costly vehicle repairs quickly ate into his meager earnings. Ongoing U.S. airstrikes made navigating the streets at night far too dangerous. Eventually, he had to rely on extended family to stay afloat. Personal plans, including starting a family, have been completely shelved.
"I thought that after marriage I could keep working and traveling, going places together," Rasoul said. "But since we got married, nothing."
Other industries have faced complete collapse due to supply chain blockades and regional instability. Kayvan, a 42-year-old materials engineer from Tehran, helped a Chinese firm establish a business supplying raw materials to Iran's vital oil sector.
When fighting escalated, the maritime trade came to a halt.
"The environment became so unsafe," Kayvan said. "Transit routes and shipping routes were shut down, the Strait of Hormuz was closed, sea transport became impossible."
With clients unable to place orders, the business collapsed.
"It was like those American movies where people dump their belongings into a box and clear out their desk," Kayvan said about the day he had to leave his job.
"Passengers on a Train"
To survive the job loss, Kayvan's family relied entirely on his wife's income and rapidly dwindling personal savings—a cushion eroding fast against extreme economic headwinds.
"Terrifying inflation, unprecedented price hikes... we've genuinely never experienced days like these before," Kayvan said, adding that the conflict simply needs to stop. "We're all just falling apart."
For some, temporary relief has come, though it offers little peace of mind. In July, Rasoul managed to secure a new role as a sales manager. Yet with the conflict continuing and the broader economy in freefall, stability feels like an illusion.
"We're like passengers on a train," Rasoul said. "We don't know if the bridge ahead is broken or intact."

Your guide to the U.S. midterms, and why they're crucial for Donald Trump
Republican control of House, Senate at stake in nationwide elections on Nov. 3
The upcoming U.S. midterm elections will determine whether Republican President Donald Trump will be free to pursue his agenda during his final two years in office or whether he'll face constraints from a Congress where the Democrats hold new power.
Here's what you need to know about the midterms.
Why do U.S. midterms matter?
The midterms are a contest for control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, which together make up the U.S. Congress.
The party that controls the Senate holds sway over presidential appointments to cabinet, the courts and senior posts in federal agencies. The party that controls the House can launch impeachment proceedings and has the power to initiate budget bills .
If one party controls both, it has broad influence over legislation as well as the potential to thwart some presidential actions.
How is the race shaping up?
The Democrats are generally excited about their prospects in the midterms and the Republicans a little worried.
History gives the Republicans plenty of reason to fret. The incumbent president's party has suffered a net loss of seats in Congress in all but two midterms since the 1930s. The only exceptions were Bill Clinton (1998) and George W. Bush (2002), when each had sky-high approval ratings.
Trump's approval rating is anything but sky-high.
What's at stake?
With slim majorities in each chamber, the Republicans have little wiggle room to lose seats and still maintain their hold on Congress.
The Democrats need to flip just four districts to take control of the House (if they hold on to all their current seats). The Democrats also need to take just four Republican-held states to win control of the Senate. But that's a tougher task than flipping the House because there are far fewer Senate seats up for election and winning each requires a statewide victory.
All 435 seats in the U.S. House of Representatives are up for grabs, as members of the House are elected to two-year terms.
Only 35 of the 100 seats in the Senate are up for election this fall. U.S. senators are elected to six-year terms.
When does voting happen?
Midterms, like the word implies, come at the two-year mark of a president's four-year term. This year, midterm election day is Nov. 3.
Many U.S. voters will choose to vote before then, either in advance polls or by mail-in ballots, a method the Trump administration is trying to restrict.
You may also have heard that people across the U.S. have been voting at various times since the spring in primaries, which are the contests to select each party's candidates. In most states, only people who are registered Republicans or Democrats can vote in the party's primaries.
How does Trump factor in?
Trump is not on the ballot in the midterms, but his influence on the campaign will be unavoidable.
Only one president since 1950 has headed into a midterm with an approval rating below 40 per cent: George W. Bush in 2006 (at 37 per cent), when his Republicans lost 30 seats in the House and six in the Senate.
Despite his low polling numbers, Trump is vowing to give "a lot of speeches" in states and districts where the races are tight to help Republican candidates. Some of those candidates are quietly asking the White House to keep him away, according to reporting by Politico.
What are the key issues in the midterms?
While U.S. polls differ slightly on the precise numbers, there's a strong thread of consistency suggesting the top issue of concern among voters right now is the cost of living.
Whether it's gas prices pushed up as a result of the war against Iran or the prices of consumer goods rising because of Trump's tariffs, pocketbook issues predominate the midterm polling.
Trump, as the dominant figure in U.S. politics for the past decade, will undoubtedly be an issue, particularly for moderate Republican or swing voters who backed him in the 2024 presidential election but have soured on him since then, according to polling.
Turnout in midterms is always lower than during presidential election years, so each party will be striving for ways to motivate their base. For the Democrats, weakening Trump's power could be that driving force. For the Republicans, stoking fear about what a Democratic-controlled Congress would do to the economy is a key advertising message.
Where are the key Senate races?
Of the 35 Senate seats up for election this time, fewer than 10 are considered by campaign analysts to be at risk of changing hands.
The Republicans are considered most vulnerable in North Carolina and Maine, but polling suggests they also are in tough to hang on to their Senate seats in Ohio, Alaska, Iowa and even Texas, where no Democrat has won a statewide election since 1988.
The Democrats' biggest challenges to hold appear to be in the Senate races in Michigan and New Hampshire.
- A Michigan Democrat wants to put Canada on the ballot during the midterms. Are voters listening?
- With U.S. midterm elections looming, Democrats are clashing over how to win
Where are the key House races?
More than 80 per cent of House seats are considered safe for either the Republicans or the Democrats, according to the University of Virginia Center for Politics newsletter Crystal Ball, which has forecast and analyzed every election for U.S. president, House, Senate and state governors since 2002.
That political inertia leaves only a few dozen districts across the country truly "in play," as campaign strategists describe races where the outcome is in doubt.
Crystal Ball has labelled 17 Republican-held districts as toss-ups, including three in Pennsylvania and two in Michigan. All will be races to watch because they're prime targets for the Democrats as they try to win back control of the House.

Celine Dion shed tears as she kicked off her eagerly anticipated 16-date residency tonight at Plenitude Arena on the outskirts of Paris, marking her first major series of live shows since stepping away from the spotlight in 2022.
“I had promised myself not to cry,” Dion told thousands of adoring fans in the opening moments of her show. “I don’t keep my promises. But I’m so happy to see you all. I missed you. I’m going to sing like you without crying.”
Dion’s arrival in Paris two weeks ago has dominated headlines and sparked a frenzy on social media as well as in the streets of the French capital. The metro station near the concert venue has also been renamed Celine and has been decorated with some of her most famous lyrics. Fans from every corner of the world have been camping in front of the Royal Monceau hotel behind security barriers and have been singing her more popular songs every time she comes out. Clips of Dion engaging with fans, singing a capella with them and making some dance moves in front of the Parisian palace have gone viral.
Popular on Variety
Not all of those hardcore fans will make it to the Paris concerts, however. Some may be turned away if they unknowingly bought fake tickets from the more than 200 fraudulent websites and social media accounts that popped up right when pre-sale tickets went on sale in April, according to the Associated Press, which quoted Group-IB, a Singapore-based cybersecurity firm.
Her comeback isn’t just being eagerly anticipated by fans — it’s also being touted as a potential lifeline for France’s state coffers heading into 2027. French newspaper Liberation dedicated the cover of its weekend edition to Dion’s residency with a picture of the singer doing a prayer-like gesture, looking upward with a bright halo of light behind her, and a headline that reads, “Celine Dion — is she going to save the 2027 budget?” Her Paris concerts could indeed generate €1 billion in economic impact for France, that’s four times more than what Beyoncé’s Paris concerts in June 2025 brought and roughly a fifth of what the entire Paris 2024 Olympics generated, according to French radio Europe 1.
More than 33,000 people are expected at the Plenitude Arena. As much as 60% of the set list is expected to be from her French repertoire, mainly songs penned and composed by Jean-Jacques Goldman, including “Pour que tu m’aimes encore” and “J’irai où tu iras.” She’s also teased that her first show will last over two hours in an informal chat with fans in front of her hotel and told them to wear comfortable shoes, as reported by France Info.
Rumors have been circulating about a potential surprise duo with Beyonce who happens to be in the French capital with Jay Z, who gave a concert in Paris two days ago.
An estimated nine million people signed up for advance tickets for the shows after Dion announced her concert comeback on her birthday, on March 30, during a glamorous bash (which she didn’t attend but delivered a message on video) in front of the Eiffel Tower, which was illuminated in tribute, with a choreographed light show set to Dion’s greatest hits.
Dion made her stage return singing Edith Piaf’s “Hymne A L’Amour” by the Eiffel Tower at the 2024 Paris Olympics opening ceremony.
Dion’s Paris concerts were originally scheduled for 2020 at Paris La Défense Arena as part of her Courage World Tour, but were postponed due to the pandemic and then delayed again due to her health issues. In 2022, Dion was diagnosed with Stiff Person Syndrome (SPS), a rare neurological and autoimmune disorder that causes muscular stiffness, inhibiting the ability to walk and sing. Her fans lost hope she would ever come back after seeing Dion struggle against this illness in the 2024 documentary “I Am: Celine Dion,” which was directed by Irene Taylor.

America Has Forfeited Its Greatest Strength
Osama bin Laden wanted to eradicate faith in American power. Twenty-five years later, his dream is on the verge of coming true.
Perhaps the most famous conclusion of the 9/11 Commission Report is that America’s inability to prevent the September 11 attacks resulted from a “failure of imagination.” With respect to the 9/11 Commission, that is not quite right.
Long before September 11, members of the U.S. intelligence community understood the awful scale of Osama bin Laden’s ambitions. The presidential daily brief on August 6, 2001, included an item titled “Bin Ladin Determined to Strike in US,” which even referenced al-Qaeda’s desire to hijack an American aircraft. This was just one of 36 articles in presidential briefings that year that mentioned bin Laden or al-Qaeda.
As an FBI special agent, I participated in investigations of al-Qaeda both before and after 9/11. Based on my experience, the main reason the U.S. didn’t stop 9/11 was not a failure of imagination but a failure of trust. America’s intelligence institutions lacked confidence in one another. In fact, they hid intelligence from their peers. This particular problem has improved since the attacks, but new, even graver, failures of trust have emerged.
As 9/11 and its aftermath have shown, American security depends on many kinds of faith. Allies must trust U.S. leadership. Citizens must have confidence in their government. Policy makers must believe in America’s deepest norms and values. Over the past 25 years, the U.S. has frayed each of these bonds of trust.
This is exactly what bin Laden sought to achieve. He often referred to a text called “Management of Savagery,” dubbed the “al-Qaeda manual,” which recalled the collapse of the Roman empire in the face of sustained pressure from small frontier tribes. The jihadist mission was to subject the U.S. to the same fate—turning its allies into enemies by eradicating the world’s trust in American power and ideals.
The 9/11 attacks alone did not accomplish that goal. But 25 years later, America’s own mistakes have brought it closer to fulfillment than bin Laden ever could.
Several weeks before 9/11, the FBI sent me to Sanaa, Yemen, to join an interagency team investigating al-Qaeda’s murder of 17 U.S. sailors. Al-Qaeda had bombed USS Cole in October 2000 as the ship lay at anchor in a Yemeni port. We soon learned the first of a series of details about the attack that have played in my mind ever since.
In January 2000, when planning for the bombing was well under way, two al-Qaeda operatives left Yemen for Thailand with $36,000 in cash. Both would participate in the eventual attack. A few days later, a third, more senior al-Qaeda operative known as Khallad flew from Malaysia to Thailand and collected the money.
We knew that al-Qaeda had been plotting to attack a U.S. warship in Yemen. So why would the group move two operatives and a large amount of cash out of the country? We sought answers from our partners across the U.S. intelligence community. Each time, the response was the same: No one knew anything that could help our investigation.
I was still in Sanaa on September 11. From thousands of miles away, I saw images of smoke billowing from the Pentagon, twin fireballs bringing down the World Trade Center, and wreckage lying strewn across a field in my home state of Pennsylvania. Along with the rest of the Cole team, I was ordered to evacuate Yemen.
The next day, when I was already at the airport, I got a call: Someone had information to share about the attacks. Instead of boarding my flight, I raced to the U.S. embassy, where a CIA officer handed me a file with the answers my team had been seeking.
The $36,000 hadn’t been meant for Khallad, as we’d thought. Apparently it had paid for two other al-Qaeda members, Khalid al-Mihdhar and Nawaf al-Hazmi, to travel to the United States. The purpose of their trip had just been revealed: Al-Mihdhar and al-Hazmi were two of the hijackers who crashed American Airlines Flight 77 into the Pentagon.
The pair had been in the United States for months, and had left a significant paper trail. As both the CIA inspector general and the 9/11 Commission would conclude years later, the two hijackers could have been tracked down and arrested if this information had been shared with the Cole team. The “planes operation,” as al-Qaeda called it, might have been stopped.
All at once, I realized that we could have saved thousands of lives if only we’d had the relevant intelligence. I have yet to overcome the horror of that discovery. I suspect I never will.
After the attacks, the intelligence community and law enforcement worked together on a sweeping investigation to track down those responsible and prepare the government to retaliate. In Yemen, a colleague and I questioned Abu Jandal, a suspect in the Cole investigation, gleaning crucial information from him about al-Qaeda and bin Laden. In keeping with traditional American interrogation methods, we pretended that we were his friends and made him believe that we already knew the information we needed.
These techniques worked, as they usually did. Jandal identified several of the 9/11 hijackers as al-Qaeda members. This information allowed President George W. Bush to inform the American people that bin Laden was responsible for the attacks. It was also instrumental in persuading several leaders in the Muslim world, most notably Pervez Musharraf of Pakistan, to acquiesce to the invasion of Afghanistan.
The 9/11 investigation progressed in parallel with military action against al-Qaeda and its Taliban enablers. Interagency cooperation improved. More suspects were apprehended. At that moment, it was still possible to believe that America’s response to the attacks would be sober, measured, and led by sound intelligence. Within a few months, however, I would be disabused of that notion.
By the spring of 2002, I had joined another interagency team and began interrogating Abu Zubaydah, a fixer who often worked with al-Qaeda, though he wasn’t a member. Almost as soon as we sat down, he identified himself as “Daood.” I smiled. We had caught him in a lie.
“How about I call you Hani?” I said, using his childhood nickname. Zubaydah’s jaw dropped. He seemed to realize that we would know if he continued trying to deceive us, so he started cooperating. Within an hour, Zubaydah had divulged the details of a developing terrorist plot. We reported the information to Washington, and the attack was foiled. Zubaydah proceeded to tell us everything he knew about the “planes operation,” including the identity of its mastermind, Khalid Sheikh Mohammed.
After about 10 productive days, a team from the CIA’s Counterterrorism Mission Center arrived alongside an external contractor, who claimed that he could get even more information out of Zubaydah. He described a series of techniques that were designed to establish the interrogator in Zubaydah’s mind as “God.”
The contractor had Zubaydah stripped naked, pumped loud music into his cell, and deprived him of sleep. These were part of a set of methods that would come to be known euphemistically as “enhanced interrogation techniques.”
It is important to recognize that these techniques did not reflect the CIA’s usual practice, or the painstaking work of most of its veteran officers. The agency’s traditional interrogation program, which combined lawful questioning with the exploitation of well-documented evidence, achieved great successes when it was not compromised by ineffective torture methods. Indeed, many of the 9/11 investigation’s early breakthroughs, including with Zubaydah, were achieved with the help of CIA officers. Their valuable work must not be confused with the torture program, which was largely designed and implemented by contractors.
Subjected to the new, unproven techniques, Zubaydah immediately clammed up. This was unsurprising: Most jihadist terrorists are trained to withstand even harsher methods, including ones involving physical and sexual violence. Eventually, the contractor was pulled back and the interagency team was allowed to interrogate Zubaydah once more. He started talking again, identifying additional al-Qaeda members and associates.
Still, the promoters of the new techniques were not satisfied. They insisted that Zubaydah was a top al-Qaeda official rather than an outside fixer, and turned the temperature in his cell as low as it would go. Once again Zubaydah stopped talking, until the interagency team was called back in. This back-and-forth continued until the contractor’s methods became so extreme and grotesque—one involved a custom-built coffin in which he planned to imprison Zubaydah—that FBI headquarters became unwilling to be associated with the techniques.
The torture program not only breached American norms and values; it yielded fake intelligence. Among other falsehoods, Zubaydah “confessed” under torture to being the third-ranking al-Qaeda official. He later told more conventional interrogators that he had said that only to make the torture stop.
These methods introduced violence into our intelligence gathering and ignored decades of accumulated wisdom about effective interrogation. They also alienated our allies. The Senate Select Committee on Intelligence found that the program “caused immeasurable damage to the United States’ public standing, as well as to the United States’ longstanding global leadership on human rights in general and the prevention of torture in particular.”
The interrogation program was just one example of a cardinal error that the U.S. government made after 9/11: It abandoned norms and values embodied in the Constitution; America’s commitment to human rights; and more practical guidelines, such as the Army Field Manuals, which enshrine the traditional, highly effective interrogation methods that my colleagues and I used on Jandal and Zubaydah. These were replaced with untested, ad hoc experiments that appeared to prioritize seeking vengeance over protecting American lives. The CIA inspector general did not identify a single imminent plot that the enhanced interrogation techniques had actually thwarted.
The program was finally outlawed by Congress in 2015, but it continues to undermine American security. Torture produced faulty intelligence that has shaped policy decisions whose effects still linger. Most notable, it contributed to arguably the United States’ worst misstep since 9/11: the decision to go to war in Iraq.
In the months following the attacks, many counterterrorism professionals came under pressure to find a link between al-Qaeda and Saddam Hussein’s government in Iraq. I was one of them. In addition to the intelligence and counterterrorism work I was doing during the day, I returned to my quarters every evening to a barrage of emails seeking proof of a connection that did not exist.
The enhanced interrogation techniques played an important role in the search for the longed-for link. The same contractor who had compromised Abu Zubaydah’s interrogation participated in the interrogation of Zubaydah’s partner, the al-Qaeda operative Ibn al-Shaykh al-Libi. I wasn’t involved in al-Libi’s interrogation, but, like Zubaydah, he had reportedly been cooperating under the traditional approach.
After the contractor arrived, al-Libi was subjected to torture in a third country. As al-Libi later freely confessed, he “decided he would fabricate any information the interrogators wanted in order to gain better treatment and avoid being handed over” to a foreign government. One such fabrication was the purported link between al-Qaeda and the Iraqi regime. This became a key piece of evidence used by policy makers seeking to justify war in Iraq.
America’s leaders began the war in Afghanistan with clear mandates, limited goals, and broad coalitions. The 2003 invasion of Iraq, by contrast, featured vague, ambitious aims and took place over the objections of many U.S. allies. It looked more like a war of vendetta—or, worse, one of empire building. The Senate Select Committee on Intelligence found that George W. Bush’s administration had “repeatedly presented intelligence as fact when in reality it was unsubstantiated, contradicted, or even non-existent.”
The consequences have been devastating. When it became clear that the Iraq War had begun under false pretenses, American citizens’ faith in their government took a nosedive, and allies’ confidence was shaken. Moreover, the conflict played directly into al-Qaeda’s core narrative: the false idea that the West and its henchmen were waging an epochal war against Islam.
The invasion of Iraq, the torture program, the humiliating conditions at Guantánamo Bay and prisons such as Abu Ghraib, America’s apparent indifference to civilian casualties from air strikes—each became a powerful recruitment tool for terrorists. As of September 11, 2001, al-Qaeda likely had only a few hundred members, most of them based in Afghanistan. Today, the U.S. intelligence community estimates that the group has 15,000 to 28,000 members worldwide.
Finally, by splitting its attention and resources across two wars, the United States doomed its fortunes in both. In 2011, the withdrawal from Iraq after eight grueling years paved the way for the Islamic State to take over much of the country. At the same time, U.S. objectives in Afghanistan crept further from the limited goals articulated in 2001. It became U.S. policy to attempt to shape Afghanistan into a Western-style, centralized republic, whether the Afghan people wanted that or not. Pursuing that doomed, messianic mission for 20 years ultimately cost the United States about $2.3 trillion; 2,219 American military members’ lives; and a great deal of trust around the world.
The eventual withdrawal from Afghanistan, shortly before the 20th anniversary of 9/11, seemed stage-managed to show just how steeply American power had declined over those two decades. The images of desperate Afghans clinging to departing aircraft became defining symbols of the end of America’s longest war. Much like the fall of Saigon and the evacuation of the U.S. embassy there in 1975, those scenes will continue to taint the world’s perceptions of American power, credibility, and commitment.
Even worse, the U.S. is repeating the same mistakes today.
In February, the United States began its war against Iran without broad support from its allies in the region. Soon the conflict unleashed significant political, military, and economic damage on many of those allies, prompting some of them to question the value of U.S. security guarantees.
Some American allies, previously content to rely on the U.S. security umbrella, have begun making alternative arrangements. In August, Turkey, a NATO member, entered into a mutual-defense pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan. Hakan Fidan, Turkey’s foreign minister, didn’t hide his country’s reasoning: “External hegemons coming into the region do not solve the problems; they make them more acute, and the cost becomes very high.”
America’s relationships with the Muslim world have suffered in other ways too. In March, as the threat of Iranian drone and missile attacks escalated, the State Department ordered nonemergency embassy personnel to leave Qatar, Bahrain, Jordan, Oman, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates. Meanwhile, operations at embassies in Iraq and Lebanon have been hampered for some time by threats and attacks from Iranian-backed militants. These disruptions have compounded a bigger problem: The U.S. has far fewer active embassies in the region today than it did before 9/11.
This will have significant long-term consequences. When diplomatic channels disappear, cooperation between militaries and law enforcement erodes, as do bilateral trade and investment. Intelligence agencies lose human eyes and ears on the ground. Peaceful relations become harder to maintain. Miscalculation grows likelier.
Even as it disengages from important relationships in the Middle East, the United States has introduced confusion into alliances elsewhere. In recent years, American policy makers have given Taiwan mixed messages, oscillating from staunch support to requests for the country to shoulder a greater security burden. The U.S. has called into question its formal security guarantee with Japan and, in the opening weeks of the Iran war, redeployed some 2,500 Marines that had previously been stationed there. Around the same time, Washington reportedly diverted missile-defense interceptors from South Korea to the Middle East. All of these moves threaten to diminish U.S. power in the Indo-Pacific at a time when Chinese influence is growing.
In Europe, the Iran conflict may have distracted attention and resources from the war in Ukraine. According to the Associated Press, a “sizable number” of Patriot missiles had been moved out of Europe, bound for the Middle East. Peace negotiations stalled, reportedly because U.S. attention suddenly pivoted toward Iran. Thanks to spiking energy prices, Russian oil revenues and tax receipts surged, leading one prominent think tank to characterize the war in Iran as “an economic gift for Putin.”
The conflict has also coincided with a decline in trust among America’s hitherto staunchest allies. In May, polling by the European Council on Foreign Relations found that only 11 percent of respondents across 15 European democracies still considered the United States an ally. As Europe and Asia drift further from America’s orbit, the U.S.-led international order comes closer to collapse, just as Osama bin Laden dreamed.
America’s own citizens are scarcely less skeptical than those of its allies. At the outset of hostilities with Iran, 62 percent said they had not been given a clear explanation of the reasons for war. It is not difficult to see why. As recently as June 2025, senior administration officials had claimed that the United States had “destroyed the Iranian nuclear program.” Less than nine months later, the same officials were citing the continued existence of that program as a casus belli.
The shifting official justifications have resembled the obfuscation and outright lies that underpinned America’s invasion of Iraq. But whereas the Iraq War was popular at the outset—about three-quarters of Americans favored military action—a majority of U.S. voters opposed the Iran conflict as soon as it started.
Americans have many reasons for opposing the war. But the profound skepticism with which so many U.S. citizens regard their government has clear roots in 9/11. The distrust has only grown since the attacks because of a systematic lack of accountability.
Families who lost spouses, partners, parents, and children in the 9/11 attacks have spent 25 years waiting for justice. Some have died before seeing those responsible enter a courtroom.
The U.S. government has denied accountability not only for the attackers but also for American officials who made significant mistakes. To use a personal example: The CIA inspector general recommended that an accountability board review the performance of the officials who failed to hand over information my team had asked for in Yemen. This recommendation was summarily rejected by the CIA director.
As recently as 2024, prosecutors reached plea deals with Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and two other suspects, partly designed to induce them to give depositions in exchange for lifelong imprisonment rather than the death penalty. Yet the Department of Defense revoked those plea deals just two days later. Not all of the victims’ families supported them, but the deals would not have been necessary in the first place if the U.S. government had simply followed its own laws while interrogating suspects, rather than compromising evidence by obtaining it through torture.
Still, the families continue to fight, including Terry Strada, whose husband was killed in the World Trade Center. “The question is whether the United States will stand with the victims of terrorism or with those who financed and enabled it,” Strada wrote in 2024. “Our grief has not faded. Neither has our determination. We will not accept selective memory or performative sympathy, and we will not be silent, because without accountability our national security is weakened, and our country is more vulnerable to a recurrence of past threats.”
In the years since 9/11, a lack of accountability has become endemic across the U.S. government. The enhanced-interrogation-techniques program is another example: Not a single official has been prosecuted, not even those who were connected to the two detainees who died in U.S. custody. Instead, the contractors who devised the program received indemnity and $81 million for their services.
As the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence found, some agencies of the U.S. government obscured or misrepresented the truth about the techniques not only to the CIA inspector general but to Congress, the Department of Justice, and even the White House. It appears that nobody has been held accountable.
At the end of 1974, in the midst of the Vietnam War and the fallout from Watergate, the proportion of Americans who trusted their government to do the right thing “just about always” or “most of the time” fell to what was then an unprecedented low of 36 percent. Faith in government later rebounded somewhat. On the eve of 9/11, it stood at 44 percent, then peaked at 55 percent as Americans rallied around their government in the month after the attacks. But by 2025, this trust had declined to 17 percent—less than half of its post-Watergate nadir.
Such low trust in the state degrades the social contract. It reduces support for everything the government does, including—and perhaps especially—national security. Faced with a redacted page or a whitewashed report, people will choose something else to believe in—in many cases something considerably darker than the truth. Conspiracy theories, amplified by social media, further erode the public’s confidence.
September 11, 2001, is a day that never really ended. Its consequences continue to be felt whenever America is tempted to risk the little trust that it still enjoys, whether by confusing vengeance with security, impunity with strength, or callousness with patriotism. The only way for the United States to rebuild its global leadership is by recommitting to the values our enemies hoped to make us abandon: truth, accountability, law, decency, and the protection of innocent life. Only then will we have escaped the long shadow of 9/11.

A former Guilford county detention officer in North Carolina faces forgery charges in connection to 20 alleged forged Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detainment documents, according to a Guilford county sheriff’s office (GCSO) news release.
Guilford county’s sheriff, Danny H Rogers, reported that on Friday the Guilford county magistrate’s office notified the GCSO of a potentially forged court document submitted by GCSO detention officer Michael Diehl, 40.
“The document, entitled ‘Order After Receipt of ICE Detainer and Administrative Warrant’, an AOC-CR-662 form, was associated with an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detainer issued for inmate Claudio Nepornuceno,” the statement read.
“Upon review, the Magistrate’s Office and GCSO Detention staff determined that the document contained the allegedly forged signature of a different magistrate who didn’t process Nepornuceno’s initial arrest,” the statement added.
Under North Carolina law, when inmates are subject to an ICE detainer, they must see a magistrate with a copy of the ICE detainer. Afterwards, the magistrate can issue an AOC-CR-662 form, which allows the detention center to hold the inmate for up to 48 hours beyond the time they would otherwise be entitled to be released from custody. The 48-hour window allows ICE an opportunity to take custody of the inmate.
However, the GCSO found that Nepornuceno was not presented before the magistrate with the detainer. Instead, the form containing the magistrate’s allegedly forged signature was submitted.
A further investigation into the GCSO’s jail booking records identified 19 additional AOC-CR-662 forms associated with 19 additional inmates that contained allegedly forged signatures of magistrates.
The investigation found that in each of these 20 cases, ICE had issued a detainer based on evidence that the inmate who was the subject of the detainer was in violation of US immigration law.
During the GCSO’s criminal investigation into the matter, Diehl’s employment with the sheriff’s office was terminated.
And as a result of the investigation, Diehl was arrested and charged with 20 counts of felony common law forgery.
He received a $5,000 secured bond and has since been released from custody.
The investigation remains ongoing and additional charges may follow.
The investigation into Diehl comes as the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown continues across the country. 
 Since Trump’s inauguration, a record number of individuals – more than 70,000 – have been detained by ICE.

Ndiaye's journey from non-league football to £65m Man City move
- Published
Iliman Ndiaye's journey to Manchester City has been something of a scenic route after he completed a move to Etihad Stadium from Everton in a deal worth up to £65m.
The deadline day move for the Senegal winger, 26, is worth £60m plus a further £5m in add-ons - a little over six years since he made his professional debut playing in the seventh tier of English football.
"I've worked my whole life for an opportunity like this," said Ndiaye, who has signed a five-year contract with the club.
"City are one of the best clubs in the world and I've seen them win everything as I've grown up. To be able to write my own chapter in a story that special is the chance of a lifetime and I'm determined to grab it with both hands."
Ndiaye had held talks with Saudi Pro League side Al-Hilal earlier in the summer while Tottenham had agreed terms with Everton on Friday night for Ndiaye, when it looked as though Richarlison would move the other way in a separate transfer.
However, sources indicated Richarlison failed to agree personal terms with his former club and as a result, Spurs were unable to proceed with the Ndiaye transfer.
The move comes on the same day City agreed to pay a joint-British transfer record fee of £125m for Chelsea midfielder Enzo Fernandez.
The Argentian international is set to become City's eighth summer arrival with Enzo Maresca's side having also signed Elliot Anderson, Geronimo Rulli, Ayyoub Bouaddi, Allan Elias, Jeremy Monga and Pierce Charles.
Ndiaye's journey from non-league football to City
As a 19-year-old living in London, Ndiaye was in the youth ranks of Boreham Wood and playing Sunday league football when he was invited for a one-week trial with Sheffield United.
Two trial games were enough for the then-Premier League club to sign the talented teenager, although it would be another 18 months until he made an appearance for the Blades.
Instead, he spent the second half of the 2019-20 campaign on loan at Hyde United in the Northern Premier Division, six levels below the top division.
He made six appearances in his very first taste of professional football, often risking missing the last train back to Sheffield to stay out on the training pitch.
"It's not always been easy in my career," said Ndiaye.
"But I always had the belief that I could play for a team challenging for the biggest prizes and now I'm here."
After returning to Bramall Lane, Ndiaye made his Premier League debut in March 2021 against Leicester City but it would be another three-and-a-half years until he became established at the highest level following the Blades' relegation.
Two seasons in the Championship culminated in Ndiaye spearheading their return to the top flight in 2023 with 14 goals in 43 starts but he was then sold to Marseille that summer.
Ndiaye struggled during a season in France before joining Everton for an initial £16m fee in July 2024.
A firm fan favourite on Merseyside, "Skiliman" scored 15 goals and provided four assists in 67 Premier League games for the Toffees before his City move.
Is £65m a fair price for Ndiaye?
In a summer of highly-inflated transfer fees, value has become increasingly hard to determine.
On one hand, the Senegal international is a player of superlative skill, evasive, quick and wonderfully entertaining with the ball at his feet.
Ndiaye was responsible for 73 of Everton's 250 completed dribbles last season, the highest share of any Premier League player.
Everton fans may also point to recent moves in the Premier League involving City, such as the sale of Savio to Tottenham for an initial £75m, as further evidence that the club should have demanded more for Ndiaye.
On the other hand, Everton are effectively quadrupling the initial £16m they paid Marseille to sign Ndiaye two years ago for a player whose underlying numbers, at this stage at least, are not truly elite.
In the Premier League last season, Ndiaye only ranked joint third at Everton alone for goal contributions (nine), with Beto (10) and Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall (12) providing more.
It is reasonable to assume that those numbers for Ndiaye will improve in a more attacking team at City but his general creativity is also middling as things stand.
He created 36 chances in total in the Premier League last season, ranking him only fourth at Everton. Toffees midfielder James Garner created 26 more. Jack Grealish, whose season ended in January because of injury, created eight more.
Grealish has effectively replaced Ndiaye at Everton following his loan move from Enzo Maresca's side.
Casting the net a little wider, 45 Premier League players have recorded more goal contributions than Ndiaye's 19 since he made his Everton debut two years ago.
As a 26-year-old set to be surrounded by better players, it would be no surprise should his numbers flourish at the Etihad.
But even in today's money, £65m for Ndiaye's current output may not be as questionable a deal as it sounds.

Almost half of the world’s farmers are poisoned by pesticides every single year, a study has found.
Using publicly available data from 2006-2023, the study, which was commissioned by Pesticide Action Network, found there to be an estimated 402-433m cases of unintentional acute pesticide poisoning of farmers and farm workers every year.
Based on a worldwide farming population of 934 million, this means approximately 46% of farmers are being poisoned every year. The greatest estimated number of poisonings was in southern Asia, followed by south-east Asia and east Africa.
The overall highest national incidence of poisoning was in Burkina Faso in west Africa, where nearly 84% of farmers and farm workers were reported to have experienced poisoning.
The study, published in the journal Frontiers in Public Health on Wednesday, also found that an estimated 11,000 deaths occur every year due to pesticide poisoning, with nearly 60% of these in India.
Jayakumar Chelaton, the executive director of Pesticide Action Network India, said the research exposed a “crisis that can no longer be ignored”.
The authors of the study are calling for “immediate action”, including the implementation of a UN recommendation to phase out highly hazardous pesticides.
The study states that despite global efforts to highlight the dangers, pesticide use has continued to grow steadily, with 3.8m tonnes used in 2023, a doubling since 1990.
Dr Sheila Willis, the head of international programmes at Pesticide Action Network UK, said: “Now that the scale of suffering has been revealed, farmers must be supported to access safer alternatives to protect their health and that of their families.”
The study did not consider the impact of pesticide exposure on the estimated 84 million children working in agriculture and did not look at the long-term health impacts, with acute pesticide poisoning defined in the study as any illness or health effect experienced a short time after exposure.
Génon Jensen, the executive director of the Health and Environment Alliance, said: “We are extremely concerned about the devastating health impacts from pesticide poisonings – both the acute impacts mentioned in this study but also chronic exposures that farm workers and communities suffer.”
Hélène Nicora, the director general of Parkinson’s Europe, said there was also “overwhelming evidence” to suggest that Parkinson’s was an environmentally driven disease, with growing evidence linking pesticide exposure to the development of Parkinson’s.
Parkinson’s disease is a progressive disorder in which parts of the brain become damaged over time, affecting movement and balance. The global burden of the disease is rising, with France, Germany and Italy all recognising it as an occupational disease for farmers.
Farmers and farm workers are mainly exposed to pesticides during preparation and application, as well as when touching treated crops and contaminated equipment or clothing.
Speaking at a webinar organised by Friends of the Earth Europe earlier this year, Rendert Algra said he believed his Parkinson’s disease was linked to the pesticides he had used when working at his family farm in the Netherlands.
“Being the eldest son, I did all the spraying of pesticides in our fields for several years in a row,” he said.
Despite being the most robust study to date, the report highlights that available information on pesticide poisoning is inadequate, with the authors calling for standardised surveillance and reporting protocols so that pesticide-related poisonings become reliable and comparable.

Christian Harrison and Neal Skupski beat Kevin Krawietz and Tim Puetz 6-4 7-6(6) on Saturday (September 12, 2026) to win the U.S. Open men's doubles title.
The reigning Australian Open champions took the first set after Harrison struck a two-handed backhand return winner to break for a 4-3 lead. The American-British duo held serve the rest of the way to take the set 6-4.
Their German opponents fought back in the second set and moved 3-2 ahead but Harrison and Skupski responded with a love hold to level at 3-3.
The 2024 runners-up went up 4-3 and later 5-4 after saving a set point, but Harrison and Skupski stayed in contention. Harrison, serving with the sun in his eyes, held in a five-point game to force a tiebreak.
Puetz gave the Germans a 4-3 lead in the breaker with a volley but Harrison and Skupski recovered. Skupski sealed the victory with a return that forced Krawietz into an error, giving the pair their second Grand Slam doubles title of the year.
The victory was a moment of redemption for Skupski, who finished runner-up with Dutchman Wesley Koolhof in 2022. He suffered a second defeat in last year's final alongside fellow Briton Joe Salisbury.
Salisbury later took a break from tennis because of anxiety, and Skupski began the 2026 season with Harrison.
The pair had known each other for years and had lost in the first round of a Futures event together in England in 2013.
Their partnership produced immediate results when they clinched the Australian Open in January.
"It's been obviously an amazing couple of weeks for us," Skupski told reporters. "It's just total focus throughout the match, believing in each other, looking at our team, trying to give us as much energy as possible."
"When we play with energy and belief, we're a very dangerous team. We both believe in each other's games. I feel like we complement each other very well on the court," the 36-year-old player added.
For Harrison, 32, the home victory carried particular significance after an injury-hit career in which he underwent eight bouts of surgery and spent years trying to return to the top level.
"Of course, there's always a little bit of doubt, especially as you're getting older and you realise your body is not recovering the same, but I never lost my joy for playing."

39 pupils and staff fall ill after eating school lunches in Sha Tin
Authorities are investigating a suspected outbreak of food poisoning at Baptist (Sha Tin Wai) Lui Ming Choi Primary School
Hong Kong health authorities are investigating an outbreak of suspected food poisoning that hit 39 pupils and staff members who ate lunch at a Sha Tin school earlier this week.
Twenty-three boys and 14 girls, aged between five and 11, from Baptist (Sha Tin Wai) Lui Ming Choi Primary School and two employees, aged 34 and 38, were affected.
They developed stomach pain and diarrhoea about eight to 22 hours after eating school lunches provided by a supplier on Wednesday.
A spokesman for the school, located at 8 Yuen Chau Kok Road in Sha Tin, could not be reached for comment on Saturday night.
The Centre for Health Protection did not name the supplier in a statement on Saturday.
“Initial investigations of the [centre] revealed that the affected persons consumed the same type of lunchboxes before the onset of symptoms, pointing to food poisoning likely related to the consumption of marinated chicken leg and penne provided by the lunch supplier,” it said.
Two pupils sought medical advice but did not require hospitalisation. They were in a stable condition.

In Summary
- Apple’s new CEO John Ternus is expected to take centrestage on 9 September in Apple’s “Surprise and shine” event. This will be
- Ternus’ first appearance in an Apple event since he took over from Tim Cook.
- Apple is expected to launch new iPhones at the event, including the much-talked-about iPhone Ultra, its first foldable phone.
- As the event draws near, we write an open letter to Apple’s new CEO, requesting something that was once very much Apple – being different.
Dear John,
You will shortly be making your first public appearance as CEO at a major Apple event. Over the years, the iPhone launch pretty much sets out the tech agenda for the rest of the year. For the iPhone is not just a tech launch but a trend setter of sorts – it influences which colors, shapes, features, and functions matter in the industry in the coming days. About a decade ago, we would have laughed at the notion of a notch in any device. Until last year, orange was associated more with juice than tech. You get the idea.
Indeed, very few names have influenced our lives in the way in which Apple has over the past few decades. The brand made computers and touchscreen smartphones that were effortlessly easy to use, put thousands of songs in our pockets, created notebooks that could be carried in stationery envelopes, showed us that Bluetooth earbuds could exist without wires, added a third screen to many of our lives in the form of a tablet, got us looking at our watches for more than just the time, made us realize that there was “an app for that…”, and much more. It was seldom the first to come out with a particular product, but it often put a different spin on products, making them easier to use. It was the brand that thrived on its legendary motto, ‘Think Different’. Other brands could match Apple’s features and spec sheet, perhaps, but never the ‘feel’ or ‘vibe’ of an Apple product.
In recent times, however, this Apple feel or vibe has been getting increasingly diminished. Some would say that perhaps an “inspired” (read “copycat”) competition is closing the gap on the market leader. Perhaps. But then, it is not as if competition and “copy and paste” mode did not exist in the past. Remember how Steve Jobs went ballistic at Google for Android, claiming that it had been copied from Apple? “I’m going to destroy Android, because it’s a stolen product. I’m willing to go thermonuclear war on this,” Jobs raged when speaking of the topic, in Walter Isaacson’s biography. But even then, Apple’s products continued to be strikingly different. The competition could offer a similar appearance (camera units, straight sides, similar colors), but beneath that familiar surface, it was clear that they were just knockoffs.
That is no longer the case. Somewhere in its pursuit of market share over the past decade, Apple started losing its mystique, going from Hogwarts to Harvard. The brand’s sales volumes and capital value have shot up exponentially, but all this has come at a creative cost. Apple now seems more a part of the crowd rather than apart from it. Don’t get me wrong. Apple’s products are still very good, but while their pricing is more premium than ever, the products themselves are not as different as they used to be. In fact, in many cases, they do not even seem to be too different from their own predecessors.
The brand that championed “Think DIfferent” has been increasingly thinking similarly of late. From being among the first to popularise graphical UIs, capacitive touchscreens, app screens and face unlock systems, it has graduated to being last in line in the foldables and AI race. It might end up winning both of those contests even now, such is its market domination, but that would be a victory of volumes rather than delivered value, similar to how IBM ended up bossing the PC market in the early eighties even though it was a latecomer. IBM’s motto was incidentally “Think,” and is believed to have inspired Apple’s “Think Different.” Oh, the irony.
There has always been a large section of people who believed that most people who bought Apple products did so just to “show off the logo,” as products from other brands were just as good. For a while, this was a very unfair accusation, as in spite of their premium price tags (even more so in India, because of customs duties, we are told), Apple’s products seemed to be in a totally different league. Today, Apple still has the high ground in privacy and security and its face unlock remains unmatched, but in many other regards (yes, even in apps and interface), the brand seems content to swim in the mainstream, rather than walloping the competition from within its famous “walled garden.”
We are coming to the stage when a lot of people are actually buying Apple products for the logo on them rather than what they do. At one level, it tells us that the Apple brand has such equity that people are willing to invest large amounts in a product because it has an apple engraved on it. At another, it tells us that the products are now being defined by the brand rather than the other way around – a foldable phone is special because it comes from Apple, rather than Apple being special because it made a foldable phone.
Today, Apple is arguably the world’s greatest tech brand, but it has more money than mojo. For other brands, that would be just perfect. But since when was Apple just another brand? Mind you, money is a wonderful thing. After all, it enables one to do things and invest in ideas that don’t have a short-term payback. We did not say that; Steve Jobs did. Well, Apple has the money. Perhaps it is time for it to do things. Differently.
All this is easier said than done, of course. My colleague Akriti Rana recently wrote eloquently of how you now hold not just the reins of arguably the most high-profile tech company in the world, but also bear the burden of two massive, yet contrasting legacies. How you decide to honor them is your choice. You could choose to sail in a sea of successful sameness. Or maybe just spend more time in that walled garden.
Still, as someone whose first ever story in tech was about an Apple product (the iBook in 1999) and who confidently predicted that the first iPhone would fail (and was delighted to be proved wrong) in 2007, I have a request.
I am not asking for slimmer portfolios. Or lower price tags. I am asking for something much more basic – the experience of going to an event without having any idea of what will happen.
Of seeing a product without having seen it being leaked more often than a local municipal pipeline.
Of feeling a sense of wonder while using a product, because there is nothing else quite like it.
Of looking at the Apple logo and thinking of wizardry rather than wealth.
The universe is waiting, John Ternus. Go put a ding in it.
Regards,
Nimish Dubey

A united Ireland would be 'fantastic' says Trump
- Published
US President Donald Trump has said he would love to see a united Ireland while at a meeting with the Taoiseach (Irish Prime Minister) during a visit in Dublin.
Trump is on a two-day visit to the country where earlier he had a courtesy call with the Irish President Catherine Connolly at the Áras an Uachtaráin - the official residence of the Irish president.
He will also attend events at the US Ambassador to Ireland's residence, before attending the Amgen Irish Open golf tournament.
Trump said a united Ireland would happen eventually and that the Taoiseach was "the right man over here to get it moving".
During his meeting with Micheál Martin at Farmleigh House in Phoenix Park, in Dublin, Trump said a united Ireland would be a "fantastic thing".
"I think it would be a fantastic thing; now the UK would have something to say about it obviously but I think it would be a great thing, I mean, how can it be bad?"
Trump also said his country's relationship with Ireland is "stronger than ever".
During his meeting with the Taoiseach, Trump said: "We've a big relationship with Ireland."
"The two countries do very well together," he said, adding: "It's never been as good as it is right now."
He said they discussed various topics, including trade.
He was greeted by Tánaiste (Irish deputy prime minister) Simon Harris and Irish Foreign Minister Helen McEntee at Dublin Airport on Saturday morning.
Trump was welcomed at the Áras an Uachtaráin by President Connolly.
President Connolly, an outspoken Gaza activist who has been critical of the US and said Trump is acting "like a bully" over tariffs, has come under pressure to raise issues in the Middle East during her brief meeting with the US president.
Sinn Féin and a series of other parties in the Republic who backed her in the Irish presidency campaign last year have called on her to raise Gaza during her meeting with Trump.
Ireland is one of the most pro-Palestinian countries in the European Union and has been criticised for its stance by Israel.
Irish authorities have been planning for Trump's visit for months in what is one of the biggest security operations in the history of the state.
