The 2,400-seat Miami theater lit up like a Coldplay concert when the QR code dropped at the Miss USA pageant. A sea of phones — held up by supportive parents, partners, and past pageant queens — trained their cameras on the massive barcode being projected from center stage, ready to vote for their favored contestant.
Twelve minutes on the clock: The countdown was on.
Fingers tapped rapidly as the audience used their free vote or purchased more in bundles — $50 for 50, $250 for 250, $500 for 500 — alongside viewers at home. The top 20 contestants' headshots shifted around the leaderboard as the votes tallied live on the pageant's website, revealing exactly how far each woman was from the top spot.
Two minutes left on the clock, a banner flashed across: Now, votes counted double. As the seconds ticked closer to zero, the votes burst in like a flash flood. The gap between first and second place was 1,794 votes at the 36-second mark. When the clock struck zero, it was more than 14,000.
Fans have never had more of a say at Miss USA — especially if they're willing to pay. At last month's pageant, paid voting helped determine three top 20 spots, while a fourth went to the contestant who sold the most Westgate Resorts vacation packages, an unprecedented incentive that tied a contestant's placement to sales for a pageant sponsor. The winner was determined by a panel of six judges, including a mix of Miss USA and Miss Universe winners, but fans also had the opportunity to vote for the top 10 as the "seventh judge."
Nearly a dozen of this year's Miss USA contestants spoke to Business Insider about the changes. Some believe it's a savvy strategy by CEO Thom Brodeur, who took over the pageant in September 2025, to keep the business afloat and increase fan engagement, especially at a time when pageants struggle to remain relevant. Others worry the competition is turning into what one called a "pay-to-play" model, making it less accessible to women who don't have money or big social media followings.
Nobody is arguing with Beyoncé or Taylor Swift's teams over the standing-room ticket prices of four-figures and higher, and we're not going to apologize either.Miss USA CEO Thom Brodeur
"There's a lot of fatigue," Miss Arizona Kaitlyn Humphrey told Business Insider. "It's an expensive sport already, and it breaks my heart that a lot of people can't compete purely because there's such a barrier to entry in the financial aspect of things. And then we're just adding layers to that."
The bygone days of network TV
Nearly 40 million people tuned in to watch Miss USA in the 1960s and '70s, but viewership dwindled over its 60 years on television. In 2023, the Miss USA final peaked at 1.1 million viewers on The CW. It was a far cry from its heyday, but still enough for a multiyear deal. The network ultimately dropped the pageant in 2025 amid fallout from former CEO Laylah Rose's tenure, during which Miss USA 2023 Noelia Voigt and Miss Teen USA 2023 UmaSofia Srivastava relinquished their crowns due to her leadership.
This year, the competition was set to return to The CW, but, as Business Insider first reported, the network dropped the show on August 20, a week before the final. Miss USA cited a "contractual issue with our production arrangements" and moved it to Queen Beauty Network, a streaming service focused on the pageant industry, where Brodeur is listed as vice president and chief marketing officer.
When the crown was placed on Justus Kelley's head on August 27, making her the first married woman and mother to win the title, a live viewer counter on the Queen Beauty Network showed around 4,000 people watching.
Shrinking viewership hasn't only affected Miss USA's ratings — it's put a serious dent in the pageant's coffers. Paula Shugart, who oversaw Miss USA from 2001 to 2020 as president of the Miss Universe Organization, told Business Insider that the pageant once received $3 to $5 million in licensing fees from the networks. Those days are gone.
"Network television has completely changed," Shugart said. "You don't have the viewership, and you're not going to get the license fees that you used to get. You have to figure out different ways to pay for it and defray the costs."
It's a reality that Brodeur knows well.
"The days of 'free lunch' for pageants and pageant fans are over," he told Business Insider last week. "They've been over for some time. Introducing new revenue streams — whether that's through fan voting, contests, or other unique opportunities we're exploring — are the way this industry lives to see its next 75 years."
Competing at Miss USA wasn't cheap to begin with, although the cost varies widely depending on who you ask. Contestants who spoke to Business Insider estimated costs ranging from $3,000 to $50,000.
Brodeur compared the investment to that of any competitive sport. "There is nothing new under the sun about creating opportunities and spaces for all of us to exercise our God-given gifts in this world," he said. "Unfortunately, there are also costs attached to the creation of those opportunities and spaces, and that's the reality of life."
A new way to engage fans
Traditionally, contestants make it to Miss USA by winning a state pageant.
Those are organized and funded by individual directors, who pay the organization a franchise fee. Contestants must live, work, or study in the state for at least 90 days prior to the competition and are allowed to compete in two state pageants a year.
When Brodeur took over as CEO, he had five weeks to put on the Miss USA 2025 pageant. Some departed state directors had not been replaced, and eight states were missing titleholders. His solution: an open casting call in which women from any state could apply for a state title. Five judges selected the titleholders.
This year, 16 states were left without directors. Brodeur said only the Miss Universe Organization can legally issue franchise agreements to new state directors, so the open casting call returned — this time with fans getting a say.
Before the applicants could be seen by a judging panel of former Miss USA winners, they had to make it through three rounds of fan voting over the course of a month. People could use a daily free vote or purchase bundles that ranged from $4.99 for 10 votes to $499 for 2,000 votes on a third-party website. The votes did not roll over from round to round, so each contestant started each round back at square one.
"It was crazy," said Amber Uhler, who was selected to represent Michigan through the casting call. "I had to get everyone I knew to put in paid votes for me. [I said], 'If you were ever going to buy me a Christmas gift, just make it this.'"
Miss USA split the 16 states into two casting calls. Women who didn't get selected in the first, which ran from May 20 to June 30, were automatically entered into the second, from June 29 to July 28. That meant some women were campaigning for votes for two months.
Malory Hudson, who has competed at 12 Miss USA state pageants since 2017, was one of them. "I love competing, but I hated this open casting call," said Hudson, who did not make it through the judges' panel. "There was just anxiety every single day. You have to post so much, and it's exhausting."
Other contestants, like Uhler, enjoyed the process because it "made it more fun" as people were invested in the contestants' journeys. Jordyn Owen, who won Miss Colorado through the open call, said it brought "a lot more buzz and attention" to Miss USA.
"Last year, it was completely anonymous. No one knew if you submitted in the open call or not," she added. "Having it be very public this year, I actually kind of liked it because it did make it feel a little bit more invested."
Brodeur said that the multiple rounds of voting were designed to engage fans and give contestants the "absolute best chance and most opportunity for their fans to advance them into the final judging round."
"We recognize that both open casting and fan voting are 'new ways' of thinking about and approaching this journey in pageantry," he added. "Not everything that is innovative is accepted universally right away."
Some contestants worried that the process was a barrier for women who didn't have generous sponsors via their family, friends, or followers. Uhler said her family spent $4,000 to $5,000 in votes during the last round; Hudson said she had a sponsor who bought around $30,000 worth of votes.
Brodeur disputed that the new fan voting made Miss USA less accessible, saying nearly 70% of the open-call winners advanced with a "much higher ratio of free votes from their fans than paid votes."
"There are two types of competitors in this sport," he said. "The first… has such a deeply engaged fan base she could repeatedly encourage her fans to 'vote for me for free' and she advanced. The other was the candidate who wasn't afraid to seek the financial support of her friends, family, and fans to drive their participation."
"How is this any different than Instagram and TikTok influencers monetizing their content or their 'journeys/stories' through fans on behalf of the brands they're repping?" he added. "It's absolutely the same process."
Brodeur said the open casting call is here to stay for at least another year. "As we work through this next season's contract process, we are likely going to be forced to execute a similar strategy as we did during this last cycle," he added.
The People's Choice(s)
The campaign for votes wasn't over after the open casting call. Next, contestants had to go through People's Choice, which let fans vote for their favorite among all 51 Miss USA 2026 contestants. As with the casting call, fans could use a daily free vote or purchase them in bundles.
Most pageants — including Miss Universe and Miss America — have traditionally allocated one spot in the semifinals for the contestant who receives the most fan votes. Under Brodeur's leadership, that single spot in Miss USA's top 20 expanded to four in 2025, and three this year.
It's been a controversial decision among contestants, including Miss Kansas Madilynn Becker, who won this year's People's Choice award with Miss Louisiana Ella Clark and Miss Colorado's Owen.
"People's Choice is a path, but it's almost like the shortcut, in a sense," said Becker. "I think I would have felt even more proud if I got in on my own merit."
"I would love to see the voting become a free thing because, essentially, it comes down to who has the most money to champion for them," said Miss California Acacia McBride.
Brodeur said he expanded the number of People's Choice contestants to give fans a larger say. "One of the rallying cries for the better part of a decade has been, 'We want more of a voice in who makes it and where,'" he added.
He said that's why fans were also given the chance to vote for the top 10 on finals night. The Miss USA website said these votes were "combined into a seventh score and counted with the judges' six when the top 10 is decided." Brodeur confirmed that the fan voting counted as 14% of the contestants' overall score.
While a number of contestants who spoke to Business Insider thought the voting was a great way to keep the audience engaged, comparing it to the real-time voting on "Love Island" or "Dancing with the Stars," others were surprised to learn that fans could purchase votes.
"It definitely stirred up a lot of feelings backstage," Arizona's Humphrey said. "Some of the girls have different financial situations than others, and you feel like things are getting ripped away from you for factors that you can't control, and we've already spent so much money to be there."
Tens of thousands of votes poured in, but, in the end, the three women who received the most votes — Humphrey, Miss Louisiana Ella Clark, and Miss Montana Lisbeth Fernández — did not advance to the top 10.
"I feel very blessed to know that I have a big audience that is willing to show up for me," said Fernández, who received the most votes. "But at the end of the day, the judges are the ones who make the ultimate call."
Parents and pageant fans tossed around the phrase "money grab" throughout the weeklong 2026 competition in Miami.
Brodeur said the organization made "five or six figures" from fan voting but declined to share an exact number. He also noted that some revenue from fan voting was used to fund new cash prizes — ranging from $3,500 to $15,000 — for every contestant who made it into the top five. The salary for this year's Miss USA winner also increased to $150,000; it was $75,000 in 2025.
"There were a lot of different aspects where I was like, 'OK, you have to pay to play,'" said McBride. "However, I do think, on the flip side of that, incorporating the cash prizes and the salary balanced it out."
A new top 20 incentive
An additional top 20 spot was reserved for the contestant who sold the most Westgate Resorts vacation packages: $99 for a two-night stay at one of six US properties.
Miss USA announced the new partnership in April. Brodeur told Business Insider that it was a way to tap into what he calls "one of the largest micro and nano-influencer networks of women aged 14 to 45 in the United States."
Some women dove headfirst, traveling to a Westgate property to film Instagram content. Fernández, who secured the "Westgate Brand Ambassador" title, said she sold almost 200 packages and will now have the opportunity to interview for a six-figure position at the company.
"A lot of the girls were focused on the People's Choice, but I really didn't give it any thought at all because I wanted to win the 'Westgate Brand Ambassador,'" she told Business Insider. "I put my selling skills in action, and I promoted that all over with my friends, family, and community. I also sold some corporate packages."
Uhler, who estimates she sold 103 packages, was also a fan of the incentive. Although she didn't make it into the top 20, she appreciated that Miss USA offered a new avenue for contestants to advance.
"It's great that you can work hard and earn something rather than just, you know, being the prettiest, or having the best walk, or having the best body," she added. "I don't think that I have any of those things, but you almost can't outwork me — except for this time, someone did! I really thought I was going to nail it with 100."
Some contestants who spoke to Business Insider worried that the placement was out of reach for those without built-in social media followings. Others, like Miss USA 2004 Shandi Finnessey, didn't think it fit the brand.
"I don't think they should be selling real estate," Finnessey said. "Miss USA is not a salesperson; she should be a spokeswoman."
Brodeur said he believes that it's part of Miss USA's job to be a "brand ambassador, a salesperson, a spokesperson… for brands that are willing to test their skills and see who rises to the occasion."
The $99 Westgate resort deal was also included in the $500 ticket for this year's Miss USA competition, a steeper price than in years past. One contestant said her parents spent $2,000 on tickets for the preliminary, final, and state costume shows this year. Others told their relatives to save their money and watch from home.
"At the end of the day, I would rather my dad be in the stands than go on a vacation," Becker said.
Brodeur defended the cost, saying he wanted to "elevate the Miss USA brand."
"We're not a high school musical production. We're not a prom or homecoming queen event," he said. "Nobody is arguing with Beyoncé or Taylor Swift's teams over the standing-room ticket prices of four-figures and higher, and we're not going to apologize either."
Brodeur hopes the changes can catapult Miss USA into its next chapter after years of scandals. The challenge is proving to prospective contestants that there will be a return on their investment.
Is it enough for Miss USA to be another influencer? The stage used to be a launching pad for stars like Halle Berry and Kenya Moore. Some pageant queens aren't convinced it still has that power.
"Anyone these days can pick up your phone and go on TikTok," said Owen. "I'm not saying it's easy. It takes a lot to build followers and a brand, but what pageants used to have were a household name. Miss USA needs to have that celebrity quality again."

Ahead of the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks, people shared a rumor claiming U.S. President Donald Trump posted on Truth Social that the National September 11 Memorial & Museum in New York said he wouldn't be allowed to speak at the museum's remembrance ceremony, adding that his administration was "looking into shutting them down permanently."
For example, on Sept. 1, a Facebook user shared (archived) an image showing the alleged Truth Social post:
(Irmawati via Facebook)
The purported Trump post read as follows:
"The National September 11 Memorial and Museum commission decided I'm not allowed to speak at the remembrance. Imagine that? A native new Yorker. The greatest president in history. We're looking into shutting them down permanently, remove the memorial and building a statue of me as tall as the World Trade Center. Not to brag or anything, but I single handedly saved 500 thousand people in those burning buildings. I ran 110 floors at least 50 times within 30 minutes pulling people out of tight spaces. I almost died." DJT
According to a reverse image search of the supposed Trump post screenshot, users primarily shared the image on Facebook. It also appeared on the 9GAG meme website.
Snopes readers emailed us to investigate the alleged screenshot's legitimacy, asking, for example, "I believe the fact that he won't attend is true, but is this X post for real?"
To investigate the rumor, we first checked Trump's Truth Social page and found no such post. We then searched on DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo for reports about the supposed post possibly being shared then deleted. If Trump had falsely posted he saved 500,000 people and mentioned plans of building a massive statue after removing the memorial and museum, journalists with reputable news outlets, such as The Associated Press or The New York Times, would have widely reported on it, and our search inquiries would have uncovered such evidence. We found no such articles.
While some Facebook commenters questioned whether the post was real, many others recognized the image as fabricated humor, specifically calling it "satire."
In sum, the purported Trump Truth Social post screenshot's fake nature and extremely outlandish, false claims, suggested the image originated as satire. We will update this article if we locate the origin of the image.
Trump reportedly not going to NY ceremony
The story spread in the days before the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, which killed nearly 3,000 people. Ahead of that anniversary, Trump and the White House disputed a New York Times report alleging he decided against attending the New York remembrance because he couldn't speak at the event. The reporting cited three anonymous sources "with knowledge of the events." We did not locate evidence that might conclusively confirm or debunk that claim.
A spokesperson for the 9/11 Memorial & Museum previously told Snopes that the organization has historically "intentionally worked to keep the commemoration free of politics because remembering those we lost on 9/11 should never be a partisan issue," and that politicians are not to deliver remarks and must "remain in a designated area."
In an authentic post on Aug. 28, Trump posted (archived) an attack on Times journalist Maggie Haberman, one of several reporters who worked on the Times' story, calling her "Maggot Hagerman" and writing, "I would love not to speak, because I'm speaking all the time, and this is a day to remember the victims, and their beautiful family members."
Trump's post also said he plans to attend the remembrance at the Pentagon.
Via email, White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told Snopes of Trump's plans:
As a proud New Yorker, President Trump has spoken about his own experiences watching the horrific events of September 11, 2001. On the 25th anniversary of this tragic day, the President will remember those who were killed at the hands of evil terrorists, honor their loved ones, and pay tribute to the brave first responders who put their lives on the line to rescue their fellow Americans.
The White House also said Vice President JD Vance plans to travel to New York, as well as that all three 9/11 sites, including Shanksville, Pennsylvania, will be represented with administration officials in attendance.
For further reading, we previously reported about the claim Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth wore nothing but underwear during a visit to the 9/11 memorial.
Since the effectiveness of satire is subjective, we use "originated as satire" or "labeled satire" ratings based on creators' description of their work.

The National Payments Corporation of India’s (NPCI’s) consolidated net profit fell 32.4% to ₹989.4 Cr in the financial year ended March 2026 from ₹1,463.2 Cr in FY25, as a sharp rise in tax expenses offset growth in its pre-tax profit. The payments infrastructure operator’s revenue from operations grew 21.8% to ₹4,240 Cr in FY26 from ₹3,480.8 Cr in the previous fiscal year, according to its annual report. Including other income of ₹632.6 Cr, total income rose 20% YoY to ₹4,872.6 Cr in FY26. Income from payment services, NPCI’s biggest revenue stream, increased 16.3% to ₹3,735.8 Cr during the year under review from ₹3,212 Cr in FY25. The segment accounted for 88.1% of the revenue from operations in FY26. The UPI operator’s other revenue streams include network income, implementation services, certification income, fetching fees, among others. NPCI’s profit before tax grew 5.4% to ₹1,888 Cr from ₹1,791.8 Cr. However, its tax expense surged 173.4% to ₹898.5 Cr from ₹328.7 Cr, pulling down its net profit. Current tax rose 19% YoY to ₹568 Cr, while deferred tax expense stood at ₹330.7 Cr compared with a deferred tax credit of ₹11.1 Cr in FY25. The previous year’s tax expense had also benefited from a prior-year tax adjustment of ₹137.6 Cr. It is pertinent to note that as NPCI is incorporated as a not-for-profit company under Section 8 of the Companies Act, its financial statements use “surplus” instead of profit and report profit after tax as “surplus for the period”. Where Did NPCI Spend In FY26? NPCI’s total expenses increased 31.5% to ₹2,984.6 Cr in FY26 from ₹2,269.8 Cr in the previous year. Marketing: This remained NPCI’s biggest cost head, accounting for nearly 48% of its total expenses. Marketing expenses rose 27.3% to ₹1,420.3 Cr from ₹1,116 Cr in FY25. Within this, marketing and branding expenses increased 10.2% YoY to ₹770.3 Cr, while product incentives and cashback expenses jumped 55.8% to ₹650 Cr. NPCI said these expenses included payments to banks for RuPay cards, cashback campaigns to promote digital transactions, RuPay media and advertising campaigns, business-to-business initiatives, and sponsorships. Employee Benefit Expenses: This cost head rose 22.6% to ₹534.4 Cr from ₹435.8 Cr in the previous year. NPCI reclassified outsourcing costs from employee benefit expenses to administrative and other expenses from April 1, 2025. In FY26, it booked ₹54 Cr in outsourcing costs under administrative expenses, compared with ₹31.6 Cr included under employee expenses in FY25. Consequently, administrative and other expenses rose 54.4% to ₹293.4 Cr in FY26 from ₹190 Cr in the previous year. Operating Expenses: NPCI’s operating expenses grew 38.6% to ₹291.4 Cr from ₹210.3 Cr in FY25. These included annual maintenance charges on network and IT equipment, network costs, testing and certification charges, and data centre expenses. Notably, data centre rental expenses jumped nearly 20X to ₹10.4 Cr from ₹52.5 Lakh, while data centre power and fuel costs increased 51.5% YoY to ₹33 Cr. BHIM’s Loss Widens Loss of NPCI BHIM Services Ltd (NBSL), the wholly owned subsidiary that operates the BHIM app, widened nearly sixfold to ₹390.6 Cr in FY26 from ₹68.1 Cr in FY25. NBSL generated a turnover of ₹27.8 Cr during the year and reported a loss before tax of ₹372.6 Cr. The subsidiary was incorporated in June 2024 as a for-profit entity to drive the growth and expansion of BHIM. NPCI transferred its BHIM strategic business unit to NBSL with effect from October 1, 2024. In comparison, NPCI Bharat BillPay Ltd’s net profit grew 33.6% to ₹31.5 Cr from ₹23.6 Cr on a turnover of ₹161.1 Cr. NPCI International Payments Ltd, which is responsible for taking UPI and RuPay to overseas markets, reported a loss of ₹19.4 Cr, nearly double the ₹10 Cr loss recorded in FY25. Its turnover stood at ₹83 Cr. The financial performance comes as UPI continues to scale to new highs. The payments system processed a record 24.51 Bn transactions worth ₹29.82 Lakh Cr in August 2026. Meanwhile, NPCI continued to expand its digital payments ecosystem at the Global Fintech Fest 2026 this week, unveiling agentic AI platforms and open-source Android ATMs capable of instantly issuing RuPay cards and generating merchant UPI QR codes.

US President Donald Trump on Saturday commented on the possibility of a UK-run Ireland. He is currently on a weekend visit to a tournament at his Irish golf course. During a meeting with the Irish PM Micheal Martin in Dublin, Trump said that a unified Ireland would be 'fantastic.' He also said that eventually the Republic of Ireland will be merging with the United Kingdom's Northern Ireland. “I don’t want to cause any problems but I’d love to see it unified," Trump told a reporter as quoted by AP. He was asked for his opinion on the issue. "It’s going to happen eventually. It may as well happen now." “I think it would be a fantastic thing," the Republican president said, adding "the UK will have something to say about it, obviously.” However, during his next stop, Trump changed his earlier candid stance. He acknowledged there is “no good answer” to the reunification question while addressing business leaders from both countries at a gathering which took place at the US ambassador's residence. Trump's statement is likely to draw mixed reactions from the Irish people. Previously, a section of people or demonstrators were spotted against Trump's visit in the country. People carried banners, suggestive balloons and Irish flags during a protest against the visit of the US President in Dublin. The subject of Irish unification remains a deeply sensitive issue among the Irish people. This is because Northern Ireland is divided between two communities with competing views on its constitutional future. Nationalists, who are predominantly Catholic, generally support joining the Republic of Ireland. However, unionists, who are largely Protestant, want Northern Ireland to remain part of the United Kingdom. The issue runs deep in Irish history. It stems from Ireland’s partition and decades of sectarian and political violence known as the Troubles. The 1998 Good Friday Agreement largely ended the conflict and established a framework for deciding Northern Ireland’s future through democratic consent. Under the agreement, a referendum on Irish unification can be held if it appears likely that a majority would vote in favour of leaving the UK and joining the Republic of Ireland. However, any move towards a referendum remains politically contentious. As predicted by experts, it is expected to reopen divisions between nationalist and unionist communities. Meanwhile, the UK government has maintained that a referendum should only be considered when there is clear evidence that a majority in Northern Ireland wants unification. The Special Investigation Team (SIT) of police and drug inspectors, formed to probe the fake medicine racket busted near Bidadi recently, raided a private facility, Krupa Healthcare near Minerva Circle, on Saturday and recovered a large stock of suspected counterfeit medicines.
This raid was part of simultaneous raids at 10 locations in six states including Karnataka, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Maharashtra.
The owner of Krupa Healthcare, Veeresh Kumar Jain, said to be a former business partner of the absconding alleged kingpin of the racket Prashanth, has been arrested in connection with the case.
Investigators suspect that counterfeit cancer medicines, life-saving drugs and injections used in intensive care units (ICUs) were being supplied to hospitals, clinics and medical stores.According to investigators, the medicines may have been supplied to more than 90 hospitals and clinics in Bengaluru. The team is examining seized batch numbers and records to identify all establishments that received the suspected counterfeit medicines. We have seized documents pertaining to procurement and distribution which is being verified, a senior officer supervising the operation, said.
The network came to light during a raid on a farmhouse in Bidadi on August 18. During the operation, authorities seized suspected counterfeit medicines worth approximately ₹4.91 crore, along with fake bills, injection-filling equipment and counterfeit labels.
The officials found that Veeresh Kumar Jain, operating his firm for the last five years, had close links with Prashanth, described by investigators as a key accused in the suspected counterfeit drug network.
How it operated?
Investigators suspect that low-cost rebranded medicines were purchased and sold under different brand names. Expired medicines were allegedly collected, transferred into new containers and repackaged using counterfeit labels and packaging material. Even medicines associated with reputed pharmaceutical companies were allegedly given fake labels before being distributed.
The suspected counterfeit medicines were reportedly stored at the Minerva Circle warehouse before being supplied to hospitals, clinics and medical shops across Bengaluru and surrounding areas.
The medicines were allegedly supplied to hospitals at discounts of around 50%.
A network of more than 15 medical representatives is also suspected to have been involved in distributing the medicines to hospitals and pharmacies.
The seized medicines have been sent to laboratories to determine their chemical composition, authenticity and quality. Batch numbers of medicines suspected to be counterfeit have reportedly been blocked on the Karnataka FDA portal as a precautionary measure.
Authorities are now tracing the distribution chain to identify hospitals, clinics and medical stores that may have received the suspected fake medicines.
Manhunt
Meanwhile, the hunt is on for the alleged kingpin Prashanth, who is currently on the run. His questioning is expected to provide further details about the alleged racket, including its financial transactions, procurement network and distribution channels.

WHO welcomed Mr Javier Padilla Bernáldez, Spain’s Secretary of State for Health and his delegation on 23 and 24 April 2024 to discuss joint global health priorities. Amongst others, Spain's focus is on universal health coverage and health systems strengthening; pandemic response and emergency medical teams; organ and tissue transplantation; malaria and other tropical diseases; and polio.
During the visit, participants focused on plans and on-going work across a number of areas, including WHO’s Transplantation Program to increase availability; ethical access and oversight of transplantation of human cells; tissues and organs. They also discussed social determinants of health; tobacco and alcohol control; primary health care; access to medicines; universal health coverage; ensuring healthy lives at all ages; nutrition and food safety; health workforce; and emergencies.
Mr Javier Padilla was accompanied by Ms Paola Cannata Molero, Director of the Cabinet of the Secretary of State for Health, Mr Jacobo Fernández Álvarez, Technical Secretary General, Mr Héctor Tejero Franco, Advisor in the Cabinet of the Minister of Health and Responsible for Health and Climate Change, and Mr Roberto Carro Vázquez, Senior Technician of the Office of the Secretary of State for Health. The delegation also had representatives of Spain’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations Office and Other International Organizations in Geneva, including H.E. Ambassador Ms A. Díaz-Rato Revuelta, H.E. Ambassador Ms Clara Cabrera Brasero, and Counsellor Ms María del Carmen Martínez de la Peña.

WHO’s Management and their teams thanked Spain for their financial and technical support over the years. Spain’s support was instrumental in the last biennium in improving access to quality essential health services and medicines; addressing climate change and healthier environments; and strengthening country capacity in both data and innovation. Spain continues to be a champion of the Global Polio Eradication Initiative.
Spain also contributes to WHO’s work in tackling malaria and neglected and other tropical diseases, and has helped the Organization strengthen countries’ preparedness, readiness, prevention and response for health emergencies, epidemics and pandemics. Spain’s contribution to WHO’s Health Emergency Appeal has helped to protect health in humanitarian emergencies to break the cycles of poverty.
As a world leader in the field of organ and tissue transplantation, Spain plays a key role in WHO’s efforts through its Ministry of Health to improve the safety, quality, efficacy and access to transplants. WHO appreciates and acknowledges Spain as a partner who is not only leading and sharing expertise in support of countries’ development of sustainable, self-sufficient organ transplant systems, but also more generally, a key partner to WHO in health for all.

Tobacco use is linked to infertility in women as well as poorer sperm quality and sexual function in men, according to the latest World Health Organisation (WHO) report, which further warned that second-hand smoke may also affect fertility. Women who quit smoking may have a 25% lower infertility risk than continuing smokers, it said.
The report highlighted evidence that tobacco use is associated with potentially lower chances of success for some fertility treatments. It said that evidence on newer products, including e-cigarettes, waterpipes, and smokeless tobacco, is still emerging, stating that while evidence is strongest for cigarette smoking, other tobacco and nicotine products may also pose risks to fertility and require further research.
Globally, one in six people of reproductive age will experience infertility at some point in their lifetime. Infertility is defined as the failure to achieve pregnancy after 12 months or more of regular unprotected sex.
40% rise in risk
The publication cites decades of evidence showing that smoking can harm women’s reproductive health. A systematic review of studies conducted between 2000 and 2026 found that women who currently smoke tobacco have a 40% higher risk of infertility compared to those who do not smoke.
The publication also notes that women who smoked tobacco in the past but are not currently smoking may have a 25% lower risk of infertility compared with women who continue to smoke, suggesting that quitting tobacco can make a meaningful difference.
The WHO stressed that infertility is not only a women’s health issue. "A recent review of 44 studies involving more than 60,000 men found that smoking was associated with reproductive dysfunction, including semen abnormalities and sexual dysfunction. The evidence indicated that men who smoke were more likely to have erectile dysfunction, ejaculation problems, and related issues such as absence of sperm in semen, poor sperm motility and abnormal sperm shape," it said.
Impact on treatments
For people using fertility treatment, tobacco smoking may reduce the chance of success. The publication cites earlier research from 21 studies, showing that cigarette smoking was linked to fewer live births and fewer pregnancies following assisted reproduction, such as in vitro fertilisation, with findings suggesting that the chances of successful outcomes may be roughly halved by cigarette smoking.
The WHO has recommended that healthcare providers inform individuals and couples planning a pregnancy about the reproductive risks of tobacco use and offer evidence-based support to help them quit. It also recommended that brief advice on quitting be consistently provided to all tobacco users in all healthcare settings.
